t: Mutations in the nerve growth factor (NGF) gene are stated to cause congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis (CIPA), also known as HSAN type IV.
CSF/blood neurofilament light chain levels were highest in PSP-Richardson-syndrome and did not differ significantly among PSP-parkinsonism, Parkinson's disease, and controls.
No significant subgroup interactions were found (e.g., by age, sex, blood pressure parameters, nadir systolic BP threshold of 100mmHg) for the association between OH variants and outcomes.
The C-terminal TECPR repeat domain of TECPR2, rather than the HOPS-binding middle region, mediates colocalization with VPS18 and binding to the early endosomal GTPase RAB5.
Supine and nocturnal hypertension has been associated with damage to target organs.
The Schellong test (orthostatic blood pressure and heart rate measurement) was reported as the only useful test for diagnosing POTS in this adolescent case series.
Impaired esophageal peristalsis in LPRD patients was associated with diminished vagal nerve function.

Synucleinopathies (Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, pure autonomic failure, multiple system atrophy) typically feature baroreflex failure, which underlies their associated neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.
Tilt table testing reproduced the majority of PASC symptoms, supporting orthostatic intolerance as a driver of symptom burden.
Some homozygous knockout mice developed limb damage, consistent with self-mutilating behavior seen in sensory neuropathies.

EMG/nerve conduction studies revealed a severe diffuse motor neurogenic process, while MRI brain/spine and spinal fluid analysis were normal, and serum inflammatory, infectious, and autoimmune markers were negative.
Genetic testing showed no abnormalities in the AAAS gene, effectively excluding Triple-A syndrome as the diagnosis in this patient.
A pilot study reported reduced urinary GABA levels in ME/CFS patients.
The title indicates a report of orthostatic intolerance occurring in association with Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome, a congenital vascular malformation disorder.
PPH is more common than orthostatic hypotension in older adults with dementia with Lewy bodies.
Golgi bodies in dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons appeared turgid/swollen in knockout mice on transmission electron microscopy.
The prevalence of in-hospital falls was higher among patients with type 2 diabetes than among those without.
Distal symmetric polyneuropathy (DSPN) independently predicted stroke risk in patients with type 1 diabetes.
Supine and orthostatic hypocapnia (low end-tidal CO2) was observed in PASC patients, indicating respiratory dysregulation.
The guideline weakly recommends against the use of intravenous corticosteroids for GBS treatment.
Disorders of gut-brain interaction represent the strongest gastrointestinal association identified in patients with hEDS/HSD.
The presence of orthostatic hypotension in some patients suggests an underlying sympathetic nervous system dysfunction in children with PWS.
Knockdown of MFSD7b reduced choline influx in mammalian cells, supporting its role as a choline transporter.
Subtle motor signs were more common among all patients who later phenoconverted to MSA, PD, or DLB.
Two affected patients had microcytic anemia without hemolysis, an atypical finding that initially raised suspicion for Majeed syndrome before genetic testing clarified the diagnosis as HSAN2B.
Affected individuals exhibited autonomic dysfunction, including hyperhidrosis, urinary incontinence, and absent sympathetic skin responses on electrophysiological testing.
No significant sex/gender differences were observed among nOH(+), non-nOH(+), and OH(-) groups.
The Task Force does not recommend any specific treatment for fatigue in GBS.
Beta-blockers are not recommended for pediatric vasovagal syncope according to guideline consensus.
Autonomic neuropathy is identified as a distinct category of neurological immune-related adverse event associated with ICI cancer treatment.
No specific treatment for fatigue in GBS is recommended by the guideline.
Gastrointestinal symptom frequency did not differ based on presence of benign joint hypermobility syndrome.
Gastrointestinal symptom occurrence did not significantly differ between children with and without BJHS.
The patient's autonomic reflex screen test, which assesses control of blood pressure, heart rate, and sweating, was positive, supporting a diagnosis of AAG.
The guideline does not recommend a specific treatment for fatigue in GBS patients.
The Task Force does not recommend plasma exchange followed immediately by IVIg as a combined treatment strategy.
The patient had a negative (absent flare/swelling) histamine intradermal reaction test, a finding classically associated with familial dysautonomia due to sensory/autonomic nerve impairment.
The guideline does not recommend plasma exchange followed immediately by IVIg as a combined treatment.
No significant changes in plasma catecholamines or heart rate variability were observed after metreleptin initiation, despite thyroid hormone and energy expenditure changes.

Males with PD show worse performance than females on most cognitive parameters (semantic fluency, MoCA, phonemic tasks), and OH and RBD are more common in males, although MMSE shows no sex difference.
Care must be taken regarding micturition syncope, a phenomenon linking bladder voiding and cardiovascular autonomic instability in these patients.
The guideline does not recommend plasma exchange followed immediately by IVIg as a combined treatment for GBS.
Ultrastructural arteriopathic changes on skin biopsy were characteristic of CADASIL (cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy).
Pacing is described as a promising treatment approach for managing post-exertional malaise in post-COVID patients.

COMPASS-31 scores are elevated across PTSD, depression, and anxiety, conditions highly comorbid with functional disorders, with each showing characteristic autonomic patterns (sympathetic predominance in PTSD/anxiety, widespread hypoactivation in depression).

The review notes that women show an increased incidence of orthostatic intolerance compared to men, a sex-linked difference observed terrestrially that warrants further study in the spaceflight context.
Anxiety levels correlated with the severity of reflux symptoms in LPRD patients.
Demyelination of the sciatic nerve was commonly observed in knockout mice via microscopy.
At baseline, left ventricular mass index was similar between POTS patients and healthy controls.
No single factor was found to explain the family stress reported during the pandemic, suggesting a multifactorial contribution.
Small fiber neuropathy is noted to be common in EDS and is proposed as a contributor to autonomic dysfunction relevant to hypoglycemia.
Baseline plasma GFAP levels did not differ significantly between groups at baseline.
Baseline plasma DDC levels did not differ significantly between groups.
Electrochemical skin conductance, used to assess sudomotor (sweating) function, was normal in children with Prader-Willi syndrome.
Targeted sequencing of LPIN2 coding exons did not identify any variants, excluding Majeed syndrome as the cause of the family's recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis.
Serum BDNF correlated with acetylcholine in the MPS cohort.
Serum BDNF correlated with neuropeptide Y (NPY) in the MPS cohort.
The patient's anti-gAChR antibody assay was negative despite an autonomic and gastrointestinal clinical picture consistent with AAG, leading to a diagnosis of seronegative AAG.
Drugs used to treat orthostatic hypotension may worsen post-void residual urine volume in patients with PD or MSA.
Vestibular symptoms (vertigo, dizziness) were reported less frequently than cochlear symptoms across the reviewed conditions.
Despite classic MIRAGE syndrome features (myelodysplasia, growth restriction), the patient did not develop adrenal insufficiency.
No associated mortality was found linked to dysautonomia in this GBS cohort.
The review discusses the efficacy of combined immunotherapy as a treatment approach for AAG, though no specific outcome data are given in the abstract.
No adverse events were reported during the 8-week taVNS intervention, including no local discomfort, skin irritation, or transient autonomic symptoms.
Malignancy screening was negative in all patients with CASPR2-related Morvan syndrome, arguing against a paraneoplastic etiology in this cohort.
CSF analysis was normal in most anti-CASPR2 patients, indicating that normal CSF does not exclude the diagnosis.
HRV scores did not differ significantly between DAN(+) and DAN(-) groups as defined by COMPASS-31, indicating poor agreement between HRV and COMPASS-31.
Among individuals with ME/CFS, those whose illness was labeled 'CFS' rather than another term had an increased risk of dying by suicide compared to other ME/CFS patients.
ME/CFS patients with more limited overall functioning had an increased risk of dying by suicide compared to those with less functional impairment.
ME/CFS patients without comorbid illnesses had an increased risk of dying by suicide compared to those with comorbid conditions.

The commentary argues that CBT and graded exercise therapy (GET) are inappropriately framed as treatments for ME/CFS, and that numerous experts, not just patients, have rejected the research underlying this treatment approach.

The authors contend that ME/CFS lacking identified diagnostic biomarkers does not equate to it being an 'illness without disease', noting that many leading scientists and physicians view ME/CFS as a biomedical disease.

A freedom-of-information survey of 57 NHS-affiliated ME/CFS specialist clinics in England found that clinics were highly inconsistent in how they addressed treatment-related harm from graded exercise therapy and cognitive behavioural therapy.
Maximal muscle strength and strength endurance of the knee flexors/extensors were significantly lower in hEDS/HSD patients than controls at both baseline and 8-year follow-up.
Maximal muscle strength of the knee flexors showed a significantly different evolution over 8 years between groups, decreasing in the control group.
Strength endurance of the knee extensors decreased over 8 years in the hEDS/HSD group while it increased in controls, indicating a differential longitudinal decline.
Muscle density, assessed by peripheral quantitative computed tomography, decreased over 8 years in the hEDS/HSD group with a significantly different evolution compared to controls.

Aside from knee flexor strength, knee extensor endurance, and muscle density, no other significant differences in the 8-year evolution of muscle strength parameters were found between hEDS/HSD patients and controls.
Participants with Joint Hypermobility Syndrome/EDS-Hypermobility Type reported significant healthcare limitations, including a lack of awareness of the condition among healthcare professionals.
Participants described a 'restricted life' as a major theme, reflecting limitations on daily activities and independence imposed by the condition.
Participants reported experiencing social stigma related to their hypermobility condition.
Participants expressed 'fear of the unknown' regarding disease progression and prognosis, linked to inadequate information provision.
Effective coping strategies identified included acceptance of the condition, building social networks, learning about joint hypermobility, and adapting activities.
Physiotherapists knowledgeable about Joint Hypermobility Syndrome/EDS-Hypermobility Type were cited by participants as important sources of support, hope, and encouragement for regular exercise.
Participants receiving help from family members to complete activities described feelings of guilt and shame, indicating a need for rehabilitation focused on maintaining independence.

Participants reported difficulties with sexual relationships due to prolapse or erectile dysfunction, along with associated anxieties, indicating a need for greater awareness of these issues in primary care.
Nearly all subjects with HSD/hEDS met criteria for at least one Rome IV functional gastrointestinal disorder, compared with less than half of controls.
Bowel-related FGIDs were more common in HSD/hEDS subjects than controls.
Gastroduodenal FGIDs were more common in HSD/hEDS subjects than controls.
Esophageal FGIDs were more common in HSD/hEDS subjects than controls.
Anorectal FGIDs were more common in HSD/hEDS subjects than controls.
A significantly higher proportion of HSD/hEDS subjects had FGIDs affecting two or more gastrointestinal regions compared with controls.
HSD/hEDS subjects reported a significantly higher number of non-GI, non-musculoskeletal somatic symptoms than controls.
HSD/hEDS subjects reported lower quality of life than controls.
Almost 40% of subjects with HSD/hEDS reported a diagnosis of chronic fatigue syndrome and/or fibromyalgia.
After adjusting for the number of non-GI/non-musculoskeletal somatic symptoms, the association between HSD/hEDS and FGIDs was reduced by up to 4-fold and in some cases became non-significant.
Subjects with HSD/hEDS had greater healthcare use than controls, including higher rates of abdominal surgeries and analgesic medication use.
Subjects with HSD/hEDS reported lower quality of life compared with controls.

A female infant born at 35 weeks gestation with a pathologic skull fracture after vaginal delivery was found to carry a pathogenic COL1A1 splice-site variant (c.472-1G>C), consistent with arthrochalasia type Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome.

This case expands the phenotypic spectrum of arthrochalasia type EDS to include pathologic bone fractures, a feature previously reported in only one other study, suggesting bone fragility can occur alongside the classic joint hypermobility and dislocation features.
Serum lithium levels were significantly lower in women with generalized joint hypermobility compared to controls.
Serum zinc levels were significantly higher in women with generalized joint hypermobility compared to controls.
Serum strontium levels were significantly higher in women with generalized joint hypermobility compared to controls.
TNXB gene expression was significantly higher in the blood of women with generalized joint hypermobility compared to controls and correlated positively with the Beighton score.
SLC39A13 gene expression was significantly higher in the blood of women with generalized joint hypermobility compared to controls and correlated positively with the Beighton score.
COL1A1 gene expression was significantly lower in the blood of women with generalized joint hypermobility compared to controls and correlated negatively with the Beighton score.
COL1A2 gene expression was significantly lower in the blood of women with generalized joint hypermobility compared to controls.
COL5A1 gene expression was significantly lower in the blood of women with generalized joint hypermobility compared to controls.
FKBP14 gene expression was significantly lower in women with generalized joint hypermobility compared to controls.
DSE gene expression was significantly lower in women with generalized joint hypermobility compared to controls.
Beighton score showed a strong negative correlation with B4GALT7 gene expression.
Beighton score showed a strong negative correlation with FKBP14 gene expression.
Beighton score showed a strong negative correlation with COL1A1 gene expression.
Beighton score showed a strong negative correlation with serum lithium level.
Beighton score showed a significant positive correlation with SLC39A13 gene expression.
Beighton score showed a significant positive correlation with TNXB gene expression.
Serum zinc levels showed a significant positive correlation with the Beighton hypermobility score.
Serum strontium levels showed a significant positive correlation with the Beighton hypermobility score.
B3GALT6 expression showed a significant positive correlation with the Beighton hypermobility score.
Absence or hypoplasia of the lingual frenulum was found in 90% of pediatric EDS patients compared to only 1.8% of controls.
Absence of the lingual frenulum demonstrated a sensitivity of 90% and specificity of 98.2% for diagnosing EDS in this population.
The authors propose that absence of the lingual frenulum should be included as a minor diagnostic criterion for Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome.

Qualitative thematic analysis identified three main themes regarding employment participation in hypermobile EDS: facilitators of employment participation, limitations in employment participation, and unemployment due to the condition.
Work was reported to have positive effects on the well-being of people with hypermobile EDS, functioning as a facilitator when job requirements match functional abilities.
Some patients with hypermobile EDS reported becoming unemployed as a direct consequence of their condition.
Gastrointestinal functional disorders were among the most common comorbidities and were significantly more frequent in the EDS cohort compared with matched controls.
Hernias were significantly more common among patients with EDS compared with the matched control cohort.
Asthma was significantly more common among patients with EDS compared with matched controls.
Pneumonia was significantly more common among patients with EDS compared with matched controls.
Osteoporosis was identified as one of the most common comorbidities in patients with EDS.
All disease categories and unique ICD-10 codes examined were significantly more frequent in the EDS cohort than in the matched control cohort, particularly those related to common EDS manifestations.

Adolescents with asymptomatic generalized joint hypermobility showed higher knee extensor muscle strength (peak torque/body weight) in the dominant leg than non-hypermobile controls, after adjusting for age and gender.

Apart from dominant-leg knee extensor strength, no other significant associations were found between asymptomatic GJH and other measures of muscle strength, motor performance (single-leg-hop-for-distance), or physical activity level compared to non-hypermobile controls.

Perceived harmfulness of physical activity (measured with PHODA-youth) was not more pronounced in adolescents with asymptomatic GJH than in non-hypermobile controls, and its negative impact on physical functioning was not amplified in the GJH group.
Altered bowel function was more prevalent among LDS patients compared to vEDS patients.
Ventral hernias were more frequent and more often postoperative in vEDS patients compared to LDS patients, despite similar overall hernia prevalence between groups.
LDS patients had a significantly higher prevalence of arterial aneurysms overall than vEDS patients.
A higher proportion of LDS patients required arterial repair compared to vEDS patients.
Autonomic dysfunction was reported as a more prevalent comorbidity in LDS patients than in vEDS patients.
Psychopathology, most commonly anxiety, depression, and adjustment disorder, was more prevalent in LDS patients than vEDS patients.
Allergy was more prevalent as a comorbidity in LDS patients than in vEDS patients.
Gastrointestinal symptoms were frequently and similarly reported across both vEDS and LDS patients, and hernias occurred in similar overall proportions between the two groups.
Psychopathology, most commonly anxiety, depression, and adjustment disorder, was more prevalent in patients with Loeys-Dietz syndrome than in those with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Allergy was more prevalent as a comorbidity in patients with Loeys-Dietz syndrome compared to those with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Three patients with typical CRPS showed orderly clinical evolution over time to full-blown fibromyalgia.
The authors describe DRG hyperexcitability and small fiber neuropathy as shared pathogenetic mechanisms recently demonstrated in both CRPS and fibromyalgia.

The authors propose that after trauma, DRG perineuronal glial cells produce proinflammatory mediators, and immune cells including macrophages, lymphocytes, and satellite glial cells may spread this response to other spinal cord sites, potentially explaining widespread pain and autonomic dysfunction.
The authors propose that DRG metabolic changes may lead to small nerve fiber degeneration, contributing to development of widespread pain and autonomic dysfunction.

Active high-frequency rTMS over primary motor cortex combined with multicomponent therapy did not reduce weekly mean self-reported pain more than sham rTMS plus multicomponent therapy in fibromyalgia patients.

Pain VAS, cardiorespiratory fitness, quality of life, depression, and pain catastrophizing all improved significantly by week 14 and remained stable through 6-month follow-up (week 40), regardless of rTMS group assignment.
Cardiac autonomic adaptations did not change significantly with the combined rTMS and multicomponent therapy program in fibromyalgia patients.
Sleep efficiency did not change significantly following the combined rTMS and multicomponent therapy program in fibromyalgia patients.

Pain thresholds decreased during stress induction and recovery in healthy controls, but no such change occurred in women with fibromyalgia, suggesting a blunted stress-induced hypoalgesic response in FM.
In healthy controls, the pain intolerance threshold decreased during acute stress induction but returned to (was maintained at) basal level during the recovery period.
Women with fibromyalgia without PTSD (FM-PTSD) showed a delayed pain modulation response, with a drop in intolerance threshold appearing only at recovery rather than during stress.
Women with fibromyalgia and comorbid PTSD (FM+PTSD) showed no change in pain intolerance/tolerance levels across stress and recovery phases.
Systolic blood pressure and heart rate reactivity to the stress task did not explain the observed group differences in pain modulation response.

The authors interpret the blunted pain modulation response to stress in FM as consistent with a broader pattern of hypoactive (hypo-reactive) stress responsiveness previously reported in FM across autonomic and neuroendocrine axes, potentially contributing to chronic pain maintenance.
Serum cesium levels were significantly lower in patients with schizophrenia than in healthy controls, even after adjusting for age, sex, and BMI, and this remained significant after FDR correction.
Serum rhenium and rubidium levels did not differ significantly between patients with schizophrenia and healthy controls.
Serum CCL11 (eotaxin), IL-1β, and TNF-α levels were significantly higher in patients with schizophrenia than in healthy controls.

All cognitive test scores (verbal episodic memory, working memory, semantic and letter fluency, attention, executive functions) were significantly lower in patients with schizophrenia than in healthy controls.

Lower serum cesium was significantly correlated with higher psychiatric symptom severity scores (BPRS, SANS, and HAM-D) across the combined sample of patients and controls, and these correlations survived FDR correction and adjustment for age, sex, and BMI.

Lower serum cesium was significantly correlated with higher scores on the FibroFatigue (FF) scale, an instrument assessing fibromyalgia and chronic-fatigue-type symptoms, in the combined sample of schizophrenia patients and controls; this scale was used here as a symptom-severity measure within a schizophrenia cohort rather than in diagnosed fibromyalgia patients.

Higher serum cesium was significantly correlated with better performance on multiple cognitive tests (Tower of London, Symbol Coding, Controlled Word Association, Category Instances, Digit Sequencing Task, and List Learning), and these correlations persisted after FDR correction and in an education-restricted subsample.
Serum cesium was significantly and inversely correlated with CCL11 (eotaxin) and TNF-α, but not with IL-1β, and these associations survived FDR correction and adjustment for age, sex, and BMI.
Antipsychotic drug use (risperidone, olanzapine, fluphenazine) and tobacco use disorder had no significant effect on serum cesium, rhenium, or rubidium levels.
The authors state that increasing appreciation suggests mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) may be prevalent in up to 17% of the general population.
The authors assert that most MCAS patients, regardless of how long they were ill before diagnosis, can eventually identify a treatment that yields sustained improvement.

Two differing diagnostic proposals for MCAS ('consensus-1' from 2012 and 'consensus-2' from 2011) lead to substantially different numbers of patients qualifying for diagnosis and treatment, with underdiagnosis via consensus-1 criteria considered the larger problem compared to potential overdiagnosis via consensus-2 criteria.
At baseline, airway hyperresponsiveness to mannitol (a marker of airway mast cell activation) was similar between patients with T2-high and T2-low asthma.

Both T2-high and T2-low asthma patients showed a similar, significant improvement (reduced hyperresponsiveness, i.e. higher provoking dose) in AHR to mannitol after 12 months of specialist asthma management.
Unlike mannitol, airway hyperresponsiveness to methacholine did not show concomitant improvement after 12 months of specialist management.
Patients with diabetic symmetrical polyneuropathy had significantly higher sensory perception thresholds than healthy controls.
Patients with DSPN had significantly higher spinal reflex thresholds compared with healthy controls.
Fewer patients with DSPN were able to complete the full recording session compared with healthy controls (34/48 vs 21/21).
DSPN markedly reduced the odds of successfully eliciting a nociceptive withdrawal reflex compared with healthy controls.
DSPN was associated with overall changes in somatosensory evoked cortical potentials compared with healthy controls.
Post hoc analysis showed the N1 peak amplitude of the somatosensory evoked potential was reduced in DSPN patients compared with controls.
Post hoc analysis showed the N1 peak latency of the somatosensory evoked potential was prolonged in DSPN patients compared with controls.

Botulinum toxin inhibits acetylcholine release from nerve endings and is used as a therapeutic alternative for spastic gastrointestinal tract disorders including achalasia, gastroparesis, sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, chronic anal fissures, and pelvic floor dyssynergia.
Long-term efficacy of botulinum toxin has not been observed in many gastrointestinal disorders, primarily due to its relatively short duration of action.
Not all patients respond to botulinum toxin therapy, and large randomized controlled trials are lacking for many conditions commonly treated with it.
Bindarit at 300 μM significantly reduced Col3A1 expression in SSCT fibroblasts from CTS patients compared to vehicle control.
Bindarit at 300 μM significantly reduced CTGF expression in SSCT fibroblasts from CTS patients compared to vehicle control.
Bindarit at 300 μM significantly reduced SERPINE1 expression in SSCT fibroblasts from CTS patients compared to vehicle control.
In a fibrosis gene array, INHBE expression was significantly down-regulated by Bindarit at 300 μM.
In a fibrosis gene array, ACTB expression was significantly down-regulated by Bindarit at 300 μM.
In a fibrosis gene array, EDN1 expression was significantly down-regulated by Bindarit at 300 μM.

Hypoxanthine phosphoribosyltransferase 1 (HPRT1) expression was significantly down-regulated in CTS-derived SSCT fibroblasts treated with Bindarit at 300 μM compared to vehicle control on the fibrosis gene array.
Integrin beta-3 (ITGB3) expression was significantly up-regulated in CTS-derived SSCT fibroblasts treated with Bindarit at 300 μM compared to vehicle control on the fibrosis gene array.

Bindarit at 300 μM significantly reduced TGF-β1-induced Smad signal transduction activation compared to vehicle control plus TGF-β1 in CTS SSCT fibroblasts, as measured by a Smad luciferase reporter assay.
SD208, a TGF-β receptor type 1 inhibitor, at 1 μM significantly reduced TGF-β1-induced Smad signal transduction activation compared to vehicle control plus TGF-β1 in CTS SSCT fibroblasts.
The authors conclude that combination therapy with Bindarit and SD208 may offer potential benefit as a medical treatment for SSCT fibrosis associated with carpal tunnel syndrome.
The large majority of gastroparesis patients had elevated serum TNF-alpha levels.
The large majority of gastroparesis patients had elevated serum IL-6 levels.
Nearly all patients had elevated cutaneous electrogastrogram frequency, indicating gastric electrophysiologic abnormality.
Nearly all patients had abnormal inner interstitial cell of Cajal counts on gastric biopsy.
All patients had abnormal outer interstitial cell of Cajal counts on gastric biopsy.

Measures of inflammation correlated with abnormalities across autonomic, enteric anatomic, electrophysiologic, and hormonal domains in gastroparesis patients, suggesting inflammation is a fundamental driver affecting multiple organ systems.
Gastroparetic GI symptoms were similar regardless of baseline gastric emptying results or diabetic versus idiopathic etiology.
New onsets of IBS, CFS and FM occurred at incidence rates of 48.9, 8.8 and 20.6 per 10,000 person-years respectively over 2.4 years of follow-up.
Female sex was a strong predictor of new-onset IBS (OR 1.88, stable in 100% of imputed datasets).
Female sex was the strongest predictor of new-onset CFS (OR 3.16, stable in 100% of imputed datasets).
Disturbed sleep at baseline was a shared predictor of new onset for all three syndromes, though the effect sizes were small.
Higher somatization score (SCL-90 SOM) at baseline was a shared predictor of onset of IBS, CFS and FM.
Poorer perception of general health (RAND General Health scale) at baseline predicted new onset of all three syndromes.
Stress related to chronic ill health (Long-term Difficulties Inventory) was the strongest of the four predictors shared by all three syndromes.
Having an allergy predicted onset of both IBS and FM, one of four predictors shared between these two syndromes.
Lifetime diagnosis of gastrointestinal disorders (e.g. stomach ulcer, IBD, celiac disease, gallstones) predicted onset of both IBS and FM.
Low alcohol consumption predicted onset of both IBS and FM.
Body mass index predicted both IBS and FM onset but in opposite directions: higher BMI lowered IBS onset probability while raising FM onset probability.
High negative life-events score in the year prior to baseline (excluding serious illness/injury/assault) predicted onset of both CFS and IBS.
A lifetime diagnosis of fibromyalgia at baseline predicted new onset of IBS.
A lifetime diagnosis of IBS at baseline predicted new onset of fibromyalgia.
Unlike IBS and FM, CFS was not predicted by baseline IBS or FM diagnosis, nor was CFS itself a predictor of onset of the other two syndromes.
Use of drugs for functional gastrointestinal disorders (ATC A03A) at baseline was the strongest IBS-specific predictor of new onset IBS.
Use of drugs for constipation (ATC A06A) at baseline predicted new-onset IBS.
Use of hormonal contraceptives at baseline predicted a lower risk of new-onset IBS.
Use of antiandrogen medication (ATC G03H) at baseline predicted new-onset IBS.
Prior musculoskeletal disorders (e.g. osteoarthritis, joint inflammation, fractures) was among the strongest FM-specific predictors of new onset.
Medication for peptic ulcer or gastro-esophageal reflux disease (ATC A02B) at baseline predicted new-onset FM.
Having no GP or specialist contact in the past 5 years increased risk of new-onset FM, whereas a serious illness, injury or assault in the prior year decreased FM onset risk.
Lifetime diagnosis of high cholesterol showed the largest effect among only two syndrome-specific predictors identified for CFS onset.
Reduced vitality (RAND scale) at baseline showed a small association with new-onset CFS.
Overall, three-quarters of the identified predictors were syndrome-specific and only a quarter were shared across two or more syndromes, arguing against a fully shared etiology for IBS, CFS and FM.
The LASSO-based prediction models showed low predictive accuracy for onset of all three syndromes, as measured by area under the recall-precision curve.
Use of ATC-A03A drugs for functional gastrointestinal disorders at baseline was the strongest medication predictor of new-onset IBS.
Use of ATC-A03F propulsive drugs at baseline predicted new-onset IBS.
Use of ATC-A06A drugs for constipation at baseline predicted new-onset IBS.
Baseline use of hormonal contraceptives (ATC G03A) was associated with a reduced probability of new-onset IBS.
Baseline use of peptic ulcer/GERD medications (ATC A02B) was among the strongest syndrome-specific predictors of new-onset fibromyalgia.
Use of other ophthalmological preparations (e.g. artificial tears) at baseline predicted new-onset fibromyalgia.
Use of nasal decongestants at baseline predicted new-onset fibromyalgia, part of a shared allergy-related cluster with IBS.
Use of thyroid hormone preparations at baseline was an additional predictor of new-onset fibromyalgia.
Use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory/antirheumatic drugs at baseline was associated with new-onset fibromyalgia in the LASSO model.
Being a student at baseline (relative to not working) was a small positive predictor of new-onset IBS.
Having paid work at baseline (relative to not working) was associated with a slightly reduced probability of new-onset IBS.
The authors note that the shared allergy-related predictor cluster between IBS and FM is consistent with recent findings implicating local mast cell activation in IBS.

The authors suggest that gut dysbiosis or small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (including long-term proton pump inhibitor use) may underlie the gut-brain axis changes linking IBS and FM, though this has not previously been shown to precede IBS onset.

Prior literature cited shows the number of tender points is strongly associated with IBS severity (but not bowel-habit subtype), suggesting a common abnormality of pain perception underlying IBS-FM co-occurrence.
The authors note that the high rate of medical comorbidity found among FM predictors partly explains the previously documented high mortality of fibromyalgia.
Gastric retention time measured by 3D-MAGMA was prolonged in people with type 2 diabetes compared to healthy controls.
Median transit time in the duodenum was shorter in people with type 2 diabetes compared to healthy controls.
Transit time through the first 50 cm of jejunum did not differ substantially between diabetes patients and healthy controls.

The 3D-MAGMA magnetic detector system was able to detect differences in gastric and small bowel motility between diabetic and healthy participants, suggesting clinical utility for diagnosing diabetic motility disorders.
Colonic transit time correlated with the symptom of postprandial fullness in type 1 diabetes participants.
Colonic transit time correlated with the symptom of constipation in type 1 diabetes participants.
Decreased colonic motility index was correlated with the presence of diarrhea in type 1 diabetes participants.
Decreased colonic motility index was correlated with decreased bloating in type 1 diabetes participants.
GI symptoms were not correlated with gastric or small bowel transit time or motility index, unlike colonic measures.
In participants with low cardiac vagal tone, gastric motility index was increased compared to those with normal vagal tone.
Abdominal pain was decreased in type 1 diabetes participants with peripheral neuropathy compared to those without.
Decreased cardiac vagal tone was correlated with decreased abdominal pain in participants with type 1 diabetes.
Unlike low cardiac vagal tone, presence of peripheral neuropathy was not associated with increased gastric motility index or colonic transit time.
TNF gene expression in the multifidus muscle was higher in patients with high intramuscular fat infiltration compared to those with low fat infiltration.
Leptin expression was greater in intra-muscular and subcutaneous adipose tissue of participants with high multifidus fat infiltration than those with low infiltration.
Arginase-1, a marker of anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages, was lower in intra-muscular and subcutaneous adipose tissue of participants with high multifidus fat infiltration.
TNF expression was greater in epidural fat of participants with high multifidus fat infiltration compared to those with low infiltration.
Adiponectin expression was greater in epidural fat of participants with high multifidus fat infiltration.
Nitric oxide synthase 2 (a marker of pro-inflammatory M1 macrophages) was more highly expressed in epidural fat of participants with high multifidus fat infiltration.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the COL3A1 gene, leading to arterial and organ fragility and premature death.
Patients treated with celiprolol had significantly better overall survival compared to those not treated.
The mortality reduction from celiprolol was dose-dependent, with the greatest protection observed at 400 mg/day compared to lower doses.
Overall patient survival in the cohort was dependent on the specific type of COL3A1 variant, age at diagnosis, and medical treatment received.
Over half of vEDS patients (51%) had previous arterial events or arterial lesions already present at the time of molecular diagnosis.
Despite a high baseline burden of arterial events/lesions, more than two-thirds of vEDS patients remained clinically silent during follow-up.
The ratio of hospitalizations for acute arterial events versus hospitalizations for regular follow-up significantly changed after 2011, suggesting improved overall medical care over time.
Ninety-seven percent of hEDS patients reported severe chronic pain.
There was a marked delay between pain onset (age 10), chronicity (age 20), and formal hEDS diagnosis (age 24).
Pain intensity gradually increased over time in three-quarters of patients.
Pain in hEDS primarily localized to joints, predominantly in the lower limbs.
Patients with generalized pain presentation had an older age at chronic pain onset and a greater impact on the affective component of pain compared to others.
Neuropathic pain was frequently observed at the most painful joint and was associated with heat hypoesthesia on quantitative sensory testing.
Asymmetric proprioception was found in about one third of hEDS patients.
A very high rate of attempted suicide was observed among hEDS patients with chronic pain.
The authors conclude that central sensitization appears to be a key step in the evolution of chronic pain in hEDS, alongside frequent peripheral neuropathic pain.
A very high rate of attempted suicide was observed among patients with hEDS-related chronic pain.
The authors conclude that central sensitization appears to be a key mechanistic step in the evolution of pain in hEDS, alongside frequent peripheral neuropathic pain.
Non-motor symptom burden increased with advancing Hoehn and Yahr disease stage, while the amplitude of non-motor symptom fluctuations between On and Off states decreased with disease progression.
In patients at Hoehn and Yahr stage 5, no significant non-motor symptom fluctuations were detected between On and Off states.
Multivariate regression adjusting for major demographic and clinical covariates confirmed that both motor and non-motor symptom fluctuation amplitudes decrease with disease stage progression.
Among 187 patients with Guillain-Barré syndrome, 71 (38%) had at least one manifestation of dysautonomia.
Demyelinating GBS was the most common subtype (72% of the cohort), and 36% of patients with demyelination had dysautonomia.

The most common autonomic manifestations in GBS patients with dysautonomia were ileus (42%), hypertension (39%), hypotension (37%), fever (29%), tachycardia or bradycardia (27%), and urinary retention (24%).
Quadriparesis, bulbar and neck flexor weakness, and need for mechanical ventilation were clinical predictors associated with autonomic dysfunction in GBS.

Patients with dysautonomia more commonly had cardiogenic complications, syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH), and posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) compared to those without.
Patients with dysautonomia had higher GBS disability scores and higher (worse) Erasmus GBS Outcome Scores (EGOS) than those without dysautonomia.
Mortality was significantly higher in GBS patients with dysautonomia (6%) compared to the entire cohort (2%).
ALS patients showed decreased total sleep time and sleep efficiency compared with healthy controls.
ALS patients experienced increased nocturnal awakenings compared with controls.
ALS patients showed an inverted stage 1 (N1) to stage 3 (N3) sleep ratio relative to controls.
REM sleep was reduced in ALS patients compared with healthy controls.
ALS patients had a decreased cyclic alternating pattern (CAP) rate with fewer A phases and an inverted A1/A3 subtype ratio, indicating altered EEG oscillatory activity during sleep.
A significant reduction in heart rate variability (HRV) parameters was observed during all sleep stages in ALS patients, indicating impaired cardiac autonomic modulation during sleep.
Despite objective polysomnographic sleep disruption, ALS patients subjectively perceived their sleep quality as satisfactory.
Adults with osteogenesis imperfecta reported significantly higher fatigue severity scores than both an American and a Dutch healthy control population.
Total FSS fatigue scores did not differ significantly between men and women with OI, although women scored numerically higher on nearly all items.
Women with OI scored significantly higher than men on the FSS item rating fatigue as among the three most disabling symptoms.
There were no significant differences in mean total FSS fatigue score among OI type 1, type 3, and type 4 patients.
The FSS score for the item on motivation being lower when fatigued was significantly lower in the 41–45 age category compared to other age groups.
A Norwegian study using the FSS found that adults with OI did not differ significantly in fatigue from age- and gender-matched healthy controls, contrasting with the present Dutch cohort's findings.
A cited study in children with OI reported that a 12-week individual, supervised physical training program decreased fatigue levels, with fatigue increasing again after the program stopped.
Nearly a quarter of confirmed EDS patients surveyed had undergone ophthalmic surgery, and almost half of those reported at least one surgical complication.
EDS patients undergoing refractive surgery (LASIK/PRK/RK/LASEK) had a much higher complication rate than reported for the general population.
The most common refractive surgery complaint among EDS patients was under-correction or regression of the surgical result.
A subset of refractive surgery patients reported postoperative pain, though this is common after LASIK generally and may not represent a true complication.
A small number of refractive surgery patients reported impaired night vision or halos postoperatively.
A small number of refractive surgery patients reported dry eye, which the authors note is common post-LASIK generally and may not be a true complication.
A subset of refractive surgery patients reported induced or acquired astigmatism, potentially reflecting the corneal collagen abnormalities of EDS.
Two EDS patients reported findings suggestive of possible corneal ectasia after refractive surgery, consistent with EDS being considered a contraindication to LASIK due to collagen abnormalities.
EDS patients undergoing cataract/lens surgery had a complication rate substantially higher than typically reported after cataract surgery in the general population.

One EDS patient reported retinal detachment following cataract surgery, a rate the authors note is not well characterized in EDS patients specifically compared to established general-population incidence.
EDS patients undergoing retinal surgery had a substantial complication rate, with nearly a quarter experiencing recurrent retinal detachment.
EDS patients undergoing strabismus correction surgery reported a high complication rate.
The reoperation rate after strabismus surgery among EDS patients was substantially higher than the reoperation rate reported for the general population.
After excluding complications deemed not clinically true (floppy eyelid, headache from positioning), oculoplastic surgery in EDS patients had a moderate complication rate.

After excluding complications judged to be unrelated to the surgery itself (e.g., debris from an accident, difficulty suturing), no true complications remained among EDS cornea surgery patients, despite an initial 60% complication report rate.
Half of EDS patients undergoing laser surgery for glaucoma reported a complication, though the small sample and vague descriptions limit interpretation.
The majority of surveyed EDS patients underwent their ophthalmic surgery before receiving an EDS diagnosis, which is concerning given that EDS is considered an FDA contraindication for LASIK.
Recovered and symptomatic groups reported similar pre-injury post-concussive symptoms, with group differences emerging at 2 days post-injury across most symptom subscales.

Children who did not recover by 2 weeks had a higher rate of pre-injury psychiatric diagnoses, more acute CT scans, and more severe parent-rated post-concussive symptoms at 2 days than those who recovered.
Both recovered and symptomatic groups showed lower parent-rated post-concussive symptoms and less internalizing behavior over time, with statistically significant changes (p<0.01).
No differences between recovered and symptomatic groups were found for child age, sex, injury mechanism factors, pre-injury parent-rated symptoms, or acute physical and cognitive status.
The study concludes that both pre- and post-injury mental health status are important considerations in managing post-concussion recovery in children.
Both online and investigator-confirmed idiopathic hypersomnia patients had significantly higher composite autonomic symptom scores (COMPASS-31) than matched controls.
Within the COMPASS-31 subdomains, orthostatic intolerance and vasomotor symptoms showed the greatest symptom burden in idiopathic hypersomnia patients.
Both online and confirmed idiopathic hypersomnia patients reported greater daytime sleepiness on the Epworth Sleepiness Scale than controls.
Online-recruited idiopathic hypersomnia patients reported more fatigue on the Chalder Fatigue Scale than controls.
Investigator-confirmed idiopathic hypersomnia patients did not show significantly greater fatigue on the Chalder Fatigue Scale compared with controls, unlike the online cohort.
Epworth sleepiness scale scores were positively correlated with COMPASS-31 autonomic symptom scores in idiopathic hypersomnia patients.
Chalder fatigue scale scores were positively correlated with COMPASS-31 autonomic symptom scores in idiopathic hypersomnia patients.
Patients with idiopathic hypersomnia reported lower quality of life across all domains of the RAND 36-item health survey compared to controls.
RAND-36 quality of life scores were negatively correlated with COMPASS-31 autonomic symptom scores.
Low bone mineral density and fractures appear to be frequent in some of the rarer EDS subtypes, including kyphoscoliotic, arthrochalasia, spondylodysplastic, and classic-like EDS.
In hypermobile and classic EDS, case-control studies found mildly decreased bone mineral density compared with controls, but it was not clear that fracture rates were increased.
Abnormalities in vertebral shape appear common in both classical and hypermobile EDS types.
In a cohort of individuals with EDS followed prospectively since birth, no fractures were observed during infancy.
Bone mineral density varies widely across the different EDS subtypes.
Bone mineral density is highly variable across the different subtypes of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
The authors suggest it may be justified to perform spine radiographs and bone mineral density assessments in individuals newly diagnosed with EDS.
Arthroscopic ligamentum teres reconstruction significantly improved modified Harris Hip Score from 44.1 preoperatively to 71.8 postoperatively.
Non-Arthritic Hip Score improved from a mean of 47.5 preoperatively to 78.6 postoperatively after LTR.
Visual analog scale pain score decreased from 7.8 preoperatively to 3.6 postoperatively after LTR.
Average patient satisfaction after LTR was 7.88 (range, 4-10).
Among patients undergoing LTR, the subgroup with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (5 patients, 7 hips) showed a higher failure rate than the overall cohort.
Two of 11 hips that underwent LTR were converted to total hip arthroplasty at a mean of 21.12 months postoperatively.
ME/CFS patients, both with and without fibromyalgia, showed a significant decrease in pressure pain threshold after head-up tilt testing compared to healthy controls.
ME/CFS patients with comorbid fibromyalgia had markedly lower pressure pain thresholds both before and after head-up tilt testing compared to ME/CFS patients without fibromyalgia.
Prior to head-up tilt testing, temporal summation (windup) was significantly increased in both ME/CFS patients with and without fibromyalgia compared to healthy controls.
Windup did not significantly change from pre- to post-head-up tilt testing in either ME/CFS patients or healthy controls.
Healthy controls showed no significant change in pressure pain threshold between pre- and post-head-up tilt testing at either the finger or shoulder.
Children with ME/CFS showed lower objectively measured (ActiGraphy) activity levels compared to healthy control children.
Participants with ME/CFS showed increased nighttime activity compared to healthy control children.
Participants with ME/CFS showed a delayed initiation of daytime activity compared to healthy control children.
Self-reported activity levels of children with ME/CFS significantly correlated with their ActiGraph-measured activity data, suggesting accurate self-perception of activity.
20.1% of adolescents with CFS/ME met DSM-5 criteria for major depressive disorder on the KSADS diagnostic interview.
27.4% of adolescents with CFS/ME met DSM-5 criteria for at least one anxiety disorder on the KSADS.
Among those with a mental health diagnosis, about a third (34.5%) had co-occurring anxiety and depression together.
Social anxiety disorder was one of the most prevalent anxiety diagnoses, present in 11.6% of participants.
Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) was found in 10.4% of participants, described by the authors as a new finding in this population.
Specific phobia was diagnosed in 8.5% of participants, a rate comparable to general population adolescent samples.
Only one participant (0.6%) met full diagnostic criteria for separation anxiety disorder, much lower than previous questionnaire-based estimates, although 9.8% showed subthreshold symptoms.
More females than males were diagnosed with depression (69.7% of MDD cases were female) and anxiety (75.6% of anxiety cases were female), consistent with the female-predominant sample.
In adolescents with comorbid MDD, fatigue perceived to be linked to and exacerbated by low mood (over and above CFS/ME fatigue) was reported by the vast majority (90.9%).

Cognitive difficulties were pervasive among those with comorbid MDD (87.9%), while suicidal ideation/worthlessness was comparatively low (18.2%), a symptom pattern differing from typical CAMHS-referred depressed adolescents.

The RCADS-Anxiety subscale (both 37-item and brief 15-item, self- and parent-report versions) showed the best diagnostic accuracy for anxiety disorders, with AUC values of 0.879-0.890, meeting the required sensitivity ≥0.8 and specificity ≥0.7 thresholds.
The RCADS-Depression subscale showed moderate accuracy (AUC 0.789 raw score) but did not meet the pre-specified sensitivity/specificity accuracy thresholds for detecting MDD.

The HADS did not meet the required accuracy criteria for detecting either depression (AUC 0.714) or anxiety (AUC 0.774), leading the authors to recommend against its use for screening in this population.
The SCAS showed moderate accuracy for anxiety (AUC 0.744) but did not meet the required sensitivity/specificity thresholds.
Inter-rater reliability for KSADS diagnostic decisions between two independent raters (blind to each other's conclusions) was 94.2% agreement but only fair kappa agreement (κ=0.20).
A high proportion (35-48%) of adolescents with chronic musculoskeletal pain also report generalized joint hypermobility, supporting GJH as a risk factor for CMP.

The authors propose that a vulnerability to heightened pain-related fear, catastrophizing thoughts and generalized anxiety, as described by the fear-avoidance model, may underlie the relationship between generalized joint hypermobility and pain-related disability in adolescents.

Across the eight controlled trials, only three (Celenay & Kaya, Daman et al., Reychler et al.) showed consistent superiority of exercise-based conservative management over no-treatment controls post-treatment, while the remainder showed inconsistent or absent between-group differences.

All 11 studies (controlled trials and cohort studies) reported significant improvements from pre- to post-treatment across a wide range of patient-reported, parent-reported and objective outcomes, regardless of whether a between-group effect was found.

In an RCT of women with joint hypermobility syndrome, an 8-week spinal stabilisation exercise programme significantly reduced pain intensity and improved trunk endurance and one postural stability measure compared to a no-intervention control group.

In an RCT of women with knee-pain-associated JHS, combined closed kinetic chain and proprioception exercise therapy significantly improved pain, joint position sense and physical functioning compared to no-treatment control, but not mental health.

In an RCT of women with EDS-HT/JHS, 6 weeks of inspiratory muscle training (IMT) significantly improved inspiratory muscle strength (SNIP), FEV1 and 6-minute walk distance compared to control, with no significant effect on anxiety, depression or physical activity level.

In a paediatric RCT, an individual multidisciplinary physiotherapy/occupational therapy programme showed no significant difference from standard care on any outcome (pain, function, QoL, motor skills, grip strength) at 3 or 12 months, although both groups combined improved over time in pain, motor skills and grip strength.

In a paediatric RCT comparing targeted versus generalised physiotherapy for JHS-related arthralgia, no outcome differed between groups at 2 months, and only parental global assessment favoured targeted physiotherapy at 5 months, with all other outcomes showing no group difference.

In children with JHS and knee pain, exercising into the hypermobile range versus neutral range produced inconsistent effects: parent-reported physical quality of life favoured the neutral-range exercise while parent-reported psychosocial quality of life favoured the hypermobile-range exercise, with no differences on child-reported or physical outcome measures.

In adults with benign JHS, an 8-week supervised proprioception exercise programme (balance and kinaesthesia exercises) significantly improved pain on movement and at rest, joint position sense, and the occupational activity subscale of function compared to baseline, though a direct statistical comparison with the control group was not reported.

In a single-arm cohort study, an 8-week home exercise programme with progressive closed kinetic chain exercises significantly improved knee proprioception, balance, muscle strength, pain intensity and quality of life (SF-36) from baseline in adults with JHS and knee pain.

In a pilot cohort study, a 15-week multidisciplinary rehabilitation programme with a cognitive behavioural approach significantly improved activity performance, performance satisfaction, muscle endurance measures and kinesiophobia in adults with EDS-HT/JHS, but did not significantly improve pain intensity or stair-descent ability.

A three-group cohort study found that people with JHS had significantly lower baseline concentric and eccentric leg press torque than non-hypermobile controls and generalised joint hypermobility (GJH) participants, but improved at the same rate as other groups following an individualised exercise programme, with significant improvements in pain, knee function and activity.

In a pilot RCT feasibility study, adding a comprehensive whole-body physiotherapy intervention to advice-only self-management led to continued improvement in impact scores (BIoH) from 4 to 7 months, whereas the advice-only group reverted to baseline; no formal statistical comparison was performed given the pilot design.

A cited study (Rombaut et al.) found that only 33.9% of EDS-HT patients who underwent surgery reported a positive effect, compared to 63.4% of those who received physiotherapy, though the authors caution that indications for each intervention likely differed.

Cited prevalence studies found that syndromic hypermobility (historical JHS via Brighton criteria) was common among UK musculoskeletal service referrals: 30% of musculoskeletal triage referrals, and 39.1% of pain management, 37.0% of rheumatology, and 10.9% of orthopaedic lower-limb clinic referrals met JHS criteria.

A case report describes use of digital dental technologies for oral rehabilitation of a 6-year-old with ectodermal dysplasia and a 20-year-old with Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome, both presenting with congenitally missing teeth or premature tooth loss and underdeveloped, easily traumatized oral structures.
Most respondents with Loeys-Dietz or vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome had received advice about physical activity and had modified their activity habits.
Physical activity levels were mixed among the cohort, with half at an appropriate level, 40% too low, and 10% too high due to excessive intensity.
Lower fatigue severity scores were associated with higher physical activity levels among patients with Loeys-Dietz or vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Lower anxiety subscale scores on the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale were associated with higher physical activity levels.
About a third of respondents with Loeys-Dietz or vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome reported unmet rehabilitation needs.
In a 59-year-old man with classical EDS and osteoporosis, 48 months of denosumab therapy increased lumbar spine BMD by 1.6%.
In the same 59-year-old man with classical EDS, 48 months of denosumab therapy increased total hip BMD by 11.4%.
In a 42-year-old man with vascular EDS and osteoporosis, 18 months of denosumab therapy increased lumbar spine BMD by 5.0%.
In the same 42-year-old man with vascular EDS, 18 months of denosumab therapy increased total hip BMD by 1.8%.
No fractures or other complications were observed in either EDS patient during denosumab treatment, suggesting the drug was safely administered.

Generalized lack of attached gingiva was present in all 12 children who inherited the familial C1R/C1S pathogenic variant and absent in all 7 children who did not inherit it, indicating this gingival phenotype is a pathognomonic pediatric feature of periodontal EDS.
Easy bruising was reported in 8 of the affected children and in none of the unaffected children.

Most affected children did not fulfill the full clinical diagnostic criteria for pEDS, with only 2 of 12 variant-carrying children (aged 8 and 13) meeting the criteria, showing other pEDS manifestations are rarely present in childhood.
Periodontal Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in adults is caused by dominant pathogenic variants in the C1R or C1S genes, underlying the disorder's main clinical features.
Chst14 gene-deleted (Chst14-/-) mice showed significantly decreased skin tensile strength compared with wild-type (Chst14+/+) mice.
Electron microscopy showed that collagen fibrils in Chst14-/- mouse skin were oriented in various directions, forming disorganized collagen fibers in the reticular layer.

Cupromeronic blue EM staining revealed that glycosaminoglycan chains in Chst14-/- mice were rod-shaped, attached at one end to collagen fibrils and protruding outward, in contrast to the round, fibril-wrapping GAG chains seen in wild-type mice.
Anion-exchange HPLC analysis after enzymatic digestion showed a very low level of dermatan sulfate disaccharides in the skin of Chst14-/- mice.

The authors conclude that Chst14-/- mice, which exhibit similar decorin GAG structure and collagen network abnormalities as human patients, represent a reasonable animal model for the skin fragility of mcEDS-CHST14.
The prevalence of EDS diagnosis among pregnancies increased significantly over the 16-year study period.
Women with EDS had significantly increased odds of prematurity compared to women without EDS.
Women with EDS had significantly increased odds of cervical incompetence compared to women without EDS.
Women with EDS had significantly increased odds of antepartum hemorrhage compared to women without EDS.
Women with EDS had significantly increased odds of placenta previa compared to women without EDS.
Women with EDS had a markedly increased risk of maternal death during pregnancy compared to women without EDS, though the confidence interval was wide.
Pregnant women with EDS were significantly more likely to be delivered by cesarean section than women without EDS.
Women with EDS had a higher risk of prolonged postpartum hospital stay (>7 days) compared to women without EDS.
Neonates born to mothers with EDS had a higher risk of intra-uterine growth restriction compared to neonates of mothers without EDS.
Women with EDS were more likely to be Caucasian, belong to a higher income quartile, and smoke compared to the general obstetrical population.
Resting heart rate variability indexes reflecting vagal (parasympathetic) modulation were significantly lower in women with fibromyalgia compared with healthy women.
Chronotropic reserve during maximal incremental exercise was significantly lower in women with fibromyalgia than in healthy women.

Heart rate recovery at 30, 120, 180, 300, and 600 seconds post-exercise was significantly lower in fibromyalgia patients compared with healthy women, indicating impaired parasympathetic reactivation after exertion.

Cardiac autonomic abnormalities (reduced vagal HRV, chronotropic reserve, and HR recovery) in fibromyalgia patients persisted even when analysis was restricted to a subgroup matched for physical fitness, indicating the dysautonomia is independent of fitness level.
Over half of biopsied adolescents with juvenile fibromyalgia had epidermal neurite density below the 5th centile, compared to only a small fraction of matched healthy controls.
Mean epidermal neurite density was significantly lower in juvenile FM patients than in healthy controls.
A prior meta-analysis in adults with fibromyalgia found a pooled prevalence of about 45% for abnormally low epidermal neurite density, similar to the prevalence found in this juvenile cohort.
Adolescents with FM reported greater functional disability, dysautonomia symptoms, and pain compared to healthy controls on validated questionnaires.

Schizophrenia patients with higher physiosomatic (FF) symptom scores showed greater psychosis, hostility, excitement, formal thought disorder, psychomotor retardation, and negative symptoms compared with those with lower FF scores.
Plasma IL-6 was positively associated with the FF (physiosomatic) score in schizophrenia patients, contributing to a regression model explaining 55.1% of its variance.
Plasma IL-10 was inversely associated with the FF (physiosomatic) score, suggesting lowered immune regulation contributes to physiosomatic symptoms.
Poorer performance on digit sequencing, token motor and list learning tasks was inversely associated with higher FF physiosomatic symptom scores.
Older age was inversely associated with the FF physiosomatic symptom score in the regression model.
HMGB1 was among the top predictors (ranked highest along with IL-6) of the FF physiosomatic symptom score in a neural network analysis.
Plasma IL-6 was positively and independently associated with the fibromyalgia/chronic fatigue (FF) symptom score in schizophrenia patients.
Plasma IL-10 was inversely and independently associated with the FF symptom score, suggesting lowered immune regulation contributes to physiosomatic symptoms.
Poorer performance on digit sequencing, token motor and list learning cognitive tasks was inversely associated with higher FF (fibromyalgia/chronic fatigue) symptom scores.
Older age was inversely associated with FF symptom scores in the regression model.

HMGB1 was identified as the top or second-ranked predictor of FF symptom score in neural network analysis and also contributed to a latent vector combining cognitive, schizophrenia symptom, and FF measures.
MOR was among the top predictors of FF symptom score in neural network analysis and also contributed to the latent vector combining cognitive, symptom, and FF measures.
KOR was among the top-6 predictors of FF symptom score in neural network analysis.

Schizophrenia patients with higher Fibromyalgia and Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (FF) rating scores showed more severe psychosis, hostility, excitement, formal thought disorder, psychomotor retardation and negative symptoms than patients with lower FF scores.
β-endorphin, one of the endogenous opioid system markers measured, was not among the significant predictors of the FF score or the latent physiosomatic-symptom vector reported in the models.

The authors conclude that neurotoxic immune pathways together with lowered immune regulation and alterations in the endogenous opioid system appear to drive the physiosomatic (fibromyalgia/chronic-fatigue-like) symptoms of schizophrenia.

The paper's overarching conclusion is that chronic-fatigue/fibromyalgia-like physiosomatic symptoms, as measured by the FF scale, are an integral component of the schizophrenia phenome rather than an incidental comorbidity.
Intramuscular pressure measured in the trapezius muscle was nearly three times higher in fibromyalgia patients compared to patients with other rheumatic diseases.
Patients with fibromyalgia showed significantly greater tenderness on dolorimetry testing compared to rheumatic disease controls.
Patients with fibromyalgia showed significantly greater tenderness on digital palpation compared to rheumatic disease controls.
Patients with fibromyalgia reported significantly higher pain scores than rheumatic disease controls.
In fibromyalgia, both aerobic and strengthening exercise were similarly effective and superior to stretching alone for pain management.
For chronic whiplash-associated disorders, body awareness exercises had similar effects to combined exercises, and adding sling exercises to a strengthening program made no difference.
For chronic idiopathic neck pain, motor control exercises and nonspecific muscle strengthening had similar effects.

The authors conclude that global, low-to-moderate intensity exercise programs sustained over longer periods should be prioritized for nociplastic pain conditions such as fibromyalgia and CWAD, whereas more specific, focused, and intense short-duration exercises are better suited to nociceptive pain conditions like CINP.
TPSAB1 copy number gains consistent with hereditary alpha-tryptasemia were significantly more common in mastocytosis patients than in sex-matched controls.
Mastocytosis patients with hereditary alpha-tryptasemia had significantly higher basal serum tryptase levels than those without it, independent of mast cell burden.
Hymenoptera venom hypersensitivity reactions were more frequently observed in mastocytosis patients with hereditary alpha-tryptasemia than in those without it.
Severe cardiovascular mediator-related symptoms and anaphylaxis occurred more frequently in mastocytosis patients with hereditary alpha-tryptasemia than in those without it.
Findings on the association between HαT and severe mediator-related symptoms in mastocytosis were confirmed in an independent validation cohort of 61 additional patients.

In a cigarette-smoke-induced COPD model, therapeutic anti-Siglec-8 antibody significantly reduced total leukocytes, neutrophils, and lymphocytes in bronchoalveolar lavage compared to isotype control-treated mice.
Anti-Siglec-8 treatment significantly reduced smoke-induced elevations of the chemokines CXCL1 and CCL2 in BAL fluid compared to isotype control.
Anti-Siglec-8 treatment significantly reduced the number of total and degranulating lung mast cells increased by chronic cigarette smoke exposure.
Serum MCPT1, elevated by chronic smoke exposure, was significantly decreased with anti-Siglec-8 treatment.
Anti-Siglec-8 treatment significantly reduced histopathologic airway, parenchymal, and vascular inflammation scores caused by chronic smoke exposure.
Anti-Siglec-8 treatment improved smoke-induced changes in lung function, reducing total lung capacity and improving tissue elastance and FEV100/FVC ratio.
A single dose of anti-Siglec-8 given during acute bleomycin-induced lung injury significantly suppressed infiltration of neutrophils, monocytes, and macrophages into BAL fluid.
Anti-Siglec-8 significantly decreased BLM-induced IL-6, CXCL1, and IP-10 levels in BAL fluid.
Anti-Siglec-8 treatment reduced acute BLM-induced lung fibrosis, as measured by Ashcroft score, and lowered BAL collagen and TGFβ levels.
Anti-Siglec-8 treatment decreased lung mast cell numbers, activation state (CD63+), and MCPT1/MCPT4 protease levels in the acute BLM lung injury model.
In a chronic subcutaneous bleomycin model, anti-Siglec-8 treatment reduced BAL neutrophils and macrophages and reduced lung fibrosis by histology, Ashcroft score, and hydroxyproline levels.
Intraperitoneal IL-33 administration dose-dependently induced neutrophil, eosinophil, and monocyte influx into the peritoneal cavity without changing mast cell numbers.

Pre-dosing with anti-Siglec-8 significantly reduced IL-33-induced peritoneal neutrophil, monocyte, and eosinophil infiltration without reducing mast cell numbers, indicating an inhibitory rather than depleting mechanism.
Depletion of eosinophils with anti-CCR3 antibody did not reduce IL-33-induced neutrophil influx, indicating eosinophils are not required for this response.

Anti-Siglec-8 treatment significantly decreased IL-33-induced peritoneal cytokines and chemokines associated with neutrophil, monocyte, and eosinophil infiltration, including IL-6, CCL2, CXCL2, CXCL1, TNF, IL-13, CCL3, and CCL4.
Anti-Siglec-8 treatment significantly reduced IL-33-induced systemic serum levels of CCL2 and CXCL1.

RNA-seq of FACS-sorted peritoneal mast cells showed that IL-33 administration significantly changed the mast cell transcriptome, enriching pathways including mTORC signaling, TNF/NF-κB signaling, unfolded protein response, and IL-6/STAT3 signaling.

Anti-Siglec-8 treatment significantly modulated 498 IL-33-induced mast cell genes including Hdc, Tnf, Slc6a19, Nfkb1, Il1f9, and Tpsab1, downregulating pathways such as unfolded protein response, TNF/NF-κB, mTORC1, IL-2/STAT5, and PI3K/AKT signaling.

In non-activated (no IL-33) mast cells, anti-Siglec-8 treatment alone increased expression of genes associated with inhibitory/TLR-regulatory function, including Tmem176a, Ticam2, Tifab, and Unc93b1, suggesting engagement of additional inhibitory pathways.
In human peripheral blood-derived mast cells expressing Siglec-8, anti-Siglec-8 antibody significantly reduced IgE-pathway (anti-FcεRI-induced) mast cell activation as measured by CD63 expression.

Anti-Siglec-8 treatment of IL-33-activated human peripheral blood-derived mast cells reduced their capacity to induce neutrophil migration and decreased IL-8 levels in supernatant compared to isotype control.
Intramucosal mast cell density in colonic mucosa was similar among IBS, IBD-in-remission, and normal control groups.
Mast cell counts did not significantly differ between IBD patients in remission and IBS patients.
Mast cell counts did not significantly differ between Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis biopsies.
Mast cell counts did not significantly differ between IBS patients with diarrhea and those without diarrhea, indicating no correlation with symptoms.
Biopsies with high mast cell counts (≥20 per HPF) were equally distributed across IBS, IBD, and control disease groups.
CD117 immunohistochemical staining was sensitive for detecting mast cells in colonic mucosa biopsies.
The authors concluded that mast cell count (≥20/HPF) is not a reliable diagnostic criterion for IBS or for distinguishing IBS from IBD in remission.
The purified centipede venom allergen Sco m 5 promoted degranulation of the human mast cell line HMC-1, indicating direct mast cell-activating potential.
Sco m 5 showed an 83.3% IgE-binding frequency among centipede-allergic patients as detected by immunoblotting.
Sco m 5 elicited a 66.7% positive reaction frequency on skin prick testing among centipede-allergic patients.
IgE-binding to Sco m 5 was detected in 9%-16% of the general Chinese population, suggesting substantial background sensitization potential.
Sera positive for Sco m 5 IgE-binding showed cross-reactivity against venom from the wasp Vespa mandarinia, suggesting shared or similar allergenic epitopes between centipede and wasp venoms.
The incidence of maternal cardiac arrest in Maryland from 2013-2017 was estimated at 10 per 100,000 deliveries, comparable to prior US national estimates.
Maternal cardiac arrest incidence was significantly higher among non-Caucasian patients compared to Caucasian patients in Maryland.
Hemorrhage was the most common apparent cause of maternal cardiac arrest in this Maryland cohort.
Maternal survival following maternal cardiac arrest was 59.4%, while fetal survival was much higher at 93.8%.
No significant differences in maternal cardiac arrest incidence were observed across maternal age groups.
There is substantial heterogeneity in the diagnostic criteria used across studies for idiopathic small fiber neuropathy (iSFN).
The most common diagnostic criteria set for iSFN (any iSFN symptoms, absence of large fiber involvement, and reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density) was used in only 14% of studies.
Any sensory symptoms were required as a mandatory diagnostic criterion for iSFN in 60% of the reviewed studies.
Pain was required as a mandatory diagnostic criterion for iSFN in 19% of the reviewed studies.
Small fiber signs were required as a mandatory diagnostic criterion for iSFN in 20% of the reviewed studies.
Absence of large fiber signs was required as a mandatory diagnostic criterion for iSFN in 62% of the reviewed studies.
Reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD) was required as a mandatory diagnostic criterion for iSFN in 38% of the reviewed studies.
Autonomic symptoms were rarely required as a mandatory diagnostic criterion for iSFN, appearing in only 1% of the reviewed studies.

Across the reviewed literature, there was substantial heterogeneity in the diagnostic criteria used to define idiopathic small fiber neuropathy, with no single standardized approach being predominant.

MR neurography-detected T2-weighted hyperintense lesion load in the sciatic/tibial nerve increased with diabetic polyneuropathy severity, with the highest burden at the mid-thigh sciatic nerve and a proximal-to-distal gradient.
Both T2-weighted hyperintense and hypointense sciatic nerve lesions on MR neurography increased with diabetic polyneuropathy in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes patients.

T2-weighted hypointense sciatic nerve lesions were more prevalent in type 2 diabetes patients than in type 1 diabetes patients, suggesting a possible etiological difference (dyslipidemia vs glycemic control) between the two types.
T2-weighted hyperintense sciatic nerve lesions on MR neurography were associated with nerve conduction function and glycated hemoglobin levels.
T2-weighted hypointense sciatic nerve lesions correlated positively with triglyceride levels and negatively with high-density lipoprotein cholesterol.

T2-weighted hyperintense lesion load in the sciatic nerve was significantly associated with decreased Aα-, Aβ- and Aδ-fiber function but not C-fiber function in type 2 diabetes patients versus healthy controls.
T2-weighted hypointense sciatic nerve lesions were negatively correlated with mechanical detection threshold, peroneal nerve conduction velocity and amplitude.
Quantification of intra-epidermal nerve fiber density by PGP9.5 immunostaining of skin biopsy samples is established as a reliable method for diagnosing diabetic small-fiber neuropathy.
Corneal confocal microscopy-measured corneal nerve fiber length and density are reported as a reliable marker of diabetic small-fiber neuropathy.
MR neurography of diabetic polyneuropathy shows large overlap between patients and healthy controls, making it difficult to distinguish normal from abnormal nerve findings.

Neurodegeneration from uncontrolled diabetes might promote progression from diabetic small-fiber neuropathy to diabetic sensory neuropathy (large-fiber involvement), though it is unclear whether this progression is consistent.
Intraepidermal nerve fiber density measured using PGP9.5 did not differ between DPN patients with pain and those without pain.

Patients with painful diabetic polyneuropathy showed increased density of dermal peptidergic nerve fibers (substance P and CGRP-containing) compared with patients with painless DPN and healthy controls.
Peptidergic nerve fiber density correlated with pain intensity ratings in patients with painful diabetic polyneuropathy.
Peptidergic nerve fiber density did not correlate with quantitative sensory testing (QST) results.
GCSI symptom scores improved from baseline in both periods but did not differ significantly between prucalopride and placebo treatment arms.
Meal-related symptom scores (MRSS), both over time and cumulatively, were not significantly different between prucalopride and placebo periods.
Gastric emptying was significantly accelerated during the prucalopride treatment period compared to placebo, shown by lower four-hour gastric meal retention.
Weekly bowel movement frequency was significantly higher during prucalopride treatment than during placebo.
Patients reported a higher perception of weight loss while on prucalopride compared to placebo.
Restricting analysis to only the diabetic gastroparesis subgroup (n=13) did not change the overall study conclusions.
Injection of mast cells into mice induced cholestatic-like liver injury with increased ductular reaction, fibrosis, and TGF-β1 secretion.
Injecting mast cells pretreated with a TGF-β1 receptor inhibitor (TGF-βRi, LY2109761) reversed the increased ductular reaction, fibrosis, and angiogenesis caused by mast cell injection.
Mast cell-conditioned medium induced cholangiocyte (biliary) proliferation and senescence in vitro.
Mast cell-conditioned medium activated hepatic stellate cells (HSCs), increasing markers of activation including α-SMA, SYP-9, and collagen type-1a expression.
Mast cell injection increased markers of angiogenesis, including von Willebrand factor and VEGF-C expression, in the liver.

The nodose ganglia contained the most abundant population of purely nNOS-immunoreactive neuronal somata among all examined structures, suggesting a role for neuronal NO in cardiac afferent innervation.
