All nitrergic neuronal somata in the nucleus ambiguus co-expressed choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) and represented only a small subset (6%) of neurons in this nucleus.
In the dorsal nucleus of the vagal nerve, biphenotypic nNOS-IR/ChAT-IR neurons made up 7.0 ± 1.0% of neurons, while purely nNOS-IR small neurons were rare.
Nitrergic neuronal somata were plentifully distributed within the nuclei of the solitary tract, a key visceral afferent relay for cardiac reflexes.
In dorsal root ganglia and stellate ganglia, nitrergic neuronal somata were only sporadically present, indicating a minor sympathetic/somatic sensory contribution to cardiac nitrergic innervation.

The majority of sympathetic neuronal somata in the intermediolateral nucleus of the spinal cord were simultaneously immunoreactive for nNOS and ChAT, implicating nitrergic co-transmission in sympathetic preganglionic cardiac control.

Retrograde tracing with DiI in ex vivo human colon myenteric plexus was used to establish that motor neuron projections rarely exceed 8 mm, allowing long ascending/descending interneurons to be distinguished from motor neurons by projection length.
The most abundant type of long ascending interneuron in human colon myenteric plexus was immunoreactive for both choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) and enkephalin (ENK).
A second type of long ascending interneuron was triple-labeled for ChAT, enkephalin, and substance P (SP).
A third type of long ascending interneuron was double-labeled for ChAT and calbindin.
A fourth type of long ascending interneuron was triple-labeled for ChAT, enkephalin, and calbindin.
One type of long descending interneuron in human colon myenteric plexus was immunoreactive for nitric oxide synthase (NOS) without ChAT co-expression.
A subset of long descending interneurons in human colon myenteric plexus co-expressed choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) and calretinin immunoreactivity.
A further subset of long descending interneurons co-expressed ChAT and 5-hydroxytryptamine (serotonin) immunoreactivity, with or without nitric oxide synthase.
Long ascending and descending interneurons, which do not innervate the muscularis externa, are proposed to coordinate neural activity over distances of many centimeters along the human colon.
Mutations in FBN1 disrupt fibrillin microfibril networks and cause a spectrum of skin phenotypes ranging from thick, fibrotic skin to thin, lax, hyperextensible skin.

Fibrillin-2, along with fibrillin-1, assembles into microfibrils that form supramolecular networks essential for skin homoeostasis, and mutations in FBN2 also contribute to fibrillinopathy skin phenotypes.

Fibrillin microfibrils control the bioavailability of growth factors targeted to the extracellular matrix, providing a mechanistic explanation for the spectrum of fibrotic and lax skin phenotypes seen in fibrillinopathies.
Mutational inactivation of ligands associated with fibrillin microfibrils leads to forms of cutis laxa, distinct from fibrillin-dependent fibrosis.

Flow cytometry identified two distinct pulmonary mast cell populations in naive C57BL/6 mice distinguished by β7 integrin expression and granularity: β7Low (dense, constitutive CTMC-like) and β7High (hypogranular, inducible MMC-like).
Repeated house dust mite (HDM) challenge over 3 weeks caused a fourfold increase in β7High mast cell concentration relative to stromal cells, while β7Low mast cells remained unchanged.
Sensitization and challenge with Alternaria alternata mold extract also selectively expanded β7High mast cells, showing this response generalizes across diverse type 2 inflammatory triggers.

MCpt5/DTA mice, in which Cma1 (mMCP-5)-expressing cells are deleted, lack β7Low CTMCs entirely but retain a small β7High mast cell compartment that still expands normally after Alt challenge, confirming these as distinct lineages.

RNA-seq showed β7Low mast cells were significantly enriched for the connective tissue MC (CTMC) transcriptional signature, including MRGPR family receptors and canonical CTMC proteases mMCP-4, -5, -6, and -11.

β7High mast cells unexpectedly showed significant enrichment for Mcpt8, a protease transcript previously thought to be basophil-specific, without accompanying enrichment of other basophil signature genes, indicating this is genuine mast cell expression rather than basophil contamination.

β7Low mast cells were enriched for heparin sulfate biosynthetic enzymes while β7High mast cells were enriched for chondroitin sulfate synthase (Chsy1), matching CTMC vs MMC granule glycosaminoglycan phenotypes.

β7Low and β7High mast cells expressed divergent receptor repertoires: β7Low enriched for receptors for C3a, IL-6, IL-10, and IL-33, while β7High enriched for LTB4 receptor, GM-CSF/PDGF-B receptors, and the succinate receptor Sucnr1.

Upon HDM challenge, β7High mast cells upregulated 62 genes (and downregulated 9), including cytokines, chemokines, cox-1, and multiple activating receptors, while β7Low mast cells showed minimal transcriptional change.
β7High mast cells significantly upregulated the serotonin biosynthetic enzymes Tph1 and Ddc following HDM challenge, with a trend toward upregulation of the tryptophan transporter Slc7a5.

mMCP-1 protein was significantly upregulated in β7High mast cells following Alternaria challenge (similar trend with HDM), with minimal expression in β7Low mast cells, identifying β7High cells as the dominant pulmonary source of mMCP-1 during inflammation.

Genetic deletion of the constitutive CTMC (β7Low) compartment in MCpt5/DTA mice had no effect on lung CD45+ cell influx, eosinophilia, or serum IgE increases following Alt sensitization/challenge, indicating CTMCs are dispensable for this model of allergic airway inflammation.

β7High mast cells upregulated multiple TGF-β/Smad2/3 target genes (Skil, Ldlrad4, Itgae, Mcpt1, Mcpt2) following HDM challenge, suggesting a TGF-β signaling axis drives the inducible MMC phenotype in vivo.
TGF-β1 and SCF acted synergistically to greatly enhance mMCP-1 and αE integrin protein expression in bone marrow-derived mast cells (BMMCs) in a TGF-β1 dose-dependent manner in vitro.
TGF-β signaling downregulated expression of CTMC-marker MRGPR family genes (Mrgprb1, Mrgprb2, Mrgprx2) in BMMCs in vitro.

SCF-dependent TGF-β1 stimulation recapitulated 21 of the 62 genes upregulated in vivo in HDM-elicited β7High mast cells, and β7High (but not β7Low) MCs from HDM-treated mice were highly significantly enriched for the TGF-β1+SCF BMMC gene signature.

Reclustering of human distal lung scRNA-seq data from healthy donors identified an MCTC cluster (CTSG, CMA1) analogous to mouse β7Low CTMCs and an MCT subcluster enriched for TGF-β signature genes (SKIL, LITAF, SMAD3) and inflammation-associated genes (IL1RL1, PIM2, PRNP), with IL13 detectable only in this cluster, suggesting a conserved TGF-β-driven MMC-like phenotype in human lung mast cells.

Primary airway epithelial cells express TGF-β1 and directly induce mMCP-1 and αE integrin upregulation in cocultured BMMCs; this induction was blocked in a dose-dependent manner by the TGF-βR1/R2 dual inhibitor LY2109761, confirming epithelial TGF-β as a driver of MMC-like mast cell maturation.
Patients diagnosed with EDS reported slightly lower physical health-related quality of life (SF36-PCS) than patients diagnosed with HMS, a small but statistically significant difference.

Aside from SF36-PCS, no statistically significant differences were found between patients coded as EDS versus HMS across pain, distress, and quality-of-life measures, supporting clustering the two groups together for further analysis.
Female sex was disproportionately represented among EDS/HMS and fibromyalgia patients compared to spinal pain and WAD groups.
Patients with EDS/HMS were significantly younger on average than patients with fibromyalgia, spinal pain, or WAD, with a large effect size.
Despite being younger, EDS/HMS patients reported the longest duration of chronic pain among the four diagnostic groups, longer than fibromyalgia, spinal pain, and WAD patients.
EDS/HMS patients showed a spread of pain across body regions nearly as extensive as fibromyalgia patients, and substantially greater than spinal pain or WAD patients.
Both EDS/HMS and fibromyalgia patients reported markedly lower vitality (a proxy for fatigue) than the spinal pain group, with WAD intermediate.
Fibromyalgia patients reported the most severe pain intensity and severity compared to EDS/HMS, spinal pain, and WAD groups, confirming prior research.

Although statistically significant group differences existed for HADS anxiety scores, the magnitude of difference between groups was clinically small, with all groups scoring between possible and probable anxiety case levels.
HADS depression scores showed a similarly small range of clinical difference across the four diagnostic groups.
Fibromyalgia patients scored highest on MPI Interference (pain interference with life), with no significant difference among EDS/HMS, spinal pain, and WAD groups.
Fibromyalgia patients reported the lowest sense of control over their life situation (MPI Control), with EDS/HMS and WAD intermediate and spinal pain patients reporting the most control.
EDS/HMS patients rated their physical health (SF36-PCS) similarly to fibromyalgia patients but significantly worse than spinal pain and WAD patients.

In a multivariate OPLS-DA model, age, pain intensity (NRS-7days and MPI Pain Severity), depressive symptoms, and SF36-MCS significantly differentiated EDS/HMS from fibromyalgia, though the model explained less than 10% of variance.

In a multivariate OPLS-DA model, female gender, age, pain duration, SF36-PCS, and SF36-Vitality significantly differentiated EDS/HMS from spinal pain, with relatively more women, lower age, longer pain duration, and lower vitality/physical health in EDS/HMS.
The strongest multivariate model differentiated EDS/HMS from WAD, with pain duration, female gender, SF36-PCS, and age as significant regressors, though still explaining only 29% of group variance.
The proportion of patients classified as EDS/HMS within the SQRP registry (1.9%) was somewhat smaller than the estimated 3% general population prevalence.

The current cohort's EDS/HMS vitality (fatigue proxy) scores were lower than those reported by members of the Swedish National EDS Association, likely reflecting selection of more severe cases referred to specialist clinics.
An analysis of US health insurance claims data reported a high narrow-sense heritability estimate for CFS.
An analysis of UK Biobank participants self-reporting a CFS diagnosis found a modest SNP-based heritability estimate with low confidence.
A large twin-based study of CFS-like cases produced an inconclusive heritability estimate, with the 95% confidence interval including zero.

Individuals with a CFS diagnosis show significant excess relatedness compared to the wider population for both close (first/second-degree) and distant (third-degree) relatives, supporting a heritable component.
Independent studies confirm that clinically proven mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) variants do not commonly explain ME/CFS.
People with ME/CFS appear more likely to carry mtDNA that lacks even mildly deleterious variants, a finding requiring further investigation.
The HLA-C*07:04 allele, carried by ~10% of ME/CFS individuals, was found to be significantly associated with ME/CFS status and alters risk by ~1.5-2.0-fold.
The HLA-DQB1*03:03 allele, carried by ~10% of ME/CFS individuals, was found to be significantly associated with ME/CFS status and alters risk by ~1.5-2.0-fold.
The UK Biobank contains 1829 participants (~0.45% of the cohort) who self-reported a clinical CFS diagnosis, with prevalence of 0.61% in females and 0.26% in males, consistent with known female bias.
Five independent GWAS analyses of the same UK Biobank CFS dataset failed to reach consensus, with not a single associated DNA variant replicated across multiple analyses.

The rs7337312 variant, identified in a female-only UK Biobank CFS GWAS, lies within a 51 kb region containing SLC25A15 and predicts SLC25A15 mRNA expression, suggesting SLC25A15 could be a causal gene for altered CFS risk.

A person carrying the rs7337312 CFS risk allele is predicted to have reduced SLC25A15-mediated mitochondrial ornithine transport, resulting in higher blood ornithine, a prediction partly supported by Yamano et al. and Naviaux et al. but not Armstrong et al.
The variant rs148723539, one of the highlighted GWAS hits in UK Biobank CFS studies, is a multi-allelic site likely reflecting a technical genotyping artefact rather than a true association.
TCOF1 showed a greater number of copy number variants (gains or losses) in UK Biobank CFS cases compared with controls after multiple-testing correction.
THUMPD2 showed a greater number of copy number variants (gains or losses) in UK Biobank CFS cases compared with controls after multiple-testing correction.
A small GWAS (40 cases, 40 controls) reported 65 variants associated with CFS at a highly permissive threshold, but none remained significant at the standard genome-wide threshold.
A small GWAS (42 cases, 38 controls) reported 299 variants at a permissive threshold and 15 genome-wide significant variants, none of which were replicated in the UK Biobank cohort.

A study of 383 self-reported ME/CFS cases (Fukuda criteria) restricted to gene-disrupting variants reported 5693 DNA variants at 2-fold different frequency between cases and controls, using non-standard frequency thresholds.

A candidate gene study of nine NR3C1 variants in 40 CFS cases and 42 controls found four variants nominally significant, but none survived Bonferroni correction, and none replicated in the UK Biobank CFS cohort.

Testing genetic associations from 11 prior CFS studies (from a systematic review of 16 studies, 2003-2015) for replication in the UK Biobank CFS cohort yielded a P-value distribution showing no skew toward small values, indicating no evidence of replication.

Replication P-values for 77 DNA variants from Marshall-Gradisnik et al. and 23 from Schlauch et al. showed a similar lack of skew toward small values when tested in the UK Biobank CFS cohort, further indicating no replication.
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is described as a significant challenge to managing joint instability, with the hip being particularly affected.
Ligamentum teres tears of the hip have been found to be more common than previously thought, though their clinical significance remains poorly understood.

In patients with both Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and ligamentum teres tears, surgical reconstruction combined with capsular plication achieved moderate success, though outcomes were not favorable in all cases.
Families described paediatric ME/CFS as a persistent and disabling condition that impacted mobility, hobbies, schooling and social activities.
Reported symptoms in this younger cohort included severe fatigue, weakness, unrefreshing sleep, digestive symptoms resembling IBS, joint and muscle pain, sore throats and headaches.
Parents reported post-exertional malaise, describing children becoming severely incapacitated days after physical exertion.
Families reported emotional difficulties, such as crying and hyperventilation, secondary to the physical disability of ME/CFS.
Some parents felt the specialist CFS/ME service under-addressed co-morbid anxiety and low mood, wanting more psychological support.

Parents commonly attributed illness onset to a viral trigger combined with psychosocial stressors, immune dysfunction and gut health, though this was a lay causal theory rather than a tested mechanism.

Children aged 5-7 (KS1) struggled to engage in and understand clinical consultations and to verbally report their symptoms, compared with children aged 8-11 (KS2) who were more active participants and gave richer symptom accounts.
Parents of KS1 (5-7 year old) children felt that medical terminology such as 'chronic fatigue syndrome' or 'myalgic encephalomyelitis' and standard treatment resources were not age-appropriate.

Only a minority of KS2 (8-11 year old) children reported independently using self-management strategies such as relaxation apps, identifying low-energy activities, and visual timer/card systems to regulate activity.

Families found it challenging or impossible to monitor and restrict a child's activity via activity diaries, frequently abandoning them, and instead made broader lifestyle adjustments such as 'pyjama days'.
Parents/carers reported feeling isolated, unsupported and disbelieved during the diagnostic and referral process, but valued the specialist service for validation and reduced isolation.
The authors suggest that parent/carer-only clinical sessions may be beneficial for children aged seven and under, based on observed limited engagement of this age group in consultations.

The authors propose that body mapping, emoji cards and card-sorting arts-based tools may effectively help children over eight describe their ME/CFS experience, based on their use in this study's interviews.

The authors suggest wearable technology could be integrated into paediatric CFS/ME interventions to support self-monitoring of activity/sleep, though no such intervention currently exists for this condition and none was tested in this study.

The paper cites prior epidemiological data (Collin et al., 2015) that the gender split in CFS/ME is more balanced in younger children than adolescents (57% vs 74% female), and that younger children less often report cognitive dysfunction, sleep problems or headaches but more often present with sore throats, tender lymph nodes and dizziness.
A cited review found that full recovery from CFS/ME is uncommon in adults, with an average of only 5% of patients reaching this status.
The same review found that symptomatic improvement (short of full recovery) is more common, reported in 8% to 63% of patients across studies.
CFS/ME is estimated to affect around 0.76% of the population.
Undertaking treatments such as cognitive behavior therapy or graded exercise therapy is reported to improve chances of recovery from CFS/ME.

Participants' definitions of 'recovery' varied widely, from being fully symptom-free ('100%') and able to do everything healthy people could do, to more relative or partial notions of recovery involving symptom management and lifestyle adaptation.

Some participants considered themselves 'recovered' despite ongoing symptoms, defining recovery as resumption of societal roles (e.g., paid employment, daily activities) and effective symptom self-management rather than complete symptom freedom, consistent with 'leaving the sick role' rather than freedom from illness.

Longer illness duration (many participants ill more than 10 years), advancing age, comorbid conditions, negative feedback from health professionals, lack of treatment options, and past unsuccessful treatments were associated with participants viewing full recovery as unlikely.

Postexertional malaise, a characteristic and unpredictable symptom of CFS/ME not relieved by rest, may drive a 'boom and bust' cycle in which patients overexert when feeling well, leading to worsened symptoms, and may complicate efforts to leave the sick role behind through unhelpful management approaches.

One participant described rejecting the CFS/ME label due to associated stigma and disbelief (including from family), defining herself as 'not' having ME despite managing ongoing symptoms, illustrating how stigma affects adoption of illness identity/sick role.

Some participants redefined 'recovery' as achieving more modest, obtainable goals (e.g., regaining part-time functionality, more typical post-exertion recovery time, distinguishing 'normal tired' from 'ME tired') rather than a full return to pre-illness health, consistent with prior findings (Brown et al., 2017) that even self-reported 'recovered' patients continue to manage symptoms via pacing and rest.
The primary outcome, the proportion of patients with a CIS score of 76 or higher after 8 weeks, did not significantly differ between the SJDBT and placebo groups.
The mean change in CIS scores did not significantly differ between the SJDBT and placebo groups after 8 weeks.
Overall fatigue severity measured by VAS decreased significantly more in the SJDBT group than in the placebo group at 8 weeks.
VAS score for post-exertional malaise significantly decreased in the SJDBT group compared to placebo at week 8.
VAS score for unrefreshing sleep significantly decreased in the SJDBT group compared to placebo at week 8.
VAS score for muscle pain significantly decreased in the SJDBT group compared to placebo at week 8.
The mean change in Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS) score differed significantly between SJDBT and placebo groups at the treatment endpoint, favoring SJDBT.
Chalder Fatigue scale (ChFi) scores decreased by a significantly greater extent in the SJDBT group than in the placebo group at week 8.
Quality of life measured by EQ-5D-5L showed no significant difference between SJDBT and placebo groups after 8 weeks.
Subjective happiness level (VAS) showed no significant difference between SJDBT and placebo groups after 8 weeks.
Sleep quality measured by PSQI-K showed no significant difference between SJDBT and placebo groups after 8 weeks.
Qi deficiency scores (QBYY-Q) improved significantly more in the SJDBT group than in the placebo group at the treatment endpoint.
Blood, yin, and yang deficiency scores (QBYY-Q subscales) did not change significantly after 8 weeks of SJDBT administration compared with placebo.
Adverse events did not significantly differ between the SJDBT and placebo groups, and all reported AEs were mild and judged unrelated to the study drug.
Vital signs, HRV parameters, and laboratory test results showed no significant differences between SJDBT and placebo groups, and any significant within-group changes remained within normal ranges.

A cited case-control cerebrospinal fluid study found decreased IL-12 p40 levels among cytokines differing between CFS patients and healthy subjects, supporting an immune dysfunction hypothesis in CFS pathogenesis.
An in vitro study cited in the discussion showed that SJDBT enhanced immunity by augmenting the production of IL-12 p40, offering a proposed mechanistic link to its potential clinical effects.
Chronic fatigue syndrome reduced the number of blastocyst implantation sites in pregnant mice compared to non-CFS pregnant mice.
CFS increased the incidence of absorbed, stillborn, and malformed fetuses in pregnant mice.
The morphology and structure of the placenta were abnormal in pregnant mice with CFS compared to controls.
Oxidative stress markers were increased in the serum, uterus, and placenta of pregnant mice with CFS compared to controls.
Levels of antioxidase (antioxidant enzymes) were decreased in pregnant mice with CFS relative to controls.
CFS inhibited the Wnt/β-catenin signalling pathway in the placenta of pregnant mice compared to controls.
The authors propose that inhibition of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway together with enhanced oxidative stress mechanistically drives abnormal placentation in CFS pregnant mice.
Cartilage defects on hip MRI were much less prevalent in hypermobile (GJH) dancers compared to non-GJH dancers at baseline.
Lower Beighton scores (less hypermobility, <5/9) were predictive of the presence of cartilage defects at baseline, independent of age and sex.
Hip pain scores (HAGOS) at baseline and follow-up were similar between hypermobile and non-hypermobile dancers.
Hip-related injury incidence over 5 years was similar between hypermobile and non-hypermobile dancers.
Hypermobility was more prevalent among dancers who remained active than those who retired over the 5-year period, independent of age, rank, and sex.
None of the 12 dancers who retired by follow-up did so because of hip injury or joint hypermobility.
The title indicates that medical therapy has an effect on the arteriopathy seen in vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, but no further detail is provided in the given text.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is a rare monogenic disease caused by pathogenic variants in procollagen 3A1 (COL3A1), and all 40 patients in this cohort carried pathogenic COL3A1 sequence variants.
Of 38 patients undergoing dose uptitration, 26 (65%) successfully reached the target celiprolol dose of 400 mg daily.

The annual risk of a major vascular event on celiprolol was 4.7% (5/106 patient-years), similar to the celiprolol treatment arm of the BBEST trial (5%) and lower than the control arm of that trial (12%).
Logistic regression analysis did not identify any significant predictor of vascular events among the patients in this cohort.
Whole-exome sequencing identified a COL5A1 missense variant c.1588G>A (p.Gly530Ser) in the proband, present in trans with a second COL5A1 variant, and inherited from one parent.
A second COL5A1 missense variant, c.4135C>T (p.Pro1379Ser), was identified in trans with c.1588G>A in the proband, inherited from the other parent.
Functional assays showed a significant decrease in collagen α1(V) chain expression in cells from both heterozygous parents compared with control cells.
The two COL5A1 variants had an additive effect in the proband, further lowering collagen α1(V) chain expression compared to either parent alone.
Both heterozygous parents manifested very subtle EDS signs including atrophic scars, recurrent bone fractures, colonic diverticulosis, varicose veins, and osteoarthritis.

The c.1588G>A COL5A1 variant, previously reported both as 'disease modifying' and as a biallelic causative mutation with subtle heterozygous cEDS signs, is proposed to have variable functional significance depending on additional genetic hits.
Across the fibromyalgia cohort as a whole, corneal nerve density did not significantly correlate with any of the symptom severity questionnaires assessed.
In fibromyalgia patients without severe anxiety or depression (n=13), lower corneal nerve density was strongly correlated with higher Small-Fiber Symptom Survey scores.
In the same non-severe anxiety/depression subgroup (n=13), lower corneal nerve density was strongly correlated with higher COMPASS-31 (autonomic symptom) scores.

Fibromyalgia patients with severe anxiety or depression (n=15) reported more intense symptoms but showed no correlation between corneal nerve density and symptom scores, suggesting anxiety/depression confounds the clinical-pathological relationship.
Small fiber neuropathy can present without a length-dependent pattern and is sometimes mistaken for fibromyalgia or complex regional pain syndrome.
New testing methods, including autonomic function tests and skin punch biopsy, have emerged to improve diagnosis of small fiber neuropathy.
New treatments have recently become available for TTR amyloid neuropathy, a cause of small fiber neuropathy.
New treatments have recently become available for Fabry disease, a genetic cause of small fiber neuropathy.
Ongoing clinical trials are evaluating the efficacy of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) for inflammatory small fiber neuropathy syndromes.
Seven of 11 IC/BPS patients (63.6%) had reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density consistent with small fiber polyneuropathy.
Small fiber polyneuropathy was significantly more prevalent in non-bladder-centric IC/BPS patients (85.7%) than bladder-centric patients (25.0%).
Non-bladder-centric IC/BPS patients reported significantly more overall comorbid nonurologic syndromes than bladder-centric patients.
Fibromyalgia was significantly more prevalent among non-bladder-centric IC/BPS patients compared with bladder-centric patients.
Migraine was significantly more prevalent among non-bladder-centric IC/BPS patients compared with bladder-centric patients.
Anxiety/panic disorder was significantly more prevalent among non-bladder-centric IC/BPS patients compared with bladder-centric patients.
Allergies were significantly more prevalent among non-bladder-centric IC/BPS patients compared with bladder-centric patients.
Asthma was significantly more prevalent among non-bladder-centric IC/BPS patients compared with bladder-centric patients.
At 12 weeks post-treatment, PENFS plus standard therapy showed a nonsignificant trend toward improved pain scores compared with standard therapy alone.
PENFS treatment significantly improved pain interference with sleep at 12 weeks compared with standard therapy controls.

Following PENFS treatment, resting-state functional connectivity MRI seeded at the right posterior insula showed increased connectivity to cerebellar and executive control network regions compared with the standard therapy control group.

Pain and functional outcomes correlated with altered resting-state functional connectivity MRI network connectivity, and neuroimaging results differed between groups, suggesting an alternative underlying mechanism for PENFS analgesia.
Patients with fibromyalgia reported a significant reduction in average pain intensity on a 10-point numeric pain scale when exposed to green light-emitting diodes but not white light-emitting diodes.
Quality of life as measured by the EQ-5D-5L survey was significantly improved in fibromyalgia patients exposed to GLED compared to white light exposure.
Pain as measured by the Short-Form McGill Pain Questionnaire was significantly improved in fibromyalgia patients exposed to GLED.
Fibromyalgia-related functional impact, as measured by the Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire, was significantly improved in patients exposed to GLED.
GLED therapy was not associated with any measured adverse side effects in fibromyalgia patients over the 10-week exposure period.
Higher pain catastrophizing scores were positively correlated with greater pain widespreadness across the body in fibromyalgia patients.
Whole-brain regression showed that pain widespreadness was positively associated with resting salience network connectivity to the posterior cingulate cortex, a default mode network node.
SLN-posterior cingulate cortex connectivity statistically mediated the relationship between pain catastrophizing and pain widespreadness in fibromyalgia patients.
Fibromyalgia patients showed moderately high pain widespreadness, most frequently in the spinal region from the lower back to the neck, averaging 26.1% of total body area.

Across chronic fatigue syndrome, irritable bowel syndrome, and fibromyalgia patients combined, RMSSD (a time-domain HRV index of parasympathetic activity) was significantly lower than in healthy controls.

Across chronic fatigue syndrome, irritable bowel syndrome, and fibromyalgia patients combined, high-frequency HRV (HF-HRV), a marker of parasympathetic activity, was significantly lower than in healthy controls.

Meta-regression showed that sample age and publication year accounted for substantial heterogeneity in RMSSD effect sizes, whereas statistical adjustment for confounders accounted for heterogeneity in HF-HRV effect sizes across studies.
Resting-state EEG in FMS participants showed increased slow-rhythm (theta) power over fronto-central cortical regions compared to healthy controls in the majority of the sample.
Alpha1 band relative power increased at the end of the stimulation cycle after beta-tACS compared to random noise stimulation over bilateral M1.
Pain intensity (VAS) significantly decreased from baseline to end of stimulation cycle after tACS, in 9 of 14 participants.
Pain did not significantly decrease after random noise stimulation (sham) between baseline and end of cycle, nor between end of cycle and follow-up.
Depressive symptoms (BDI-II) significantly decreased after tACS both at end of stimulation cycle and after the 4-week wash-out, and after RNS in the short term.
The BSI Global Severity Index, reflecting overall perceived psychopathology, significantly decreased after both tACS and RNS between baseline and end of cycle.
Self-reported cognitive skill loss (PROCOG-P subitem) improved after tACS between baseline and 4-week follow-up.
Everyday memory functioning (EMQ-R) was significantly better in the tACS condition compared to RNS at end of stimulation cycle.
MoCA global cognitive scores significantly improved after tACS both at end of stimulation cycle and after wash-out.
Trail Making Test A speed significantly increased in the RNS group between baseline and follow-up.
Trail Making Test B completion time significantly decreased (improved) in the tACS group between baseline and follow-up, reflecting better divided attention/set-shifting.
Phonemic verbal fluency total scores increased and errors decreased in the tACS group between baseline and follow-up; RNS group also improved between end of cycle and follow-up.

Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure copy time-score improved after tACS at both cycle end and follow-up, and after RNS at follow-up.
Several SF-36 health-related quality of life subitems (functionality, energy, social activity, pain) improved after both tACS and RNS combined with physiotherapy.
A phased carboplatin desensitization protocol allowed the patient with idiopathic MCAS to receive chemotherapy without hypersensitivity complications in the first cycle.

During the final chemotherapy cycle the patient developed a minor hypersensitivity reaction (flushing, back pain) during paclitaxel infusion, which resolved with treatment and allowed completion of infusion at a slower rate.
Registry studies have found significantly increased prevalence of melanoma and cancers of the breast, ovary, cervix uteri, thyroid and lung in patients with MCAS.
Systemic mast cell activation diseases such as systemic mastocytosis are associated with an increased risk of solid cancers including melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancers.
Paclitaxel is associated with a higher incidence of hypersensitivity reactions (8-45%), typically immediate (within 10 minutes), with only 1.3% classified as severe (grade 3/4).
Carboplatin hypersensitivity incidence is low (<1%) up to 6 cycles but rises sharply to 27% beyond 6 cycles, with half of those reactions being moderate or severe.
Concomitant administration of carboplatin and paclitaxel is associated with a higher hypersensitivity risk than alternative carboplatin combination regimens.
In primary MCAS, mutations in the tyrosine kinase receptor KIT result in monoclonal mast cell proliferation.
Chemotherapeutic agents including carboplatin and paclitaxel are known potent mast cell stimulators requiring careful consideration before administration.

Patients with pre-existing hypersensitivity disorders, including mast cell disorders, are predisposed to more severe hypersensitivity reactions to chemotherapy that are less responsive to pre-medication and treatment strategies.
Treatment with mepolizumab (anti-IL-5) reduced serum tryptase levels and improved clinical symptoms in a patient with eosinophilic asthma and idiopathic mast cell activation.
The paper proposes an interaction between eosinophils and mast cells as a contributing mechanism in a patient with concurrent eosinophilic asthma and mast cell activation disease.

MRGPRX2, a mast cell receptor (with mouse orthologue MRGPRB2), mediates mast cell degranulation upon binding a broad range of cationic molecules including neuropeptides, quorum-sensing molecules, venom peptides, host defense peptides, and some FDA-approved drugs.

Upon MRGPRX2 activation, mast cells release granule-associated proteases, lipids, and cytokines that can modulate vascular permeability, immune cell recruitment, and activation of tissue-projecting nociceptive sensory neurons.

The authors propose MRGPRX2-dependent skin mast cell activation as a mechanism underlying pruritus, pain, and inflammation, and suggest it as a potential therapeutic target for inflammatory pain, itch, atopic dermatitis, and drug-induced injection site reactions.
Multivalent antigen-induced aggregation of FcεRI rapidly depolymerized actin filaments in mast cells.
Disaggregation of FcεRI by monomer hapten rapidly restored actin polymerization following antigen-induced depolymerization.
Cofilin, an actin-severing protein, was transiently dephosphorylated several minutes after multivalent antigen stimulation of mast cells.
Addition of monomer hapten rapidly increased cofilin phosphorylation within 30 seconds, coinciding with actin re-polymerization.

Removal of extracellular Ca2+, instead of monomer hapten addition, did not restore cofilin phosphorylation, indicating that the decrease in intracellular Ca2+ was not the critical driver of actin rearrangement.

In mast cells pretreated with jasplakinolide (an actin depolymerization inhibitor), monovalent hapten did not completely reduce intracellular Ca2+, linking actin depolymerization state to Ca2+ signaling regulation.
Response to intramuscular epinephrine in treating anaphylactic uterine contractions was inconsistent across reported cases.
A small number of reported cases showed good response of anaphylactic uterine contractions to beta-2 agonist treatment.
Pretreatment with antihistamines generally failed to prevent recurrence of anaphylactic uterine contractions.
Pretreatment with montelukast generally failed to prevent recurrence of anaphylactic uterine contractions.
NSAIDs were used successfully in some reports to prevent or treat anaphylactic uterine contractions.
Subcutaneous immunotherapy was the most frequent trigger of anaphylaxis-associated painful uterine contractions, followed by food and drugs.

Mast cell degranulation induced by compound 48/80 enhanced the dose-dependent vasopressor response to big ET-1 in wild-type mice but not in mMCP-4 knockout mice, in a chymase inhibitor-sensitive manner.
Mast cell stabilization with cromolyn repressed the vasopressor response to big ET-1 in wild-type mice but not in mMCP-4 knockout mice.
mMCP-4-dependent hydrolysis of a fluorogenic chymase substrate was depleted in peritoneal mast cells isolated from mice pretreated with the mast cell degranulator C48/80.
mMCP-4-dependent hydrolysis of the same fluorogenic substrate was enhanced in peritoneal mast cells from mice pretreated with the mast cell stabilizer cromolyn.
C48/80-induced mast cell degranulation markedly increased conversion of exogenous big ET-1 to ET-1(1-31) in vitro using WT peritoneal fluid-isolated mast cells.
Cromolyn abolished ET-1(1-31) conversion from exogenous big ET-1 in vitro in WT peritoneal mast cells.
Vasopressor responses to angiotensin I were unaffected by mast cell activation (C48/80) or stabilization (cromolyn), in contrast to big ET-1 responses.
Cromolyn pretreatment abolished conversion of exogenous big ET-1 to ET-1(1-31) in mast cells isolated from mouse peritoneal fluid in vitro.
Vasopressor responses to angiotensin I were unaffected by mast cell activation (C48/80) or stabilization (cromolyn) in mice, in contrast to big ET-1 responses.
Vasopressor responses to the ACE-resistant angiotensin I analog [Pro11, D-Ala12] Ang I were potentiated by mast cell degranulation with C48/80, unlike native Ang I.

A fluorescent NPY-mRFP reporter construct can be co-transfected with a gene of interest into mast cells to selectively track regulated exocytosis of transfected cells, overcoming low transfection efficiency and high signal-to-noise limitations of bulk secretion assays.

Acid challenge of duodenal biopsy specimens increased mast cell and tryptase-positive cell density in all subjects, with a significantly greater increase in functional dyspepsia patients than controls.
Release of mast cell mediators histamine, NGF, PGD2, and tryptase from duodenal mucosa was significantly increased in FD patients after acid exposure.

Blocking enteric neurotransmission with tetrodotoxin (TTX) significantly inhibited acid-induced mast cell recruitment/activation and mediator release in both FD and control tissue, indicating a neuronally-mediated mechanism.
Acid challenge increased TRPV1 and TRPV4 expression in duodenal mucosa of both FD and control subjects, with a significantly greater increase in FD patients.

Western blot confirmed higher acid-induced TRPV1 and TRPV4 protein expression in FD patients than controls, and immunofluorescence showed this overexpression localized mainly to NeuN-positive nerve fibers.
TTX pretreatment inhibited acid-induced TRPV1 and TRPV4 upregulation, with a more pronounced effect in dyspeptic than control subjects, confirming neuronal mediation.
Acid challenge significantly increased PEA release in control duodenal mucosa but not in dyspeptic patients, indicating an impaired PEA release response in functional dyspepsia.
TTX pretreatment significantly inhibited acid-induced PEA release in both FD and control subjects, suggesting PEA release is neuronally dependent.
PPARα protein expression increased significantly in controls upon acid stimulation, paralleling PEA release, but not in FD subjects.

Exogenous PEA administration significantly and concentration-dependently reduced acid-induced mast cell/tryptase-positive cell numbers, TRPV1/TRPV4 immunopositivity and protein expression, and release of histamine, tryptase, PGD2, and NGF in FD duodenal biopsy specimens.
PEA's anti-inflammatory effects on FD duodenal tissue were abolished by the PPARα antagonist MK866 but unaffected by the PPARγ antagonist GW9662, indicating a PPARα-dependent mechanism.

In acid-treated control biopsy specimens, exogenous PEA also reduced MC density, tryptase-positive cells, TRPV1/TRPV4-expressing cells, and mediator release via a PPARα-mediated pathway, replicating the effect seen in FD tissue.
PEA had no effect on acid-induced mast cell/TRPV1/TRPV4 responses in PPARα knockout mice, confirming that PEA's protective effects strictly require PPARα.

Among 10,234 patients who underwent cerebral angiography over a 9-year period, 9 (0.088%) were identified with a twig-like middle cerebral artery (Tw-MCA) configuration, a rare vascular anomaly replacing the normal M1 segment with a plexiform network.
Of the 9 patients with Tw-MCA, 5 (62.5%) were admitted due to an intracranial hemorrhage, indicating a strong association between this vascular anomaly and hemorrhagic presentation.

Among the hemorrhagic Tw-MCA patients, two had a ruptured intracranial aneurysm on the anterior communicating artery (one with multiple brain aneurysms), two presented with intraparenchymal hematoma due to a periventricular anastomosis, and one had an intraventricular hemorrhage of unclear origin.
The authors conclude that Tw-MCA is a very rare vascular anomaly associated with hemorrhagic events and that its accurate identification is essential to avoid misdiagnosis as steno-occlusive disease.
Across the entire study population, Brachyspira colonisation of the colonic mucosa was found in 31% of IBS patients but in none of the 31 healthy controls.

Restricting analysis to participants with consistent results across at least two diagnostic methods, Brachyspira colonisation prevalence was 28% in IBS versus none in controls, and reached 42% among IBS-D patients specifically.
Membrane-associated spirochetosis (direct epithelial attachment) was detected in 21% of IBS patients but no controls, and was significantly more common in IBS-D (38%) than IBS-C (0%).

Different Brachyspira species preferentially occupied different colonisation niches: B. aalborgi/hominis dominated membrane-associated spirochetosis while B. pilosicoli dominated mucus-restricted colonisation.
Extracolonic Symptom Severity Scores were significantly lower in patients with membrane-associated spirochetosis compared with other IBS patients.
A combined stool score (frequency plus Bristol consistency) was higher in membrane-associated spirochetosis than in IBS patients without Brachyspira and controls, indicating more diarrhoeal symptoms.
Oro-anal transit time was accelerated in patients with membrane-associated spirochetosis compared with other IBS patients.

Host mucus proteome analysis showed a global increase in proteins related to bacterial adhesion and invasion, notably the Arp2/3 complex, along with induction of complement, inflammasome and immunoglobulin components in Brachyspira-colonised patients.
KEGG pathway analysis of mucus proteome alterations in Brachyspira-colonised patients showed strong resemblance to pathways activated in enteric infections such as shigellosis and salmonellosis.
Guanylin, an endogenous ligand of the guanylate cyclase-C receptor that promotes fluid secretion, was increased in the mucus of patients with spirochetosis.
Somatostatin, which promotes intestinal fluid absorption, was decreased in the mucus proteome of patients with spirochetosis, proposed as a contributor to diarrhoea.
Glycocalyx and desmosomal proteins were reduced in patients with dense membrane Brachyspira colonisation, suggesting multilevel mucosal barrier weakening.
Lamina propria immune cell infiltration, including plasma cells and eosinophils, was increased in patients with membrane-associated spirochetosis compared with IBS patients without Brachyspira.
Total and activated mucosal mast cells were significantly more abundant in IBS patients with Brachyspira colonisation than in IBS patients without Brachyspira, based on toluidine blue staining.

Subepithelial mast cell numbers correlated closely with abdominal pain scores in patients with spirochetosis but not in IBS patients without Brachyspira, suggesting Brachyspira status modulates the mast cell-pain relationship.
Mast cell granule proteins (tryptase, chymase, beta-hexosaminidase) and histamine-metabolising enzymes were more abundant in mucus from patients with spirochetosis.
Ingenuity Pathway Analysis of mucus proteome changes predicted CD40LG, IL13 and IL4 as major upstream cytokine regulators, suggesting a Th2-driven immune response to Brachyspira colonisation.

The thickness of the impenetrable mucus layer tended to be reduced in spirochetosis but did not reach statistical significance, alongside occasional bacterial invasion of crypts and goblet cells by other (Gram-positive) genera.

Open-label metronidazole treatment (500 mg three times daily for 14 days) in four patients with membrane-associated spirochetosis resulted in sustained clinical improvement (IBS-SSS reduction >50 points at 15 months) in three of four patients, with reductions in pain, bloating and quality-of-life interference.

Despite clearance of Brachyspira from the epithelial surface after metronidazole treatment, the spirochetes relocated into crypt lumina and goblet cell mucus granules in all four treated patients, a phenomenon paradoxically induced by the antibiotic and potentially representing a bacterial immune/antibiotic evasion strategy.
Following metronidazole treatment, plasma cell, mast cell and eosinophil counts were reduced, with the mucosal immune cellular composition shifting from a Th2-like to a Th1-like pattern.

Routine histology and faecal 16S rDNA sequencing failed to detect Brachyspira colonisation confirmed by proteomics/immunofluorescence/PCR, likely due to primer incompatibility with standard 16S amplicon methods, explaining why the association had previously gone undetected.
ALA dose-dependently reduced serum histamine, chemokine release, vasodilation, eosinophil infiltration, and mast cell degranulation in a mouse model of passive cutaneous and systemic anaphylaxis.
ALA reduced Compound 48/80- or Substance P-induced calcium influx, degranulation, and cytokine/chemokine release in LAD2 mast cells via the Lyn-PLCγ-IP3R-Ca2+ and Lyn-p38/NF-κB signaling pathways.
ALA inhibited C48/80- and Substance P-induced calcium influx in MrgX2-transfected HEK293 cells, implicating the MrgX2 receptor pathway in ALA's anti-pseudo-allergic effect.
In vitro kinase assays showed that ALA directly inhibited Lyn kinase enzymatic activity, reducing it relative to C48/80-stimulated levels.
The title describes a case of cutaneous sarcoidosis presenting with small-fiber neuropathy that clinically resembles leprosy.

Patients with small-fiber neuropathy showed reduced white matter connectivity between the thalamus and the insular cortex and sensorimotor areas (postcentral and precentral gyri) compared to controls.

The degree of skin nerve fiber degeneration (IENFD) was associated with reduced thalamic connectivity to pain-related brain areas, with the specific regions involved depending on the neuropathic pain phenotype (burning, electrical shocks, tingling, mechanical allodynia, numbness).
Despite altered thalamic structural connectivity, white matter integrity as measured by fractional anisotropy was unchanged in SFN patients.
Keratinocytes from patients with small fiber neuropathy showed higher expression of the axon guidance cue netrin-1 (NTN1) than keratinocytes from healthy controls.
Human keratinocytes were shown to attract the neurites of murine dorsal root ganglion neurons in coculture, supporting a role for keratinocyte-nerve interaction.
Exogenous NTN1 slowed and reduced the outgrowth of murine sensory neurites in vitro.
NTN1 exposure did not alter keratinocyte cytokine expression.
In the naive state, keratinocytes from patients with SFN showed significantly higher expression of transforming growth factor-β1 compared with controls.
Fibroblasts from patients with SFN showed significantly higher expression of the algesic cytokine IL-6 compared with controls.
Fibroblasts from patients with SFN showed significantly higher expression of the algesic cytokine IL-8 compared with controls.
Human keratinocytes were shown to attract murine dorsal root ganglion neuron neurites in coculture systems, supporting a chemoattractive role for keratinocytes in cutaneous nociceptor innervation.
Chronic prebiotic (FOS) treatment decreased body weight and fasting hyperglycaemia and improved glucose tolerance in high-fat-diet diabetic mice without changing insulin release.
FOS treatment decreased mRNA expression of inflammatory markers F4/80, Cd11c and Tnfα in epididymal white adipose tissue of diabetic mice.
FOS treatment reduced duodenal contraction frequency and decreased nNos and Chat mRNA expression in the duodenum of diabetic mice.
Prebiotic FOS treatment selectively increased colonic levels of the bioactive lipid 12-HETE in diabetic mice, but not in the duodenum.
12S-HETE dose-dependently (10 nM to 1 µM) reduced ex vivo duodenal mechanical contraction.
Chronic oral 12S-HETE decreased duodenal contraction amplitude (not frequency), and this effect was blocked by the PPARγ antagonist GW9662, indicating a PPARγ-dependent mechanism.
Chronic oral 12S-HETE increased nNos mRNA expression (but not Chat) in the duodenum of diabetic mice.
Chronic oral 12S-HETE treatment decreased body weight and fasting blood glucose and improved glucose tolerance in diabetic mice without altering blood insulin levels.
12S-HETE treatment specifically increased glucose uptake in epididymal white adipose tissue, identifying eWAT as the preferred target tissue.
12S-HETE decreased F4/80 mRNA expression in eWAT of FOS-fed diabetic mice, with a trend toward reduction in Cd11c and Tnfα mRNA (p=0.06) that did not reach significance.
12S-HETE increased Penk and Oprm1 mRNA expression in the mouse duodenum, linking the lipid to enkephalin/mu-opioid receptor signalling.
12-HETE concentration in the duodenum of patients with diabetes was 38% lower than in healthy volunteers, but this difference did not reach statistical significance.
In human diabetic duodenum, Chat mRNA was increased while nNos and Penk mRNAs were decreased compared with healthy volunteers, with no significant change in Oprm1 expression.

In diabetic (HFD-fed) mouse duodenum, Chat mRNA was increased and Penk mRNA decreased (similar to humans), with no change in nNos, but Oprm1 mRNA was markedly increased, contrasting with human findings and suggesting a compensatory response.
Immunohistochemistry showed that mu-opioid receptors (MOR) are expressed on ChAT-expressing and nNOS-expressing neurons within the enteric nervous system.
The 12-HETE-synthesising enzyme Alox12 was localised to ChAT-expressing and nNOS-expressing neurons in the enteric nervous system.
The selective MOR agonist DAMGO decreased ex vivo mechanical activity of the diabetic mouse duodenum.

Chronic oral DAMGO decreased body weight, fasting blood glucose and improved glucose tolerance in diabetic mice without changing insulin release, while increasing glucose uptake in eWAT and decreasing eWAT inflammatory markers.

Chronic DAMGO treatment decreased Chat mRNA (but not nNos mRNA) expression in the duodenum, and its effect on contraction amplitude was blocked by the PPARγ antagonist GW9662, implicating 12S-HETE/PPARγ signalling downstream of MOR activation.
Injection of the noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor reboxetine into the BNST significantly decreased the bradycardic component of the baroreflex without altering the tachycardic component.

Prior administration of an alpha-1 (but not alpha-2) adrenoceptor antagonist into the BNST prevented the reboxetine-induced decrease in bradycardic baroreflex response, indicating alpha-1 receptor mediation of this effect.

Prior injection of NMDA receptor antagonists and nitric oxide pathway blockers into the BNST inhibited the reboxetine-induced reduction in bradycardic baroreflex response, indicating that BNST noradrenergic effects on baroreflex depend on NMDA/nitric oxide signaling.

The study demonstrates for the first time an interaction between BNST noradrenergic, glutamatergic, and nitrergic neurotransmission systems in the modulation of the bradycardic component of the baroreflex.
Heart failure rats showed a greater EFS-induced vasoconstrictor response in the superior mesenteric artery than sham-operated rats, regardless of endothelium integrity.
The alpha-adrenoceptor antagonist phentolamine reduced EFS-induced vasoconstriction to a greater extent in HF rats than in sham-operated rats, indicating increased adrenergic contribution in HF.
The noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor desipramine increased EFS-induced vasoconstriction more in HF than in sham-operated rat SMA segments, suggesting altered noradrenaline reuptake dynamics in HF.
EFS-induced noradrenaline release was greater in HF animals, attributed to higher tyrosine hydroxylase expression and activity.
The P2 purinoceptor antagonist suramin reduced EFS-induced vasoconstriction only in sham-operated rats, not in HF rats, indicating diminished purinergic cotransmission in heart failure.
EFS-induced ATP release from perivascular nerves was lower in HF rats than in sham-operated rats.

The NO synthase inhibitor L-NAME enhanced EFS-induced vasoconstriction to a similar extent in both HF and sham-operated groups, and EFS-induced NO release and vasodilator response to sodium nitroprusside did not differ between groups, indicating nitrergic innervation was unchanged in HF.

The NO synthase inhibitor L-NAME enhanced EFS-induced vasoconstriction to a similar extent in both heart failure and sham-operated rat SMA segments, and EFS-induced NO release was not altered in heart failure.

The vasodilator response to the NO donor sodium nitroprusside was unchanged between heart failure and sham-operated SMA segments, indicating preserved smooth muscle sensitivity to NO despite altered sympathetic neurotransduction.

Overall, post-myocardial infarction heart failure enhanced noradrenergic sympathetic function and diminished purinergic (ATP) cotransmission in the superior mesenteric artery while leaving nitrergic innervation unchanged, resulting in a net increase in sympathetic vasoconstrictor participation.
In the mucosa of the human sigmoid colon, hpChAT-immunoreactive fibers and a few neuronal cell bodies form a local micro-neuronal network that was digitally reconstructed in 3D.
Three interconnected layers of submucosal plexus were visualized in 3D, and hpChAT-immunoreactive neurons were only rarely co-labeled with nNOS in this region.

In the myenteric plexus, 30.1% of hpChAT-immunoreactive somas, including Dogiel type I and II neurons, were co-labeled by nNOS, and three classes of hpChAT-ir nerve fiber strands were identified in 3D.
The density and intensity of hpChAT-immunoreactive fibers in 3D reconstructions were significantly higher in the circular muscle layer than in the longitudinal muscle layer of the sigmoid colon.
94% of patients with alcoholic chronic liver disease showed impaired cardiovascular autonomic reflex tests (R index and/or S/S-HR), indicating autonomic dysfunction.
Seventy-five percent of patients with alcoholic chronic liver disease had gastroparesis, evidenced by a delayed gastric half-emptying time (T1/2).

A significant negative correlation was found between the R index (parasympathetic cardiovascular reflex) and gastric half-emptying time (T1/2), supporting a link between autonomic dysfunction and gastroparesis.

Whole exome sequencing identified a heterozygous TGFBR2 missense mutation (c.1441G>A, p.Glu481Lys) as the causal genetic lesion in a female infant diagnosed with Loeys-Dietz syndrome, reported as the youngest such case in China.

The infant underwent systematic rehabilitation and standard high-risk infant follow-up, resulting in continued developmental improvement including walking with assistance, standing unaided, and improved visual tracking and eye movement.

Diagnosis of Loeys-Dietz syndrome was confirmed based on the combination of skeletal changes, ocular hypertelorism, ocular exotropia, micrognathia, and high-vaulted palate together with the identified pathogenic TGFBR2 mutation.

In the patient with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, 3D phase-contrast imaging showed irregular dermal fiber architecture with fibers of varying thickness radiating in different directions and slightly increased ground substance, compared with the tightly packed, regular fibers seen in the healthy control.

In the patient with idiopathic enteric dysmotility and overweight, dermal fibers were thin and loosely arranged with moderately increased inter-fibrillar ground substance compared with the healthy control.
Across the four dysmotility patients, no dermal architectural changes distinguished those with normal IENFD from those with decreased IENFD.
Immunohistochemical assessment showed decreased IENFD in two of the four gastrointestinal dysmotility patients, while the other two had IENFD similar to healthy controls.
Laboratory phase-contrast µCT of unstained skin biopsies clearly resolved the distinct layers of the epidermis and dermal components such as sebaceous glands, hair follicles, and blood vessels.
High-resolution synchrotron nanoCT (GINIX) clearly visualized keratinocytes, but could not differentiate other epidermal cell types such as melanocytes, Langerhans cells, and Merkel cells.

In the patient with type 1 diabetes, a filament-like structure interpreted as a single nerve fiber was identified in the epidermis and could be tracked through repeated high-resolution imaging sections.

In the patient with type 1 diabetes and normal IENFD, dermal fibers appeared parallel and coarse, contrasting with the disorganized pattern seen in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and the loosely arranged fibers in drug-induced CIPO.
In the patient with drug-induced chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction and reduced IENFD, upper dermal fibers were fine, parallel, and loosely arranged on high-resolution nanoCT.

X-ray phase-contrast CT screening of skin biopsies achieved a volume throughput of about 1 mm3 per minute at sub-micron voxel size, exceeding conventional histology/electron microscopy in scanning speed for sparse structures despite inferior cellular resolution.
Cardiac septal 18F-dopamine PET radioactivity, a marker of sympathetic noradrenergic innervation, was markedly reduced in patients with Lewy body synucleinopathies (PD±OH, PAF) compared to controls.
Cardiac septal 18F-DA radioactivity was increased in MSA patients relative to controls, contrasting with the decrease seen in Lewy body synucleinopathies.
18F-DA radioactivity in the left ventricular chamber was higher in MSA patients than in controls.
18F-DA radioactivity in the liver was higher in patients with Lewy body synucleinopathies than in controls.
18F-DA radioactivity in the liver was also higher in MSA patients than in controls.
18F-DA radioactivity in the submandibular glands was decreased in patients with Parkinson's disease compared to controls.
18F-DA radioactivity did not differ among groups in the spleen, pancreas, stomach, renal cortex, renal pelvis, or thyroid.
Postmortem myocardial norepinephrine content was substantially decreased (approximately 97% below controls) in Lewy body disease compared to the non-Lewy body (MSA and control) group.
Postmortem tissue norepinephrine concentrations did not differ between the Lewy body and non-Lewy body groups in the liver, spleen, pancreas, thyroid, submandibular glands, or sympathetic ganglia.

In a subset of 10 patients with both in vivo and postmortem data, cardiac 18F-DA-derived radioactivity correlated strongly with myocardial tissue norepinephrine content, validating the PET tracer as a biomarker of cardiac noradrenergic deficiency.

A single pathologically confirmed MSA patient had both low cardiac 18F-DA radioactivity and low myocardial norepinephrine, along with an elevated peripheral 'synuclein index' in arrector pili muscles during life, suggesting an early peripheral Lewy body-like process in this atypical case.

Neither in vivo neuroimaging nor postmortem neurochemistry suggested pancreatic noradrenergic deficiency in synucleinopathies, in the first study to examine pancreatic sympathetic innervation in this disease group.
Mean postmortem myocardial norepinephrine content was normal in the small group of MSA patients, contrasting with the severe depletion seen in Lewy body disease.
Plasma total antioxidant capacity was significantly decreased in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
Plasma lipoperoxide levels were significantly increased in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
IL-1β levels were significantly increased in ME/CFS patients versus healthy controls, consistent with low-grade systemic inflammation.
IL-6 levels were significantly increased in ME/CFS patients versus healthy controls.
IL-10 levels were significantly increased in ME/CFS patients versus healthy controls.
TNF-α levels were significantly increased in ME/CFS patients versus healthy controls.
C-reactive protein levels were significantly increased in ME/CFS patients versus healthy controls.
IL-8 levels did not significantly differ between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
Circulating FGF21 levels were significantly higher in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
Circulating NT-proBNP levels were significantly higher in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
In ME/CFS patients, NT-proBNP levels were significantly positively correlated with IL-1β and IL-6 levels.
FGF21 levels did not significantly correlate with inflammatory cytokines in ME/CFS patients.
In healthy controls, neither FGF21 nor NT-proBNP levels showed significant correlations with inflammatory markers.
PBMC oxidative phosphorylation was significantly depressed in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls, with no change in glycolysis.

ATP synthesis as a percentage of basal respiration was decreased in ME/CFS compared to controls, suggesting a defect in ATP synthase (complex V) with compensatory increases in other electron transport chain complexes.
Two studies found mitochondria in ME/CFS patients had a lower reserve capacity for energy production compared to healthy controls, offering a possible explanation for post-exertional fatigue.
Structural studies found branching/fusion (skeletal muscle) or condensation (PBMCs) of mitochondrial cristae in ME/CFS patients, attributed to increased energy demand.

No differences in the levels of specific ETC complexes I-IV were found between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls, suggesting dysfunction stems from external stimuli or oxidative damage rather than the complexes themselves.
Castro-Marrero et al reported higher lipid peroxidation as a cause of lowered ATP levels in ME/CFS compared with healthy controls.
Castro-Marrero et al found significantly lower levels of CoQ10 in PBMCs in 23 ME/CFS participants compared to 15 controls, along with decreased ATP levels and increased lipid peroxidation.

Maes et al studied 58 ME/CFS participants and 22 healthy controls and found many ME/CFS participants had CoQ10 concentrations lower than the lowest healthy control value, with a significant negative correlation between CoQ10 concentration and fibrofatigue symptom scores.
In contrast to other studies, Wood found no statistical differences in CoQ10 in PBMCs or plasma between an ME/CFS cohort and healthy controls.
Jammes et al showed increased markers of oxidative stress in 38 ME/CFS participants, with greater oxidative stress observed after exercise.
Richards et al found an association between increased levels of oxidative stress and ME/CFS symptoms in 33 patients.
Miwa and Fujita found levels of oxidative stress were increased during the relapse state of ME/CFS.
In an uncontrolled, open-label study, d-ribose supplementation produced significant improvement in fatigue as measured by visual analogue scales in ME/CFS patients.
ME/CFS patients taking methylphenidate with vitamins and minerals supporting mitochondrial function reported some improvement in fatigue scores, but this was non-significant compared to placebo.
In an uncontrolled, open-label study, 45% of participants had reduced fatigue when treated with sodium dichloroacetate, a pyruvate dehydrogenase/glycolysis inhibitor.

Fukuda et al found that CoQ10 supplementation significantly increased plasma CoQ10 levels in ME/CFS patients, with the increase in CoQ10 significantly correlated with decreasing oxidative stress and fatigue.

Castro-Marrero et al found that supplementation with NADH plus CoQ10 produced a statistically significant increase in ATP levels and NAD+/NADH ratio in ME/CFS patients, along with improvement in fatigue and biochemical parameters.

A systematic review of sixteen studies on CoQ10 supplementation for fatigue concluded that CoQ10 was more effective at decreasing fatigue in disorders such as fibromyalgia and statin-related fatigue than in ME/CFS.

An online randomised controlled trial of MitoQ versus placebo in 51 ME/CFS participants found no statistically significant improvement in symptoms, with limitations including inability to confirm diagnosis, compliance, and reliance on self-reported data.

Proteomic analysis of ME/CFS patients versus healthy controls found a significant proportion of proteins with changed expression were involved in mitochondrial function, oxidative phosphorylation, ETC complexes I and V, and redox/ROS regulation.
MitoQ prevented hydrogen peroxide-induced apoptotic cell death in a mitochondrial cell model, outperforming non-targeted antioxidants.

Simultaneous Components Analysis identified two perpetuating components of fatigue in CFS/ME patients, labeled 'psychological discomfort' and 'activity', from 22 EMA-registered behaviours, cognitions and affects.
At the group level, neither the psychological discomfort nor the activity component predicted fatigue at a subsequent time-point in multilevel vector autoregressive modelling.

At the individual patient level, the strength and direction of associations between perpetuating components and fatigue varied considerably, indicating heterogeneity in fatigue perpetuation across CFS/ME patients.

None of the individual associations between perpetuating components (psychological discomfort, activity) and fatigue significantly predicted outcome of cognitive behaviour therapy for fatigue severity.
Across the reviewed studies, maladaptive perfectionism showed a moderate-to-strong positive association with depression in people with CFS/ME.
The perfectionism subcomponent 'concern over mistakes' was positively associated with depression in CFS/ME patients.
The perfectionism subcomponent 'doubts about actions' was positively associated with depression in CFS/ME patients.
The relationship between perfectionism and anxiety in CFS/ME remains under-researched, limiting conclusions on this association.
Perineural (Tarlov) cysts ≥5 mm were found on lumbar/sacral MRI in 39% of patients diagnosed with fibromyalgia and/or chronic fatigue syndrome.
The prevalence of Tarlov cysts differed markedly by sex among FM/CFS patients, being 12% in males versus 42% in females.

The authors conclude that TC prevalence in FM/CFS patients was three times higher than in the general population, supporting a shared pathophysiology between symptomatic Tarlov cysts and FM/CFS involving elevated cerebrospinal fluid pressure irritating dorsal root ganglia.
Patients with hEDS/HSD reported significantly higher levels of pain and foot dysfunction than healthy controls.
Patients with hEDS/HSD showed a significantly increased eversion position of the medial forefoot during the stance phase of gait, suggestive of a hypermobile first ray.
Significantly more dorsiflexion was found in the medial and lateral forefoot and the rearfoot during gait in hEDS/HSD patients compared to controls.
An increased plantar flexion at the midfoot was found in subjects with hEDS/HSD compared to controls during gait.
Decreased dorsiflexion at the hallux was found in subjects with hEDS/HSD compared to controls during gait.
Increased inversion and abduction at the hallux were found in subjects with hEDS/HSD compared to controls during gait.
hEDS/HSD patients with multidirectional shoulder instability showed significantly less scapular upward rotation during arm elevation compared to healthy controls.

hEDS/HSD patients with multidirectional shoulder instability showed significantly less scapular upward rotation during arm elevation compared to subjects with multidirectional shoulder laxity (MDL) without instability.
hEDS/HSD patients showed significantly less scapular posterior tilt compared to subjects with multidirectional shoulder laxity (MDL).
hEDS/HSD patients with multidirectional shoulder instability showed significantly higher EMG activity of the infraspinatus muscle during arm elevation.
hEDS/HSD patients with multidirectional shoulder instability showed significantly higher EMG activity of the middle trapezius muscle during arm elevation.
hEDS/HSD patients with multidirectional shoulder instability showed significantly higher EMG activity of the posterior deltoid muscle during arm elevation.
Wearing the compressive jacket significantly increased the power of shoulder external rotators at 180°/s compared to not wearing it.
At 90°/s angular speed, no significant difference in shoulder rotator power or strength was found between wearing and not wearing the jacket.
When comparing on versus off jacket wear, a significant difference in external and internal rotator power was observed regardless of angular speed tested.
The occurrence of shoulder subluxation events decreased significantly after wearing the compressive jacket.
The occurrence of shoulder dislocation events decreased significantly after wearing the compressive jacket.
Pain scores decreased from 3.5/10 to 2.5/10 after jacket wear, but the change was not statistically significant.
Over 70% of patients reported satisfaction with the jacket's effect on arthralgia, instability, or function, with high overall QUEST satisfaction scores.

A heterozygous TNXB splice donor site variant c.12463+2T>C was identified in five subjects from two unrelated CAH families with previously unexplained CAH-X and was associated with a moderate hypermobility EDS phenotype.
In both families, the TNXB splice site variant shared an allele with a CYP21A2 c.955C>T (p.Q318X) pathogenic CAH variant rather than with a 30-kb deletion.
PCR and Sanger sequencing confirmed the absence of the known TNXA/TNXB chimeras (CAH-X CH-1 or CH-2) in these subjects, ruling out the more common cause of CAH-X.

Clinically, the three CAH patients carrying the variant showed a moderate EDS phenotype including significant joint and skin manifestations in adult siblings, and joint hypermobility, spongy skin, and minor cardiac defects (patent ductus arteriosus, patent foramen ovale) in the pediatric patient; all three had a history of hernia.
RT-PCR and Sanger sequencing of skin biopsy RNA showed that mRNA transcribed from the variant TNXB allele was less abundant than from the normal allele, without a detectable splicing error.

In dermal fibroblasts (but not skin biopsies) from variant carriers, RT-PCR detected a premature TNX RNA form that failed to remove intron 42, transcribed exclusively from the variant allele, along with a trace of nascent RNA in one subject.

qRT-PCR showed a moderate decrease in overall TNX mRNA abundance in dermal fibroblasts from three adult variant carriers compared with non-EDS CAH controls, though the reduction was less severe than in a subject with a CAH-X CH-1 haploinsufficiency chimera.

A CAH carrier (B-I-2, non-CAH-affected) with the TNXB splice variant had only mild joint involvement and no generalized hypermobility despite low fibroblast TNX mRNA, consistent with milder EDS manifestations previously observed in CAH carriers compared to CAH-affected patients.

A heterozygous TNXB c.12218G>A (p.Arg4073His) variant, predicted to be damaging in silico, was found in family A and might contribute biallelically to the CAH-X phenotype, though its high population allele frequency (0.029-0.122) makes it unlikely to be pathogenic alone.
The splice variant is annotated in gnomAD as a high-confidence predicted loss-of-function variant with an allele frequency of 0.01096 in the general population.
Subject B-II-1 (pediatric TNXB variant carrier) had a history of allergic disorders, which prior GWAS work has suggested may be associated with TNXB.
Pain was the most commonly perceived symptom affecting day-to-day activities, reported by 73% of parents.
Fatigue was the second most commonly perceived symptom affecting day-to-day activities, reported by 68% of parents.
Parents were more satisfied with their child's self-care abilities (61%) than with school participation (33%).
Difficulty keeping up with handwriting at school was the most frequently reported school-based difficulty, affecting 71% of children.
Gross motor activity difficulties at school were reported by 70% of parents.
Most parents (65%) reported leisure activity difficulties for their child, with pain (64%) and fatigue (60%) being the main contributing factors.
A case report describes absence of myocardial support at the base of the left coronary aortic sinus in a patient with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, a potential structural cardiac vulnerability.
The patient carried a de novo heterozygous STXBP1 mutation (c.560C>T, p.Pro187Leu) associated with epileptic encephalopathy presenting as electrical status epilepticus during slow-wave sleep (ESES).
Treatment with a 3:1 classical ketogenic diet led to cessation of the patient's refractory seizures by the third month of therapy.
The case highlights a rare co-occurrence of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome with STXBP1-related epileptic encephalopathy, noting that epilepsy is not a common neurological finding in EDS.
Serum tau protein levels were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients compared with age-matched healthy controls.
Serum beta-amyloid-42 levels were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients compared with age-matched healthy controls.
Higher serum tau levels in fibromyalgia patients were positively correlated with worse sleep quality as measured by the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index.
Among all symptom scores assessed (pain, impact, depression, anxiety, sleep), only sleep disturbance was significantly associated with higher serum tau levels in fibromyalgia patients.
Electroacupuncture (EA), which provides somatosensory afference, produced a greater reduction in fibromyalgia pain severity than mock laser acupuncture (ML), which lacks somatosensory afference.

Patients receiving EA, compared to those receiving ML, showed increased resting-state functional connectivity between the leg representation of primary somatosensory cortex (S1leg) and the anterior insula.
Following EA therapy, increased S1leg-anterior insula functional connectivity was associated with reduced pain severity on the BPI.
Following EA therapy, increased S1leg-anterior insula connectivity was associated with increased levels of GABA+ in the anterior insula.
Increased levels of GABA+ in the anterior insula were associated with reduced pain severity as measured by the BPI.
Post-EA changes in anterior insula GABA+ levels statistically mediated the relationship between changes in S1leg-anterior insula connectivity and reduced pain severity on the BPI.

Using normalized mutual information on resting-state fMRI data, the global network architecture of intrinsic functional brain communities was found to be less stable (more variable) in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls, replicated across two independent cohorts.
Node community assignment analyses showed that the composition of intrinsic functional brain communities differed between fibromyalgia patients and healthy controls.

Differences in functional network organization were associated with changes in community composition across fibromyalgia patients with varying levels of clinical pain, suggesting a link between network reorganization and pain severity.
The ACE rs4646994 genotype showed no significant association with susceptibility to developing fibromyalgia syndrome in this Jordanian cohort.
The MTHFR rs1801133 genotype showed no significant association with susceptibility to developing fibromyalgia syndrome in this Jordanian cohort.
The VDR rs2228570 genotype showed no significant association with susceptibility to developing fibromyalgia syndrome in this Jordanian cohort.
Among FM patients, the ACE rs4646994 genotype was associated with the presence of restless leg symptoms.
Bone marrow mast cells in MCAS-T patients were significantly larger in size compared with controls.
Bone marrow mast cells in MCAS-T patients were hypogranular compared with controls.
Mast cells in MCAS-T patients were more frequently located in paratrabecular bone marrow regions compared with controls.
Mast cells in MCAS-T patients were more frequently located in perivascular bone marrow regions compared with controls.
MCAS-T patients showed bone marrow eosinophilia compared with controls.
All 10 MCAS-T patients available for tryptase genotyping were confirmed to have hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (HaT), caused by extra copies of TPSAB1.

MCAS-T patients had a negative work-up for clonal mast cell disorders such as systemic mastocytosis and monoclonal mast cell activation syndrome, indicating their bone marrow findings are distinct from clonal MC disease.
Internalisation of Staphylococcus aureus into host cells appears to enhance bacterial survival by modulating host immune responses and activating mast cells.
Sophoricoside treatment reduced allergic and asthmatic symptoms in ovalbumin-induced mice by suppressing airway inflammation and antibody-antigen reactions.
Sophoricoside suppressed immune cell recruitment into airway lumens and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine production in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid of OVA-induced mice.
Sophoricoside decreased the amount of histamine released in OVA-induced mice and in antibody-antigen stimulated mast cells.
Sophoricoside decreased release of arachidonic acid metabolites in OVA-induced mice and antibody-antigen stimulated mast cells.
Sophoricoside decreased differentiation of naïve CD4+ T cells into Th1, Th2, and Th17 cell subsets.
