Neuromuscular-blocking agents and other agonists activate MRGPRX2 on human LAD2 mast cells, inducing calcium mobilization and cytokine release in an MRGPRX2-dependent manner.
Unlike other MRGPRX2 agonists tested, rocuronium induced calcium mobilization and cytokine release but did not trigger mast cell degranulation.
Co-treatment of mast cells with sugammadex and some MRGPRX2 agonists significantly reduced cell activation.
When sugammadex was given a few minutes after MRGPRX2 stimulation, it failed to attenuate mast cell degranulation, arguing against its use for acute control of NMBA-induced anaphylactic symptoms.
Addition of sugammadex up to 180 minutes after MRGPRX2 stimulation significantly reduced CCL2 mRNA and protein induction, suggesting a possible role in dampening delayed mast cell mediator release.
Cellular and animal studies show that mast cells can induce esophageal smooth muscle cells to proliferate and differentiate into a more contractile phenotype.
Mediators released by degranulating mast cells, including tryptase and histamine, can activate esophageal smooth muscle contraction pathways.

The authors propose that mast cell degranulation in the esophageal myenteric plexus could cause loss of enteric neurons, a hallmark of achalasia, analogous to mast cell involvement in neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's.
The paper presents a novel conceptual model proposing an allergy-induced form of achalasia mediated by mast cell activation in the esophageal muscularis propria.
The neurokinin-1 receptor mediates inflammatory processes, including immune cell differentiation, cytokine release, and mast cell activation.
Because substance P and human hemokinin-1 have similar peptide structures, the neurokinin-1 receptor does not discriminate between them, and both show biological receptor affinity.
Using the newly applied mass spectrometric assay, substance P was quantified in porcine brain tissue at a concentration of 4.49 ± 0.53 nM.
Substance P was quantified in human saliva at 113.3 ± 67.0 pM using the mass spectrometric assay.
Substance P was quantified in human seminal fluid at 0.52 ± 0.15 nM using the mass spectrometric assay.
Consistent with prior reports, neither substance P nor human hemokinin-1 could be detected in human plasma by mass spectrometry.
Neither substance P nor human hemokinin-1 could be detected in human plasma using the selective mass spectrometric assay, consistent with prior reports.

Despite mass spectrometry detecting no SP in plasma, a commercial immunoassay of the same plasma samples reported SP-like immunoreactivity concentrations ranging from 37.1 to 178.0 pM, revealing a discrepancy between the two methods.

The previously reported carboxylic acid form of substance P was confirmed by high-resolution mass spectrometry but showed no cross-reactivity in the immunoassay and did not contribute to the SP-like immunoreactivity signal.

Compound discovery on immunocaptured plasma material identified a precursor of substance P as a possible cross-reactor, which may explain the previously reported high variance in SP plasma level measurements.
The tick salivary peptide IPDef1 induced itch-related behavior (pruritus) in mice.
IPDef1 had greater pruritogenic potency than IRDef2 and induced itch through a histamine-independent mechanism.
IPDef1 induced itch by activating mouse MrgprC11 and human MRGPRX1 receptors on dorsal root ganglion (sensory) neurons.
Activation of MrgprC11/MRGPRX1 by IPDef1 sensitized the downstream ion channel TRPV1 in dorsal root ganglion neurons, contributing to pruriceptor signaling.
IPDef1 also activated mouse MrgprB2 and its human ortholog MRGPRX2, receptors selectively expressed on mast cells, triggering release of inflammatory cytokines and driving acute inflammation in mice.
Despite IPDef1-induced mast cell activation via MrgprB2/MRGPRX2, this mast cell activation did not contribute to the itch caused by oxidated IPDef1.
IPDef1 activated mouse MrgprB2 and its human ortholog MRGPRX2 on mast cells, triggering release of inflammatory cytokines and driving acute inflammation in mice.
Despite activating mast cells via MrgprB2/MRGPRX2, mast cell activation did not contribute to the itch induced by oxidated IPDef1, indicating itch and inflammation arise from distinct mechanisms.
KIT mutations are present in more than 85% of both adult and pediatric mastocytosis cases, but the D816V mutation is found in most affected adults and only about half of affected children.
Cutaneous mastocytosis (CM) regressed in 210 of the 272 included pediatric-onset patients (77.2%), with a mean time to regression of 6.10 years.
The rare cases of aggressive systemic mastocytosis in the cohort were symptomatic from the outset of disease.
Congenital onset of mastocytosis was significantly associated with regression of cutaneous mastocytosis (odds ratio 0.48, P = .031).
Presence of the KIT D816V mutation was significantly associated with regression of cutaneous mastocytosis (odds ratio 0.173, P = .031).
Aggravation of mast cell activation symptoms (MCASs) over time was correlated with persistence (non-regression) of cutaneous skin lesions.
In 19% of patients who had MCASs at baseline and whose CM subsequently regressed, MCASs nonetheless became more intense, supporting the need for long-term follow-up even after skin regression.
SELE expression was significantly increased in blood samples from chronic idiopathic urticaria (CIU) patients compared to normal individuals.

In a mouse model of CIU induced by intradermal ovalbumin IgE antiserum injection, mast cell degranulation and directional histamine release were increased along with elevated TNF-α, HRF, and IL-6 expression.
SELE silencing (loss-of-function) in CIU mice decreased mast cell degranulation, reduced the rate of histamine directional release, and suppressed TNF-α, HRF, and IL-6 expression in serum.
Ketotifen treatment rescued (reduced) the increased TNF-α, HRF, and IL-6 expression that was caused by SELE overexpression in the CIU model.
FAHF-2, derived from the classical formula Wu Mei Wan, prevented systemic anaphylaxis in murine models and showed preliminary immunomodulatory effects on T cells and basophils.
A retrospective practice-based evidence study found comprehensive TCM therapy effectively prevented frequent and severe food anaphylaxis triggered by skin contact or protein inhalation.
The traditional Japanese herbal medicine Kakkonto suppressed allergic diarrhea and decreased mast cell numbers in the intestinal mucosa of a murine model.

Active compounds derived from TCM potently inhibited IgE, mast cell activation, and proinflammatory cytokines/signaling (TNF-alpha, IL-8, NF-κB), suggesting relevance to both IgE- and non-IgE-mediated food allergy.

Triple TCM therapy combining ingestion, bath, and cream markedly improved skin lesions, itching, and sleep loss in patients with corticosteroid-dependent, recalcitrant, or topical steroid withdrawal eczema.
Xiao Feng San along with other Japanese and Korean herbal formulas were found effective in treating eczema.
Acupuncture reduced wheal size, skin itching, and basophil activation in patients with atopic dermatitis.
Xiao Feng San and various Japanese and Korean herbal formulas were reported to be effective in treating eczema.
Acupuncture reduced wheal size, skin itching, and basophil activation in patients with atopic dermatitis.
The review concludes that traditional Chinese medicine is generally safe as a therapy for food allergy and eczema.
The paper reports cutaneous sensory and autonomic small fiber neuropathy occurring in patients with HTRA1-related cerebral small vessel disease.
The incidence and prevalence of small fiber neuropathy are estimated at 12 per 100,000 and 53 per 100,000 respectively, and are expected to rise with increasing clinical awareness.
Non-length-dependent SFN is likely associated with immune-mediated conditions and presents more often in younger women.

Approximately 30% of idiopathic SFN patients carry a SCN9A mutation, and mutations can be gain-of-function (causing pain disorders including SFN) or loss-of-function (causing congenital insensitivity to pain).

In a study of 1139 patients with pure SFN, over seventy different SCN9A/SCN10A/SCN11A mutations were found in 11.6% of participants, leading to a recommendation for genetic screening in all pure SFN patients regardless of clinical presentation.
Intra-epidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD) reduction is the most frequently reported pathological finding in SFN, though similar changes occur to a lesser extent in healthy subjects.
Sweat gland nerve fiber density (SGNFD) decreases and sweat gland atrophy occurs in SFN, but the assay is labor-intensive (30-40 hours per biopsy) limiting routine clinical use.

Corneal confocal microscopy (CCM) exploits the cornea's very high small-fiber density (300-400x that of skin) to quantify nerve fiber length, branching and tortuosity in vivo, and corneal nerve fiber density correlates with IENFD.

Ultrasound of the sural nerve shows significantly increased cross-sectional area in SFN patients compared with healthy volunteers, while the superficial peroneal nerve and thickness-to-width ratio show no difference.
Subjects with SFN show volume reduction in the anterior cingulate cortex (a pain-processing brain region), and the degree of volume reduction correlates with the degree of IENFD decrease.
Laser Doppler imaging flare (LDIflare), an axon-reflex-mediated blood flow test, is reduced in diabetic patients compared with healthy controls and correlates with nerve fiber density.

In diabetic patients, axon swelling seen on skin biopsy can predict progression from distal SFN to proximal large-fiber or polyneuropathy, whereas a separate study excluding diabetic patients found SFN to be a stable disorder that rarely progresses.

A definite SFN diagnosis has been proposed to require at least two abnormal findings among clinical examination, QST, and skin biopsy, though an alternative group proposes substituting QSART for skin biopsy or using a four-method combination (skin biopsy, electrochemical skin conductance, laser evoked potentials, QST).

QSART sweat output normative values differ by sex, with mean output of 2-3 μl/cm2 in males versus 0.25-1.2 μl/cm2 in females, and QDIRT shows near-absent responses in female subjects due to low sweat volume and rapid evaporation.

MIBG SPECT heart-to-mediastinal uptake ratio correlates highly with IENFD in Parkinson's disease patients but not in diabetic patients, indicating disease-specific differences in cardiac sympathetic denervation patterns.
Sodium-channel blockers are only effective in SFN patients with a proven sodium-channel mutation, supporting a phenotype-based diagnostic and treatment approach.
Gain-of-function variants in Nav1.7, including I228M, are found in 5% to 10% of patients with idiopathic painful small-fiber neuropathy.
DRG neurons from Nav1.7 I228M knock-in mice show hyperexcitability compared with wild-type littermate-control neurons, measured by whole-cell patch-clamp and multielectrode array recordings.
Despite DRG neuron hyperexcitability, Nav1.7 I228M knock-in mice do not display mechanical or thermal hyperalgesia in vivo.
Nav1.7 I228M knock-in mice do not show intraepidermal nerve fiber loss, in contrast to the fiber loss characteristic of human small-fiber neuropathy.

The authors conclude that the relationship between sensory neuron hyperexcitability and patient-reported pain in Nav1.7-related small-fiber neuropathy is more complex than previously appreciated, highlighting challenges in modelling channelopathy pain disorders in mice.
Across four diagnostic models, the frequency of small fiber neuropathy (SFN) among patients with probable or definite DPN ranged widely from 1.4% to 13.1%.
Large fiber neuropathy (LFN) frequency among patients with probable or definite DPN varied from 9.3% to 21.5% depending on the diagnostic model applied.
Mixed fiber neuropathy (MFN) was the most common subtype among patients with probable or definite DPN, with frequency ranging from 51.4% to 83.2% depending on the diagnostic model.
Non-classifiable neuropathy (NCN), representing patients whose neuropathy could not be subtyped, ranged from 0.5% to 14.5% across diagnostic models among probable or definite DPN cases.
Restricting analysis to patients with definite DPN, SFN frequency across diagnostic models ranged from 1.6% to 13.5%.
Among patients with definite DPN, LFN frequency across diagnostic models ranged from 5.6% to 20.6%.
Among patients with definite DPN, MFN was again the most frequent subtype, ranging from 61.9% to 89.7% across diagnostic models.
In the definite DPN group, the frequency of non-classifiable neuropathy (NCN) ranged from 0.0% to 6.3% depending on the diagnostic model applied.

The authors conclude that the frequency of polyneuropathy subtypes (SFN, LFN, MFN, NCN) in type 2 diabetes patients depends substantially on the type and number of diagnostic criteria used, independent of DPN certainty level, highlighting a need for standardized future consensus criteria.
Optimizing electrode design parameters for an intra-epidermal electrode increased the activation threshold ratio between Aβ- and Aδ-fibers by up to 289% compared to existing electrode designs.
Optimizing electrode design parameters for a planar concentric electrode increased the activation threshold ratio between Aβ- and Aδ-fibers by up to 595% compared to existing electrode designs.
A small cathode area was found to be essential for producing high current density in the epidermal skin layer, which enables activation of small nerve fibers.
Small anode area and short anode-cathode distance minimize current spread to deeper tissues, reducing the likelihood of activating large Aβ-fibers.
In the optimization, all electrode parameters were optimal at their lower bound except cathode protrusion, which was optimal a few micrometers above the location of the Aδ-fiber model.
Genetic deletion of one myostatin allele increased hindlimb muscle weights in mice regardless of OI (G610C) genotype.
Postnatal treatment with the anti-myostatin monoclonal antibody Regn647 increased hindlimb muscle mass in both wild-type and +/G610C mice.
Female mice heterozygous for both myostatin and G610C (Dbl.Het) tended to show trabecular and cortical bone parameters similar to wild-type, indicating reversal of the G610C OI bone phenotype.
Male +/G610C mice with concurrent myostatin heterozygous deficiency showed minimal effect on bone parameters, unlike the improvement seen in females.
Pharmacologic myostatin inhibition with Regn647 did not improve trabecular or cortical bone properties in either male or female +/G610C (OI) mice.
Pharmacologic myostatin inhibition improved skeletal microarchitectural and biomechanical properties in male wild-type mice, in contrast to the lack of effect seen in +/G610C OI mice.
A 4-week treatment holiday following pharmacologic myostatin inhibition did not alter skeletal outcomes compared to continuous treatment.
High-fat diet (HFD) consumption from adolescence to adulthood significantly increased body weight in rats without altering food intake.
HFD-fed adult rats showed increased visceral fat mass accompanied by delayed gastric emptying.
Bethanechol-induced contractile responses were attenuated in antral and fundic gastric strips of HFD-fed rats.
Sodium nitroprusside (SNP)-induced relaxant responses were attenuated in antral and fundic gastric strips of HFD-fed rats.
HFD markedly decreased the number of myenteric neurons in both fundus and antrum, as assessed by cuprolinic blue staining and PGP 9.5 immunostaining.
Neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS) immunoreactivity was markedly decreased in both fundus and antrum of HFD-fed rats.
HFD markedly decreased choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) expression in gastric tissue.
HFD increased vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) immunoreactivity in the antrum.
High-fat diet exposure from adolescence to adulthood markedly reduced the number of myenteric neurons in both the gastric fundus and antrum.
HFD consumption decreased neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS) immunoreactivity in both the fundus and antrum.
HFD consumption markedly decreased ChAT expression, indicating reduced cholinergic enteric innervation.
HFD consumption increased VIP immunoreactivity specifically in the antrum, consistent with altered non-adrenergic non-cholinergic inhibitory neurotransmission.

An in vitro study of skin biopsies identified the αvβ3-ILK-Snail1/Slug signalling axis as promoting fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transition in hEDS and HSD patients, a change absent in classical and vascular EDS biopsies.
The distribution of joint hypermobility across genders is well reported to show a female predominance.
Females with joint hypermobility have increased odds of developing pelvic girdle pain during pregnancy compared to those without joint hypermobility.
A study of pregnancy complications in EDS patients found the prevalence of pelvic pain and instability was almost four times greater than in those without EDS.
Small case series report that up to 88% of hEDS patients experience pelvic girdle pain during pregnancy.
The combined prevalence of all EDS subtypes is estimated at 1 in 5000, with 80-90% believed to be hEDS.
Epidemiological studies estimate joint hypermobility prevalence to range between 2% and 35%.
Studies investigating pelvic pain in females suggest generalised-HSD can affect up to 24% of women, which may not differ meaningfully from general population figures.
Pelvic girdle pain during pregnancy affects between 23% and 65% of pregnant women in general.
Pelvic girdle pain prevalence during pregnancy was higher in HSD individuals (26%) compared to controls (7%).

Among women with continuous pelvic girdle pain 11 years after birth, 29% were known to have a diagnosis of joint hypermobility, while 8.6% and 10% of women had persistent PGP at 2 and 11 years postpartum respectively.
The composition, proportion, structure and distribution of collagen types are altered in hypermobile individuals, with an increased ratio of type III to type I collagen.
Twin studies suggest a strong genetic component to joint hypermobility with multifactorial influences, showing 60% concordance in monozygotic twins and 36% in dizygotic twins.
Radiographic studies of asymptomatic individuals showed up to five millimetres of physiological motion at the pubic symphysis, informing thresholds used to define pathological instability.
Studies investigating Relaxin's relation to pelvic girdle pain found it unlikely to cause musculoskeletal disease, and Relaxin levels do not predict PGP development.

Haploinsufficiency and missense variants of tenascin-X, encoded by TNXB, have been reported in a small subset of hEDS phenotype individuals, though penetrance varies and it accounts for only a minority of cases.
Variations of the LZTS1 gene have been identified in a family with hEDS, though the mechanistic process remains poorly understood.
Females with chronic pelvic pain are at significantly increased risk of anxiety and depression compared to pain-free controls or population norms.
Women with pelvic girdle pain screened three months postpartum had 3.58 times the odds of screening positive for depression compared to women without pelvic or lumbar back pain.
A prospective cohort of 130 women with pregnancy-related PGP found 83% reported substantial recovery within 6 weeks postpartum, with 44% recovering within 2 weeks.

A cross-sectional study of 50 SIJ fusion patients found that patient-reported outcomes at 1-year post-surgery were maintained 23 years later, but were not statistically different from patients managed without surgery over a 17-year follow-up.

A prospective study of 8 patients with severe PGP undergoing SIJ fusion found significant reductions in ODI and VAS pain scores and improvements in SF-36 scores, though with notable postoperative complications.
Minimally invasive SIJ fusion had a significantly lower revision surgery rate (3.5%) compared to open fusion (44%), along with lower operating time, blood loss and length of admission.
A meta-analysis found minimally invasive SIJ fusion significantly reduced VAS and ODI scores, indicating improved pain and functional outcomes.
A randomised controlled trial found that minimally invasive iFuse SIJ fusion significantly improved VAS, ODI and EQ-5D scores 24 months post-procedure compared to conservative management.
A case series of nine patients using BMP-7 with type I collagen for pelvic fusion found no local or systemic complications, with bone healing in 89% of cases and fusion at a median of 5 months.
Students who later developed severe ME/CFS had significantly lower IL-6 levels at baseline (before developing mononucleosis) compared to those who remained asymptomatic.
Students who later developed severe ME/CFS had significantly lower IL-13 levels at baseline (before developing mononucleosis) compared to those who remained asymptomatic.

Prior to developing infectious mononucleosis, students who would later develop severe ME/CFS did not differ from those who remained asymptomatic in stress, coping, anxiety, or depression, though they did differ on several behavioral measures.
At the time of developing infectious mononucleosis, both ME/CFS groups tended to have more autonomic complaints and behavioral symptoms than the recovered/asymptomatic group.
At the time of developing infectious mononucleosis, the severe-ME/CFS group had higher levels of IL-12 than the recovered (asymptomatic) group.
At the time of developing infectious mononucleosis, the severe-ME/CFS group had lower levels of IL-13 than the recovered (asymptomatic) group.
Among 4501 college students, 238 (5.3%) developed infectious mononucleosis, and 6 months later 55 of these (23%) met criteria for ME/CFS while 157 (66%) were asymptomatic.
In ME/CFS patients, the WHOQOL-BREF Physical Health domain score was significantly lower than the Psychological, Social Relationships and Environment domain scores.

Family members of adult ME/CFS patients had significantly higher (worse) FROM-16 total scores, indicating greater QoL burden, than family members of patients with 25 other diseases reported in the FROM-16 validation study.

A statistically significant negative correlation was found between patients' self-rated overall QoL (WHOQOL-BREF Question 1) and their family members' mean FROM-16 total scores, indicating poorer patient QoL is associated with greater family burden.

Significant negative correlations were found between the WHOQOL-BREF Physical Health domain and the Environment domain, each with the mean FROM-16 total score, while weaker correlations were seen for Psychological and Social Relationships domains.
Patients' self-rated overall QoL and their health satisfaction ratings were strongly and significantly correlated.

Mean FROM-16 scores were similar across parents, children, and partners/spouses of ME/CFS patients, while siblings and grandparents (a small subgroup) scored notably higher, though this did not reach the estimated minimal clinically important difference.
The FROM-16 questions with the highest reported impact on family members concerned worry, disruption of family activities, frustration and sadness.
Cerebrospinal fluid glutamate was significantly elevated in the postexercise GWI STOPP subgroup compared to nonexercise sc0, cfs0, and gwi0 groups and the postexercise START subgroup.
There was no significant difference in CSF glutamate among the three nonexercise groups (sc0, cfs0, gwi0), and no bimodal distribution predictive of later START vs STOPP status.

CSF C5-OH acylcarnitine was significantly higher in postexercise sedentary controls (SC) than nonexercise sedentary controls (sc0), indicating an exercise effect, and was also higher in SC than the postexercise GWI groups.

There were no differences in carnitine levels between nonexercise GWI (gwi0) and postexercise GWI subjects, suggesting exercise did not increase carnitine production via fatty acid oxidation in GWI, unlike in controls.
LysoPC a C28:0 was significantly higher in nonexercise GWI (gwi0) than nonexercise ME/CFS (cfs0), and gwi0 was also higher than the combined postexercise GWI (START+STOPP) groups.

Unlike previously reported plasma findings, the summed concentrations of carnitine, lysophospholipid, phosphatidylcholine, and sphingomyelin lipid families in CSF were not significantly different between GWI, ME/CFS, control, or exercise groups.

ME/CFS (cfs0), GWI (gwi0), and postexercise START/STOPP subjects showed high symptom load and disabling quality of life scores ('ceiling' effects) compared to 'floor' effects seen in sedentary control groups (sc0, SC).

In patients diagnosed with the broad Oxford criteria (CF, no PEM requirement), GET added to specialist medical care moderately improved fatigue and physical functioning up to 1-year follow-up, though APT was not effective.
Adaptive Pacing Therapy was not an effective addition to specialist medical care and was associated with more frequent physical deterioration than GET.

In CFS patients diagnosed mainly with Fukuda criteria (PEM optional), several interventions including GET, adaptive pacing, qigong and yoga were moderately effective in reducing fatigue at post-treatment only, but effects on physical functioning were largely absent or negative.

The only RCT in patients diagnosed with criteria requiring PEM (CCC, ME) found a self-management and activity-pacing program effective for fatigue and self-efficacy at short-term follow-up, but not for physical functioning, with no sustained long-term effect.
In the Nùñez trial, MRT combining GET and CBT was not superior to usual treatment at 12 months and the intervention may have been harmful to some participants due to increased pain.
In the Moss-Morris GET trial, physiological assessment testing was experienced as harmful by more than half of the participants.
In the GES trial, about a quarter of participants in both intervention and control groups reported deterioration of physical functioning despite overall reported safety.

A review of 11 patient surveys found that more than half of ME/CFS patients who underwent GET reported negative outcomes, whereas pacing had the lowest negative response rate and highest reported benefit.
An independent re-analysis of the PACE trial found that most of the modest improvements reported for GET did not reach statistical significance compared to control.

Analyses across PACE and two other CBT studies showed that reported effect sizes for exercise/CBT interventions increased as the subjectivity of the outcome measure increased, while objective outcomes showed no clinically significant improvement with GET.
A patient survey found that about half of ME patients had received physiotherapy and 53% of these reported that physiotherapy worsened their ME symptoms.
High mean baseline CFQ scores across trials indicate a ceiling effect, meaning the instrument can capture improvement but not exacerbation of fatigue symptoms in ME/CFS patients.

In a GET-like case-control study using accelerometry, ME/CFS patients initially met prescribed activity goals but became unable to sustain them after 4-10 days, with pronounced symptom worsening, demonstrating objective non-compliance and exertion intolerance.
Qigong and isometric yoga interventions were generally well tolerated with adverse events uncommon or absent, and no PEM was reported after yoga.
Home orthostatic training was well tolerated and generally complied with in CFS patients, though it did not significantly improve fatigue impact scores compared to sham training.
Only two of eighteen included RCTs assessed PEM occurrence as an outcome measure, and its operationalization was unclear, limiting the ability to evaluate intervention effects on PEM specifically.
A chronic post-viral syndrome with fatigue, myalgia, depression and sleep disturbance resembling CFS/fibromyalgia was previously reported after the 2003 SARS coronavirus outbreak.
In a cohort recovering from hospital admission for COVID-19, persistent breathlessness, cough and fatigue remained common at follow-up.
Olfactory dysfunction was reported in the large majority of patients with mild-to-moderate COVID-19 and preceded other symptoms in a substantial minority.

In a hamster model, SARS-CoV-2 nasal instillation caused massive olfactory epithelium damage and cilia loss within 2 days, driven by infection of sustentacular support cells rather than olfactory sensory neurons themselves.
In mice, chemical ablation of olfactory sensory neurons removed the low-resistance CSF pathway and disrupted CSF drainage through the cribriform plate.
In sheep, acute surgical obstruction of the cribriform plate CSF outflow pathway increased resting intracranial pressure, supporting the olfactory pathway as a major CSF drainage route.

In a large ME/CFS clinic cohort, MRI-derived optic nerve sheath/eyeball diameter ratios indicated possible intracranial hypertension in 83% of patients, with 32% showing more severe elevation, versus 5% prevalence of such ratios in the normal population.
Lumbar puncture in 20 CFS patients with prominent headache found CSF pressure above 20 cmH2O in five, with a mean pressure of 19 cmH2O, towards the high end of normal.

CSF withdrawal (lumbar puncture) produced symptomatic improvement — reduced headache, heightened alertness, reduced fatigue — in 85% of CFS patients with headache, including those with normal-range CSF pressures.

A single CFS patient with transverse sinus narrowing typical of IIH experienced a life-changing, sustained remission of headache, fatigue, concentration and pain symptoms after bilateral transverse sinus stenting.
In an online survey of COVID-19 patients, nearly a quarter reported tinnitus, with a small fraction describing it as pulsatile.
In COVID-19 patients, headache was common and persisted at 6 weeks in over a third of cases; headache was significantly associated with concurrent anosmia/ageusia.

In a subset of COVID-19 patients with severe persistent headache, CSF opening pressure was frequently elevated in the absence of meningitis/encephalitis, consistent with an intracranial hypertension-like state.
A human multi-phase MRI tracer study found no significant enrichment of intrathecal CSF tracer in the nasal mucosa, questioning the importance of nasal lymphatic CSF drainage in humans.

A dynamic PET study measuring CSF clearance in humans found significant CSF tracer levels in the superior nasal turbinates, supporting the nasal turbinate as part of the CSF clearance system, consistent with postmortem anatomical findings.

The author's central hypothesis is that SARS-CoV-2-induced death of olfactory sensory neurons increases resistance to CSF outflow through the cribriform plate, causing glymphatic system congestion and toxic CNS build-up that manifests as post-COVID-19 fatigue syndrome, analogous to a subclinical form of idiopathic intracranial hypertension seen in ME/CFS.

The author proposes that osteopathic manipulative therapy (e.g., the Perrin technique) to promote lymphatic/glymphatic drainage could be a treatment approach for ME/CFS and post-COVID-19 fatigue syndrome.
Natural killer cells from chronic fatigue syndrome/myalgic encephalomyelitis patients show reduced TRPM3 expression and altered cytoplasmic calcium flux compared to healthy controls.
Multiple single nucleotide polymorphisms in TRP ion channel genes, including TRPM3, TRPA1 and TRPC4, have been reported in ME/CFS patients.
Reduced natural killer cell cytotoxic activity is described as the most consistently reported immune finding in ME/CFS.
TRPM3 expression is significantly reduced on both NK cells and B lymphocytes in ME/CFS patients, altering cytosolic and stored Ca2+ concentrations and potentially the NK cell activation threshold.
Colonic biopsies from inflammatory bowel disease patients show increased TRPA1+TRPV1+ leukocyte and T cell infiltration, with TRPA1 upregulated and TRPV1 downregulated relative to controls.

Loss-of-function mutations (stop, frameshift, splice-site, exon deletions) in TRPM6 cause primary hypomagnesemia with secondary hypocalcaemia via impaired intestinal magnesium absorption and renal wasting.

TRPM2-deficient mice show improved neurological outcomes and are protected from ischaemic stroke, as TRPM2 in peripheral neutrophils and macrophages promotes migration to ischaemic brain and exacerbates injury.
Capsaicin, a TRPV1 agonist, is used clinically as an analgesic for neuropathic and nociceptive pain, with side effects including altered body temperature and reduced stimulus response.
Resiniferatoxin, a potent TRPV1 agonist, selectively ablates nociceptors when delivered intrathecally and is under phase 1 trials for palliative pain relief with minimal reported side effects.

Cannabidiol, a relatively selective TRPV2 agonist, induces apoptosis in human T24 bladder cancer cells via continuous TRPV2-mediated Ca2+ influx, and is proposed as a potential urothelial carcinoma therapeutic.
Teachers consistently reported cognitive difficulties in their pupils with CFS/ME, including 'foggy head', slowed work pace, poor multitasking, memory and concentration problems.
Teachers consistently noted debilitating fatigue as a core feature of their pupils' presentation of CFS/ME.

Beyond fatigue and cognitive dysfunction, teachers described a heterogeneous range of additional symptoms among pupils with CFS/ME including decreased mobility, pain, nausea, digestive problems, hypersensitivity, headaches and pale complexion.
Teachers described that CFS/ME had a social impact on pupils, including peer stigmatisation and isolation resulting from visible symptoms and restricted activity/absences.
Teachers reported that pupils with CFS/ME showed emotional difficulties including general and school-specific anxiety, low self-esteem, and negative cognitions.

Two of eleven teachers reported not observing any symptoms of illness and expressed scepticism about the CFS/ME diagnosis, with one questioning whether symptoms were stress/anxiety-related rather than physical.
Teachers reported that receiving formal written confirmation of the CFS/ME diagnosis from the clinical service was an important enabler that facilitated implementation of school support.
Teachers negotiated individualised reduced school timetables with families to manage activity and avoid overexertion in pupils with CFS/ME.
Teachers facilitated planned and impromptu rest breaks and provided quiet/comfortable spaces for pupils with CFS/ME to manage fatigue.
Teachers made cognitive/academic accommodations such as simplified tasks, extra time, scribing, and use of iPads to support pupils with cognitive difficulties from CFS/ME.
One teacher described using relaxation and mindfulness meditation via iPad, which the pupil reported as helpful for managing symptoms.

Most teachers reported that their pupil with CFS/ME was not good at verbalising symptoms, feelings, needs and preferences, prompting use of communication aids such as feeling cards and check-in systems.

Most teachers had little to no prior knowledge of CFS/ME and received minimal information or guidance from the clinical team, leading them to base support strategies on intuition rather than formal training.
Some teachers reported using strategies inconsistent with evidence-based CFS/ME management, such as encouraging the child to take naps, due to lack of formal guidance.

None of the interviewed teachers reported using Individual Health Care Plans, a tool mandated by the UK Department of Education to facilitate communication between teachers, families, and health services for children with medical needs.
Widespread brain hypometabolism seen on 18F-FDG PET in a patient/patients with chronic fatigue syndrome reversed (improved) following hyperbaric oxygen therapy.
Vascular EDS most often results from variants in COL3A1, which encodes the pro-alpha1 chain of Type III collagen, disrupting collagen synthesis and structural integrity.
Classical EDS is caused by COL5A1/COL5A2 variants leading to malfunctioning collagen alleles and haploinsufficiency of Type V collagen, compromising fibrillogenesis.
In a minority of hypermobile EDS cases, variants in TNXB and COL3A1 have been reported with autosomal dominant inheritance, though the primary causative gene for hEDS remains unidentified.
Kyphoscoliotic EDS results from deficiency of the FKBP14 enzyme (peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase), affecting Type III, VI, and X collagen, inherited autosomal recessively.
Classical-like EDS is caused by variants in the tenascin XB coding gene (TNXB), inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.
Arthrochalasia EDS is caused by variants in COL1A1 and COL1A2, which encode Type I collagen alpha1 and alpha2 chains, inherited autosomal dominantly.
Dermatosparaxis EDS arises from functional abnormality of procollagen-N-proteinase, associated with the ADAMTS2 gene, affecting procollagen Types I, II, and III.
Spondylodysplastic EDS is caused by variants in B4GALT7, B3GALT6, or SLC39A13, each producing distinct clinical phenotypes, and is inherited autosomal recessively.
Musculocontractural EDS is caused by variants in CHST14 and DSE, inherited autosomal recessively.
Myopathic EDS's causative gene is COL12A1, which controls the alpha chain of Type XII collagen; inheritance can be autosomal dominant or recessive.
Periodontal EDS is an autosomal dominant condition caused by variants of the C1R and C1S genes, affecting the C1r and C1s complement proteins.
Vascular EDS accounts for about 4-5% of all EDS cases and affects approximately 1 in every 50,000 to 250,000 individuals.
Pregnant patients with vascular EDS face a 5% risk of mortality during each pregnancy, particularly due to uterine rupture in the third trimester.
Joint hypermobility, a hallmark feature of hypermobile EDS, is reported to be more common in females than in males.
Psychiatric and psychological symptoms such as anxiety, depression, eating disorders, and drug abuse are reported to be more prevalent in hypermobile EDS compared to other EDS forms.

The authors state that a reported association between MCAS, hypermobile EDS, and POTS is scant and unsubstantiated, with virtually no original research supporting it, and note MCAS is poorly defined and POTS lacks a clearly defined pathogenic mechanism.
Ascorbic acid, a collagen fibril cross-linking cofactor, has been reported to help with wound healing, chronic bruising, and hematoma formation in EDS patients.
Beta-blockers may be beneficial in EDS patients with aortic dilatations and aneurysms.

About 60% of individuals diagnosed with vascular EDS during childhood have a positive family history, while 50% of those without known family history experience major complications by a mean age of 11 years.

hEDS patients' skin fibroblasts exhibit phenotypic features of myofibroblasts, widespread extracellular matrix disarray, and perturbation of ECM-cell contacts, as previously demonstrated by the authors.
Proteomic profiling of 6 hEDS dermal myofibroblasts compared to 12 control fibroblasts revealed differential expression of proteins principally involved in cytoskeleton organization.
Proteome analysis identified differentially expressed proteins related to energy metabolism and redox balance in hEDS dermal myofibroblasts versus controls.
Proteome analysis identified differentially expressed proteins related to proteostasis (protein homeostasis) in hEDS dermal myofibroblasts versus controls.
Proteome analysis identified differentially expressed proteins related to intracellular trafficking in hEDS dermal myofibroblasts versus controls.
Two siblings were diagnosed with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, apparently transmitted from their unaffected mother through maternal germline mosaicism for a COL3A1 variant.

Five unrelated patients presenting with features of connective tissue disorders and a family history consistent with autosomal dominant transmission were found to carry the same heterozygous ADAMTSL2 Gly421Ser missense variant previously reported in a dermatosparaxic EDS family.
Patients with the ADAMTSL2 Gly421Ser variant exhibited generalized joint hypermobility and pain along with fragility of internal and external tissues including skin, dura, and arteries.

A previously reported family with three affected members across two generations displayed features of dermatosparaxic EDS with autosomal dominant transmission, carrying the same heterozygous ADAMTSL2 Gly421Ser missense variant.
Variation in ADAMTSL2 is also known to cause autosomal recessive geleophysic dysplasia, distinct from the dominant connective tissue phenotype described in this report.

Two sibling young adults with periodontal Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (pEDS) had early-onset periodontitis appearing at age 3, which was misdiagnosed for years despite this being a major diagnostic criterion of pEDS.
The report argues that dental practitioners can play a key role in early diagnosis of pEDS by recognizing and responding appropriately to periodontal manifestations at early stages.

Among 62 MFS probands whose parents were tested with both direct sequencing and HRMA, parental somatogonadal mosaicism for the FBN1 disease-causing variant was detected in 3 cases, giving an estimated frequency of 4.8% (95% CI 1.1-13.6%).
The observed frequency of de novo FBN1 variants in this cohort (56.0%, 79/141) was substantially higher than the classically reported ~25% de novo rate for Marfan syndrome.

A paternal somatogonadal mosaicism for a COL5A1 disease-causing variant (c.3179G>A, VAF 11% in blood) was identified in the father of a boy with classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, representing the first reported case of parental mosaicism in COL5A1.
Despite carrying the COL5A1 mosaic variant at 11% VAF in blood, careful clinical examination of the father did not reveal any skeletal, skin, or other diagnostic criteria for classical EDS.

Direct sequencing failed to detect the FBN1 c.3158G>A mosaic variant with the lowest estimated allele fraction (VAF 5-10%, patient M0277), demonstrating limited sensitivity of direct sequencing for low-level mosaicism compared with HRMA and NGS.
In one mosaic parent (M0078), the variant allele frequency for FBN1 c.1095C>A was lower in cheek cells (10%) than in blood cells (20%), indicating tissue-specific variation in mosaicism level.

Modeling by Campbell et al. shows that detecting somatic parental mosaicism in blood is the strongest predictor of sibling recurrence risk in MFS, estimated at 5.21% for a single affected child when mosaicism is detected in a parent, versus 0.048-2.6% when no mosaicism is detected.

Clinical signs tended to be milder in FBN1 mosaic carriers than in fully heterozygous MFS patients; only one of the three mosaic parents reported here (VAF 7%) displayed cardiovascular involvement (mild aortic root dilatation), and the systemic score under the Ghent nosology remained below diagnostic threshold (<7) in all three.

The father (M0277) carried the FBN1 c.3158G>A [p.(Cys1053Tyr)] variant in mosaic state (VAF 7% in blood) located in the exon 24-32 'neonatal region' associated with early-onset MFS, and transmitted it to two children who developed severe early-onset Marfan syndrome, representing the first molecularly proven recurrence of early-onset MFS due to parental mosaicism.

Across this study and prior literature, parental FBN1 mosaicism has been reported in both sexes, with six maternal and four paternal cases identified, suggesting no single sex-specific mitotic mechanism underlies parental mosaicism.
Estimation of variant allele fraction for the four mosaic variants was concordant between HRMA and NGS, with only a 0-6% difference between the two methods.
Half of the 295 MFS probands with available family history data were sporadic (149/295) while half had a family history evocative of MFS (146/295).

In two families with a family history suggestive of MFS in a sibling, parental molecular testing showed the FBN1 variant occurred de novo and was absent in the suspected affected relative, resolving diagnostic uncertainty since neither relative displayed major MFS signs on Ghent nosology re-evaluation.
A significantly higher proportion of persons with EDS had prescription claims for at least one GI drug group compared to matched controls.
Among children, 25.7% of those with EDS had GI drug prescription claims compared to 7.4% of matched controls.
Among adults, 45.1% of those with EDS had GI drug prescription claims compared to 21.0% of matched controls.
Women with EDS had a 44.0% rate of GI drug prescription claims compared to 19.2% in matched female controls.
Men with EDS had a 25.3% rate of GI drug prescription claims compared to 9.6% in matched male controls.

EDS patients had significantly higher prescription claims than controls for drugs in each of four categories studied: acid suppressants, anti-emetics, irritable bowel syndrome drugs, and visceral hypersensitivity medications.
Predominant GI medication burden occurs among women with EDS, with onset beginning peri-pubertally for anti-emetic and visceral hypersensitivity drug use.
Small nerve fiber pathology has been described in a sizable subgroup of fibromyalgia patients, supporting a neuropathic-autonomic basis for the disease.
Fibromyalgia overlaps clinically with ME/CFS, POTS, gulf war illness, macrophagic myofasciitis, and post-HPV vaccination syndrome, suggesting shared pathophysiology.
The authors previously reported that the DRG sodium channel Nav1.7 rs6754031 GG genotype is associated with severe fibromyalgia.
Fibromyalgia patients exhibit norepinephrine-evoked pain, implicating sympathetic-nociceptive crosstalk.

After moderate exercise, ME/CFS patients with comorbid fibromyalgia showed greater increases than healthy controls in gene expression of metabolite-sensing DRG receptors ASIC3 and P2X purinoreceptors 4 and 5.
ME/CFS patients had increased expression of adrenergic receptor genes (alpha-2A, beta-1, beta-2), COMT, and immune genes IL-10 and TLR4 after exercise, unlike normal subjects.
A pilot postmortem study of four ME/CFS patients found DRG inflammation in three of them.

IgG from fibromyalgia patients, but not from controls, induced hyperalgesia in mice and was found robustly localized to DRG satellite glial cells, fiber tracts, and macrophages, but not brain or spinal cord.
Small fiber neuropathy has been described in approximately half of fibromyalgia patients, providing the most robust evidence linking fibromyalgia to DRG pathology.
In fibromyalgia patients without marked anxiety or depression, corneal denervation strongly correlates with small fiber neuropathy symptom burden.
MRI of human DRG shows significantly increased permeability and interstitial leakage compared to spinal nerves, particularly in the nuclei-rich area.
Female gender is associated with significantly increased DRG vascular permeability compared to male on MRI.

Magnetic resonance neurography has consistently demonstrated increased DRG perfusion in patients with painful neuropathy associated with Sjogren's syndrome, Fabry disease, and oxaliplatin-induced polyneuropathy.
MRI assessment of DRG volume has not shown adequate clinical-pathological correlation, in contrast to perfusion measures.
DRG stimulation has been reported to reduce sympathetic muscle nerve traffic, which may benefit fibromyalgia patients via lowered sympathetic outflow.
In a rat hind-limb injury model, DRG stimulation decreased BOLD fMRI activity in pain-related brain areas.

In mice, sound stress exposure caused long-lasting hyperalgesia associated with lysophosphatidylcholine 16:0 overexpression, which triggered nociceptive signaling via ASIC3 activation and DRG phospho-ERK upregulation.

In rodents, sciatic nerve ligation leads to DRG sympathetic sprouting via nerve growth factor overexpression, creating abnormal sympathetic-nociceptive connections in which norepinephrine induces pain.
DRG Nav1.8 sodium channels have been shown to modulate lymphocyte trafficking, linking DRG to immune-nociceptive crosstalk.
DRG sensory neurons can sequester antigen-specific antibodies released by plasma cells, potentially explaining immune-mediated hyperalgesia despite DRG lacking antibody-producing machinery.
Human DRG neurons express the SARS-CoV-2 receptor ACE2, which is speculatively proposed to explain post-COVID-19 chronic pain and fatigue.
Dorsal root ganglionitis with neuropathic pain is a well-recognized complication of Sjogren's syndrome.
Autoimmune disorders including Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Sjogren's syndrome, and lupus frequently coexist with fibromyalgia.
In rare instances, vaccination has been reported to induce a severe fibromyalgia-like illness.

TRPV1 channel expression was found to be upregulated in the prefrontal cortex, somatosensory cortex, hippocampus and thalamus in an intermittent cold-stress model of fibromyalgia-like pain, suggesting a central role in sustained hyperalgesia.

TRPV1 gene deletion (knockout) mice were used to determine that the TRPV1 receptor plays a functional role in the development and expression of fibromyalgia-like pain in the intermittent cold-stress model.

Electroacupuncture (EA) applied bilaterally at the ST36 acupoint successfully attenuated both mechanical and thermal hyperalgesia in the fibromyalgia-like pain model, indicating an analgesic effect likely mediated through neuromodulation.
Across 13 meteorological studies examining ambient temperature and fibromyalgia pain, the majority (9 of 13) found no uniform relationship between temperature and pain.
All 17 QST studies assessing cold pain thresholds found numerically reduced CPTs in fibromyalgia patients compared with controls, with this difference statistically significant in 14 of 17 studies.
Beyond cold pain thresholds, other thermal thresholds (e.g. warm detection/pain thresholds) were often found to be abnormal in fibromyalgia patients relative to controls in QST studies.

The review concludes that the literature provides consistent evidence for abnormal sensitization of the temperature-sensation system in fibromyalgia patients, with a subgroup perceiving low ambient temperatures as painful.

Independent Component Analysis of resting-state fMRI showed a significant reduction in functional connectivity across several component pairs, with the largest changes involving the retrosplenial cortex, a central node of the default mode network.
The periaqueductal gray, a key pain-processing area, also showed reduced functional connectivity, though to a lesser extent than the retrosplenial cortex.

Seed-to-seed analysis of 14 pain-related brain areas showed the strongest functional connectivity reduction for the retrosplenial cortex with several cortical areas, including somatosensory, prefrontal, and insular cortex.

Seed-to-seed analysis showed that the periaqueductal gray had reduced functional connectivity with somatosensory cortex as well as subcortical structures including habenula, thalamus, and parabrachial nucleus.
Functional connectivity between the retrosplenial cortex and periaqueductal gray was reduced, and this reduction tended to positively correlate with individual subject pain levels.
Seed-voxelwise analysis focused on the periaqueductal gray confirmed prior seed-to-seed findings and additionally detected reduced PAG functional connectivity with the anterior cingulate cortex.
Intracellular calcium mobilization following IgE/antigen stimulation was significantly reduced in mast cells from NHERF1+/- mice compared to wild-type.
Activation of MAPKs ERK1/2 and P38 after FcεRI stimulation was significantly reduced in NHERF1+/- mast cells relative to wild-type.
Cytokine production of IL-13 and IL-6 following IgE/antigen exposure was significantly reduced in NHERF1+/- mast cells.
Mast cell-mediated passive cutaneous anaphylaxis was reduced in NHERF1+/- mice compared to wild-type mice.
Passive systemic anaphylaxis was reduced in both NHERF1+/- mice and in mast cell-deficient KitW-sh/W-sh mice engrafted with NHERF1+/- mast cells.
Levels of miRNA 155-3p and miRNA 155-5p, which regulate mast cell responses, were altered in mast cells from NHERF1+/- mice.
NHERF1 rapidly localized to the nucleus of mast cells following FcεRI stimulation.
NHERF1 acts as an adapter molecule that promotes IgE/antigen-induced mast cell activation via FcεRI signaling.

Radiolabeled Ara h 1, Ara h 2, and β-lactoglobulin were transported across pig intestinal epithelium at similarly low rates (0.1-0.4% of applied dose) with no significant differences between proteins.
All four apical (non-transported) peanut allergens activated basophils sensitized with peanut-allergic patient serum, whereas the negative control β-lactoglobulin did not.
After transport across the intestinal epithelium, Ara h 1 lost its ability to activate basophils, with a significant drop compared to non-transported apical Ara h 1.
Ara h 3 similarly lost its capacity to activate basophils after intestinal epithelial transport.
Ara h 2 retained basophil-activating capacity after intestinal epithelial transport, with no significant difference between apical and basolateral samples.
Ara h 6 similarly retained basophil-activating capacity after intestinal epithelial transport with no significant apical-basolateral difference.

Pepsin digestion rapidly fragmented the major bands of Ara h 1 (64 kDa) and Ara h 3 (45/42/23 kDa) within 15 seconds, but IgE from peanut-allergic patients still bound to the resulting peptide fragments on immunoblot.
All pepsin digestion time-point mixtures of Ara h 1, 2, 3, and 6 retained the ability to activate basophils in the in-BAT assay across three patient sera.

Ara h 1 digested for 60 minutes prior to intestinal transport elicited significantly higher mast cell degranulation than Ara h 1 digested for 0 seconds, though not significantly different from 30-second digestion.
Ara h 3 digested for 60 minutes prior to transport produced significantly higher mast cell degranulation than either 30-second or 0-second digestion.
Digestion time did not significantly affect Ara h 2's ability to activate mast cells after epithelial transport.
Digestion time did not significantly affect Ara h 6's ability to activate mast cells after epithelial transport.

The authors hypothesize that Ara h 1 and 3 are preferentially degraded by lysosomal proteases during transcellular enterocyte transport, destroying IgE-binding epitopes and explaining their loss of allergenicity after transport, supported by prior dendritic cell phago-lysosomal degradation data.

The authors propose that small pepsin-digested fragments of Ara h 1 (<5 kDa) may cross the epithelium via paracellular transport, bypassing lysosomal degradation, and may re-aggregate in the intestinal alkaline environment to form new immunoreactive epitopes, explaining restored mast cell activation after digestion plus transport.
Neonatal maternal separation triggered activation of mast cells in the hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus (PVN) and induced visceral hypersensitivity in adult rats.
Intra-PVN infusion of the mast cell stabilizer cromolyn repressed maternal separation-induced PVN mast cell activation and visceral hypersensitivity.
Mast cell-deficient KitW-sh/W-sh mice did not develop chronic visceral hypersensitivity following neonatal maternal separation, unlike wild-type mice.
Maternal separation increased expression of proinflammatory mediators, the number of CRF-positive cells, and CRF protein levels in the PVN, and these increases were prevented by intra-PVN cromolyn.

Intra-PVN infusion of the mast cell degranulator compound 48/80 induced mast cell activation, proinflammatory mediator release, CRF neuronal sensitization, and visceral hypersensitivity, all of which were suppressed by cromolyn.
Lyn, a Src-family tyrosine kinase, has both positive and negative regulatory roles in the IgE/FcεRI signaling pathway and is essential for mast cell activation via its interaction with FcεRIβ.

Pediatric patients with maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis (MPCM) appear to have a higher rate of vaccination reactions attributable to mast cell activation than the general population, though the reactions were mild.
Mast cell-specific mediators and adrenomedullin, the proteolytic precursor of the MRGPRX2 agonist PAMP-12, are upregulated in inflamed compared to uninflamed regions of ulcerative colitis tissue.

MRGPRX2 stimulation of lamina propria cells induces carboxypeptidase secretion specifically from inflamed ulcerative colitis tissue, indicating functional MRGPRX2-mediated mast cell degranulation in active disease.

Among all protein-altering GPCR variants tested in an Ashkenazi Jewish UC case-control cohort, the MRGPRX2 Asn62Ser variant was the allele most strongly associated with UC and was bioinformatically predicted to alter arrestin recruitment.

Functional validation in transfected CHO and HMC1.1 cells showed the UC-protective serine (Ser62) allele of MRGPRX2 enhances beta-arrestin recruitment, decreases IP-1 accumulation, and increases phosphorylated ERK in response to MRGPRX2 agonists, consistent with decreased downstream mast cell activation.
Single-cell RNA sequencing showed that adrenomedullin, an MRGPRX2 agonist precursor, is expressed by activated fibroblasts and epithelial cells in inflamed UC tissue.
Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis identified interferon gamma as a key upstream regulator of mast cell gene expression in ulcerative colitis tissue.
In mice, bacterial infection and bacterial toxins triggered an immune response producing dietary-antigen-specific IgE antibodies that were confined to the intestine.
Oral ingestion of the sensitizing dietary antigen induced increased visceral pain through an IgE- and mast-cell-dependent mechanism in mice.
Aberrant visceral pain signalling resulted from histamine receptor H1-mediated sensitization of visceral afferent neurons.
In patients with irritable bowel syndrome, injection of food antigens (gluten, wheat, soy and milk) into the rectosigmoid mucosa produced local oedema and mast cell activation.
At day 6 post-infection, C57BL/6 mice had significantly higher numbers of parasitic adults in the small intestine than BALB/c mice, replicating prior reports.
F1 (BALB/c x C57BL/6) mice showed intestinal S. ratti burden similar to BALB/c mice and lower than C57BL/6 mice, indicating BALB/c-like inheritance of the resistance phenotype.
Infection with S. ratti increased the frequency of Foxp3+ Treg cells in F1 and C57BL/6 mice but not in BALB/c mice compared to naive mice.
CD49b+LAG-3+Foxp3- type 1 regulatory (Tr1) T cell frequency expanded in all three infected mouse genotypes (BALB/c, F1, C57BL/6) compared to non-infected controls.
Infected C57BL/6 mice had markedly lower total numbers of CD4+ T cells in mesenteric lymph nodes than infected BALB/c and F1 mice.
Absolute numbers of Foxp3+ Treg in mesenteric lymph nodes were lower in infected C57BL/6 mice compared to infected BALB/c and F1 mice.
Foxp3+ Treg from C57BL/6 mice expressed higher levels of CTLA-4, BTLA(high), CD49b and VISTA than Treg from BALB/c mice, with F1 mice showing intermediate or BALB/c-like expression.
PD-1 expression on Foxp3+ Treg was not induced by S. ratti infection but was constitutively lowest in F1 mice and significantly higher in Treg from infected BALB/c and C57BL/6 mice.
LAG-3 expression on Foxp3+ Treg was not altered by murine genotype or by S. ratti infection.

ILT3 expression by Foxp3+ Treg was already higher at steady state in C57BL/6 mice and remained significantly higher than BALB/c and F1 mice during infection, while infection did not alter ILT3 expression in BALB/c or F1 Treg.
Among Foxp3- CD4+ T effector cells, expression of CTLA-4, BTLA(high), CD49b, LAG-3 and PD-1 was highest in C57BL/6 mice, lowest in BALB/c mice, with F1 mice showing intermediate levels.
VISTA expression on Foxp3- CD4+ T cells was similar across BALB/c, F1 and C57BL/6 mice and was not upregulated by S. ratti infection in any strain.

ILT3 expression by Foxp3- CD4+ T cells from C57BL/6 mice was higher at steady state and increased further with infection, remaining significantly higher than in BALB/c and F1 mice, whose ILT3 levels were unchanged by infection.
TIM-3 was barely detectable on Treg and Foxp3- T cells and its expression level was similar across BALB/c, F1 and C57BL/6 mice.

Transient diphtheria-toxin-mediated Treg depletion in DEREG mice improved eradication of S. ratti (reduced worm burden) in BALB/c and F1 mice, but C57BL/6 DEREG mice did not benefit from Treg depletion.

Treg depletion increased serum mast-cell-specific protease mMCPT-1 (indicating mast cell degranulation) in BALB/c and F1 DEREG mice, but mMCPT-1 levels were comparable between Treg-depleted and non-depleted C57BL/6 DEREG mice.

Despite increased type 2 immune responses and elevated S. ratti-specific IL-9 production in Treg-depleted C57BL/6 mice, this was not sufficient to trigger increased mast cell activation or accelerate parasite clearance, suggesting additional regulatory layers compensate for Treg loss in C57BL/6 mice.
Omalizumab is described as the standard of care for chronic spontaneous urticaria patients unresponsive to H1 antihistamines.
IL-5 pathway blockade is highlighted as a promising emerging therapeutic target with sufficient data to advance to later-stage clinical trials in patients unresponsive to omalizumab.

Mast cell activation, triggered by factors such as infections, drugs and food, along with immune system alterations, is proposed as the main driver of increased vascular permeability and inflammatory cell extravasation in urticaria.

Emerging biomarkers are reported to correlate with severity and/or prognosis of chronic spontaneous urticaria and can help differentiate it from disorders such as vasculitis and autoinflammatory diseases.
A patient with extremely severe anaphylaxis to paper wasp venom was found to carry a mutation (P542R) in the KARS gene encoding lysyl-tRNA synthetase.
Biochemical and structural analyses showed that the P542R mutation alters the subcellular location of LysRS compared to wild-type protein.

The P542R mutation resembles constitutively active LysRS and causes constitutive activation of the microphthalmia transcription factor (MITF), which regulates mast cell mediator synthesis and granule biogenesis.
The aberrant LysRS-P542R function was linked to exacerbated mast cell activation with increased release of proinflammatory mediators following antigen-IgE-dependent stimulation.

Oral administration of 300 mg/kg ethanol extract of Bombyx mori pupa-incubated Cordyceps militaris significantly alleviated sneezing/scratching, mast cell activation, eosinophil infiltration, and Syk activation in an ovalbumin-induced allergic rhinitis mouse model.
Treatment with the ethanol extract significantly suppressed the release of β-hexosaminidase, a marker of mast cell degranulation, in activated RBL2H3 cells.
The ethanol extract significantly suppressed mRNA expression levels of IL-3, IL-10, and IL-13 in activated RBL2H3 mast cells.
Both the ethanol extract and its purified constituent β-sitostenone reduced Ca2+ ion mobilization in activated RBL-2H3 mast cells.
Western immunoblotting demonstrated that the ethanol extract significantly retarded the Ca2+ ion mobilization-initiated signaling cascade that provokes expression of allergic cytokines.
The extract interfered with p38 activation as part of its inhibitory effect on mast cell signaling.
The extract interfered with NF-kB activation as part of its inhibitory effect on mast cell signaling.
The extract interfered with Nrf-2 nuclear translocation as part of its inhibitory effect on mast cell signaling.
Among asthmatics with concordant systemic and airway eosinophilia, the largest subgroup (45%) had raised total serum IgE together with atopy.
IgE-low non-atopic concordant eosinophilic asthma was characterized by predominantly late-onset disease with more intense airway eosinophilic inflammation compared to the IgE-high atopic group.
Patients with IgE-low non-atopic eosinophilic asthma required maintenance oral corticosteroid treatment more often than the IgE-high atopic group.

Despite more severe airway eosinophilic inflammation, IgE-low non-atopic asthmatics showed reduced bronchial hyperresponsiveness to methacholine compared to the IgE-high atopic group, despite similar baseline airway calibre impairment.

The authors conclude that the more severe airway eosinophilic inflammation in IgE-low non-atopic asthmatics, despite similar inhaled corticosteroid treatment and higher oral corticosteroid burden, suggests a degree of corticosteroid resistance in this asthma phenotype.
Imperatorin reduced substance P-induced calcium flux and suppressed mast cell degranulation.
Substance P promotes phosphorylation of ERK and CamKII in mast cells, which regulates synthesis of inflammatory factors such as MIP-2 and TNF-α.
Imperatorin ameliorates mast cell-mediated allergic airway inflammation by inhibiting MRGPRX2 and the CaMKII/ERK signaling pathway.

In mouse models, imperatorin mitigated substance P-induced passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) and active systemic anaphylaxis (ASA), indicating suppression of IgE-independent (pseudo-allergic) mast cell responses.
Imperatorin mitigated lung inflammation in an ovalbumin-induced allergic asthma mouse model by inhibiting mast cell activation in lung tissue.
Imperatorin binds directly to the MRGPRX2 protein with a binding constant (KD) of 4.48 ± 0.49 × 10^-7 M, as determined by surface plasmon resonance and supported by molecular docking.
Diabetic peripheral sensory neuropathy (DPN) affects up to 50% of people with long-standing diabetes and is the most common presentation of diabetic neuropathy.
Over the past 50 years, numerous agents have failed in trials aimed at treating diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN) as a disease-modifying therapy.
Several approved agents can relieve pain from diabetic neuropathy but do not alter the underlying pathologic disease process.

The authors attribute the failure to develop disease-modifying diabetic neuropathy treatments to complex trial design and the slow disease progression requiring long-duration trials to demonstrate efficacy.

The authors propose modifying regulatory processes to allow early introduction of agents with demonstrated safety and suggested benefit, alongside extended marketing exclusivity while long-term efficacy trials continue.
In vivo corneal confocal microscopy showed no significant differences in corneal nerve fiber length or branch density between PD patients with RLS, PD patients without RLS, and controls.
UENS scores, a clinical measure sensitive to small fiber neuropathy, were significantly higher in both PD groups compared to controls, but did not differ between PD patients with and without RLS.
No difference in UENS scores was found between PD patients with and without RLS, indicating small fiber neuropathy signs were not associated with RLS status.
QST (small fiber function) and NCS (large fiber function) showed no significant differences between PD+RLS, PD-RLS, and control groups.

Densities of mature dendritic cells, immature dendritic cells, and globular cells in the corneal subbasal nerve plexus did not differ significantly between PD+RLS, PD-RLS, and controls, arguing against corneal immune activation in PD.

A borderline-significant difference in the proportion of globular cells among the three groups suggested a possible increase in PD+RLS relative to PD-RLS and controls, though the biological meaning is unclear.
Among PD patients, longer duration of l-dopa therapy was associated with lower corneal nerve branch density and fiber length, with CNBD remaining significant after adjusting for age and sex.

Plasma neurofilament light (p-NfL), a marker of axonal degeneration, correlated negatively with the electroneurography index (indicating worse large fiber function with higher p-NfL) after adjusting for age and sex.

Plasma NfL correlated positively with UENS scores (worse peripheral neuropathy signs) after adjusting for age and sex, suggesting a link between axonal degeneration marker and clinical small fiber neuropathy scale.
Modified Hoehn and Yahr stage, indicating more advanced PD, correlated with worse warmth and cold perception thresholds in the hand after adjustment for age and sex.
Levels of vitamin B6, MMA, folate, and homocysteine did not differ significantly between PD+RLS, PD-RLS, and controls, and were within normal range overall.

In a subgroup analysis of all PD patients, peripheral nerve parameters (corneal, electrophysiological, clinical) did not differ significantly between those taking versus not taking B-vitamin/multivitamin supplements, despite the supplemented group having significantly longer disease and l-dopa duration.
Plasma NfL correlated significantly with modified Hoehn and Yahr stage after adjustment for age and sex, suggesting NfL may reflect both central and peripheral axonal neurodegeneration in PD.
PD patients with RLS had significantly higher (worse) modified Hoehn and Yahr disease severity stage rank compared to PD patients without RLS.

A majority (81%) of PD+RLS patients had a positive sensory suggested immobilization test, supporting the reliability of RLS diagnosis in this cohort even though not all patients were tested during an active symptomatic period.
The main finding of the study is that small fiber neuropathy (assessed by IVCCM, QST, and UENS) and large fiber neuropathy (assessed by NCS) are not associated with RLS status in Parkinson's disease.
CGRP treatment of mast cells altered expression of 29 genes, with 28 upregulated and only 1 downregulated.

Bioinformatics analysis showed that the higher-ranked DEGs following CGRP treatment were enriched for genes involved in response to corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), transcriptional regulation, and mast cell activation/proliferation.

Nr4a3 was verified as upregulated by CGRP treatment via Western blot and was the predominant gene overexpressed in colonic mast cells located near CGRP-containing fibers in water-avoidance stress mice.
Although Crem was verified as a CGRP-responsive DEG by Western blot in vitro, it showed little to no expression in colonic mast cells near CGRP-containing fibers in WAS mice in vivo.
Gpr35 was confirmed as a CGRP-responsive DEG by Western blot in vitro but showed little to no expression in colonic mast cells near CGRP-containing fibers in WAS mice in vivo.
FosB was confirmed as a CGRP-responsive DEG by Western blot in vitro but showed little to no expression in colonic mast cells near CGRP-containing fibers in WAS mice in vivo.
Sphk1 (referred to as Sphlk1) was confirmed as a CGRP-responsive DEG by Western blot in vitro but showed little to no expression in colonic mast cells near CGRP-containing fibers in WAS mice in vivo.

Bioinformatics analysis of the CGRP-induced DEGs in mast cells showed enrichment for genes involved in response to corticotropin-releasing hormone, regulation of transcription, mast cell activation, and mast cell proliferation, overlapping with genes implicated in stress-induced mast cell activation in IBS.

In colonic tissue from water-avoidance stress-induced visceral hyperalgesia mice, the majority of mast cells located near CGRP-containing nerve fibers overexpressed Nr4a3, while showing little to no expression of FosB, Gpr35, Sphk1, or Crem.
Knockdown of Nr4a3 reduced the CGRP-induced increase in mast cell viability, indicating Nr4a3 mediates CGRP's promotion of mast cell activity.
Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) treatment restored gut Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes phyla levels in hypertensive rats to levels similar to normotensive controls.
MMF increased acetate- and lactate-producing gut bacteria to levels comparable with normotensive WKY rats.
MMF increased the abundance of butyrate-producing gut bacteria in hypertensive rats.
MMF increased the percentage of anaerobic bacteria in the gut of hypertensive rats.
Improvement of gut dysbiosis by MMF was associated with enhanced colonic integrity in hypertensive rats.
MMF treatment was associated with decreased sympathetic nervous system drive in the gut of hypertensive rats.
MMF inhibited neuroinflammation in the hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus (PVN) in hypertensive rats.
MMF treatment increased the proportion of regulatory T cells in the mesenteric lymph nodes of SHR, which had been lower prior to treatment.
MMF treatment altered Th17 and Th1 cell infiltration in the aorta of SHR, coinciding with improved vascular immune profile.
MMF treatment improved aortic endothelial function in spontaneously hypertensive rats.
MMF treatment reduced systolic blood pressure in spontaneously hypertensive rats.
Diurnal fluctuations in salivary cortisol were linked to pain, which was associated with peaks of increased stress in FM patients.
In women with FM, higher salivary cortisol levels were directly related to the presence of depression.
Early-stage FM was associated with greater cortisol release compared to healthy individuals.
A meta-analysis of 28 studies comparing saliva, serum, and urine cortisol between women with FM and healthy women found low cortisol levels associated with FM due to HPA axis alterations.
The reduction in salivary cortisol levels in FM patients was found to be greater with longer disease duration.
Several studies described significantly increased salivary alpha-amylase (sAA) levels in patients with FM, an adrenergic biomarker of SAM axis stimulation.
Ahmadi-Motamayel et al. and Vahedi et al. found a correlation between pain intensity and sAA level, suggesting utility as a pain-intensity biomarker.
Fischer et al. found that the relationship between momentary stress and pain in FM patients was mediated by cortisol but not by alpha-amylase.
Attempts to reduce salivary alpha-amylase levels in FM patients using music therapy or physical activity as stress-control strategies were unsuccessful.
Bazzichi et al. observed transaldolase overexpression in saliva of women with FM using 2-DE and Western blot, potentially reflecting increased tissue oxidative stress.
Thermal treatments (balneotherapy or mud therapy) had no effect on transaldolase expression in women with FM.
Ciregia et al. confirmed increased transaldolase expression in FM patients via 2-DE, but this increase did not distinguish FM from migraine.
Bazzichi et al. demonstrated PGM1 overexpression in FM patients using ELISA and Western blot.
Ciregia et al. found PGM1 to be a good biomarker of FM but also increased in patients with migraine, limiting specificity.
PGM1 expression was markedly decreased in FM patients after 12 weeks of mud-balneotherapy, unlike transaldolase which was unaffected.

Bazzichi et al. found overexpression of calgranulin A and C (S100A8/S100A12) in saliva of FM patients versus healthy individuals, confirmed by mass spectrometry in Giacomelli et al., possibly reflecting a protective role against oxidative stress.
Cyclophilin A is overexpressed in women with FM, possibly secreted by smooth muscle cells and macrophages in response to oxidative stress.
Rho GDP-dissociation inhibitor 2, which regulates cell morphology and motility, is overexpressed in women with FM.
Proteasome subunit-alpha-type-2, related to intracellular protein proteolysis, is overexpressed in women with FM.
Haptoglobin-related protein precursor, involved in innate immune response, is overexpressed in women with FM although its mechanism of action is unknown.
CRP has been proposed as a biomarker of FM providing information on inflammatory status, though its role in FM remains poorly understood.
Elevated IL-1β and IL-1 receptor antagonist levels have been reported in serum, and increased IL-1β in skin samples, of FM patients.
Cê et al. did not observe altered IL-1β salivary levels in patients with fibromyalgia.
Many studies described increased serum/plasma IL-6 levels in FM patients, correlated with pain intensity, and elevated in skin biopsies and PBMCs, related to hyperalgesia, fatigue, and depression.
Geiss et al. described increased IL-6 levels with pressure pain stimulation at tender points in women with FM, associated with pain and fatigue.
IL-8 elevation in serum is well documented in FM patients and has been related to reflex sympathetic pain and pain severity; Kadetoff et al. found elevated IL-8 in serum and cerebrospinal fluid.
Kutu et al. found no significant differences in serum IL-8 levels between FM patients and controls, but levels were related to pain severity.
Elevated IL-10 levels in the serum of FM patients led to its proposal as an FM biomarker, though some authors found no relationship between this cytokine and FM.
Elevated serum IL-17 levels have been widely reported in FM patients and related to anxiety and pain.

Elevated TNF-α levels in serum or skin biopsies have been related to FM presence, with a positive correlation to pain severity reported by Kutu et al., although other authors found no significant serum TNF-α differences between FM patients and controls.
Higher serum chemokine levels have been observed in patients with FM than in healthy individuals, implicating chemokines in peripheral/central sensitization and FM pathogenesis.
In wild-type cells, TGF-β/Activin stimulation induces rapid degradation of SKI and its paralog SKIL within one hour, which is blocked by the TGFBR1 inhibitor SB-431542.
CRISPR/Cas9 deletion of SMAD4 in HEK293T and HaCaT cells abolished ligand-induced SKI/SKIL degradation, showing SMAD4 is required for this process.
Knockout of SMAD2 and SMAD3, individually or together, confirmed these R-SMADs are absolutely required and act redundantly for TGF-β/Activin-induced degradation of SKI and SKIL.
SMAD4 mutants D351H and D537Y, which cannot bind phosphorylated R-SMADs, failed to rescue TGF-β-induced SKIL degradation in SMAD4-null cells, despite retaining SKIL binding.
SMAD4 mutants A433E and I435Y, designed to abolish SKI/SKIL binding via the SAND domain interface, retained R-SMAD binding but likewise failed to rescue TGF-β-induced SKIL degradation.

Reintroduction of wild-type SMAD4 into SMAD4-null HaCaT cells restored TGF-β-induced SKIL degradation, causing a 50% reduction in SKIL protein by Western blot and a 52% reduction by flow cytometry after 1 hr of TGF-β treatment.
SGS mutations introduced into the SKI 11-45 peptide abolished binding of PSMAD2, PSMAD3, and consequently SMAD4, in peptide pulldown assays.

A mutational peptide array screening all substitutions across SKI residues 19-35 identified eight residues intolerant to substitution for PSMAD3-SMAD4 binding, six of which correspond to known SGS disease mutation sites.

Crystal structure of the SKI N-terminal peptide bound to a phosphorylated SMAD2 MH2 domain trimer (resolved at 2.0 Å, PDB 6ZVQ) revealed the SKI peptide binds a three-helix bundle only accessible in the trimeric phosphorylated state, explaining phospho-trimer-specific recognition, with binding affinity in the low nanomolar range (Kd 1.33 nM).

CRISPR knockin of the SGS mutation P35S into SKI in HEK293T cells severely compromised binding to phosphorylated SMAD2 while leaving SMAD4 binding intact, and rendered SKI protein completely resistant to Activin-induced degradation, whereas SKIL degradation was unaffected in these cells.
Unlike WT SKI, which loses DNA binding at SBE sites after Activin stimulation, P35S mutant SKI remains bound to SMAD-binding elements together with SMAD4 even after ligand stimulation.
