P35S SKI knockin HEK293T cells showed significantly reduced Activin-induced CAGA12-Luciferase (PSMAD3-SMAD4-dependent) reporter activity compared to parental cells, while BMP4-induced BRE-Luciferase activity (SKI/SKIL-independent) was unaffected, demonstrating attenuated TGF-β/Activin transcriptional output caused by SGS mutation.
Introducing the SGS-equivalent mutation G103V into SKIL reduced SMAD2 binding (residual binding was via SMAD4) and rendered SKIL resistant to Activin-induced degradation.

In dermal fibroblasts from two SGS patients (heterozygous L32V or ΔS94-97 SKI mutations), SKI protein remained relatively stable after TGF-β stimulation, whereas in healthy control fibroblasts SKI was abrogated within 1 hr, though the effect was incomplete due to heterozygosity.

RNA-seq of SGS patient (L32V) fibroblasts showed that 60% of genes significantly induced/repressed by 1 hr TGF-β in healthy fibroblasts were less efficiently regulated in mutant cells, and after 8 hr, 75% (3556 of 4769) of genes were less efficiently regulated, with a substantial subset showing no significant response at all.

The authors conclude that SGS mutations in SKI cause attenuated, not excessive, TGF-β/Activin signaling, contradicting the prior assumption that loss-of-function mutations in a negative regulator (SKI) would increase TGF-β signaling in Marfan-related syndromes.
LPA acting through the LPA2 receptor activates a Gα-αβ-integrin-TGFB1 pathway that increases PDGFB and CTGF production and secretion by proximal tubule cells.
LPA2, β-integrin, PDGFB, and CTGF levels increase in kidneys after ischemia-reperfusion injury, coinciding with the development of fibrosis.
The TGFB1 receptor antagonist SD-208 prevents post-IRI increases in β-integrin, TGFB1-SMAD signaling, and PDGFB/CTGF expression and ameliorates renal fibrosis.
LPA1 receptor signaling through EGFR-ERK1/2-activator protein-1 cooperates with LPA2-dependent TGFB1 signaling to additively increase PDGFB/CTGF production and secretion in proximal tubule cells.

Combined inhibition of both LPA1 and LPA2 pathways produces greater suppression of PDGFB/CTGF production/secretion and greater proximal tubule cell differentiation than inhibiting either pathway alone.

Combined inhibition of both LPA1 and LPA2 signaling pathways produced greater suppression of PDGFB/CTGF secretion and promoted greater proximal tubule cellular differentiation than blocking either pathway alone.
Antagonism of the LPA-generating enzyme autotaxin suppressed signaling through both the LPA1 and LPA2 pathways, and autotaxin protein was increased in kidneys after ischemia-reperfusion injury.

After ischemia-reperfusion injury, kidneys showed increased LPA1 and autotaxin proteins together with enhanced EGFR/ERK1/2 activation, in addition to previously known increases in LPA2, nuclear SMAD2/3, and PDGFB/CTGF.
The TGFB1 receptor antagonist SD-208 prevented all IRI-induced signaling abnormalities except the increase in LPA2, indicating it inhibits only the LPA2-Gα-αβ-integrin-dependent arm of LPA signaling.

The authors propose translational potential for concurrent use of TGFB1 receptor antagonists with LPA1 and LPA2 inhibitors, and autotaxin inhibitors, in acute kidney injury to prevent progression to chronic kidney disease.
L. plantarum CCFM8610 administration significantly reduced colonic IL-1β expression in the IBS mouse model, an effect not seen with the other seven tested strains.
L. plantarum CCFM8610 significantly reduced colonic IL-6 expression in the IBS mouse model.
L. plantarum CCFM8610 significantly reduced colonic PAR-2 (protease-activated receptor 2) expression in the IBS mouse model, a receptor implicated in visceral hypersensitivity.
L. plantarum CCFM8610 significantly reduced mast cell tryptase expression in the IBS mouse model.
L. plantarum CCFM8610 treatment significantly increased intestinal barrier function in the IBS mouse model.
L. plantarum CCFM8610 inhibited visceral hypersensitivity symptoms in the IBS mouse model.
L. plantarum CCFM8610 modulated gut microbiota diversity and composition in the IBS mouse model.
Among physiological characteristics of Lactobacillus strains, the ability to synthesize conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) was the factor most strongly correlated with IBS-alleviating effects.
Comparative genomic analysis identified COG1028-related functional genes as the genetic feature most strongly associated with the IBS-alleviating effects of Lactobacillus strains.

Among eight tested Lactobacillus strains, only L. plantarum CCFM8610 significantly reduced inflammatory and hypersensitivity markers, indicating strain-specific IBS-alleviating effects rather than a general Lactobacillus effect.

A 31-year-old woman with sacroiliac joint dysfunction and temporomandibular joint disorder was treated with neural therapy using lidocaine injections to the TMJ, masseter muscle, and C4 segmental level, resulting in reduced back pain and TMJ tenderness maintained over 3 months.
The paper suggests a possible relationship between temporomandibular joint dysfunction and sacroiliac joint dysfunction, though this link remains unclear.
Vasoconstriction response to cold showed a significant inverse correlation with gastric emptying time (GET TS50), decreasing as gastric emptying delay worsened.
Finger capillary pulse response to positional changes (PAR) showed a significant inverse correlation with gastric emptying time, decreasing with delayed gastric emptying.
Gastric myoelectrical activity measured by EGG showed a significant inverse correlation with gastric emptying time, decreasing with delayed gastric emptying.

Cardiovagal RRI response to deep breathing significantly predicted gastric emptying category via ordinal logistic regression, with higher RRI values associated with 0.93 times the likelihood of rapid gastric emptying.
EGG value significantly predicted gastric emptying category via ordinal logistic regression, with higher EGG values associated with 0.14 times the likelihood of rapid gastric emptying.
A combined panel of autonomic (RRI, VC, PAR) and enteric (EGG) measures predicted disordered gastric emptying with an AUROC of 0.72, outperforming EGG alone (AUROC 0.59).
Targeted NGS/WES identified a pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant in FBN1, TGFBR1, TGFBR2 or SKI in 44 of 53 index patients (83.0%), with one additional VUS in FBN1.
Among 45 patients with a rare variant, 36 (80.0%) carried an FBN1 variant, comprising missense (58.3%), splice (13.9%), small indel (8.3%), nonsense (5.6%), and multi-exon deletions (13.9%).
Four patients (8.9%) carried a TGFBR1 missense variant, consistent with Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
Three patients (6.7%) carried a TGFBR2 missense variant, consistent with Loeys-Dietz syndrome, including two novel variants p.(Arg485Ser) and p.(Arg485Pro).
Two patients carried a SKI missense variant, including a novel variant in the R-SMAD binding domain, consistent with Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome.

A homozygous FBN1 missense variant c.2861G>A/p.(Arg954His) was identified in a child of consanguineous parents, both parents being heterozygous carriers, producing a classical Marfan syndrome phenotype in the child.

Of 41 distinct rare variants identified across four genes, 21 (51.2%) were novel and not previously reported in HGMD or UMD-FBN1 databases; 20 of these were classified pathogenic/likely pathogenic and one FBN1 intronic variant was a VUS.
De novo occurrence of the pathogenic variant was confirmed by parental testing in 17 of 45 index patients (37.8%), including 11 in FBN1, 3 in TGFBR1, 2 in TGFBR2, and 1 in SKI.

Eight index patients (15%) with clinical features suggestive of an HCTD had no disease-associated variant detected across 62 panel genes plus MLPA analysis, suggesting further genetic heterogeneity or phenocopies.

In patients with confirmed Marfan syndrome variants, aortic root dilatation was the most common cardiovascular finding (77%), followed by mitral valve prolapse (67%) and tricuspid valve prolapse (53%).
Ocular and skeletal manifestations were common in the Marfan syndrome cohort, with myopia in 60%, lens subluxation in 49%, dolichostenomelia in 71%, and pectus abnormality in 47% of patients.

In patients with Loeys-Dietz syndrome (TGFBR1/TGFBR2 variants), cardiac abnormalities occurred in all individuals, with aortic root dilatation in 75% and characteristic craniofacial features (long/narrow face, hypertelorism, downslanted palpebral fissures, micro/retrognathia) present in all eight patients.

Seven of 36 FBN1-positive index patients had disease-causing variants in the exon 24-32 region previously associated with early-onset, rapidly progressive Marfan syndrome; five of these seven had ocular, cardiac and skeletal manifestations.
A proband and his paternal half-sister shared an FBN1 nonsense variant not found in the father's leukocyte DNA, indicating paternal germline mosaicism.

The paper discusses that certain FBN1 missense variants (e.g., p.(Arg2726Trp), p.(Pro1424Ala), p.(Ala986Thr)) show incomplete penetrance in the heterozygous state but appear fully penetrant when in trans with a second pathogenic variant, supporting a hypomorphic allele model for biallelic FBN1-related Marfan syndrome.
Among the aggregated ME/CFS sample, 25.7% (549 of 2138) of participants were classified as homebound based on self-reported functional status.
Among homebound ME/CFS participants, 16.2% (89 of 549) were further classified as bedridden, while 83.8% were homebound but not bedridden.
More severe post-exertional malaise (PEM) domain scores increased the odds of a participant with ME/CFS being classified as homebound compared to not homebound.
Higher SF-36 physical functioning scores decreased the odds of a participant being homebound.
Higher SF-36 social functioning scores decreased the odds of a participant being homebound.
Worse scores for the PEM symptom 'next day soreness or fatigue after non-strenuous, everyday activity' increased the odds of being homebound.
Worse scores for the PEM symptom 'physically drained or sick after mild activity' increased the odds of being homebound, showing the strongest effect among tested PEM symptoms.

Among homebound ME/CFS participants, more severe PEM domain scores decreased the odds of being bedridden compared to homebound but not bedridden, contrary to the direction seen in the homebound vs not-homebound comparison.

Among homebound participants, more severe scores for the symptom 'minimum exercise makes you physically tired' decreased the odds of being classified as bedridden versus not bedridden, the strongest predictor in this comparison.
Homebound participants differed demographically from not-homebound participants, with a smaller percentage of males and fewer having completed at least a college degree.
Homebound-bedridden participants were significantly younger and less likely to be married than homebound-not bedridden participants.

Extrapolating from the homebound proportion (25.7%) to a US ME/CFS prevalence estimate of 1.5 million, the authors estimate approximately 385,000 persons with ME/CFS are homebound in the US, and about 62,000 are also bedridden.
NICE's draft updated guideline concluded that graded exercise therapy should not be used in ME/CFS.
NICE's draft guideline concluded that cognitive behavioural therapy is only a supportive therapy for ME/CFS, not a treatment or cure.
The draft NICE guidance highlighted that subjective outcome measures in non-blinded ME/CFS trials are unreliable.
The authors call for high quality randomised controlled ME/CFS trials to identify pharmacological treatments producing substantial objective improvement and restoring work capacity.
81% of fibromyalgia and/or ME/CFS patients met the Brighton criteria for hypermobility syndrome, with an odds ratio of 7.08 compared to controls.
18% of fibromyalgia and/or ME/CFS patients met the 2017 diagnostic criteria for hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Hypermobility scores significantly predicted the level of symptoms reported by patients with fibromyalgia and/or ME/CFS.
There was substantial symptomatic overlap between patients diagnosed with fibromyalgia and those diagnosed with ME/CFS.

Among Gulf War Illness (GWI) veterans, men had significantly higher plasma autoantibody levels against tubulin and myelin-associated glycoprotein (MAG) than women with GWI, with no marker showing the reverse pattern.
No significant differences were found between GW healthy male and GW healthy female controls on any of the 10 autoantibodies, though the analysis was underpowered given only 4 healthy women.
GWI men had significantly higher levels than healthy GW men for 9 of the 10 autoantibodies (all except S100B).
GWI women had significantly higher autoantibody values than healthy GW women for 2 of the 10 markers: GFAP and tubulin.

Men with GWI showed significantly higher mean levels of 9 of 10 neural autoantibodies (tubulin, tau, MAP-2, MBP, NFP, MAG, CamKII, alpha-synuclein, GFAP) compared with a combined control group of male IBS, ME/CFS, and healthy GW veterans, with no difference for S100B.

Women veterans with GWI exhibited significantly increased mean levels of 8 of 10 autoantibodies (tubulin, tau, MAP-2, MBP, MAG, NFP, CamKII, alpha-synuclein) compared with a combined female control group of IBS, ME/CFS, and healthy GW veterans.
The combined CAI score (mean of all 10 autoantibodies) was significantly higher in men with GWI (41.1) than in women with GWI (32.4).
The CAI score was significantly higher in GWI men (41.1) than in healthy GW male controls (21.4) and in the combined male control group (21.5).
The CAI score was significantly higher in GWI women (32.4) than in healthy GW female controls (12.0) and in the combined female control group including ME/CFS and IBS (18.7).

S100B, a marker of acute/current blood-brain barrier disruption, did not differ significantly between GWI men and their male controls (healthy GW veterans or combined controls), suggesting the elevated autoantibody profile reflects more chronic rather than acute glial/BBB injury.

Organophosphate compound exposure is proposed to increase CaMKII activity and expression, causing hyperphosphorylation of neural proteins that leads to their aggregation, slowed axonal transport, and neuronal cell death, providing a mechanistic basis for elevated neural autoantibodies in GWI.
Tender lymph nodes/swollen glands scores did not significantly differ between CFS/ME and FM groups.
The FM group reported significantly more muscle aches and pains than the CFS/ME group, with a medium effect size.
FM participants reported more unrefreshing sleep symptoms than CFS/ME participants, though the effect size was small.

Except for total score, joint pain, muscle aches/pains, and unrefreshing sleep, there were no statistically significant differences between CFS/ME and FM on the CDC Symptom Inventory, and even the significant differences were mostly small in magnitude, suggesting the groups were similar at baseline.

Structural equation modelling confirmed measurement invariance between CFS/ME and FM groups on the McGill Pain Questionnaire, Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory, SF-36 V2, Multidimensional Health Locus of Control Scale, and Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale, indicating both groups responded similarly to these symptom measures.

SEM invariance testing found that CFS/ME and FM groups were non-invariant (i.e., responded differently) on the American CDC Symptom Inventory, the Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (FIQ), and the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS).
On item-level constraint testing, the 'muscle aches and pains' item of the CDC Symptom Inventory was identified as specifically responsible for the non-invariance between CFS/ME and FM groups.
Two FIQ items ('the symptoms' and 'how tired have you been') were identified as responsible for the non-invariance between CFS/ME and FM groups on the Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire.

On the HADS, two items ('I can laugh and see the funny side of things' and 'I can enjoy a good book or radio programme') were identified as responsible for non-invariance between CFS/ME and FM groups.

A combined 'Syndrome Model' incorporating the CDC Symptom Inventory, FIQ, HADS, and ACR pain-point criteria showed invariance between CFS/ME and FM groups, supporting the conclusion that both groups experience a similar overall symptom syndrome.
The FM group had a much higher proportion meeting the ACR tender-point criteria (≥11 pain points) than the CFS/ME group, though many CFS/ME participants still reported substantial pain point counts.

Hierarchical cluster analysis of 37 biological markers across five domains (endocrine, inflammatory, cardiovascular, pain threshold, cognition) identified six clusters, but overlap between clusters was substantial and no distinct subgroups of adolescent CFS patients could be identified.
Patients in Cluster 5 (pain intolerant & poor cognitions) were significantly more likely to meet the Canada 2003 (Carruthers) diagnostic criteria for CFS than patients in other clusters.
Cluster 5 (pain intolerant & poor cognitions) had significantly poorer functional disability (FDI) and quality of life (PedsQL) scores compared with clusters 1-3.
Fatigue (Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire), post-exertional malaise, and depressive symptom (MFQ) scores did not differ significantly across the six biomarker-based clusters.
There were no significant differences between clusters in demographic and constitutional variables, including candidate genetic markers (COMT, ADRA2A, ADRB2, SLC6A4/5-HTTLPR).
Cluster 2 was characterized by a high urine cortisol:creatinine ratio, interpreted as signaling restored HPA axis dynamics relative to the attenuated HPA activity typically seen in CFS.
Cluster 3 was characterized by a strong tachycardia response with a corresponding fall in stroke volume during head-up tilt testing, typical of orthostatic intolerance.
Cluster 4, comprising only 4 patients, was characterized by high levels of interferon gamma (IFNγ) and interferon gamma-induced protein 10 (IP-10), indicative of low-grade inflammation.
Cluster 6, comprising only 3 patients, was characterized by strong high-frequency heart rate variability power, reflecting high vagal (parasympathetic) activity.
Restored HPA axis activity (higher urine cortisol:creatinine ratio) was positively associated with better functional abilities in adolescent CFS patients, consistent with prior NorCAPITAL findings.

Contrary to the assumption that the Canada 2003 criteria reflect an inflammatory pathophysiology, the low-grade inflammation cluster (Cluster 4) was not associated with Canada 2003 criteria adherence, while the cluster associated with Canada 2003 adherence (pain intolerant & poor cognitions) actually had the lowest inflammation scores.

There were no significant differences between clusters in change of symptoms and function from baseline to 30-week follow-up, though there was a non-significant trend toward greater functional improvement in Cluster 5 (pain intolerant & poor cognitions).
Cluster 1 was characterized by high pressure pain thresholds and high cognitive function test scores, labelled 'pain tolerant & good cognitions'.
Cluster 5 was characterized by low pressure pain thresholds and low cognitive test scores, representing a mirror image of Cluster 1, and was labelled 'pain intolerant & poor cognitions'.

The index patient carries a heterozygous single nucleotide deletion in COL5A1 predicted to cause a frameshift and premature stop codon, likely causing haploinsufficiency of the collagen V alpha-1 chain, confirming classical EDS.

The mother, who displays a milder classical EDS phenotype (Beighton score 5, hyperelastic skin, atrophic scars), also carries the same heterozygous COL5A1 mutation as her daughter, while the father does not.

A novel de novo heterozygous C1R missense variant, predicted pathogenic by multiple in-silico tools and absent from population/disease databases, was identified in the proband and confirms the diagnosis of periodontal EDS.
Radiographic examination of the proband revealed generalized alveolar bone loss of up to 80%, consistent with severe periodontal EDS.

Lack of attached gingiva, predisposing to gingival recession, is described as a pathognomonic feature of periodontal EDS that is consistently present already in childhood, and was found in the proband.

Despite carrying the COL5A1 mutation and having classical EDS, the mother showed no periodontal destruction (CPITN grade 0, no radiological bone loss, healthy attached gingiva), supporting that periodontitis is not a feature of classical EDS.
The proband showed generalized joint hypermobility with a Beighton score of 8 alongside muscular hypotonia, flat feet, scoliosis, and craniomandibular dysfunction.
Two lower primary incisors (teeth 71 and 81) were prematurely lost due to periodontal bone loss at age four, without root resorption.
Across the literature, 108 individuals with molecularly confirmed periodontal EDS have been reported, with early severe periodontitis diagnosed in 99% of adult cases.

A prior study of 12 children (age 4-13) with molecularly confirmed periodontal EDS found the only consistent finding was generalized lack of attached gingiva; periodontal destruction was seen only in the oldest (13-year-old) proband.
Severe (inflammatory) periodontitis has never been reported in any case of molecularly confirmed classical EDS to date, in contrast to periodontal EDS.

Periodontal EDS mutations cause constitutive intracellular activation of C1s (and C1r) serine proteases, resulting in C4 cleavage and local complement cascade activation, which is implicated in inflammatory bone loss in periodontitis.
Periodontitis patients have significantly higher salivary IL-6 levels than healthy subjects, consistent with C1-mediated cytokine upregulation.
Periodontitis patients present significantly higher serum and salivary immunoglobulins against periopathogens compared to healthy controls.
This case represents only the second published report of two concomitant monogenic types of EDS in a single individual, the first being a family with periodontal and vascular EDS in 2018.
The CH1 TNXA/TNXB chimera was the most frequent TNXB alteration, found in 41% of alleles carrying the CYP21A2 deletion.
The CH2 TNXA/TNXB chimera was found in 29% of alleles carrying the CYP21A2 deletion.
The rarer CH3 TNXA/TNXB chimera was found in only 1% of alleles carrying the CYP21A2 deletion.
Overall, 71% of CYP21A2-deletion-carrying alleles were found to also carry a contiguous TNXB gene deletion (TNXA/TNXB chimera).
Sixty-seven percent of CAH patients analyzed had a monoallelic form of TNXB alteration.
Six percent of CAH patients analyzed had a biallelic form of TNXB alteration.

All CAH patients with the biallelic TNXA/TNXB chimeric form had severe skin hyperextensibility and generalized joint hypermobility, consistent with an Ehlers-Danlos syndrome phenotype (CAH-X syndrome).

CAH-X syndrome arises from a contiguous gene deletion affecting both CYP21A2 and TNXB, producing TNXA/TNXB chimeric alleles that cause tenascin-X deficiency and connective tissue dysplasia alongside congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

The authors recommend routine evaluation of TNXB status in CYP21A2 deletion carriers and assessment of connective tissue dysplasia, including cardiologic evaluation, in those found positive for chimeras.
A case report describes a 21-year-old woman with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome presenting with persistent lightheadedness, suggesting a clinical association between EDS and orthostatic/autonomic symptoms.
A case of type IV (vascular) Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is reported in which massive pulmonary thrombosis occurred following an episode of haemoptysis.
A patient with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type IV (vascular type) developed a posterior tibial artery dissection with associated aneurysmal degeneration.
The patient's posterior tibial artery dissection and aneurysm were successfully treated with a Flow Diversion Stent (FDS), which preserved vessel patency while excluding the aneurysm.

Flow Diverting Stent technology offers a low-profile, micro-catheter-deliverable alternative to conventional stent grafts for excluding aneurysms in EDS-IV patients, who may be prone to vessel spasm and dissection with more conventional stent graft technology.
ATF6 expression, an endoplasmic reticulum stress marker, was significantly higher in the dermis of vEDS patients compared with infants and controls.
Cartilage oligomeric matrix protein (COMP), a binding partner for collagen fibrils, was significantly lower in vEDS patients compared with infants and controls.
COL3A1 expression levels were significantly lower in the dermis of vEDS patients compared with infants and controls.
Electron microscopy revealed anomalies in collagen fiber size in vEDS patients, with fragile and small, newly formed collagen fibrils potentially resulting from ER stress.
Infants without vEDS showed collagenous formations similar to those seen in vEDS patient samples, suggesting an overlapping immature collagen phenotype.
A greater proportion of JHS participants took a recovery step during the first perturbation than GJH or NF participants.
Muscle onset latency following perturbation did not differ significantly between JHS, GJH, and NF groups at any of the six perturbations.
At the first perturbation, JHS participants took significantly longer than NF participants to reach peak EMG amplitude in tibialis anterior, rectus femoris, vastus medialis, and vastus lateralis.
At the first perturbation, JHS participants took significantly longer than GJH participants to reach peak EMG amplitude in gluteus medius and vastus lateralis.

At the final (sixth) perturbation, JHS participants still showed significantly delayed time-to-peak EMG amplitude in gluteus medius compared to GJH, indicating this difference persisted despite repeated perturbations.
Time-to-reversal (TTR) of ankle, knee, and hip joint angles showed no significant within- or between-group differences at any perturbation.
At the first perturbation, JHS participants had significantly greater cumulative joint angle (CA) than both GJH and NF groups at the hip and knee.
At the second perturbation, JHS participants continued to show significantly greater cumulative angle than GJH and NF at the hip and knee, and greater than NF at the ankle.
At the sixth and final perturbation, JHS retained significantly greater cumulative angle than NF at the hip and knee, but no longer differed significantly from GJH.
All three groups (JHS, GJH, NF) significantly reduced cumulative angle at the hip, knee, and ankle between the first and second perturbations, showing an initial adaptation response.

In the JHS group only, hip cumulative angle continued to decrease significantly from the second to sixth perturbation, whereas GJH and NF groups showed no further significant change, suggesting slower ongoing adaptation in JHS.

No significant differences in cumulative angle were found between the GJH and NF groups at any perturbation, suggesting that joint hypermobility alone does not account for the postural instability observed in JHS.

In JHS participants, EMG amplitude recorded during a perturbation was up to three times greater than that recorded during a maximal voluntary contraction (MVC), preventing reliable amplitude normalisation.
The NF group had a significantly lower Beighton Score than the JHS group, confirming correct classification of hypermobility status, with no other significant baseline differences between groups.
Fibromyalgia patients had significantly higher depression scores (BDI-II) than healthy controls at baseline.
Fibromyalgia patients showed a significant reduction in overall FIQR symptom severity/impact scores after a 12-week Tai Chi mind-body intervention.
Depression scores (BDI-II) significantly decreased in fibromyalgia patients after the Tai Chi intervention.
Change in FIQR score after Tai Chi was significantly associated with change in BDI-II depression score.
At baseline, fibromyalgia patients showed increased medial hypothalamus resting-state functional connectivity with the bilateral subcallosal cingulate cortex compared to healthy controls.
Fibromyalgia patients showed decreased medial hypothalamus resting-state functional connectivity with the right thalamus compared to healthy controls at baseline.
Fibromyalgia patients showed decreased medial hypothalamus functional connectivity with bilateral amygdala compared to healthy controls at baseline.
Fibromyalgia patients showed decreased medial hypothalamus functional connectivity with the bilateral cerebellum compared to healthy controls at baseline.
Medial hypothalamus-thalamus functional connectivity increased after Tai Chi intervention, overlapping with and normalizing the region of decreased connectivity seen versus healthy controls.
Medial hypothalamus-amygdala functional connectivity increased after Tai Chi intervention, overlapping with the region of decreased connectivity seen versus healthy controls.
Both medial and lateral hypothalamus functional connectivity with the rostral anterior cingulate cortex increased after Tai Chi intervention, accompanying clinical improvement.
Medial hypothalamus functional connectivity additionally increased with the right DLPFC/operculum, right occipital gyrus, and left cerebellum after Tai Chi intervention, with no reductions observed.
At baseline, fibromyalgia patients showed increased lateral hypothalamus functional connectivity with the right temporal pole compared to healthy controls.
At baseline, fibromyalgia patients showed decreased lateral hypothalamus functional connectivity with the right inferior occipital gyrus/cerebellum compared to healthy controls.
Lateral hypothalamus functional connectivity with the bilateral rACC, MPFC, right middle/superior temporal gyrus, and left PCC increased in fibromyalgia patients after Tai Chi intervention.
Change in medial hypothalamus-thalamus functional connectivity after Tai Chi correlated significantly with change in FIQR function subscore, though uncorrected for multiple comparisons.
No significant association was found between lateral hypothalamus-thalamus connectivity changes and clinical outcome (FIQR/subscore) changes.

Dynamic causal modeling showed distinct directional (effective) connectivity between the medial hypothalamus and thalamus across groups: thalamus-to-hypothalamus in controls, bidirectional in untreated fibromyalgia, and hypothalamus-to-thalamus after Tai Chi treatment.

At a more lenient, uncorrected statistical threshold, medial hypothalamus-PAG functional connectivity was decreased in fibromyalgia patients versus healthy controls and increased after Tai Chi intervention.
ASP0819 activated the human KCa3.1 channel in a concentration-dependent manner with an EC50 of 102.4 nM and Emax of 99.0% in CHO cells.
ASP0819 also activated the rat KCa3.1 channel with an EC50 of 392.9 nM and Emax of 102.4%.

ASP0819 showed no meaningful activity (<50% response) on rat KCa2.2 (up to 10 µM), human KCa1.1 (up to 100 µM), L-type Ca2+ channels (up to 10 µM), or rat Na+ channel (up to 100 µM), and did not appreciably bind 54 other receptors/channels/transporters or inhibit 3 enzymes at 10 µM, indicating high selectivity for KCa3.1.

In the reserpine-induced myalgia (RIM) rat model of fibromyalgia-like pain, oral ASP0819 at 0.1, 0.3, and 1 mg/kg significantly and dose-dependently recovered the reserpine-induced decrease in muscle pressure threshold.

In the vagotomy-induced myalgia (VIM) rat model, ASP0819 (0.1-1 mg/kg) significantly recovered the decreased muscle pressure threshold both after a single dose and after 14 days of repeated daily dosing, with effects persisting at reduced magnitude up to 48 hours post-dose.

In vivo single-fiber electrophysiology in RIM rats showed that IV ASP0819 (0.3 and 1 mg/kg/h) significantly reduced spontaneous and mechanically evoked Aδ-fiber firing rates at the dorsal root, and also reduced mechanically evoked C-fiber responses.

Spontaneous and mechanically evoked peripheral nerve (dorsal root) firing rate was significantly increased in RIM rats compared with control rats, consistent with peripheral nerve hyperexcitability underlying FM-like pain.
In a rat adjuvant-induced arthritis (AIA, inflammatory pain) model, ASP0819 at 1 and 3 mg/kg significantly increased the withdrawal threshold compared with vehicle.

In the monoiodoacetate-induced (MIA) osteoarthritis rat model (non-inflammatory pain), single and repeated oral ASP0819 (0.1-1 mg/kg) significantly improved the weight-bearing deficit, whereas single-dose diclofenac had no effect.
Single oral administration of diclofenac (an NSAID) had no effect on pain in the MIA osteoarthritis model, suggesting this model reflects non-inflammatory pain that is less responsive to NSAIDs.
In a colorectal distension (CRD) model of visceral pain, oral ASP0819 at 0.3 and 1 mg/kg significantly reduced the number of abdominal contractions induced by balloon distension.

Following IV infusion of ASP0819 at 0.3 mg/kg/h in normal rats, mean plasma concentrations were 89.1, 714, and 2080 ng/mL at 10, 30, and 60 min, respectively, with a plasma-to-brain ratio of less than 1%, indicating low CNS penetration.
The Hmax/Mmax ratio measured in the flexor carpi radialis muscle was significantly higher in patients with fibromyalgia than in healthy controls.

The Hmax/Mmax ratio measured in the gastrocnemius-soleus muscle was significantly higher in patients with fibromyalgia than in healthy controls, and this elevation was not confined to the site of maximum pain.
The minimum latency of the H wave, measured in both the FCR and GCS muscles, did not differ significantly between FM patients and healthy controls.
In FM patients, the Hmax/Mmax ratios in the FCR and GCS did not significantly correlate with pain severity (VAS), pain duration, SSS, WPI, HAM-D, TMAS, or FIQR scores.
In FM patients, changes in the Hmax/Mmax ratio in the upper limb were significantly positively correlated with changes in the lower limb.
Patients with fibromyalgia had significantly higher depression scores (HAM-D) than healthy controls.
Patients with fibromyalgia had significantly higher anxiety scores (TMAS) than healthy controls.
There were no significant differences between FM patients and healthy controls in age, sex, marital status, BMI, or upper and lower limb lengths.
9.6% (43/450) of medical students met ACR 2010 diagnostic criteria for fibromyalgia, a higher prevalence than reported in the general Saudi population.
Among students who met FM diagnostic criteria, a large majority (81.4%) were female compared to only 18.6% male.
FM prevalence did not differ significantly across academic years (2nd through 6th year).
Fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, and cognitive dysfunction (memory/concentration problems) were all significantly more severe among students meeting FM criteria.
Sleep duration under seven hours per night was similarly common among students with and without FM.
Pain significantly impaired the ability to exercise among students with FM symptoms compared to those without.
Fewer than half (41.9%) of students meeting FM criteria reported taking any medication (e.g., NSAIDs, PPIs, TCAs, SNRIs, SSRIs) to control their symptoms.
Widespread pain index (WPI) scores were similar between FM students who took medication and those who did not.

A majority (77.8%) of students who reported a prior physician diagnosis of FM did not actually meet the ACR 2010 diagnostic criteria, indicating discordance between clinical diagnosis and criteria-based diagnosis.
The 9.6% FM prevalence found among medical students is higher than the pooled general population prevalence of 4.4% reported in the region.
The prevalence found in this study (9.6%) is broadly comparable to the 8.2% FM prevalence previously reported among physicians in training in Riyadh using a similar questionnaire.

A much lower FM prevalence (2.0%) was found in a prior study of medical students by Eyigor et al., a discrepancy attributed to their use of the less reliable ACR 1990 tender-point criteria versus the ACR 2010 criteria used here.

Additional somatic and psychological symptoms — irritable bowel syndrome, muscle pain, anxiety, depression, headache, heartburn, chest pain, and back pain — were assessed and compared between FM and non-FM students using chi-squared tests (Table 2).
Duodenal biopsies from patients with hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (HαT) showed significantly higher mast cell counts than both MCAS patients with normal tryptase and GI-controls.
Mast cells in HαT patients were significantly found clustered together (in groups of fewer than 15 cells) compared with MCAS-NT and GI-control patients.
Mast cells in HαT patients were distributed throughout the mucosa and submucosa, including superficial villi, distinct from the distribution seen in MCAS-NT and GI-control patients.
Spindle-shaped mast cells were observed across all three groups, including GI-controls, suggesting this morphology is not specific to HαT or MCAS.

Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia is characterized by extra copies of the mast cell tryptase gene TPSAB1 and is associated with increased small intestinal mast cells that may contribute to prevalent GI manifestations in these individuals.
The patient developed mast cell activation syndrome with pruritus, severe skin reaction, stomatitis, leukopenia, and bladder inflammation after methotrexate treatment for ectopic pregnancy.
Two weeks after starting carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia, the patient developed Stevens-Johnson syndrome with fever, generalized macular rash, buccal ulceration, and ocular burning.

The authors propose that a prior history of drug-induced mast cell activation syndrome may predispose patients to severe reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome upon exposure to carbamazepine, and recommend avoiding carbamazepine in such patients.
Laboratory investigations during the SJS episode showed mild leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, no eosinophilia, and mildly elevated liver enzymes (AST, ALT) and CRP.
The patient was treated with intravenous methylprednisolone 40 mg daily for 5 days plus supportive care, and was discharged on hospital day 10 with clinical improvement.
In a cited observational study of 113 SJS patients, early withdrawal of the causative drug reduced the risk of death by 30% for each day before the onset of blisters and erosions.
Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia is caused by multiple copies of the alpha-tryptase gene at the TPSAB1 locus and is associated with mast cell activation symptoms and anaphylaxis.
Baseline serum tryptase averaged 17.2 ng/mL among the 101 HαT patients, ranging from 6.2 to 51.3 ng/mL.
Tryptase levels were below 11.4 ng/mL in 8.9% of patients and above 20 ng/mL in 22.3% of patients, demonstrating a broad range of baseline tryptase in HαT.
The KIT D816V mutation, associated with clonal mast cell disease, was negative in all tested subjects with HαT.
The 2α:3β genotype was the most common TPSAB1 genotype found but did not correlate with baseline tryptase levels.
Unprovoked anaphylaxis occurred in 57% of subjects, across genetically heterogeneous HαT genotypes.
Patients with HαT most commonly reported gastrointestinal, cutaneous, psychiatric, pulmonary, cardiovascular, and neurologic symptoms.
85% of patients were taking H1- or H2-antihistamines, which provided only partial symptom relief.
Omalizumab was effective at suppressing anaphylaxis or urticaria in 94% of treated patients.
Patients with hereditary alpha-tryptasemia most commonly reported gastrointestinal, cutaneous, psychiatric, pulmonary, cardiovascular, and neurologic symptoms.
Most patients (85%) were treated with H1- or H2-antihistamines and experienced only partial symptom relief.
Omalizumab suppressed anaphylaxis or urticaria in 94% of treated patients with hereditary alpha-tryptasemia.

A 37-year-old woman with indolent systemic mastocytosis and severe mast cell mediator-related symptoms tolerated the first dose of BNT162b2 mRNA COVID-19 vaccine without side effects after premedication with antihistamines and montelukast.

A 47-year-old woman with KIT D816V-positive indolent systemic mastocytosis, prior drug anaphylaxis, and multiple MC mediator symptoms tolerated the first BNT162b2 vaccine dose with premedication, experiencing only myalgias the following day.

The authors note that although PEG (a vaccine excipient) is a known rare cause of IgE- and complement-mediated anaphylaxis and has been speculated to contribute to initial vaccine-related anaphylaxis reports, there is no evidence that mastocytosis/MC activation disorder patients have increased sensitization or reactivity to PEG.

Overall, the two cases are presented as initial evidence that mRNA COVID-19 vaccines are safe in patients with mastocytosis and mast cell activation symptoms, including those with a history of anaphylaxis, provided premedication and medical surveillance are used.
Inhibition of ADP-induced platelet aggregation by the NO donor sodium nitroprusside was reduced in patients with chronic coronary artery spasm compared with healthy controls.
Platelet resistance to NO showed a further, statistically non-significant worsening during acute symptomatic crises compared with the chronic phase.
Plasma syndecan 1, a marker of glycocalyx shedding, increased during symptomatic crises in coronary artery spasm patients.
Plasma tryptase, a marker of mast cell activation, increased during symptomatic crises in coronary artery spasm, suggesting mast cell involvement in acute exacerbations.
Plasma platelet microparticles increased during symptomatic crises in coronary artery spasm patients, indicating platelet damage/activation.
High-dose N-acetylcysteine combined with glyceryl trinitrate rapidly increased platelet responsiveness to sodium nitroprusside in coronary artery spasm patients.
Treatment with N-acetylcysteine plus glyceryl trinitrate decreased plasma syndecan 1 concentrations, indicating reduced glycocalyx shedding.
The effect of NAC on platelet responsiveness to SNP was mimicked in vitro by the H2S donor NaHS, implicating H2S as the mediator of NAC's action.
The effect of NAC on platelet responsiveness to sodium nitroprusside was mimicked in vitro by the H2S donor NaHS, suggesting NAC acts via H2S release.
Inhibition of enzymatic H2S production attenuated the beneficial effect of NAC on platelet NO responsiveness, supporting an H2S-dependent mechanism.
The authors conclude that H2S donors may correct the underlying pathophysiological anomalies of coronary artery spasm, including platelet NO resistance and glycocalyx shedding.
The patient's serum tryptase level was markedly elevated at initial diagnostic workup, supporting a diagnosis of systemic mastocytosis.
The patient showed eosinophilia at admission workup, a comparatively rare laboratory finding in ISM patients.
Inguinal lymph node biopsy demonstrated mast cell infiltration accompanied by vascular proliferation, eosinophilia, and fibrosis, consistent with systemic mastocytosis.
Bone marrow biopsy showed 40-50% cellularity with a significant increase in mast cells, confirming bone marrow involvement in systemic mastocytosis.
Immunohistochemical staining positive for CD117, CD34, and MPO in lymph node and bone marrow biopsies supported the diagnosis of indolent systemic mastocytosis.
Following initiation of antihistamine, cromolyn sodium, vitamin D, and glucocorticoids, the patient's symptoms markedly improved and serum tryptase declined from 73 to 20 ng/ml.

SARS-CoV-2 infection was temporally associated with sudden worsening of mast cell activation symptoms (pruritus, urticaria, flushing, fever, cough) in this ISM patient despite epinephrine self-injection.

Replacing glucocorticoids with omalizumab (alongside resuming antihistamines, cromolyn, vitamin D) while treating concurrent COVID-19 with remdesivir and supportive care was associated with ISM stability and improved COVID-19 symptoms two weeks later.

Because ISM presents with highly diverse and nonspecific symptoms, diagnosis is frequently delayed by up to 10 years, consistent with the delay observed in this patient (initially misdiagnosed as Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma).
Across ISM patients generally, elevated serum tryptase (>20 ng/dl) is reported in 71% of cases, making it a key screening parameter.
The KIT D816V activating point mutation is detectable in more than 70% of ISM patients and serves as a key diagnostic/screening marker.

Generalized lymphadenopathy, present in this patient, is an infrequent ISM manifestation (reported in ~3% of cases) and is more commonly associated with smoldering or aggressive mastocytosis subtypes rather than classic ISM.
MRGPRX2 is a receptor that activates mast cells and contributes to pseudo-allergic drug reactions, pain, itching, and inflammatory diseases.
MRGPRX2 ligand binding and G protein coupling likely triggers phosphorylation cascades, Ca2+ mobilization, and degranulation with cytokine/chemokine generation via MAPK and NF-κB pathways.
Diverse MRGPRX2 ligands use conserved residues in the transmembrane domains and carboxyl-terminal Ser/Thr residues to mediate ligand binding and G protein coupling.

Agonists that activate MRGPRX2 on mast cells are classified into peptides (antimicrobial peptides, neuropeptides, MC degranulating peptides, peptide hormones) and nonpeptides, including FDA-approved drugs.

MRGPRX2 inhibitors described in the literature include non-selective GPCR inhibitors, herbal extracts, small-molecule MRGPRX2 antagonists, and DNA aptamer drugs, which could reduce MRGPRX2-mediated mast cell activation.
Among 59 clinically diagnosed PD patients, 12 (20.3%) carried the LRRK2 G2385R variant.
PD patients carrying the LRRK2 G2385R variant had significantly higher nonmotor symptom burden (NMSS) than noncarriers.
RBD prevalence was significantly higher in LRRK2 G2385R carrier PD patients than noncarriers.
G2385R carrier PD patients required a higher levodopa equivalent dose than noncarriers.
Both LRRK2 G2385R carrier and noncarrier PD patients had a much higher prevalence of small fiber neuropathy symptoms than healthy controls.
COMPASS-31 autonomic symptom scores were significantly higher in G2385R carriers than in noncarriers, although SFN-SIQ scores did not differ.
SFN-SIQ and COMPASS-31 scores were markedly higher in both PD carrier and noncarrier groups compared with healthy controls.
SFN-SIQ scores were positively correlated with COMPASS-31 scores across PD patients.
Distal leg intraepidermal nerve fiber density was significantly lower in LRRK2 G2385R noncarrier PD patients than in healthy controls.
The reduction in distal IENFD in G2385R carriers versus HC was attenuated and did not reach statistical significance.
Distal IENFD did not differ between G2385R carrier and noncarrier PD patients.
Distal IENFD was mildly negatively correlated with COMPASS-31 autonomic symptom scores across the whole PD group.
No correlation was found between distal IENFD and SFN-SIQ score, disease duration, Hoehn and Yahr stage, UPDRS-III, or levodopa equivalent dose.
Phosphorylated α-synuclein deposits colocalized with PGP9.5-positive cutaneous nerve fibers were present in both G2385R carrier and noncarrier PD patients but absent in healthy controls.
Overall p-syn deposition positivity in the whole PD group was 79.7%, higher at the proximal cervical (C7) site (69.5%) than the distal leg site (40.7%).

LRRK2 G2385R carriers showed a homogeneous proximal-distal p-syn deposition pattern (no significant site difference), whereas noncarriers and the whole PD group showed a proximal-to-distal gradient with higher positivity at C7 than distal leg.
IENFD, SFN-SIQ, and COMPASS-31 scores did not significantly differ between PD patients with and without cutaneous p-syn deposition, in carriers, noncarriers, or the whole group.
Secretomotor symptom scores were significantly higher in G2385R carrier PD patients than noncarriers.
Prevalence of orthostatic intolerance, gastrointestinal symptoms, and bladder symptoms was higher in G2385R carrier PD patients than noncarriers.

A cited prior study reported the G2385R variant altered LRRK2 interaction strength/quality and increased synaptic vesicle fusion rate, suggesting a loss-of-function-like effect, discussed as possible mechanistic context for this study's findings.
Tympanic core body temperature was significantly higher in women with fibromyalgia than in healthy controls.
Hand skin temperature measured by infrared thermography was significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.

Serum nitric oxide levels were negatively associated with minimum skin temperature at the dorsal center of the dominant hand in healthy controls, an association not observed in fibromyalgia patients, suggesting dysfunctional sympathetic cutaneous control in fibromyalgia.

Serum nitric oxide levels were negatively associated with maximum skin temperature at the center of the palm of the non-dominant hand in healthy controls, an association absent in fibromyalgia patients.

Serum nitric oxide levels were negatively associated with minimum skin temperature at the center of the palm of the non-dominant hand in healthy controls, an association not seen in fibromyalgia patients.

Serum nitric oxide levels were negatively associated with mean skin temperature at the center of the palm of the non-dominant hand in healthy controls, an association not observed in fibromyalgia patients.
Serum nitric oxide levels were negatively associated with maximum skin temperature at the thenar eminence of the dominant hand in healthy controls, an association not seen in fibromyalgia patients.
Serum nitric oxide levels were negatively associated with tympanic core body temperature in healthy controls but this association was not observed in fibromyalgia patients.

The absence of the expected negative association between nitric oxide and skin/core temperatures in fibromyalgia patients, in contrast to healthy controls, suggests a dysfunction of sympathetic cutaneous neural control in fibromyalgia.
AIHA patients had reduced serum complement C3 levels compared with control subjects.
Serum C4 levels were lower specifically in DAT-positive AIHA patients but did not differ from controls in DAT-negative AIHA patients.
Among AIHA subtypes, patients with warm AIHA secondary to connective tissue disease and those with cold agglutinin disease/cold agglutinin syndrome had the lowest serum C3 and C4 levels.
Serum C4 levels were negatively correlated with cold agglutinin test (CAT) titers.
Serum C4 levels were negatively correlated with direct antiglobulin test (anti-C3d) titers.
In AIHA patients with positive CAT and/or DAT (anti-C3d) but negative DAT (anti-IgG), serum C3 levels were negatively correlated with indirect bilirubin.
In the same serologically defined subgroup (CAT and/or DAT anti-C3d positive, DAT anti-IgG negative), serum C4 levels were negatively correlated with indirect bilirubin.
Women with central sensitivity syndromes (CSS) had significantly higher pre- and post-operative pelvic organ prolapse symptom (POP-SS) scores than women without CSS.
Fewer women with CSS achieved a minimum 6-point improvement on the POP-SS scale after surgery compared to those without CSS, though this difference was not statistically significant.
McGill pain scores were higher in women with CSS than in those without, both before and after prolapse surgery.
Women with CSS were less likely to achieve their surgical goals and be satisfied with pelvic organ prolapse surgery compared to women without CSS.
Microcurrent-treated fibroblasts (F+MC) showed higher Ctgf expression than untreated fibroblasts (F) on day 4.
Microcurrent-treated fibroblasts (F+MC) showed lower Tenascin C (Tnc) expression than untreated fibroblasts (F) on day 4.
Microcurrent-treated fibroblasts (F+MC) showed lower Fibromodulin (Fmod) expression than untreated fibroblasts (F) on day 4.
No difference in Tgfb expression was observed between microcurrent-treated and untreated fibroblast groups.
No difference in Fn1 (Fibronectin) expression was observed between microcurrent-treated and untreated fibroblast groups.
No difference in Scleraxis (Scx) expression was observed between microcurrent-treated and untreated fibroblast groups.
Microcurrent-treated fibroblasts showed greater migration into the scratch wound area than untreated fibroblasts on day 4.
Cell viability assay showed no significant difference between fibroblasts treated with microcurrent and untreated fibroblasts after 4 daily applications.
The authors report a case of gallstone ileus in a 69-year-old woman with a 30-year history of ALS who had not used medical management since diagnosis.
Autonomic symptoms, most commonly urinary or gastrointestinal dysfunction and orthostatic intolerance, are reported in more than a quarter of ALS patients.
ALS patients on chronic tracheostomy ventilation were reported to have a significantly higher risk of developing cholelithiasis or cholecystitis.
The authors propose that intestinal hypoperistalsis in ALS may impair gallbladder contractility, leading to biliary stasis and sludge formation.
Hyperfunction of the adrenergic sympathetic nervous system may cause splanchnic hypoperfusion, worsening gallbladder contractility and promoting gallstone formation.
A cited study found that gastric emptying was delayed by more than 160 minutes in 83% of ALS patients compared to healthy controls, supporting GI dysmotility in ALS.
Colonic transit times in the right and left colon were significantly delayed in ALS patients compared to age-matched controls.
Unlike the right and left colon, rectosigmoid transit time in ALS patients was within normal limits compared to healthy controls.
Surgical management with enterolithotomy, open cholecystectomy, and fistula takedown successfully resolved the patient's gallstone ileus with an uncomplicated recovery.

After partial hysterectomy (axotomy of uterine horn-innervating axons), the proportion of FB-traced PCG neurons showing tyrosine hydroxylase immunoreactivity decreased markedly on the right side and mildly on the left side compared to sham-operated controls.
Dopamine beta-hydroxylase immunoreactivity in FB-traced PCG neurons decreased significantly after hysterectomy, more so in the right PCG than the left.
Galanin immunoreactivity, absent in PCG neurons innervating the uterine horn in controls, appeared in a substantial proportion of these neurons after hysterectomy, particularly on the right side.
The proportion of FB-traced PCG neurons showing NPY immunoreactivity increased significantly in the right PCG after hysterectomy, with a smaller, non-significant increase on the left.
Somatostatin immunoreactivity in FB-traced PCG neurons innervating the uterine horn did not change significantly after hysterectomy compared to sham controls.

No FB-traced PCG neurons innervating the uterine horn showed cholinergic markers (ChAT, VAChT) in either control or hysterectomized animals, indicating PCG neurons projecting to the uterus do not undergo an adrenergic-to-cholinergic phenotype switch after axotomy.

Neuronal nitric oxide synthase, VIP, PACAP, and substance P were not detected in FB-traced PCG neurons innervating the uterine horn in either control or hysterectomized pigs, indicating PCG neurons projecting to the uterus are not a source of nitrergic, VIPergic, PACAPergic or SP-containing innervation and do not adopt these phenotypes after axotomy.
In control (sham-operated) pigs, virtually all FB-traced PCG neurons innervating the uterine horn were adrenergic, expressing both tyrosine hydroxylase and dopamine beta-hydroxylase.

The case illustrates that indolent systemic mastocytosis confined to the GI tract, without cutaneous involvement, produces non-specific symptoms that mimic inflammatory bowel disease or irritable bowel syndrome.

Biopsy with histopathological analysis is described as necessary to confirm a diagnosis of indolent systemic mastocytosis in the absence of cutaneous mast cell aggregates (papules, nodules, or plaques).

The authors argue that indolent systemic mastocytosis should be considered in the differential diagnosis of patients with persistent, treatment-refractory GI symptoms even without cutaneous findings, since missing this diagnosis delays appropriate treatment.
The TNXB gene, encoding tenascin-X, was discovered because it overlaps the CYP21A2 gene (encoding steroid 21-hydroxylase) on the opposite DNA strand.
Current data show TNXB has 44 exons spanning 68 kb and encodes a tenascin-X protein of 4,244 amino acids totaling 458,220 Da.

A patient with CAH and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome had a genomic deletion extending from the XA region through CYP21A2 into TNXB, and lacked TNX protein and mRNA in dermal fibroblasts, demonstrating that TNX deficiency causes EDS.
An immunoassay found absent serum TNX fragment in 146 of 151 patients with EDS, and the remaining 5 patients had TNXB mutations not involving CYP21A2.
Tnxb-knockout mice had skin hyperextensibility, reduced skin tensile strength, and reduced skin collagen content.
In contrast to Tnxb knockouts, mouse knockouts of TNC and TNR lacked abnormal phenotypes.
TNX appears to associate with and stabilize newly produced collagen fibrils, suggesting that recessive forms of EDS concern post-translational modification of collagens.
TNX-deficiency has been associated with primary myopathy.
TNX-deficiency has been associated with recurrent gastrointestinal perforation.
TNX-deficiency has been associated with vesicoureteral reflux.
TNXB single nucleotide polymorphisms are associated with schizophrenia.
Tnxb-knockout mice showed increased anxiety, improved memory, and higher sensorimotor coordination than control mice.
Among 20 obligate heterozygotes for a severely defective TNXB allele, 9 of 14 females but no males had hypermobility-type EDS.
Heterozygous TNXB mutations causing TNX haploinsufficiency produce a mild hypermobility form of EDS, often associated with CAH, together comprising the unique CAH-X syndrome.
7% of patients with 21-hydroxylase deficiency (21OHD/CAH) had symptomatic TNX haploinsufficiency, defining a CAH-X subtype.
A more recent study reported that 14% of 21OHD patients have symptomatic TNX haploinsufficiency (CAH-X), a higher estimate than the earlier 7% figure.
Expression of the short adrenal-specific TNX isoform XB-S is induced by hypoxia, and XB-S associates with the mitotic motor kinesin Eg5, though its precise function remains unclear.
Recessive TNX-deficient EDS (now termed classic-like EDS) was found to be clinically distinct from dominant EDS caused by collagen mutations.
In normothermic control rats, 41% of myenteric plexus neurons in the ileum showed constitutive phosphorylated Tau (AT8) immunoreactivity, whereas in the colon only 10% did.

Synthetic torpor (pharmacologically induced deep hypothermia) significantly increased the percentage and intensity of AT8 (phospho-Tau) immunoreactivity in myenteric neurons of the ileum compared with normothermic controls.
Synthetic torpor significantly increased the percentage and intensity of AT8 immunoreactivity in myenteric neurons of the colon compared with controls.
In control rats, AT8 signal intensity was significantly higher in the ileum than in the colon, but this regional difference disappeared during synthetic torpor.

Synthetic torpor significantly decreased the percentage of nitrergic (nNOS-immunoreactive) neurons in the ileum myenteric plexus compared to controls, while cholinergic (ChAT) neuron percentage was unchanged.
In the colon, unlike the ileum, synthetic torpor did not significantly change the percentages of nitrergic (nNOS) or cholinergic (ChAT) myenteric neurons, though immunolabeling brightness increased.
In the ileum, the great majority of AT8-immunoreactive (phospho-Tau) neurons co-expressed the cholinergic marker ChAT in both control and torpor rats, with no significant difference between groups.

In the colon, the proportion of AT8-positive neurons co-expressing ChAT was significantly reduced during synthetic torpor compared with controls, suggesting a shift in the neurochemical phenotype of phospho-Tau-expressing neurons.

Only a small percentage of AT8-immunoreactive neurons co-expressed the nitrergic marker nNOS in the ileum and colon of control rats, with a non-significant trend toward increased co-expression during torpor.
Multiple studies report altered mast cell count and density in the intestinal mucosa of IBS patients, though findings across studies are inconsistent.
Most reviewed studies suggest intestinal mast cell infiltration is present in patients with IBS.
Risk factors for IBS including dietary habits, psychological factors, infection, and dysbiosis are implicated in inducing intestinal mast cell infiltration.
Food may trigger immune-related allergic reactions and affect intestinal microbiota activity, contributing to mast cell involvement in IBS.
Exogenous pathogens and altered commensal bacteria profiles promote intestinal mast cell recruitment through enhanced chemokine release from epithelial cells or direct immune activation.
Psychological factors may affect the microenvironment in which intestinal mast cells reside, potentially influencing their behavior in IBS.
Mast cells interact closely with enteric neurons and other immunocytes, evidenced by close spatial proximity and regionally altered immune system components.

Mediators released by enteric neurons, immunocytes, and mast cells themselves—such as neurotrophins, neuropeptides, cytokines, and chemokines—may stimulate mast cells by modulating their survival, proliferation, and recruitment in the intestine.
Retinal Ccn2/Ctgf mRNA expression was reduced by approximately 50% in heterozygous CTGFLacZ/+ mice compared to wild-type littermates.
CCN2/CTGF protein levels in the retina, assessed by Western blot, were significantly reduced in CTGFLacZ/+ mice compared to WT littermates, paralleling the mRNA reduction.

Despite reduced CCN2/CTGF levels, heterozygous CTGFLacZ/+ mice showed no obvious structural or ultrastructural abnormalities in cornea, Descemet's membrane, trabecular meshwork, Schlemm's canal, or retina compared to wild-type mice at 9 weeks of age.
During early eye development (E11.5), all cell types forming the lens vesicle, optic cup, and surrounding neural crest showed positive Ccn2/Ctgf promoter activity.

At E16.5, neural crest-derived cells forming the sclera, choroid, ciliary body, and iris stroma, along with corneal epithelium/endothelium and lens epithelium, showed intense Ccn2/Ctgf promoter activity, while lens fibers and retinal pigment epithelium were negative.

Throughout postnatal life and adulthood, Ccn2/Ctgf promoter activity remained persistently intense in the stroma of the ciliary body and adjacent chamber angle tissues including the trabecular meshwork, while staining in sclera, cornea, and lens weakened with age.

Cells in the inner wall endothelium of Schlemm's canal and adjacent trabecular meshwork showed intense Ccn2/Ctgf promoter activity both at P15 and in adulthood, identified via CD31 double-immunolabeling.

Retinal astrocytes, Müller cell processes and endfeet, and starburst amacrine cells all showed Ccn2/Ctgf promoter activity, identified by co-labeling with GFAP, glutamine synthetase, and choline acetyltransferase respectively.
Endothelial cells of retinal and choroidal blood vessels homogenously expressed Ccn2/Ctgf promoter activity, identified via CD31 co-labeling.
An unexpectedly high and persistent Ccn2/Ctgf promoter activity was found in astrocytes of the glial lamina at the optic nerve head from P10 through adulthood, colocalizing with GFAP.

The authors propose that CCN2/CTGF, by amplifying TGF-beta signaling, contributes to neural crest morphogenesis during eye development, and that its continued expression in adult retinal/choroidal vessels and astrocytes may counteract VEGF-driven neovascularization and support mechanical resilience of the optic nerve head glial lamina.

A waterborne E. coli gastroenteritis outbreak in the United States was followed by development of IBS-like symptoms with comorbid depression and anxiety disorder in affected individuals, illustrating post-infectious IBS as a gut-brain axis disorder.
A meta-analysis found that prenatal antibiotic exposure significantly increased the risk of autism spectrum disorder in children.

Treatment with the non-absorbable antibiotic vancomycin, which mainly targets Gram-positive bacteria such as Clostridium spp., improved eye contact behavior and reduced constipation in autistic children.
A longitudinal population-based study reported that early-life antibiotic exposure is associated with an increased risk for psychiatric disorders.
A clinical study found altered auditory processing and recognition memory responses in infants who received intravenous antibiotics after delivery.

Broad-spectrum postnatal antibiotic use reduced amyloid plaque deposition in aged APPSWE/PS1ΔE9 transgenic mice, suggesting selective microbiome-based treatments may benefit early-stage Alzheimer's disease.
Antibiotic-induced gut microbiota depletion resulted in defective microglia, which could be restored by microbiota-derived metabolites such as short-chain fatty acids (SCFA).
α4β7 gut-homing T cells are described as a marker of intestinal inflammation in both functional dyspepsia and irritable bowel syndrome.
Treatment with probiotic Bifidobacteria can increase the amount of tryptophan, the precursor of serotonin.
Some Lactobacilli species alter GABA metabolism and change brain GABA receptor expression and behavior.
Lactobacillus rhamnosus produced a central nervous system effect in animals that was abolished by vagotomy, indicating vagal mediation of gut microbiota-brain communication.
Patients with a history of vagotomy have a diminished risk for certain neurological diseases.
Germ-free animal experiments show altered hippocampal neurogenesis and decreased expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, implicating gut microbiota in neurodevelopment.

Broad-spectrum antibiotic cocktails in animal studies produced impaired social behaviors, neurogenesis, and cognitive function alongside gut microbiota perturbations, comparable to results seen in germ-free mice.
Antibiotic-induced disruptive effects on brain and behavior in some studies could be rescued by probiotic administration.

Antibiotic use, especially in early life, may cause long-lasting effects on the microbial community and immunity that increase predisposition and susceptibility to disease progression such as inflammatory bowel disease.
Of 98 EDS patients reviewed, 75 (76.5%) were diagnosed with the hypermobile subtype (EDS-HT), making it the most common subtype in this clinic cohort.
The EDS cohort was overwhelmingly female, with 94 of 98 patients (95.9%) being women.
On average, each EDS patient had involvement of 5.4 joints, with the shoulder, knee, and lumbar spine being the most commonly affected sites.
EDS patients had an average of 2.8 comorbid systemic conditions among those assessed (autonomic dysfunction, headaches/migraines, GI conditions, cardiovascular anomalies, MCAS, and TMJ dysfunction).
Autonomic dysfunction was reported as the most common comorbid systemic condition among EDS patients in this cohort.
Headaches/migraines were assessed as a comorbid systemic condition in this EDS cohort.
Gastrointestinal conditions were assessed as a comorbid systemic condition in this EDS cohort.
Cardiovascular anomalies were identified as one of the systemic comorbid conditions present among the EDS patient cohort.
Mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) was recorded as a comorbid systemic diagnosis in this EDS cohort.
Temporomandibular joint (TMJ) dysfunction was reported as a systemic comorbid condition among EDS patients.
The shoulder, knee, and lumbar spine were the most frequently involved joints reported among EDS patients with musculoskeletal pain.
In the core demographic-adjusted model, each 1-SD decrease in distribution entropy (DistEn) was associated with a 36% increased risk of all-cause mortality.

DistEn remained an independent predictor of all-cause mortality even after full adjustment for demographics, lifestyle, cardiovascular risk, comorbidities, and autonomic measures (heart rate, RMSSD, mean arterial pressure).

Participants in the lowest decile of DistEn had a 55% higher risk of all-cause mortality than those in the highest decile, a magnitude comparable to being nearly 9 years older, being a former smoker, or having diabetes.
DistEn predicted cardiovascular-related mortality in the core demographic model, with a larger effect size than for all-cause mortality.
DistEn predicted respiratory-disease-related mortality in the core demographic model, with the largest effect size among cause-specific outcomes.

DistEn's weak association with cancer-related mortality was no longer significant after adjustment for resting heart rate, RMSSD, and mean arterial pressure, whereas resting heart rate alone remained predictive.
The mortality risk from lower DistEn was significantly stronger in younger participants (<55 years) than in older participants (>65 years), representing an interaction with age.

The mortality risk from lower DistEn was significantly stronger in participants with prior myocardial infarction compared with those without, representing an interaction with MI history; combined, those <55 years with prior MI had a 56% higher risk than those >65 years without prior MI.

DistEn (heartbeat complexity) was lower in older participants, men, non-Europeans, those with low physical activity, higher socioeconomic deprivation, obesity (BMI>35), and high cardiovascular risk burden.

DistEn was only marginally lower in beta-blocker users and showed no significant difference in patients with a history of atrial fibrillation/arrhythmias, suggesting relative robustness to common cardiac medications/conditions.
DistEn was negatively correlated with resting heart rate and positively correlated with RMSSD, but had no relationship with mean arterial pressure.
Resting heart rate, RR interval, and RMSSD were each individually predictive of all-cause mortality, but none of these associations remained significant once DistEn was included in the same model.
In direct comparison, DistEn showed superior predictive performance (higher concordance index) for all-cause mortality compared with RR interval-based survival models across follow-up years.

Halpin et al. found significantly increased anti-EBV/HHV-6 dUTPase antibody levels in longitudinal and single serum samples from ME/CFS patients compared to controls, with 30.91–52.7% of patients showing multi-herpesvirus dUTPase antibody positivity versus 17.21% in controls.
Loebel et al. reported a significant reduction of EBNA-1 and VCA antibody-secreting EBV-specific memory B cells in two separate ME/CFS cohorts diagnosed by Fukuda criteria.
Analyses of CD4+ and CD8+ T cell subsets in a small ME/CFS cohort revealed significantly diminished frequencies of EBNA-1-specific triple TNF-α/IFN-γ/IL-2 producing cells.
A higher frequency of EBER-DNA, but not BZLF-1 RNA, was observed in PBMCs of ME/CFS patients compared to healthy individuals, suggesting frequent latent EBV replication.

Peptide microarray and suspension multiplex immunoassay studies (including Blomberg et al.) found the EBV anti-IgG response in ME/CFS patients was not significantly different from controls, apart from small non-significant differences to EBNA-3C and EA-D.
Shikova et al. was the only study to report active EBV infection in some ME/CFS patients, in contrast to the majority of studies finding no increased viral load.
The overall result of multiple studies was that no significant increase in EBV or HHV-6 viral load occurred in ME/CFS patients compared to controls.
Multiple studies by the same research group showed that FOXP3+ regulatory T cells (Tregs) were significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to controls, suggesting overall immune dysregulation.

Kerr and co-investigators identified 88 PBMC genes clustering into eight ME/CFS gene expression subtypes; EBI2 was the most highly induced gene in a female subgroup with the most severe clinical phenotype, lowest SF-36 functional scores, and high frequency of muscle pain and sleep problems.
Cornaby et al. reported that the EBV BRRF1 gene product induces upregulation of the cellular gene EBI2, whereas a BRRF1-deficient virus could not induce EBI2.

Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of ME/CFS cytokine studies produced conflicting results: one study found TGF-β alone elevated, another found TNF, IL-2, IL-4 and CRP elevated, while two others found no significant differences in plasma cytokines.

EBV dUTPase was shown to induce increased secretion of multiple cytokines and chemokines, including TNF-α, TGF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-12p40, IL-23, CCL5, CCL20 and IFN-γ, in PBMCs and human primary monocyte-derived dendritic cells.

EBV dUTPase-induced cytokine/chemokine expression was shown to be dependent on Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) signaling, resulting in NF-κB activation, and dUTPase secreted in exosomes was sufficient to trigger this pathway in dendritic cells and PBMCs.

The ability to act as a PAMP ligand for TLR2 was shown to be a common feature of dUTPases encoded by other herpesviruses (HSV-2, HHV-6A, HHV-8, VZV) and human endogenous retrovirus-K, though these differentially activated NF-κB via TLR2/TLR1 heterodimers rather than TLR2 homodimers.

Multiple studies have reported the presence of autoantibodies in ME/CFS patients against numerous cellular components, supporting the hypothesis that ME/CFS may involve autoimmune mechanisms possibly triggered by EBV molecular mimicry.
Cox et al. found significant increases in serum activin A and IL-21 (but not CXCL13) in ME/CFS patients, correlating with seropositivity for anti-EBV and anti-HHV-6 dUTPase antibodies.

EBV and HHV-6 dUTPases induced secretion of activin A in human dendritic cells sufficient to promote differentiation of naive CD4+ T cells into a TFH cell-like phenotype; serum from ME/CFS patients was also sufficient to drive this differentiation.

Immunophenotyping showed that EBV dUTPase protein induced a significant in vivo increase in the frequency of iNKTFH cells, marginal zone B (MZB) cells, and plasmablasts/plasma cells, supported by gene expression analyses.

While a single ME/CFS study found no difference in MZB cell frequency versus controls, several other studies reported increased iNKT cells in ME/CFS patients that positively correlated with disease severity in some reports.
Neuroinflammation is described as a common feature affecting 85–90% of all ME/CFS patients, although the underlying mechanisms and extent of astrocyte/microglial activation remain largely unclear.

A mouse model study found that EBV dUTPase altered expression of 34 genes with central roles in blood-brain-barrier integrity, fatigue, pain, synapse structure/function, and tryptophan, dopamine, and serotonin metabolism.

EBV dUTPase downregulated LIN7b, SYNPO, and RAB33A while upregulating Egr-1 in mouse brain, implicating disruption of NMDAR localization, long-term potentiation, and vesicle trafficking important for synaptic plasticity.

In vitro studies using human cerebral microvascular endothelial cells, astrocytes, and microglia demonstrated that EBV dUTPase potently induced TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, cytokines known to disrupt the blood-brain barrier.
EBV dUTPase induced a transient increase in COX-2 (PTGS2) expression in human astrocytes but a significant and sustained (>24 h) increase in microglia.

EBV dUTPase increased IDO1 and KMO expression in microglia (suggesting increased quinolinic acid synthesis), increased Gch1, and downregulated Tph2, Th, Drd1, Drd5 and Slc6a4, changes proposed to reduce dopamine and serotonin availability and contribute to cognitive symptoms and oxidative stress.
49 to 93% of patients who develop ME/CFS report that their symptoms began after an illness with flu-like symptoms, suggesting an infectious trigger.
A study comparing 36 matched pairs found no statistically significant difference in ACTH pulsatility between ME/CFS patients and controls.
Another study found a differential pattern of ACTH release over 24-hour periods in ME/CFS patients, contrasting with a prior null pulsatility study.
ME/CFS patients showed the same number of cortisol secretory events as controls but secreted lower quantities in the early morning hours.
A group of ME/CFS patients had adrenal glands 50% smaller than controls, resembling adrenal atrophy seen in prolonged critical illness.
Some studies found low nocturnal GH secretion in ME/CFS patients, while others found normal 24-hour urinary GH excretion.
Some studies found reduced GH response to induced hypoglycemia in ME/CFS patients, while others describe normal GH responses to stimulation.
There are no consistent differences in IGF-1 levels between ME/CFS patients and controls, consistent with findings in prolonged critical illness.
Fibromyalgia studies show relative GH deficiency and low or low-normal IGF-1 levels, with some patients failing to exhibit a GH response to exercise, consistent with loss of GH pulsatility.
ME/CFS patients had similar TSH levels to controls but lower Free T3, Total T4, and Total T3, and a significantly higher rT3-to-T3 ratio, resembling non-thyroidal illness syndrome (NTIS).
Depressed thyroid hormone levels appear to reduce natural killer cell activity, which is a signature finding in ME/CFS.
Montoya et al. found that 17 cytokines were positively correlated with ME/CFS severity, of which 13 were pro-inflammatory.
ME/CFS patients show high brain lactate and low brain glutathione levels, likely arising from oxidative stress mechanisms.
Numerous studies have found increased oxidative and nitrosative stress in ME/CFS, identified as a factor in observed metabolic dysfunction.

ME/CFS patients show decreased baseline cortisol levels, blunted HPA axis responses to stressors, reduced responsivity to CRH/ACTH provocation tests, and a heightened inhibitory feedback loop, with dysfunction severity increasing with illness duration and symptom severity.

HPA axis dysfunction is present in the majority of fibromyalgia patients, involving depressed CRH secretion, CRH receptor deficiency on the pituitary, and adrenal atrophy from reduced ACTH stimulation.
The most common peri-onset events reported by ME/CFS patients are infection-related episodes (64%), stressful incidents (39%), and exposure to environmental toxins (20%).
Of 101 ME/CFS patients treated with low-dose aripiprazole, 74% experienced improvement in at least one symptom category (fatigue, brain fog, unrefreshing sleep, or PEM frequency).
12% of patients showed no observable change in symptoms even at the maximum dose of 2 mg/day.
14% of patients discontinued aripiprazole due to worsening symptoms or side effects.
In responders, average self-rated fatigue score decreased significantly from 5.76 to 2.86 after low-dose aripiprazole.
In responders, average brain fog score improved significantly from 4.39 to 2.06 after aripiprazole.
In responders, unrefreshing sleep rating improved significantly from 5.80 to 3.75 after aripiprazole.
In responders, frequency of post-exertional malaise episodes decreased from once every 4.2 days to once every 8.3 days on aripiprazole.
Among responders, 57 patients described PEM episodes as milder and shorter, and 18 reported complete resolution of PEM with no new episodes.
Non-responders showed no significant change in fatigue scores (5.85 to 5.65) after aripiprazole.
