Non-responders showed no significant change in brain fog scores (4.25 to 3.60) after aripiprazole.
Non-responders showed a non-significant worsening of sleep quality (5.89 to 6.32) after aripiprazole.
Non-responders showed no significant change in PEM frequency (0.23/day to 0.25/day) after aripiprazole.
Beyond the titration phase, reported side effects of low-dose aripiprazole included headache, irritability/agitation, insomnia, and rare extreme agitation.

Bodyweight changes during aripiprazole treatment were highly variable, averaging a 0.15 kg/month gain, with some patients gaining 5–12 kg and others losing 6–14 kg, not clearly attributable to the drug.
Concurrent antidepressant use did not significantly differ between responders and non-responders, suggesting it does not predict aripiprazole response.
Quality-of-life improvements from aripiprazole enabled six patients with ME/CFS to return to work.
Four ME/CFS patients with comorbid myoclonic dystonia reported improvement of their movement disorder while taking aripiprazole.

The authors cite prior evidence that dopamine D2 receptor agonists mediate neuroinflammation, microglial activation, and cell death, providing rationale for testing the dopamine-modulator aripiprazole in ME/CFS.

Cited prior evidence indicates elevated inflammatory cytokines in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid correlating with symptom severity, and PET imaging shows activated microglia/astrocytes in various brain regions of ME/CFS patients.
ME/CFS prevalence in the U.S. is estimated at 0.5-1.5% of the population.
ME/CFS prevalence is reported to be higher among females than males.
Viral infection is described as an established trigger for the onset of ME/CFS symptoms, raising concern that COVID-19 could increase ME/CFS prevalence.
Immune dysregulation is described as a common feature across the heterogeneous ME/CFS patient population.
Mitochondrial dysfunction is described as a common feature across the heterogeneous ME/CFS patient population.
Current ME/CFS treatments are largely palliative, limited to symptom alleviation and addressing psychological sequelae of long-term disability.

After 84 days of open-label (-)-OSU6162 treatment, Clinical Global Impression of Change scores showed significant within-group improvement from day 7 through day 112, with 78.6% of participants showing some degree of improvement at day 84.
Fatigue Severity Scale total scores significantly decreased following 84 days of (-)-OSU6162 treatment.
Mental Fatigue Scale scores decreased from the severe to moderate range at the group level after 84 days of (-)-OSU6162 treatment, interpreted as clinically relevant improvement.
Beck Depression Inventory scores decreased from mild to minimal depression range following 84 days of (-)-OSU6162 treatment.
FibroFatigue scale total scores significantly improved following 84 days of (-)-OSU6162 treatment.
SF-36 subscales for Vitality, Social function and Physical function significantly improved (higher scores indicating less disability) after 84 days of (-)-OSU6162 treatment.
Blood leukocyte counts showed a slight but statistically significant decrease from baseline to end of (-)-OSU6162 treatment.
Serum prolactin levels significantly increased, as expected pharmacologically, from baseline to end of (-)-OSU6162 treatment.
(-)-OSU6162 dose at visit 7 was strongly correlated with its plasma concentration at that visit.
(-)-OSU6162 plasma concentration was significantly correlated with the change in serum prolactin but not with change in blood leukocyte concentration.
No significant correlations were found between (-)-OSU6162 plasma concentrations and changes observed in the clinical efficacy rating scores.
One patient discontinued the study due to a treatment-related adverse event of affect lability starting during the second month of treatment.
Two participants experienced serious adverse events (appendicitis; bronchopneumonia followed by anxiety requiring hospitalization) during the study, neither judged related to treatment.

The therapeutic response to (-)-OSU6162 on fatigue appeared larger in ME/CFS patients who were also on concomitant pharmacological antidepressant treatment compared to those who were not, consistent with a prior double-blind ME/CFS study.

The Mental Fatigue Scale appeared to be a more sensitive instrument than the validated Fatigue Severity Scale for detecting clinical improvement in mental fatigue and related symptoms in ME/CFS and other neurological disorders.
Combined CoQ10 and NADH supplementation significantly reduced Fatigue Impact Scale (FIS-40) scores in ME/CFS patients.
NADH supplementation alone significantly reduced fatigue scores compared to placebo in ME/CFS patients.
KPAX002 (methylphenidate hydrochloride plus a mitochondrial modulator) significantly reduced symptom scores, with the greatest response seen in patients with higher baseline symptom severity.

Acetyl-L-Carnitine (ALC) significantly reduced mental fatigue and Propionyl-L-Carnitine (PLC) significantly reduced general fatigue, but the ALC+PLC combination was a less effective intervention than either alone.
Two of the nine included studies found no significant change in fatigue levels following nutraceutical intervention.

CoQ10 plus NADH supplementation significantly lowered age-predicted maximum heart rate during a cycle ergometer task and significantly reduced fatigue perception at all follow-up visits, though sleep and pain scores were unchanged.
CoQ10 plus NADH supplementation significantly increased NAD+/NADH, CoQ10, ATP, and citrate synthase levels in ME/CFS patients.
CoQ10 plus NADH supplementation significantly reduced lipoperoxide levels in ME/CFS patients, consistent with reduced oxidative stress.
Guanidinoacetic acid (GAA) supplementation significantly increased muscular creatine levels and improved muscular strength and aerobic power in ME/CFS patients.
Improvement in depression scores following ubiquinol-10 supplementation was dependent on an increase in total plasma CoQ10 levels in ME/CFS patients.

Ubiquinol-10 supplementation significantly improved Clinical Global Impression (CGI) and Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) scores, but Patient Global Impression (PGI) scores were not significantly changed.

In the ALC, PLC and combination ALC+PLC intervention groups, performance on the Stroop attention concentration test significantly improved in all groups, while McGill Pain Questionnaire scores did not significantly change in any group.
A prior study found no significant differences in mitochondrial DNA between ME/CFS patients and comparators, suggesting ME/CFS is not primarily a mitochondrial DNA-based disorder.
The authors propose that impairments in calcium (Ca2+)-dependent mitochondrial pathways contribute to the oxidative stress reported in ME/CFS patients across several intervention studies.

Across the nine included studies, six reported significant improvements in fatigue levels following mitochondrial-targeting nutraceutical intervention, while fatigue was the primary outcome measure in eight of the nine studies.
RNase1 was one of nine plasma proteins significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls at q<0.05.
RABP2, a retinoic-acid shuttling protein, was significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to controls.
AIF1L, an actin-bundling cytoskeletal protein, was significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to controls.
PXDN (peroxidasin), an extracellular matrix crosslinking enzyme, was significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to controls.
Ephrin-A4 (EFNA4) was significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to controls, implicating ephrin-Eph signaling.
TIMD3 (HAVCR2), an immune tolerance receptor that inhibits Th1 and CD8+ T-cell activity, was significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to controls.
MXRA7, a protein involved in wound healing and neovascularization, was significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to controls.
TNF soluble receptor-I (TNFRSF1A), which sequesters TNF-α and inhibits inflammation, was significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to controls.
IL-18 binding protein alpha, which inhibits IL-18-driven Th1 proinflammatory responses, was significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to controls despite IL-18 itself being unchanged.
CFTR was the only relaxed-threshold protein found significantly reduced in ME/CFS patients compared to controls, at q<0.15.
ROR1, a neurite-growth-modulating receptor, was found significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients at the relaxed q<0.15 threshold.
DCP1A and BAMBI (TGF-beta pathway components) and PPIC (protein folding chaperone) were among proteins elevated in ME/CFS patients at the relaxed q<0.15 threshold.
DR6, a TNF-receptor-family protein involved in axonal pruning and T-cell regulation, was significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients in the less-standardized dataset analysis.

Ephrin-A5 (EFNA5), involved in cell-cell adhesion, axon fasciculation, and glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, was significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients in the less-standardized dataset analysis.

STRING functional enrichment analysis of the entire dataset showed statistically significant enrichment restricted to ephrin receptor and ligand family proteins, identifying ephrin-Eph signaling as centrally disrupted in ME/CFS.
FYN, RhoA, and LYN, which interact with all ephrin family proteins, showed fold changes inverted relative to (and significantly higher than) the ephrin family proteins in ME/CFS patients.

STRING gene-set analysis of the 391 nominally significant proteins showed enrichment of multiple immune-related Reactome pathways including cytokine signaling, platelet activation/degranulation, and neutrophil degranulation.
The top nine individual proteins by ROC AUC (>0.85) for distinguishing ME/CFS from controls were the same nine proteins significant at q<0.05.
The plasma abundance ratio of FXN (frataxin) to HAVCR2 (TIMD3) achieved the highest ROC AUC (~0.95) of all protein ratios tested for distinguishing ME/CFS from controls.

Four protein abundance ratios with plausible biological rationale showed highly significant differences between ME/CFS patients and controls, with most subjects' ratio values clearly separating the two cohorts.
DAVID functional annotation clustering of the top 3000 differentially abundant proteins identified a cluster related to regulation of Janus kinase (JAK) activity and JAK-STAT cytokine signaling.
A GO cluster centered on glucose metabolism (glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, glucose phosphorylation) was significantly enriched among differentially abundant proteins.
The C3-ZPBP2 protein-protein correlation was the most inverted between cohorts (from strongly negative in controls to strongly positive in ME/CFS patients), implicating complement system disruption.
The NSDHL-IMPAD1 protein correlation showed the largest positive-to-negative inversion between cohorts, linking cholesterol biosynthesis and skeletal element formation pathways.
CILP2 and the CGA/FSHB proteins had over 7% of their total protein-protein interaction correlations inverted in ME/CFS patients compared to controls, disproportionately more than other proteins.
ME/CFS patients scored significantly worse than controls on both the Bell scale and SF-36 quality-of-life survey, reflecting substantial illness burden.
No significant correlations were detected between collected clinical/symptom survey data and plasma protein abundance levels.
PXDNL, an antagonist homolog of PXDN, was found at lower levels in ME/CFS patients despite PXDN itself being elevated, though not reaching the primary significance threshold.
Unlike TIMD3 upregulation seen with T-cell exhaustion in cancer/chronic viral infection, PD-1 (PDCD1) expression was not elevated in the ME/CFS cohort.
TNF ligand (TNF-α) plasma levels were not significantly different between ME/CFS patients and controls, despite elevated soluble TNF receptor-I.
The C3-ZPBP2 protein pair showed the most extreme flip in correlation between cohorts, with a negative correlation in controls becoming positive in ME/CFS patients.
The NSDHL-IMPAD1 protein pair showed the largest positive-to-negative correlation flip between controls and ME/CFS patients.
CILP2 and the CGA/FSHB pair each had over 7% of their total protein-protein interactions inverted in the ME/CFS cohort compared to controls.
The abundance ratio of Fraxatin (FXN) to HAVCR2 (TIMD3) yielded the highest AUC of any protein pair, nearly 0.95, for distinguishing ME/CFS patients from controls.
The LAYN-CLEC4D protein abundance ratio was among the top pairs distinguishing ME/CFS from controls and was proposed to have biological relevance given both proteins' roles in T-cell function.

The EPHA5-CFTR protein ratio was one of the top distinguishing pairs and is supported by prior experimental evidence linking both proteins to hypoglycemic response regulation in the ventromedial hypothalamus.

The four biologically-rationalized protein ratios (FXN-HAVCR2, LAYN-CLEC4D, EPHA5-CFTR, and CFTR-KRT16) each differed significantly between ME/CFS patients and controls with high statistical significance.

STRING rank-based functional enrichment analysis of the full dataset identified the ephrin receptor/ligand family as significantly enriched, with the 'EPHA-mediated growth cone collapse' pathway (28 proteins, 17 measured) being the largest and most inclusive pathway detected.
FYN, RhoA, and LYN, which interact with all measured ephrin family proteins, showed fold changes inverted relative to the ephrin proteins, being significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than controls.

STRING gene set-based enrichment of the 391 nominally significant proteins highlighted Reactome pathways centered on the immune system, including cytokine signaling, platelet activation/degranulation, and neutrophil degranulation, in addition to the Ephrin signaling pathway.
DAVID functional annotation clustering of the top 3000 UniProt IDs by p-value identified a cluster related to regulation of Janus kinase (JAK) activity, part of JAK-STAT cytokine signal transduction.

A DAVID functional annotation cluster centered on glucose metabolism biological processes (glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, glucose-6-phosphate conversion) was enriched among differentially abundant proteins.
A DAVID functional cluster related to axon guidance and cell migration signaling, functionally intertwined with the ephrin-Eph pathway, was enriched among differentially abundant proteins.
A DAVID functional cluster linked to PI3K signaling, involved in cell proliferation and neural long-term potentiation, was enriched among differentially abundant proteins.
While PXDN was elevated in ME/CFS patient plasma, its antagonist PXDNL, a related peroxidase-like protein, showed a nominal decrease in patients.

Unlike the T-cell exhaustion phenotype seen in cancer where TIMD3 upregulation accompanies PD-1 upregulation, PD-1 (PDCD1) levels were not different between ME/CFS patients and controls in this cohort.
Circulating TNF ligand levels did not differ significantly between ME/CFS patients and controls, despite elevated TNF sR-I (soluble receptor).
IL-18 levels were comparable between ME/CFS patients and controls, distinguishing this cohort from Crohn's disease patients in whom both IL-18 and IL-18BPa are elevated relative to controls.
IFN-gamma was slightly lower (not significantly) in the ME/CFS cohort, indicating the observed increase in IL-18BPa was not driven by increased IFN-gamma.

EFNA4, EFNA5, and TNFRSF1A were previously reported as upregulated members of a correlation network in a heart failure study, and almost all other proteins in that network were likewise found upregulated in the current ME/CFS cohort.

KRT16, along with several other keratin family proteins, has previously been reported as significantly different in the cerebrospinal fluid of a primarily male ME/CFS cohort compared to controls, and was slightly higher in plasma in the current female cohort.

CFTR has a prior modest link to ME/CFS through a gene-expression-based drug repurposing study that identified a CFTR-associated gene module ('M46-recycling pathway of L1') linked to the drug Ivacaftor as a candidate repurposed treatment.
Correlation analysis between the collected clinical/symptom survey data and plasma protein abundances found no significant correlations.
ME/CFS patients scored significantly worse than controls on both the Bell scale and SF-36 quality-of-life metrics, reflecting substantial illness burden.

Individual protein abundance ROC analysis showed the top nine proteins by AUC (all >0.85) for distinguishing ME/CFS from controls were the same nine proteins found significantly different by the strict statistical threshold (Table 2).

The discussion notes that genetically diverse viruses, including Epstein-Barr virus, utilize Eph receptors for viral entry, which the authors connect to the controversial association between EBV and ME/CFS given their ephrin-Eph pathway findings.

A prior study of circulating extracellular vesicles in ME/CFS patients found evidence implicating the ephrin-Eph pathway, including PI3K signaling, actin cytoskeletal regulation, and focal adhesions, corroborating the current dataset's findings.

A prior ME/CFS cerebrospinal fluid proteome study also implicated axonal guidance pathways linked to ephrin-Eph signaling and complement pathways including C3, consistent with the disrupted C3 correlation network observed in the current plasma dataset.
Cognitive exertion caused greater increases in fatigue and pain in women with ME/CFS than in controls, while cognitive performance was unaffected.
At baseline, ME/CFS patients showed altered functional connectivity between default-mode network seeds and frontal brain areas compared to controls.
At baseline, ME/CFS patients exhibited stronger functional connectivity between all salience network seeds and left temporal areas and the medulla compared to controls.

Cognitive exertion caused significantly greater increases in functional connectivity between the right insular seed and frontal and subcortical areas in ME/CFS patients than controls, and these increases correlated with symptom worsening.
A pediatric patient presenting with chronic fatigue syndrome/ME was found to have an underlying organic cause identified via cardiopulmonary exercise testing.
The report emphasizes the need to rule out organic causes of CFS in pediatric patients to avoid missing a preventable or treatable underlying condition.
CFS/ME is estimated to affect approximately 0.4% of the population, with no known biomarker for diagnosis.

An estimated 10-25% of the CFS/ME population fall into the severe or very severe category, equating to roughly 82,000 housebound/bedbound individuals across England who may not be receiving appropriate treatment.

The PACE trial used a 6-minute walk test as part of eligibility/consent assessment, which would have precluded severe and very severe CFS/ME patients from participating, meaning trial conclusions (e.g., on CBT/GET) may not generalize to this subgroup.
All five participants deteriorated when attempting to increase activity/exercise or return to 'normal' function, consistent with unidentified exercise intolerance and a 'boom or bust' pacing pattern.
One participant reported that Graded Exercise Therapy (GET)-type activity (physically pushing past symptom limits) made her worse, leading her to avoid CFS clinics and GET entirely.
Dissociation and detachment, including loss of sense of self/identity, was expressed by four of the five participants and suspected in the remaining participants.
One participant described disturbed sleep attributed to autonomic/hyperadrenergic disturbance, including overheating, waking hourly, bad dreams, and hallucinations.
Basic daily activities such as personal hygiene and eating appeared to engage the sympathetic nervous system, often leading to dysautonomia affecting heart, blood vessels, digestion, and breathing.
Prior research cited indicates that CBT and GET do not restore the ability of a person with CFS/ME to work.

It has been reported that 88 suicides were partly attributed to CFS/ME between 2001 and 2016, driven mainly by extrinsic factors (lack of medical/social support, uncontrolled symptoms, inadequate financial help) rather than depression alone.
Two of the five participants reported difficulty navigating the disability benefits system, including loss of benefits following reassessment despite ongoing illness.

Illness onset coinciding with a life transition (e.g., new job, new parenthood, school-to-work transition) and an imbalance between illness burden and available support resources were identified as potential risk factors for developing the severe/very severe CFS/ME presentation.
All five participants reported delayed diagnosis and poor relationships with healthcare professionals, consistent with previously identified risk factors for severe CFS/ME presentation.
The discussion notes that fatigue is a major symptom of long-haul COVID-19, prompting the authors to call for re-evaluation of approaches to CFS/ME given the anticipated surge in long-COVID cases.

17.5% of COVID-19 survivors (21/120) showed fatigue-syndrome spectrum symptoms 6 months after discharge, with 10% chronic idiopathic fatigue, 5% CFS-like with insufficient symptoms, and 2.5% meeting full CFS criteria.

The strict CFS prevalence measured after COVID-19 (2.5%) was comparable to the estimated general population prevalence of CFS using Fukuda criteria (~2%), suggesting minimal added contribution of COVID-19 to future CFS risk.
5.8% of COVID-19 survivors (7/120) screened positive for PTSD using the PCL-5 six months after discharge, with a mean total severity score of 9.27 ± 10.76.
All patients who screened positive for PTSD also fell within the fatigue-syndrome spectrum, with the majority classified as chronic idiopathic fatigue.

Sex, PTSD, comorbidity, and chloroquine phosphate administration were significantly associated with asthenia severity in univariate analysis, but none remained significant predictors in multivariate logistic regression.

Female sex was associated with increased risk of CFS/ME in univariate analysis, consistent with literature showing 1.5- to 2-fold higher susceptibility in women, but this association did not remain significant after multivariate adjustment.
Oxygen saturation at admission, primary presenting symptoms, ICU admission, and laboratory test parameters were not associated with occurrence of asthenia/fatigue after COVID-19.
The brainstem shows relatively high ACE2 receptor expression compared with other brain regions, which may explain SARS-CoV-2 tropism for this region.
Neuropilin-1, a co-receptor facilitating SARS-CoV-2 entry, may also be expressed in the brainstem, potentially contributing to viral tropism there.
Autopsy studies have detected SARS-CoV-2 RNA and proteins directly in brainstem tissue of COVID-19 cases.
The brainstem is highly susceptible to damage from pathological immune or vascular activation, as observed in autopsy findings of COVID-19 cases.

The authors hypothesize that persistent brainstem dysfunction, arising from limited neuronal regeneration after damage, may underlie the chronic respiratory, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, and cognitive symptoms seen in long-COVID.

Brainstem dysfunction has previously been implicated in other chronic disorders with symptom overlap, including chronic pain, migraine, and myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS).
40.9% of adolescents with CFS/ME met the diagnostic threshold for depression based on their own RCADS self-report.

Parents reported fewer symptoms than children, resulting in a lower proportion of adolescents meeting diagnostic thresholds for depression, anxiety and any mental health disorder on the RCADS-P compared with the RCADS-C.
Bland-Altman analysis showed a small mean difference between parent and child depression subscale scores (0.7 points), with limits of agreement ranging from -6.6 to 8.0 points.
Bland-Altman analysis showed greater variability between parent and child anxiety subscale scores at higher total scores, with a mean difference of 5.3 points and wide limits of agreement.
For total RCADS scores, the mean difference between parent and child report was 6.0 points, with wide limits of agreement considered clinically unacceptable.
RCADS-C depression subscale scores accurately predicted a KSADS depression diagnosis in 69.9% of children, compared with 75.3% accuracy for RCADS-P.
RCADS-C anxiety subscale scores accurately predicted an anxiety diagnosis on the KSADS in 76.3% of cases, versus 79.6% for RCADS-P.
RCADS-C total scores accurately predicted a diagnosis of any mood disorder in 78.5% of children, compared with 75.2% for RCADS-P.
Item-level parent-child agreement on the RCADS, assessed by Cohen's kappa, was generally slight to moderate, but was moderate specifically for observable symptoms.
Both child- and parent-reported RCADS depression subscale scores significantly and similarly predicted KSADS depression diagnosis in logistic regression models.
Both child- and parent-reported RCADS anxiety subscale scores significantly predicted KSADS anxiety diagnosis with nearly identical odds ratios.
Both child- and parent-reported RCADS total scores significantly predicted any KSADS mental health diagnosis with similar odds ratios.
Approximately one-third of children with paediatric CFS/ME meet criteria for a mental health problem, a higher rate than in the general paediatric population.
Children with HSD or hEDS had a significantly higher rate of verified ADHD diagnosis than the general child population in the same catchment area.
A verified ADHD diagnosis was significantly more common in children with hEDS than in those with HSD.
The proportion of children with HSD or hEDS diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (including Asperger's syndrome) was significantly higher than in the general child population.
Fatigue was significantly more common in children with hEDS than in those with HSD.
Pain was very common (78%) across the whole cohort but did not differ significantly between the hEDS and HSD groups.
Sleep-related symptoms (sleep problems, snoring, or sleep apnea) were present in 45% of the whole cohort with no significant difference between hEDS and HSD groups.
Gastrointestinal symptoms were present in 52% of the whole cohort with no significant difference between hEDS and HSD groups.
Within the whole HSD/hEDS cohort, children with a verified ADHD diagnosis had significantly higher rates of fatigue, sleep problems, and urinary tract problems than those without ADHD.
Pain and other gastrointestinal symptoms were not significantly different by ADHD status, though there was a non-significant tendency toward more reflux/gastritis in the ADHD group.
Sleep problems were markedly overrepresented among children currently undergoing ADHD assessment compared to the rest of the cohort.
Within the HSD subgroup, ADHD diagnosis was associated with significantly more fatigue, sleep problems, and reflux/gastritis.
Within the hEDS subgroup, ADHD diagnosis was associated with significantly more sleep problems and urinary tract problems.

Among children with ADHD, those treated with CNS stimulants (56%) showed no statistically significant difference in sleep problems or pain compared to untreated ADHD children, though there was a non-significant trend toward fewer sleep problems in the treated group.
Children with ASD had a substantially higher prevalence of sleep disorders than those without ASD.
Fatigue was significantly more common among children with coexisting ASD than in those without ASD.
Children with ASD had significantly higher Beighton hypermobility scores than those without ASD.
Boys with hEDS or HSD were diagnosed significantly earlier than girls.
The proportion of children with HSD or hEDS who had an ADHD diagnosis increased markedly with age, reaching nearly half in the oldest age group.
Degree of joint hypermobility (Beighton score) was not significantly related to the overall burden of associated symptoms, suggesting hypermobility is only a sub-symptom of a broader condition.
Joint hypermobility syndrome was present in 54% of functional dyspepsia patients compared with only 7% of healthy subjects.

Non-JHS functional dyspepsia patients showed a smaller drop in intragastric pressure (less gastric accommodation) during nutrient drink infusion compared with JHS-FD and healthy subjects, though the difference did not reach statistical significance.

Non-JHS functional dyspepsia patients tolerated less nutrient drink volume/calories before maximal satiation compared with JHS-FD patients and healthy subjects, though the difference was not statistically significant.
The paper reports a case in which intestinal pseudo-obstruction occurred as an atypical clinical manifestation of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

The infant was found to carry a homozygous duplication of exons 10–16 (c.1067_1846dup) in the PLOD1 gene on chromosome 1p36.3-p36.2, confirming a diagnosis of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome kyphoscoliotic type (EDS VIA).

Initial targeted gene sequencing for PLOD1 and FKBP14 was reported as normal/negative, which apparently excluded EDS, but later MLPA analysis revealed the causative exon duplication that targeted sequencing had missed.

Urinary lysyl pyridinoline to hydroxylysyl pyridinoline (LP/HP) crosslink ratio was abnormally high in the patient, testing positive despite initially negative PLOD1/FKBP14 targeted sequencing, and this ratio is diagnostic for EDS VIA versus normal controls.

FKBP14 mutations, a less common cause of EDS kyphoscoliotic type with abnormal collagen crosslink formation, are distinguished from PLOD1-related disease by a normal (rather than elevated) LH/HP ratio.

The absence of the inferior labial and lingual frenulum, together with joint hypermobility and early-onset kyphoscoliosis/hypotonia, is described as a distinctive clinical clue suggesting EDS in a floppy infant workup.
Hip dislocations are described in 25% of EDS VIA patients at birth, contributing to long-term walking impairment as one of the disorder's major long-term complications.

Vascular rupture (of a medium-sized artery) is identified as the major life-threatening complication in EDS kyphoscoliotic type, warranting cardiovascular assessment including echocardiography for aortic root size by age 5.

Osteoporosis occurs in all individuals with EDS kyphoscoliotic type, and adults with severe kyphoscoliosis are at risk of chronic respiratory failure, recurrent pneumonia and cardiac failure; microcornea is common, with glaucoma and retinal detachment also occurring.
Nearly one-third of women with hEDS had a history of suicide attempt.
Nearly 43% of hEDS patients showed some degree of suicide risk at the time of evaluation, mostly mild.
hEDS patients who had attempted suicide were younger than those who had not attempted suicide.
hEDS patients with a history of suicide attempt scored higher on personality disturbance subscores including depressive, avoidant, antisocial, and borderline traits compared to non-attempters.
hEDS patients who attempted suicide had an increased lifetime prevalence of major depression, mania/hypomanic episodes, and anxiety disorders compared to non-attempters.
Binary logistic regression showed that personality disturbances and anxiety disorders increased the probability of belonging to the suicide attempters group among hEDS patients.
The authors report that small fiber neuropathy (SFN) is increasingly suspected to underlie many of the unexplained symptoms seen in patients with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS).
Two EDS patients with presumed immune-mediated small fiber neuropathy were successfully treated with intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIG).

The authors highlight that small fiber neuropathies are underrecognized and have limited treatment options, underscoring a need for further research into immunosuppressant therapies and the EDS-SFN link.

A 3-year-old child with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and a confirmed COL3A1 variant developed an intraperitoneal bladder rupture after minor abdominal trauma, reported as the first such case in the literature.

Tissue fragility leading to internal organ rupture after minor trauma is described as a known complication of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and this case demonstrates such rupture can occur in young children.
Women with EDS reported significantly more gastrointestinal symptoms than healthy controls.
Women with EDS reported significantly more food allergies/intolerances compared to healthy controls.
Women with EDS had increased prevalence of history of eating disorders and higher risk of current eating disorder compared to controls.
Women with EDS had lower BMI compared to healthy controls.
Within the EDS group, risk of eating disorder was associated with the presence of GI symptoms.
Restricted eating in EDS patients was associated with GI symptoms, food allergies/intolerances, and dysphagia.
Uncontrolled eating in EDS patients was associated with GI symptoms.
BMI in EDS patients was associated with GI symptoms and food allergies/intolerances.
Overall, 57.3% of surveyed fibromyalgia patients scored ≥50/100 on the Neuropathic Pain Symptoms Inventory, indicating severe neuropathic pain.

Severe neuropathic pain (NPSI≥50) was substantially more prevalent in patients meeting Fibromyalgia Research Criteria (FM+, 62.4%) than in those with FM-like symptoms not fulfilling criteria (FM-, 21.0%).
Approximately 46% of patients reported three or more small-fiber neuropathic symptoms (SFNS) potentially suggestive of small fiber pathology, most commonly dry eyes/mouth, allodynia, and dyshidrosis.
NPSI score showed a moderate-to-strong positive correlation with self-reported disability (Spearman's rho=0.61).
NPSI score showed a moderate-to-strong positive correlation with overall pain level (Spearman's rho=0.66).
NPSI score showed a moderate positive correlation with stiffness level (Spearman's rho=0.46).
NPSI score showed a weak-to-moderate positive correlation with the number of painful sites (Spearman's rho=0.40).
NPSI score showed a weak-to-moderate positive correlation with small-fiber neuropathic symptoms (SFNS) (Spearman's rho=0.44).
NPSI neuropathic pain scores showed a moderate positive correlation with the number of small-fiber neuropathic symptoms reported.
Despite the high prevalence of neuropathic pain and small-fiber neuropathic symptoms, objective neurophysiologic testing was performed in only 43.6% of enrolled patients.
Skin punch biopsy, the gold-standard test for small-fiber neuropathy, was performed in only 1.9% of surveyed fibromyalgia patients.
Only 13.2% of fibromyalgia patients surveyed reported taking anti-neuropathic pain drugs, despite high reported prevalence of neuropathic pain symptoms.
Pain acceptance moderates the relationship between pain catastrophizing and pacing patterns in women with fibromyalgia.
At low levels of pain acceptance, pain catastrophizing was significantly and positively associated with pacing patterns.
At high levels of pain acceptance, pacing patterns were independent of pain catastrophizing, suggesting acceptance decouples this relationship.

The paper hypothesizes that a broad set of pro-inflammatory molecules termed the 'inflammatome' is repeatedly elevated in cerebrospinal fluid and blood of fibromyalgia patients and underlies disease pathogenesis.
Gut dysbiosis is proposed as the primary trigger of the inflammatome in fibromyalgia and has recently been detected in individuals with FM.
Sarcopenia-associated processes are proposed to act as the peripheral nociceptive source contributing to fibromyalgia pathogenesis and have been recently detected in FM patients.
Neuroinflammation is proposed as the central mechanism driving pain sensitization, transmission, and overall symptomatology in fibromyalgia.

The authors propose that specialized pro-resolving mediators (SPMs), which have repeatedly been shown to prevent and attenuate pain in animal experiments, could be a safe therapeutic strategy to alleviate fibromyalgia symptoms, potentially combined with anti-dysbiotic treatment.

Vagus nerve stimulation, whether invasive or transcutaneous, has been shown in small open-label pilot studies to significantly reduce disease activity in rheumatoid arthritis by dampening the inflammatory response of circulating peripheral cells.
Studies have shown that vagus nerve stimulation could limit fatigue in Sjogren's syndrome and systemic lupus erythematosus.
Vagus nerve stimulation has been reported to decrease pain in patients with fibromyalgia.
Vagus nerve stimulation has also been reported to decrease pain in erosive hand osteoarthritis.
During the final four weeks of each condition, generalized body pain did not differ significantly between placebo and low-dose dextromethorphan treatment.
Physical activity ratings during the final four weeks of treatment did not differ significantly between placebo and DXM.
When analyzing the entire treatment period (rather than just the last four weeks), generalized pain was significantly lower during DXM treatment than during placebo.
The rate of decline in pain over time differed by condition, with pain decreasing over time during placebo but remaining flat during DXM treatment (significant time-by-condition interaction).
Highest reported pain (maximum pain) was significantly lower during DXM treatment than during placebo across the entire treatment period.
In sensitivity analyses over the entire treatment period, no significant effects of DXM condition were found for muscle pain, fatigue, or depressed mood.
Age and duration of FM did not significantly moderate the treatment effect of DXM on generalized pain.
Day-to-day medication compliance did not predict generalized pain scores beyond the general treatment effect, and did not interact with treatment condition.
Elevated alanine aminotransferase was the most frequently observed adverse event, occurring during DXM treatment but absent during the placebo phase.
Participants could not reliably distinguish whether they were receiving placebo or DXM, correctly guessing only 57% of the time on average, not significantly above chance in any period.

Chronic overlapping pain conditions (COPC) as defined by the US NIH include chronic fatigue syndrome, chronic low back pain, chronic tension headache, endometriosis, fibromyalgia syndrome, migraine, painful bladder syndrome, temporomandibular disorder and vulvodynia.
COPCs share etiological risk factors including familial aggregation, childhood adversities, and major or traumatic life events.
A major shared pathophysiological mechanism across COPCs, including endometriosis and fibromyalgia, is altered central nervous system processing of stimuli (central sensitization).
Guidelines recommend that patients with endometriosis should be screened for other chronic pain conditions (including fibromyalgia) and for psychological distress.
Physical examination in endometriosis patients should check for local myofascial trigger points and generalized signs of hyperalgesia and allodynia indicating central sensitization.
In cases of endometriosis with chronic overlapping pain conditions, repeated surgery for pain relief should be avoided.
Amitriptyline and duloxetine are recommended as pharmacological treatment options for endometriosis patients with chronic overlapping pain conditions.

A multimodal therapy approach including physiotherapy and pain-related psychological treatment, possibly combined with centrally acting pain modulation medication, is recommended for endometriosis patients with COPCs.
MCAS diagnosis includes documenting a rise in serum tryptase of more than 20% plus 2 ng/mL within 1-4 hours of an acute symptomatic episode.
MCAS is defined by three criteria: typical episodic systemic mast cell activation symptoms, a documented tryptase rise, and clinical response of symptoms to antimediator therapy.
Antimediator therapy responsiveness of mast cell activation symptoms is used as one of the diagnostic criteria for MCAS and reflects a treatment approach.
The Spanish Network on Mastocytosis score is used as a predictive model to identify MCAS patients likely to have an underlying clonal mast cell disorder, guiding selection for bone marrow biopsy.
MCAS diagnosis requires a substantial rise in serum tryptase above the patient's individual baseline (baseline x1.2 + 2 ng/mL) during a symptomatic episode.
Systemic reactions to hymenoptera stings are much more common in mastocytosis patients (22–49% in adults, 6–9% in children) than in the general population (0.3–8.9%).
Male patients with systemic mastocytosis without skin lesions and lower basal serum tryptase levels represent a unique subgroup with the highest reported risk of severe sting-induced anaphylaxis.
A particularly high prevalence of sting-induced anaphylaxis was reported in mastocytosis patients with tryptase levels between 20.4 and 29.9 µg/L.
Lowering the diagnostic threshold for hymenoptera venom-specific IgE to 0.17 kUA/L improves sensitivity for detecting insect venom allergy in mastocytosis patients without losing good specificity.

The basophil activation test yielded positive results in sensitized mastocytosis patients with reported sensitivity ranging between 81% and 87% in some studies, though data are inconsistent across centers.
Venom immunotherapy (VIT) side effect incidence in mastocytosis patients ranges from about 18.9% to 34%, with most reactions occurring during the induction phase (73%) versus maintenance (27%).
The frequency of common atopic diseases in mastocytosis patients (21–31%) is similar to that reported in the general population.
Among 11 systemic mastocytosis patients with persistent nasal symptoms studied by Dollner et al., only one had a confirmed documented allergy (to grass pollen).

Matito et al. found local anesthetic administration was symptomatic in only 4 of 515 administrations (<1%) in mastocytosis patients, with 2 of 76 (2.5%) epidural anesthesia recipients having an adverse event and only one severe anaphylaxis case overall.

The incidence of perioperative anaphylaxis in mastocytosis patients was estimated at 0.4%, substantially higher than the 0.01% incidence in the general population, though this estimate derives from a small, potentially biased cohort with only 3 anaphylactic cases.
Mastocytosis patients who received benzodiazepines as premedication had a lower risk of developing perioperative anaphylaxis than those who did not.

Between 9% and 14% of mastocytosis patients report severe symptoms after taking aspirin or other NSAIDs, though only about 2% have a confirmed positive oral provocation test according to Hermans et al.

Jennings et al. reported that 50.3% of mastocytosis patients report reactions to food and 23.2% report food hypersensitivity, with 73.5% overall reporting diet-associated symptoms, most commonly triggered by fruits, vegetables (especially tomatoes and citrus), dairy, cereal grains, seafood, food additives, and spices.

Jarkvist et al. systematically studied 204 Swedish patients with clonal mast cell disorders and found food hypersensitivity prevalence of only 20.6% (comparable to the general population), with confirmed IgE-mediated food allergy in only 6% after thorough workup.

Hereditary alpha tryptasemia (HAT), caused by additional copies of the alpha tryptase gene TPSAB1, is associated with elevated basal serum tryptase and a higher risk of severe mediator-related symptoms, and is present in about 5% of the general population.

Hereditary alpha tryptasemia (HAT) is present in about 15–20% of all patients with systemic mastocytosis and is associated with higher rates of hymenoptera venom allergy (30.0% vs. 9.9% in SM patients without HAT).

In a British cohort, HAT was associated with a broad range of clinical findings including urticaria/angioedema (51%), abdominal pain (43%), aches/pain (41%), skin flushing (41%), food intolerance (39%), diarrhea (36%), nausea/vomiting (27%), behavioral issues (24%), asthma (20%), eczema (19%), rhinitis (19%), joint hypermobility (17%), dizzy spells (16%) and constipation (13%).

Midostaurin, a KIT and SYK-targeting multi-kinase inhibitor, blocks IgE-dependent mediator release from normal and neoplastic mast cells and basophils and rapidly suppresses mediator-related symptoms while improving quality of life in patients with systemic mastocytosis.
Omalizumab has been suggested as an effective agent for mastocytosis patients suffering from severe IgE-related allergic reactions.
Current pharmacological and diagnostic approaches remain ineffective in about 10–20% of all MCAS patients and about 10% of all mastocytosis patients.
Over 90% of mastocytosis patients carry a somatic gain-of-function KIT D816V mutation causing SCF-independent constitutive activation and enhanced survival of neoplastic mast cells.
A rise in serum total tryptase greater than 20% above baseline plus 2 ng/mL is used to define laboratory-confirmed mast cell activation for MCAS diagnosis.
Urinary 9alpha,11beta-PGF2 was found to be more sensitive than tryptase for MCAS and more specific for mast cell activation because, unlike tryptase, it is not produced by basophils.

In a multicenter European study of 2083 patients with functional gastrointestinal disorders, 85% showed clinical overlap with MCAS, though this was likely an overdiagnosis due to non-consensus diagnostic criteria.
Mastocytosis prevalence is estimated at 9 per 100,000 in the USA and 13 per 100,000 in the Dutch population aged over 15.
About 35% of cutaneous mastocytosis and 1.8% of systemic mastocytosis cases occur in children.
Localized cutaneous mastocytomas regress at a rate of 10% per year, while maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis regresses more slowly at 1.9% per year.
Systemic mastocytosis with associated hematological neoplasm (SM-AHN) accounts for up to 40% of all SM cases, making it the second most frequent SM subvariant.
Aggressive systemic mastocytosis (ASM) is a relatively rare form representing 12% of SM cases, characterized by tissue infiltration potentially leading to multi-organ dysfunction.

Hereditary Alpha-Tryptasemia (HAT), an autosomal dominant increase in alpha-tryptase gene copy number causing elevated baseline serum tryptase, occurs in up to 4% of the general population and can mimic MCAS with atopy (94%), GERD (up to 100%), abdominal pain/diarrhea (87%), and cutaneous symptoms (up to 80%).

A Spanish retrospective study of 726 anesthetic procedures in 501 mastocytosis patients found a higher frequency of perioperative anaphylaxis than in the general population, though anesthesia was still recommended with high-risk premedication.
Venom immunotherapy (VIT) for hymenoptera stings, the most frequent anaphylaxis risk factor in MCAS/mastocytosis patients, appears safe and significantly reduces the risk of anaphylactic recurrence.
Omalizumab, an anti-IgE monoclonal antibody, has been shown to be effective in reducing symptoms in primary, secondary, and idiopathic MCAS, as well as in pediatric diffuse cutaneous mastocytosis.
The only well-designed RCT identified in a systematic review demonstrated rupatadine to be superior to placebo with globally significant clinical improvement in adults with MCAS symptoms.
Mast cell stabilizers, especially cromolyn sodium, have shown efficacy in different RCTs for mast cell disorders.
Patients treated with acetylsalicylic acid who had elevated urinary 9a-11b-PGF2 responded with symptom improvement and normalization of 9a-11b-PGF2 levels, consistent with COX-mediated PGD2 blockade.

Trials of tyrosine kinase inhibitors (Imatinib, Dasatinib, Masitinib, Nilotinib) in systemic mastocytosis showed the D816V KIT mutation confers resistance to these drugs due to conformational change of the receptor activation loop.
A multicenter study of Imatinib in advanced mast cell disease reported 29% efficacy, only in patients without the D816V KIT mutation.
Imatinib has been found useful in systemic mastocytosis with transmembrane-domain KIT mutations, mainly F522C and K509I.
In a multicenter phase II single-arm trial, midostaurin achieved a 60% response rate in advanced systemic mastocytosis patients, but 52% required temporary discontinuation due to poor tolerability.

In five patients with aggressive systemic mastocytosis unresponsive to less invasive therapies, interferon alpha-2b combined with prednisolone achieved complete or partial response in 60% and disease stabilization in 20%, while 20% discontinued due to side effects.
Cladribine has been used in systemic mastocytosis since 2001, achieving response rates greater than 50%.

Pediatric mastocytosis patients show a range of vaccination reactions, from mastocytoma formation at injection sites to severe anaphylaxis, with combination hexavalent vaccines associated with more reactions than single-antigen vaccines.

Compound 48/80 at 2 mg/kg activated mast cells and produced anticonvulsant effects, extending the onset time of both myoclonic jerk and generalized tonic-clonic seizures induced by pentylenetetrazole.
Mast cell activation by compound 48/80 (2 mg/kg) shortened the duration of generalized tonic-clonic seizures compared to saline-treated pentylenetetrazole controls.
The mast cell stabilizer cromolyn reversed the anticonvulsant effects of compound 48/80-induced mast cell activation, indicating the effect is mast-cell-mediated.
In mast cell-depleted rats, compound 48/80 no longer produced anticonvulsant effects, confirming that the effect requires intact mast cells.

Exogenous serotonin administration (10 mg/kg) also produced anticonvulsant effects against pentylenetetrazole-induced seizures, similar to mast cell activation with compound 48/80, suggesting serotonin mediates the mast cell effect.
Administration of serotonin (10 mg/kg) produced anticonvulsive effects against pentylenetetrazole-induced seizures similar to those seen with mast cell activation by compound 48/80.
The authors propose that the anticonvulsive effects of mast cell activation are mediated by serotonin release from activated mast cells.
Compound 48/80 acts as an anticonvulsant through dose-dependent activation of mast cells, indicating a graded relationship between mast cell activation and seizure suppression.
IBS prevalence in the general population varies markedly by diagnostic criteria, with 9% meeting Rome III and only 4.6% meeting the stricter Rome IV criteria.
A large Swedish survey found that 45% of IBS patients had anxiety and 26% had depression scores exceeding the normal range.
Combined multicentre data showed that pain induced by rectal distension (visceral hypersensitivity) was strongly correlated with overall gastrointestinal symptom severity in IBS.

Classical food allergy in the gut is mediated by antigen-specific IgE bound to mast cells throughout the body, triggering systemic symptoms including urticaria, asthma and gut pain/diarrhoea after ingestion.
In murine studies, gut mast cells could be sensitized to react to food given at the time of an infectious gastroenteritis episode, without any detectable specific IgE in serum.
Gut mast cells can be activated directly by psychological stressors as well as by lectins such as those in raw potatoes and uncooked red kidney bean agglutinins.

Confocal laser endomicroscopy with direct duodenal food instillation in IBS patients showed acute increases in lymphocytes and permeability with increased claudin 2, with wheat the commonest trigger (60% of responses), followed by yeast (20%), milk (9%) and soy (7%).

Caecal biopsy studies showed that atopic IBS-D patients had more severe symptoms, higher mucosal mast cell numbers, greater mast cell tryptase release, and greater mucosal permeability than non-atopic IBS-D patients.
The number of mast cells located near enteric nerves correlates with the severity of pain in IBS.
A low FODMAP diet reduces urinary histamine excretion while a high FODMAP diet increases it, suggesting FODMAP metabolic products can cause mast cell activation.
In post-infectious IBS patients with impaired intestinal barrier function, glutamine treatment improved both barrier function and symptoms.
A large UK primary care study found atopy in 44.8% of IBS patients compared to 32.7% of healthy controls, with the strongest effect for allergic conjunctivitis and hay fever.
In a large gastroenterology outpatient survey, 32% reported adverse food reactions but only 3% had allergy confirmed by endoscopic allergen provocation and/or dietary challenge.

Larger population-based studies of IBS patients with adequate controls found no difference in food-specific IgG4 antibody levels, which appeared instead to reflect dietary intake, contradicting earlier small-clinic findings.

In a double-blind, placebo-controlled study, documented lactose malabsorbers who reported milk intolerance tolerated a lactose dose equivalent to 240 mL of milk with no difference from lactose-free placebo.
A meta-analysis of 7 RCTs (397 IBS patients) found the low FODMAP diet significantly reduced the risk of not improving compared to usual/high FODMAP diet.
Adherence to the low FODMAP diet after 6 weeks averaged only 41%, with much greater adherence in IBS-D (51%) than IBS-C (10%) patients, and adherers had a high prevalence of eating disorders.

IBS-D patients carrying sucrase-isomaltase (SI) hypomorphic variants had gene dose-dependent reduced response rates to both low FODMAP and NICE diets, falling from 42.1% with one or no copies to 16.7% with two copies.
Double-blind placebo-controlled encapsulated food challenge identified 276 of 920 (30%) IBS patients as wheat sensitive, reproducing key IBS symptoms.

In a challenge study comparing gluten vs fructan vs placebo in self-identified gluten-sensitive IBS patients on a gluten-free diet, fructans induced symptoms but gluten did not, suggesting wheat-free diet benefit is due to fructan exclusion rather than gluten.
Unselected IBS patients meeting Rome III criteria have a 7-fold increased risk of having coeliac disease compared to controls.

Several randomised placebo-controlled trials show that kiwifruit increases small bowel/colonic water content, associated with increased bowel frequency and softer stools, of potential benefit for constipation-predominant patients.

A general population survey in Australia found 14.9% reported wheat intolerance, but only 1.2% had coeliac disease, and IBS patients were 3.5 times more likely than controls to report wheat intolerance.
Patients with idiopathic anaphylaxis show a higher percentage of activated T cells during acute episodes than at their own baseline.
IA patients have more activated B cells than control patients or patients with chronic idiopathic urticaria, both during acute episodes and at baseline.
Soluble CD25 levels were higher after an acute anaphylaxis episode compared to healthy controls, but lower than in mastocytosis patients.
DNA microarray analysis found that cells from IA patients differentially expressed genes correlating with CD203c levels, some of which regulate mast cell/basophil degranulation.

IA patients showed increased IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 cytokine levels after lymphocyte stimulation compared to atopic subjects and healthy controls, supporting a Th2-driven mast cell hyperreactivity hypothesis.
A prospective ex vivo study of cultured mast cells from IA patients found no evidence of a hyperresponsive mast cell phenotype using IgE-mediated beta-hexosaminidase release assays.
Peripheral blood from IA patients yielded higher mast cell numbers in culture compared to healthy controls.
Elevated tryptase levels during an acute IA episode support mast cell degranulation as the underlying mechanism.
Bone marrow biopsy identified a clonal mast cell population in 5 of 12 IA patients without cutaneous mastocytosis features or histologic systemic mastocytosis on local biopsy.
Bone marrow examination in 30 IA cases without cutaneous mastocytosis found 47% had an aberrant mast cell population diagnosed as clonal MC disorder.
In 56 subjects with unexplained anaphylaxis (>3 episodes/year) undergoing bone marrow examination, 14% showed evidence of clonal mast cell disease.
The REMA scoring tool predicts underlying mast cell clonality in anaphylaxis patients using gender, clinical symptoms, and baseline serum tryptase cut-offs of <15 or >25 ng/mL.

The Karolinska modification of the REMA score, using a tryptase cut-off of 11.4-20 ng/mL, achieved 93% sensitivity and 94% specificity for predicting clonal mast cell disorder when retrospectively applied.
The NICAS score combines clinical symptoms, gender, a tryptase cut-off of 11.4 ng/mL, and allele-specific PCR for KIT D816V mutation to identify clonal mast cell disorder in anaphylaxis patients.
Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia, caused by TPSAB1 gene duplication/extra copy numbers, occurs in about 6% of the general population and is associated with basal serum tryptase typically above 8.0 ng/mL.

Patients with hereditary alpha-tryptasemia may present with a broad symptom complex including EDS-like joint hypermobility, POTS, GI hypomotility/IBS, vibratory urticaria, eosinophilic esophagitis, neuropsychiatric diagnoses, and chronic musculoskeletal pain, though this may reflect referral bias.

Increased germline copies of alpha-tryptase are associated with more severe venom anaphylaxis, are more prevalent among people with idiopathic anaphylaxis and systemic mastocytosis, and confer increased relative risk of anaphylaxis in systemic mastocytosis patients.
Re-evaluation of 70 patients previously diagnosed with IA found 6 had reactions related to alpha-gal sensitization (2 of whom also had mastocytosis).
Alpha-gal sensitization prevalence in the general adult population ranges from 5.5 to 8.1% in an urban environment.

Alpha-gal-sIgE sensitivity was 20% overall in patients consulting an Allergy Unit, with the highest prevalence (30.2%) among patients with insect venom allergies, and prior tick bite significantly increased the risk of positivity.
The prevalence of alpha-gal sensitization among patients with clonal mast cell disorders was 18%, comparable to the general population.
In a literature review of 234 FDEIA cases, food/exercise challenges performed in 81 patients were negative in 36% of cases, showing a negative challenge does not exclude the diagnosis.

In a series of 335 IA patients, all experienced angioedema and urticaria; 63% had upper airway obstruction, 39% bronchospasm, 23% hypotension/syncope, and 22% GI symptoms, with no isolated cardiovascular collapse reported.
Clonal MCAS patients presenting with idiopathic anaphylaxis symptoms may more prevalently suffer cardiovascular symptoms, reported to be over 90% in one study.

In a case report, a 68-year-old man with recurrent unexplained anaphylactoid episodes had a baseline tryptase of 15 ng/mL that rose to 31 and 35 ng/mL during two documented acute episodes, confirming systemic mast cell activation, and symptoms resolved with desloratadine and montelukast therapy.

In the largest published IA series with 132 of 335 patients available for follow-up, 87 achieved remission (lasting 1-14 years); of 56 patients given prednisone for frequent episodes, about 20% had recurrent symptoms as the dose was tapered.
The REMA scoring tool combines clinical features (gender, symptoms) with a baseline serum tryptase cut-off (<15 or >25 ng/mL) to predict underlying clonal mast cell disease in anaphylaxis patients.
A modified 'Karolinska-score' using a baseline tryptase cut-off of 11.4-20 ng/mL achieved 93% sensitivity and 94% specificity for identifying clonal mast cell disease when retrospectively applied.

The NIH Idiopathic Clonal Anaphylaxis Score (NICAS) combines clinical symptoms, gender, a tryptase cut-off of 11.4 ng/mL, and allele-specific PCR for KIT D816V mutation to predict clonal mast cell disease.

Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (HaT) is caused by duplication or increased copy number of the alpha-tryptase gene TPSAB1 and is found in approximately 6% of the general population, with serum baseline tryptase typically greater than 8.0 ng/mL.

Patients with hereditary alpha-tryptasemia may present with EDS-like joint hypermobility with arthritis, POTS, flushing, GI hypomotility, vibratory urticaria, IBS, eosinophilic esophagitis, neuropsychiatric diagnoses, and chronic musculoskeletal pain, though this may reflect referral bias.

Increased germline copies of alpha-tryptase are associated with increased severity of venom anaphylaxis and are more prevalent among individuals with idiopathic anaphylaxis and systemic mastocytosis, with an increased relative risk for anaphylaxis among SM patients.

Alpha-gal syndrome, caused by IgE sensitization to the mammalian oligosaccharide galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose, can present with delayed anaphylactic symptoms up to 6 hours after ingestion of mammalian meat, unlike typical IgE-mediated food reactions.

In a cohort of 70 patients previously diagnosed with idiopathic anaphylaxis, further evaluation found 6 patients (two of whom also had mastocytosis) had reactions attributable to alpha-gal sensitization.

Alpha-gal sensitization prevalence in the general adult urban population ranges between 5.5 and 8.1%, while overall alpha-gal-sIgE-sensitivity was 20% among patients consulting an Allergy Unit and highest (30.2%) among those with insect venom allergies.
A reported tick bite within the 12 months prior to blood sampling significantly increased the risk of alpha-gal-sIgE positivity.
The prevalence of alpha-gal sensitization in patients with clonal mast cell disorders was found to be 18%, comparable to that of the general population.

In a literature review of 234 cases of food-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis (FDEIA), food/exercise challenges were performed in 81 patients and 36% of these had a negative challenge, showing a negative challenge does not exclude FDEIA.

A subgroup of patients describing subjective symptoms consistent with IA but without documented objective signs is termed undifferentiated somatoform IA, including patients with panic attacks, vocal cord dysfunction, or Munchausen syndrome.

A case report describes a 68-year-old man with 11 unexplained mast cell activation episodes whose baseline tryptase was 15 ng/mL but rose to 31 and 35 ng/mL during two separate emergency-documented symptomatic episodes, confirming a systemic mast cell activation process despite a negative bone marrow biopsy for clonal disease.

The 68-year-old patient's mast cell activation symptoms resolved with regular treatment of desloratadine 5 mg three times daily and montelukast 10 mg once daily, with no severe reactions in subsequent years.
Evidence suggests that treatment of systemic anaphylactic reactions with epinephrine prevents progression to more severe symptoms.

In the largest published IA series, of 132 patients available for follow-up, 87 achieved remission (lasting 1-14 years); prednisone was given to 56 patients for frequent episodes, with approximately 20% experiencing recurrent symptoms as the dose was tapered.

Omalizumab, a monoclonal anti-IgE antibody, has been reported in anecdotal reports and case series to reduce the frequency of idiopathic anaphylaxis episodes with varying success, though no randomized controlled trials exist.

Ketotifen, an H1-antihistamine and mast cell stabilizer dosed at 1-2 mg orally two to three times daily, has published steroid-sparing evidence in IA and demonstrated mast cell stabilizing properties in mastocytosis, though it can cause significant sedation.

Oral cromolyn sodium, a local mast cell stabilizer, can help patients with prominent gastrointestinal symptoms of IA, but limited systemic absorption reduces its value as a systemic prophylactic and some patients do not tolerate it due to bloating, cramping, and diarrhea.
The frequency and severity of idiopathic anaphylaxis episodes tend to decrease over time, with the vast majority of patients following a benign, gradually improving course.
MRGPRX2 is a mast cell GPCR that, when activated by certain peptide drug candidates, mediates a pseudo-allergenic mast cell degranulation response leading to histamine release.

A commercially-available cell-based MRGPRX2 assay reliably identified compounds that induce histamine release or localized edema in ex vivo human and rodent skin samples, supporting its use as an in vitro predictor of in vivo pseudo-allergenic injection site reactions.
Implementation of the MRGPRX2 in vitro assay as a substitute for postmortem injection-site evaluation in rats achieved a significant reduction in animal use during peptide drug candidate screening.
Resveratrol reduced compound 48/80-induced calcium flux in mast cells in vitro.
Resveratrol inhibited mast cell degranulation induced by compound 48/80 in vitro.
Resveratrol suppressed compound 48/80-induced hind paw extravasation in a mouse model of pseudo-allergy in vivo.
Resveratrol suppressed active systemic anaphylaxis induced by compound 48/80 in a mouse model in vivo.
Resveratrol suppressed mast cell degranulation in mouse models of pseudo-allergy in vivo.
PCR and immunohistochemistry showed that resveratrol up-regulates Nrf2 expression.
A Nrf2 inhibitor attenuated the protective effects of resveratrol, indicating the Nrf2 pathway mediates resveratrol's inhibition of MRGPRX2-mediated mast cell activation.
Aloe-emodin significantly inhibited IgE/FcεRI- and Mrgpr-mediated mast cell degranulation both in vitro and in vivo.
Aloe-emodin rapidly and reversibly decreased cytosolic Ca2+ concentration in mast cells by enhancing mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake.
Genetic silencing or pharmacologic inhibition of MCU significantly weakened aloe-emodin's effect on cytosolic Ca2+ level and mast cell degranulation, indicating MCU mediates the drug's action.

Aloe-emodin showed a more potent inhibitory effect on mast cell degranulation than six clinically used mast cell stabilizers (amlexanox, tranilast, ketotifen, cromolyn disodium salt, dexamethasone, and pimecrolimus).
Higher epithelial mast cell burden in nasal polyps was associated with earlier recurrence of polypoid edema after FESS.
Higher stromal mast cell burden in nasal polyps was associated with earlier recurrence of polypoid edema after FESS.
The percentage of TIM-3-expressing mast cells in epithelial or stromal polyp layers was not significantly associated with earlier recurrence of polypoid edema.
Mast cell burden was not significantly associated with the need for future steroid treatment after FESS.
TIM-3+ mast cell expression was not significantly associated with the need for future steroid treatment after FESS.

Skin punch biopsy showed reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density, consistent with small fiber neuropathy, in seven of nine female patients carrying the p.D313Y GLA variant compared to sex- and age-matched reference values.
The study examined the pathophysiological significance of the non-classical Fabry-related GLA variant p.D313Y in relation to small fiber neuropathy and neuropathic pain.
Four of the nine patients reported acral paresthesias and neuropathic pain with an average visual analogue scale score of 7 out of 10.
Two patients experienced acute pain crises.
Six of the seven patients diagnosed with small fiber neuropathy had a history of hypohidrosis and/or hyperhidrosis, suggesting associated autonomic nervous system dysfunction.

Overall gut microbial community structure (beta diversity) differed significantly among CD, T1DM, T1DM+CD and healthy control groups, with CD and T1DM+CD each significantly divergent from healthy controls.

Healthy controls exhibited greater alpha (within-sample) microbial diversity than the disease groups, with CD patients showing markedly lower diversity and T1DM patients the highest diversity among the disease groups.
Higher serum tTG-IgA levels (a serological marker of coeliac disease) were significantly negatively correlated with observed gut bacterial OTU diversity.
Serum Vitamin D, Folic acid and Vitamin B12 levels showed no significant correlation with gut microbial alpha diversity in this cohort.
Levels of Shigella/E.coli (pathogenic Proteobacteria) were significantly higher in the coeliac disease group compared to healthy controls.
Coeliac disease patients showed an exclusive microbial signature with decreased Dialister and Parabacteroides and increased Ruminococcus compared to other groups.
A significant increase in Akkermansia and Barnesiella genera was found to be exclusive to the T1DM group compared to other groups.
A decrease in Coprococcus genus was identified as a distinguishing hallmark of the gut microbiome in patients with both T1DM and CD.

Seven ASVs shared among the three disease groups showed opposing abundance trends between CD and T1DM/T1DM+CD: Bacteroides decreased in CD but increased in T1DM/T1DM+CD, while Prevotella, Alistipes, Oscillospira and Clostridium increased in CD but decreased in T1DM/T1DM+CD.

Parabacteroides genus abundance was significantly negatively correlated with corneal nerve fiber length (CNFL), a marker of small fiber/corneal neuropathy, suggesting a protective role against neurodegeneration.

Bacteroidetes phylum abundance was negatively correlated with corneal nerve fiber length, indicating an association between reduced abundance of this phylum and greater corneal small fiber neuropathy.
No significant correlation was observed between Vitamin D or Vitamin B biochemical markers and corneal small fiber neuropathy in this cohort.

PICRUSt-predicted microbial functional pathways including retinol metabolism, biosynthesis of unsaturated fatty acids, and ethylbenzene degradation were significantly downregulated in patients with neuropathy compared to those without.
No statistically significant differences in gut microbiota composition were observed between the four study groups at the phylum or family taxonomic levels.
All 14 included patients had positive anti-FGFR3 antibody titers (≥3000), with an average titer of 14,285.71.
Painful paresthesia was the most common presenting symptom, occurring in 100% of patients with anti-FGFR3 antibody-related polyneuropathy.
Autonomic symptoms, including orthostatic hypotension and neurogenic bladder, were reported in 28.6% of patients with anti-FGFR3 antibody polyneuropathy.
Impaired vibration sensation was noted in 78.6% and impaired proprioception in 35.7% of patients on sensory examination.
Deep tendon reflexes were reduced or absent in the lower limbs in 57.1% of patients and in the upper limbs in 14.3% of patients.
Three patients (21.4%) had co-existing facial pain meeting ICHD-3 diagnostic criteria for trigeminal neuralgia.
Nerve conduction study/EMG was abnormal in 11 of 14 patients, showing sensorimotor axonal neuropathy in 50% and sensory axonal neuropathy in 28.6%, with no evidence of demyelination.

In three patients with normal NCS/EMG, skin biopsy showed reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD) in the thigh (4.1, 3.8, 4.2 fibers/mm), below the 5th percentile (5.2 fibers/mm), consistent with non-length-dependent small fiber neuropathy, while distal leg IENFD was within normal limits.

Co-existing autoimmune conditions (type 1 diabetes mellitus, Grave's disease, rheumatoid arthritis) were present in 21.4% of patients with FGFR3 antibody-related polyneuropathy, similar to rates reported in prior studies.

Of 100 patients tested for FGFR3 antibody due to suspected autoimmune neuropathy, 25% (25/100) tested positive, a relatively high positivity rate potentially reflecting false positives due to lack of serum-specific background noise (SSBN) normalization at the testing laboratory and broader inclusion criteria.

Four FGFR3 antibody-positive patients were excluded because their neuropathy was attributed to alternative etiologies (nerve biopsy-proven vasculitis in two, TTR amyloidosis in one, chemotherapy-induced neuropathy in one), indicating FGFR3 antibody positivity does not exclude other causes.
Women exposed to domestic abuse had more than double the risk of developing chronic lower back pain compared to unexposed women.
Women exposed to domestic abuse had over three times the risk of developing chronic headaches compared to unexposed women, though the confidence interval was wide.
Women exposed to domestic abuse had a 41% increased risk of developing irritable bowel syndrome compared to unexposed women.
Women exposed to domestic abuse had a near 89% increased risk of developing restless legs syndrome compared to unexposed women.
No positive association was found between domestic abuse exposure and the development of interstitial cystitis.
No positive association was found between domestic abuse exposure and the development of vulvodynia.
No positive association was found between domestic abuse exposure and the development of myofascial pain syndrome.
Fibromyalgia is characterized by chronic generalized pain, fatigue, disordered sleep, and cognitive difficulties persisting for at least 3 months.
Fibromyalgia is commonly associated with irritable bowel syndrome symptoms, headaches, intermittent paresthesias, and mood disorders.
Women are more commonly affected by fibromyalgia than men.
Management of fibromyalgia should be individualized, addressing mood disorders, sleep, exercise, maladaptive pain responses, and stress coping.
Among 239 pediatric patients diagnosed with gastroparesis by 4-hour gastric emptying scintigraphy, idiopathic gastroparesis was the most common etiology identified.
Over a median follow-up of 22 months, outcomes among children with gastroparesis were 34.8% no improvement, 34.8% some improvement while remaining on therapy, and 30.3% complete symptom resolution.
Compared to younger children with gastroparesis, adolescents showed a higher female predominance.
Adolescents with gastroparesis were more likely to report nausea compared to younger children.
Girls with gastroparesis were more likely than boys to report abdominal pain.
Girls with gastroparesis were more likely than boys to report nausea.
Girls with gastroparesis were more likely than boys to have a documented diagnosis of dysautonomia.
Among pediatric gastroparesis patients, girls were more likely than boys to report nausea.
Girls with pediatric gastroparesis were more likely than boys to have a documented diagnosis of dysautonomia.
Boys with pediatric gastroparesis were more likely than girls to have regurgitation.
Boys with pediatric gastroparesis were more likely than girls to have gastroesophageal reflux disease.
Boys with pediatric gastroparesis were more likely than girls to have rumination.
The authors propose that overexpression of TGF-β drives a protracted state of immunosuppression and fibrosis underlying persistent post-COVID syndrome (PPCS).
TGF-β is described as elevated during and after both sepsis and COVID-19, consistent with a counter-regulatory anti-inflammatory response.

In a retrospective case series of 214 patients in Wuhan, China, 36.4% had neurologic symptoms involving the central nervous system (24.8%), peripheral nervous system (8.9%), or skeletal muscle (10.7%).
The two most common CNS symptoms in this COVID-19 cohort were dizziness (16.8%) and headache (13.1%).
Approximately 5–8% of patients infected with SARS-CoV-2 develop ARDS, characterized by hypoxemia, bilateral infiltrates, and decreased lung compliance.

SARS-CoV-1 patients followed for 12 years demonstrated cardiovascular abnormalities in 40%, used as a proxy to predict long-term cardiac consequences of SARS-CoV-2 given genetic similarity between the viruses.
COVID-19 patients commonly show myocardial injury, heart failure, and myocarditis, evidenced by elevated troponin T and BNP levels.
Severe COVID-19 infection can trigger DIC-like coagulopathy with delayed clotting times, low platelets, and decreased fibrinogen (<1.0 g/L) due to consumption.

The authors propose repurposing existing cancer-directed TGF-β inhibitors (e.g., galunisertib, vactosertib, fresolimumab, trabedersen, tasisulam, belagenpneumatucel-L, AdAPT-001) to treat persistent post-COVID syndrome by targeting fibrosis and immunosuppression.
Nintedanib and pirfenidone, FDA-approved antifibrotic medications, are non-curative but slow the progression of pulmonary fibrosis and are proposed for post-ARDS/post-COVID fibrosis management.

TGF-β signaling dysregulation is linked to multiple neurological/psychiatric disorders (AIDS dementia complex, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, Huntington's, ALS, multiple sclerosis, anxiety, depression, schizophrenia), supporting its candidacy as a therapeutic target for COVID-19-induced neuropsychiatric symptoms.

Recursive ensemble feature selection (REFS) run on the CAMDA mRNA dataset (118 PBMC samples) identified 23 genes as the optimal predictor set distinguishing ME/CFS patients from healthy controls, with a statistically significant MANOVA difference between groups.
All 23 REFS-selected predictor genes showed downregulated mRNA expression in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.

The 23-gene REFS signature classified ME/CFS cases versus controls with an average global accuracy of 91.57% and a best single-classifier (Passive Aggressive) accuracy of 95.87%, with a ROC AUC of 0.92.
The IWGCNA-derived 20-gene set (Presson et al.) performed only slightly better than chance in classifying ME/CFS status on the same CAMDA data.
Univariate chi-squared feature selection (23 genes) performed only slightly better than chance for classifying ME/CFS status on the CAMDA data.

The 23-gene mRNA signature (18 overlapping genes) validated on an independent Affymetrix dataset (GSE14577, post-infectious male ME/CFS patients and controls) achieved 91.11% classification accuracy and ROC AUC of 0.95.

REFS applied to merged DNA methylation data (278 CpGs mapped to the 23 candidate genes) identified 48 CpG sites as predictive of ME/CFS, with a statistically significant MANOVA difference between cases and controls.
The 48 predictor CpG sites classified ME/CFS cases versus controls with 90.17% global accuracy and ROC AUC of 0.97.

Most of the 48 predictor CpG sites showed enhanced (increased) DNA methylation in ME/CFS patients compared to controls, inversely paralleling the downregulated mRNA expression of the corresponding genes.
MAPK4 (ERK4), which normally phosphorylates AKT to activate mTOR signaling for cell survival and proliferation, was among the genes downregulated in ME/CFS patients.

ARRB1 (beta-arrestin 1), which inhibits phosphorylated G-protein coupled receptors in lymphocytes, was downregulated in ME/CFS patients, consistent with prior reports of ARRB1 decrease following Epstein-Barr virus infection in mice.

GOLGA4, whose upregulation normally increases TNF trafficking and secretion upon macrophage LPS activation, was downregulated in ME/CFS patients, potentially impairing TNF secretion and immune response to inflammation.

ABCE1, which inhibits antiviral RNase L activity, was downregulated in ME/CFS patients, consistent with a prior report linking ABCE1 downregulation in PBLs of ME/CFS patients with upregulated RNase L.

PHKA2, required for glycogen breakdown to glucose for ATP production, was downregulated in ME/CFS patients, potentially contributing to impaired glycolysis in immune cells and reduced dendritic cell function.

IL2RB, the beta-subunit of the IL2 receptor involved in T cell differentiation, was downregulated in ME/CFS patients; a prior study found a 3'UTR SNP in IL2RB associated with ME/CFS that may interfere with miRNA binding and reduce receptor function.
