CCR4, a chemokine receptor involved in leukocyte trafficking, was downregulated in ME/CFS patients; pharmacologic blockage of CCR4 by mogamulizumab has been reported to induce fatigue in humans.
HLA-DQA1, encoding the alpha-chain of MHC class II involved in antigen presentation to T cells, was downregulated in ME/CFS patients.

PRG4 (proteoglycan 4), which coats immune cells and prevents activation by low-grade pro-inflammatory cytokines, was downregulated in ME/CFS patients, possibly reducing its anti-inflammatory action and contributing to low-grade inflammation.

OGG1, a DNA repair enzyme excising oxidative 8-oxoguanine lesions, was downregulated in ME/CFS patients, which combined with reportedly increased oxidative stress could increase DNA damage and innate immune activation via DAMPs.
At baseline, ME/CFS patients showed no significant differences in AIx75, carotid-radial PWV, or blood pressure measures compared to healthy controls.
In healthy controls, AIx75 significantly decreased 48 h after a maximal exercise test, indicating improved (reduced) arterial stiffness, whereas no such improvement occurred in the ME/CFS group.

ME/CFS patients showed no significant change in AIx75 from baseline to either 48 h (p=0.7) or 72 h (p=0.7) recovery after maximal exercise, unlike the vasodilatory improvement seen in healthy controls.
No significant changes in carotid-radial PWV were observed after exercise in either ME/CFS or control groups at 48 h or 72 h, despite minor non-significant reductions in both ME/CFS groups.

The study's overall interpretation was that ME/CFS patients may not experience the systemic arterial vasodilation seen in healthy controls after aerobic exercise, suggesting impaired vascular recovery contributing to post-exertional malaise.
A prior study (Spence et al., 2008) found ME/CFS patients had significantly higher mean AIx75 than healthy controls, indicating increased arterial stiffness.
CRP levels were found to be elevated in the ME/CFS cohort compared to controls in the Spence et al. (2008) study, supporting a link between chronic inflammation and arterial stiffness in ME/CFS.
A prior study (Scherbakov et al., 2020) found that peripheral endothelial dysfunction was associated with increased ME/CFS symptom severity.

A prior study (James et al., 2016) found exercise-induced oxidative stress was higher in CFS patients who had been regularly active (≥6 h/week) before illness onset, and in those who had a severe infection within 4 months prior to onset.
A prior 6-month vitamin D3 supplementation trial (Witham et al., 2015) in ME/CFS found no change in AIx75 or PWV, nor in blood markers of oxidative stress.
A geneticist identified a heterozygous mutation in PSTPIP1 in Case A during work-up of debilitating fatigue and recommended mitochondrial cofactor support to decrease oxidative stress.

A mitochondrial function test on Case A yielded a mitochondrial score of 0.24, indicating only 24% cellular energy availability and significant blocking of mitochondrial active sites and translocation proteins.

Invasive cardiopulmonary exercise testing (iCPET) in Case A revealed deficiencies in anaerobic threshold, ventricular refill, and muscle oxygen uptake, leading to diagnoses of preload failure, mitochondrial myopathy, and disordered ventilatory control.
Treatment with Mestinon (pyridostigmine bromide) combined with mild recumbent bicycle exercise helped Case A recover enough stamina to resume a modest work schedule.
Case A had a mild IgG1 deficiency and absence of antibodies to 10 pneumococcal serotypes; Pneumovax vaccination markedly reduced subsequent sinus and bronchial infections.
Case A was diagnosed with generalized autonomic failure and orthostatic hypotension, for which no effective treatments were identified.
Case A's vestibular migraine was treated with some benefit using vitamin B2 (riboflavin).
iCPET testing in Case B led to diagnosis of severe autonomic dysfunction in the form of preload failure.
Case B was diagnosed with small fiber polyneuropathy by a neurologist, which along with the preload failure diagnosis helped secure SSDI approval.
Mestinon for preload failure and midodrine for low blood pressure slightly improved Case B's functioning.
In Case B, an antiviral for trace EBV findings and an antibiotic for trace tick-borne illness had no effect, while vitamin B-12 injections helped with getting out of bed and walking.
Telemedicine appointments dramatically improved Case B's access to care and reduced post-appointment PEM duration from weeks to a few days compared to in-person visits.
Immune function testing in Case C revealed low levels of some natural killer cells and an abnormal cytokine profile, along with traces of immune response to EBV and HHV-6.
Nine months of treatment with the antiviral famciclovir (Famvir) produced no improvement in Case C's physical condition.
Immunomodulators Nexavir and low-dose naltrexone provided no benefit to Case C and caused intolerable side effects of increased dizziness and neurological symptoms.
Case C was diagnosed with neurally mediated hypotension (NMH) and postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS) by two cardiologists, described as common autonomic problems in pwME.
Fludrocortisone (Florinef) did not help Case C's POTS/NMH symptoms, while extra salt and midodrine helped a little.
Case C, suffering from very severe ME/CFS for two decades with poor quality of life and no improvement despite extensive treatment, died by suicide at age 38.

Suicide risk is elevated among pwME relative to the general population and tends to occur at a younger average age, with risk factors including disease stigma, chronic pain, and reduced functionality.
All three patients experienced lengthy diagnostic delays for ME/CFS (3, 13, and 12 years respectively), often after being told by physicians they were healthy despite debilitating symptoms.
A prospective Australian study found that 11% of patients with acute EBV, Q-fever, or Ross River virus infection met ME/CFS diagnostic criteria at six months.
Studies of long-term SARS sequelae found that 27% of survivors met ME/CFS diagnostic criteria four years after infection.
Disability studies estimate that 75% of pwME are housebound most of the time, 50% are unemployed, and 25% are bedbound most of the time.
Full recovery from ME/CFS is rare, estimated at less than 5%, though some patients experience extended remission followed by relapse.
ME/CFS research in the US is underfunded by about a factor of 14 relative to its disease burden, which the authors link to female predominance and historical stigmatization of the disease.
70% of EUROMENE expert respondents reported that there are no lists of registered ME/CFS patients maintained by GPs in their country.
65% of respondents reported that there is no specific national guidance on treatment pathways for ME/CFS in their country.
Experts estimated, via a weighted average of survey responses, that around 60% of people with ME/CFS remain undiagnosed.
Experts estimated that on average 66% of people with ME/CFS present to a GP.
Experts estimated that only about 23% of GPs recognise ME/CFS as a genuine clinical entity, with 61% of respondents putting GP recognition at just 0-20%.
78% of respondents reported that only 0-20% of GPs are confident in their ability to diagnose ME/CFS, giving a weighted average confidence estimate of just 17%.
91% of respondents reported that only 0-20% of GPs are confident in their ability to manage ME/CFS patients, giving a weighted average confidence estimate of just 14%.
Experts estimated that only around 26% of ME/CFS patients who consult a GP are actually diagnosed by that GP.
Experts estimated that on average 46% of ME/CFS patients presenting to a GP are referred to specialist care, with considerable variation across countries.
Experts estimated that on average 51% of ME/CFS patients self-refer to specialist services, though variability may reflect differing interpretation of the question.
91% of respondents strongly agreed there should be more teaching about ME/CFS in undergraduate medical curricula.
91% of respondents strongly agreed that postgraduate training about ME/CFS should be available for doctors and other healthcare professionals, with the remainder agreeing.

Prior published GP surveys from Ireland, Scotland, South Wales, and South-West England found that between 28% and 46% of GPs did not accept ME/CFS as a genuine clinical entity, consistent with the current EUROMENE expert survey findings.

Experts identified doctors' disbelief in ME/CFS, or misattribution of it as a psychiatric or functional disorder, as a major barrier to patients' access to primary and specialist care in multiple countries including Austria, Finland, and Greece.
No specialist ME/CFS care was reported to be available in Austria, Denmark, the Netherlands, or Romania, and only limited specialist care was reported in France, Germany, Ireland, and Poland.

Finland's forthcoming official ME/CFS guidance will state that pacing has a role in management, while graded exercise therapy (GET) and cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) will not be considered effective treatments, aligning with the current UK NICE draft guideline.
Whole-cell proteomics of ME/CFS versus control lymphoblasts showed significantly more upregulated than downregulated proteins overall.
Whole-cell transcriptomics showed significantly more downregulated than upregulated transcripts in ME/CFS lymphoblasts, contrasting with the proteomic pattern.

After FDR correction for pathway-level testing, 123 pathways were significantly over-represented among downregulated transcripts in ME/CFS lymphoblasts, while none were over-represented among upregulated transcripts.
Mitochondrial fatty acid β-oxidation enzymes were significantly upregulated as a group at the protein level in ME/CFS lymphoblasts.
In contrast to the protein-level elevation, transcripts encoding fatty acid β-oxidation enzymes were slightly but significantly reduced in ME/CFS lymphoblasts.

Five individual mitochondrial β-oxidation-related proteins spanning multiple fatty-acid chain lengths and electron transfer were each significantly upregulated at the protein level in ME/CFS lymphoblasts.
ACOX1, the rate-controlling enzyme of peroxisomal β-oxidation, was significantly upregulated at the protein level but unchanged at the transcript level in ME/CFS lymphoblasts.
Pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) enzymes were significantly upregulated at the protein level in ME/CFS lymphoblasts, with no significant change at the transcript level.
G6PD, the rate-limiting enzyme of the oxidative PPP, was significantly elevated in ME/CFS lymphoblast proteomes.
All 16 detected glycolytic enzymes, including the rate-controlling phosphofructokinase and hexokinase, showed unchanged protein expression in ME/CFS lymphoblasts.

Despite unchanged glycolytic protein levels, glycolytic enzyme transcripts trended slightly higher in ME/CFS lymphoblasts, consistent with accumulation of untranslated mRNA during a metabolic shift favoring fatty acid oxidation.

Enlarged proteomics confirmed upregulation of all five OXPHOS complexes, TCA cycle enzymes as a whole, and SLC25 mitochondrial solute carriers, but not the TIMM/TOMM/SAMM protein import machinery, at the protein level in ME/CFS lymphoblasts.

At the transcript level, Complex II expression was elevated, SLC25/TCA transcripts were unchanged, but Complexes I, III, IV, V and mitochondrial protein import complex transcripts were downregulated, implying posttranscriptional regulation of OXPHOS protein upregulation.
Western blotting validated proteomic findings: ACO2 and SDHA were unchanged, while MDH1 was confirmed elevated in ME/CFS lymphoblasts.
qRT-PCR confirmed the directional trends of SDHB, GLS, NDUFB1 and NDUFB10 transcripts seen in the transcriptomic dataset.
SIRT2 transcript was significantly upregulated while SIRT3 and SIRT6 were downregulated in ME/CFS lymphoblasts; SIRT1, SIRT4, SIRT5 and SIRT7 were unchanged.
At the transcript level, CD19, CD47, CD52 and CD79A were downregulated while CD164 was upregulated in ME/CFS lymphoblasts, though none are B-cell subset-specific markers.
At the protein level, CD226, CD48 and CD70 (markers of activated lymphocytes) were significantly upregulated in ME/CFS lymphoblasts, consistent with compensatory metabolic hyperactivation.
The Reactome pathway for PKN activation by RHO GTPases was the most significantly downregulated pathway with tissue relevance among proteins reduced in ME/CFS lymphoblasts.

The three key glutamine/glutamate-degrading enzymes GLS, GLUD1 and GOT2 were all significantly elevated at the protein level in ME/CFS lymphoblasts, supporting increased mitochondrial amino acid catabolism.
Neither cytosolic BCAT1 nor mitochondrial BCAT2 transcript expression differed significantly between ME/CFS and control lymphoblasts.

Both subunits of the rate-controlling BCKDH complex were significantly elevated at the protein level, and BCKDHB was also elevated at the transcript level, indicating increased mitochondrial BCAA degradation in ME/CFS lymphoblasts.

GCDH (lysine/tryptophan degradation) and FAH (phenylalanine degradation) proteins were significantly elevated in ME/CFS lymphoblasts, suggesting increased catabolism of these essential amino acids as mitochondrial substrate.
Proteasome complex subunits were significantly upregulated at the protein level in ME/CFS lymphoblasts, indicating elevated targeted protein degradation.

Fatty acid biosynthesis enzymes ACC1 and FASN were unchanged at both protein and transcript levels in ME/CFS lymphoblasts, contrasting with upregulated β-oxidation, consistent with a shift favoring fatty acid catabolism over synthesis.
Mean ACC phosphorylation (a marker of AMPK activity) was ~17% higher in ME/CFS lymphoblasts but did not reach statistical significance.
SLC25A11, the mitochondrial transporter that shuttles α-ketoglutarate to activate mTORC1, was significantly elevated in ME/CFS lymphoblast proteomes.

Whole-cell proteomics comparing ME/CFS and control lymphoblasts identified 218 upregulated and 41 downregulated proteins out of 2861 unchanged, with significantly more proteins upregulated than downregulated.

Whole-cell transcriptomics revealed 843 upregulated and 1409 downregulated transcripts out of 11,128 unchanged, with significantly more transcripts downregulated than upregulated in ME/CFS lymphoblasts.

PANTHER over-representation analysis of the transcriptome, with FDR correction for multiple pathway comparisons, found 123 pathways over-represented among downregulated genes and none among upregulated genes.
Without FDR correction, 51 pathways were over-represented among upregulated transcripts, mostly relating to innate immune activation or small-molecule import/intracellular transport.
Among sirtuin transcripts, SIRT2 was significantly upregulated while SIRT3 and SIRT6 were significantly downregulated in ME/CFS lymphoblasts, with SIRT1, SIRT4, SIRT5 and SIRT7 unchanged.
At the transcript level, CD19, CD47, CD52 and CD79A were significantly downregulated while CD164 was significantly upregulated in ME/CFS lymphoblasts, though none are specific B-cell subset markers.
At the protein level, CD226, CD48 and CD70 were significantly upregulated in ME/CFS lymphoblasts, consistent with a general hyperactivated lymphocyte phenotype.
The Reactome pathway for activation of protein kinase Ns (PKNs) by RHO GTPases was the most significantly over-represented pathway among downregulated proteins in ME/CFS lymphoblasts.
Mitochondrial biogenesis and TCA cycle/respiratory electron transport pathways were among the most significantly over-represented pathways in the upregulated protein fraction of ME/CFS lymphoblasts.
Nearly half (9/20) of the most significantly upregulated pathways in the ME/CFS lymphoblast proteome pertained directly to fatty acid β-oxidation.
Seven of the top twenty upregulated proteomic pathways related to innate and adaptive immune response activation, consistent with immune activation trends also seen in the transcriptome.
The mitochondrial α-ketoglutarate transporter SLC25A11, which shuttles α-KG to activate mTORC1 via prolyl hydroxylases, was significantly elevated in ME/CFS lymphoblast proteomes.
Western blotting confirmed unaltered expression of ACO2 and SDHA and confirmed elevated MDH1 protein levels in ME/CFS lymphoblasts, validating the proteomic dataset.
qRT-PCR confirmed the directional transcript-level trends of SDHB, GLS, NDUFB1 and NDUFB10 seen in the transcriptomic dataset, validating those findings independently.
The BCKDH-inhibitory kinase BCKDK was not significantly different in expression between ME/CFS and control lymphoblasts, indicating BCKDH regulation may not involve BCKDK-mediated inhibition.

An independent proteomic study of ME/CFS PBMCs by Sweetman et al. also reported elevated acyl-CoA dehydrogenases and HADHB, corroborating the current lymphoblast findings across a different, non-immortalised cell type.

Sweetman et al. also reported elevated OXPHOS Complex I and V subunits, TCA cycle proteins, and proteasome subunits/assembly factors in ME/CFS PBMCs, mirroring findings in this study's lymphoblasts and supporting a shared lymphoid-cell phenotype independent of immortalisation.

In an independent epigenetic study by Helliwell et al. using reduced representation bisulphite sequencing, the Complex I subunit gene NDUFA11 was found to be hypomethylated in ME/CFS PBMCs, consistent with the elevated Complex I protein expression observed in this and prior lymphoblast/PBMC studies.

A total of 259 proteins and 2243 transcripts were significantly altered in expression after multiple-comparison correction, suggesting the potential for future diagnostic biomarker panels based on differential expression.
Because the non-significant elevation in AMPK activity co-occurs with elevated mTORC1 activity, the authors could not determine whether autophagy is increased or decreased in ME/CFS lymphoblasts.

Although the ME/CFS and control cohorts differed significantly in gender proportion and age distribution, neither age nor gender significantly affected the experimental outcomes analysed in either group.

Patients with pernicious anaemia report markedly higher frequencies of neurological symptoms (fatigue 87%, memory complaints 78%, sleep disturbance 87%) than patients assessed 6 months after COVID-19 hospitalisation (fatigue 34%, memory complaints 31%, sleep disturbance 26%), despite overlapping symptom profiles between the two conditions.
Cerebrospinal fluid homocysteine is very markedly elevated in ME/CFS patients with no overlap versus controls, and CSF homocysteine correlates significantly with objective fatigue ratings.
A metabolomic study suggests ME/CFS is a hypometabolic syndrome potentially amenable to interventions targeting folate, B12, glycine, serine and B6 pools.

In silico screening against a computational model of SARS-CoV-2 nsp12 (RdRp) identified methylcobalamin as the best-matching molecule for the enzyme's natural substrate binding site, suggesting it could act as an RdRp inhibitor.
In SARS-CoV-2-infected Vero-E6 cells, hijacked host METTL3 adds m6A modification to viral RNA and interacts with viral RdRp, which in turn boosts METTL3 expression, facilitating viral replication.
Porcine epidemic diarrhoea virus (PEDV) infection increases the m6A ratio in host RNA, suggesting a host defensive attempt to restrict viral replication via m6A modification.
A study of ten European countries found that suboptimal vitamin B12 consumption correlates with increased COVID-19 incidence and mortality.
COVID-19 patients hospitalized and given daily vitamin D, magnesium and vitamin B12 supplementation had a significantly improved clinical course compared with non-supplemented patients.

A case report of four women with confirmed COVID-19 found a normal GSH/GSSG ratio in two with mild disease, whereas the two with more severe disease had a low GSH/GSSG ratio indicating GSH deficiency and oxidative stress.
Two patients with shortness of breath due to COVID-19 pneumonia showed a dramatic and rapid symptomatic response within hours of glutathione treatment.
There are reports of good clinical responses to high-dose, frequent subcutaneous B12 injections combined with folic acid in ME/CFS patients.

Elevated blood homocysteine is common in patients with cognitive impairment and dementia including Alzheimer's disease, an association argued to fulfil Bradford-Hill criteria for causality, and lowering homocysteine with high-dose B vitamins slows cognitive decline and brain atrophy.
Reducing serum serine and glycine levels via dietary intervention dramatically decreases pathogen-driven T-cell expansion, indicating these amino acids are required for the T-cell response.

The authors hypothesize that SARS-CoV-2-associated cytokine storm and oxidative stress oxidise the cob(I)alamin intermediate of the methionine synthase reaction to cob(II)alamin, requiring SAM for re-activation and resulting in net SAM depletion and elevated homocysteine.

The authors hypothesize that SARS-CoV-2-driven increased methylation demand lowers intracellular SAM, reducing cystathionine beta synthase (CBS) activity and diverting homocysteine away from glutathione synthesis, prioritizing methylation over transsulfuration/antioxidant defense.

In the largest included trial, CBT had the highest probability of being the most cost-effective option for adults with CFS/ME compared with graded exercise therapy, specialist medical care, and adaptive pacing therapy.
In a smaller primary-care trial, counselling was found to dominate CBT (lower cost and greater improvement) when cost-effectiveness was expressed per unit improvement in fatigue score.
CBT was found to be more cost-effective than multidisciplinary rehabilitation treatment (MRT) for adults with CFS/ME despite MRT producing a larger QALY gain.
CBT dominated guided support groups and was more cost-effective than natural course in a Dutch trial, at €21,375 per QALY versus natural course.
GET was found to be more effective and cheaper than counselling and cost-effective relative to usual care plus a self-help booklet above a modest willingness-to-pay threshold for fatigue improvement.
Home-based fatigue self-management (FSM) was cheaper and produced greater QALY gains than usual care (dominant) in US primary care patients with severe chronic fatigue.
Treatment as usual was found to be cheaper and more effective than both pragmatic rehabilitation and supportive listening in UK primary care patients with chronic fatigue.

In the only pediatric economic evaluation, adding the lightning process to specialist medical care was more costly but also more cost-effective than specialist medical care alone in adolescents with CFS/ME.

Long-term follow-up of the PACE trial showed that the advantage of CBT and GET over comparator groups on fatigue and physical function narrowed over time, raising concerns about durability of cost-effectiveness estimates based on short-term outcomes.
Productivity losses and informal caregiver costs frequently dominated overall cost estimates across the included economic evaluations but were inconsistently measured or omitted.
CFS/ME is associated with substantially higher healthcare use, lost income, and informal caregiver support compared with chronic fatigue that does not meet CFS/ME diagnostic criteria.

CFS/ME imposes a large economic burden, estimated at around €40 billion per year across the EU-28 and over £100 million per year in the UK from productivity loss due to early workforce exit prior to specialist assessment.
Baseline EQ5D utility scores in the reviewed CFS/ME trials were substantially lower than working-age population norms, indicating a major impact of the condition on health-related quality of life.

In one Dutch trial, significant improvements in the CIS fatigue score with CBT did not translate into any significant difference in QALYs, indicating discordance between fatigue and utility-based outcome measures.
Both CFS/ME and FM participants reported significant pain, sleep disturbance, and fatigue that adversely affected their health-related quality of life.
Unlike the other symptom domains, anxiety and depression were not confirmed as significantly debilitating in either the CFS/ME or FM groups.
The similarity in symptom profiles between CFS/ME and FM participants suggests an underlying relationship between the two conditions that warrants further research.

The authors propose that ME/CFS and Longhaul COVID-19 share a common underlying process and should be jointly conceptualized as Post Active Phase of Infection Syndromes (PAPIS), triggered by acute infection or reactivation of persistent viral infection.
Approximately 10 percent of COVID-19 patients are estimated to develop Longhaul COVID-19 symptoms.
The authors cite evidence that oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction are shared pathological processes involved in both Longhaul COVID-19 and ME/CFS.

Epstein-Barr virus has historically been considered the most frequent precipitating viral trigger of ME/CFS, though other viruses have also been reported as triggers, and the authors argue SARS-CoV-2 will now become a frequent precipitant as well.

The authors note that non-viral triggers such as Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome, cervical spine compression, post-traumatic injury, toxic exposure, or a metabolic defect could also precipitate ME/CFS-like illness and cannot be excluded from a unifying etiological explanation.
The historical 'mass hysteria' hypothesis for the Royal Free Hospital ME cluster outbreak has since been challenged and discredited.

Baseline chronic fatigue syndrome in MERS survivors was independently associated with an approximately 7.6-fold increased risk of suicidality over the 2-year follow-up period, even after adjusting for sex, depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, coping strategy, and psychotropic use.
Suicidality prevalence among MERS survivors declined over the follow-up period, from 22.2% at 12 months to 15.1% at 18 months and 10.0% at 24 months.
At the 12-month baseline assessment, 29 of 63 MERS survivors (46%) met the FSS cutoff for chronic fatigue syndrome.
MERS survivors with and without chronic fatigue syndrome at baseline did not differ significantly in socio-demographic or MERS-infection-related clinical characteristics.
UK health guideline authorities moved to revise recommendations for chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), with advocates welcoming the rejection of graded exercise therapy as a treatment.
The guideline revision also reflects rejection of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) as a recommended treatment for ME/CFS, according to patient advocates.
The pattern of muscle fiber conduction velocity change with increasing static force differed significantly between the CFS group and both the fibromyalgia group and healthy controls.
In the CFS group, muscle fiber conduction velocity increased excessively as static force load increased.
In healthy controls, muscle fiber conduction velocity increased only slightly with force and this change was not statistically significant.
In the fibromyalgia group, muscle fiber conduction velocity did not increase at all with increasing static force load.
In the CFS group, the number of motor unit potentials showing very high conduction velocities increased abundantly with force, accompanied by narrowing of the MUPs.
The authors conclude that CFS patients show disturbed muscle membrane function in motor units involved in low force generation, potentially contributed to by central neural deregulation.
A glycine substitution mutation in the COL5A1 gene was identified in a patient diagnosed with classic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, caused by pathogenic variants in COL3A1, is associated with a high prevalence of supra-aortic trunk (cervical) artery lesions.
Nearly half of all SAT lesions were identified at first arterial work-up, with a cumulative incidence of first SAT lesion identification of 41.7% by age 40.
Among 183 identified SAT lesions, 132 were dissections and 33 were aneurysms, occurring predominantly in the internal carotid arteries (56.3%) and vertebral arteries (28.9%).
SAT lesions were less frequent among patients carrying COL3A1 null mutations compared with other variant types.
Transient ischemic attack or stroke occurred in 19.5% of patients with SAT lesions and was not significantly related to age, sex, treatment, or hypertension.
During dominant leg cutting, asymptomatic hypermobile individuals showed lower minimum knee valgus angles than nonhypermobile individuals.
During dominant leg cutting, hypermobile individuals showed greater peak knee external rotation angles than nonhypermobile individuals.
During nondominant leg cutting, hypermobile individuals showed lower peak ankle plantarflexion angles than nonhypermobile individuals.

The authors concluded that although some kinematic differences were found, these are not crucial biomechanical risk factors that would predispose asymptomatic hypermobile individuals to noncontact knee or ACL injuries.

EDS type IV (vascular subtype) arises from a genetic defect in collagen synthesis and presents with characteristic facial features, translucent skin, easy bruising, and risk of spontaneous arterial rupture and visceral perforation.
A 15-year-old male with no prior medical history experienced spontaneous sigmoid colon perforation requiring emergency laparotomy, later found to be due to EDS type IV.
Chest CT angiography revealed a right subclavian artery aneurysm in the patient, which was treated with endovascular stent grafting.
Family history and clinical presentation raised suspicion of EDS type IV, and DNA analysis subsequently confirmed the diagnosis.
The authors note that anaesthetic management of EDS type IV patients remains challenging due to a lack of evidence-based recommendations.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the COL3A1 gene, which the authors note is characterized by recurrent arterial, digestive, and pulmonary events.
Among 136 enrolled vEDS patients, 24 (17.6%) had a history of respiratory events, including 17 with pneumothorax, 4 with hemothorax, and 3 with hemoptysis, with 11 requiring thoracic surgery.
CT scans detected lung parenchymal abnormalities in 78 of 136 (57.3%) vEDS patients.
Emphysema, mostly centrilobular and paraseptal, was found in 44 of 136 (32.3%) patients and was comparable between smokers and non-smokers.
Clusters of calcified small pulmonary nodules were identified on CT in 9 of 136 (6.6%) patients.
Cavitated pulmonary nodules were found in 4 of 136 (2.9%) vEDS patients on CT.
Histologic examination of 5 surgical samples showed arterial abnormalities and emphysema with alveolar ruptures in 3 samples, accompanied by diffuse hemorrhage and increased hemosiderin resorption.
Presence of lung parenchymal changes was associated with a slightly higher incidence of respiratory events, but this association was not statistically significant.
Vascular EDS is caused by pathogenic variants in the COL3A1 gene, and all 136 enrolled patients had molecularly confirmed vEDS.
The presence of lung parenchymal changes on CT was associated with a slightly higher incidence of respiratory events, but this association did not reach statistical significance.
The frequency of emphysema on CT was comparable between smokers and non-smokers among vEDS patients.

Histologic examination of surgical lung samples from vEDS patients showed arterial abnormalities and emphysema with alveolar ruptures accompanied by diffuse hemorrhage and increased hemosiderin resorption.
Of the patients who experienced respiratory events, 11 required thoracic surgery, most commonly related to hemoptysis or recurrent pneumothorax/hemothorax.
Fibromyalgia patients showed significantly greater sleep disturbance scores compared to healthy controls on the Medical Outcomes Study Sleep Scale-12.
Fibromyalgia patients had markedly poorer sleep quality than controls as measured by the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index.
Fibromyalgia patients had significantly worse quality of life than controls, which further worsened with increasing fibromyalgia severity.
Twelve of the thirty fibromyalgia patients had autonomic dysfunction as assessed by cardiovascular autonomic function tests and heart rate variability.
Autonomic dysfunction in fibromyalgia patients was not significantly associated with the degree of sleep disturbance or with quality of life.

The authors conclude that autonomic dysfunction is not an early feature of fibromyalgia, while sleep disturbance and poor sleep quality are prominent early features that significantly impact quality of life.
RNA sequencing of keratinocytes revealed 141 differentially expressed protein-coding genes between patients with small fiber neuropathy and healthy controls.
No differentially expressed keratinocyte genes were found between patients with fibromyalgia syndrome and healthy controls.
Comparing SFN and FMS patients directly revealed 167 differentially expressed keratinocyte genes, with 129 upregulated and 38 downregulated in SFN relative to FMS.
Pathway enrichment analysis of the differentially expressed genes between SFN and FMS identified inflammatory pathways as enriched.
In an independent validation cohort, interleukin-8 expression was higher in keratinocytes from SFN patients compared with FMS patients.
In an independent validation cohort, CXCL3 expression was higher in keratinocytes from SFN patients compared with FMS patients.
In an independent validation cohort, endothelin receptor type A expression was higher in keratinocytes from SFN patients compared with FMS patients.
In an independent validation cohort, Nav1.7 (SCN9A) expression was higher in keratinocytes from SFN patients compared with FMS patients.
Fibromyalgia patients showed lower cardiac branch baroreflex sensitivity (SBP-IBI covariation) compared to healthy controls.
Fibromyalgia patients showed lower myocardial branch baroreflex sensitivity (SV-PEP covariation) compared to healthy controls.
Fibromyalgia patients showed lower vasomotor branch baroreflex sensitivity (TPR-related) compared to healthy controls.
Fibromyalgia patients exhibited lower baroreflex effectiveness index (BEI) in the cardiac branch compared to healthy controls.
Fibromyalgia patients exhibited lower baroreflex effectiveness index (BEI) in the vasomotor branch compared to healthy controls.
Fibromyalgia patients showed blunted reactivity of cardiac BRS, BEI, SBP, IBI, SV, and PEP during the cold pressor test and mental arithmetic task compared to controls.
Lower baroreflex sensitivity and effectiveness were inversely related to clinical pain severity in fibromyalgia patients.
Lower baroreflex sensitivity and effectiveness were inversely related to cold pressor test-induced pain in fibromyalgia patients.
Lower baroreflex sensitivity and effectiveness index were associated with greater cold pressor-induced pain among fibromyalgia patients.
Lower baroreflex sensitivity and effectiveness index were associated with higher depression scores in fibromyalgia patients.
Lower baroreflex sensitivity and effectiveness index were associated with higher trait anxiety in fibromyalgia patients.
Lower baroreflex sensitivity and effectiveness index were associated with greater sleep problems in fibromyalgia patients.
Lower baroreflex sensitivity and effectiveness index were associated with greater fatigue in fibromyalgia patients.
The authors propose that reduced baroreflex function diminishes the normal antinociceptive effect of baroreceptor afferents, potentially contributing to the hyperalgesia seen in fibromyalgia.

In female fibromyalgia patients, the DN4 questionnaire showed a numerically higher AUC-ROC than the Pain Detect Questionnaire for identifying neuropathic pain features suggestive of small fiber neuropathy, but the difference was not statistically significant.

An ultrasonographic sural nerve cross-sectional area cut-off of 3 mm2 identified neuropathic pain features suggestive of small fiber neuropathy in fibromyalgia patients with 70% sensitivity and 90% specificity.
Antigen (DNP-BSA) activation of IgE-sensitized MC/9 mast cells dose-dependently suppressed ORMDL3 mRNA and protein expression, with maximal suppression at 100 ng/ml DNP-BSA.
The reduction in ORMDL3 expression following antigen activation was not associated with increased mast cell death.
ORMDL3 was localized to the endoplasmic reticulum in MC/9 mast cells and its ER-localized expression was reduced following antigen activation.

ORMDL3 overexpression significantly suppressed antigen-induced mast cell degranulation (histamine, β-glucuronidase, tryptase release), whereas ORMDL3 knockdown significantly increased it, in Ag-activated MC/9 cells.

ORMDL3 overexpression significantly reduced antigen-induced release of cytokines (IL-6, IL-13, TNF-α) and chemokines (CCL3, CCL4), while ORMDL3 knockdown increased their release, with no differences seen in non-activated cells.
ORMDL3 overexpression increased mRNA and protein levels of ER stress markers SERCA2b and ATF6 in Ag-activated mast cells, while ORMDL3 knockdown decreased them.

ORMDL3 overexpression increased autophagy markers Beclin 1 and LC3B (mRNA, protein, and LC3B puncta by confocal imaging) in Ag-activated mast cells, while ORMDL3 knockdown decreased them, with no difference in non-activated cells.
Levels of XBP1u, XBP1s, PERK, and BiP were unaffected by ORMDL3 overexpression or knockdown, indicating ORMDL3 selectively engages the ATF6 arm of the UPR rather than IRE1α or (mRNA-level) PERK arms.

Phosphorylated eIF2α protein was upregulated by ORMDL3 overexpression and downregulated by ORMDL3 knockdown in activated mast cells, despite PERK mRNA levels being unchanged, suggesting ORMDL3 affects eIF2α phosphorylation independent of PERK transcription.

Doxycycline-inducible ATF6 knockdown (100 ng/ml) in ORMDL3-overexpressing cells significantly reversed ORMDL3-OE-mediated suppression of degranulation and cytokine/chemokine production, though not fully to baseline (unmanipulated) levels.

A lower dose of doxycycline (10 ng/ml), producing only 15-25% ATF6 knockdown, did not rescue ORMDL3-OE-induced impairment of degranulation but did partially restore cytokine/chemokine (IL-6, IL-13, TNF-α, CCL4) production, suggesting cytokine responses are more sensitive to ORMDL3/ATF6 pathway modulation than degranulation.
ATF6 knockdown (both 100 and 10 ng/ml doxycycline) markedly reversed the ORMDL3-OE-induced increase in Beclin1 and LC3B mRNA/protein, indicating autophagy acts downstream of the ORMDL3/ATF6 pathway.

Pharmacological autophagy inhibition with 3-methyladenine (3-MA) reversed ORMDL3-overexpression-mediated suppression of degranulation and cytokine/chemokine production, with an enhanced reversal when combined with ATF6 knockdown, confirming autophagy as a mediator of ORMDL3's inhibitory effect.

In a mouse passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) model, intradermal ORMDL3-overexpressing VLPs inhibited Evans blue extravasation (a measure of mast cell degranulation), while ORMDL3 knockdown and/or ATF6 knockdown VLPs enhanced extravasation, and combined ORMDL3-OE + ATF6-KD reversed the ORMDL3-OE-mediated inhibition.

The authors note their finding of enhanced cytokine/chemokine expression with ORMDL3 knockdown in Ag-activated MC/9 cells is consistent with prior BMMC data, but contrasts with Bugajev et al., who reported elevated cytokine/chemokine mRNA in unstimulated ORMDL3-KD BMMCs and no effect of ORMDL3 knockdown on degranulation — differences attributed to cell line vs primary cell and antigen differences.

In a cohort of 28 patients with mast cell disorders, COVID-19 mortality was low (1 death) and comparable to general population rates, with the death attributable to significant pre-existing comorbidities rather than the mast cell disorder.
None of the 28 patients with mast cell disorders reported clinical mast cell activation symptoms such as urticaria or anaphylaxis during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Several patients with baseline mast cell activation symptoms (pruritus, bloating, diarrhea) reported improvement in these symptoms during acute COVID-19 infection, with symptoms recurring after convalescence.

Highly purified bone marrow mast cells from mastocytosis patients and healthy controls did not express detectable levels of ACE2, the SARS-CoV-2 entry receptor, suggesting mast cells are unlikely to be directly infected by the virus.

Bone marrow mast cells from mastocytosis patients showed elevated TLR3 gene expression relative to healthy controls, suggesting a potential pathway for indirect mast cell activation during viral infection.

Bone marrow mast cells from mastocytosis patients showed elevated expression of IL1RL1 (encoding the IL-33 receptor ST2) relative to healthy controls, suggesting a possible route for indirect mast cell activation via IL-33 signaling during viral infection.

Inpatient hospitalization for COVID-19 was required in 43% of the mast cell disorder cohort, a higher rate than general U.S. population hospitalization rates at the time, possibly reflecting international site variation or prophylactic hospitalization due to comorbidity.
Symptom duration during COVID-19 infection in this cohort ranged from 7 days to over two months, with an average duration of 29 days.
In the single patient for whom mast cell mediator levels were measured during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection, levels were unchanged from baseline, suggesting a lack of acute mast cell activation.
PM2.5 exposure enhanced IgE-mediated degranulation and increased cytokine expression in mast cells.
In a BALB/c passive cutaneous anaphylaxis mouse model, PM2.5 treatment increased Evan's blue extravasation and serum cytokines.
PM2.5 treatment markedly increased expression of Gadd45b, an oxidative stress molecule that activates downstream MEKK4/JNK signaling.
PM2.5 treatment activated MEKK4 and JNK1/2 but did not activate ERK1/2 or p38, indicating pathway specificity.
PM2.5 treatment did not activate ERK1/2 signaling, distinguishing it from the JNK pathway response.
PM2.5 treatment did not activate p38 MAPK signaling.
Knockdown of Gadd45b significantly attenuated PM2.5-mediated JNK1/2 activation and cytokine expression in mast cells.
The JNK1/2-specific inhibitor SP600125 blocked IgE-mediated mast cell activation and cytokine release in the PCA model mice.

PM2.5 treatment increased ROS levels in mast cells, and an ROS inhibitor blocked PM2.5-induced ROS production and reversed PM2.5-mediated gene expression changes in the mitochondrial respiratory chain.
Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (HαT) is caused by germline copy-number gains on one allele of the TPSAB1 gene encoding α-tryptase, leading to elevated basal serum tryptase.

In the original 35 HαT families, frequently reported clinical manifestations included cutaneous flushing, pruritus, urticaria, autonomic dysfunction including POTS, functional GI symptoms (IBS, dysmotility, GERD), chronic pain, sleep disruption, Hymenoptera reactions and connective tissue abnormalities such as joint hypermobility.
A gene-dose effect was observed such that higher numbers of extra alpha-tryptase copies were associated with progressively higher basal serum tryptase levels.
Sabato et al. reported that a Belgian family with germline TPSAB1 α-quintuplications had significantly higher basal serum tryptase levels compared to individuals with duplications or triplications.
The prevalence of hereditary alpha-tryptasemia in the general population is estimated at 3-8%, similarly found across independent cohorts including a British birth cohort (5%).

HαT prevalence was significantly higher among patients with idiopathic anaphylaxis (17%) compared to healthy individuals (5.6%) and nonatopic disease controls (5.3%), and increased alpha-tryptase copy number gains were associated with increased risk for severe Hymenoptera venom-triggered anaphylaxis.

In vitro cultures of primary mast cells derived from CD34+ blood cells of HαT individuals showed increased TPSAB1 and TPSB2 mRNA levels and more spontaneous tryptase secretion compared to non-HαT controls, without differences in cell growth, morphology, intracellular tryptase protein or IgE-mediated degranulation.

2α:2β-tryptase heterotetramers are particularly increased in individuals with HαT and correlate with higher symptom severity, showing enhanced proteolytic activity and stability compared to α or β homotetramers.

Incubation of skin mast cells with 2α:2β-tryptase heterotetramers, but not β-homotetramers, led to vibration-triggered mast cell degranulation via proteolytic cleavage of EMR2 subunits, and only individuals with an HαT genotype showed a vibration-induced cutaneous effect in a challenge of 56 volunteers.
Heparin-stabilized 2α:2β-tryptase heterotetramers, but not β-homotetramers, produced dose-dependent PAR2 activation in Jurkat cells in vitro.

Mature tryptase, but not α-β heterotetramers, promoted PAR2-dependent transmigration of human umbilical vein endothelial cells in vitro, suggesting a role for enhanced vascular permeability in severe anaphylaxis in HαT patients.

In a cohort of 180 mastocytosis patients, HαT prevalence was 17.2%, confirmed in an independent validation cohort of 61 patients (21.3%), with the highest prevalence in indolent SM (18.8%); HαT carriers had higher tryptase levels, lower KIT D816V allele burden, and more severe mediator-related symptoms.

In mastocytosis patients, HαT was strongly associated with Hymenoptera venom hypersensitivity reactions (30%) and severe cardiovascular mediator-related symptoms including anaphylaxis and hypotension (35.5%).

An independent study by Lyons et al. confirmed a high prevalence of HαT in systemic mastocytosis (12.2%) with an increased risk of severe systemic anaphylaxis in HαT-positive SM patients, comparable to the Viennese cohort's control prevalence.

Giannetti et al. described atypical, larger, hypogranular bone marrow mast cells with abnormal paratrabecular/perivascular localization and associated eosinophilia in patients with MC activation symptoms and elevated basal serum tryptase, some diagnosed with HαT, suggesting intrinsic mast cell abnormalities predisposing to SM and MCAS.

In a retrospective multicenter study, 12 of 13 HαT patients treated with omalizumab experienced improvement in about half of reported symptoms (urticaria, nausea, flushing, fatigue, abdominal pain) after a median of 8 weeks, but autonomic dysfunction, palpitations, diarrhea and joint hypermobility showed no improvement.

Autonomic dysfunction, palpitations, diarrhea and joint hypermobility symptoms in HαT patients did not improve with omalizumab treatment, unlike IgE/mast-cell-mediator symptoms such as urticaria and flushing.

A noncompetitive inhibitory antibody targeting both α- and β-tryptases dissociates active tetramers into inactive monomers and reduced IgE-induced systemic anaphylaxis responses in a humanized mouse model.

The majority of systemic mastocytosis patients carry a somatic KIT D816V mutation causing constitutive receptor activation, and HαT carriers with mastocytosis show a significantly lower KIT D816V allele burden than non-HαT mastocytosis patients.

Only a few inherited single-gene disorders, such as autosomal recessive Gaucher's disease and GATA2 haploinsufficiency, have been identified as associated with elevated basal serum tryptase levels aside from HαT.
Serum tryptase was markedly elevated during a symptomatic attack and declined to near-normal levels over the following days.
White blood cell and neutrophil counts markedly increased during the mast cell activation episode and normalized after remission.
Blood potassium transiently decreased during the mast cell activation episode, possibly due to redistribution of intracellular/extracellular potassium ions.
Bone marrow mast cells strongly stained positive for CD117 (KIT receptor) and showed multifocal dense infiltration meeting the major diagnostic criterion for systemic mastocytosis.
Testing for the KIT D816V mutation in the patient's bone marrow was negative, despite this mutation being present in over 80% of adult SM cases in the literature.
Serum total IgE was mildly elevated above the normal range in this patient, suggesting a possible allergic component, though specific allergen testing was negative.

A head-up tilt test induced with nitroglycerin was positive in this patient, though the induced syncope did not reproduce the characteristic skin flushing and conjunctival hyperemia seen in spontaneous episodes.
Adrenaline (epinephrine) was used as first-choice treatment for mast cell mediator-induced hypotension/shock, with the patient carrying an adrenaline pen as precautionary self-treatment.

For indolent systemic mastocytosis, symptom control drugs including H1/H2 antihistamines (e.g., cetirizine, ranitidine), mast cell membrane stabilizers, leukotriene inhibitors (e.g., montelukast), and NSAIDs are used, alongside avoidance of mast cell activation triggers.
Imatinib is the only FDA-approved drug for SM patients with KIT mutations sensitive to imatinib or without the KIT D816V mutation.
Midostaurin is the only tyrosine kinase inhibitor approved as monotherapy for aggressive systemic mastocytosis, following phase 2/3 trials.

Indolent systemic mastocytosis has a relatively good prognosis with median survival of 198 months, showing no significant difference in survival compared with healthy controls, whereas aggressive SM, SM-AHN, and mast cell leukemia have progressively worse prognoses.
Serum tryptase levels parallel bone marrow mast cell infiltration in indolent SM but correlate poorly with clinical symptom severity of mast cell mediator release.
Peanut-sIgE levels were significantly higher in peanut-allergic than peanut-sensitized-tolerant children.
Peanut-sIgE levels strongly correlated with peanut-induced mast cell activation in the mast cell activation test (MAT).
Ara h 2-sIgE correlated with mast cell activation and was the most diagnostically discriminant allergen component.
IgE specific activity (sIgE/tIgE ratio) to peanut and its major components was significantly higher in peanut-allergic than sensitized-tolerant children.
Ara h 2 specific activity showed the highest diagnostic accuracy for peanut allergy among all IgE variables tested.
Peanut IgE specific activity showed a significantly greater diagnostic AUC than peanut-sIgE alone.
Peanut specific activity correlated most strongly with mast cell activation among the SA measures.
Peanut-allergic children had significantly higher IgE avidity for peanut allergen than sensitized-tolerant children, though with overlap between groups.
Peanut IgE avidity showed only a weak, non-significant correlation with mast cell activation.
Diversity of the IgE repertoire against peanut allergens (Shannon diversity index) was significantly greater in peanut-allergic than sensitized-tolerant children.
Overall IgE diversity across the whole 112-allergen ISAC array did not discriminate between peanut-allergic and sensitized-tolerant children.
Peanut IgE diversity had high diagnostic accuracy for peanut allergy and correlated strongly with mast cell activation.
In multivariable regression modeling mast cell activation, peanut IgE diversity to peanut allergens was the single most influential IgE characteristic, exceeding sIgE level and avidity.
When peanut-sIgE was replaced by peanut specific activity in the multivariable model, both peanut SA and PD retained significant, comparable influence on mast cell activation.
In basophil activation test (BAT) univariable regression, both peanut specific activity and peanut diversity showed the highest standardized beta coefficients, mirroring effects seen with mast cells.
MAT and BAT responses to peanut were markedly higher in peanut-allergic than sensitized-tolerant or non-allergic children, validating these assays as reflecting clinical allergic status.
A high-throughput calcium mobilization screen identified a group of commonly used drugs, largely antidepressants, antiallergic drugs, and antipsychotics, that activate the mast cell receptor MRGPRX2.
Three-dimensional pharmacophore modeling showed the identified MRGPRX2 agonists share structural similarities, classifying them as cationic amphiphilic drugs.
Clomipramine caused concentration-dependent, MRGPRX2-dependent degranulation of the human mast cell line LAD2.
Paroxetine caused concentration-dependent, MRGPRX2-dependent degranulation of the human mast cell line LAD2.
Desipramine caused concentration-dependent, MRGPRX2-dependent degranulation of the human mast cell line LAD2.
Clomipramine, paroxetine, and desipramine induced degranulation of primary human skin mast cells and murine peritoneal mast cells.
Intradermal injection of clomipramine, paroxetine, or desipramine elicited dose-dependent scratching behavior in C57BL/6 mice, which was attenuated in MRGPRB2-mutant mice.
Clomipramine, paroxetine, and desipramine induced degranulation of primary human skin mast cells and murine peritoneal mast cells.
Intradermal injection of clomipramine, paroxetine, and desipramine elicited dose-dependent scratching behavior in C57BL/6 mice, an effect that was reduced in MRGPRB2-mutant mice.
Intradermal injection of the identified cationic amphiphilic drugs produced wheal-and-flare reactions in human skin, indicating pseudoallergic mast cell activation in vivo in humans.

The study concludes that characterizing structure-activity relationships of MRGPRX2 ligands can help predict adverse drug reactions such as drug-induced pruritus and prevent severe drug hypersensitivity reactions.
24 hours of 10% cyclic tension simulation reduced collagen II gene expression in chondrocytes.
24 hours of 10% cyclic tension simulation increased collagen I gene expression in chondrocytes.
24 hours of 10% cyclic tension simulation increased collagen III gene expression in chondrocytes.
24 hours of 10% cyclic tension simulation increased Runx2 gene expression in chondrocytes, consistent with hypertrophic/fibrotic shift.
24 hours of 10% cyclic tension simulation increased MMP13 gene expression in chondrocytes.
24 hours of 10% cyclic tension simulation increased ADAMTS-5 gene expression in chondrocytes.
Culturing chondrocytes with recombinant human TGF-β1 (without cyclic tension) raised cellular CCN2 expression, indicating TGF-β1 acts upstream of CCN2.
Exogenous recombinant TGF-β1 or CCN2 protein supplementation increased integrin-α5β1 mRNA levels in chondrocytes, placing integrin-α5β1 downstream of both TGF-β1 and CCN2.

Knockdown of TGF-β1 or CCN2 did not alter integrin-α5β1 expression regardless of whether cyclic tension stimulation was applied, indicating integrin-α5β1 is not solely regulated downstream of TGF-β1/CCN2 knockdown under these conditions.
Swimming-trained rats showed reduced iNOS gene and protein expression in the RVLM compared to sedentary rats.
Trained rats exhibited resting bradycardia relative to sedentary rats.
Swimming-trained rats showed a lower sympathovagal balance based on power spectral analysis of pressure and heart rate variability.
Trained rats displayed higher antioxidant capacity in RVLM tissue, including glutathione, FRAP and ABTS radical scavenger measures, compared to sedentary rats.
Decreased RVLM iNOS expression was positively correlated with reduced heart rate in trained rats.
Pressor and tachycardic responses to local RVLM microinjection of L-glutamate were smaller in trained rats than in sedentary rats.

Unilateral RVLM iNOS inhibition with aminoguanidine reduced sympathetic activity in sedentary rats but did not change sympathetic activity in trained rats, which already had reduced RVLM iNOS content.
E2 stimulation for 24 hours increased TGFβ1 transcript levels 1.4-fold in primary human dermal fibroblasts compared to vehicle-treated cells.
E2 stimulation for 24 hours increased TGFβ2 transcript levels 1.7-fold in primary human dermal fibroblasts compared to vehicle-treated cells.
Unlike TGFβ1 and TGFβ2, TGFβ3 transcript levels did not increase significantly 24 hours post E2 stimulation in primary dermal fibroblasts.
E2 stimulation for 1 hour induced a 3.7-fold increase in phosphorylated/activated ERK1/2 relative to total ERK1/2 in primary human dermal fibroblasts.
Unlike ERK1/2, the MAPK family members p38 and JNK were not activated by E2 stimulation in dermal fibroblasts.
Pre-treatment with the MEK/ERK inhibitor U0126 blocked E2-induced ERK1/2 phosphorylation in dermal fibroblasts.
MEK/ERK inhibition with U0126 prior to E2 stimulation prevented E2-induced TGFβ1 and TGFβ2 transcription at 24 hours and TGFβ1 protein translation at 48 hours.
E2 stimulation significantly increased EGR1 transcript levels at 6 hours and EGR1 protein levels at 16 hours in primary human dermal fibroblasts, though not at 30 minutes.
EGR1 transcript levels remained elevated 8 hours post E2 stimulation in dermal fibroblasts.
siRNA knockdown of EGR1 significantly diminished E2-induced levels of EGR1 and TGFβ2 in primary human dermal fibroblasts, with only a non-significant trend for TGFβ1 reduction.
In the ex vivo human skin organ culture model, TGFβ2 transcript levels increased 24 hours post E2 stimulation compared to vehicle-treated skin, an effect that subsided by 48 hours.
E2 induced Col22A1 transcription in ex vivo human skin at 48 hours post stimulation, but not at 72 hours.
In the ex vivo skin model, TGFβ1 transcript levels similarly increased at 48 hours post E2 stimulation.
Col IA2, Col IIIA1, and fibronectin (FN) transcript levels were significantly increased 72 hours post E2 stimulation in ex vivo human skin, but not at 24 or 48 hours.
Col IA1, CTGF, and alpha-SMA transcript levels were not significantly induced by E2 in ex vivo human skin at the timepoints tested.

The TGFβ type I receptor inhibitor SB-431542 reduced E2-induced Col22A1 transcript levels in ex vivo skin, but did not reduce Col IA2, Col IIIA1, or FN transcription below E2-treated levels, indicating Col22A1 induction by E2 occurs via TGFβ signaling while the other ECM genes are induced through a TGFβ-independent route.
Pre-treatment with the ERα inhibitor fulvestrant (ICI 182,780) significantly decreased E2-induced Col22A1 transcription in ex vivo human skin.

The authors propose a novel cellular mechanism in which E2 induces TGFβ1 and TGFβ2 through ERα signaling, MAPK/ERK activation, and EGR1 induction, which in turn drive Col22A1 induction and dermal fibrosis.
PKG1α, but not the PKG1β isoform, immunoreactivity co-localized with neuronal markers HuC/D and β3-tubulin in both the myenteric and submucosal plexuses of the guinea pig enteric nervous system.
PKG1α immunoreactivity co-localized with the IPAN marker calbindin in 100% of labeled myenteric neurons.
PKG1α immunoreactivity co-localized with cytoplasmic NeuN, another IPAN marker, in 98 ± 1% of submucosal plexus neurons.

CGRP-immunoreactive dorsal root ganglion neurons identified as visceral afferents via retrograde tracing were shown to express PKG1α, linking IPANs and DRG visceral nociceptors through shared PKG1α expression.

Blocking neuronal action potentials with tetrodotoxin or abolishing synaptic transmission with low Ca/high Mg media both prevented Fos activation in myenteric neurons induced by intraluminal cholera toxin, indicating that mucosal stimulation requires intact neurotransmission to activate enteric neurons.

The PKG inhibitor N46 (100 µM) inhibited Fos activation in myenteric neurons following mucosal stimulation with cholera toxin, indicating that PKG1α activity is functionally necessary for this IPAN-mediated reflex activation.
Blocking synaptic transmission with low-calcium/high-magnesium media inhibited Fos activation in myenteric neurons induced by mucosal stimulation with cholera toxin.
The PKG inhibitor N46 (100 µM) inhibited Fos activation in myenteric neurons following mucosal stimulation, indicating a functional requirement for PKG1α in this pathway.
N46 concentration-dependently inhibited peristaltic reflexes in isolated preparations of guinea pig distal colon, with an IC50 of 83.3 ± 1.3 µM.
Cultured lung fibroblasts from systemic sclerosis (SSc) patients showed significantly higher basal CCN2 protein expression than fibroblasts from healthy controls.
siRNA knockdown of CCN2 significantly reduced TGF-β-induced CCN2 protein expression in healthy control lung fibroblasts.
CCN2 knockdown lowered constitutive (basal, non-TGF-β-treated) fibronectin expression in SSc lung fibroblasts.
CCN2 knockdown significantly lowered TGF-β-induced CCN2 expression in SSc lung fibroblasts.
CCN2 knockdown significantly reduced TGF-β-induced fibronectin expression in SSc lung fibroblasts.
CCN2 knockdown significantly reduced TGF-β-induced collagen type I expression in SSc lung fibroblasts.
CCN2 knockdown significantly reduced TGF-β-induced TIMP-1 expression in SSc lung fibroblasts.
CCN2 knockdown significantly reduced TGF-β-induced α-SMA (myofibroblast marker) expression in SSc lung fibroblasts.
CCN2 knockdown reduced secreted IL-6 in TGF-β-treated healthy control lung fibroblasts.
Tamoxifen-induced fibroblast-specific CCN2 gene deletion significantly reduced CCN2 mRNA expression in mouse lung tissue compared to untreated controls.
CCN2 protein staining was significantly increased in bleomycin-treated wild-type mouse lungs compared to saline-treated wild-type lungs.
CCN2 protein staining was significantly reduced in bleomycin-treated CCN2 knockout mice compared to bleomycin-treated wild-type mice.
Fibroblast-specific CCN2 deletion reduced the histological fibrotic index (modified Ashcroft score) by 20% following bleomycin challenge compared to wild-type mice.
Pulmonary pressures (RVSP) were significantly reduced in bleomycin-treated CCN2 knockout mice compared to bleomycin-treated wild-type mice, indicating protection against pulmonary hypertension.
Bleomycin treatment significantly upregulated COL1α2, COL3 and EDA-fibronectin mRNA expression in wild-type mouse lungs compared to untreated lungs.
Bleomycin-induced COL1α2 and COL3 mRNA expression was reduced in CCN2 knockout mouse lungs compared to wild-type lungs.
Chronic hypoxia combined with SU5416 (VEGF receptor inhibitor) induced significantly elevated RVSP in wild-type mice compared to normoxia/SU5416, modelling pulmonary arterial hypertension.
Fibroblast-specific CCN2 deletion significantly reduced RVSP compared to wild-type mice under hypoxia/SU5416 conditions.
Fibroblast-specific CCN2 deletion significantly reduced hypoxia/SU5416-induced right ventricular hypertrophy (RV/LV+S ratio) compared to wild-type mice.
In control animals, the right anterior pelvic ganglion (APG) contained more than twice as many Fast Blue-labeled (bladder trigone-projecting) neurons as the left APG.

Unilateral right-sided axotomy of nerve fibers projecting to the urinary bladder trigone caused loss of more than half of bladder-projecting neurons in both the ipsilateral (right) and contralateral (left) APG.
The proportion of adrenergic (TH/DBH-immunoreactive) bladder trigone-projecting neurons in the right APG dropped markedly after axotomy.
The proportion of cholinergic (VAChT/ChAT-immunoreactive) neurons in the right APG increased slightly after axotomy.
The percentage of NANC (non-adrenergic, non-cholinergic) bladder trigone-projecting neurons in the right APG rose sharply after axotomy.
The proportion of VIP-immunoreactive bladder trigone-projecting neurons in the right APG increased dramatically after axotomy.
The proportion of galanin-immunoreactive bladder trigone-projecting neurons in the right APG increased dramatically after axotomy.
bNOS-immunoreactive bladder trigone-projecting neurons, absent in controls, newly appeared in the right APG after axotomy.
The percentage of NPY-immunoreactive bladder trigone-projecting neurons in the right APG did not change significantly after axotomy despite gene-level changes.

Unlike the ipsilateral (right) ganglion, the contralateral left APG showed no significant change in the immunohistochemical (protein-level) chemical coding of its bladder trigone-projecting neurons after right-sided axotomy.
qPCR showed marked downregulation of VAChT and ChAT gene expression in both the right and left APG following unilateral axotomy.
qPCR showed downregulation of DBH and TH gene expression in both the right and left APG following unilateral axotomy, despite an increase in adrenergic fiber density.
qPCR showed marked downregulation of NOS gene expression in both the right and left APG following unilateral axotomy, despite an increase in bNOS-immunoreactive neurons.

Despite the large increase in VIP-immunoreactive neurons, qPCR showed VIP gene expression was significantly lower in both ganglia after axotomy, a discordance the authors attribute to termination of already-elevated protein synthesis.

GAL gene expression rose sharply (34-fold) and NPY gene expression rose modestly (1.61-fold) in the ipsilateral right APG after axotomy, but neither changed significantly in the contralateral left APG.

Intraganglionic TH- and DBH-immunoreactive fiber density increased substantially in both right and left APG after axotomy, a phenomenon the authors could not fully explain and speculate reflects compensatory mechanisms.
Intraganglionic VAChT-immunoreactive fiber density decreased dramatically in both right and left APG after axotomy.

Intraganglionic VIP- and galanin-immunoreactive fiber density increased significantly in both right and left APG after unilateral axotomy, forming basket-like structures around neuropeptide-containing neurons.
Post-operative morphine consumption mediated 79% of the effect of peri-operative IV acetaminophen on shortening hospital length of stay after spinal surgery in youth with acute pain.
GI-specific avoidance behaviour mediated 67% of the effect of internet-delivered CBT versus waitlist control on reducing GI symptoms in adolescents with IBS.
GI-specific avoidance behaviour mediated the effect of internet-delivered CBT versus treatment as usual on reducing GI symptoms in children with functional abdominal pain disorder (FAPD).
GI-specific anxiety mediated the effect of internet-delivered CBT versus treatment as usual on reducing GI symptoms in children with functional abdominal pain disorder.

Perceived pain threat mediated the effect of social-learning CBT on reducing pain intensity at 3 and 6 months, but not at 12 months, and did not mediate reduction of GI symptom severity at any timepoint, in youth with FAPD.

Pain catastrophizing mediated the effect of social-learning CBT on reducing GI symptom severity at 3 months only, but not at 6 or 12 months, and did not mediate pain intensity outcomes at any timepoint, in youth with FAPD.
Perceived stress did not significantly mediate the effect of internet-delivered CBT versus waitlist control on outcomes for adolescents with IBS.
Parent solicitousness did not significantly mediate the effect of social-learning CBT versus education on GI symptom severity or pain intensity at any timepoint in youth with FAPD.

Pain reactivity mediated the effect of ACT compared to multidisciplinary treatment with amitriptyline on reducing pain interference at 3.5 and 7 months and depression at 3.5 months, but not depression at 7 months, in youth with mixed chronic pain.

Pain impairment beliefs mediated the effect of ACT compared to multidisciplinary treatment with amitriptyline on reducing depression at 3.5 and 7 months, but did not mediate pain interference at either timepoint, in youth with mixed chronic pain.
Pain catastrophizing did not mediate the effect of CBT versus fibromyalgia education on functional disability or depression at 6 months in youth with juvenile fibromyalgia.

Pain catastrophizing did not mediate the effect of ACT compared to multidisciplinary treatment with amitriptyline on pain interference or depression at 3.5 or 7 months in youth with mixed chronic pain.
Pain coping and coping efficacy did not mediate the effect of CBT versus fibromyalgia education on functional disability or depression at 6 months in youth with juvenile fibromyalgia.

Self-efficacy, kinesiophobia, and pain intensity did not mediate the effect of ACT compared to multidisciplinary treatment with amitriptyline on pain interference or depression at any timepoint in youth with mixed chronic pain.

Across six studies testing 53 mediation models of paediatric pain treatments, only 12 models identified a significant mediator of treatment effect while 41 did not, and methodological quality was generally poor (no power calculations, minimal confounder adjustment, no sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounding).
Somatic symptom severity (PHQ-15) showed a large within-group reduction from pre- to post-treatment following internet-administered EAET.
The large reduction in somatic symptoms was fully maintained, and slightly increased, at 4-month follow-up after I-EAET.
Nearly a quarter of participants achieved a 50% or greater reduction in somatic symptoms post-treatment, rising slightly at follow-up.
The majority of patients reached a minimally clinically important difference (MCID) reduction in PHQ-15 scores at both post-treatment and follow-up.
Anxiety symptoms (GAD-7) showed a small-to-moderate reduction post-treatment that was maintained at follow-up.
Depressive symptoms (PHQ-9) decreased moderately post-treatment and continued to improve substantially by 4-month follow-up.
Trauma-related symptoms (PCL-5) decreased modestly post-treatment and further improved by 4-month follow-up.
Functional impairment (Sheehan Disability Scale) improved after treatment, with a substantially larger effect at 4-month follow-up.
Feasibility criteria for adherence and attrition were met, with 85% average module completion and 29% attrition, better than the pre-specified thresholds.
A meaningful minority of participants reported a treatment-related increase in symptoms during I-EAET, more frequently than other negative-effect domains.
Over 80% of the SSD-CS sample had a comorbid psychiatric diagnosis, with depression and panic disorder being most common.
Fibromyalgia was the most common self-reported somatic condition in the SSD-CS sample, and over half reported at least two somatic conditions.

A prior meta-analysis found a 3-fold increased prevalence of psychological trauma in patients with functional somatic syndromes, including IBS, fibromyalgia, and chronic fatigue syndrome, compared to healthy controls.
The symptom reduction rate observed with I-EAET was notably higher than the 50% responder rate reported for traditional CBT in fibromyalgia in a prior meta-analysis.

A prior meta-analysis of internet-administered, primarily CBT interventions for similar samples found only a small reduction in somatic symptoms at follow-up compared to passive controls, smaller than the effect found for I-EAET in this study.
TGF-β1 stimulation of HK2 cells reduced miR-133b expression in a concentration-dependent manner, with no significant difference between 8 and 10 ng/mL.
miR-133b expression in HK2 cells decreased with increasing duration of TGF-β1 (8 ng/mL) exposure, plateauing between 48 and 72 hours.
Overexpression of miR-133b preserved epithelial (cobblestone) morphology of HK2 cells despite TGF-β1 stimulation, whereas NC-miR-transfected cells adopted a fibroblast-like morphology.
Bioinformatic target prediction (TargetScan, miRBase, PicTar) identified CTGF as a potential direct target of miR-133b, with a predicted binding site at 1027–1033 bp of the CTGF 3'-UTR.

Transient transfection of a miR-133b mimic into HK2 cells increased miR-133b expression by approximately 21,566-fold, confirming successful overexpression, and this was accompanied by a significant decrease in CTGF mRNA and protein.

Dual-luciferase reporter assay confirmed that miR-133b directly binds the CTGF 3'-UTR: the miR-133b mimic significantly decreased luciferase activity of the wild-type CTGF construct but had no effect on the mutant construct.
miR-133b overexpression significantly inhibited TGF-β1-induced downregulation of E-cadherin and upregulation of α-SMA, fibronectin, Col3A1, and CTGF at both mRNA and protein levels in HK2 cells.

Immunofluorescence confirmed that miR-133b reduced TGF-β1-induced increases in α-SMA, Col3A1, fibronectin, and CTGF fluorescence intensity and increased E-cadherin intensity, with no change seen with NC-miR.

Exogenous CTGF overexpression reversed miR-133b-mediated inhibition of α-SMA, fibronectin, and Col3A1 upregulation and the increase in E-cadherin, demonstrating CTGF acts downstream of miR-133b in EMT regulation.
Intravenous administration of a miR-133b transfection complex significantly increased renal miR-133b expression in aged UUO mice compared with sham and UUO+NC-miR groups at both 7 and 14 days.
miR-133b treatment significantly reduced relative renal interstitial collagen deposition (Masson's trichrome) in aged UUO mice at both 7 and 14 days compared with the UUO+NC-miR group.

In aged UUO mouse kidneys, miR-133b treatment significantly decreased mRNA and protein levels of CTGF, fibronectin, Col3A1, and α-SMA and increased E-cadherin compared with UUO+NC-miR at both 7 and 14 days, though levels remained abnormal relative to sham.
miR-133b treatment significantly lowered BUN at day 7 and both BUN and sCr at day 14 post-UUO compared with the UUO+NC-miR group, indicating improved renal function.

UUO produced significantly higher CTGF, fibronectin, Col3A1, and α-SMA and lower E-cadherin mRNA/protein in the kidney compared with sham mice, with fibrosis worsening from 7 to 14 days, validating the aged UUO model of renal interstitial fibrosis.
Next-generation sequencing of the clone-based IGHV/IGHD/IGHJ repertoire revealed biased usage of several IGHV genes in peripheral blood B cells from ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
ROC analysis of the skewed B cell repertoire indicated the potential to distinguish ME/CFS patients from healthy controls.
B cell clones using IGHV3-30 and IGHV3-30-3 genes were more frequent in ME/CFS patients who had an obvious infection-related episode at disease onset.
Frequency of IGHV3-30/IGHV3-30-3-using B cell clones correlated with expression levels of interferon response genes in plasmablasts from ME/CFS patients.

Fecal Bacteroidetes relative abundance was significantly increased and Firmicutes reduced in CFS/ME patients compared with external controls, with the Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio reduced ~60% in patients and ~50% in relatives.
The order Clostridiales within Firmicutes was significantly reduced in CFS/ME patients compared to external controls.
Bacteroidales within Bacteroidetes phylum was significantly increased in both CFS/ME patients and their relatives compared to external controls.
Lachnospiraceae, a family of butyrate-producing bacteria, was significantly reduced in CFS/ME patients compared to external controls.
Bacteroidaceae was roughly 10-fold more abundant in CFS/ME patients and 6-fold more abundant in relatives compared to external controls.
Barnesiellaceae was significantly increased in both CFS/ME patients and their relatives compared to external controls.
Anaerostipes, a lactate-to-butyrate converting genus, was significantly reduced in both CFS/ME patients and their relatives compared to external controls.
Bacteroides genus and Phascolarctobacterium were about 10-fold more abundant in CFS/ME patients versus external controls; Bacteroides was also ~6-fold higher in relatives.
Ruminococcus was significantly increased in patients' relatives compared to external controls (not significant in patients themselves).
Bacteroides ovatus was about 10-fold more abundant in both CFS/ME patients and their relatives than in external controls.
Bacteroides uniformis was about 10-fold more abundant in both CFS/ME patients and their relatives than in external controls.
Ruminococcus bromii showed a significant increase only in patients' relatives compared to external controls, with no significant change in patients themselves.
Fecal alpha-diversity metrics (total OTUs, Chao1, Simpson's evenness) did not significantly differ between CFS/ME patients, relatives, and external controls.

Canonical Correspondence Analysis of fecal microbiota showed disease status (CFS/ME vs relatives vs controls) was a significant, though modest, source of variability in bacterial community composition.
Salivary Actinobacteria phylum, and specifically the order Actinomycetales, was significantly increased in CFS/ME patients compared to external controls.
The genus Rothia (family Micrococcaceae) was significantly more abundant in the saliva of CFS/ME patients compared to external controls.
Rothia dentocariosa was significantly increased in the saliva of both CFS/ME patients and their relatives compared to the external control group.
Fecal glutamic acid was significantly up-accumulated in CFS/ME patients compared to external controls, identified as a top discriminant metabolite by both Volcano plot and PLS-DA/OPLS-DA analyses.
Fecal argininosuccinic acid was strongly up-accumulated in CFS/ME patients versus controls, suggesting possible alteration of the NO-citrulline/urea cycle.
Fecal alpha-tocopherol (vitamin E) was strongly down-accumulated in both CFS/ME patients and their relatives compared to external controls, consistent with increased oxidative stress.
Fecal lithocholyltaurine and eicosapentaenoic acid were significantly up-accumulated in patients' relatives compared to external controls.

Among the 35 CFS/ME patients, 71% reported gastrointestinal disturbances and 31% had comorbid Irritable Bowel Syndrome, versus only 20% GI symptoms in relatives and none reporting IBS in either comparison group.
Post-exertional malaise was reported by the majority (85%) of CFS/ME patients, compared to only 5% of patients' relatives.
Family whole-exome sequencing revealed compound heterozygous MTHFR mutations (c.677C>T and c.1298A>C), inherited one from each parent, considered the cause of the patient's hyperhomocysteinemia.
The patient's serum homocysteine was markedly elevated during illness and decreased after combined folate/B-vitamin/carnitine therapy.
A standing test showed an exaggerated heart rate increase from supine to upright posture accompanied by lightheadedness, confirming a diagnosis of POTS.
The patient had markedly elevated EBV capsid antigen IgG and nuclear antigen IgG (with normal IgM and viral load), suggesting past EBV infection speculated to be linked to CFS onset.
Testing revealed intensified/enhanced flow-mediated vasodilation, interpreted as reflecting impaired endothelial function and abnormal vasoconstriction contributing to POTS.
Multiple sleep latency testing showed markedly shortened sleep latency and three sleep-onset REM periods in five naps, with an Epworth Sleepiness Scale score of 19, confirming narcolepsy.
The authors cite literature indicating that nearly 11% of adult CFS patients are also diagnosed with POTS, with higher POTS incidence in pediatric CFS patients than adults.
The authors cite a retrospective study reporting that treating narcolepsy obviously relieved fatigue in 75% of CFS patients with comorbid narcolepsy.

Combined oral folate, vitamin B6, vitamin B12, and L-carnitine therapy was given for hyperhomocysteinemia, previously providing limited benefit and again used in this admission alongside other treatments.
Oral midodrine hydrochloride was prescribed to target excessive vasodilation in POTS, partially relieving dizziness after one month but not improving drowsiness/fatigue.
