Methylphenidate hydrochloride was added to treat the narcoleptiform sleep disorder, resulting in markedly reduced daytime drowsiness and shortened total sleep duration, enabling return to school.
Cited cross-sectional research found that therapeutic response and required oral folate dose in CFS patients correlate with MTHFR c.677C>T and c.1298A>C single-nucleotide polymorphisms.
Two of three patients with treatment-resistant CFS treated with modafinil plus CBT showed clinically meaningful improvement in energy and pain/concentration on Likert-scale ratings.
All three treatment-resistant CFS patients treated with modafinil plus CBT achieved social recovery, defined as return to work or full-time training.
The authors conclude that repeat/medium-term prescription of modafinil may potentiate the benefits of CBT in patients with refractory CFS.
Self-reported physical activity level via activity diary showed only a weak correlation with accelerometer-measured activity in CFS patients, both for weekdays and weekend days.
In healthy controls, self-reported and accelerometer-measured activity levels were moderately strongly correlated, a stronger association than seen in CFS patients.
A linear mixed model showed that older age was associated with a smaller discrepancy between self-reported and objectively measured physical activity level, in both CFS patients and healthy controls.

The discrepancy between self-reported and objectively measured physical activity level in CFS patients was not explained by illness-related complaints, health-related quality of life domains, or demographic factors.

The authors hypothesize a possible physiopathological link between Gorlin–Goltz syndrome and Ehlers–Danlos syndrome based on the chromosomal proximity of the PTCH1 and COL5A1 genes, both located on chromosome 9.
Simultaneous occurrence of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and odontogenic keratocyst is extremely rare, with only two prior cases reported in the literature before this one.
Unlike the two previously reported EDS-OKC cases, which involved only mandibular lesions, this patient's odontogenic keratocysts were found in both the mandible and the maxilla.
Unlike prior reported EDS-OKC cases, this patient experienced recurrence of odontogenic keratocysts after surgical treatment (enucleation and curettage).
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome affects collagen synthesis, resulting in friable oral mucosa, increased intraoperative bleeding risk, and slower wound healing that may progress to scarring or keloids.
Following surgical enucleation of an OKC lesion performed at another institution in 2019, the patient developed post-operative paraesthesia in the territory of the left inferior alveolar nerve.
Recurrence risk of odontogenic keratocyst varies by treatment method, ranging from 32.3% for marsupialization down to 8.4% for bone resection.
Gorlin–Goltz syndrome mutations are autosomal dominant and may involve PTCH1, PTCH2, or SUFU genes.

The patient was diagnosed with classic-type Ehlers-Danlos syndrome at age 7 based on major criteria (skin hyperextensibility, joint hypermobility) and minor criteria (smooth skin, easy bruising, positive family history with affected father).

The patient additionally met clinical criteria for Gorlin-Goltz syndrome, with multiple odontogenic keratocysts as the major criterion plus four minor criteria (frontal bossing, hypertelorism, scoliosis, Sprengel's deformity), though this was not confirmed with genetic testing.
A patient with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome presented with an inferior vena cava aneurysm, reported as a case of vascular pathology co-occurring with EDS.
A novel gross deletion mutation, c.-105_4042+498del, in the TNXB gene was identified in a Japanese woman diagnosed with classical-like Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Despite carrying a TNXB gross deletion causing classical-like EDS, the patient had an uneventful pregnancy and delivery.

Surgical lung biopsy demonstrated dendriform-type diffuse pulmonary ossification with irregular-shaped ossifications containing bone marrow, surrounding fibrosis, and compression of normal lung structure.
Genetic testing for COL3A1 mutations, which cause vascular EDS, was negative in this patient despite pathological suspicion of vEDS.
The patient lacked classic external physical signs of vEDS such as skin hyperextensibility and hemoptysis, and had no family history of the disease.
Pulmonary function testing showed moderately restrictive changes with reduced diffusion capacity, and a 6-minute walk test showed desaturation to a minimum SpO2 of 88%.
Citing prior literature (Tseung et al.), the authors note that DPO has a frequency of 0.16%, with a median patient age of 72 years (range 32-91) and 88% of affected individuals being men.

The authors propose that vEDS can cause secondary diffuse pulmonary ossification through chronic repetition of pulmonary hemorrhage and hemostasis, with hematoma formation followed by organization and ossification.
A prior epidemiological study found DPO frequency of 0.16% with median patient age 72 (range 32-91) and 88% of affected individuals being men, contrasting with the present 30-year-old male patient.
COL3A1 mutations are reported to be detectable in over 95% of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome patients using sequence analysis.

Approximately 50% of vEDS patients are reported to carry a de novo pathogenic variant, which the authors note as a possible explanation for the negative COL3A1 test despite clinical suspicion in this patient without family history.
Most pulmonary manifestations of EDS occur in the vascular subtype and typically present with bloody sputum, hemoptysis, and pneumothorax.
The authors propose that vEDS can cause secondary diffuse pulmonary ossification through chronic repeated cycles of pulmonary hemorrhage and hemostasis.

Nodular pulmonary ossification is typically linked to chronic congestion from cardiac disease such as mitral stenosis, whereas dendriform ossification (as in this patient) is typically linked to chronic inflammatory pulmonary disease such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, amyloidosis, ARDS, COPD, or asbestosis, though idiopathic cases are also common.
EDS is currently classified into 13 subtypes per the 2017 international classification, caused by mutations in specific collagen-encoding genes or collagen-processing enzymes.
Gene-based mutation burden and variance component tests showed enrichment of genetic variation in COL2A1 in keratoconus patients compared to controls.
COL5A1, a known Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome gene, showed enrichment of genetic variation across gene-based tests in keratoconus patients versus controls.
TNXB, a known Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome gene, showed enrichment of genetic variation across gene-based tests in keratoconus patients versus controls.
ZNF469, a known Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome gene, showed enrichment of genetic variation across gene-based tests in keratoconus patients, confirming its previously disputed role in KC susceptibility.
A common variant in COL12A1, another known Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome gene, was the top hit in the single-variant association test for keratoconus.

Resequencing of 34 candidate genes in keratoconus patients and controls demonstrates a shared genetic etiology between keratoconus and Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome, being the first study to show a consistent role of EDS gene variants in KC etiology.
The study resolves previous disagreement in the literature by confirming that ZNF469 genetic variation contributes to keratoconus susceptibility.
The gene-based associations for COL2A1, COL5A1, TNXB, and ZNF469 were consistently detected across independent Belgian, French, and Italian subpopulations, supporting replication of the findings.
Adolescents with chronic musculoskeletal pain had decreased muscle strength compared to adolescents without chronic pain.
Adolescents with chronic musculoskeletal pain had decreased muscular endurance compared to adolescents without chronic pain.
Adolescents with chronic musculoskeletal pain had lower motor performance compared to adolescents without chronic pain.
Higher levels of pain-related fear were associated with decreased muscle strength, endurance, and motor performance.
No differences in physical functioning or pain-related fear were found between hypermobile and non-hypermobile adolescents with chronic musculoskeletal pain.
The patient was genetically diagnosed with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome after missense variants were found in COL3A1.

The patient died from a common hepatic artery aneurysm rupture that occurred five days after emergency colon resection surgery for sigmoid colon perforation, with no aneurysm detectable on preoperative CT.
In a cohort study, 15% of vEDS patients with intestinal complications also developed vascular complications during follow-up.
A study of Japanese vEDS patients found that 66% experienced both intestinal and vascular complications.
Celiprolol is reported to reduce vascular complications in patients with vEDS, and the patient had been taking celiprolol 400 mg/day before surgery but it was discontinued postoperatively.

The average age of death from vEDS is reported to be 48 years, and vascular rupture is the most common cause of death, with bowel rupture accounting for 8% of deaths and surgical mortality reported at 7%.
Only 38% of patients with vEDS have a family history of the disease, and characteristic physical/facial features may be absent even in confirmed cases.
Chronic constipation, present in approximately half of vEDS patients, is thought to increase intestinal pressure and may induce ischemic colitis and intestinal rupture.

Microscopic examination of the perforated sigmoid colon showed inflammatory cell infiltration, rupture of the muscular layer, and thin collagen fibers in the submucosal layer, consistent with vEDS-related connective tissue fragility.

The authors propose that surgery-related invasion (colon resection plus pan-peritonitis) may have elevated collagenase activity, contributing to a 'remote vascular catastrophe' with hepatic artery rupture distinct from direct surgical injury.
The patient's EDS diagnosis was confirmed by a private rheumatologist based on clinical history and examination after her GP raised suspicion.
A specialist suggested the patient's neurological symptoms could be associated with EDS-related cranio-cervical instability following a fall sustained during a suicide attempt.

The patient developed disabling vertigo, syncope, and nausea in late adolescence, becoming fearful that standing and movement would provoke fainting, seizures, or joint dislocations, eventually becoming wheelchair-dependent.

Physiotherapy assessment found full power in all limbs and no sensory deficits, leading the physiotherapist to conclude the patient's impaired mobility was functional rather than due to structural EDS-related damage.
Trauma-focused physiotherapy combined with balance and strength training helped the patient regain confidence in her physical abilities and resume walking after years of wheelchair use.

Consistent emotional validation and mindfulness-based behavioral strategies, along with self-alerting staff before episodes, reduced the frequency and duration of the patient's psychogenic nonepileptic seizures.
By discharge, the patient had been seizure-free for several months, compared to twice-weekly seizures on admission.
The patient transitioned from full-time electric wheelchair use to mostly unaided or walker-assisted mobility indoors by the time of discharge, requiring wheelchair use only for long journeys.
The patient showed improvement across all nine structured outcome measures (symptomatology, quality of life, mindfulness, recovery) from admission to discharge, sustained at six-month follow-up.
Following the one-year inpatient programme, the patient no longer met diagnostic criteria for Emotionally Unstable Personality Disorder.
At discharge the patient had been self-harm free for 200 days and denied suicidal ideation, plans, or intent.
Several psychotropic medications (Buscopan, Quetiapine, Clonazepam regular dosing, Duloxetine, and Zopiclone) were discontinued through shared decision-making with the patient during the admission.
The authors note that comorbid EUPD, EDS, and FND is frequently encountered in clinical practice despite no prior published case reports on this specific combination.
Generalized joint hypermobility (GJH) was not correlated with self-reported knee health as measured by KOOS domains.
Knee-specific hypermobility (KSH) showed a very weak correlation with one of the five KOOS domains.
Prevalence of generalized joint hypermobility was significantly higher in non-Caucasians than Caucasians.
Prevalence of generalized joint hypermobility was significantly higher in females than males.
Prevalence of knee-specific hypermobility did not differ significantly between ethnic groups.
Prevalence of knee-specific hypermobility did not differ significantly between gender groups.
Non-Caucasian participants reported better (higher) scores in all five KOOS domains compared to Caucasians.

Individuals meeting age- and gender-specific criteria for GJH or KSH did not report worse knee health than non-hypermobile counterparts, suggesting these traits are not associated with lower knee function.
Among 47 IPSG survey respondents, 94% (44/47) reported never having encountered a case of noniatrogenic medial patellar dislocation, confirming the rarity of the condition.
Four of the six confirmed cases of noniatrogenic medial patellar dislocation occurred in patients with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, suggesting connective tissue laxity as a risk factor.
Three of the four EDS patients had bilateral medial patellar instability, and two of these had prior contralateral knee surgery for recurrent medial instability.
One EDS patient with recurrent medial patellar instability had rotational malalignment of both lower extremities, with increased femoral anteversion of 22° and increased tibial torsion of 46°.

All 4 EDS patients with noniatrogenic medial patellar dislocation were managed with physical therapy and bracing, with surgical intervention reserved for cases in which an adequate trial of nonoperative treatment failed.

A 19-year-old male collegiate basketball player with upper extremity hyperlaxity sustained a noniatrogenic acute medial patellar dislocation with bone contusions of the anterior medial femoral condyle and lateral patella; treated with reverse J-shaped bracing, physical therapy, and arthroscopic chondroplasty, he returned to full collegiate play with no recurrence at 1.5-year follow-up.

A 21-year-old female collegiate soccer player sustained a traumatic medial patellar dislocation with spontaneous reduction and a large displaced chondral flap injury; treated with arthroscopic chondroplasty and viscosupplementation injections, she completed her final collegiate season with only mild residual patellofemoral discomfort at 14 months.

In the two acute noniatrogenic medial patellar dislocation cases, MRI showed a bone contusion pattern involving the anterior medial femoral condyle and lateral patella, the reverse of the pattern classically seen in lateral patellar dislocation (lateral femoral condyle and medial patella).
Nearly one-third of FMS patients (31.0%) showed QST-defined signs of central sensitization (abnormal mechanical pain sensitivity, mechanical pain threshold, or dynamic mechanical allodynia).
Patients with signs of central sensitization had significantly higher average and minimal pain intensity than those without such signs.
Average pain intensity positively correlated with mechanical pain sensitivity and mechanical pain threshold values.
Patients with higher pain intensity (NRS≥6) showed increased mechanical and pressure pain sensitivity (higher MPT, MPS, and PPT) compared to those with lower pain intensity.
The number and type of psychiatric comorbidities (depression, anxiety, sleep disorder) did not significantly influence the overall QST profile in FMS patients.

Patients with substantial depressive symptoms showed higher frequencies of abnormal mechanical pain sensitivity and vibration detection threshold than non-depressed patients, though overall z-value differences were not significant.
When controlling for pain intensity (NRS) as covariate, MPS abnormality was significantly explained by pain intensity but not by depression status itself.
Patients with higher pain intensity scored positive for depression more often than those with lower pain intensity, and HADS-D correlated with average pain intensity.
Depressive symptom severity (BDI-II) and disease impact (FIQ) both showed mild positive correlations with pressure pain threshold values.
No significant differences in QST parameters were found between patients with and without anxiety symptoms.
No significant QST differences were observed between subgroups based on age or pain duration.

Nearly half of FMS patients (45.9%) showed loss of large-fiber function (hyposensitivity to nonnoxious mechanical stimuli such as vibration and light touch), suggestive of large-fiber afferent or central pathway impairment.

Only a small subgroup (11.4%) of FMS patients showed thermal detection loss suggestive of small-fiber pathology, contrasting with some prior studies and suggesting small-fiber neuropathy may not be a major mechanism in FMS.
Comorbid anxiety and depressive disorders were highly prevalent among FMS patients based on HADS screening.
Sleep disturbances were extremely common among FMS patients, with the majority showing abnormal sleep somnolence, disturbance, and inadequacy scores.
Most FMS patients suffered from multiple overlapping comorbidities simultaneously, with nearly half having all three (depression, anxiety, sleep disorder) concurrently, while very few had none.
Post hoc analysis showed no significant differences between the FM group and control group in eyeblink response to prepulse inhibition (PPI) conditions.
The FM group showed a significantly greater eyeblink reactivity to the prepulse facilitation (PPF) conditioned stimulus compared with controls.
A significant GROUP*CONDITION interaction indicated that the difference in eyeblink amplitude between the FM and control groups varied depending on whether the condition was PPI or PPF.
The authors suggest that interventions decreasing autonomic drive or rebalancing autonomic/parasympathetic tone, such as vagal stimulation, might be effective for treating people with FM.
Mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and inflammation have been implicated in the pathophysiology of fibromyalgia.
A deficit in CoQ10 status has been associated with fibromyalgia.
CoQ10 supplementation is proposed to improve mitochondrial activity, restore cellular antioxidant capacity, and ameliorate inflammation, contributing to symptomatic relief in fibromyalgia.
Individuals with fibromyalgia and individuals with both fibromyalgia and rheumatoid arthritis reported worse daily well-being than individuals with rheumatoid arthritis alone.

After controlling for age, pain duration, and daily pain, differences between FM and RA remained significant only for social well-being and completion of plans, implying other well-being differences may be explained by these covariates.
After adjustment for covariates, individuals with both FM and RA diagnoses differed significantly from RA-only individuals in completion of plans, negative affect, and isolation.
Individuals with fibromyalgia reported more perceived stigmatization than individuals with rheumatoid arthritis.

Individuals with both fibromyalgia and rheumatoid arthritis reported similar levels of stigmatization to individuals with fibromyalgia alone, but more than individuals with rheumatoid arthritis alone.
Increased levels of daily perceived stigma were associated with lower daily well-being across participants.
Visual discomfort, as measured by the L-VISS and VDS, was highest in people with fibromyalgia, followed by those with CRPS, relative to general chronic pain and pain-free controls.
The Leiden Visual Sensitivity Scale (L-VISS) and Visual Discomfort Scale (VDS) demonstrated good internal consistency across the studied groups.
Both the L-VISS and VDS were positively related to experimentally induced visual distortions for mid-spatial frequency striped patterns, supporting good construct validity.
L-VISS and VDS scores were positively correlated with each other and dissociated pain and pain-free groups in similar ways.
There was no relationship found between age and L-VISS scores.
A small negative relationship was found between age and VDS scores, indicating slightly lower visual discomfort with increasing age.
Stat5B-deficient (KO) mice showed reduced responses to IgE-mediated anaphylaxis compared to wild-type mice.
Stat5B KO mice retained normal mast cell tissue distribution despite functional deficits.
Mast cells from Stat5B KO mice showed diminished IgE-induced degranulation and cytokine secretion in vitro.
Stat5B KO mice have elevated IgE production compared to wild-type mice, which does not appear to stem from an intrinsic B cell defect.
Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia is an autosomal dominant trait present in 4-6% of the general population, caused by extra copies of the alpha-tryptase gene at TPSAB1.
Elevated basal serum tryptase above 8 ng/mL is a defining feature of HαT and reflects increased pro-alpha-tryptase synthesis and secretion rather than mast cell activation.
Approximately one-third of individuals with HαT have associated symptoms spanning cutaneous, gastrointestinal, atopic, musculoskeletal, autonomic, and neuropsychiatric domains.
HαT occurs at a disproportionately high rate among patients with systemic mastocytosis and idiopathic anaphylaxis.
HαT independently increases both the incidence and severity of anaphylaxis, acting as a modifying genetic factor.

The varied phenotypes of HαT may partly result from coinheritance of other genetic variants, increased alpha-/beta-tryptase heterotetramer expression, and/or pro-alpha-tryptase overexpression, though further study is needed.
HαT independently increases both the incidence and severity of anaphylaxis, acting as a modifying genetic factor.
The varied clinical phenotypes seen in HαT may partly result from coinheritance of other genetic variants alongside the TPSAB1 duplication.
Increased expression of α-/ß-tryptase heterotetramers is proposed as a contributor to the variable clinical phenotypes of HαT.
Overexpression of pro-alpha-tryptase is proposed as another contributor to the varied clinical phenotypes seen in HαT.
An accurate genetic diagnostic test exists to confirm HαT and, combined with serum basal tryptase, can help risk-stratify patients being considered for bone marrow biopsy.

There is no specific treatment for HαT-associated symptoms; management focuses on controlling manifestations using mast cell mediator antagonists, aspirin, inhalers, epinephrine, omalizumab, and multidisciplinary specialist involvement.
IVIG did not significantly improve pain compared with placebo in patients with painful idiopathic small fiber neuropathy on the primary outcome measure.
A subset of secondary pain and quality-of-life outcomes showed statistically significant differences between IVIG and placebo but were inconsistent and not considered clinically meaningful.
Patient Global Impression of Change (PGIC) ratings of much/very much improved did not differ significantly between IVIG and placebo at 12 or 24 weeks.
IVIG showed no significant benefit over placebo on autonomic symptoms, overall disability, or pain relief measures.
Adverse events including headache, nausea, vomiting, and rash occurred significantly more frequently in the IVIG group than the placebo group.
Serious adverse events occurred more frequently in the IVIG group than in the placebo group.
Number-needed-to-treat and cost analysis showed IVIG is not cost-effective for achieving pain responses beyond placebo in I-SFN.
Complete knockout or conditional knockout of Scn9a in specific cell populations in mice reduces sensitivity to various pain stimuli.
Complete knockout of Scn10a in mice reduces sensitivity to various pain stimuli.
Possum mutant mice carrying a dominant hypermorphic (gain-of-function-like) mutation in Scn10a show increased sensitivity to noxious stimuli.
Several gain-of-function mutations in these sodium channel genes have been identified in patients with painful small fiber neuropathy.
DIO3OS expression was significantly upregulated in BPH prostate tissues compared with normal prostate tissues.
Within BPH tissue, DIO3OS levels were higher in stromal tissue than in epithelial tissue.
DIO3OS was significantly upregulated by TGF-β1 treatment and downregulated by resveratrol treatment in both BPH-1 epithelial cells and WPMY-1 stromal cells.

A Smad2/Smad3/Smad4 complex binding site was predicted and validated in the DIO3OS promoter region, with luciferase and ChIP assays confirming Smad-DIO3OS promoter interaction and transcriptional activation.
TGF-β1 stimulated phosphorylation of Smad2 and Smad3 in BPH-1 and WPMY-1 cells, while resveratrol blocked TGF-β1 signaling by repressing this phosphorylation.

TGF-β1 induced epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) of BPH-1 cells, and this effect was attenuated by DIO3OS silencing (shRNA), while DIO3OS overexpression enhanced EMT and was repressed by resveratrol.
TGF-β1 promoted proliferation of WPMY-1 stromal cells, an effect reversed by DIO3OS silencing, while DIO3OS overexpression facilitated proliferation and was inhibited by resveratrol.
DIO3OS was found to be predominantly localized in the cytoplasm of BPH-1 and WPMY-1 cells, consistent with a potential role interacting with miRNAs.
miR-656-3p and miR-485-5p were identified as direct binding targets of DIO3OS, confirmed by RNA pull-down and luciferase reporter assays.
miR-656-3p and miR-485-5p inhibitors reversed the EMT inhibition caused by DIO3OS shRNA, while their mimics alleviated EMT caused by DIO3OS overexpression in TGF-β1-stimulated BPH-1 cells.

miR-656-3p and miR-485-5p inhibitors attenuated the proliferation suppression induced by DIO3OS shRNA, while their mimics abated the proliferation acceleration caused by DIO3OS overexpression in TGF-β1-treated WPMY-1 cells.
CTGF and ZEB1 were identified as direct downstream targets of both miR-656-3p and miR-485-5p, validated by luciferase reporter and Western blot assays.

TGF-β1 upregulated CTGF and ZEB1 expression via the DIO3OS/miR-656-3p/miR-485-5p axis, and DIO3OS increased CTGF and ZEB1 expression which could be eliminated by resveratrol or by miR-656-3p/miR-485-5p.
Electrical stimulation of choroidal superior salivatory nucleus (SSN) with a metal electrode increased choroidal blood flow at the anterior temporal recording site.
SSN stimulation also increased choroidal blood flow at the anterior nasal recording site.
SSN stimulation increased choroidal blood flow at a posterior nasal recording site, demonstrating that SSN influence on choroid extends beyond the anterior eye, unlike a prior report.
Systemic arterial blood pressure did not rise significantly during SSN stimulation at any of the three choroidal recording sites, indicating perfusion pressure was not driving the ChBF increases.
Fine glass-micropipette electrical stimulation of SSN, which produces less current spread than metal electrodes, still significantly increased ChBF at the anterior nasal site.

Regression analysis across stimulation sites showed choroidal blood velocity increases were more strongly correlated with, and a greater contributor to, SSN-evoked ChBF increases than choroidal blood volume increases.
Across pooled stimulation trials, ABP changes showed no significant positive correlation with SSN-evoked ChBF increases, with a flat regression slope.
Pharmacological nNOS inhibition (NPA/LNAME) reduced basal choroidal blood flow and blunted the SSN-evoked ChBF increase, implicating NO as a key mediator of parasympathetic choroidal vasodilation.
Electrolytic destruction of choroidal SSN impaired the ability of ChBF to compensate and remain stable during systemic hypotension, unlike eyes with lesions that missed SSN.
Choroidal SSN destruction reduced the ipsilateral (right) eye scotopic ERG a-wave amplitude, with the deficit present by 4 weeks and worsening by 10 weeks post-lesion.
Choroidal SSN destruction significantly reduced the ipsilateral (right) eye ERG b-wave amplitude by 10 weeks post-lesion.
Unilateral right choroidal SSN destruction unexpectedly also reduced ERG a-wave and b-wave amplitudes in the contralateral (left, unlesioned) eye by 10 weeks post-lesion.

Rats with lesions that missed choroidal SSN showed no significant ERG a-wave change at 4 weeks and only a slight reduction at 10 weeks, and no b-wave deficit at either time point, confirming specificity of the SSN-lesion effect.

Choroidal SSN destruction significantly increased GFAP immunolabeling of retinal Müller cell processes, with processes penetrating deeper into the inner plexiform layer, in both ipsilateral and contralateral retinas.
qPCR confirmed an 8-fold increase in retinal GFAP mRNA expression after choroidal SSN destruction compared to controls.

Immunostaining showed that choroidal parasympathetic (nNOS, VIP) and sympathetic (VMAT2) nerve fiber distribution was present throughout the eye and was not obviously altered by choroidal SSN destruction.

In a prior study cited here, nNOS heterozygous-null mice had markedly reduced basal choroidal blood flow at 3 months of age compared to wild-type, although baroregulation was still intact at that age.

In the same cited prior mouse study, nNOS+/- mice showed normal visual acuity at 3 months but a marked decline in visual acuity and photoreceptor abundance by 200-500 days of age, consistent with progressive outer retinal damage from chronic parasympathetic ChBF deficiency.
The paper cites a study showing the AMD-risk CFH Y402H polymorphism may itself compromise autonomic sympathetic control of choroidal blood flow early in life.
The paper cites evidence that CFH-deficient mice show progressive choroidal pathology, supporting a direct link between AMD-risk polymorphisms and neurogenic control of choroidal blood flow.
Women with fibromyalgia showed significantly higher hypothenar eminence (hand) skin temperature measured by infrared thermography than healthy controls.
Core body (tympanic) temperature did not significantly differ between FMS women and healthy controls in the direct group comparison.
Visual Analogue Scale pain intensity scores were significantly higher in FMS women than in healthy controls.
Central Sensitization Inventory scores were significantly higher in FMS women compared with healthy controls.
Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores indicating worse sleep quality were significantly higher in FMS women than in healthy controls.
Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory scores were significantly higher (more fatigue) in FMS women than in healthy controls.
Beck Anxiety Inventory scores were significantly higher in FMS women than in healthy controls.
Pressure pain thresholds at all 18 ACR tender points were significantly lower (indicating hyperalgesia) in FMS women than in healthy controls.
FMS women had a mean Revised Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire total score reflecting high disease severity.
Within FMS women, those with higher core body temperature showed significantly different daytime dysfunction scores (PSQI) compared to those with lower core body temperature.
Within FMS women, mental fatigue scores (MFI) differed significantly between those with higher versus lower core body temperature.
Within FMS women, subjective pain intensity (VAS) differed significantly between those with higher versus lower hypothenar hand temperature.
Core body temperature was significantly positively associated with the FIQ-R overall impact subscale in FMS women after adjustment for age, menopause status and BMI.
Core body temperature was significantly positively associated with daytime dysfunction (PSQI) in FMS women after adjustment for age, menopause status and BMI.
Core body temperature was significantly positively associated with reduced activity (MFI) in FMS women after adjustment for age, menopause status and BMI.
Hypothenar eminence skin temperature was significantly associated with dominant greater-trochanter pressure pain threshold in FMS women after adjustment for age, menopause status and BMI.
Hypothenar eminence skin temperature was significantly associated with non-dominant greater-trochanter pressure pain threshold in FMS women after adjustment for age, menopause status and BMI.
Hypothenar eminence temperature was significantly negatively associated with use of sleep medication (PSQI subscale) in FMS women after adjustment for age, menopause status and BMI.

Prior histological work cited in this paper found that hypothenar AVAs in FMS patients show altered neural vasoregulation, with over-representation of peptidergic sensory innervation relative to noradrenergic sympathetic innervation.
The paper cites prior studies showing excessive blood concentrations of substance P and CGRP in FMS patients, proposed to relate to elevated core body temperature and symptom impact.
In 6-OHDA-lesioned rats, the gastrointestinal transit rate, total myenteric neuron number, and myenteric ChAT, nNOS, TH, and GFAP expression were unchanged compared to controls.
Chronic central NPS treatment reversed 6-OHDA-induced impairment of motor performance and solid gastric emptying in the PD rat model.
Chronic NPS treatment prevented the loss of dopaminergic (TH-positive) neurons in the substantia nigra induced by 6-OHDA.
Chronic NPS treatment prevented the loss of cholinergic (ChAT-positive) neurons in the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus induced by 6-OHDA.
NPS attenuated 6-OHDA-induced phosphorylated alpha-synuclein (Ser129) pathology in both the substantia nigra and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus.
NPSR protein was detected in gastro-projecting neurons within the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, suggesting a direct site of action for NPS on vagal outflow to the stomach.

A genome-wide association meta-analysis linked AHR to stool frequency, a trait often disrupted in disorders of gut-brain interaction, and microbiota-derived tryptophan ligand deficiency for AHR was proposed to contribute to IBS.

Enteric neuron-specific deletion of Ahr reduced colonic peristaltic activity similarly to microbiota depletion, while supplementing Ahr ligands restored motility, suggesting Ahr acts as a luminal biosensor in enteric neurons.
Alterations in enterochromaffin cells, serotonin-producing enteroendocrine cells, have been observed in IBS patients alongside microbiota effects on the serotonergic signaling system.
The number of mast cells in close contact with enteric neurons correlates positively with the degree of abdominal pain in IBS patients, though this is not established as causal.
Mucosal supernatants from IBS patients, rich in mast cell-derived mediators, triggered enteric neuron excitability with preferential activation of submucosal plexus neurons.
Chronic exposure to mucosal mast cell-derived mediators from IBS patients stimulated enteric neuron activation and sprouting, and induced hyperexcitability of visceral and somatic pain pathways.

Single-cell mRNA sequencing and transgenic Trpv1-Cre reporter mouse studies suggest that TRPV1 expression in the gut wall, relevant to visceral hypersensitivity, is largely of extrinsic rather than intrinsic enteric neuronal origin.
Blocking histamine receptor H1 (H1R) was associated with reduced abdominal pain and visceral hypersensitivity in IBS patients.
Histamine via H1R mediated ATP-induced calcium responses in enteric glial cells, and a reduction in S100B-positive glia in the colonic mucosa of IBS patients was inversely related to abdominal pain.
Antagonizing NK2R signaling restricted the occurrence of a reactive enteric glial cell phenotype and increased neurogenic contractions, implicating EGCs in disorders of gut-brain interaction.
Inhibition of tachykinin signaling pathways is proposed as a potential therapeutic target for treating IBS patients.
Antagonizing RET signaling attenuated post-inflammatory and visceral hypersensitivity in pre-clinical IBS studies.

Blocking enteric glial connexin-43 hemichannel communication reduced M-CSF-driven macrophage activation and protected against development of visceral hypersensitivity in a chronic inflammatory mouse model.
Defective maturation and altered numbers of macrophages have been documented in IBS patients.
Increased infiltration and activation of mast cells, along with elevated histamine, proteases, miRNAs, and neurotrophins, has been documented in disorders of gut-brain interaction including IBS.

Enteric neural crest-specific inactivation of the planar cell polarity gene Celsr3 caused moderate axonal disruption in the mature ENS but profound uncoordinated motor activity resembling disorders of gut-brain interaction in mice.
Disorders of gut-brain interaction, including IBS, are projected to affect roughly 40% of people worldwide and are the leading cause of gastroenterology consultations globally.
IBD and IBS frequently co-occur, IBS-like symptoms persist in IBD patients even during remission, and both show shared mucosal immune activation and neurochemical coding alterations.
Central (intracisternal) administration of the adenosine receptor antagonist DPCPX blocked the ghrelin-induced improvement of intestinal hyperpermeability in rats.
Antagonists of dopamine, cannabinoid, or opioid receptors did not block the ghrelin-induced improvement of intestinal hyperpermeability, indicating these pathways are not involved.
Intracisternal injection of an adenosine A2B receptor agonist improved colonic hyperpermeability in rats.
Intracisternal injection of an adenosine A1 receptor agonist did not improve colonic hyperpermeability, distinguishing it from the A2B subtype.
Peripheral (non-central) injection of the adenosine A2B receptor agonist failed to improve colonic hyperpermeability, indicating the effect is centrally mediated.
Vagotomy blocked the intracisternal adenosine A2B agonist-induced improvement of colonic hyperpermeability, showing dependence on an intact vagus nerve.
Alloxazine, a specific adenosine A2B receptor antagonist, blocked the improvement of intestinal hyperpermeability induced by intracisternal ghrelin.

Alloxazine also blocked the improvement of intestinal hyperpermeability induced by central vagal stimulation with 2-deoxy-d-glucose, indicating A2B receptors act downstream in the central vagal pathway independent of ghrelin administration.

The authors conclude that central activation of adenosine A2B receptors mediates the vagal-dependent improvement of leaky gut by brain ghrelin, with potential relevance to both gastrointestinal and non-gastrointestinal diseases involving altered intestinal permeability.
In a fatigue-load rat model, plasma lactate, succinate, and branched-chain amino acids (valine, leucine, isoleucine) were increased compared with control rats.
Citrulline and hydroxyproline levels decreased in the fatigue-load rat group relative to controls, indicating altered urea cycle and proline metabolism.
Cis-aconitate and isocitrate levels significantly decreased and citrate tended to decrease in the fatigue-load rat group, indicating impaired first-half TCA cycle function.
ATP levels in the liver and muscle were significantly lower in fatigue-load rats than in control and dietary restriction groups, while ATP in cerebral cortex and erythrocytes was unchanged.

Plasma NOx, a marker of oxidative stress, was significantly increased in the fatigue-load rat group compared with control and dietary restriction groups, suggesting increased systemic oxidative stress with fatigue.
In an excess-fatigue rat model, spermine, propionylcarnitine, butyrylcarnitine, and phenylalanine were significantly down-regulated compared with control rats.
In an open-label study of 30 patients, acetyl-L-carnitine supplementation improved fatigue and cognitive function in up to 59% of ME/CFS patients.
Compounds in the choline-carnitine pathway were reported to be reduced in patients with ME/CFS compared with controls.

In a female rat stress-induced ME/CFS model (restraint, forced exercise, crowding/noise), urinary alpha-ketoglutaric acid was markedly decreased compared with control rats, indicating TCA cycle dysfunction.
Magnetic resonance spectroscopy studies found lactate to be increased in brain ventricles of ME/CFS patients, a finding associated with neuroinflammation.
Choline was found to be increased in the left basal ganglia and occipital cortex of ME/CFS patients, a potential marker of glial activation and blood-brain barrier permeability.

NMR-based metabolomics of urine and serum in ME/CFS patients showed a glycolytic anomaly with reduced pyruvate/acetyl-CoA utilization in the TCA cycle, accumulation of aspartate via amino acid transamination, and increased creatinine production.

Broad-spectrum metabolomics has characterized ME/CFS as a hypometabolic response to environmental stress that traces to mitochondrial dysfunction, with reported decline in energy metabolism across multiple studies.

Taurine and hypotaurine metabolism, a central compound of lipid metabolism and bile acid biosynthesis, was reported to be dysregulated in ME/CFS patients, with decreased concentrations reflecting broader metabolic pathway effects.
A metabolomics study of immune and nervous system function in ME/CFS found decreased acyl-cholines and steroids, including cortisol, cortisone, and corticosterone, compared with healthy subjects.
Higher plasma levels of CCL11, CXCL10, IL-7, TNF-alpha, and TGF-beta-1 were significantly associated with more impaired cognitive processing and greater musculoskeletal pain in ME/CFS.

CE-TOFMS plasma metabolomics comparing ME/CFS patients and healthy subjects (study 1) found differences in pyruvate, citrate/isocitrate (TCA cycle) and ornithine/citrulline (urea cycle), with SVM-feature selection identifying these four metabolites as most useful for distinguishing patients from healthy individuals: pyruvate and ornithine were increased while isocitrate and citrulline were decreased in patients.

The metabolite ratios pyruvate/isocitrate and ornithine/citrulline were significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than healthy subjects in both a training (study 1) and validation (study 2) cohort, and a combined multivariate model of these ratios distinguished patients from healthy subjects with an AUC of 0.801 in study 1 and 0.750 in study 2.
Positron emission tomography (PET) detected neuroinflammation in widespread brain regions of ME/CFS patients, which was associated with the severity of specific neuropsychological symptoms.
Endothelial dysfunction is proposed as a pathological mechanism linking ME/CFS to angina and other coronary diseases, and correlates with disease severity.

A 23-year-old woman met Fukuda, Canadian Consensus, and Institute of Medicine criteria for ME/CFS after 9 months of unrelenting fatigue, autonomic dysfunction (orthostatic disorder on head-up tilt test), neurocognitive symptoms, myalgia, joint pain, and headache, with normal ECG, chest X-ray, and blood tests.
Kampo (traditional Japanese herbal) medicine was prescribed for the patient's ME/CFS and her condition gradually improved, allowing her to recover and resume work after 9 months.

ME/CFS symptoms recurred one year after the initial recovery, with worsening fatigue, transient chest pain with light exertion, and severe impairment in activities of daily living including reduced food intake.

During the second hospitalization, the patient exhibited negative ST changes in leads II, III, and aVF on ECG, transient nocturnal/early morning chest discomfort, ST depression with tachycardia on 24-hour Holter monitoring during fatigue exacerbation, and wide ST depression with negative T waves during a two-step exercise test, despite negative troponin and near-normal echocardiography.

The patient was diagnosed with vasospastic or microvascular angina and treated with a calcium channel blocker in addition to Kampo medicines, ibudilast, vitamin C, and coenzyme Q10, resulting in slight improvement in food intake and decreased anginal symptoms.

A prior study found that a significantly larger proportion of ME/CFS patients with angina-like symptoms showed negative T-wave changes on 24-hour ECG monitoring compared to patients with similar symptoms without ME/CFS.
Heart failure accounts for approximately one-fifth of deaths among patients with ME/CFS, as cited from prior literature.
Endothelial dysfunction was reported to reduce cerebral blood flow, which correlates with ME/CFS disease severity and results in further fatigue.
ME/CFS patients had significantly lower flow-mediated dilation (a marker of large-vessel endothelial function) at baseline compared to healthy reference women.
ME/CFS patients showed significantly reduced post-occlusive reactive hyperemia, a measure of microvascular endothelial function, compared to healthy controls.

After sublingual nitroglycerin, endothelium-independent (smooth muscle) vasodilation was actually higher in ME/CFS patients than in healthy reference individuals, indicating intact smooth muscle vasodilatory capacity despite reduced endothelium-dependent FMD.
Despite 22 of 40 patients meeting criteria for clinical response after cyclophosphamide treatment, there were no statistically significant changes in FMD or PORH from baseline to 12 months.
GLM repeated-measures analyses showed no significant difference between clinical responders and non-responders to cyclophosphamide in the change of FMD or PORH from baseline to 12 months.
There was no significant correlation between FMD and PORH measurements within the patient group, either at baseline or in change from baseline to 12 months.

No statistically significant associations were found between FMD or PORH and age, BMI, ME/CFS severity (clinical or self-reported), SF-36 Physical Function, disease duration, or physical activity (steps/24h).
Serum SDMA, a risk marker for endothelial dysfunction, was significantly lower in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls.
A significant inverse correlation was found between serum SDMA levels and FMD values, linking higher SDMA to lower flow-mediated dilation.
Serum levels of arginine, homoarginine, asymmetric dimethylarginine (ADMA), and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein did not differ significantly between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
Among the 22 of 40 ME/CFS patients classified as clinical responders to cyclophosphamide, SF-36 Physical Function scores improved substantially from baseline to follow-up.
A phase III double-blind randomized controlled trial found that B-lymphocyte depletion therapy with rituximab did not produce symptomatic improvement in ME/CFS patients.
In an open-label study by Miwa, minocycline treatment improved performance status score by at least 2 points within 6 weeks in 27% of ME/CFS subjects.
38% of subjects in the minocycline trial discontinued treatment due to side effects such as nausea and vertigo, raising concerns about dosing appropriateness.
Minocycline is reported to attenuate microglial activation and exert anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, and neuroprotective effects.
Microglial activation, indicative of neuroinflammation, has been identified in the brains of ME/CFS patients.
ME/CFS patients used significantly less problem-focused coping strategies compared to patients with other recognised chronic diseases during COVID-19 containment.
ME/CFS patients used significantly less seek-social-support coping strategies compared to patients with other recognised chronic diseases during COVID-19 containment.
ME/CFS patients showed similar use of emotion-focused coping strategies compared to patients with other recognised chronic diseases.
Brain fog symptoms in long-COVID syndrome closely resemble those seen in chemotherapy-related cognitive impairment (chemofog/chemobrain), ME/CFS, and MCAS.

The authors propose that brain fog pathogenesis may involve neuroinflammation in which mast cells, stimulated by pathogenic and stress stimuli, release mediators that activate microglia and cause hypothalamic inflammation.
A phytosomal formulation of the flavonoid luteolin (in olive pomace oil) is proposed as a potential agent to mitigate the mast cell/microglia-driven neuroinflammatory processes underlying brain fog.
ME/CFS patients in all three countries reported a statistically significant decline in self-rated quality of life comparing the year before illness onset to the most recent year.

Pre-illness quality of life was significantly higher in Italy and lowest in Latvia, while during illness Latvian patients reported significantly higher quality of life than Italian or UK patients, indicating the smallest QoL decline occurred in Latvia and the largest in Italy.
Within the Italian cohort, having more than 10 symptoms and being treated with more than 5 treatments was associated with a large (>50 point) reduction in self-reported quality of life.
Italian respondents reported significantly more investigations, symptoms, and treatments than Latvian or UK respondents, with Latvians reporting the fewest and UK intermediate.
UK respondents were significantly more likely than Italian or Latvian respondents to report that their symptoms fluctuated in severity.
Physiotherapy was the most widely used non-pharmacological treatment across all three countries, most commonly in Italy (41.7%), then Latvia (30.8%), and least in the UK (14.3%).
Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) use varied by country, reported by 23.5% of Italians, 33.3% of Latvians, and 7.0% of UK participants.
Perceived effectiveness of non-pharmacological treatments differed markedly by country: only 8% of Italian patients rated them effective compared with 52% of Latvians and 57.7% of UK patients.
Graded exercise therapy (GET), reported only by UK respondents, was found to be almost universally ineffective, with only one respondent rating it effective.
GPs were significantly more likely to hold primary responsibility for medical care of ME/CFS patients in Latvia than in Italy or the UK.
Non-physician healthcare professionals were involved in the care of a significantly higher proportion of UK respondents than in Italy or Latvia.
Significantly fewer Latvian respondents had family assistance with personal care compared with Italy or the UK.
Difficulty explaining illness to physicians was reported by roughly three-quarters of Italian and UK respondents, but only about a quarter of Latvian respondents, a significant difference.
Difficulty explaining the illness to family was significantly greater in Italy (nearly 75%) than in Latvia or the UK (both under 50%).
Difficulty explaining the illness to friends was reported by about a quarter of Latvian respondents, two-thirds of British, and over four-fifths of Italian respondents, a significant difference.

In all three countries, ME/CFS patients' household incomes were substantially lower than national averages, with only 44.1% of Italian and 54.6% of UK respondents earning above €15,000, and no Latvian respondents above that threshold.

Among Latvian GPs, diagnostic coding for ME/CFS was inconsistent: 14% used Fukuda criteria, 67% used ICD-10 R53 (malaise/fatigue), 20% used G93.3 (post-viral fatigue syndrome), and 5.5% used B94.8 (sequelae of infectious disease).
70% of Latvian GPs reported that their ME/CFS patients had difficulty describing their symptoms.

All participating Latvian GPs used laboratory tests in diagnosing ME/CFS, with 38% using more than ten different tests, and 71% referring patients to specialists (62% neurology, 30% psychiatry/psychotherapy, 13% infectious disease/other).
70% of Latvian GP respondents indicated the presence of comorbidities in their ME/CFS patients.
59% of Latvian GP respondents regarded ME/CFS as an incurable disease.
Twelve included papers used 11 different definitions of recovery, reflecting substantial heterogeneity in how recovery was measured and defined in paediatric CFS/ME.
Reported recovery rates at follow-up ranged widely from 4.5% to 83% across all 12 papers, including both treatment and control arms.

Within randomised trials reporting separate arm data, children allocated to active interventions (e.g., CBT) had higher recovery rates than controls, with intervention arm rates 43-79% versus control arm rates 4.5-64%.
Recovery rates were lower when composite outcome measures (combining multiple domains) were used to define recovery compared with single unidimensional measures.
At 6-month follow-up, recovery rates ranged from 58% to 83% in intervention groups (CBT or psychoeducation) compared with 8% to 31% in children receiving usual care or no intervention.
At 12-month follow-up, one study found a recovery rate of 64% in those receiving CBT compared with 8% in those receiving usual care, with recovery rates stable between 6 and 12 months in both arms.
In one RCT with a psychoeducation control arm, recovery rates were similar between CBT (59%) and psychoeducation (65%).
School attendance and change in fatigue were the two most commonly used outcome measures to define recovery, each incorporated in seven of nine papers using multiple unidimensional outcomes.
No included studies specifically explored recovery outcomes in children under 12 (or under 10) years old, so the review could not determine whether recovery rates differ by age group.

Four studies excluded participants with comorbid psychiatric conditions, potentially limiting the applicability of recovery findings given the high prevalence of comorbid mental health disorders in paediatric CFS/ME.

Recovery rates reported in this contemporary review (across composite and single measures) are broadly consistent with a 1997 systematic review reporting 54%-94% recovery/good improvement at 13-72 months, though that earlier review used only patient/parent-reported outcomes and included both adult and paediatric populations.
The majority of participants across included studies were female, with the proportion female ranging from 63% to 90% across papers.
Same-day chromium-51 release assay (CRCA) on whole blood correlated well with next-day CRCA performed on PBMCs isolated from shipped/stored samples.
Next-day CRCA results were compromised when using whole blood or frozen (cryopreserved) PBMCs, indicating these processing/shipping conditions degrade assay reliability.
Next-day Flow Cytometry Cytotoxicity Assay (FCCA) in PBMCs correlated strongly with same-day CRCA in PBMCs.
Next-day FCCA in PBMCs also correlated with next-day CRCA in PBMCs.
CD107a surface expression (an indirect surrogate marker of NK degranulation) induced by PMA and ionomycin did not correlate with the direct cytotoxicity measures (CRCA/FCCA).

NK function can be reliably measured in PBMCs isolated after overnight shipping/storage at ambient temperature, with CRCA and FCCA results on this sample type well correlated, suggesting feasibility for standardized multi-site testing including for ME/CFS biomarker research.

Intracerebroventricular injection of TGF-β1 in mice significantly reduced immobility duration in the forced swimming test compared with sham-injected mice, interpreted by the authors as depressive-like behavior.
TGF-β1-injected mice spent more time in the dark (closed) compartment in the elevated plus maze test compared with sham mice, indicating anxiety-like behavior.
TGF-β1-injected mice showed decreased locomotor activity (zone transitions) in the open field test compared with sham, but this difference was not statistically significant.
Mice injected with TGF-β1 showed decreased latency time to fall on the rotarod test compared with sham mice, indicating fatigue-like behavior.
TGF-β1 injection greatly reduced latency time to escape from the light box in the passive avoidance test, indicating impaired learning and memory.
TGF-β1-injected mice showed increased pain sensitivity (higher pain score) in the von Frey test compared with sham mice, indicating hypersensitivity/allodynia.
Serum LDH, a marker commonly elevated in chronic fatigue syndrome, was significantly increased in TGF-β1-injected mice compared with sham mice.
Serum CK, a marker commonly elevated in chronic fatigue syndrome, was significantly increased in TGF-β1-injected mice compared with sham mice.
TGF-β1 injection significantly reduced tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression in the ventral tegmental area of mouse brain, and altered its subcellular distribution to be concentrated in the cytoplasm.
TGF-β1 injection decreased dopamine levels in the striatum of mice as shown by immunofluorescence, suggesting suppression of dopamine production/secretion underlies fatigue-like behaviors.
TGF-β treatment of SH-SY5Y dopaminergic neuroblastoma cells reduced TH protein expression as measured by Western blot.
TGF-β treatment of SH-SY5Y cells reduced TH mRNA expression in a concentration-dependent manner as measured by real-time PCR.
A prior case-control study found that CFS patients had significantly higher serum TGF-β levels than healthy controls.
A cross-sectional study of 192 ME/CFS patients and 392 healthy controls found 17 cytokines elevated in patients, with TGF-β being the only one completely (consistently) elevated among them.
A meta-analysis demonstrated that TGF-β, IL-2, and IL-4 were markedly elevated in CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
A prior study reported that tyrosine, a dopamine precursor, was low in CFS patients compared with controls.
A prior study reported suppressed activation of the basal ganglia, including impaired function of the right caudate and right globus pallidus (dopamine-rich regions), in CFS patients.
In an adrenalectomy mouse model of CFS, TGF-β levels were increased in serum and in brain regions including the prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, hypothalamus, and raphe nuclei.

In vitro RRV-ADE infection of macrophages disrupted expression of TNF, NOS2, IFN-β and IP-10, associated with temporary ablation of the STAT-1, IRF-1 and NF-κB transcriptional complexes concurrent with enhanced viral growth.
Alongside downregulation of proinflammatory/antiviral genes, IL-10 and the transcription factor Sp1 expression were significantly increased following RRV-ADE infection.
Similar to RRV, dengue virus (DEN) and arterivirus PRRSV showed post-ADE suppression of IL-12 and IFN-γ with altered STAT/IRF transcription factors, while IL-10 was unaffected or increased.
Unlike RRV/DEN/PRRSV, SARS-CoV ADE showed abortive longer-term infection with no alteration in post-ADE mRNA expression of IFN-α/β, MCP-1, IP-10, TNF, or MIP-1.
In immortalized ex vivo lymphoblasts from ME patients, the rate of Complex V (ATP synthase) ATP synthesis was significantly reduced compared to healthy control lymphoblasts.
ME patient lymphoblasts showed a statistically significant difference in lymphocyte death rate compared to healthy controls.

ME patient lymphoblasts exhibited chronic TORC1 (TOR-Complex I) hyperactivation, suggested to be a compensatory response upregulating proteins needed for oxidative phosphorylation and mitochondrial function.
Serum Activin B, a member of the TGF superfamily, was found to be significantly different in ME patients compared to healthy volunteers.

In mouse models of disease, pharmacological inhibition of PI3K isoforms diminished the severity of inflammation, relevant to FcγRIIb-mediated ADE suppression of inflammatory pathways via PIP3-to-PIP2 conversion.
mTORC2 regulation is necessary for expression of IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs), linking TOR signaling to antiviral cytokine responses disrupted post RRV-ADE.

In Hawkes's original 1964 ADE studies, antibody-mediated enhancement produced up to 12-fold growth enhancement of Togaviruses (Getah) and Flaviviruses (Murray Valley Encephalitis, West Nile, Japanese Encephalitis) in chick embryo fibroblast cultures, specific to IgG from domestic fowl antisera.
SF-36 scores rose from 47.6 at baseline to only 57.5 at discharge and 58.5 at 3-month follow-up, remaining below the 65-point threshold previously used to identify serious disability in CFS research.

Of the 995 participants initially enrolled, 31% were lost to follow-up, and those lost had significantly worse baseline depression, work/social adjustment, and physical function than those retained, indicating non-random attrition and survivor bias.

Only 58% and 51% of the original sample completed the Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire at discharge and follow-up respectively, and only 44% and 41% completed the SF-36 at discharge and follow-up, meaning key outcome statistics were based on a substantially depleted dataset not disclosed in the Abstract.

The absence of a control group or control condition in the Adamson et al. study means the data cannot support causal inferences that CBT led to the observed improvements, despite the original authors making such causal claims.
NICE's 2020 review of 172 CBT outcome studies for CFS/ME classified all of the evidence as being of only 'low' or 'very low' quality, with none exceeding the low-quality threshold.

There was inconsistency in diagnostic criteria met by the sample: all 995 participants met the 2007 NICE CFS/ME criteria (4 months of fatigue), but only 76% met the Oxford criteria and only 52% met the CDC criteria (both requiring 6 months of fatigue), raising questions about diagnostic homogeneity and whether post-exertional malaise was present.

The study relied exclusively on subjective self-report measures (SF-36, Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire, and generic scales) and included no objective outcome indicators such as walk tests, step tests, or return-to-work/disability-benefit data.
Prior intervention research found that CBT-based therapies self-reported as producing 'improvements' had no effect whatsoever on physical endurance, fitness, or socio-economic outcomes.

Therapeutic allegiance—researchers' professional investment in a given therapy—has been shown to be a statistically significant source of investigator bias in psychotherapy trials, with allegiant researchers reporting larger effect sizes.

The originally reported 129,000-fold higher frequency of a GPBAR1 SNP in CFS patients versus Kaviar controls was reduced to a ratio of 0.8 when compared to properly matched 23andMe controls, reversing the apparent association.

One of two CYP2D6 SNPs flagged as CFS-predisposing showed more than a third erroneous 23andMe base calls, indicating the original reported association likely reflects a genotyping artifact rather than a true CFS risk allele.

When the 50 originally reported top CFS-associated SNPs were recalculated using matched 23andMe control data (or ALFA where unavailable), only 11 (22%) still exceeded the original study's ratio-of-2 threshold for note-worthiness.

Of the 11 SNPs that still met the ratio-of-2 criterion after recalculation, eight had very few (17 to 0) 23andMe control samples versus a median of nearly 3,000 elsewhere, so these could not actually be shown to have higher CFS prevalence.

The EFCAB4B SNP, involved in calcium ion channel function, remained one of only three SNPs (of the original 50) with an allele frequency ratio of about 2.0 in CFS patients versus a comparable 23andMe control.
The MORN2 SNP, related to cell differentiation, remained one of three SNPs with a ratio of about 2.0 in CFS patients versus matched 23andMe controls after reanalysis.
The LINC01171 SNP, a long non-coding RNA transcript, remained one of three SNPs with a ratio of about 2.0 in CFS patients versus matched 23andMe controls after reanalysis.

Comparing the three control datasets, 29 of 48 SNPs showed 23andMe and ALFA control frequencies in good agreement with each other but substantially higher than Kaviar, indicating a systematic Kaviar-related underestimation error (Type A).

For 8 of 48 SNPs, 23andMe control frequencies were higher than both ALFA and Kaviar (which agreed with each other), pointing to a 23andMe genotyping error (Type B) that further explains the original study's inflated ratios.

Excluding erroneous genes and low-sample SNPs, allele frequencies from 23andMe and ALFA control datasets correlated well (r=0.93), supporting general reliability of 23andMe data outside identified error sites.

Alongside GPBAR1 and CYP2D6, the genes PLA2G4D, CYP2A6, and DDX5 showed 23andMe genotyping errors also present at high frequency in the 23andMe control population itself, undermining their originally reported CFS association.
Patients with peptic ulcer disease had a significantly higher incidence of and adjusted risk for developing chronic fatigue syndrome compared to matched non-PUD patients.
The association between PUD and subsequent CFS risk was stronger in women than in men.
The CFS incidence density increased with age in both PUD and non-PUD cohorts, with PUD patients showing higher risk than non-PUD patients across all age groups.
PUD patients without any of the studied comorbidities still had a significantly elevated risk of CFS, as did those with comorbidities, though the magnitude differed.
Patients with only obesity as a comorbidity showed a markedly elevated risk of CFS compared to non-PUD patients without comorbidities, among joint-effect analyses.
Patients with only renal disease as a comorbidity showed elevated risk of CFS in joint-effect analyses.
Among PUD patients, having two or more comorbidities was associated with a higher CFS risk than having only one comorbidity, showing a dose-response pattern.
The authors propose that abnormal HPA axis activity, including hypocortisolemia and blunted ACTH/cortisol responses, is a possible shared mechanism linking PUD and subsequent CFS.
The authors propose that Helicobacter pylori-induced gut dysbiosis and chronic systemic inflammation may mediate the pathway from PUD to increased CFS risk.

Autonomic symptom frequency and severity significantly differed between people meeting 2017 hEDS diagnostic criteria and those with hypermobility spectrum disorder, while most other symptom domains were similar.
Fewer than 20% of hEDS GENE study participants had autoantibodies known to be associated with dysautonomia, suggesting these autoantibodies are not a major driver of symptoms in most participants.

People with hypermobility (hEDS/HSD) report a broad symptom burden concentrated in fatigue, kinesiophobia, gastrointestinal, and autonomic domains, associated with significantly reduced health-related quality of life.
Use of custom finger orthoses significantly reduced the time required to complete the targeted Box and Block Test with the dominant hand, with a large effect size.
Finger orthoses also significantly reduced time to complete the targeted Box and Block Test with the non-dominant hand, though with a moderate rather than large effect size.
Time to complete a handwriting test was significantly shorter when participants wore their finger orthoses, with a large effect size.
Picking-up-coins test performance with the dominant hand was significantly faster when using finger orthoses, with a large effect size, consistent with the other two tests.
No significant difference in time to complete the picking-up-coins test with the non-dominant hand was found between orthosis and no-orthosis conditions.

Cortical (DLPFC) oxygenated haemoglobin activity measured by fNIRS did not differ significantly between orthosis and no-orthosis conditions during the tBBT and writing tests, despite improved functional performance.

Right DLPFC cortical activity (OxyHb) was significantly reduced when participants used finger orthoses during the picking-up-coins test with the dominant hand, the only test showing a measurable cognitive load benefit.

A significant negative correlation was found between time to complete the coin test with the non-dominant hand and right DLPFC cortical activity, meaning slower performance was associated with lower cortical activation.
All participants with JHS/hEDS/cEDS reported pain both at rest and, more severely, during repetitive hand tasks.
Six of the 14 participants had taken early retirement due to disability related to their hypermobility disorder.

Whole exome sequencing identified a heterozygous COL5A2 c.1977G>A synonymous mutation in the patient that was absent in both unaffected parents, consistent with a de novo causative variant for classical EDS.

RT-PCR and sequencing of COL5A2 mRNA from patient skin confirmed that the synonymous c.1977G>A mutation abolishes the exon 29 donor splice site, producing a transcript with in-frame skipping of exon 29 (18 amino acid deletion, p.Gly642_Pro659del).

The patient presented with skin hyperextensibility, widened atrophic (papyraceous) scars, extreme joint hypermobility (Beighton score 9/9), easy bruising, and scoliosis, meeting the main diagnostic criteria for classical EDS.

Transmission electron microscopy of patient skin revealed collagen bundles composed of fibrils of variable diameter that were loosely packed, with thickened rope-like longitudinal fibrils, in contrast to the regularly and tightly organized bundles of normal skin.

Hematoxylin and eosin staining of patient skin showed reticular dermis filled with deep-staining 'cloudy' masses of collagen and connective tissue that was less closely packed than normal, appearing to disintegrate.

Despite more than 200 distinct pathogenic mutations described in COL5A1/COL5A2 causing classical EDS, only one pathogenic synonymous COL5A2 variant (c.1977G>A) had previously been reported, underscoring the rarity of recognized synonymous causative mutations.

Compared with the previously reported 21-year-old cEDS patient carrying the identical COL5A2 c.1977G>A mutation (Ritelli et al., 2013), the current pediatric patient shared molluscoid pseudotumor and distinctive facial features (epicanthus, strabismus, anteverted nostrils) but lacked additional skeletal abnormalities, chronic articular pain, and chronic fatigue reported in the older patient, possibly reflecting his younger age.

The authors propose that the in-frame exon-skipping mutant α2(V) chain likely incorporates into collagen molecules and interferes with type V collagen heterotrimer formation, potentially explaining the growth of thicker, abnormal collagen fibrils observed by electron microscopy.
The paper describes the histopathological characteristics of molluscoid pseudotumours, a skin lesion seen in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Naal et al. found the prevalence of generalized joint hypermobility to be 33% in a cohort of 55 patients with femoroacetabular impingement syndrome compared to 3% in the normal adult population.
The combined incidence of hypermobility spectrum disorder and hypermobile EDS is estimated at 10 per 5,000 individuals in the general population.
Monozygotic twins show higher concordance rates of joint hypermobility than dizygotic twins, suggesting a strong multifactorial genetic component.
New genes coding for LZTS1 have recently been associated with the hEDS phenotype.
Heterozygous TNXB deficiency has been associated with the hEDS phenotype but accounts for only a small percentage of cases.
A genetic mutation seen in a family with hEDS overlaps with a mutation typically causing vascular EDS, resulting in intracellular retention of type III collagen.
A validated five-point screening questionnaire developed by Hakim and Grahame demonstrated 84% sensitivity and 85% specificity for identifying hypermobility.
A Beighton score greater than 4 out of 9 points indicates the presence of joint hypermobility.
Charbonnier et al. found via MRI that significant subluxation of the femoral head occurred at extremes of motion in ballet dancers and directly correlated with impingement.
Wassilew et al. found high rates of posterior femoral head subluxation in positions associated with impingement, supporting the link between hypermobility, impingement, and instability.
In a cadaveric study, hip capsular laxity caused increased joint rotations, femoral head translations, and abnormal femoral head movement leading to microinstability.
Devitt et al. demonstrated that in patients undergoing hip arthroscopy for FAIS, generalized joint hypermobility was predictive of a thinner hip capsule (<10 mm) compared to patients without GJH.

A cadaveric biomechanical study by Waterman et al. showed that capsular plication (T-capsulotomy) and capsular shift (interportal capsulotomy) significantly reduced intra-articular hip volume compared to the native hip.
In a systematic review, ligamentous laxity was cited as a possible risk factor for dislocation following hip arthroscopy, present in 11.1% of dislocation cases.

Kalisvaart and Safran examined 32 patients with hip instability treated with capsular plication and found significant improvements in modified Harris Hip Score and iHOT score at a minimum of 12 months, with 9 of 11 collegiate/professional athletes returning to sport.

Larson et al. reported significant improvements in mHHS, SF-12, and VAS pain score at a mean of 45 months in 16 hips with hEDS treated with meticulous capsular plication, with no iatrogenic dislocations.
Stone et al. compared outcomes of female patients with and without GJH and found no significant difference in postoperative range of motion, pain, and functional outcomes at 2-year follow-up.

Ukwuani et al. examined return to sport in dancers following hip arthroscopy (33% with GJH) and found hypermobility did not affect 2-year postoperative functional outcome scores or return to dancing activity.

Maldonado et al. performed a matched cohort analysis and found no significant difference in mHHS, Non-arthritic Hip Score, HOS-SSS, and VAS pain at 2-year follow-up between patients with ligamentous laxity and those without.
In a cohort of 63 competitive dancers with hip pathology and hypermobility, hip arthroscopy produced significant improvement in mHHS and HOOS scores at 3-year follow-up, with 84% returning to sport.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome can present with life-threatening surgical complications, including total abdominal wound dehiscence and multiple enterocutaneous fistulas.

IV allogeneic mesenchymal stromal cells combined with high-dose vitamin C was trialed in a patient with EDSv abdominal wound dehiscence and led to near-complete wound healing with a 94% reduction in wound bed size.
High-dose IV vitamin C was proposed and trialed alongside MSCs as a therapy for complex wounds in EDSv, discussed in relation to collagen synthesis deficits underlying the disorder.
Following the combined MSC and vitamin C treatment, maturation of the patient's enterocutaneous fistulas also occurred.
A 12-year-old boy with no relevant medical history presented with acute dissection and rupture of the thoracoabdominal aorta, treated with open surgical repair.

In pediatric aortic dissection, connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome are commonly implicated, though up to 22% of cases have no identifiable predisposing condition.
Preoperative VAS pain scores did not differ significantly between the OFA-plus and OP groups prior to surgery.
Opioid-free anesthesia plus multimodal lidocaine/ketamine/dexmedetomidine infusion (OFA-plus) reduced postoperative day-1 VAS pain scores by up to 32% compared to opioid-based anesthesia (OP).
VAS pain scores remained significantly lower in the OFA-plus group than the OP group at hospital discharge.
There was no significant difference in length of hospital stay between the OFA-plus and OP groups.
Fewer OFA-plus patients required methadone rescue for breakthrough pain compared to the OP group, and required doses were lower.
During the first postoperative day, sufentanil requirements in the OFA-plus group were lower than equivalent morphine requirements in the OP group.
No significant differences were found between groups in equivalent opioid (sufentanil/morphine) doses on postoperative days 2, 4, and 6.
OFA-plus was associated with reduced postoperative paralytic ileus and nausea/vomiting compared to opioid-based anesthesia.
Constipation incidence was similar between the OFA-plus and OP groups.
Anxiolytic requirements during hospitalization were substantially reduced in the OFA-plus group compared to the OP group.
17.4% (n=4) of OFA-plus group patients experienced visual hallucinations, likely attributable to ketamine, requiring temporary suspension/dose reduction and haloperidol in two patients.
60.9% of OFA-plus patients showed reduced opioid requirements at hospital discharge relative to preoperative levels, whereas 63.2% of OP patients showed increased requirements.

The paper cites literature suggesting that germline duplications/triplications of TPSAB1 encoding alpha-tryptase raise basal serum tryptase and may underlie opioid intolerance and the co-occurrence of MCAS, POTS, and EDS-HT/JHS.

The paper describes a proposed mechanism whereby cranio-cervical instability causes traumatic axonal deformation, triggering abnormal Na+ influx via mechanosensitive channels, subsequent Ca2+ influx via voltage-gated channels, glutamatergic pathway upregulation, chronic neuroinflammation, and apoptosis, underlying Cervical Medullary Syndrome.
MCAS and POTS are frequently comorbid with EDS-HT/JHS, and a thorough preoperative history is recommended to avoid opioid triggers of mast cell activation.
Despite opioid use in both groups throughout hospitalization, no adverse events associated with MCAS were observed.

The authors note that low-dose ketamine's antidepressant effects are described as better in young women/adolescent females, with lower incidence of psychomimetic adverse effects than in men, which may explain the hallucination pattern observed in this predominantly female cohort.
Preoperative depression or anxiety has been associated with greater likelihood of adverse outcomes and increased opioid consumption in patients undergoing cervical spine surgery.
EDS patients undergoing shoulder arthroplasty showed significant improvement in VAS pain score from 6.5 preoperatively to 1.7 postoperatively.
EDS patients showed significant improvement in shoulder elevation range of motion from 96° preoperatively to 138° postoperatively after shoulder arthroplasty.
External rotation improved from 36° to 57° in EDS patients after shoulder arthroplasty, but this change did not reach statistical significance.

Shoulder arthroplasty produced similar postoperative pain, range of motion, complications, and reoperation rates in EDS patients compared to matched non-EDS controls undergoing arthroplasty for primary osteoarthritis or cuff tear arthropathy.

Despite lack of statistical significance versus controls, EDS patients undergoing shoulder arthroplasty had a relatively high absolute complication rate of 30% (3 of 10 patients), including instability and acromial fracture.
No shoulder in the EDS cohort required reoperation despite occurrence of complications.
Skin punch biopsy with PGP 9.5 immunolabeling to measure intraepidermal nerve fiber density has a sensitivity up to 94% and specificity up to 97% for diagnosing small fiber neuropathy.
Normative immunofluorescence data show IENFD 5th-percentile cutoff decreases by 0.54 fibers/mm per decade of age.
Normative IENFD data show females have a 1.0 fiber/mm greater 5th-percentile cutoff than males, indicating a sex difference in normal nerve fiber density.
Biopsy site affects IENFD normative values, with calf biopsies showing a 3.4 fibers/mm lower 5th-percentile cutoff compared to the lateral distal lower leg.
