QST combining warm and cold detection thresholds at the feet using both limit and level methods achieved 85.1% sensitivity and 80.9% specificity for diagnosing SFN.
Prior studies have found 30-76% of patients diagnosed with fibromyalgia have small fiber neuropathy as determined by IENFD from skin punch biopsy.
A systematic review and meta-analysis found the pooled prevalence of small fiber neuropathy in fibromyalgia patients to be 49%.
The extent of small fiber pathology in fibromyalgia may be related to symptom severity, suggesting a dose-response relationship between nerve fiber loss and disease severity.

In fibromyalgia patients, 62.4% of those meeting FM diagnostic criteria and 21% of those with FM-like symptoms not meeting criteria reported severe neuropathic pain, yet only 1.9% had received skin punch biopsies and 13.2% received anti-neuropathic pain medications.

Genome-wide association studies identified SLC64A4 (as stated), TRPV2, MYT1L, and NRXN3 as genes potentially associated with fibromyalgia susceptibility, which may be responsible for up to 50% of disease susceptibility.
Fibromyalgia is characterized by a hypomethylated DNA pattern in genes implicated in stress response, DNA repair, autonomic system response, and subcortical neuronal abnormalities.
Fibromyalgia affects approximately 2-5% of the adult US population, with a female to male ratio of 2.3:1 per ACR 2010 modified guidelines.
Fibromyalgia remains undiagnosed in as many as 3 out of 4 people with the condition, with an average of 5 years between symptom onset and diagnosis.

Autonomic dysfunction in fibromyalgia commonly includes irritable bowel symptoms and orthostatic intolerance presenting as dizziness, lightheadedness, palpitations, muscle weakness, fatigue and headache, typically without orthostatic hypotension.

SFN evaluation is proposed to guide FM subclassification, since some FM patients found to have SFN may have an alternative underlying cause (e.g., diabetes, autoimmune disease) that requires distinct management, and it has been suggested that FM may represent a spectrum of centrally and/or peripherally mediated disease processes.
Patients with migraine with aura had a higher rate of current smoking compared with migraine-free controls.
Thyroid disease was more prevalent among patients with migraine than among controls.
Depression was more prevalent among patients with migraine than among controls.
Fibromyalgia was more prevalent among patients with migraine than among migraine-free controls.
Chronic migraine was associated with a greater number of significant comorbidities than episodic migraine.
Migraine with aura was associated with a greater number of significant comorbidities than migraine without aura.
Female sex among migraine patients was associated with a greater number of significant comorbidities than male sex.

At steady state, WT BALB/c mice showed antigen passages restricted to goblet cells (GAPs), whereas Il4raF709 mice with enhanced IL-4Rα signaling exhibited both goblet and non-goblet cell antigen passages (SAPs).

Carbachol (CCh) treatment significantly increased goblet-cell antigen passage (GAP) frequency in WT BALB/c mice and induced a marked increase in both WGA+ and WGA- antigen passages (SAPs) in Il4raF709 mice.

Total CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the small intestine lamina propria were significantly increased in Il4raF709 mice compared to WT BALB/c mice at steady state, while Th2, ILC2, Treg, γδ T cell, dendritic cell, and mast cell frequencies were unaltered.

Systemic antigen challenge of CCh-treated Il4raF709 mice previously exposed orally to egg induced a shock response (hypothermia) in 55% of mice compared to 0% of saline-treated mice, indicating oral antigen exposure with SAP activation predisposes to sensitization.

A strong negative correlation was observed between antigen-specific IgE and body temperature change (shock response), and a positive correlation between antigen-specific IgE and hemoconcentration, evidence of hypovolemic shock in Il4raF709 mice.
Serum MCPT-1, a marker of mast cell activation, was positively correlated with antigen-specific IgE in Il4raF709 mice, demonstrating IgE-mast cell activation following systemic allergen challenge.
Thermoneutral (Tn) housing significantly decreased systemic corticosterone levels in WT BALB/c mice compared to standard temperature (Ts) housing.
Thermoneutral housing increased systemic IL-4 (1.2-fold) and IL-13 (2-fold) levels in WT C57BL/6 mice compared to standard housing.
Serum IL-4 levels were significantly increased in Tn-housed compared to Ts-housed Il4raF709 mice.

Small intestine lamina propria Th2, ILC2, and Treg cell numbers were not significantly different between Ts- and Tn-housed Il4raF709 mice, indicating housing temperature has minimal effect on the steady-state Type-2 immune compartment.
SI epithelial Il25 mRNA levels were similar between Ts- and Tn-housed Il4raF709 mice, suggesting housing temperature has minimal impact on the pro-Type-2 immune phenotype at steady state.
Overall fecal microbiome community composition (16S rRNA V4 amplicon sequencing) showed no significant separation between Ts- and Tn-housed Il4raF709 mice.
Relative abundance of OTU0116 (Clostridium_XIVa) was significantly reduced in Tn-housed compared to Ts-housed Il4raF709 mice.

Under thermoneutral conditions, CCh treatment of Il4raF709 mice led to a ~10-fold increase in crypt SAP frequency, indicating Tn housing shifts the antigen passage landscape from villus toward crypt without increasing overall SAP frequency.

CCh-treated Il4raF709 mice housed under thermoneutral conditions exhibited significantly higher egg-specific IgE and IgG1 than saline-treated Tn-housed Il4raF709 mice, with greater than 80% exhibiting systemic shock upon challenge, compared to 55% under standard housing.

CCh-treated Il4raF709 mice housed under thermoneutral conditions showed increased small intestinal mast cell frequency and mucosal mast cell activation (elevated serum MCPT-1) 8 weeks after sensitization following oral antigen challenge.

WT BALB/c mice housed under thermoneutral conditions developed both goblet (WGA+) and non-goblet (WGA-) antigen passages (SAPs) at steady state, present in both villus and crypt, in contrast to the goblet-only GAPs seen under standard housing.

Repeated oral egg exposure with CCh treatment in thermoneutral-housed WT BALB/c mice induced significantly higher egg-specific IgG1 and IgE, increased hemoconcentration, and increased serum MCPT-1 following systemic challenge compared to saline-treated Tn-housed WT mice, demonstrating adjuvant-free sensitization without genetic manipulation.

In a retrospective cohort of 1,620 hospitalized COVID-19 patients, propensity-matched famotidine users had a significantly reduced risk of death or intubation and of death alone compared to non-users.
Several subsequent retrospective studies (Cheung, Shoaibi, Yeramaneni) found no significant effect of famotidine on COVID-19 outcomes, contrasting with the initial Freedberg report.
Mather et al. reported protective odds ratios for famotidine similar to the original Freedberg study, with reduced odds of death and death or intubation.
Famotidine at 1-100 µM did not significantly reduce PLpro-mediated cleavage of ISG15 in vitro, indicating famotidine does not inhibit SARS-CoV-2 PLpro.
In Vero E6 cell-based assays, famotidine showed no inhibition of SARS-CoV-2 infection, whereas remdesivir and hydroxychloroquine both showed antiviral activity.
Radioligand competition binding assays showed famotidine had no detectable binding to sigma-1 or sigma-2 receptors at concentrations up to 10 µM.
Famotidine binds the H2 receptor with much higher affinity (Ki ~14 nM) than cimetidine (Ki ~586-590 nM).
Famotidine acts as a highly efficacious inverse agonist at H2, reducing basal Gs signaling activity by 75% with a potency of 33 nM.

Unlike cimetidine, famotidine acts as a partial agonist for arrestin recruitment at H2 (efficacy ~15% of histamine, EC50 105 nM), suggesting biased signaling that promotes receptor internalization and non-canonical downstream effects.
A screen of 318 human GPCRs found no reproducible agonist activity of famotidine besides at the H2 receptor, indicating specificity for H2.

Pharmacokinetic modeling shows famotidine achieves steady-state plasma concentrations 2-5 fold (oral) to >20-fold (IV) above the H2 receptor IC50 at clinically used doses, while cimetidine at standard doses achieves only a fraction of its IC50, explaining the differential clinical benefit between the two drugs.
SARS-CoV-2-infected African green monkeys showed increased mast cell infiltration in pulmonary interstitium across all lung lobes compared to naive controls, in both mild and severe pneumonia.

In a case report, a 47-year-old male with severe COVID-19 symptoms reported complete relief from chest pressure and reduced cough overnight after initiating high-dose famotidine, though fever persisted.

Photomicrographs of early-stage COVID-19 lung tissue and autopsy specimens show non-inflammatory transudative alveolar edema with preserved septal architecture, a pattern the authors interpret as consistent with histamine release from mast cells rather than typical viral inflammation.
A large autopsy study found that over 50% of patients dying of COVID-19 had pulmonary microthrombosis, a small vessel coagulopathy distinct from typical DIC.

The authors propose that mast-cell-released cytokines, proteases, histamine, and heparinase degrade the endothelial glycocalyx, potentially contributing to COVID-19-associated pulmonary microthrombosis.

H2 receptor activation by histamine inhibits neutrophil effector functions (superoxide release, PAF-induced chemotaxis, leukotriene biosynthesis) and eosinophil effector functions (peroxidase release, chemotaxis).
Famotidine pre-incubation blocks histamine-induced cAMP increase in human skin mast cells, indicating direct famotidine action on mast cell H2 receptor signaling.
SARS-CoV-2-reactive CD4+ T cells were detected in approximately 40-60% of unexposed individuals, suggesting pre-existing cross-reactive T cell immunity from prior common-cold coronavirus exposure.

IgE-mediated degranulation of rat peritoneal mast cells increases lactate export, indicating upregulated glycolysis, and the degree of glycolytic stimulation correlates positively with histamine release.
Pre-treatment of mast cells with the glycolysis inhibitor 2-deoxyglucose (2-DG) inhibited antigen-stimulated histamine release.

Mitochondrial respiration (oxygen consumption) in rat peritoneal mast cells markedly increased 15-20 minutes post IgE-mediated activation, with a greater increase in glucose-free media, suggesting compensatory upregulation of oxidative phosphorylation when glycolysis is unavailable.

ATP levels correlated positively with histamine release, but separately inhibiting glycolysis (2-DG) or respiration (oligomycin) did not significantly change ATP production despite inhibiting histamine release, suggesting pathway intermediates rather than ATP alone drive activation.

Long-term culture of murine bone-marrow derived mast cells (BMMCs) in high glucose increased IgE-mediated degranulation (β-hexosaminidase) and late-phase mediator release (LTC4, PGD2) without changes in FcεR1 surface expression or intracellular ATP.
M2-type pyruvate kinase directly binds the gamma chain of FcεR1 in an inhibitory manner in RBL-2H3 cells; activation through FcεR1 downregulates this interaction to permit degranulation.

Nitric oxide nitrates a tyrosine on aldolase A, reducing its function in human LAD2 and HMC-1 mast cell lines; this did not change ATP but increased the AMP:ATP ratio and paradoxically increased glycolysis (lactate, pyruvate).
Reduced aldolase A activity led to higher fructose-1,6-bisphosphate levels, which was shown to inhibit IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation.
Antigen-stimulated activation of RBL-2H3 and LAD2 mast cells induces translocation of mitochondria from perinuclear regions to exocytosis sites during both early and late phase activation.

IgE-mediated degranulation significantly increased mitochondrial respiration in a STAT3-dependent manner across RBL-2H3, LAD2, and BMMC cell lines; blocking mitochondrial STAT3 phosphorylation or OXPHOS-derived ATP inhibited degranulation.

Inhibiting pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) reduced IgE-mediated degranulation and TNFa/IL-6 secretion in RBL-2H3 and BMMCs, and resulted in lower histamine levels in vivo in allergen-sensitized mouse lungs.
Overexpression of the mitochondrial transcription factor MITF decreased PDH function, leading to higher pyruvate levels, lower oxygen consumption, and lower ATP production.
Non-IgE mediated degranulation induced by compound 48/80 significantly upregulates the pentose phosphate pathway by up to 80%, potentially for post-exocytosis regenerative purposes.

IL-33 stimulation increases both glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation in BMMCs; blocking glycolysis with 2-DG significantly inhibits IL-33 induced cytokine release (TNFa, IL-6, CCL2) and reduces neutrophil recruitment in vivo, an effect reversed by ATP administration.
LPS exposure suppressed cytokine production (IL-6, CCL2) in BMMCs and peritoneal mast cells, an effect potentiated by lactic acid and recreated by glycolytic inhibitors, and rescued by ATP dosing.

Co-exposure of BMMCs to extracellular adenosine and antigen induces degranulation synergistically at antigen concentrations that would otherwise produce no response, linking purinergic (non-IgE) and IgE signaling.

Quiescent hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) rely on glycolysis rather than aerobic metabolism to avoid ROS production and are commonly found in hypoxic niches, whereas increased ROS from unhealthy mitochondria forces HSCs out of quiescence into differentiation and proliferation.

When HSCs symmetrically divide into two differentiated daughter cells, the mother HSC relies on fatty acid oxidation, potentially reflecting increased cellular energy demand during commitment to differentiation.
The p38 MAPK pathway is required for cell cycle progression and differentiation of progenitor cells, utilizing glycolysis as the primary metabolic process during these developmental stages.

SCF/Kit receptor activation drives MAPK and PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling, and mTOR activation upregulates glycolytic enzyme transcription, shifting mast cell progenitor metabolism from mitochondrial respiration toward glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway to support proliferation.
Lyn-deficient mice display mast cells that are unable to proliferate, indicating a requirement for Src family kinase signaling upstream of mast cell growth.

Differentiation from bipotent basophil/mast cell progenitors to immature mast cell progenitors is accompanied by increased GATA-3, which in T-cells modulates mitochondrial biogenesis via PGC1α, suggesting a similar role in driving increased aerobic metabolism during mast cell development.

CEBPα transcription factor is increased during differentiation to immature mast cell progenitors (known to upregulate glucose and lipid metabolism in other tissues) and then decreased upon further differentiation into mature mast cells.
CRH acting through CRH-R1 on mast cells triggers histamine release, increasing vascular permeability and causing vasodilation.
Single-nucleotide polymorphisms in the CRH-R1 gene are reported to be associated with a significantly increased risk of neurodegenerative diseases.
Expression levels of CRH and its receptors are increased in patients with mastocytosis.
CRH-signal activation of mast cells leads to degranulation and release of inflammatory factors including IL-6 and TNF-alpha.
CRH-mediated mast cell activation increases cAMP and selectively induces VEGF secretion without release of tryptase, histamine, TNF-alpha, IL-6 or IL-8.
Human mast cells synthesize and secrete large amounts of CRH, suggesting autocrine regulation of mast cells via CRH and its receptors.
The CRH-R1 antagonist antalarmin alleviated mast-cell-degranulation-induced symptoms and hypothermia in a mast-cell-dependent IgE-mediated passive systemic anaphylaxis model.
Knockout of CRH-R1 on mast cells restored serum histamine, body temperature and clinical score to control levels and inhibited mast cell degranulation and intestinal permeability changes.
CRH-induced VEGF secretion from mast cells was blocked by the CRH-R1 antagonist antalarmin but not by astressin 2B, a CRH-R2 antagonist.
IL-1 or lipopolysaccharide exposure for 6 hours selectively increased CRH-R2 gene expression on mast cells, suggesting upregulation under inflammatory stimulation.
Loss of CRH-R2 function aggravates mast cell degranulation and promotes IgE-mediated anaphylaxis and stress-induced intestinal barrier dysfunction, indicating a negative regulatory role for CRH-R2.
Injection of the mast cell stabilizer sodium cromoglycate into the hypothalamus reduced CRH-induced blood-brain barrier damage.
Stress caused blood-brain barrier destruction in wild-type mice but had no effect on the BBB in mast-cell-knockout mice, indicating mast cells are required for stress-induced BBB disruption.
Psoriasis is associated with increased serum CRH-mediated mast cell activation but decreased CRH-R1 gene expression in lesioned skin, possibly due to receptor downregulation.
Colon mucosal CRH content is significantly higher in IBS patients compared with control subjects.
Administration of alpha-helical CRH, a non-selective CRH-receptor antagonist, produced higher colonic motility indices in IBS patients compared with controls after rectal stimulation.
Intestinal CRH and receptor content is positively correlated with the number of intestinal mast cells in IBS mice, suggesting mast cells as a major source of intestinal CRH.

Descending colon activity following intravenous CRH injection is significantly higher in IBS patients than in healthy controls, and CRH promotes colonic mucus secretion and mast cell protease release.
Injecting CRH into the peritoneal cavity and ventricles of mast-cell-deficient mice did not stimulate colonic electrical activity, indicating CRH's gut effects are mast-cell-dependent.
CRH and norepinephrine levels are significantly upregulated in the CSF of Alzheimer's disease patients compared with control subjects.
CRHR1 knockout mice show blocked tau phosphorylation, whereas CRHR2 knockout mice do not, suggesting CRHR1-specific involvement in Alzheimer's disease pathology.
CRHR1 signaling pathways are reported to show women as more vulnerable to Alzheimer's disease than men.
The CRHR1 antagonist R121919 decreased stress-mediated neuroinflammation, prevented cognitive damage and reduced amyloid-beta deposition in an AD mouse model.
CRH expression levels were reported to be decreased in the cerebral cortex in Parkinson's disease.
Urocortin was found to arrest the development of Parkinsonian-like features in the 6-hydroxydopamine-lesioned hemiparkinsonian rat model.
Pro-inflammatory cytokines and neuropeptides including CRH and neurotensin are significantly increased in children with autism spectrum disorder compared with non-ASD controls.
IL-6 expression levels are upregulated in the brain of patients with autism spectrum disorder.
Patients with mastocytosis show increased mast cell proliferation and activation along with upregulated serum IL-6 levels.
IL-37 is significantly increased along with pro-inflammatory IL-18 and its receptors in the amygdala and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex of children with autism spectrum disorder.
CRH-deficient mice are resistant to experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, showing decreased clinical disability and reduced brain infiltration of immune cells.

CRH-deficient mice are resistant to experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis, showing decreased clinical disability and reduced immune cell infiltration into the brain, implicating CRH in MS-related autoimmune inflammation.

Mast cell and microglial activation are increased in transgenic mouse models carrying ALS-associated mutations (TARDBP, SOD1, FUS, OPTN, ANG), accompanied by reactive astrocytosis and release of proinflammatory mediators.
Dysregulation of CRH protein levels is implicated in ALS pathogenesis, though the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.

In traumatic brain injury, mast cells directly communicate with glial cells and release neuroinflammatory mediators including IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6, CCL2, IL-8, tryptase, histamine, ROS, CRH and MMPs, contributing to secondary brain injury.

Synovium from rheumatoid arthritis patients shows a significantly increased mast cell population compared with healthy controls, with numbers increased 5- to 24-fold, and increased MC infiltration at end-stage disease.
Mast cell-deficient mice were resistant to the development or progression of rheumatoid arthritis in animal models.
The HPA axis response through CRH and its receptors is differentially modulated by CRH gene promoter polymorphisms in patients with rheumatoid arthritis.
Degranulated mast cell numbers increase more than 3-fold in multiple rheumatoid arthritis animal models.
Mast cell-derived tryptase directly triggers synovial fibroblasts via protease-activated receptor 2, resulting in degraded cartilage and bone in RA.

CRH is locally secreted in the synovial tissue and fluids of patients with osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis, and CRH and its receptors along with urocortin have been identified on mast cells from RA joints.
Stress-induced activation of mast cells via CRH is proposed to worsen or induce migraines through release of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines.
Inflammatory pathways linked to mast cells and stress are associated with chronic depression in patients with mastocytosis.
Colon mucosal CRH content is significantly higher in IBS patients compared with the control group.

Administration of alpha-helical CRH, a non-selective CRH-R antagonist, significantly stimulated the rectum and resulted in higher colonic motility indices in IBS patients compared with the control group.
The content of CRH and its receptors is positively correlated with the number of intestinal mast cells in IBS mice, suggesting mast cells may be a major source of intestinal CRH and its receptors.
Injecting CRH into the peritoneal cavity and ventricles of mast cell-deficient mice failed to stimulate colonic electrical activity, indicating CRH's intestinal effects depend on mast cells.

The mast cell stabilizer cromolyn sodium antagonized stress-induced increases in colonic mucosal permeability in mice, indicating CRH and mast cells jointly mediate stress-induced intestinal barrier dysfunction.
Pre-injection of the mast cell stabilizer sodium cromoglycate into the hypothalamus alleviated CRH-induced blood-brain barrier injury in an acute stress rat model.
Stress causes blood-brain barrier damage only in wild-type mice with mast cells present, but has no effect on the BBB in mast cell knockout mice.
Urocortin, acting via CRH-R1, arrested the development of Parkinsonian-like features in the 6-hydroxydopamine-lesioned hemiparkinsonian rat model and reduced PD-like pathology.
Expression levels of CRH were decreased in the cerebral cortex in Parkinson's disease patients.
The CRHR1 antagonist R121919 decreased stress-mediated neuroinflammation, prevented cognitive damage and reduced amyloid-β deposition in an Alzheimer's disease mouse model.

CRHR1 knockout mice exhibit blocked phosphorylation of tau (but CRHR2 knockout mice do not), suggesting a specific role for CRHR1-mediated signaling in Alzheimer's disease tau pathology, and CRHR1 signaling appears to render women more vulnerable to AD than men.
IL-37 is significantly increased along with the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-18 and its receptors in the amygdala and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex of children with autism spectrum disorder.
IL-6 expression levels are upregulated in the brain of ASD patients and serum IL-6 is linked to the autistic phenotype in mouse models.
Patients with mastocytosis show increased proliferation and activation of mast cells along with upregulated serum IL-6 levels.
Psoriasis is associated with increased serum CRH-mediated mast cell activation but decreased CRH-R1 gene expression in lesioned skin, possibly due to receptor downregulation.

Intraepithelial administration of CRH and urocortin activates CRH-R1 on human and mouse skin mast cells to promote activation and increase skin vascular permeability, an effect absent in mast cell-deficient mice or with the CRH-R1 antagonist antalarmin.

Surgical tibial fracture in rats increased brain mast cells, BBB permeability, microglial activation and neuronal apoptosis, leading to increased central inflammation and decline in learning/memory, which was prevented by an MC stabilizer injected into the lateral ventricle.

CRH and norepinephrine levels are significantly upregulated in the cerebrospinal fluid of Alzheimer's disease patients compared with control subjects, and a significant correlation exists between brain glucose metabolism and CRH levels in AD.
Serum IgE concentration was significantly higher in OVA-sensitized/challenged AR model guinea pigs than in healthy normal guinea pigs.
Fyn mRNA expression was significantly higher in nasal mucosa fibroblasts of AR model guinea pigs compared to normal guinea pigs.
SCF mRNA expression was significantly higher in AR model fibroblasts than in normal fibroblasts.
IL-10 mRNA expression was significantly lower in AR model fibroblasts than in normal fibroblasts.
Fyn protein level was significantly increased in AR model fibroblasts compared with normal fibroblasts on western blot.
STAT5 protein level was significantly decreased in AR model fibroblasts compared with normal fibroblasts.

TGF-β1 treatment (5-25 ng/ml) increased nasal mucosa fibroblast viability in a concentration- and time-dependent manner, with 25 ng/ml for 24h producing the greatest increase, while higher doses (50-100 ng/ml) at 24h decreased viability.
XGND (10-100 μg/ml) significantly increased nasal mucosa fibroblast viability after 24h treatment, with 25 μg/ml producing an optimal increase.
XGND treatment for 12h and 24h significantly decreased Fyn and SCF mRNA and significantly increased IL-10 mRNA in AR fibroblasts compared with the untreated model group.
IL-10 mRNA remained significantly elevated in the XGND group after 48h of treatment, and its upregulation was greater than in the TGF-β1 group at this time point.
XGND treatment for 12h and 24h decreased Fyn protein and increased STAT5 protein compared with the model group, similar to TGF-β1 and Rhinocort effects, but this effect was not sustained at 48h.

XGND showed no significant difference from budesonide nasal spray (Rhinocort) in its effects on Fyn, SCF, IL-10 mRNA, and Fyn/STAT5 protein expression at matched time points, suggesting a similar regulatory mechanism.

Fyn can induce phosphorylated STAT5 to localize near FcεRI in an IgE-dependent, non-IL-3/SCF-dependent manner, forming an immune complex that deposits in unactivated mast cells, and pathway activation leads to mast cell degranulation and allergic reactions, as reported in prior literature discussed by the authors.

Prior clinical studies cited by the authors reported that XGND significantly reduces serum IgE, FcεRI, TSLP, and IL-4 levels and inflammatory cell aggregation in nasal mucosa, with more stable and lasting efficacy on symptom/QoL scores compared with intranasal corticosteroids.

Prior in-vivo studies cited by the authors found that XGND significantly reduces NF-κB and NF-κB p65 mRNA/protein expression in nasal mucosa and lowers IL-5, GM-CSF, and CCL-1 concentrations in serum and nasal lavage fluid of AR guinea pigs.

Prior studies cited by the authors found that XGND reduces serum concentrations of IgE, IL-4, IL-5, LTE4, and tryptase and decreases nasal mucosa eosinophilia in AR guinea pigs and rats by downregulating the PLCE1-PKC-NF-κB signaling pathway and correcting Th1/Th2 imbalance.
Systolic and mean middle cerebral artery flow velocities were significantly higher in males than in females among healthy volunteers.

Systolic, mean, and diastolic middle cerebral artery flow velocities and peak straight sinus venous flow velocity increased with age across the lifespan, with the most pronounced increase in elderly females.

The title reports a case (or case series) describing small fiber neuropathy occurring after COVID-19 vaccination, but no further details, mechanisms, or quantitative data are provided in the available text.
Colonic mucosal GFAP (a marker of enteric glial cell activation) was increased in IBS patients compared to healthy controls.

In healthy controls, mucosal GFAP correlated with increased mast cell numbers and VPAC1-positive mast cells, and decreased VIP-positive mast cells, a pattern that appeared to help control bacterial translocation.
In IBS patients, EGC activation (GFAP) correlated with fewer mast cells and VPAC1-positive mast cells, and more VIP-positive mast cells, opposite to the pattern seen in healthy controls.
Enteric glial cell and mast cell lines showed intracellular calcium responses when exposed to each other's secreted mediators, indicating direct bidirectional signaling.
Enteric glial cell mediators prevented VIP-induced mast cell degranulation in vitro.
Mast cell mediators induced a reactive phenotype in enteric glial cells in vitro.
In vitro, mediators released by enteric glial cells prevented VIP-induced degranulation of mast cells.
Mediators released by mast cells induced a reactive phenotype in enteric glial cells in vitro.
Application of EGC mediators decreased paracellular permeability through healthy colonic biopsies mounted in Ussing chambers.
Overall, the study concludes that imbalanced communication between enteric glial cells and mast cells contributes to the pathophysiology of IBS through altered control of colonic barrier function.
TGF-β1 treatment of Graves' orbital fibroblasts significantly increased p38 phosphorylation in a time-dependent manner over 3, 6, and 9 hours compared with untreated controls.
TGF-β1 treatment similarly increased JNK phosphorylation time-dependently in Graves' orbital fibroblasts, while ERK phosphorylation was not significantly altered.
TGF-β1 treatment of Graves' orbital fibroblasts induced overexpression of CTGF, α-SMA, and fibronectin, consistent with myofibroblast transdifferentiation.
Inhibiting p38 with SB202190 did not alter TGF-β1-induced JNK phosphorylation, and inhibiting JNK with SP600125 did not affect p38 activation, indicating the two pathways act independently.

Pretreatment with the p38 inhibitor SB202190 or JNK inhibitor SP600125 (but not the ERK inhibitor PD98059) significantly reduced TGF-β1-induced expression of CTGF, α-SMA, and fibronectin in Graves' orbital fibroblasts.
TGF-β1 treatment increased protein levels of MMP-2, MMP-9, TIMP-1, and TIMP-3 in Graves' orbital fibroblasts.
Pretreatment with p38 or JNK inhibitors significantly abolished TGF-β1-induced overexpression of TIMP-1 and TIMP-3, but did not affect MMP-2 or MMP-9 protein levels.
Despite increased MMP-2/9 protein levels, TGF-β1 treatment significantly inhibited the enzymatic activities of MMP-2/-9 in Graves' orbital fibroblasts.
The TGF-β1-induced inhibition of MMP-2/-9 enzymatic activity was recovered (restored) by pretreatment with either the p38 inhibitor SB202190 or the JNK inhibitor SP600125.
In addition to activating the noncanonical p38/JNK pathway, TGF-β1 also increased Smad2/3 phosphorylation in Graves' orbital fibroblasts, suggesting concurrent canonical pathway activation.
Heterozygous TGFB2 mutations in humans are reported to cause congenital heart defects and adult aortic valve malformation, mitral valve disease, or mitral valve prolapse.
Myocardium-specific conditional knockout (cTntCre; Tgfb2 CKO) mouse embryos show significantly reduced Tgfb2 mRNA transcript expression in ventricular myocardium compared to littermate controls.

Densitometric PCR analysis of the unrecombined floxed Tgfb2 allele showed ~30-fold enrichment in non-transgenic control myocardium compared to cTntCre-positive CKO myocardium, confirming efficient Cre-mediated deletion.
Approximately 80% of myocardial Tgfb2 CKO embryos developed interventricular septal defects, including perimembranous, atrioventricular, and muscular ventricular septal defects (VSDs).
Myocardial Tgfb2 CKO embryos show significant thinning of the right ventricular myocardium compared to littermate controls, indicating a myocardial non-compaction phenotype.

Myocardial Tgfb2 CKO embryos show a trend toward smaller atrioventricular (AV) cushion size at both E12.5–13.5 and E14.5 compared to controls, but the difference did not reach statistical significance.
Periostin, a marker of cushion maturation and differentiation, is significantly reduced in AV cushions of myocardial Tgfb2 CKO embryos compared to littermate controls.
Myocardial cell proliferation (pHH3-positive nuclei) trended toward a decrease in Tgfb2 CKO myocardium compared to controls but the difference was not statistically significant.
Myocardial Tgfb2 CKO embryos show significantly reduced numbers of TUNEL-positive (apoptotic) nuclei in endocardial cushions compared to littermate controls.

Contrary to expectation, phospho-SMAD2 (a surrogate for canonical TGFβ signaling activity) was paradoxically increased in both AV cushions and ventricular myocardium of myocardial Tgfb2 CKO embryos compared to littermate controls.
The density of pSMAD2-positive nuclei correlates with severity of cardiac phenotype among CKO embryos, with the embryo showing the weakest cardiac defects having the lowest %pSMAD2-positive nuclei.

In contrast to myocardial Tgfb2 deletion, myocardial deletion of the TGFβ receptor Tgfbr2 rarely produces cardiac defects in mouse embryos, suggesting receptor-level signaling is not required cell-autonomously in the myocardium.

A prior report found that a paradoxical increase in TGFβ signaling contributes to mitral valve disease in a Marfan syndrome mouse model, paralleling the elevated pSMAD2 signaling observed in this study's Tgfb2 CKO hearts.
Mitral valve prolapse with mitral regurgitation has been observed in individuals with TGFB2 mutations (Loeys-Dietz syndrome), though less frequently than in Marfan syndrome.

Scanning electron microscopy showed that cell diameter increased progressively during the 21-day differentiation of iMSCs into PDGFRα-positive cells, from approximately 2 µm at day 9 to approximately 30 µm at day 21.
COL I gene expression was significantly higher in fibroblasts than in either iMSCs or differentiated PDGFRα-positive cells.
HAS3 gene expression was markedly increased in iMSCs and PDGFRα-positive cells compared with fibroblasts, and higher in PDGFRα-positive cells than fibroblasts but lower than iMSCs.
ALP mRNA levels were significantly higher in differentiated PDGFRα-positive cells than in iMSCs and fibroblasts, marking it as a distinguishing feature of the differentiated phenotype.
AGG gene expression was significantly higher in iMSCs than in fibroblasts and differentiated PDGFRα-positive cells.

CD44 and FSP-1 mRNA were highly expressed in fibroblasts, with inconsistent expression patterns in iMSCs and PDGFRα-positive cells; CD44 was lower in PDGFRα-positive cells than fibroblasts but higher than in iMSCs.
FSP-1 mRNA expression was lower in iMSCs than fibroblasts but significantly higher in differentiated PDGFRα-positive cells.
p53 mRNA levels were significantly higher in differentiated PDGFRα-positive cells than in fibroblasts and iMSCs.
ALP protein expression (western blot) was significantly higher in differentiated PDGFRα-positive cells than in fibroblasts and iMSCs, corroborating the mRNA data.

Flow cytometry showed PDGFRα-positive cells shared a similar CD140α (PDGFRα) surface profile with fibroblasts, while iMSCs showed significantly lower cell count and fluorescence intensity, confirming successful differentiation.
By flow cytometry, PDGFRα-positive cells exhibited significantly lower CD44 surface profile compared to fibroblasts, though higher than iMSCs.

CD34 surface marker profile was significantly higher (cell count and fluorescence intensity) in PDGFRα-positive cells compared to fibroblasts, while iMSCs differed significantly from both, challenging the classical view of iMSCs as CD34-negative.

SK3 (KCNN3) surface expression differed among fibroblasts, iMSCs, and PDGFRα-positive cells, with higher SK3-positive cell count in PDGFRα-positive cells but higher fluorescence intensity in iMSCs, an unexpected result given SK3 is considered a PDGFRα-positive cell marker.

Treatment with the NO donor SNAP (100, 500, 1000 µM) for 24 and 48 h significantly increased survival of differentiated PDGFRα-positive cells in a concentration- and duration-dependent manner, but 72 h exposure had an adverse effect on survival.

Nitrite levels, a stable NO breakdown product, increased in a concentration- and duration-dependent manner in PDGFRα-positive cells treated with SNAP compared with low baseline levels (~25 µM) in controls.

Treatment with the NO synthase inhibitor LNNA (100, 500, 1000 µM) significantly reduced PDGFRα-positive cell survival in a concentration- and duration-dependent manner at 24 and 48 h, with no further change at 72 h.
LNNA treatment for 24 h significantly decreased nitrite levels compared to control, though at 48 h (100 µM) nitrite unexpectedly increased, at about half the magnitude of the SNAP response.
Under normal glucose concentration (25 mM), nNOS gene expression was significantly higher in PDGFRα-positive cells than in iMSCs, supporting a distinct fibroblastic differentiation phenotype.

Exposure of PDGFRα-positive cells to increasing glucose concentrations (30, 50, 70, 90 mM) produced a significant, concentration-dependent increase in nNOS gene expression, whereas 25-30 mM glucose had no significant effect, mimicking hyperglycemic stress relevant to diabetic gastroparesis.
Western blot showed significantly higher nNOS protein expression in PDGFRα-positive cells exposed to 90 mM glucose compared to 30 mM glucose.

Immunostaining showed a trend toward higher nNOS expression at 90 mM versus 30 mM glucose in PDGFRα-positive cells, but this was not statistically significant, likely due to the small number of imaged cells.
Delayed gastric emptying occurs in up to 50% of patients with type 1 or type 2 diabetes, presenting as dyspepsia, gastroparesis, or remaining asymptomatic.
Functional dyspepsia and diabetic gastroparesis have been proposed as points along the same spectrum of gastric neuromuscular disorders, sharing histopathology, clinical features, and prognosis.
A prior gastrointestinal infection is a risk factor for developing irritable bowel syndrome and functional dyspepsia in about 10% of patients.
A case-control serological study found significantly higher H. pylori antibody positivity in diabetic patients (50.7%) compared to controls (38.2%).

H. pylori infection was found to be more prevalent among diabetic patients with gastroparesis, and its eradication reduced symptoms including upper abdominal pain, distention, early satiety and anorexia.
Autonomic neuropathy, interstitial cells of Cajal depletion, and reduced neuronal nitric oxide synthase expression are key pathogenetic mechanisms underlying diabetic enteropathy.
A community-based epidemiologic study found a ten-year cumulative incidence of gastroparesis of 5.2% in type 1 diabetes versus 1% in type 2 diabetes.
The severity of delayed gastric emptying correlates poorly with the severity of gastroparesis symptoms.
A prospective observational follow-up study showed baseline HbA1c and diabetes duration were independently associated with delayed gastric emptying.
A cross-sectional study of 147 type 2 diabetics confirmed correlation of diabetic gastroparesis with blood glucose levels, HbA1c, and diabetes duration.

Full-thickness stomach biopsies showed that gastroparesis and functional dyspepsia share the same histopathological changes, including reduction of interstitial cells of Cajal and anti-inflammatory CD206+ macrophages.
In a study of 32 gastroparesis patients (20 with DM), more than 60% had a positive Carnett's sign indicating somatic rather than visceral pain, and over one-third met criteria for neuropathic pain.

Diabetic patients have a higher prevalence of depression than the general population, and severe depression contributes to GI sensorimotor dysfunction and worsens gastroparesis-related quality of life.
The 13C-octanoic acid breath test shows strong correlation with gastric emptying scintigraphy in diabetic populations, offering a non-radioactive alternative for diagnosing delayed gastric emptying.
Proton pump inhibitors are effective at relieving functional dyspepsia symptoms even in the absence of gastric acid abnormalities, with efficacy independent of concomitant GERD or H. pylori status.

Metoclopramide significantly reduces symptoms of diabetic gastroparesis via central dopamine antagonism and peripheral cholinergic effect, but is limited by hyperprolactinemia and extrapyramidal side effects.
Domperidone improves gastroparesis symptoms with sustained effect and lower risk of hyperprolactinemia/extrapyramidal symptoms than metoclopramide, but carries cardiac (QT prolongation) risk.

Erythromycin significantly reduces total symptom score acutely (IV) and chronically (oral) in diabetic gastroparesis, but long-term efficacy is limited by tachyphylaxis and it carries risk of QT prolongation and ventricular arrhythmia.

In a randomized placebo-controlled trial of 34 patients with diabetic gastroparesis, prucalopride significantly reduced gastric emptying time and improved symptoms measured by the Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index.
Aprepitant, a neurokinin-1 inhibitor, increased gastric accommodation and reduced nausea and vomiting in diabetic enteropathy, but had no effect on gastric emptying.

Relamorelin, a subcutaneous ghrelin agonist, reduced symptoms and increased gastric emptying half-time in phase 2 trials, but its main side effect was worsened glycemic control with more hyperglycemia episodes and higher HbA1c.

In murine models, miR-10b regulates ICC and pancreatic β-cell development/function through the KLF11-KIT pathway; knockout of mir-10b in KIT+ cells led to diabetes and gastroparesis, while injection of miR-10b-5p mimic or Klf11 siRNA improved glucose homeostasis and gastric motility.

Acupuncture improved gastric emptying in both murine models and human studies, apparently mediated by vagal activity, and electroacupuncture was associated with reduced apoptosis and increased proliferation of interstitial cells of Cajal in mice.
Null mutations in ADAMTS2 cause dermatosparaxis EDS rather than the arthrochalasia phenotype seen with mutations abolishing its cleavage sites in type I procollagen.
Complete or partial skipping of exon six of COL1A1 or COL1A2 (which encodes the ADAMTS2 cleavage site) is the molecular basis of arthrochalasia EDS.

N-terminomic (iTRAQ-TAILS) profiling of Wt vs ADAMTS2/14-deficient mouse skin identified 437 proteins with altered N-termini attributable to ADAMTS2 and/or ADAMTS14, including 68 secreted/cell-surface proteins.
Of the 68 extracellular/cell-surface substrates identified, 40 were common to ADAMTS2 and ADAMTS14, five were ADAMTS2-specific and 21 were ADAMTS14-specific.

Coagulation factor XIIIa and mast cell protease 4 were detected as altered N-termini only in the comparison of Wt versus double ADAMTS2/ADAMTS14-deficient mice, suggesting they require combined loss of both enzymes to manifest.
The canonical ADAMTS2 cleavage site of the COL1A1 N-propeptide (S151.152Q) showed the highest P/C ratio, confirming reliability of the N-TAILS approach.
The canonical ADAMTS2 cleavage site of the COL1A2 N-propeptide (A85.86Q) showed the highest P/C ratio, confirming reliability of the N-TAILS approach.

Several additional cleavage sites beyond the canonical site were identified in the NC2 domain of COL1A1/COL1A2, indicating ADAMTS2 cleaves within a preferred region rather than at a single fixed site.

P/C ratios for type I collagen N-propeptide cleavage sites were higher in TS2−/−TS14−/− than TS2−/− mice, suggesting ADAMTS14 can exert some aminoprocollagen peptidase activity in vivo when ADAMTS2 is absent.
The main COL5A1 processing site (P435.436A) was cleaved with similar efficacy by both ADAMTS2 and ADAMTS14, revealing a new in vivo function for ADAMTS14 in type V collagen processing.
Novel cleavage sites were identified in the NC2 domain of COL5A1, including one at an A.Q site analogous to COL1A2, a location never previously reported for type V collagen.
The N-propeptide of COL5A2 can be processed by ADAMTS2 and ADAMTS14 but at a lower rate than COL1A1, COL1A2 or COL5A1.
Cleavage of the COL3A1 N-propeptide was not detected in this in vivo experiment, likely due to the corresponding peptide not being isolated for MS/MS analysis, consistent with prior in vitro results.

Contiguous 'hot spot' cleavage sites in the central COL1 triple-helical domain of Col1A1 (positions 333-337 and 827-838) and Col1A2 (988-996) were identified, revealing a previously unknown collagenase-like activity for ADAMTS2/14.

In vitro assays with purified recombinant enzymes showed ADAMTS2 and ADAMTS14 cleave within the COL1 triple helical domain mainly or only when collagen is heat-denatured/unfolded, suggesting a quality-control function degrading misfolded collagen.

Cleavage sites within the C-propeptide of COL1A1 (F1187.1188S) and COL1A2 (three sites) were identified, revealing a previously unknown C-proteinase-like activity of ADAMTS2/14 in addition to their known N-proteinase role.

Recombinant ADAMTS2 converted pro-α2(I) into pCα2 and then mature α2 chain in vitro, demonstrating a procollagen C-proteinase activity in addition to its established aminoprocollagen peptidase function.
ADAMTS14 showed only low aminoprocollagen (N-propeptide) peptidase activity on Col1A2 but more efficiently cleaved its C-propeptide, an inverse specificity compared to ADAMTS2.

Two identical cleavage sites in type XIV collagen (COL14A1) were identified for both ADAMTS2 and ADAMTS14, at positions 630 (AQQY.LEID) and 1636 (MARY.TAIL), strongly suggesting it is a true substrate.
A cleavage site in COL4A1 (G1438.1439T) was identified corresponding to the position for release of the arresten bioactive fragment, suggesting ADAMTS2/14 involvement in arresten generation.
Cleavage sites within the VWFA domains of COL6A1, COL6A2 and COL6A3 were identified, implicating ADAMTS2/14 in type VI collagen processing relevant to fibril regulation.

PCPE-1 (a BMP-1 co-factor) and three small leucine-rich proteoglycans regulating matrix assembly (biglycan, lumican, osteoglycin) were identified as potential ADAMTS2/14 substrates, based on P/C ratios >2.

Multiple immune-related proteins including immunoglobulins, complement components (C3, C4-B, factor B, factor H), macrophage migration inhibitory factor, and annexins A1/A2/A8 were identified in the ADAMTS2/14 skin degradome, implicating these proteases in immune regulation.

Recombinant ADAMTS2 and ADAMTS14 cleaved intracellular actin in human fibroblast lysates in vitro, generating a ~40 kDa fragment (both enzymes) and an additional ~34-35 kDa fragment specific to ADAMTS14.

Two identical cleavage sites in type XIV collagen (a FACIT collagen regulating fibril formation) were identified for both ADAMTS2 and ADAMTS14 in mouse skin, within the fifth fibronectin type-III domain and the third collagen-like domain.
A potential ADAMTS2/ADAMTS14 cleavage site was identified in COL4A1 at a position corresponding to release of the bioactive fragment arresten.
Potential ADAMTS2/ADAMTS14 cleavage sites were found in the VWFA domains of type VI collagen chains (COL6A1, COL6A2, COL6A3).

PCPE-1 (a BMP-1 co-factor) and the small leucine-rich proteoglycans biglycan, lumican and osteoglycin were identified as potential ADAMTS2/ADAMTS14 substrates involved in collagen matrix assembly regulation.

The ADAMTS2/ADAMTS14 skin degradome included multiple immune-related proteins (immunoglobulins, complement proteins C3/C4-B/factor B/factor H, macrophage migration inhibitory factor, and annexins A1/A2/A8), consistent with a role for these proteases in complement activation and leukocyte recruitment.

Coagulation factor XIIIa and mast cell protease 4 were detected as potential substrates only when comparing wild-type to double ADAMTS2/ADAMTS14-deficient mouse skin, suggesting a combined/redundant effect of the two proteases on these targets.

In vitro incubation of normal fibroblast lysates with recombinant ADAMTS2 generated a ~40 kDa actin cleavage product consistent with cleavage at V19.20K and/or A21.22G, confirming actin as a direct ADAMTS2/ADAMTS14 substrate by Western blot.

Incubation of fibroblast lysates with recombinant ADAMTS2 or ADAMTS14 reduced full-length vimentin bands (58 and 53 kDa) and increased lower molecular weight fragments (48, 39, 37, 32 kDa), confirming vimentin as a substrate of both enzymes.

Sequence logo analysis of all identified extracellular cleavage sites showed that ADAMTS2 and ADAMTS14 share a common preferential cleavage motif enriched in small nonpolar, amphipathic or hydrophobic residues (G, P, F, Y, A, L, M) with acidic residues favored at P2'-P4', even after excluding fibrillar collagen sites.

Actin and vimentin cleavage patterns were not different when directly comparing electrophoretic profiles of wild-type versus ADAMTS2-deficient fibroblasts, in contrast to the clear cleavage seen when recombinant enzyme was added exogenously, suggesting these cleavages may occur extracellularly or after cell death rather than intracellularly during normal fibroblast homeostasis.
Biological process enrichment of the ADAMTS2/ADAMTS14 degradome pointed to a role in lipoprotein regulation and assembly, based on cleavage of proapolipoprotein A-II and apolipoprotein A-I.

The C-propeptide of type I collagen (which can inhibit collagen synthesis when released) contains cleavage sites for ADAMTS2 and ADAMTS14 downstream of the canonical BMP1 site, raising the hypothesis that this cleavage could modulate the propeptide's feedback regulatory function on collagen synthesis.

The authors propose a novel 'quality control' function whereby ADAMTS2/ADAMTS14 degrade incorrectly folded collagen trimers within the triple helical domain, preventing their incorporation into fibrils, which could explain the irregular collagen fibril morphology in dermatosparaxis EDS.
Total serum free light chain (FLC-κ+λ) levels were significantly elevated in patients with systemic autoimmune disease compared with healthy controls.
The FLC kappa/lambda ratio did not differ between SAD patients and healthy controls, consistent with polyclonal rather than monoclonal FLC production.
Total FLC levels correlated with IgG isotype levels but not with IgA or IgM, and were independent of sex, disease duration, and age at sample collection.

The prevalence of elevated total FLC (>37 mg/L) varied by SAD subtype, ranging from 12% in rheumatoid arthritis to 30% in mixed connective tissue disease, antiphospholipid syndrome, and systemic lupus erythematosus.

Elevated total FLC in SAD patients was significantly associated with abnormal creatinemia, inflammation, proteinuria, hypertension, leucopenia, hemolytic anemia, erosive arthritis, pericarditis, worsening lung function, gangrene of the fingers, sicca syndrome, venous thrombosis, and pleural effusion.

After excluding patients with infection, cancer, or renal impairment, elevated FLC remained associated with inflammation, leucopenia, hypertension, erosive arthritis, pulmonary hypertension, and worsening lung function, indicating the associations are not driven solely by renal clearance or comorbidities.
Patients with elevated FLC had higher disease activity scores in SLE (SLEDAI) and Sjögren's syndrome (ESSDAI) compared to those with normal FLC levels.
In systemic sclerosis, elevated FLC levels were associated with a reduced forced vital capacity (FVC), indicating worse pulmonary function.
No statistically significant differences in FLC levels were observed across SAD patients according to treatment with antimalarials, steroids, immunosuppressants, or biologics.

FLC levels were positively correlated with anti-RNA binding protein autoantibodies (SSB, SSA, Sm, U1-RNP), anti-dsDNA/chromatin antibodies, and rheumatoid factor, while showing poor or no correlation with anti-CCP2, Scl70, centromere, aCL/β2GPI, and thrombosis-associated antibodies.
Total FLC levels were negatively correlated with complement fractions C3 and C4 in SAD patients.
SAD patients with a negative Kirou IFNα/γ score had lower total FLC levels compared to those with a positive IFN score, supporting a link between IFN activity and FLC production.

FLC levels increased progressively with the number of active interferon modules, being significantly higher in patients with moderate and especially strong IFN signatures, defining an elevated polyclonal FLC as a reflection of a strong IFN signature.
Total FLC levels significantly correlated with 9 of 12 measured pro-inflammatory cytokines/chemokines, most strongly with TNF-RI and CXCL10/IP-10, both linked to type I/II interferon activity.

Excess total FLC was found across all SAD subgroups regardless of renal function status, indicating that immune stimulation rather than impaired kidney clearance, infection, or cancer predominantly drives polyclonal FLC elevation in SAD.
The prevalence of IBS among pregnant women increased substantially over the 11-year study period.
Pregnant women with IBS were more likely to have comorbid fibromyalgia than non-IBS pregnant women.
Women with IBS had increased odds of pregnancy-induced hypertension compared to women without IBS after adjustment for confounders.
Women with IBS had significantly increased odds of preeclampsia compared to women without IBS after multivariate adjustment.
Women with IBS had markedly increased odds of deep venous thrombosis during pregnancy compared to women without IBS.
Women with IBS had modestly increased odds of gestational diabetes compared to women without IBS.
Congenital anomalies were substantially more frequent among neonates born to women with IBS compared to those without IBS.
Flupirtine, a nonselective Kv7 channel activator, inhibited basal Cl- secretion in mouse distal colon.
Flupirtine abolished or attenuated the Cl- secretory response to tetrodotoxin, a neuronal sodium channel blocker, indicating suppression of neuronally-driven secretion.
Flupirtine abolished or attenuated the Cl- secretory response to veratridine, a sodium channel activator that stimulates enteric neurons.
Flupirtine abolished or attenuated the Cl- secretory response to nicotine, a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor agonist acting on enteric neurons.
Flupirtine abolished or attenuated the Cl- secretory response to hexamethonium, a nicotinic antagonist affecting enteric ganglionic transmission.
Flupirtine did not block the Cl- secretory response to VIP, an endogenous VPAC receptor ligand acting directly on epithelium, indicating a neurally-selective (not epithelial) mechanism.
Flupirtine did not block the Cl- secretory response to carbachol, a nonselective cholinergic agonist acting directly on epithelium, supporting a neurally-selective mechanism.

Flupirtine inhibited Cl- secretion in both full-thickness colon and seromuscular-stripped colon (containing submucosal but not myenteric plexus), but produced no response in isolated epithelial T84 cell monolayers, localizing the site of action to the submucosal enteric neurons rather than the epithelium.

Flupirtine had no effect on short-circuit current in T84 epithelial cell monolayers lacking any neural component, indicating its action requires enteric neurons rather than direct epithelial Kv7 channels.
Kv7.2 and Kv7.3 channel proteins were detected by immunofluorescence in whole mount preparations of the submucosa of mouse distal colon.
ICA-110381, a Kv7.2/7.3-specific activator, inhibited Cl- secretion in mouse distal colon to a degree comparable to flupirtine.

The authors conclude that Kv7 channel activators inhibit neurally driven Cl- secretion and may have therapeutic benefit for pathologies with hyperexcitable enteric nervous system, such as diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-D).

Among 21 patients with SARS-CoV-2-associated spinal cord demyelinating disease, autonomic dysfunction (including sphincter dysfunction) was reported as one of the frequent neurological manifestations alongside weakness, sensory deficit, and ataxia.

Nearly half of the reviewed COVID-19 spinal demyelination cases showed isolated long extensive transverse myelitis (LETM) on spinal MRI, with fewer showing short segment or patchy involvement, or combined brain and spinal cord demyelination.
SARS-CoV-2 was detected directly in the cerebrospinal fluid of a subset of patients with spinal cord demyelination, suggesting possible direct CNS neurotropism in some cases.
Most patients with COVID-19-associated spinal cord demyelination had elevated CSF protein and lymphocytic pleocytosis, consistent with an inflammatory/immune-mediated process.
The authors propose that the SARS-CoV-2-induced cytokine storm, mainly driven by IL-6, IL-1, and TNF-alpha, activates glial cells and may trigger demyelination in the spinal cord.

The review cites historical evidence of coronavirus RNA and antigen detected directly within CNS demyelinating plaques and CSF of MS/ADEM patients, supporting a direct neurotropic mechanism for coronavirus-associated demyelination.

Corticosteroids were the most common treatment for COVID-19-associated spinal cord demyelination, with a large majority of patients receiving intravenous methylprednisolone, and additional patients treated with IVIG or plasma exchange, with most patients improving.

Dramatic clinical response to IVIG or plasma exchange in several cases of COVID-19-associated spinal cord demyelination was interpreted by the authors as supporting an underlying immune-mediated pathogenic process rather than pure direct viral injury.
Prognosis of COVID-19-associated spinal cord demyelination was generally favorable, with most patients discharged and a mortality rate under 10%.
A systematic mapping found that all but four of 29 compiled ME/CFS symptoms were reported by at least one of the 21 selected long COVID studies.
Fatigue was the most frequently reported long COVID symptom across the selected studies, noted in 13 of 21 eligible studies (also cited as 12 of 21 in the discussion).
Only three of the 21 selected long COVID studies assessed patients at or beyond the 6-month duration threshold required for an ME/CFS diagnosis.
Some long COVID symptoms reported were not part of standard ME/CFS symptom criteria, specifically olfactory dysfunction, gustatory dysfunction, and rash.
In Huang et al., among patients assessed more than 6 months after COVID onset, 63% still reported fatigue.
In Taboada et al., 47.5% of patients reported decreased functional status more than 6 months after COVID onset.
Ortelli et al. found markedly elevated serum IL-6 levels in long COVID patients, suggesting a role for hyperinflammation in pathogenesis.
Townsend et al. did not find a correlation between fatigue severity and serum inflammatory marker levels in long COVID patients.
Alhiyari et al. reported a case of persistent cough for at least 4 months post-COVID, attributed to development of pulmonary fibrosis.
Townsend et al. found that only a small percentage of study patients developed pulmonary fibrosis post-COVID, and this was not linked to overall symptom severity.
It has been previously estimated, using conservative methodology, that approximately 10% of COVID-19 patients may go on to develop a chronic illness meeting the ME/CFS case definition.
A subset of severe ME/CFS patients show upregulation of EBV-induced gene 2 (EBI2), a gene important in immune and CNS function, potentially linking EBV infection to neurological/immune symptoms.
Natural killer cell activity, modulated by bacterial microbiome components, has been shown to be reduced in chronic fatigue syndrome patients.

ME/CFS has been consistently associated with increased activated cytotoxic CD8+ T cells, poorly functioning NK cells, increased CD16+/CD3- NK cells, increased immune activation markers, and elevated interferon gamma in serum and CSF.
Metabolomic studies in ME/CFS patients found sphingolipid and phospholipid levels significantly lower than normal, resembling a hibernation-like metabolic state.
ME/CFS patients show an abnormal rise in serum cortisol and heart rate in response to the stress of waking up, indicating an abnormal stress response.
ME/CFS, though once dismissively termed 'Yuppie Flu', has come to be understood as affecting a broad population with a female predominance.
The total annual cost of ME/CFS in Europe, based on UK experience, including healthcare and productivity losses, is estimated at approximately €40 billion.
ME/CFS predominantly affects women, who make up about three quarters of patients.
ME/CFS occurs across all age groups but most frequently emerges between ages 20 and 50.
Viral infections, including EBV, are implicated in the aetiology of most ME/CFS cases.
Anti-HHV-6 IgG and IgM antibody titres were elevated in CFS patients versus controls, but this rise was nonspecific and paralleled by increases in antibodies to other viruses.
Low-functioning NK cells and altered T-cell activation markers are proposed mechanisms by which immune dysfunction contributes to ME/CFS.
HPA axis derangement leading to low cortisol may increase inflammation and chronic immune activation in ME/CFS.
A dose-response relationship was observed between chronic fatigue scores and level of organophosphate pesticide exposure in agricultural workers.

A comparison of 146 organophosphate-exposed sheep dippers and 143 non-exposed quarry worker controls found significant differences in neuropsychological tests, neurological exam, and General Health Questionnaire scores.

Forearm skin blood flow response to acetylcholine iontophoresis was higher in ME/CFS patients than controls, but normal in Gulf War syndrome and organophosphate-exposed patients, suggesting an aetiological difference for ME/CFS.
Similar reproducible gene expression abnormalities were found in ME/CFS patients and in patients following organophosphate exposure.
Patients with unexplained persistent fatigue had higher serum DDE (organochlorine) levels compared to controls.
Cognitive and sleep symptoms were more prevalent among ME/CFS patients than MS patients in the UK ME/CFS Biobank.
Older ME/CFS patients (over 50) were much more likely to experience severe symptoms than younger patients (under 30), OR 3.23.
Severe ME/CFS symptoms were much more common among smokers and those with household incomes below £15,000 per year.
A previous history of frequent infections, including colds and influenza, was the factor most strongly associated with higher risk of ME/CFS compared to healthy controls.
A systematic scoping review of 1161 studies (1979-2019) on causal factors for ME/CFS found no single dominant causal factor and concluded the quality of evidence was too low to draw firm conclusions.
A systematic review found that old age, chronic illness, comorbid psychiatric disorders, and (controversially) belief in a physical cause of illness were associated with worse ME/CFS prognosis.
Oxidative DNA damage found in ME/CFS (also seen in severe depression) is a risk factor for atherosclerosis, potentially explaining increased cardiovascular morbidity in ME/CFS.
Reduced coenzyme Q10 may cause chronic heart failure and increased cardiovascular mortality in ME/CFS.

A UK study comparing 124 severely ill and 619 mildly ill ME/CFS patients found early management of illness was the most important determinant of disease severity, and having a mother with ME/CFS was also an important risk factor.
An earlier population-based study showed shorter illness duration was a significant predictor of sustained remission from ME/CFS, underscoring the importance of early detection.

Between a third and a half of GPs either disbelieve ME/CFS exists as a genuine clinical entity or have little understanding of it, and a similar proportion of patients are dissatisfied with primary care received; across Europe, upwards of 50% of GPs do not recognise ME/CFS as a genuine clinical entity.

Vink and Vink-Niese showed patients who rested at illness onset had the best prognosis, and avoiding pressure to over-perform on return to work minimised relapses, long-term sick leave, and medical retirement.

Cardiac dysfunction with low cardiac output due to a small left ventricle may contribute to chronic fatigue in a considerable subgroup of ME/CFS patients, and is most marked in those with orthostatic intolerance.
A cross-sectional survey found that treating orthostatic symptoms in ME/CFS patients could improve functional capacity and quality of life.

A questionnaire-based study found CFS prevalence was higher in genetically unrelated household contacts and non-resident genetic relatives of patients than in the community, implicating both household contact and genetic relationship as risk factors.
Both male and female ME/CFS patients showed strongly reduced maximal and mean handgrip strength in both the first and second (post 60-min) sessions compared to healthy controls.
Female cancer-related fatigue (CRF) patients also showed significantly reduced Fmax and Fmean in both sessions compared to healthy controls.
ME/CFS patients (both sexes) showed a significant further decline in Fmax and Fmean from the first to the second session (after 60 min rest), whereas HC remained stable or even increased.
Female CRF patients similarly showed a significant reduction in Fmax and Fmean from the first to second session.
ME/CFS patients had a stronger decrease in HGS over ten repeat pulls, reflected in significantly higher Fatigue Ratios than HC in both sessions.
Female CRF patients also showed higher Fatigue Ratios than HC in both sessions.
ME/CFS patients showed a diminished Recovery Ratio compared to HC, indicating impaired restoration of grip strength after a 60-minute rest.
In a subset of female ME/CFS patients, quadriceps maximal strength dropped significantly over a 20-minute repeated contraction protocol compared to HC, who showed no significant decline.
Lower disease severity (Bell) scores correlated with lower Fmax1 in female ME/CFS patients and with lower Fmean and higher Fatigue Ratio1 in male patients.
Higher PEM scores correlated with lower Fmean2 in females and with higher Fatigue Ratio2 in both sexes, suggesting HGS reflects PEM severity.
More severe muscle pain correlated with lower Fmean2 and impaired Recovery Ratio in female ME/CFS patients.
Vasomotor dysregulation (COMPASS subscore) correlated significantly with reduced Fmax2 and Fmean1/2 in both sexes, and with Fmax1, Fatigue Ratio2 and Recovery Ratio in males.
SF-36 physical functioning scores correlated with Fmax2 and Fmean2 in male ME/CFS patients.
In female ME/CFS patients, higher post-exertion creatine kinase (CK) levels correlated with higher Fatigue Ratio2 and lower Recovery Ratio.

Higher LDH concentrations correlated with lower Recovery Ratio and higher Fatigue Ratio1 in male ME/CFS patients, and with higher Fatigue Ratio2 in female patients, suggesting a shift toward glycolytic metabolism.
ROC analysis identified Fmean2 as the best-performing HGS parameter for discriminating ME/CFS patients aged 20-39 from healthy controls, with high sensitivity and specificity.
No significant correlations were found between handgrip strength parameters and total COMPASS-31 score or Chalder Fatigue Scale severity of fatigue.
Genuine swallowing difficulties (dysphagia) can occur in patients with very severe ME/CFS via mechanisms that remain unclear.

In one patient failing to respond to enteral/parenteral feeding, Mast Cell Activation Disorder (MCAD) was diagnosed and treatment with oral cromoglycate and antihistamines stabilized and then increased her weight.
In all five cases, clinicians attributed the patients' inability to eat/swallow to psychological causes and involved psychiatrists, despite no positive evidence of psychopathology.

Allocation of a named Home Enteral Nutrition Service (HENS) dietician with advanced enteral nutrition training was associated with the most positive improvement in nutritional management in every case, including enabling one patient to discontinue tube feeding.
All five patients were allowed to become severely malnourished and dehydrated to a life-threatening extent due to delayed recognition and initiation of tube feeding.
One patient was screened with the Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST) and scored 4, well above the threshold of 2 that denotes high malnutrition risk.

Reintroduction of nutrition after prolonged malnutrition in severe ME/CFS carries an immediate risk of re-feeding syndrome and possible longer-term consequences including poor wound healing, neurological damage, and osteoporosis.
Barium meal imaging identified gastroparesis and intestinal failure as underlying causes of persistent feeding intolerance (vomiting, abdominal pain) in one patient with severe ME/CFS.

A cited large study found that with protocols in place, trained community nurses can correctly identify nasogastric tube position without hospital attendance, yet none of the five patients in this series were offered NGT re-siting at home.
Travel to hospital and the hospital environment were reported to significantly exacerbate symptoms in patients with very severe ME/CFS, who require darkened rooms and minimal staff contact.

Once established, enteral (NGT/NJT/PEG) or parenteral (TPN) feeding successfully reversed life-threatening malnutrition and improved BMI and quality of life across all five cases, despite prior delays and misdiagnosis.
Natural autoantibodies against ß2-adrenergic receptors and M3-muscarinergic receptors are found upregulated in about one third of ME/CFS patients.
Levels of ß2AdR antibodies correlate with brain network alterations associated with pain in ME/CFS patients.
Immunoadsorption to remove IgG resulted in clinical improvement of ME/CFS.
Adolescent ME/CFS was found associated with polymorphisms of the ß2-adrenergic receptor gene.
ME/CFS patients had lower expression of ß2AdR compared to controls.
Hand grip strength assessment shows impaired strength and enhanced fatiguability in ME/CFS patients, correlating with disease severity, muscle pain and PEM.

In a controlled repeated exercise study, ME/CFS patients performed worse than controls, and previous exercise deteriorated subsequent physical performance and increased arterial lactate, opposite to the pattern in healthy subjects.
Cultured human skeletal muscle cells from ME/CFS patients show impaired glucose uptake and reduced ATP levels compared to controls.
Skeletal muscle acidosis or dysregulation of protons is found in ME/CFS patients during or after exercise, and proton efflux immediately post-exercise was found strongly but transiently diminished.
Several studies show diminished oxygen supply to muscles upon exercise in ME/CFS patients, and metabolic changes indicate hypoxia and ischemia.
Expression of the cation channel TRPM3 has been found reduced in leukocytes of patients with ME/CFS.

There is evidence for inhibition of the Na+/K+-ATPase by reactive oxygen species in ME/CFS patients, potentially stemming from inflammation or mitochondrial dysfunction, contributing to reduced potassium efflux in exercising muscle.

Total body potassium was found decreased by about 10% in a group of patients with severe fatigue, with a strong inverse correlation between total body potassium and total time spent resting (a measure of fatigue).
Myocardial fibrosis has been found in some patients with ME/CFS, which may cause diastolic dysfunction enhancing preload failure due to hypovolemia.
The long noncoding RNA MIAT is found upregulated in ME/CFS patients and is proposed as a candidate driver of NHE1 upregulation via ZEB1.
ZEB1, which can drive upregulation of NHE1, was found upregulated in ME/CFS patients as well.
PBMCs from ME/CFS patients show a dramatically different impedance response to a hyperosmotic stressor compared to controls, suggested as a potential diagnostic marker.
Actin network proteins talin-1 and filamin-A were found in circulating extracellular vesicles of ME/CFS patients, suggesting minimal structural damage to skeletal muscle.
High insulin levels have been reported in ME/CFS patients, hypothesized to reflect muscular insulin resistance analogous to metabolic syndrome.
About half of ME/CFS patients have already elevated lactate levels at rest, and these elevated resting lactate levels correlate with PEM.
A study found different miRNA signatures in response to PEM induction, allowing classification of ME/CFS patients into four clusters associated with symptom severity.

Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, which can also affect large blood vessels, is a known risk factor for ME/CFS, possibly via impaired capacitance vessel contraction limiting the ability to raise circulating blood volume during hypovolemia.

Preliminary studies reported promising effects of the acetylcholinesterase inhibitor pyridostigmine (Mestinon), presumed to reduce venous pooling and improve cardiac preload, possibly via stimulation of Na+/K+-ATPase.

The ß2AdR agonist salbutamol stimulates the Na+/K+-ATPase and increases cellular potassium uptake, lowering plasma potassium, similarly to insulin, illustrating the relevance of ß2AdR for Na+/K+-ATPase activation.
Editorial describes observations that patients with long COVID undergoing exercise-based rehabilitation experienced adverse effects and symptoms strikingly similar to myalgic encephalomyelitis.
The authors issue safety recommendations for rehabilitation of long COVID and ME patients and share resources to improve care for postviral illnesses, citing risks of exercise therapy.

The patient reports that after receiving Rituximab (Rituxan), his subsequent crashes from exceeding energy limits became permanent (a 'cliff' pattern) rather than the gradual, partially recoverable crashes he had before treatment.
The patient reports that Ativan produced both a temporary drug effect and, on first use, a lasting 'reset' that permanently improved his overall symptom severity and allowed periodic communication.

Low-dose aripiprazole, titrated slowly from 0.25 mg to 2 mg over about six months, was associated with gradually increased energy and tolerance of previously stress-inducing stimuli, improving the patient from extremely severe back toward severe ME/CFS.

Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN) via PICC line was used for 1.5 years (the reported maximum duration), and the author states this route bypasses the GI tract, risks liver damage, and causes GI tract deterioration and loss of healthy bacteria.

The author states he should have received Total Enteral Tube Nutrition via jejunostomy (J-tube) from the outset instead of TPN/PICC line, believing this would have led to earlier discovery of Ativan's benefit and better health.

The author describes post-exertional malaise (PEM) as the defining symptom of ME/CFS, in which exceeding an individual energy limit causes worsening of symptoms lasting hours to permanently, and causes the energy limit itself to drop further.

In the extremely severe state, the patient developed extreme sensitivity to visual and auditory stimuli, requiring removal of bright colors, covering text with tape, and use of earmuffs/eye coverings during any caregiver contact.

The patient describes progressive severe gastroparesis, in which his stomach's functional capacity and digesting ability behaved analogously to PEM, permanently worsening whenever intake exceeded its current limit, eventually resulting in complete inability to tolerate any food or water.

Applying ice to the abdomen was reported to improve stomach function/comfort in the setting of severe gastroparesis, and after ~6 months on Abilify the patient was able to tolerate the feeding pump without ice for the first time.

The patient describes a reproducible natural adrenaline release accompanying bowel movements that transiently supplies enough energy to get out of bed and walk a short distance, which he hypothesizes as a hardwired evolutionary mechanism.

The author states that most severe ME/CFS patients probably die or die by suicide when there is no hope, attributing this to profound suffering, lack of societal support, and absence of a safety net for undiagnosed/unsupported patients.
The patient reports developing restless leg syndrome-like tingling in his feet and legs from prolonged immobility/bed confinement.

The patient describes 'crash memory', a sensitization phenomenon resembling physically-induced PTSD in which any activity or stimulus previously associated with a crash becomes newly triggering, requiring careful timing (e.g., waiting after ambient noise) to avoid repeat crashes.
The proinflammatory chemokine RANTES/CCL5 was massively overexpressed (nearly 40-fold) in the patient's fatty-degenerative jawbone marrow defect tissue compared to normal healthy jawbone.
Histopathological analysis of the curetted jawbone medullary cavity revealed an aspergilloma (fungal ball) with fungal hyphae and spores, alongside chronic inflammatory cell infiltration.
Conventional panoramic radiograph (OPG) failed to detect any abnormal findings in the jawbone area later confirmed to harbor a bone marrow defect and aspergilloma.
Digital volume tomography combined with cone beam CT (DVT/CBCT) also failed to show resolution of bony trabecular structures indicating the bone marrow defect at area 38/39.

Trans-alveolar ultrasound (TAU) measurement, unlike OPG and DVT/CBCT, detected suspected osteolysis/reduced bone density (a bone marrow defect) at jaw area 38/39, which was later confirmed histologically.
Surgical debridement of the jawbone bone marrow defect (area 38/39) with curettage and application of platelet-rich fibrin was performed to remove the necrotic/infected tissue and aspergilloma.

The patient with a 4-year history of CFS presented with dizziness, inability to work, impaired concentration, depression, headaches, and tinnitus, which had not improved with predominantly psychologically-oriented treatment.

The authors propose that mycotoxins (aflatoxin and gliotoxin) produced by Aspergillus in the jawbone defect may contribute to chronic inflammation and CNS irritation underlying the patient's CFS via immunosuppressive and DNA-damaging effects.
In a cohort of 164 adolescents with CFS/ME, 15% (25/164) met threshold criteria for clinically significant anhedonia on a structured psychiatric interview.
An additional 27% (43/164) of adolescents reported subthreshold anhedonia symptoms, bringing the total experiencing at least some anhedonia to 42% (68/164).
Fatigue severity and physical functioning were similar between adolescents with clinically significant anhedonia and those without.
Adolescents with clinically significant anhedonia scored higher on both depression and anxiety measures than those without anhedonia.
Nearly three-quarters (72%, 18/25) of adolescents with clinically significant anhedonia met full DSM-5 criteria for major depressive disorder.
Thematic analysis found adolescents attributed loss of motivation to engage in previously enjoyable activities to their fatigue from CFS/ME.
