Participants reported that CFS/ME curtailed their ability to experience enjoyment (consummatory pleasure) during activities, with new substitute activities feeling like poor replacements for those they could no longer do.

Compared to non-depressed adolescents with anhedonia, those who were depressed described a constant lack of motivation and more negative/extreme narratives, with less residual anticipatory or consummatory pleasure.
The paper cites prior work reporting that nearly 30% of adolescents with CFS/ME have comorbid depression, roughly ten times the prevalence in the general adolescent population.
The paper cites prior data showing severe school attendance impairment in adolescents with CFS/ME, with 62% attending school less than 40% of the time.
The Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire score decreased significantly from baseline to post-intervention following the individualised activity programme.
Fatigue Severity Score decreased significantly after the activity programme.
Fatigue Impact Scale scores decreased significantly after the activity programme.
Treadmill workload normalised to body weight at anaerobic threshold significantly increased after the activity programme.
Load/body mass at maximal exercise intensity significantly increased after the activity programme.
Ventilatory threshold volume at anaerobic threshold significantly increased after the activity programme.
Peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak) significantly increased after the activity programme.
Just over half of completers (19/34) showed a clinically significant VO2peak improvement (>1.1 mL/kg/min), including 7 of 14 males and 12 of 20 females.
Plasma Mitofusin 1 levels significantly increased following the activity programme.
Plasma Mitofusin 2 levels significantly increased following the activity programme.
A mixed linear model showed a significant interaction between VO2peak and plasma Mfn1 levels, suggesting a relationship between aerobic capacity improvement and mitochondrial fusion protein levels.
Increase in submaximal VO2 (at anaerobic threshold) was associated with a decrease in the sympathovagal (LF/HF-RRI) ratio response to head-up tilt testing.
Overall, autonomic nervous system function indicators (LF/HF-RRI at rest and during HUTT) did not change significantly after the activity programme.
A substantial proportion of patients (19 of 53, with 51% overall attrition) dropped out of the exercise programme due to severe post-exertional malaise triggered by the intervention.

Resting sympathetic hyperactivity, reflected by HRV and blood pressure variability changes, has been linked in a prior meta-analysis to lower maximal heart rate in CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
Heart rate response to head-up tilt testing was higher in CFS patients compared to healthy controls, per prior literature.
A meta-analysis pooling single exercise tests found peak oxygen uptake was on average 5.2 mL/kg/min lower in CFS patients than in healthy controls, with substantial heterogeneity between subjects.
Muscle biopsy electron microscopy studies have shown mitochondrial degeneration in CFS patients, cited as evidence of mitochondrial dysfunction in this population.
IC/BPS patients had a significantly greater average number of comorbid conditions than non-IC/BPS patients.
Patients with IC/BPS had a markedly higher prevalence of comorbid NUAS conditions (chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome, migraines) than non-IC/BPS patients.
IC/BPS patients had a higher prevalence of at least one psychosocial comorbidity (alcohol abuse, PTSD, sexual trauma, or depression history) compared with non-IC/BPS patients.
The elevated comorbidity burden associated with IC/BPS was more pronounced in female patients than male patients.
Heterozygous pathogenic variants in C1R cause periodontal Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (pEDS).
Three novel C1S variants (c.962G>C, c.961T>G, c.961T>A) were identified among the reported pEDS patients, expanding the mutational spectrum of the gene.
pEDS is clinically characterized by early-onset periodontitis with premature tooth loss, pretibial hyperpigmentation and skin fragility.

Three patients and one relative in this cohort displayed widespread venous insufficiency leading to persistent varicose leg ulcers, expanding the described vascular phenotype of pEDS beyond the rare arterial complications previously reported.

One patient suffered an intracranial aneurysm, with familial vascular complications including thoracic and abdominal aortic aneurysm and dissection and intracranial aneurysm rupture also occurring in the family.
The authors recommend performing a complete non-invasive vascular evaluation at the time of pEDS diagnosis given the observed, albeit infrequent, vascular complications.
Ornithine concentrations were strongly reduced during the acute mast cell activation attack compared with baseline, indicating enterocyte dysfunction.
Citrulline concentrations were strongly reduced during the acute mast cell activation attack, further supporting enterocyte dysfunction.
Histamine concentrations were highly increased during the attack and their peak coincided with the peak of clinical symptoms.
Lactate concentrations were highly increased during the attack, accompanying the peak in clinical symptoms.
Plasma histamine concentrations strongly correlated with clinical severity parameters throughout the mast cell activation event, implicating histamine as the primary driver of the acute phase.
Plasma diamine oxidase concentrations rose approximately 100-fold and this rise coincided with reduction in histamine-driven symptoms.
The authors propose rapid elimination of elevated histamine via recombinant human diamine oxidase as a potential new treatment for life-threatening mast cell activation events.
Supplementation of lysophosphatidylcholine is proposed as a possible immunomodulatory treatment for severe mast cell activation events.
Inhibition of autotaxin activity is proposed as a potential treatment target given evidence of localized autotaxin activation during the attack.
Blockade of lysophosphatidic acid receptors is proposed as a possible treatment strategy for severe mast cell activation events.
In systemic mastocytosis, mast cell numbers are manifold elevated in various organs, and their degranulation can produce life-threatening symptoms.
MRGPRX2, discovered in 2006, is confined to the MCTC mast cell subtype and absent in MCT, serving as a signature marker of connective-tissue-type mast cells.
MRGPRX2 transcript expression is markedly higher in MCTC mast cells than in MCT mast cells.
Substance P-induced mast cell degranulation in skin-derived mast cells is mediated by MRGPRX2 rather than the neurokinin-1 receptor (NK1R), even though both receptors are co-expressed.
Substance P has much higher potency at NK1R than at MRGPRX2, with EC50 values of 0.5 nM versus 100 nM respectively.

Four naturally occurring MRGPRX2 missense variants (G165E, D184H, W243R, H259Y) fail to respond to agonists such as substance P, hemokinin-1, human β-defensin-3, and Icatibant, representing loss-of-function variants.
The MRGPRX2 missense variants V123F, R138C, R141C, and V282M were identified as loss-of-function for substance P-induced mast cell activation and degranulation.
The MRGPRX2 missense variants S325L and L329Q were identified as gain-of-function for substance P-induced mast cell activation and degranulation.

Calcium mobilization kinetics differ between IgE-mediated and MRGPRX2-mediated mast cell activation, with IgE producing slow Ca2+ mobilization and compound exocytosis, and MRGPRX2 producing transient Ca2+ mobilization with single granule fusion.
Tryptase, rather than histamine, is the major preformed mediator released during MRGPRX2-mediated mast cell degranulation, unlike IgE-mediated activation where histamine predominates.
The human MRGPRX2 gene is a two-exon gene located on chromosome 11p15, 2036 bp in length, encoding a 330-amino-acid protein.
Homology modeling identified glutamic acid 164 (E164) and aspartic acid 184 (D184) as key negatively charged residues at the MRGPRX2 ligand-binding site required for binding cationic ligands.
Compound 48/80-induced mast cell degranulation was significantly reduced in MRGPRX2 siRNA-knockdown mast cells, confirming its MRGPRX2-dependent activity.
Silencing MRGPRX2 in human mast cells inhibited human β-defensin-2-induced degranulation, confirming MRGPRX2 dependence.

Host defense peptide (LL-37/human β-defensin)-induced MRGPRX2 activation of mast cells leads to degranulation but with significantly less pro-inflammatory cytokine release compared to keratinocyte responses.
Vancomycin activates mast cells via MRGPRX2, explaining the non-IgE-mediated mechanism of vancomycin-induced red man syndrome.

Fluoroquinolone antibiotics produce concentration-dependent mast cell degranulation, calcium release, and increased vascular permeability through an MRGPRX2-dependent mechanism, though one study found no ciprofloxacin activity up to 100 μM in an MRGPRX2 stable cell line.
Rocuronium produces concentration-dependent activation of both murine and human MRGPRX2/MRGPRB2 on mast cells.
Mivacurium increased paw extravasation and decreased body temperature in wild-type mice, effects that were absent in MRGPRB2 knockdown mice, indicating MRGPRB2/MRGPRX2 dependence.
Skin mast cells, which predominantly express MRGPRX2, degranulate in response to morphine, whereas lung and heart mast cells (low MRGPRX2 expression) fail to respond.
Pethidine hydrochloride caused MRGPRX2-dependent mast cell degranulation and cytokine release, while fentanyl citrate showed no such activity, attributed to differences in chemical structure.

Cationic amphiphilic antidepressants (clomipramine, paroxetine, desipramine) show concentration-dependent MRGPRX2/MRGPRB2 activation, mast cell degranulation, and scratching behavior in mice; intradermal clomipramine injection produced a wheal-and-flare reaction and activated human skin mast cells in a healthy volunteer.

Skin mast cells from chronic idiopathic urticaria (CIU) patients show high MRGPRX2 expression compared to healthy skin mast cells, potentially explaining previously unknown precipitating factors in CIU.

A patient with severe pre-operative hypersensitivity to rocuronium carried three MRGPRX2 missense mutations (M196I, L226P, L237P) in the fifth and sixth transmembrane domains, though rocuronium itself did not induce degranulation in transiently MRGPRX2-transfected RBL-2H3 cells.

A population-based study on patients' skin mast cells found substantial inter-individual variability in MRGPRX2 ligand response, with compound 48/80 activating between 3.1% and 52.4% of cells and SP between 2.9% and 52.6%.
Removal of iodine from the radiocontrast agent iohexol significantly reduced MRGPRX2 activation and local/systemic anaphylaxis, implicating iodine as crucial to MRGPRX2 activation.
Resveratrol inhibited MRGPRX2-mediated mast cell activation via the Nrf2 pathway and attenuated compound 48/80-induced paw extravasation and systemic anaphylaxis in mice.

Genistein attenuated MRGPRX2-dependent mast cell degranulation and calcium influx in a concentration-dependent manner and reduced paw thickness and Evans blue extravasation in a mouse model of anaphylactoid shock.

Pertussis toxin blocked Gαi-mediated MC degranulation induced by host defense peptides via MRGPRX2 while having no effect on Ca2+ mobilization, indicating dual Gαi/Gαq signaling downstream of MRGPRX2.

The tripeptide QWF acted as a dual NK-1R/MRGPR antagonist, inhibiting SP-induced activation of MRGPRX2, MRGPRB2 and MRGPRA1 and blocking MC degranulation induced by compound 48/80, atracurium and ciprofloxacin.
Two small-compound antagonists significantly inhibited SP- and Icatibant-induced human MC degranulation and Ca2+ flux but failed to show similar activity in ex vivo mouse MCs.
Resveratrol inhibited MRGPRX2-mediated MC activation via the Nrf2 pathway, reducing compound 48/80-induced Ca2+ mobilization, degranulation, paw extravasation and systemic anaphylaxis in mice.
Genistein showed MRGPRX2 antagonistic activity, attenuating MC degranulation and Ca2+ influx, and offered protection against compound 48/80-induced anaphylactoid shock and paw thickness in mice.

Osthole, a coumarin from Cnidium monnieri, inhibited compound 48/80-, SP- and LL-37-induced MC degranulation, Ca2+ mobilization and chemokine/cytokine production, and attenuated in vivo degranulation and histological changes.

Kaempferol dose-dependently decreased compound 48/80-induced paw swelling, Evans blue extravasation and MC degranulation, rehabilitated hypothermia, and inhibited release of histamine, tryptase, TNF-alpha, IL-8 and MCP-1.

Paeoniflorin attenuated MC degranulation, MRGPRX2 activation and Ca2+ influx, downregulated PLCγ and MAPK/ERK phosphorylation, and inhibited Evans blue extravasation, paw inflammation, histamine and chemokine release in a mouse model.
Shikonin, a plant naphthoquinone, showed dose-dependent inhibitory activity against compound 48/80-induced pseudo-allergic reactions, systemic anaphylaxis, Ca2+ flux and MC degranulation.

Piperine inhibited MC degranulation, Ca2+ mobilization and cytokine/chemokine release, attenuated hind paw swelling and reversed hypothermia in a systemic anaphylaxis model, and showed competitive binding affinity with the agonist sinomenine hydrochloride.

Quercetin antagonized MRGPRX2, inhibiting MC degranulation, Ca2+ response and cytokine release, and showed protective effects against inflammation and hypothermia in a mouse model of local and systemic anaphylaxis.
Saikosaponin A, a triterpenoid saponin, inhibited compound 48/80-induced pseudo-allergic reactions via the MRGPRX2 pathway, attenuating Ca2+ flux, MC degranulation and skin inflammation.

Hydroxysafflor yellow A inhibited Ca2+ flux, MC degranulation and histamine release induced by compound 48/80, LL-37 and ciprofloxacin, and attenuated hind paw swelling and Evans blue extravasation in a mouse model.

Isoliquiritigenin, a plant chalcone, inhibited compound 48/80-induced Ca2+ mobilization, MC degranulation, histamine and cytokine release, and attenuated hind paw swelling, Evans blue extravasation and tissue hemangiectasis in mouse models.
DNA aptamer X35 attenuated MC degranulation and histamine release induced by compound 48/80 and SP, and subcutaneous injection decreased MRGPRX2-mediated anaphylactic shock in vivo.

IL-33 has a dual, exposure-duration-dependent effect on MRGPRX2: chronic exposure of skin MCs reduces MRGPRX2 expression and abolishes the pseudo-allergic route, whereas acute exposure increases MRGPRX2-mediated degranulation, via a JNK-dependent mechanism.

Acute exposure of MCs to stem cell factor decreased responsiveness to compound 48/80 and SP and potently inhibited MRGPRX2-mediated pseudo-allergic degranulation, in contrast to its degranulation-promoting role via FcεRI.

A population-based study of patients' skin MCs found substantial inter-individual variability in MRGPRX2 ligand response, with compound 48/80 activating between 3.1% and 52.4% of MCs and SP activating between 2.9% and 52.6%, suggesting differential susceptibility to pseudo-allergic reactions.

A humanized mouse model developed by injecting GM-CSF and IL-3 plasmid into NOD-scid IL2Rγ−/− mice was proposed as a robust in vivo model for screening drug-induced MC-MRGPRX2 cutaneous adverse reactions.

Standard IgE-based diagnostic tests (skin prick/intracutaneous tests and drug-specific IgE quantification) fail to diagnose non-IgE-mediated MRGPRX2 pseudo-allergic reactions, necessitating alternative approaches such as basophil activation tests and drug provocation tests.
Patients with perioperative hypersensitivity had significantly higher baseline serum tryptase levels than uneventful anesthesia controls (5.15 vs 2.28 ng/mL).
Acute serum tryptase during the reaction was markedly higher in POH patients than in controls during uneventful anesthesia (20.30 vs 1.92 ng/mL).
The consensus formula (aST > 1.2 × bST + 2) provided the highest diagnostic accuracy (81%) for documenting mast cell activation in perioperative hypersensitivity.
A tryptase increase over baseline of 3.2 ng/mL or more had the highest diagnostic accuracy (82%) as an alternative threshold for mast cell activation in POH.
Elevated baseline serum tryptase (>8 ng/mL) was more prevalent in patients with higher-grade perioperative hypersensitivity reactions and was associated with anaphylaxis occurrence.

Degradation of PHSP by four methods (alone or combined) significantly decreased molecular weight and viscosity while preserving the main chemical bonds and functional structure compared to native PHSP.
DPHSP showed enhanced inhibitory effects on mast cell activation compared to native PHSP in vitro.
In an ovalbumin-induced food allergy mouse model, DPHSP treatment improved suppression of the food anaphylactic response compared to native PHSP.
DPHSP treatment inhibited production of the allergic cytokine interleukin-4 in the ovalbumin-induced food allergy mouse model.
DPHSP treatment inhibited production of interleukin-13 in the ovalbumin-induced food allergy mouse model.
DPHSP treatment inhibited production of interferon-γ in the ovalbumin-induced food allergy mouse model.
DPHSP had a stronger ability than PHSP to up-regulate differentiation of regulatory T (Treg) cells and their related cytokines in the food allergy model.
Reported anaphylaxis rates after COVID-19 mRNA vaccination (5.0 per million for Pfizer-BioNTech, 2.8 per million for Moderna) are 2 to 5 times higher than rates for Tdap and trivalent flu vaccines.
Individuals experiencing anaphylactic reactions to COVID-19 mRNA vaccines have been overwhelmingly female.
Atopic individuals appear to be overrepresented among those experiencing anaphylaxis to COVID-19 mRNA vaccines.
Reported prevalence of anti-PEG antibodies in healthy volunteers varies widely (5%-70%) depending on the assay and cutoffs used.

Phase 2/3 trials of PEGylated liposomes delivering RNA aptamers were halted due to an unacceptably high rate of first-exposure anaphylaxis associated with preexisting anti-PEG antibodies, with tryptase elevated in 6 of 11 severe reaction patients and complement C3a elevated at 90 minutes.

In porcine models, Doxil infusion caused production of complement anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a that activated mast cells, resulting in severe hypotension and pulmonary hypertension (complement activation-related pseudoallergic reaction, CARPA).
Humans experiencing infusion reactions to Doxil showed evidence of complement activation as measured by sC5b-9 in serum 10 minutes post-infusion, without preexisting anti-PEG antibodies.

Anti-PEG IgE was detected in a patient who experienced immediate hypersensitivity reactions to three different PEG-containing medications (Definity liposomes, oral bowel prep, and a steroid injection).

Anti-PEG IgE was identified in 2 of 2091 serum samples from healthy control screening, suggesting allergic sensitization to PEG may be more common than expected, though functional basophil/mast cell activation was not tested in these samples.

Hereditary alpha tryptasemia, caused by increased TPSAB1 alpha-tryptase gene copy number and present in about 5% of certain populations, is significantly enriched among people with idiopathic anaphylaxis, severe hymenoptera reactions, and mastocytosis.
A rare missense mutation in KARS has been reported as a monogenic cause of predisposition to severe anaphylaxis.

A prior publication demonstrated that human mast cells can be efficiently transfected using an LNP delivery system, suggesting mast cells could take up COVID-19 mRNA vaccine LNPs and potentially become activated.

In vitro incubation of Listeria monocytogenes with mast cells produced measurable degranulation, potentially due to phagolysosome disruption and/or the direct activity of listeriolysin O toxin, offering a precedent for endosome-disruption-triggered mast cell activation relevant to LNP-vaccine reactions.
Coculture of LAM-derived cells with fibroblasts induced production of multiple CXC chemokines in the fibroblasts.
LAM lungs contained increased numbers of tryptase-positive mast cells that express CXC chemokine receptors compared with control tissue.
Mast cells located at the periphery of LAM nodules were positively associated with a faster rate of lung function decline.
Pharmacologic and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated inhibition of CXCR1 and CXCR2 blocked the attraction of mast cells to LAM spheroids.
Mast-cell tryptase release triggered by LAM spheroids induced fibroblast proliferation and increased LAM-spheroid size by approximately 1.36-fold.
The tryptase inhibitor APC366 and sodium cromoglycate (SCG) inhibited mast cell-induced LAM spheroid growth in vitro.
In an immunocompetent Tsc2-null murine homograft model, sodium cromoglycate (SCG) reduced mast-cell activation and lung tumor burden compared with vehicle.
Doxycycline-induced shRNA knockdown reduced TAZ protein by 99.1% in fetal liver-derived mast cells by day 5.
Following allergen-induced IgE-FcεRI activation, TAZ knockdown mast cells showed a 25% reduction in oxygen consumption compared with wild-type mast cells.
TAZ knockdown mast cells showed a significant 31% reduction in allergen-induced degranulation compared with wild-type controls.
TAZ knockdown significantly reduced allergen-induced secretion of TNF from mast cells.
TAZ knockdown significantly reduced allergen-induced secretion of CCL1 from mast cells.
TAZ knockdown significantly reduced allergen-induced secretion of CCL2 from mast cells.
CCL9 secretion was also impaired in TAZ knockdown mast cells following allergen stimulation.

Despite reduced secretion of multiple inflammatory mediators, gene expression of these mediators was not impaired by TAZ knockdown, suggesting TAZ acts post-transcriptionally on exocytosis rather than gene expression.
Small-fiber neuropathy, detected via electrochemical skin conductance, cold/warm detection thresholds, and laser evoked potentials, was present in 23 of 33 (70%) erythromelalgia patients.
Only 10 of 33 (30%) erythromelalgia patients showed large fiber neuropathy on nerve conduction studies.

Vascular alteration, assessed by Toe Pressure Index or clinical features of microvascular disorder, was found in 28 of 33 (85%) erythromelalgia patients, making it the most common abnormality observed.
Patients with large fiber neuropathy had a higher Utah Early Neuropathy Scale (UENS) score than those without large fiber neuropathy, unlike other subgroup comparisons which showed no difference.

Clinical severity scores (EM severity score, DN4) did not differ between erythromelalgia patients with or without small-fiber neuropathy or microvascular disorder, indicating neuropathic and vascular findings are not linked to a specific clinical phenotype.
Pain and neuropathy symptom scores (DN4, MNSI, NRS, evoked-burning pain) and HbA1c levels were highest in patients with diabetic neuropathic pain compared to the other groups.
Distal leg skin biopsies showed the lowest PGP9.5-positive intraepidermal nerve fiber density in patients with diabetic neuropathic pain, consistent with length-dependent small fiber loss.
Distal leg skin biopsies showed the highest TRPV1-positive intraepidermal nerve fiber density in patients with diabetic neuropathic pain despite overall nerve fiber loss.

Axon-reflex flare responses measured by Laser Speckle Contrast Analysis at the distal leg showed hypo-functionality of small fibers in both patients with impaired glucose tolerance and diabetic neuropathic pain, correlating with disease severity.

The authors propose LASCA-based axon-flare response measurement as a practical, objective, and rapid (within 5 minutes) method for early diagnosis of small fiber hypo-functionality without requiring specialized expertise.
Sympathetic skin response (SSR) latency from the hand was mildly but significantly prolonged in metal-exposed workers compared to controls.
SSR latency from the foot was markedly and significantly prolonged in metal industry workers compared to controls, indicating autonomic small fiber involvement in the lower limb.

Thermal (cold, warm) and pain (cold pain, heat pain) sensation thresholds in both C8 (upper limb) and S1 (lower limb) dermatomes were significantly different between heavy-metal-exposed workers and controls, indicating small A-delta and C fiber dysfunction.
Vibratory (large fiber, A-beta) thresholds were not significantly different between groups in the upper limb (C8), unlike the significant difference found in the lower limb (S1).
Dispersion between temperature sensation and pain thresholds (cold and warm) was significantly greater only in the C8 (upper limb) region in metal workers compared to controls.
Only 19.5% (8/41) of heavy-metal-exposed workers had overt clinical symptoms of polyneuropathy (impaired sensation and/or diminished/absent deep tendon reflexes), all localized to the lower limbs.

Standard nerve conduction studies showed significant differences in nearly all parameters of the peroneal nerve in metal workers versus controls, while differences in the ulnar nerve were less pronounced.
No consistent significant correlations were found between individual heavy metal levels and standard neurography, SSR, or QST parameters, with only weak correlations (maximum r=0.48) observed.

The single worker with a blood lead level (Pb-B) above the cut-off had the highest temperature and pain sensation thresholds among the study group, with cold pain thresholds completely undetectable in both regions tested.

Workers with abnormally elevated urine arsenic (As-U) levels showed the highest vibratory sensation thresholds, primarily in the S1 (lower limb) region, suggesting predominant large-fiber involvement with arsenic exposure.

Peripheral nerve damage from chronic heavy metal co-exposure showed features of both demyelination (motor latency, conduction velocity changes) and axonal loss (amplitude reductions), with sensory fibers and lower-limb nerves more affected than motor fibers and upper-limb nerves.

The authors concluded that small nerve fibers (A-delta and C fibers) are affected earlier than large fibers in chronic heavy metal co-exposure, supporting the use of small fiber function testing for early diagnosis of toxic polyneuropathy.
Gastrointestinal symptoms, anxiety, and REM sleep behavior disorder, which are known pre-motor features of PD, were more prominent in PD patients than in normal controls.
R2* values, reflecting iron content, were significantly higher in the substantia nigra of drug-naïve PD patients compared to normal controls.
R2* values were significantly higher in the putamen of drug-naïve PD patients compared to normal controls.
QSM iron values did not significantly differ between PD patients and normal controls in any measured region.
Neither R2* nor QSM values in any brain region correlated with the severity of motor symptoms (UPDRS part 3, sub-scores, or Hoehn-Yahr stage) after controlling for age and sex.
Red nucleus R2* iron content was negatively correlated with Parkinson's disease sleep scale scores, indicating higher iron associated with worse sleep.
Right amygdala R2* iron content was negatively correlated with Parkinson's disease sleep scale scores.
Right amygdala R2* iron content was positively correlated with SCOPA-Aut autonomic dysfunction scores in early PD.
Left hippocampus R2* iron content was positively correlated with SCOPA-Aut autonomic dysfunction scores in early PD.
Left hippocampus QSM value was positively associated with the cardiovascular sub-score of the Non-Motor Symptoms Scale, a measure of cardiovascular autonomic symptoms in PD.
Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia, caused by extra copies of TPSAB1, was found in 5% of a large irritable bowel syndrome cohort.
Immunophenotyping of peripheral blood mononuclear cells from individuals with HαT showed increased total and class-switched memory B cells compared to controls.
In the small bowel of individuals with HαT, there was expansion of tissue mast cells expressing CD203c, HLA-DR, and FcεRI.
Small bowel tissue from individuals with HαT showed higher intestinal epithelial cell pyroptosis compared to controls.
Small bowel tissue from HαT individuals also showed increased class-switched memory B cells locally in the gut.
Serum IgG profiles from individuals with HαT significantly differed from those with quiescent Crohn disease and from non-HαT controls.
Individuals with HαT had increased antibodies directed against GI-associated proteins compared to quiescent Crohn disease and non-HαT controls.
Patients with a comorbid mood disorder showed a less favorable CBT outcome for medically unexplained symptoms.
Patients with a comorbid anxiety disorder showed a less favorable CBT outcome for medically unexplained symptoms.
Higher symptom catastrophizing and worries were associated with a less favorable CBT outcome in patients with medically unexplained symptoms.
Higher tendencies toward somatosensory amplification predicted a less favorable CBT outcome in patients with medically unexplained symptoms.
Low symptom acceptance or self-efficacy predicted a less favorable CBT outcome in patients with medically unexplained symptoms.

Moderator analyses showed that associations between cognitive-emotional predictors and CBT treatment outcome were more pronounced specifically in patients with chronic fatigue syndrome and irritable bowel syndrome.
Fecal Bacteroidetes levels, measured by 16S rRNA gene real-time PCR, were significantly increased in FMS patients compared to healthy controls.
Fecal Bifidobacterium levels were significantly increased in FMS patients compared to healthy controls.
Fecal Firmicutes levels were significantly decreased in FMS patients compared to healthy controls.
Fecal Enterobacter levels did not differ significantly between FMS patients and healthy controls.
Fecal Streptococcus levels did not differ significantly between FMS patients and healthy controls.
Fecal Lactobacillus levels did not differ significantly between FMS patients and healthy controls.
A strong negative correlation was found between the percentages of Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes in the FMS patient samples.
A moderate positive correlation was observed between the percentages of Enterobacter and Bifidobacterium in the FMS patient samples.
IBS-D patients had significantly higher anxiety (SAS) and depression (SDS) scores than healthy controls, and 64.29% of IBS-D patients had comorbid anxiety and/or depression.
Colonic tryptase-positive mast cell staining intensity (IOD) was significantly increased in IBS-D patients compared to healthy controls.
The percentage of degranulated mast cells was significantly increased in colon tissue of IBS-D patients compared to healthy controls.
Colonic NPY2R expression (by immunohistochemistry) was significantly decreased in IBS-D patients compared to healthy controls.
Colonic PAR-2 expression (by immunohistochemistry) was significantly increased in IBS-D patients compared to healthy controls.
Colonic NPS expression (by immunohistochemistry) was significantly lower in IBS-D patients compared with healthy controls.
Colonic NPY expression (by immunohistochemistry) was significantly lower in IBS-D patients compared with healthy controls.
Peripheral blood plasma NPS levels were significantly lower in IBS-D patients compared to healthy controls.
Peripheral blood plasma NPY levels were significantly lower in IBS-D patients compared to healthy controls.
Colon tissue NPS levels (by ELISA) were significantly lower in IBS-D patients compared to healthy controls.
Colon tissue NPY levels (by ELISA) were significantly lower in IBS-D patients compared to healthy controls.
NPY2R protein expression (by Western blot) in colon tissue was significantly decreased in IBS-D patients compared to controls.
PAR-2 protein expression (by Western blot) in colon tissue was significantly increased in IBS-D patients compared to controls.

The authors propose a mechanistic model in which activated mast cells up-regulate PAR-2 function, altering neuropeptide (NPS/NPY) levels, which together drive clinical symptoms and psychological changes (anxiety/depression) in IBS-D.
aVNS increased fecal pellet number and fecal water content compared with sham-aVNS in opioid-induced constipated rats.
aVNS accelerated colon transit and whole gut transit compared with sham-aVNS.
aVNS increased choline acetyltransferase protein expression in colon tissue compared with sham-VNS.
aVNS increased GDNF protein expression in colon tissue compared with sham-VNS.
aVNS increased c-kit expression in myenteric interstitial cells of Cajal compared with sham-VNS.
aVNS decreased neural nitric oxide synthase protein expression in colon tissue compared with sham-VNS.

The prokinetic effects of aVNS were abolished by both subdiaphragmatic vagotomy and atropine administration, indicating dependence on an intact vagal efferent pathway and cholinergic muscarinic signaling.
aVNS decreased neuronal nitric oxide synthase protein expression in colon tissue compared with sham-aVNS.
The prokinetic (colon motility enhancing) effect of aVNS was abolished by subdiaphragmatic vagotomy, indicating dependence on an intact vagal pathway.
The prokinetic effect of aVNS was also abolished by atropine, implicating cholinergic muscarinic signaling in the mechanism.
aVNS increased c-fos expression in both the nucleus tractus solitarius and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, indicating central vagal pathway activation.
aVNS increased vagal efferent nerve activity compared with sham-aVNS, supporting a central-to-vagal efferent mechanism of action.

Microinjection of L-cysteine showed that brainstem sites triggering external and internal carotid vasodilation were distributed non-topographically throughout the parasympathetic parvocellular reticular formation (PcRt) in anesthetized rats.

Intravenous administration of a muscarinic receptor blocker and a nitric oxide synthase inhibitor abolished external carotid vasodilation, implicating peripheral muscarinic and nitric oxide receptor involvement in this response.
Islet transplantation, which secretes C-peptide at the implanted site, provided superior protection against diabetic nephropathy compared with simple insulin therapy in STZ-treated rats.
C-peptide treatment significantly increased expression of the podocyte slit-diaphragm proteins nephrin and synaptopodin, preventing high glucose-induced podocyte injury.

C-peptide suppressed high glucose-induced epithelial-mesenchymal transition and renal fibrosis by decreasing expression of snail, vimentin, alpha-smooth muscle actin and connective tissue growth factor.
High glucose activated the Notch signaling pathway, increasing Notch 1 and Jagged 1 expression, in podocytes.
Treatment with C-peptide down-regulated expression of the Notch signaling molecules Notch 1 and Jagged 1 that were induced by high glucose.
Treatment with C-peptide down-regulated expression of the TGF-β signaling molecule TGF-β1, which was activated by high glucose.
Women with endometriosis had a median Work Role Functioning Questionnaire score of 72.0, with the lowest scores in domains related to managing the workday and physical work demands.
Severe pelvic pain was inversely associated with work performance status among women with endometriosis.
Depressive mood was inversely associated with work performance status among women with endometriosis.
Poorer sleep quality was inversely associated with work performance status among women with endometriosis.
Self-perceived social support showed a borderline positive association with better work performance status.
A combined model of pelvic pain, depressive mood, sleep quality and social support explained 37.9% of the variance in work performance limitations in this endometriosis cohort.
Spanish women with endometriosis reported lower WRFQ scores, predominantly in work scheduling and physical demands, compared with previously published data on Spanish healthy adults.
In a pilot RCT of patients with diarrhea-predominant or mixed-type IBS, RBAC supplementation for four weeks was reported effective in 63.2% of patients versus 30% on placebo.

In the same IBS trial, RBAC supplementation was associated with significant changes in serum neutrophil and lymphocyte counts and a lower neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, suggesting reduced subclinical inflammation.
RBAC-treated IBS patients showed significant within-group improvement in reflux, diarrhea, and constipation symptoms compared to baseline, though between-group differences were not significant.
Four weeks of RBAC supplementation in mixed-type IBS patients lowered CRP and the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, indicating an anti-inflammatory effect.
In a small observational study of CFS patients taking RBAC for two months, symptom improvement occurred only in the subgroup with a clear viral etiology (4 of 10 patients).
A hypothesized mechanism links RBAC-induced increases in NK cell activity to improvement in fatigue symptoms in CFS patients with viral etiology.
A placebo-controlled RCT of 71 CFS patients found RBAC (6 g/day, 8 weeks) was not superior to placebo in reducing fatigue on the Chalder physical fatigue score.
In cancer patients with CFS from cancer treatment, combined RBAC plus oncothermia significantly reduced fatigue scores from baseline, unlike the standard-treatment-only control group.
Eccentric exercise significantly increased Collagen I protein expression in skeletal muscle compared with normal controls.
TGF-β1 protein expression was significantly higher in the exercise group than in normal controls.
CTGF protein expression was significantly higher in the exercise group than in normal controls.
The ratio of phosphorylated ERK to total ERK was significantly higher in the exercise group than in normal controls.
Acupuncture significantly reduced the exercise-induced increase in Collagen I expression.
Acupuncture significantly reduced the exercise-induced increase in TGF-β1 expression.
Acupuncture treatment significantly reduced the elevated Collagen I protein expression seen in the exercise group, compared with exercise alone.
Acupuncture significantly reversed the exercise-induced elevation of TGF-β1 protein expression compared with the exercise-only group.
Acupuncture significantly reversed the exercise-induced elevation of CTGF protein expression compared with the exercise-only group.
After acupuncture, the p-ERK/ERK ratio showed a downward trend compared with the exercise group, but this reduction did not reach statistical significance.
An intronic SNP in RNF123 (rs1491985) reached genome-wide significance for association with chronic widespread pain in the UK Biobank discovery GWAS and replicated in six independent cohorts.
An intronic SNP in ATP2C1 (rs10490825) reached genome-wide significance in discovery and showed suggestive, directionally consistent association in replication (except in ELSA using a proxy SNP).
A COMT 3'-UTR variant (rs165599) was genome-wide significant in the discovery GWAS but did not replicate in 43,080 independent individuals, with inconsistent direction of effect across cohorts.
SNP-based heritability of chronic widespread pain was estimated at 33% on the liability scale, indicating substantial common-variant genetic contribution.
Genetic correlation analysis found the strongest positive correlation between CWP genetic risk and depressive symptoms.

Body mass index showed a positive, conditionally independent genetic correlation with chronic widespread pain, supporting a genetically mediated component to the known epidemiological BMI-CWP association.
Body mass index was phenotypically significantly higher in CWP cases than controls in all cohorts except the Rotterdam Study 3 (non-significant trend).
Cases of chronic widespread pain were significantly enriched for females compared with controls across all discovery and replication cohorts.
Six additional loci near or within HNRNPA1P46, LRRC3B, PDE6A, DPYSL2, ANXA11 and AL138498.1 were identified at a suggestive genome-wide threshold (p<5E-07) but did not reach formal significance.

Colocalisation analysis showed a 93% probability that the same variant (rs6809879, in complete LD with rs1491985) drives both CDHR4 eQTL expression in skeletal muscle and the RNF123 locus association with CWP.

A second colocalisation signal showed a 72% probability that a variant (rs13093525) controlling APEH exon-level expression in dorsal root ganglion tissue shares the same causal variant as the RNF123 CWP locus.
RNF123 was more highly expressed in skeletal muscle than in other GTEx tissue types, and gene-set enrichment for CWP-associated genes was strongest in skeletal muscle.

Four independent gene-mapping strategies (gene-based, positional, eQTL and chromatin interaction mapping) converged on 89 genes overall, with 9 genes (MST1, GMPPB, APEH, RNF123, ARVCF, AMIGO3, IP6K1, TANGO2, TRAIP) implicated by all four methods.

CACNA2D2, a druggable target within the RNF123 locus, encodes the alpha-2/delta subunit of the voltage-dependent calcium channel that is the receptor for gabapentinoids used in fibromyalgia management, linking the genetic finding to an existing treatment mechanism.

The authors note that loss-of-function ATP2C1 mutations cause Hailey-Hailey disease, which can be treated with low-dose naltrexone, a drug also used in fibromyalgia management, and cite evidence that naltrexone restores calcium homeostasis in natural killer cells of chronic fatigue syndrome patients, suggesting a shared calcium-regulation mechanism.

The authors cite prior evidence that CCT5 (previously the only GWAS-identified CWP locus) has been implicated in neuropathy, and that small fibre neuropathy is increasingly recognised to underlie a subset of fibromyalgia cases.

The paper reviews that COMT rs4680, previously linked to CWP in a small 122-participant study, was not confirmed in a subsequent 3,017-participant study, and the largest COMT haplotype study to date (60,367 participants, 2,713 fibromyalgia cases) found no association with fibromyalgia.

Physical therapy (low-frequency electrical stimulation plus far-infrared irradiation) applied to cervical muscles during hospitalization was associated with recovery from ME/CFS in over half of patients.
Among the eight symptoms studied, recovery from depression showed the strongest statistical association with overall ME/CFS recovery.

Recovery of each of the eight representative whole-body symptoms accompanying ME/CFS (headache, cervical pain/stiffness, vertigo/dizziness, palpitation, dazzling, nausea/stomachache, fever of unknown etiology, depression) was significantly associated with ME/CFS recovery overall.

Pupil diameter decreased from admission to discharge in patients who recovered from ME/CFS but increased in those who did not recover, with a significant between-group difference, suggesting autonomic nervous system involvement in ME/CFS recovery.
ME/CFS recovery rate did not significantly differ by sex, age strata, or hospitalization duration.

At baseline, the majority of ME/CFS patients reported headache, cervical pain or stiffness, palpitation, dazzling, fever of unknown etiology, and depression (each >70%), while vertigo/dizziness and nausea/stomachache were somewhat less prevalent (43.1% and 56.7% respectively).

The recovery rate for cervical pain or stiffness after cervical muscle physical therapy was lower than for other symptoms, suggesting the therapy's benefit may act through a mechanism other than direct modulation of the cervical muscles themselves.

Subgroup analyses showed the pupil-diameter decrease associated with ME/CFS recovery was reproducible across sex, age, and hospitalization-duration strata, except in the longer hospitalization (61-120 days) group for raw change (D-A), and in women, younger patients (10-49 years), and the longer hospitalization group for the adjusted change ratio ([D-A]/A).
ME/CFS has a general population prevalence of 0.17-0.89% and occurs more frequently in women.
A retrospective study of 837 patients found that symptoms of acute infection preceded ME/CFS onset in 77% of patients.
A prospective study of 301 adolescents with acute EBV infection found 13% met 1994 CDC ME/CFS criteria at 6 months and 4% had still not recovered at 24 months.
Similar rates of post-infectious fatigue (about 12% at 6 months) were reported following Q Fever or Ross River Virus infection.
A prospective cohort of 618 patients diagnosed with non-specific viral infection found 12.9% met validated chronic fatigue criteria at 6 months.
Following the 1918 influenza pandemic, up to 40% of survivors remained chronically unwell with fatigue, lethargy, and difficulty concentrating exacerbated by exertion.
A Norwegian population health registry surveillance study identified an increased incidence of ME/CFS diagnosis after the 2009 H1N1 pandemic.
A study of 233 SARS survivors found that 27.1% met 1994 CDC criteria for ME/CFS at 41 months post-infection.
A meta-analysis of post-infectious symptoms in MERS and SARS found that 19.3% of patients experienced ongoing fatigue up to 39 months after infection.
A meta-analysis found higher prevalence of depression (14.9%), anxiety (14.8%), and PTSD (32.2%) in SARS/MERS survivors compared with population rates of approximately 7%.
A study found comorbid psychiatric conditions were more common in post-SARS ME/CFS patients but found no association with initial illness severity, other medical comorbidities, age, or gender.

In a murine coronavirus (MHV-A59) model, infection of astrocytes and microglia produced persistently elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines in the CNS at 30 days post-infection, unlike uninfected or non-neurotropic virus-exposed controls.
A meta-analysis found altered levels of tumor necrosis factor alpha, transforming growth factor beta, interleukin-2, and interleukin-4 in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
A separate meta-analysis analyzing 64 cytokines found no significant association with ME/CFS.
An attenuated TH1/TH17 cell response has been described in ME/CFS, resembling the pattern seen in latent infections such as EBV, along with altered natural killer and T-regulatory cell function.
In severe COVID-19 infections, significantly increased levels of anti-nuclear antibodies and rheumatic factor have been detected, suggesting heightened auto-reactive B cell activation.
Antibodies against muscarinic and adrenergic receptors have been identified in ME/CFS and are thought to be associated with postural orthostatic symptoms.

A meta-analysis of imaging findings in ME/CFS found a greater proportion of altered cerebral blood flow, structural cortical abnormalities, focal inflammation, and changes to functional connectivity compared with healthy controls.
HCoV-OC43 was found to be significantly more prevalent in CNS tissue of people with multiple sclerosis than in healthy controls.
A sleep study in SARS survivors unable to return to work found a high proportion of REM and alpha EEG sleep anomalies commonly seen in ME/CFS, suggesting a common pathologic mechanism.

A muscle biopsy study of 50 people with post-viral fatigue syndrome found mitochondrial degeneration and structural abnormalities in 80% of cases, versus minor structural changes in only 52% of healthy controls.

A small prospective gene expression study of five people with post-EBV ME/CFS found significant differences in genes associated with mitochondrial fatty acid metabolism, oxidation, membrane function, and apoptosis relative to HLA-matched healthy controls.
Coenzyme Q10, an anti-oxidant, has been found to be lower in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls in some studies.
Two systematic reviews on mitochondrial function in ME/CFS found no significant agreement in structural, genetic, metabolic, or oxidative pathway abnormalities between studies.
A large prospective cohort of 1733 patients hospitalized with COVID-19 found that 63% were still experiencing fatigue/myalgia at 6 months post-discharge.
Dyspnea, the other most common persistent symptom after coronavirus infection, was reported in up to 56% of inpatients at follow-up ranging from 1 to 6 months.

Some studies found an association between persistent post-acute COVID-19 symptoms and age, illness severity, and female gender, while ethnicity, psychiatric condition, comorbidity number, or obesity were not consistently associated.

No standard biomarker (CBC, lymphocyte/neutrophil/monocyte counts, D-dimer, CRP, LDH, IL-6, CD-25, LFTs, or creatinine) differentiated post-COVID patients who remained symptomatic from those who returned to baseline health.
Multiple post-acute COVID-19 studies found no association between illness severity, presence of chronic symptoms, and objective measures of respiratory function.

Recent evidence suggests graded exercise therapy may accentuate post-exertional malaise in some ME/CFS patients, and patient narratives describe post-acute COVID-19 symptoms worsening even with minimal exertion.
Dyspnea is seen in up to 36% of people diagnosed with ME/CFS and is considered part of the broader category of orthostatic intolerance, along with postural tachycardia and hypotension.
Reported rates of full recovery from post-acute COVID-19 symptoms ranged from 13% to 86% at follow-up periods of 30 to 186 days across studies.
In a large prospective cohort of 1733 hospitalized COVID-19 patients, 63% still reported fatigue or myalgia at 6 months post-discharge.
Dyspnea was reported in up to 56% of COVID-19 inpatients at follow-up ranging from 1 to 6 months, mirroring patterns seen after previous coronavirus outbreaks.
Pulmonary restrictive spirometry and imaging abnormalities were found in more than half of post-COVID-19 patients but did not correlate well with initial disease severity or overall symptom burden.

Some studies found an association between persistent post-COVID-19 symptoms and older age, greater illness severity, and female gender, while ethnicity, psychiatric history, comorbidity count, and obesity were not consistently associated.

No standard laboratory biomarker (CBC, lymphocyte/neutrophil/monocyte counts, D-dimer, CRP, LDH, IL-6, CD-25, liver function tests, creatinine) differentiated patients who remained symptomatic after COVID-19 from those who returned to baseline health, paralleling the lack of biomarkers in ME/CFS.

Graded exercise therapy, recommended by NICE guidelines for ME/CFS, may worsen post-exertional malaise in some patients, and this exacerbation has also been described in post-acute COVID-19 patient narratives.
Some experts have cautioned against the use of graded exercise therapy for managing fatigue in post-acute COVID-19.
Dyspnea occurs in up to 36% of people diagnosed with ME/CFS and is considered part of the broader category of orthostatic intolerance, alongside postural tachycardia and hypotension.

Unlike ME/CFS dyspnea, post-COVID dyspnea is not clearly linked to orthostatic intolerance and may instead represent pulmonary fibrosis following inflammatory lung injury, supported by imaging and pulmonary function abnormalities.

Multiple post-acute COVID-19 studies found no association between illness severity, presence of chronic symptoms, and objective measures of respiratory function, suggesting an alternate mechanism of pathogenesis beyond direct lung injury.
The higher rate of psychiatric comorbidities observed after epidemic outbreaks is likely driven by external stressors related to the pandemic rather than a direct effect of infection itself.
At least one persistent symptom was reported in 75% of post-COVID-19 patients at follow-up ranging from 7 to 12 weeks.
A systematic review of 28 post-COVID-19 symptom studies found fatigue, dyspnea, and anosmia were the most frequently reported symptoms lasting more than 3 weeks.
Reported rates of full recovery from post-acute COVID-19 symptoms ranged widely from 13% to 86% across studies with follow-up between 30 and 186 days.
Plasma miR-21 levels were increased in both mild/moderate and severely affected ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
Plasma miR-34a was increased in ME/CFS patients versus HC, though this was the weakest signal, borderline after multiple-testing adjustment.
Plasma miR-92a was increased in ME/CFS patients versus HC, consistent with prior PBMC data.
Plasma miR-126 was increased in ME/CFS patients versus HC, potentially reflecting a compensatory endothelial-protective response.
Plasma miR-200c was increased in ME/CFS patients versus HC and may relate to acetylcholine-induced endothelial dysfunction via reduced Sirt1/eNOS activity.

Reanalysis of an independent published PBMC microarray dataset confirmed increased expression of miR-21, miR-34a, miR-92a, and miR-126 in ME/CFS patients versus HC, with miR-200c showing a borderline non-significant increase.

Linear discriminant analysis using the five-miR panel correctly classified 60.8% of ME/CFS patients with at least 80% probability, versus only 30.4% of healthy controls classified as such, suggesting the miR panel discriminates disease status but not severity.
The five-miR panel could not distinguish severely affected from mild/moderate ME/CFS patients, with classification probabilities near 50% for each group.
The five studied miRs were highly and positively correlated with each other across all study participants regardless of group, suggesting coordinated regulation.

In healthy controls only, miR-34a, miR-92a, and miR-200c showed positive Spearman correlations with erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and miR-34a and miR-92a correlated with diastolic pressure; these correlations were not evident in ME/CFS patients, possibly masked by patient heterogeneity.

Bioinformatics network analysis of the five-miR target/protein-protein interaction network identified HDAC1 as the most central node (highest degree and betweenness centrality) among 135 interacting proteins.

Functional enrichment analysis of predicted miR targets showed the top over-represented biological processes included regulation of vasculature development, reproductive structure development, response to oxidative stress, ERK1/ERK2 cascade, and response to oxygen levels.
Fatigue severity scale scores were markedly higher in both mild/moderate and severely affected ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
SF-36 physical functioning and other health-related quality of life subscales were significantly lower in both mild/moderate and severely affected ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), a non-specific inflammation marker, was increased in ME/CFS patients compared to HC, consistent with a previous UKMEB cohort report.
Creatine phosphokinase (CPK) and creatinine, markers of muscle activity, were reduced in both ME/CFSmm and ME/CFSsa patients relative to HC, consistent with muscle atrophy/reduced activity.

Body composition was altered in ME/CFS: waist circumference, body metabolic rate, and body muscle bioimpedance were lower, while body fat bioimpedance was higher, in both ME/CFSmm and ME/CFSsa versus HC.
Blood pressure and CRP levels did not significantly differ between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls, consistent with immunological heterogeneity across ME/CFS cohorts.

Prior in vivo studies using flow-mediated dilatation (FMD) and EndoPAT report endothelial dysfunction in 40-51% of ME/CFS patients, supporting the hypothesis that ED is present in a subset of patients, consistent with the ~61% classified via the miR panel in this study.

Autoantibodies against the M3 muscarinic acetylcholine receptor, which normally increases endothelial NO synthesis, were reported significantly higher in ME/CFS patients compared to HC in prior literature, and this receptor pathway is also implicated in POTS.
All three adolescents/young adults with confirmed or probable COVID-19 developed ME/CFS symptoms from the outset of illness and met full ME/CFS diagnostic criteria by 6 months.

All three participants developed profound postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), with heart rate increases on standing far exceeding the diagnostic threshold, several months after COVID-19 onset.
Patient 1 showed a 70 bpm increase between lowest supine and peak standing heart rate during a 10-minute passive standing test, consistent with POTS.
Patient 1's plasma histamine was elevated at 4.2 mg/mL (reference ≤1.8) and remained elevated on repeat testing at 3 and 7 months, suggesting mast cell activation.
Patient 1's chromogranin A was mildly elevated at 144 (reference 25-140), consistent with possible mast cell activation.
Patient 1's serum tryptase was normal despite other evidence suggestive of mast cell activation.
Neurodynamic testing revealed restricted range of motion (neural gliding dysfunction) in all three post-COVID-19 patients.
Two of the three post-COVID-19 patients had an abnormal (positive) Hoffman sign on neurologic examination.
Patient 2 met diagnostic criteria for hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome as a comorbid finding in post-COVID-19 ME/CFS.
Patient 1's cardiopulmonary exercise test at 4 months showed below-average peak VO2 (84% of predicted) despite a normal exercise ECG.
Neither of the two probable (unconfirmed by PCR) COVID-19 cases developed detectable SARS-CoV-2 antibodies during convalescence, despite characteristic symptoms and household exposure.

Persistent fatigue following COVID-19 infection appears independent of the severity of the initial infection, unlike ME/CFS following infectious mononucleosis where risk is related to acute infection severity.

Two of three patients with sustained elevated plasma histamine showed improvement in fatigue and cognitive dysfunction after treatment with H1 histamine receptor-blocking drugs, consistent with a mast cell activation mechanism.

All three patients had orthostatic intolerance symptoms emerging very early in the illness course (within 1 day to 2 weeks), suggesting autonomic dysfunction may be an early, direct consequence of viral infection rather than secondary to deconditioning.
Stroke volume index measured by Nexfin CO Trek finger plethysmography was significantly higher than suprasternal aortic Doppler-derived SVI both supine and at end-tilt.
Bias, limits of agreement, and percent error between Nexfin CO Trek and Doppler-derived SVI were high, with percent errors of 37-43% before calibration.
Calibrating supine SVINexfinCOTrek to SVIDoppler reduced the percent error to an acceptable 29%, allowing SVINexfinCOTrek to be used for tracking SVI changes during tilt testing.

A 33-year-old woman with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and temporomandibular disorder was treated with an anterior repositioning splint and proprioception exercises, with pre/post assessment via surface electromyography, T-scan, and stabilometric platform.

The patient also received osteopathic manipulation treatment (OMT) as physical rehabilitation, which along with the gnathological therapy proved effective in improving symptomatology and functionality as confirmed by digital findings.
Temporomandibular disorders are described as among the most frequent complaints in EDS patients, alongside chronic generalized pain and musculoskeletal dysfunctions due to joint hypermobility.
Several studies suggest a link between chronic low back pain and joint hypermobility, including hypermobility spectrum disorder (HSD).
Lower back pain in patients on the HSD-EDS spectrum is described as multifactorial in origin and should not be considered solely in anatomical terms.
Perioperative complication rates after lumbar spinal surgery in the hypermobile EDS population have been reported to be as high as 50%.
Vascular type EDS has a particular propensity for severe bleeding complications, warranting caution in surgical management, especially when EDS subtype is unclear.
The authors advocate multidisciplinary management involving physiotherapists, pain physicians, surgeons, and psychologists for patients with coexisting hypermobility and chronic lumbar back pain.

The patient was found to carry a heterozygous splice-site variant in COL3A1 (c.1662+1G>A) causing aberrant splicing at the exon 23–intron 23 boundary, confirming a diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

The patient presented with cystic lung disease and recurrent pneumothorax as the initial and dominant clinical manifestation of vascular EDS, an atypical presentation not classically emphasized in the condition.

Physical examination revealed classic vascular EDS features including deep-set eyes with infraorbital creases, thin skin with increased venous visibility, and a history of easy bruising unrelated to trauma.

The patient's father died of a brain haemorrhage and had a history of unexplained hepatic arterial rupture, consistent with a familial pattern of vascular fragility supporting the vascular EDS diagnosis.
Genetic testing for FLCN mutations to rule out Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome as an alternative cause of cystic lung disease was negative.

Vascular imaging of the intracerebral, abdominal, and thoracic arteries was normal despite the confirmed vascular EDS diagnosis, indicating no arterial complications had yet developed at the time of evaluation.

The authors note that management recommendations for pneumothorax in vascular EDS favour a conservative approach, with surgical intervention avoided except in life-threatening situations due to risk of bleeding from fragile tissue.
The combined diagnosed prevalence of EDS and Hypermobility Spectrum Disorder is 1 in 500.

Classical EDS results from COL5A1 (type V collagen) mutations that cause either haploinsufficiency via nonsense-mediated decay or production of a structurally defective procollagen retained in the ER, impairing type I collagen fibril regulation.
Vascular EDS results from mutations in COL3A1 (type III collagen), causing the same haploinsufficiency or defective-procollagen mechanisms that impair type I collagen fibril organization.

In a large cohort of 177 EDS patients, TEM analysis found 83% of clinically diagnosed patients had a normal report, and among 24 genetically confirmed patients 29% also had a normal biopsy, with no TEM finding specific to any EDS subtype.
vEDS patient skin biopsies show collagen fibrils that are smaller, more variable in diameter, and of overall reduced density compared to normal.
Two individuals with a likely pathogenic COL5A1 variant did not present with the expected 'flower-like' collagen fibril pattern typical of classical EDS.

EDS/HSD fibroblasts across main subtypes show a shared 'integrin switch': downregulation of collagen receptor α2β1 and fibronectin receptor α5β1, with compensatory upregulation of the vitronectin receptor αvβ3, which acts as an alternative fibronectin receptor.
Adding collagen to the culture media of human EDS fibroblasts restores α2β1 integrin surface expression and reverses the integrin switch, a phenomenon termed phenotypic correction.
hEDS/HSD fibroblasts cultured on a stiff substrate show excessive actin stress fibers compared to control, but these are absent when hEDS/HSD fibroblasts are examined directly within native tissue.
In cEDS and vEDS fibroblasts, cell-ECM adhesion is specifically mediated by the αvβ3 integrin-fibronectin interaction, a dependency not observed in control cells.
Fibronectin organization is impaired in EDS/HSD, present in the ECM only as rare fibrils rather than a normal network.

cEDS and vEDS fibroblasts show a disorganized actin cytoskeleton and decreased migratory capacity, whereas hEDS and HSD fibroblasts show actin organized into stress fibers and significantly increased migration.

In animal dermatosparaxis (ADAMTS2 mutation, equivalent to human dermatosparaxis EDS), fibroblast gel contraction ability correlates with clinical severity: mildly affected sheep fibroblasts approach normal contraction while severely affected calf/sheep fibroblasts fail to contract the gel, including in less-affected tissues of the same severely affected animal.

Dermatosparaxis fibroblasts lack surface expression of a 34 kDa collagen-binding protein related to anchorin CII, preventing effective adhesion to type I and IV collagens and impairing gel contraction.

Historic gel contraction studies in human EDS fibroblasts (including dEDS with an identical genetic basis to animal dermatosparaxis) showed no contraction abnormality compared to controls, leading to the original conclusion that fibroblast dysfunction did not contribute to human EDS/HSD pathogenesis.
hEDS/HSD fibroblasts show enhanced expression of matrix metalloproteinase MMP-9, which could promote ECM disassembly and prevent collagen-α2β1 engagement.

The αvβ3 integrin specifically rescues cEDS and vEDS fibroblasts from anoikis (a form of cell death triggered by ECM detachment), suggesting the integrin switch is a survival response to defective collagen-ECM engagement.

In a related connective tissue disorder highly associated with EDS/HSD, Pelvic Organ Prolapse fibroblasts show significantly higher static expression of actin, α-tubulin, and vimentin compared to control fibroblasts, but respond abnormally (decreased actin) under mechanical strain versus controls (increased actin).
Vimentin-null fibroblasts show a reduced ability to contract collagen gels, implicating intermediate filaments in tractional force generation relevant to connective tissue maintenance.

The authors propose that fibroblast dysfunction and membrane-bound collagen assessment may also be relevant to fibromyalgia and ME/CFS, which show significant but poorly understood overlap with hypermobility and connective tissue abnormalities.
Genetic testing identified a heterozygous germline splice acceptor site mutation in intron 23 of COL3A1, a known pathogenic variant, confirming the diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

Histopathologic examination of surgical lung biopsy specimens showed intra-alveolar accumulation of red blood cells, hemosiderin-laden macrophages, and round fibro-osseous nodules scattered in a hemorrhagic background, without disruption of the vascular wall on van Gieson elastic staining.
The patient's father had a history of recurrent pneumothorax and spontaneous intraabdominal bleeding due to aneurysmal rupture of the common hepatic artery, consistent with a familial vEDS phenotype.

Vascular EDS accounts for approximately 4%-5% of EDS cases and carries a high rate of fatal cardiovascular and gastrointestinal complications, such as cerebrovascular hemorrhage or intestinal rupture, and pregnancy can be fatal due to uterine or uterine vessel rupture.

Prior literature (Kawabata et al.) reported that fragile lung parenchyma with spontaneous laceration, acute hemorrhage/hematoma, and fibro-osseous nodules are frequently identified in surgical lung biopsy specimens of vEDS patients, serving as histopathologic clues for diagnosis, consistent with the present case.
The paper reports a case series and literature review on the use of vertical sleeve gastrectomy in adolescent and young adult patients with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
The sample of individuals with suspected EDS+ showed high levels of clinically significant anxiety and depressive symptoms.
Pain severity ratings were significantly correlated with depressive symptom severity but not with anxiety severity in individuals with EDS+.
Higher perceived interoceptive attention regulation ability was significantly associated with less severe anxiety and depressive symptoms in individuals with EDS+.
Interoceptive attention regulation did not moderate the relationship between pain severity and anxiety or depressive symptom severity in EDS+ patients.

Whole-exome sequencing identified a pathogenic heterozygous missense variant c.1052G>T in COL3A1, causing substitution of glycine with valine at position 351, confirming a diagnosis of EDS type IV (vascular type) in the patient.

A 25-gauge pars plana vitrectomy with endodiathermy and laser photocoagulation under air successfully reattached the retina and restored visual acuity in this EDS type IV patient, with the retina remaining attached at 8-month follow-up.

Prior published cases of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment in EDS (types VI and VIa) managed by pars plana vitrectomy required multiple revitrectomies due to redetachment with proliferative vitreoretinopathy and resulted in poorer visual outcomes (6/60 and 1/60) compared with the favorable outcome achieved in this EDS type IV case.

EDS type IV patients have congenitally thin and fragile arterial walls due to COL3A1 mutations affecting collagen type III, predisposing them to arterial dissection, tears, and bleeding complications, which was a key surgical consideration in this case.

Intraoperative examination revealed ten retinal breaks across all four quadrants (two preoperatively identified U-shaped tears plus eight additional breaks found during surgery), consistent with widespread retinal fragility in this EDS type IV patient.

EDS has been associated with a range of ophthalmological manifestations including convergence insufficiency, blue sclera, dry eye syndrome, keratoglobus, high myopia, retinal tears, angioid streaks, corneal fragility/rupture, microcornea, conjunctivochalasis, vitreous hemorrhage, scleral rupture, and lens dislocation.

A 19-year-old female with classic-type EDS and skeletal Class II malocclusion with transverse discrepancy and severe crowding was treated with orthodontic camouflage using anchor screws and Class II elastics instead of orthognathic surgery, due to risks of skin bruising, poor wound healing, and temporomandibular disorder.

Classic EDS is characterized by joint hypermobility and fragile, easily bruised skin that heals with distinctive 'cigarette-paper' scars, which informed the decision to avoid orthognathic surgery in this patient.
The overall prevalence rate of genodermatoses in Las Tunas Province, Cuba, from 1989-2019 was 46.51 per 100,000 population.
Neurofibromatosis type 1 had the highest prevalence rate among genodermatoses studied, at 13.6 per 100,000 population.
Classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome was the second most prevalent genodermatosis in Las Tunas Province, at 7.1 per 100,000 population.
Ichthyosis vulgaris was the third most prevalent genodermatosis in Las Tunas Province, at 5.0 per 100,000 population.
Cutaneous mastocytosis had a prevalence of 2.4 per 100,000 population, among the more common genodermatoses in the province.
The incidence rate of classical Ehlers-Danlos syndrome peaked at 44.4 per 1000 genodermatosis cases in 2013.
Complications among genodermatosis patients decreased from 40% (22/55) in 1989-2009 to 21.1% (41/194) in 2010-2019, coinciding with the multidisciplinary service implementation.
Pyodermitis was the most common complication among genodermatosis patients across the whole study period, accounting for 29.1% (16/55) of complications.
Overall survival among genodermatosis patients in Las Tunas was high (98.0%), with only 5 deaths recorded across the entire 1989-2019 study period.
Consanguinity was identified among cases of epidermolysis bullosa (Herlitz type) and xeroderma pigmentosum in the study population.
The municipality of Majibacoa had the greatest proportional share of registered genodermatosis cases (0.07% of population).

The paper notes that underlying conditions associated with pediatric nonaortic arterial aneurysm formation include Ehlers-Danlos type IV syndrome, among other connective tissue and vascular disorders.

Repeated molecular genetics workups (at initial presentation and again after the second recurrence) found no evidence of an underlying genetic connective tissue or vascular condition (e.g., EDS), and the brachial artery aneurysm was classified as idiopathic.

Excision of the recurrent brachial artery aneurysm with reversed saphenous vein graft reconstruction plus circumferential reinforcement using an 8-mm Gore-Tex vascular graft wrap at the anastomotic sites and along the vein graft prevented aneurysm recurrence, with a patent graft and intact radial pulse at 18 months postoperatively.

Circumferential wrapping of the anastomotic sites with acellular dermal matrix during the second surgical repair failed to prevent aneurysm recurrence, likely because the material was incorporated and resorbed over time.

Pathology of the excised brachial artery aneurysm showed a true aneurysm with intramural capillary endothelial hyperplasia and fibrosis consistent with organized mural thrombus, and later specimens described native arterial disease with extensive myxoid lining and proliferating vascular channels sparing the interposed vein graft.
Adolescents with functional abdominal pain disorders (FAPDs) and joint hypermobility had reduced vagal efficiency compared to adolescents with FAPDs but without joint hypermobility.
Adolescents with FAPDs and joint hypermobility had reduced vagal efficiency compared to healthy controls.

Adolescents with FAPDs and joint hypermobility showed lower and less dynamic respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA) and heart period (HP) values during posture shifts (supine, sitting, standing), with the strongest differences seen in supine position and using the vagal efficiency metric.
A Beighton score cutoff of ≥4 was identified as the optimal threshold for distinguishing differences in autonomic function among adolescents with FAPDs.
Over half of cryptogenic small fiber neuropathy cases were seropositive for TS-HDS and/or FGFR-3 antibodies, with TS-HDS being the more common of the two.
Seropositive patients were more likely to show a nonlength dependent pattern of epidermal nerve fiber loss on skin punch biopsy.
Neuropathic pain was the primary presenting symptom in the large majority of seropositive patients.
A subset of seropositive patients reported widespread pain, a symptom overlapping with fibromyalgia presentations.
Seropositive cases were much more likely to present acutely compared with seronegative cases.
Nearly a quarter of seropositive patients had received an incorrect initial diagnosis, including fibromyalgia, before their SFN was identified.
Eight seropositive small fiber neuropathy patients treated with intravenous immunoglobulin had a 42% reduction in pain scores compared to pre-treatment.
IVIG-treated seropositive patients showed a 44% reduction in Utah Neuropathy Score after treatment.
Epidermal nerve fiber density on skin punch biopsy improved following IVIG treatment in seropositive patients.
TS-HDS/FGFR-3 antibody-positive small fiber neuropathy cases are frequently misdiagnosed as other conditions, including fibromyalgia.
PPG spectral entropy was significantly reduced during thermal pain stimulation compared to the no-pain control condition in healthy subjects.
EEG spectral entropy increased slightly during thermal pain stimulation compared to the no-pain control condition, with significant discrimination in the 26-30 Hz range.
Both one-dimensional and two-dimensional spectral entropy derived from combined EEG and PPG signals differentiated the painful condition from the no-pain control state.
The majority of MCAS participants reported clinically significant levels of depressive symptoms.
Younger age among MCAS participants was associated with higher rates of clinically-significant depression.
Greater loneliness among MCAS participants was associated with more severe depressive symptoms.
More disease-specific stressors among MCAS participants were associated with greater depressive symptoms.
Greater illness intrusiveness was associated with greater magnitude of depressive symptoms in MCAS participants.
Lower social support was associated with greater magnitude of depressive symptoms in MCAS participants.
Lower optimism was associated with greater magnitude of depressive symptoms in MCAS participants.

Mast cells can be activated through multiple surface receptor pathways in addition to the classic IgE-mediated route, contributing to allergic, immunologic, and infectious inflammatory conditions across organ systems.
Current consensus criteria for diagnosing MCAS require clinical symptoms of anaphylaxis correlating with elevation of a mast cell activation biomarker that improves with H1-antihistamine treatment.
Clinical symptoms of MCAS can overlap with those of neurogenic disorders such as dysautonomia, making accurate differential diagnosis important for appropriate treatment.

Anti-PD-L1 administration during the sensitization phase resulted in lower serum specific anti-OVA IgE at D27 compared with the OVA-only and isotype control groups, although still higher than PBS negative controls.
The rise in serum specific anti-OVA IgG1 seen on D27 in OVA-sensitized and isotype control mice was blocked by anti-PD-L1 administration during sensitization.
There was no significant difference in serum anti-OVA IgG2a levels among PBS, OVA, anti-PD-L1, and isotype control groups.

Anti-PD-L1 administered during the sensitization phase abolished the significant Evans blue extravasation (ACA positivity) seen in OVA-sensitized and isotype control mice, with no difference from PBS controls.

When anti-PD-L1 was administered only before the challenge (effector phase, group 5), the ACA reaction remained positive with significant Evans blue extravasation, similar to the OVA and isotype groups, unlike blockade during sensitization.

Histological quantification showed OVA-sensitized mice had fewer intact (CAE-stained) mast cells, indicating more degranulation, whereas anti-PD-L1 treatment during sensitization attenuated this reduction, preserving a higher number of resting mast cells compared to OVA alone.

The authors conclude that PD-L1 blockade specifically during the sensitization phase, but not the effector/challenge phase, inhibits Th2-driven synthesis of specific IgE and IgG1 and downstream mast cell activation, indicating PD-L1's role in Th2 lymphocyte polarization rather than direct mast cell effector function.
Costunolide administration relieved intestinal dysfunction and depression-like behaviours in mice with chronic unpredictable mild stress-induced IBS.
Costunolide treatment improved low-grade colon inflammation and intestinal mucosal permeability in IBS mice.
Costunolide inhibited the activation of colonic mast cells in stress-induced IBS mice.
Costunolide upregulated colonic Occludin expression in IBS mice.
Costunolide downregulated colonic Claudin 2 expression in IBS mice.
Costunolide upregulated GluN2A expression in hippocampal cells of IBS mice.
Costunolide treatment increased GluN2A expression in the hippocampus of stress-induced IBS mice.
Costunolide treatment increased BDNF expression in the hippocampus of stress-induced IBS mice.
Costunolide treatment increased phosphorylated ERK1/2 expression in the hippocampus of stress-induced IBS mice.
Costunolide treatment increased phosphorylated CREB expression in the hippocampus of stress-induced IBS mice.
Costunolide treatment increased 5-HT levels in hippocampal cells of stress-induced IBS mice.
Costunolide inhibited central 5-HT metabolism in stress-induced IBS mice.
Molecular docking analysis showed that costunolide could form hydrogen bonds with the serotonin transporter (SERT), suggesting it affects reuptake of 5-HT in the intercellular space.

IgE-mediated FcεRI crosslinking on mast cells alone (via OVA injection in IgE-sensitized mice) did not increase the number of endogenous 2W1S-specific CD4+ T cells in draining lymph nodes or spleen compared to controls.

In vitro, bone marrow-derived mast cells sensitized with OVA-specific IgE and stimulated with combined OVA and LPS released significantly more IL-6 than with LPS or IgE crosslinking alone, indicating FcεRI/TLR4 synergy.
