BMMCs derived from TLR4 knockout mice lost the synergistic IL-6 release seen with combined IgE, OVA, and LPS stimulation compared to wild-type BMMCs, confirming TLR4 is essential for the synergistic effect.

In vivo, combining IgE-mediated mast cell activation with the TLR4 agonist LPS significantly increased 2W1S-specific CD4+ T cell numbers in cervical lymph nodes and spleen compared to either stimulus alone.

Diphtheria toxin-mediated ablation of mast cells in Mcpt5-Cre x iDTR mice significantly diminished the 2W1S-specific CD4+ T cell response to combined IgE crosslinking and LPS in draining lymph nodes, with a less clear effect in the spleen.

TLR4-deficient mice showed significantly reduced 2W1S-specific CD4+ T cell numbers after LPS treatment compared to wild-type controls, and the IgE/OVA+LPS-induced T cell expansion seen in wild-type mice was abrogated in TLR4 knockout mice, demonstrating that global TLR4 is essential for the mast cell amplifying effect.

Mast cell-specific TLR4 deletion (Mcpt5-Cre x Tlr4-flox mice) did not abrogate the LPS-induced expansion of 2W1S-specific CD4+ T cells, indicating that TLR4 expression on mast cells themselves is not solely responsible for the synergistic effect and that other TLR4-expressing cells likely contribute.
Tamarixetin reduced degranulation in IgE/antigen-stimulated mouse bone marrow-derived mast cells.
Tamarixetin decreased leukotriene C4 generation in IgE/antigen-activated BMMCs.
Tamarixetin decreased prostaglandin D2 generation in IgE/antigen-activated BMMCs.
Tamarixetin inhibited phosphorylation of Akt in activated BMMCs.
Tamarixetin inhibited phosphorylation of IKK downstream of Akt in activated BMMCs.
Tamarixetin inhibited phosphorylation of nuclear factor κB downstream of Akt in activated BMMCs.
Tamarixetin downregulated phosphorylation of cytosolic phospholipase A2 in activated BMMCs.
Tamarixetin downregulated phosphorylation of p38 MAPK in activated BMMCs.
Tamarixetin reduced Ca2+ influx in IgE/antigen-stimulated bone marrow-derived mast cells.
The study concludes that tamarixetin inhibits mast cell degranulation and eicosanoid generation via both PLCγ1 and Akt signaling pathways.
About half of the interviewed patients reported disease-related impairments in everyday life, and 42.4% reported a psychological burden from mastocytosis.
The mean MC-QoL total score corresponded to a mild level of HRQOL impairment, with wide variation across the cohort.
About one-third of patients reported moderate or severe HRQOL impairment while another third reported no impairment at all.
Mast cell activation symptoms and perceived food intolerance were the factors with the greatest negative impact on HRQOL.
Higher patient age was associated with reduced HRQOL in mastocytosis.
Perceived food intolerance was among the symptom domains most strongly associated with reduced health-related quality of life in mastocytosis patients.
Higher patient age was associated with reduced health-related quality of life in adults with nonadvanced mastocytosis.
Higher body mass index was associated with reduced health-related quality of life in mastocytosis patients.
Higher serum tryptase level was associated with reduced health-related quality of life in patients with nonadvanced mastocytosis.
Longer duration of symptoms was associated with reduced health-related quality of life in mastocytosis patients.
Current use of drug therapy was associated with reduced health-related quality of life in mastocytosis patients.
Pathological bone density (e.g., osteoporosis/osteopenia) was associated with reduced health-related quality of life in mastocytosis patients.

Urodynamically defined diabetic cystopathy (bladder small fiber neuropathy) showed no significant correlation with systemic atherosclerotic risk markers including BMI, blood pressure, cardio-ankle vascular stiffness index, and Doppler echography plaque score/intima-media thickness in type 2 diabetes patients.

Diabetic cystopathy was not significantly correlated with peripheral nerve conduction abnormality (Dyck's criteria ≥7), suggesting bladder small fiber neuropathy may occur independently of large-fiber limb neuropathy.
No relationship was found between severity/duration of diabetes (HbA1c, disease duration) and urodynamic diabetic cystopathy in this cohort, despite prior literature suggesting such a link.
Validated patient-reported symptom questionnaires (overactive bladder symptom score and international prostate symptom score) also showed no relationship with atherosclerotic factors.

In Sjögren's syndrome, small fiber neuropathy is thought to result from immune-mediated damage to small unmyelinated/thinly myelinated fibers via perivascular inflammatory infiltrates with locally elevated proinflammatory cytokines.
Up to 32% of patients with connective tissue disorders have elevated serum anti-nerve growth factor antibodies that correlate with high disease activity and severe nervous system manifestations.
Increased expression of nerve growth factor occurs in painful vasculitic neuropathies.
Anticardiolipin antibodies may target myelin phospholipid antigenic determinants, potentially leading to demyelinating neuropathies.
Anticardiolipin antibodies are hypothesized to bind nodal axonal epitopes, potentially causing axonal variants of Guillain-Barré syndrome in SLE patients.
Primary antiphospholipid syndrome is associated with neuropathy in up to 35% of cases, most commonly sensorimotor polyneuropathy, followed by sensory polyneuropathy and carpal tunnel syndrome.

In a cohort of 22 antiphospholipid syndrome patients with autonomic neuropathy as the inaugural manifestation, 71% also had sensory small fiber neuropathy, and autonomic involvement was associated with significant thrombotic risk.
In systemic sclerosis, 35% of patients with peripheral neuropathy had an alternative, potentially reversible cause identified rather than SSc-related immune neuropathy.
Heerfordt syndrome, comprising facial palsy with uveitis, chronic fever and parotid enlargement, is a pathognomonic cranial neuropathy presentation of sarcoidosis.
Subclinical neuropathy detected by electrophysiology was found in almost 77% of Behçet's disease patients, predominantly affecting lower extremity (sural and peroneal) nerves.

Asymptomatic, biopsy-proven vasculitic neuropathy was identified in 21 patients (20 with diffuse leg neuropathy, 1 with mononeuritis multiplex), with a reported 7.8% prevalence of asymptomatic vasculitic neuropathy among biopsy-proven vasculitis patients.

Serum NFL showed 100% specificity and 82% sensitivity at a cutoff of 155 pg/ml for distinguishing active vasculitic neuropathy from non-vasculitic neuropathy or systemic vasculitis without neuropathy.
Serum and CSF NFL are elevated across many types of acquired neuropathies regardless of clinical subtype, and serum NFL correlates with disease activity and disability progression.
High resolution nerve sonography showed the distal median nerve is significantly thicker in chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy compared to vasculitic neuropathy.
Tibial nerve thickening and hypoechogenicity, possibly due to intraneural edema, was demonstrated by ultrasound in eight patients with vasculitic neuropathy.

Superficial sural nerve biopsy alone has only 50% sensitivity for vasculitic neuropathy, while combined nerve-muscle biopsy adds 5.1% additional diagnostic yield in clinically suspected cases and 15% in established cases.
Direct immunofluorescence for IgG, IgM, and C3 on combined nerve-muscle biopsy demonstrated 92% specificity for diagnosing vasculitic neuropathy.

The only randomized controlled trial for severe neuropsychiatric SLE compared IV cyclophosphamide with IV methylprednisolone and included just 7 patients with peripheral neuropathy out of 32 total patients evaluated.

Pain treatment recommendations for immune-mediated neuropathy are extrapolated from diabetic peripheral neuropathy trials, with pregabalin having class I evidence and other agents (gabapentin, duloxetine, venlafaxine, amitriptyline, valproate, opioids, capsaicin) having class II evidence.
Systemic vasculitides have an annual incidence of 60–140 per million, and up to 60–70% of patients with systemic vasculitis develop neuropathy.
Rheumatoid arthritis involves the peripheral nervous system in up to 75% of cases, with mononeuritis multiplex occurring in up to 8% of patients.
In SLE, axonal degeneration is the cardinal histopathological pattern of neuropathy, seen in 70-80% of cases, while demyelination occurs in about 20%.
In Sjögren's syndrome, peripheral neuropathies occur in 2–64% of patients, with small fiber neuropathy the most frequent phenotype, while sensorimotor polyneuropathy occurs in only 1%.
In polyarteritis nodosa, up to 72% of patients present with mononeuritis multiplex, mainly in the lower extremities, while less than 2% associate cranial nerve palsy.
In eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), peripheral nervous system involvement occurs in up to 65% of patients.

Vasculitic neuropathy is the first clinical presentation in 8% of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) patients, typically as mononeuritis multiplex, with a distinctive feature of lower cranial nerve mononeuropathy.
Motor and sensorimotor polyneuropathy occur at similar frequency (7%) in microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) as in GPA, whereas pure sensory neuropathy and cranial nerve palsy are far less common in MPA.

Serum neurofilament light chain at a cutoff of 155 pg/ml distinguished active vasculitic neuropathy from non-vasculitic neuropathy or systemic vasculitis without neuropathy with high specificity and sensitivity.
Serum and CSF neurofilament light chain levels are increased across many acquired peripheral neuropathies (not only vasculitic) and correlate with disease activity and disability progression.

High resolution nerve sonography showed that distal median nerve is significantly thicker in chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy compared to vasculitic neuropathy, aiding differential diagnosis.
A patient with vasculitic neuropathy showed bilateral nerve hypertrophy (median, ulnar, tibial and cervical nerve roots) on sonography that diminished after steroid treatment.
Tibial nerve thickening and hypoechogenicity, possibly from intraneural edema, were demonstrated by sonography in eight patients with vasculitic neuropathy.

Combined nerve-muscle biopsy adds diagnostic yield over superficial sural nerve biopsy alone (5.1% additional yield in clinically suspected, 15% in established vasculitic neuropathy), while sural nerve biopsy alone has only 50% sensitivity.
Direct immunofluorescence for IgG, IgM and C3 in combined nerve-muscle biopsy demonstrated 92% specificity for diagnosing vasculitic neuropathy.
Intraepidermal nerve fiber density is significantly reduced in small fiber neuropathy and skin biopsy is considered the gold standard test for this diagnosis.
Corneal confocal microscopy fiber density is inversely correlated with intraepidermal nerve fiber loss in the distal leg and with disease severity in small fiber neuropathy.

Up to 32% of patients with connective tissue disorders have increased serum anti-nerve growth factor antibody levels, which correlate with high disease activity and severe nervous system manifestations.
Increased expression of nerve growth factor occurs in painful vasculitic neuropathies, suggesting a role in pain pathogenesis.

A randomized controlled trial in severe neurological manifestations of SLE compared IV cyclophosphamide with IV methylprednisolone, but only 7 of 32 evaluated patients had peripheral neuropathy, limiting conclusions specific to neuropathy.

Guidelines state glucocorticoids alone or combined with immunosuppressive therapy achieve a 60-75% response rate in SLE neuropsychiatric manifestations, though this recommendation is not well referenced.

Asymptomatic, biopsy-proven vasculitic neuropathy was found in 21 patients (20 with diffuse leg neuropathy, one with mononeuritis multiplex), representing a 7.8% prevalence of asymptomatic vasculitic neuropathy among patients with biopsy-proven vasculitis.

Autonomic neuropathy was the inaugural manifestation in 22 antiphospholipid syndrome patients, with 71% also having sensory small fiber neuropathy, and autonomic involvement was associated with significant thrombotic risk.
In systemic sclerosis, 35% of patients with peripheral neuropathy had an alternative identifiable cause for nerve impairment, prompting recommendations to screen for other treatable etiologies.

ANCA involvement in vasculitic neuropathy pathogenesis is doubtful, since more than half of ANCA-negative EGPA patients have peripheral neuropathy, ANCA are rarely detected in the most common vasculitic neuropathy (non-systemic vasculitic neuropathy), and vasculitic neuropathy prevalence is similar in seropositive and seronegative ANCA-associated vasculitides.

A T-cell-mediated pathogenic model for vasculitic neuropathy has been proposed in which autoreactive T cells are recruited to the peripheral nerve, activated by antigen-presenting macrophages/endothelial cells/Schwann cells, and mature into cytotoxic T cells that destroy vessel walls, with macrophage inducible costimulator ligand upregulation restimulating effector memory T cells.
In Sjögren's syndrome small fiber neuropathy, immune-mediated inflammatory perivascular infiltrates involve elevated local proinflammatory cytokines including IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α and IL-1β.
One patient with a history of neurosarcoidosis experienced a moderate flare including small fiber neuropathy shortly after SARS-CoV-2 vaccination, which resolved spontaneously.
Across 27 cases of immune-mediated disease flare or new onset, the average time from vaccination to symptom onset was about 4 days, occurring predominantly after the first dose.
Most reported cases followed BNT162b2 mRNA vaccination, with fewer cases after mRNA-1273 or ChAdOx1 DNA vaccination.
Eleven of 27 cases presented with arthritis, mostly seronegative inflammatory arthritis, following vaccination.
Four cases of Behcet's disease flare, all with oral ulceration and limited to cutaneous/articular involvement, were reported in Israel following vaccination.
Three SLE cases were reported, including one discoid SLE that converted to systemic disease with pleuropericarditis shortly after a TLR-9 agonist-containing DNA vaccine.
Three new-onset vasculitis cases were reported, including a Henoch-Schönlein Purpura pattern and two cases of chilblain lesions linked to Type-I interferon elevation in skin.
Two new-onset myasthenia gravis cases occurred after the second dose of BNT162b2, one severe, and a new-onset multiple sclerosis case occurred a week after the first dose, responding well to therapy.
Two pericarditis cases were reported, one recurring 4 days after both first and second vaccine doses, treated successfully with NSAIDs and colchicine.
One new-onset polymyalgia rheumatica case and one new-onset RS3PE case (in a subject with prior PMR history) were reported following vaccination.
A case of ulcerative colitis with severe associated hypereosinophilic syndrome flared after vaccination.
The majority of the 27 cases (80.8%) received glucocorticoid therapy and all cases showed good therapeutic response with no severe resistant or progressive disease at time of writing.

The authors propose that mRNA/DNA vaccine stimulation of nucleic acid sensors (TLR-3/7/8/9, RIG-I, MDA5) and resultant Type-I interferon responses may mechanistically underlie the observed spectrum of immune-mediated disease flares/new onset.
Gastroparesis shows a strong female predominance in population-based epidemiological cohorts.
Type 1 diabetes confers a substantially higher 10-year cumulative risk of developing gastroparesis than type 2 diabetes or non-diabetic controls.

A subset of gastroparesis presents post-virally/post-infectiously, suggesting acute GI infection can trigger chronic gastric motor dysfunction, though the consensus panel did not endorse infection as a definitive risk factor.
Connective tissue diseases and certain neurological disorders (Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, amyloid neuropathy) are consensus-endorsed risk factors for gastroparesis.

Heart-rate variability testing showed diabetic gastroparesis was more often associated with vagal (parasympathetic) dysfunction than idiopathic gastroparesis, and combined sympathetic/parasympathetic dysfunction correlated with more severe symptoms and more delayed gastric emptying in a larger cohort.
Idiopathic gastroparesis patients frequently show impaired gastric accommodation or visceral hypersensitivity to gastric distension, each linked to distinct symptom patterns.

Functional brain imaging shows altered central processing in gastroparesis, including altered insula connectivity and a tendency toward reduced insula gray matter volume, alongside altered cortical processing of visceral afferent signals in diabetic neuropathy linked to symptom severity and quality of life.
A long polyGT repeat polymorphism in the HMOX1 (heme oxygenase-1) gene promoter, associated with lower transcriptional activity, has been linked to worse outcomes in gastroparesis and other diseases.

Bloating and symptom overlap with functional dyspepsia (FD) and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) are common in gastroparesis, with the large majority of gastroparesis patients meeting Rome criteria for FD, especially postprandial distress syndrome.

Anxiety and depression scores are elevated in gastroparesis and correlate with symptom severity and hospitalization rates, but not with disease etiology (diabetic vs idiopathic) or gastric emptying rate.

In a large online survey of self-reported gastroparesis patients, quality of life measured by SF-36 was decreased, particularly on the physical health component, and this was negatively correlated with symptom severity (nausea, early satiety, abdominal pain).
Mortality risk is higher in diabetic than idiopathic gastroparesis, driven largely by cardiovascular comorbidity, per UK CPRD database analysis.

A phase 2 RCT of intranasal metoclopramide in diabetic gastroparesis patients found no overall significant symptom benefit versus placebo, but a significant effect emerged in a female-only subgroup analysis.
The ghrelin-receptor agonist relamorelin (RM-131) was studied in two randomized, placebo-controlled trials in diabetic gastroparesis, but a subsequent phase 3 program was discontinued.
A randomized controlled trial of nortriptyline in idiopathic gastroparesis patients showed no benefit over placebo.

A sham-controlled multicenter trial of gastric electrical stimulation (GES) reported improved vomiting frequency regardless of gastric emptying status, but most other studies failed to show acceleration of gastric emptying by GES, and earlier open-label benefits were not corroborated by RCTs.
Controlled trials of intrapyloric botulinum toxin injection failed to demonstrate improvement in symptoms or gastric emptying, despite earlier open-label studies suggesting short-term efficacy.
Hypothyroidism is more frequent among gastroparesis patients than in the general population, though the consensus panel did not endorse it as an established risk factor.

Consensus panel endorsed dietary adjustments (small particle size diet) and 5-HT4 receptor agonists as having therapeutic efficacy in gastroparesis, while explicitly not endorsing PPIs, most antiemetics, prokinetics as a class, neuromodulators, herbal therapies, acupuncture, psychological therapies, GES, botulinum toxin, pyloric myotomy, or gastrectomy due to insufficient consensus.
IL-6 is reported to be elevated in individuals with irritable bowel syndrome, consistent with a role in IBS pathophysiology.
Co-application of the GLP-1 receptor agonist exendin-4 with IL-6 potentiated colonic secretory currents and transepithelial resistance in Ussing chamber experiments compared to exendin-4 alone.
Vagal afferent fibers originating in the colonic submucosal layer showed larger electrophysiological responses to exendin-4 when IL-6 was also present.
Co-application of exendin-4 and IL-6 suppressed colonic circular muscle contractile activity in organ bath experiments.
Extrinsic vagal afferent activity originating in the colonic myenteric layer was similarly suppressed by co-application of exendin-4 and IL-6.
Post-prandial GLP-1 secretion is linked to exacerbation of IBS symptoms and can influence colonic secreto-motor activity.

Circulating small extracellular vesicles (EVs) are increased in the serum of patients with systemic mastocytosis (SM) compared to healthy volunteers, correlating with serum tryptase (mast cell burden).
SM-derived EVs, but not healthy volunteer EVs, carry mast cell-specific surface markers including MRGPRX2, tryptase, high-affinity IgE receptor, and KIT.
Treatment of hFOB1.19 pre-osteoblasts with SM-EVs, but not HV-EVs, caused substantial reductions in alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity, a marker of osteoblast differentiation.
SM-EVs reduced extracellular calcium mineral deposition (mineralization) by osteoblasts by more than 50% compared to untreated or HV-EV-treated cultures.
SM-EV treatment reduced protein expression of RUNX2, osteopontin (OPN), type I collagen (COL1), and phosphorylation of AKT and ERK1/2 in differentiating osteoblasts.
EVs isolated directly from bone marrow aspirates of SM patients also markedly reduced ALP activity and RUNX2 expression in osteoblast cultures, similarly to serum-derived SM-EVs.

SM-EVs significantly reduced ALP activity and RUNX2 expression during osteoblast differentiation of primary human mesenchymal stem cell (hMSC)-derived osteoblasts, extending the effect beyond a single cell line model.

Low-density EV fractions containing exosome/microvesicle markers (Annexin 1, CD9, CD63, ALIX) from SM serum, but not higher-density non-vesicular fractions or HV fractions, inhibited osteoblast differentiation by ~80%, localizing the active components to small EVs.
SM-EVs contain significantly higher levels of miR-21, miR-23a, miR-25, miR-93, and miR-30a compared to HV-EVs, with fold changes ranging from 1.5-fold (miR-21) to 40-fold (miR-25).

Levels of miR-21, miR-23a, and miR-30a (but not miR-25 or miR-93) in individual patients' SM-EVs significantly correlated with the degree of inhibition of osteoblast differentiation, implicating miR-23a and miR-30a in the effect.
miR-23a and miR-30a levels in EVs were significantly higher in SM patients with osteopenia/osteoporosis compared to those without, independent of gender.

In three patients with smoldering (more aggressive) SM and osteopathy, EV miR-23a and miR-30a levels were higher than in indolent SM with osteopathy, and all three caused >70% inhibition of osteoblast differentiation.

Transfection of osteoblasts with miR-23a or miR-30a mimics inhibited ALP activity and reduced RUNX2 expression, reproducing the effect of SM-EV treatment, whereas miR-25 and miR-93 mimics had no effect.
Combined transfection with miR-23a and miR-30a mimics caused stronger inhibition of osteoblast differentiation than either alone, while co-transfection with miR-93 lessened the inhibitory effects.

Knockdown of miR-23a or miR-30a in osteoblasts effectively reversed the SM-EV-induced reduction in ALP activity and RUNX2 expression, whereas knockdown of miR-21, miR-25, or miR-93 had no significant effect.

EVs shed from neoplastic mast cell lines HMC-1.1 (KIT V560G) and especially HMC-1.2 (KIT V560G plus D816V, the most common SM-associated variant) contained substantial amounts of miR-21, miR-23a, miR-25, miR-30a and miR-93, and caused concentration-dependent inhibition of osteoblast differentiation and mineralization.
Knockdown of miR-23a and miR-30a in HMC-1.2 mast cells reduced these miRNAs in shed EVs by ~50%, and correspondingly reduced the EVs' inhibitory effect on osteoblast differentiation by ~50%.
SM-EV treatment significantly reduced mRNA and protein levels of RUNX2, SMAD1, SMAD5, and (to a lesser extent) SMAD2, as well as BMP2, but did not affect SATB2 or CXCL12 expression in osteoblasts.

miR-23a and miR-30a mimics both reduced RUNX2 expression but showed relative specificity for SMAD targets: miR-23a preferentially reduced SMAD5, while miR-30a preferentially reduced SMAD1, with modest effects on SMAD2.
RUNX2 mRNA expression was reduced in bone marrow cells of SM patients with osteopenia/osteoporosis compared to those without, while ALP mRNA levels did not differ between the groups.

RANKL mRNA was reduced and OPG mRNA slightly increased in BM cells of SM patients with osteopenia/osteoporosis versus those without, markedly diminishing the RANKL/OPG ratio and arguing against increased osteoclastogenesis as the driver of bone loss.

In vivo, SM-EVs (from high-tryptase or osteoporosis-associated patients) injected into mice markedly reduced mRNA expression of Alp, Runx2, Smad1/5 (and to a lesser extent Smad2) in bone marrow cells and calvaria osteoblasts, while HV-EVs had no effect.
Treatment of pre-osteoblasts with SM-derived extracellular vesicles markedly reduced BMP2 mRNA and protein expression compared to untreated or HV-EV-treated cultures.
SM-EV treatment significantly reduced RUNX2, SMAD1, and SMAD5 mRNA levels (with a lesser effect on SMAD2), while SATB2 and CXCL12 expression were unaffected.

miR-23a preferentially suppressed SMAD5 with a slight effect on SMAD1 and none on SMAD2, whereas miR-30a preferentially suppressed SMAD1 over SMAD5 with a modest effect on SMAD2, indicating distinct target specificity.
RUNX2 mRNA expression was reduced in bone marrow aspirate cells from SM patients with osteopenia/osteoporosis compared to those without, while ALP mRNA levels did not differ between the groups.

In SM patients with osteopenia/osteoporosis, RANKL mRNA was reduced and OPG was slightly increased in BM cells, resulting in a markedly diminished RANKL/OPG ratio compared to patients without bone disease.
TRAP (ACP5) mRNA was unchanged and RANK mRNA was reduced in BM cells of SM patients with osteopenia/osteoporosis compared to those without.

In vivo, mice injected with SM-EVs (high tryptase or from osteopenia/osteoporosis patients) showed markedly reduced Alp, Runx2, and Smad1/5 mRNA (and to a lesser extent Smad2) in bone marrow cells from femurs/tibias and in calvarial osteoblasts.
Satb2 and Cxcl12 mRNA expression did not change in bone tissue of mice injected with any EV group, consistent with the lack of in vitro effect of SM-EVs and miRNA mimics on these transcripts.

Mice injected with EVs from neoplastic HMC-1.2 mast cells showed reduced Alp and Runx2 expression in calvarial osteoblasts, an effect attenuated when donor HMC-1.2 cells were transfected with miR-23a and/or miR-30a antagonists prior to EV collection.

Micro-CT analysis showed that injection of SM-EVs (high tryptase or from osteopenia/osteoporosis patients) into mice caused a 28% decrease in trabecular bone volume, fewer trabeculae, increased trabecular separation, and reduced bone mineral density, with no change in cortical bone.
Histomorphological analysis of proximal tibial bone in SM-EV-injected mice showed thinner trabeculae, reduced total bone area, and fewer Runx2-positive cells compared to HV-EV-injected mice.
Osteoclast numbers (multinucleated TRAP-positive cells) per field appeared reduced in SM-EV-treated mice but did not reach statistical significance.
SM-EVs did not affect in vitro differentiation of osteoclasts from mouse bone marrow cells, indicating a selective effect on osteoblasts rather than osteoclasts.

Within the SM cohort with osteoporosis/osteopenia and documented T-scores (n=13), EV levels of miR-23a significantly correlated with T-scores, while miR-30a showed a non-significant trend toward higher levels at lower T-scores.
EV levels of both miR-23a and miR-30a significantly correlated with total serum alkaline phosphatase levels in SM patients, supporting their link to clinical bone disease.
Injury to the hepatic branch of the vagus nerve during laparoscopic pancreaticoduodenectomy was independently associated with increased risk of delayed gastric emptying.
Postoperative intra-abdominal infection was identified as an independent risk factor for delayed gastric emptying after laparoscopic pancreaticoduodenectomy.

Preservation of the hepatic branch of the vagus nerve during laparoscopic pancreaticoduodenectomy was associated with a significantly lower incidence of delayed gastric emptying compared with HBVN injury, both before and after propensity score matching.
Delayed gastric emptying occurred in 33.2% of patients after laparoscopic pancreaticoduodenectomy, with grade B in 13.9% and grade C in 7.7% by ISGPS criteria.

Univariate analysis identified longer operative time, more estimated intraoperative blood loss, HBVN injury, postoperative pancreatic fistula (grades B/C), postoperative hemorrhage, intra-abdominal infection, and Clavien-Dindo grade ≥III complications as risk factors for delayed gastric emptying.
Among LDS type 1 patients, 27% had bilateral conductive hearing loss.
In LDS type 1, 9% had unilateral mixed hearing loss.
In LDS type 1, 36% had subclinical hearing loss.
In LDS type 2, 38% had conductive hearing loss.
In LDS type 2, 38% had subclinical hearing loss.
In LDS type 3, 40% had bilateral sensorineural hearing loss.
In LDS type 4, 43% had bilateral sensorineural hearing loss.
Bifid uvula was observed only in LDS types 1 and 2, occurring in 55% of LDS-1 patients.
A small proportion of LDS-1 patients (9%) had unilateral mixed hearing loss.
Tympanic membrane perforation following tympanostomy tube placement occurred in 45% of ears (10/22) among patients with LDS-1 and LDS-2.
Middle ear cholesteatoma occurred in 3 patients, all with LDS-1 or LDS-2.
One case of external ear canal cholesteatoma was found in a patient with LDS-3.
Across LDS subtypes, the degree of hearing loss observed ranged from mild to moderate severity.
Homozygous premature truncating variants in LTBP1 were identified in eight affected individuals from four unrelated consanguineous families with a novel cutis laxa syndrome.

Affected individuals present with connective tissue features (cutis laxa and inguinal hernia), craniofacial dysmorphology, variable heart defects, and prominent skeletal features (craniosynostosis, short stature, brachydactyly, and syndactyly).

In proband-derived dermal fibroblasts, C-terminal LTBP1 variants produce an altered protein loosely anchored in the microfibrillar network and cause increased ECM deposition associated with excessive TGFβ growth factor activation and signaling.
N-terminal LTBP1 truncation results in loss of LTBP1 protein but does not alter TGFβ levels or ECM assembly in proband fibroblasts, indicating a distinct mechanism from C-terminal variants.
In vivo validation with two independent zebrafish ltbp1 mutant lines showed abnormal collagen fibrillogenesis in skin and intervertebral ligaments and ectopic bone formation on the vertebrae.
One of the two mutant zebrafish lines additionally shows voluminous and hypo-mineralized vertebrae.
Affected individuals show variable heart defects as part of the LTBP1-associated cutis laxa syndrome phenotype.
Zebrafish ltbp1 mutant lines exhibit abnormal collagen fibrillogenesis in skin and intervertebral ligaments.
Zebrafish ltbp1 mutants show ectopic bone formation on the vertebrae.
One of the two mutant zebrafish lines shows voluminous and hypo-mineralized vertebrae.
The combined human and zebrafish data indicate that LTBP1 function is crucial for skin and bone ECM assembly and homeostasis.

Bi-allelic pathogenic variants in IPO8 were identified in 12 individuals from 9 families, causing a novel connective tissue disorder with cardiovascular, skeletal, neurologic, and immunologic features.
Eleven of 12 individuals showed dilatation of the ascending aorta, with early onset before age 1 year in the youngest patient.
Joint hyperlaxity with multiple joint dislocations was present in 11 of 12 individuals, and skin hyperextensibility and/or hernia in 11 of 12.
A subset of individuals with IPO8 deficiency displayed immunological abnormalities including hyperIgE, hyperIgG, hypoIgA, and hypereosinophilia, consistent with impaired TGF-β signaling.

Predisposition to allergic or inflammatory disease, previously documented in Loeys-Dietz syndrome, was evidenced in six of 12 individuals with IPO8 deficiency, including intestinal inflammation in 5/12 and allergic symptoms in 6/12.
Developmental delay was observed in 7 of 12 individuals, with mild intellectual disability in three and severe in one, presumed consecutive to joint instability.
Immunoblot analysis showed a striking reduction of IPO8 protein level in fibroblasts or EBV-B cells from four tested individuals, including two carrying homozygous missense variants.
Maternal-zygotic ipo8-/- zebrafish mutants displayed a spectrum of dorsalization phenotypes at 24 hpf, with only 4.5% appearing normal compared to 96.5% of WT embryos.
Most ipo8-/- zebrafish larvae (81%) developed heart edema by 3 days post-fertilization, and over 70% showed abnormal arterio-venous connections and poorly differentiated central arteries in the head.
Nuclear localization of pSmad1/5/9 was significantly reduced in ipo8-/- zebrafish embryos compared to wild type, with pSMAD signal instead detected in the cytoplasm and at cell membranes.
Transcriptomic analysis showed smad7, a direct transcriptional target of TGF-β/BMP signaling, was strongly decreased in ipo8-/- zebrafish embryos at both 13 and 24 hpf compared to WT.

IPO8 deficiency syndrome clinically overlaps with other TGF-β signalopathies (Marfan syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome, Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome), sharing cardiovascular, facial, and skeletal anomalies, with immune dysregulation and allergic disease as distinguishing features.

A companion study (Van Gucht et al.) reports overlapping developmental abnormalities in seven additional IPO8-deficient individuals and shows loss of ipo8 causes severe early-onset thoracic aortic aneurysm in a mouse model.

Bi-allelic loss-of-function variants in IPO8 cause a syndromic thoracic aortic aneurysm disorder with clinical overlap with Loeys-Dietz and Shprintzen-Goldberg syndromes, identified in seven individuals from six unrelated families.
A C57BL/6N Ipo8 knockout mouse model develops thoracic aortic aneurysm from 8-12 weeks of age in both sexes, with ascending aorta dilatation and dissection propensity most prominent in males.
Compliance assays suggest augmented passive stiffness of the ascending aorta in male Ipo8 knockout mice throughout life.
Immunohistological investigation of mutant aortic walls in Ipo8 knockout mice reveals elastic fiber disorganization and fragmentation.
Aortic walls of mutant Ipo8 mice show a signature of increased TGF-beta signaling as evidenced by nuclear pSmad2 accumulation.
RT-qPCR assays of the aortic wall in male Ipo8 mice demonstrate decreased Smad6 and Smad7 expression.
SMAD1-4, components of the TGF-beta signaling pathway, have been proposed as cargo molecules transported into the nucleus by importin 8.

The IPO8-related syndromic thoracic aortic aneurysm phenotype shows clinical overlap with Loeys-Dietz syndrome and Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome, both known TGF-beta-related connective tissue aortopathies.
Male Ipo8 knockout mice show more prominent ascending aortic dilatation and a greater propensity for dissection compared to females, indicating a sex difference in phenotype severity.

The authors propose that importin 8, being the most downstream TGF-beta-related effector implicated in TAA pathogenesis identified so far, represents a candidate drug target for thoracic aortic aneurysm.

Across all 14 included studies, bariatric surgery was consistently associated with increased parasympathetic modulation and overall heart rate variability, along with a decrease in resting heart rate.
The review concluded that the literature does not establish that improved HRV after bariatric surgery is directly caused by the surgical procedure itself.
There is limited evidence suggesting patients with type 2 diabetes show greater interim improvement in HRV after bariatric surgery than patients without diabetes.
Reduction in insulin resistance following bariatric surgery was correlated with increased HRV in some studies, but this association was not supported in others.
Improvement in leptin levels after bariatric surgery was associated with a greater increase in HRV.
Improvements in leptin levels following bariatric surgery were associated with greater increases in heart rate variability.
Improvements in NT-proBNP levels after bariatric surgery were linked with greater increases in heart rate variability.
ME/CFS prevalence is estimated at 0.1-0.7% of the population with an incidence of 0.015 new cases per 1000 person-years, suggesting around 3 million affected people in Europe.
At least two-thirds of ME/CFS cases occur in women, with young people in productive life phases preferentially affected, though the disease occurs in all age groups.
Studies from the UK and US consistently show increased mortality from suicide among people with ME/CFS.
One American study found increased cardiovascular and cancer mortality in people with ME/CFS, but this finding has not been confirmed by other studies.
Quality of life in ME/CFS is on average lower than in other chronic or disabling diseases such as multiple sclerosis, cancer, rheumatoid arthritis, depression, diabetes, epilepsy, or cystic fibrosis.
Extrapolating from UK data, ME/CFS may cost approximately 40 billion Euros per year to health services and society in Europe.

Postural tachycardia (standing heart rate increase >30/min in adults over 20 or >40/min in younger patients, or >120 bpm standing at any age) may occur in ME/CFS patients due to dysautonomia or relative hypovolemia, leading to a diagnosis of POTS.

Muscle fatiguability in ME/CFS is demonstrated by lower handgrip strength compared to healthy individuals and by a rapid fall in grip strength during repetitive contractions, particularly in severely affected patients.
Low creatine phosphokinase (CK) levels suggest either severe disease or very low physical activity levels in ME/CFS patients.
Elevated LDH and GPT/GOT liver enzyme levels are found in a subset of ME/CFS patients.
Elevated NT-proBNP may be found in ME/CFS patients and is associated with lower cardiac volume, warranting further investigation.
A subset of ME/CFS patients has diminished IgG/IgA/IgM levels and/or IgG subclass deficiency.
About half of pediatric ME/postinfectious fatigue syndrome cases manifest following typical EBV-associated infectious mononucleosis.
A gene expression study identified seven genomically derived subtypes of ME/CFS, each manifesting distinct clinical phenotypes.
Cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) may have long-term benefits in chronic fatigue but evidence is limited, and it should be used cautiously as a supportive, not curative, therapy.
Some ME/CFS patients have hypermobile joints or meet clinical criteria for hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS), which should be recognized as a comorbidity.
There is considerable symptom overlap between ME/CFS and fibromyalgia, and a concomitant diagnosis of fibromyalgia is often made.
A significant minority of ME/CFS patients, often quoted as around 25%, are virtually home- or bedbound.
Non-exudative pharyngitis and crimson crescents in the oral pharyngeal region have often been described on physical examination of ME/CFS patients.
Low daily doses of hydrocortisone (5–15 mg) improved fatigue and disability scores in ME/CFS patients without further suppressing the HPA axis.
Somewhat higher hydrocortisone doses (25–35 mg/day) caused a moderate decrease in endogenous ACTH and cortisol production in ME/CFS patients via the negative feedback loop.
Fludrocortisone supplementation produced positive results in some ME/CFS trials but not others.
An uncontrolled pilot study found DHEA supplementation significantly reduced ME/CFS symptoms including pain, fatigue, helplessness, anxiety, memory loss, and sexual problems.
Pregnenolone sulfate was suggested to have therapeutic potential to restore TRPM3 ion channel function in natural killer cells in ME/CFS.
A small placebo-controlled study found GH injections over 12 months beneficial for ME/CFS patients, with some able to resume work after long sick leave.
Placebo-controlled studies in fibromyalgia patients with relative GH deficiency showed GH injections over several months reduced pain and improved quality of life.
A large double-blind RCT of rhGH infusions in critically ill patients (1999) resulted in increased mortality, leading to near-cessation of GH use in critical care.
Small placebo-controlled studies by Lowe et al. showed supraphysiologic T3 doses (75-150 mcg/day) were safe and significantly effective for fibromyalgia symptoms compared to baseline and placebo.

A placebo-controlled study by Teitelbaum et al. showed euthyroid ME/CFS and fibromyalgia patients treated with T4 or desiccated thyroid hormone plus adrenal hormones, vitamins, minerals, and antibiotics experienced significant improvement.
Recent studies suggest low thyroid hormone function at target tissues in ME/CFS despite normal TSH and T4 laboratory values, resembling euthyroid sick syndrome/NTIS.
Partial hypoadrenalism (low production of adrenal hormones) has been well-documented in ME/CFS across numerous studies.
Researchers found evidence that hypoadrenalism in ME/CFS is caused by a central deficiency of CRH, paralleling mechanisms in prolonged critical illness.
Significant adrenal atrophy has been documented in ME/CFS patients and is surmised to be present in fibromyalgia patients.
Several studies found that ME/CFS patients had a blunted cortisol/ACTH response to CRH injection compared to controls, though this normalized when CRH was combined with desmopressin.
In fibromyalgia patients, CRH injection produced an exaggerated ACTH response but a blunted cortisol response.
ME/CFS patients showed a blunted serum DHEA response curve to intravenous ACTH injection and lower overall cortisol production.
A study administering GHRH to ME/CFS patients to test HPS axis function found GH responses were no different from controls and found no GH deficiency in ME/CFS.
Pyridostigmine reversed the impaired GH response to exercise in fibromyalgia patients, correcting a depressed HPS axis, but did not improve fibromyalgia symptoms.
Placebo-controlled studies showed CoQ10 combined with NADH is beneficial for ME/CFS patients.
A placebo-controlled trial of the herbal medicine myelophil showed promising results in alleviating ME/CFS symptoms, potentially via HPA axis modulation.
ME/CFS is characterized by impaired heat shock protein (HSP) production, which combined with O&NS and low-grade inflammation could explain muscle dysfunction and exercise intolerance.
Trials of Low Dose Naltrexone (along with Nexavir/Kutapressin and IL-1 receptor antagonist anakinra) to reduce pro-inflammatory cytokines showed some positive benefits in ME/CFS, notably with LDN.
Immune-modulating treatments including the TLR3 agonist rintatolimod (Ampligen), Imunovir, and IV gamma globulin have been trialed for ME/CFS.
Antiviral trials targeting chronic viral infections have been conducted in ME/CFS patients with some positive benefits reported for a subset of patients.

Rat models showed T3 and T2 thyroid hormone injections repaired mitochondrial DNA damage resulting from oxidative stress, with T3 reducing ROS and restoring mitochondrial function in cells with mtDNA mutations.
ME/CFS disease progression may involve an early hypermetabolic state culminating in a hypometabolic state with low energy production, similar to critical illness.
At least one-quarter of ME/CFS patients are house- or bedbound at some point in their lives, reflecting the severe functional burden of the disease.

In prolonged critically ill men, coadministration of GHRP-2, TRH and GnRH reactivated GH, TSH and LH pituitary axes and produced beneficial metabolic effects absent with GHRP-2 alone and only partially present with GHRP-2+TRH.

Fibromyalgia patients injected simultaneously with CRH, TRH, GHRH and GnRH (for diagnostic testing, not treatment) showed an exaggerated ACTH secretion compared to controls, unlike when CRH was given alone.

In patients with acute myocardial infarction, NAC treatment virtually eliminated the decrease in serum T3 and prevented the rT3 increase characteristic of non-thyroidal illness syndrome, likely by relieving glutathione competition between deiodinase and antioxidant enzymes.

Controlled experiments showed sodium selenite reduces cytokine-induced oxidative stress in human cells, and selenium supplementation is associated with modest normalization of thyroid hormones during critical illness.

Administration of the chaperone co-inducer BGP-15 upregulates Heat Shock Proteins and mitigates muscle dysfunction associated with critical illness myopathy and ventilator-induced diaphragm dysfunction, also acting as a membrane stabilizer with anti-inflammatory effects.

Activation of the JAK/STAT signaling pathway, driven by IL-6, has been reported in respiratory and limb muscles in ICU studies and is a common feature of muscle wasting; the JAK1/2/STAT3 inhibitor Ruxolitinib and the prednisolone analog Vamrolone showed positive effects on muscle structure/function.
Placebo-controlled studies have shown that CoQ10, an important mitochondrial antioxidant, is beneficial to ME/CFS patients when provided in combination with the coenzyme NADH.
Following early positive results, a study is currently ongoing to determine the efficacy of NAC for neuroprotection against oxidative stress in ME/CFS symptoms.

A placebo-controlled trial of the herbal medicine myelophil, which has antioxidant and immunomodulatory properties, showed promising results in alleviating ME/CFS symptoms, possibly via modulatory effects on the HPA axis.
Studies have shown ME/CFS is characterized by impaired Heat Shock Protein production, which combined with O&NS and low-grade inflammation could explain muscle dysfunction and exercise intolerance.
In rat models, T3 and T2 thyroid hormone injections repaired mitochondrial DNA damage resulting from oxidative stress.

In cells from patients with mtDNA mutations, T3 administration reduced reactive oxygen species production and cytoplasmic Ca2+, increased cytochrome c oxidase activity and ATP levels, and restored mitochondrial membrane potential, complex V activity, and manganese superoxide dismutase levels.
T3 (but not T4) administration stimulated Na-K-ATPase activity in rat models through non-genomic pathways, an enzyme critical for maintaining cellular ion gradients.
T3 and T4 supplementation selectively affect GABA-evoked neurotransmission in rat models, possibly producing profound alterations in brain activity.
T3 treatment of human cells caused decreased viral replication.
Researchers tried unsuccessfully to cure non-thyroidal illness syndrome by blocking IL-1 cytokine receptors, reflecting the complexity of the interconnected cytokine network.
Increased plasma kynurenine levels precede the development and persistence of sepsis in critically ill patients and are associated with lower ICU survival.
Elevated kynurenic acid, a metabolite of kynurenine, is associated with myelin damage leading to neuronal and cognitive dysfunction in critical illness.
Low Dose Naltrexone has been trialed in ME/CFS to reduce pro-inflammatory cytokines, with evidence of some positive benefits.
Anakinra, an IL-1 receptor antagonist, has been trialed in ME/CFS to reduce pro-inflammatory cytokines.

Researchers have trialed immune-suppressive treatments in ME/CFS including cyclophosphamide and the monoclonal antibody rituximab, as well as immune adsorption (IgG depletion) and plasmapheresis to reduce antibodies.

Other researchers have tried to modulate (rather than suppress) the immune system in ME/CFS using TLR3 agonists (rintatolimod/Ampligen), immune-stimulants such as Imunovir, and intravenous gamma globulin.

Antivirals such as acyclovir and valganciclovir have been trialed for chronic viral infections in ME/CFS patients, with evidence of some positive benefits at least for a subset of patients, though results remain largely inconclusive.
A recent study demonstrated the safety of L-kynurenine supplementation in healthy volunteers, though impacts on ill patients (including ME/CFS) remain to be investigated.
The total economic cost of ME/CFS is estimated at $36 to $51 billion annually in the USA.
A UK study found people with ME/CFS had over a six-fold increased standardized mortality ratio for suicide compared to the general population.
In Spain, 12.75% of people with ME/CFS were found to be at risk of suicide compared to 2.3% of the general population.
One study did not find an increased risk of completed suicide in ME/CFS but did find an increased risk of non-fatal self-harm, a strong predictor of future suicide attempts.

A retrospective convenience sample identified suicide as one of the three leading causes of death in ME/CFS, with median age at completed suicide significantly younger (39.3 years) than the general population (48 years).
In a UK county-based study of suicide and physical illness, 16% of people who died by suicide had ME/CFS.
Among moderately and severely ill ME/CFS patients, 39-57.25% reported having contemplated suicide, compared with 4% of the general US population and 1-10% of primary care outpatients.
In people with POTS, lower sleep quality scores were significantly associated with suicidal ideation.

In chronic pain patients, disturbed sleep mediated the effect of chronic pain on suicide risk; once sleep was removed from the statistical model, the direct effect of chronic pain on suicide risk became nonsignificant.

In a census-based study of chronic physical illness, degree of functional limitation was the largest statistical predictor of death by suicide, with those 'limited a lot' more than three times as likely to die by suicide as those without functional limitation.

Johnson et al. found ME/CFS patients who were housebound were three times as likely to die by suicide as those who were not housebound or those who were bedridden, suggesting a floor effect where severe impairment may be protective.

McManimen et al. did not find an increased suicide mortality risk for ME/CFS patients overall, but noted over half the sample were bed-bound, which may explain the lack of significance given a possible floor effect.
Presence of any chronic pain condition was associated with increased suicide risk, both at 12-month (OR 1.5) and lifetime (OR 1.3) timeframes.
In ME/CFS patients, pain-related activity limitation was associated with approximately 1.6-fold higher odds of depression compared to those without such limitation.
Cognitive dysfunction was reported at an intense level by 31-45% of severely affected ME/CFS patients.
Hypersensitivity to light, touch, sound, and substances was more common and intense in severely ill ME/CFS patients compared to mildly and moderately affected patients.
Hopelessness was cited by 48% of non-depressed ME/CFS patients who reported contemplating suicide.
Between 54-74% of ME/CFS patients reported their health worsened after participating in graded exercise programs.

ME/CFS patients meeting depression criteria or endorsing suicidal ideation were more likely to have experienced unsupportive social interactions (distancing, minimizing, blaming) and stigma than those who did not.

Comparing ME/CFS and/or fibromyalgia patients to those with an autoimmune disorder, overall unsupportive interaction levels did not differ, but ME/CFS patients were significantly more likely to report 'distancing' and 'minimizing' interactions specifically.
In POTS patients, a suicide risk screening study found 79% of respondents reported 'high' or 'very high' loneliness on the UCLA Loneliness Scale.

The Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) had very high negative predictive value (97.93-99.63%) but low positive predictive value (8.97-16.49%) for prospective suicidal behavior across clinical trial populations.
The Ask Suicide-Screening Questions (ASQ) instrument had 100% negative predictive value and 32% positive predictive value compared to a longer reference questionnaire in medical/surgical inpatients.

PHQ-9 item 9 alone poorly discriminates suicide risk: up to 30% denying suicidal thoughts on it may actually be at risk, while 16-19% endorsing thoughts may not be, and it flagged 24% of subjects as suicidal versus 6% (C-SSRS) and 1% (clinical interview).

CDC data indicate that 54% of people who died by suicide in the US had no known mental health condition, challenging the older assumption that 90% of suicides are attributable to psychiatric disorders.

Psychological treatments such as dialectical behavioral therapy, CBT-based approaches, and Collaborative Assessment and Management of Suicidality decreased suicidal thoughts and attempts by 37.5% to 60% in clinical trials and observational studies.

Patients introduced to suicide safety planning during an emergency room visit were half as likely to attempt suicide in the subsequent 6 months compared to those receiving usual care, and were twice as likely to attend follow-up mental health appointments.
Between 21-88% of ME/CFS patients may be affected by anxiety and 17-47% by mood disorders.

The risk of suicide is 200 to 300 times higher than the general population during the first week and first month, respectively, after psychiatric hospitalization, remaining 30 times higher even after 5-10 years.

In an RCT of home-based care for people with multiple sclerosis, patients receiving care in the home showed significant improvements in multiple quality-of-life domains, including mental health-related role-emotional and social functioning.
An emergency department intervention combining a safety plan, crisis resources, and telephone follow-up calls reduced suicide attempts by 30% in the following year.
Acceptability of suicide screening in medical settings is high, with 81-95% of patients deeming it appropriate for inpatient and outpatient care.
Approximately 25-29% of ME/CFS patients experience severe reductions in functioning that render them homebound or bedbound.
Homebound ME/CFS patients showed greater impairment in home management, mobility, and overall functionality, and reported more physical problems, compared to other (non-homebound) ME/CFS patients.
ME/CFS was found to be more intrusive to patients' lives than multiple sclerosis, laryngeal cancer, end-stage renal disease, irritable bowel syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis, and insomnia.
Patients with ME/CFS and fibromyalgia reported more illness-related loss (social support, recreational activities, material possessions) than patients with other chronically fatiguing diseases.
Medical costs for ME/CFS patients are reported to be 50% higher than for patients with lupus or multiple sclerosis, and three to four times higher than for the average insured person.
Suicide has been identified as a cause of death for a significant number of ME/CFS patients.
ME/CFS patients who died by suicide appeared to lack sufficient depressive symptoms to meet criteria for a depression diagnosis, suggesting their symptoms were better attributed to grief.
Losses associated with ME/CFS and perceived stigma are likely risk factors for suicidal ideation in patients.
There is a reported relationship between suicidal ideation and illness identity in ME/CFS, whereby grieving illness-related losses can worsen the negative identity associated with the illness.
Individuals with a chronic illness or disability report higher post-traumatic growth than individuals without a chronic illness or disability.

Post-traumatic growth was found to be lower among women with ME/CFS compared to women with rheumatoid arthritis, osteoarthritis, and multiple sclerosis, potentially due to greater illness-related stigma in ME/CFS.
Evidence suggests ME/CFS has a higher prevalence in communities of color.
Lower socioeconomic status (SES) has been shown to be a risk factor for more severe presentations of ME/CFS.
Homebound ME/CFS patients are more likely to be unemployed as a result of their health status, which can further reduce their socioeconomic status.
Denial as a coping mechanism and non-acceptance of illness has been suggested to delay improvement in ME/CFS patients.
Two twin studies found increased REM sleep in ME/CFS patients compared with their healthy twin.
Sleep onset latency (SOL) showed no significant difference between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls across all 13 studies that assessed it.
Slow-wave sleep (SWS) duration was significantly longer in ME/CFS patients compared with HC in 3 of 11 studies, with the remainder showing no difference.
Microarousal index (MAI), a measure of sleep fragmentation, was increased in ME/CFS patients compared with HC in all five studies that assessed it.
Apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI) findings were inconsistent, with 5 of 8 studies showing no difference and 3 studies detecting differences between ME/CFS patients and HC.

One study found diminished alpha power during stage 2, slow wave, and REM sleep, decreased delta power during SWS (but elevated during stage 1 and REM), and reduced theta, sigma and beta spectral power during stage 2, SWS and REM in ME/CFS patients compared with HC.
One study found ultra-slow delta power was significantly lower in ME/CFS patients compared with HC during N3 sleep, while other frequency bands did not differ.
Multiple Sleep Latency Testing (MSLT) results were largely inconsistent, with only 1 of 6 studies finding reduced mean sleep latency in ME/CFS patients versus HC.

Subjective sleep quality or sleepiness scores were significantly different between ME/CFS patients and HC in all 13 studies that assessed this, despite objective PSG measures often showing no difference.
Depression scores were significantly higher in ME/CFS patients compared with HC in all six studies that reported these values.
Anxiety scores were significantly different between ME/CFS patients and HC in four of the five studies that measured this.
Insomnia was significantly higher in ME/CFS patients compared with HC in both studies that investigated it.
Fatigue levels were significantly greater in ME/CFS patients compared with HC in all seven studies that measured this variable.
One study found significant differences in emotional awareness parameters (TAS-20, TAS total, LEAS-self) in ME/CFS patients, which correlated with number of awakenings.
Total sleep time did not significantly differ between ME/CFS patients (397.03 min) and HC (400.1 min) across studies.
One study (not among the primary 20 but discussed) found significantly higher levels of sleep disruption, including brief and longer awakenings, in adolescents with ME/CFS.

One study reported higher fractal scaling index α1 (a heart rate variability measure) during non-REM sleep in the sleepier ME/CFS subgroup compared with HC, suggesting autonomic nervous system involvement despite no other significant PSG changes.

The discussion notes that reduced natural killer (NK) cell cytotoxicity is the most consistent immunological feature of ME/CFS, and is proposed as an area warranting further research in relation to sleep/melatonin pathways.
Dysregulation of the 2-5A synthetase/RNase L antiviral pathway has previously been linked with sleep disruption (alpha-delta sleep), but a study by Van Hoof et al. did not support this association.

Structural changes in the medial prefrontal cortex were found to correlate with unrefreshing sleep in ME/CFS patients, potentially explaining the discrepancy between subjective and objective sleep measures.
One included study reported a higher number of cases of sleep disorders among ME/CFS patients diagnosed with comorbid irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).
Male ME/CFS patients showed higher resting heart rate and systolic arterial pressure than male healthy controls.
Diastolic arterial pressure trended higher in male ME/CFS patients versus controls but did not reach significance.
Male ME/CFS patients reported markedly higher neurovegetative complaint scores than male healthy controls.
Male ME/CFS patients reported substantially higher physical, cognitive, psychosocial and total fatigue scores than controls.
Male ME/CFS patients had significantly increased scores in orthostatic intolerance, vasomotor, secretomotor, bladder, pupillomotor, gastrointestinal, and total COMPASS-31 domains versus controls.
Male ME/CFS patients had markedly worse subjective sleep quality across all PSQI components, with total scores 3.5-fold higher than controls.
Male ME/CFS patients reported significantly higher anxiety and depression scores (10-11 points more) than controls.
In men, no significant differences were found between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls in any HRV time-domain or frequency-domain parameter, though controls trended higher on all measures.
In men, greater gastrointestinal autonomic dysfunction (COMPASS-31 GI domain) was negatively correlated with SDNN, RMSSD, pNN50 and LF.
Physical fatigue score (FIS-40) was negatively correlated with pNN50 in the total male sample.
In male ME/CFS patients only, physical fatigue was significantly predicted by reduced SDNN, RMSSD, LF, HF, and pNN50, an association absent in male healthy controls.
Global scores across all self-reported symptom questionnaires were highly and positively intercorrelated in the male sample.
Independent of ME/CFS status, women had lower systolic blood pressure, higher heart rate, and higher COMPASS-31 vasomotor (and marginally secretomotor) scores than men.

Female ME/CFS patients showed a greater increase in neurovegetative complaints relative to female controls than male ME/CFS patients did relative to male controls, indicating a sex-specific ME/CFS effect on autonomic complaints.

Across the combined male/female dataset, HF, HFnu, and LF/HF ratio showed significant overall gender effects, with women showing higher HF/HFnu and lower LF/HF than men, indicating greater parasympathetic predominance in women overall.

Female ME/CFS patients showed decreased HF and HFnu values compared to female controls, whereas the two male groups did not differ from each other or from female ME/CFS patients, indicating that ME/CFS reduces the typically higher parasympathetic predominance seen in healthy women to a male-like level.
Female healthy controls had the lowest LF/HF ratio, differing significantly from female ME/CFS patients and both male groups, mirroring the HF/HFnu pattern.
In the combined male and female dataset, ME/CFS patients showed significantly lower cardiac variability (all time-domain HRV parameters) than healthy controls, regardless of gender.
In a survey of 4038 ME/CFS patients, 62% reported they were not confident their GP understood the condition.
18% of ME/CFS patients surveyed waited longer than six years to receive a diagnosis.
Up to 90% of ME/CFS patients are estimated to be undercounted, undiagnosed and under-treated.
Between a third and half of general practitioners lack confidence in acknowledging, diagnosing and managing ME/CFS.

Exercise in ME/CFS has been reported to worsen symptoms and cellular bioenergetics, with studies showing cognitive abnormalities, altered brain spectroscopy, reduced metabolic energy generation, immune dysregulation and neuroinflammation following repeated exertion.
Of the 22 UK medical schools that responded to the survey, 41% (9 schools) did not teach ME/CFS in their curriculum at all.
Among the 13 schools that teach ME/CFS, most devote only 1-2 hours to the subject, with two schools devoting more than 3 hours and one less than 1 hour.
Only 3 of the 13 schools that teach ME/CFS (23%) include contact with ME/CFS patients as part of the curriculum.
Only 7 of 22 responding schools (32%) set examination questions on ME/CFS.
14 of 22 responding schools (64%), including 7 of 9 schools that do not currently teach ME/CFS (78%), expressed interest in receiving further teaching aids on the subject.
In a European survey of ME/CFS experts, 91% strongly agreed there should be more teaching about ME/CFS in undergraduate medical curricula.
A comparable US study found only 5.6% of medical schools were judged to deliver sufficient clinical, curricular and research content on ME/CFS.
Fatigue measured by the Chalder Fatigue Scale significantly decreased during s.c. IgG treatment at months 6, 9 and 12 but not after the initial dose-escalation phase at month 3.
Physical functioning measured by SF-36 significantly increased during s.c. IgG treatment at months 6, 9 and 12 but not at month 3.
Five of twelve patients completing 12 months of IgG treatment (P2, 9, 11, 13, 16) met the pre-defined clinical response criterion (≥6-point CFQ decrease and/or ≥25-point SF-36 increase) at month 12.
Two additional patients (P4, P8) met the response definition at months 6 and 9 but no longer met it at month 12.
Three months after IgG treatment cessation (month 15), physical functioning decreased and fatigue increased again, indicating loss of benefit after stopping treatment.
Fatigue (CFQ) and physical functioning (SF-36) scores were closely inversely correlated across treatment.
Cognitive and immune symptom severity (Canadian Consensus Criteria scoring) significantly improved at months 6, 9 and 12 of IgG treatment.
Muscle pain severity showed no overall improvement during IgG treatment.
Autonomic symptom severity assessed by COMPASS-31 significantly improved from baseline (moderate-to-severe autonomic dysfunction in all patients) to months 6 and 9 of IgG treatment.
Daily step counts increased during IgG treatment in responding patients (including transient responders) but not in non-responders.
Endothelial dysfunction (reactive hyperemia index ≤1.8) was present pretreatment in over half of tested patients and improved post-treatment in most, but did not correlate with clinical response.
The frequency of infections (mostly respiratory tract) significantly decreased during the 12-month IgG treatment period compared to the year prior.
No significant differences in age, sex, Bell disease-severity score, disease duration, or baseline SF-36/CFQ/COMPASS-31/symptom scores were found between treatment responders and non-responders.
All treatment responders had an infection-triggered ME/CFS onset, suggesting infection-triggered disease may be more responsive to IgG therapy.
Baseline serum LDH level was significantly higher in patients who responded to IgG treatment (including transient responders) compared to non-responders.
Baseline soluble IL-2 receptor (sCD25) level was significantly lower in patients who responded to IgG treatment compared to non-responders.
Serum LDH levels significantly decreased during IgG treatment from month 6 onward, but not during the initial dose-escalation phase at month 3.
Serum IgG levels increased during s.c. IgG treatment, consistent with expected pharmacodynamic effect of substitution therapy.
Unlike a prior study, pretreatment lymphocyte count was not associated with IgG treatment response in this cohort.
Patients who did not tolerate IgG treatment or had early disease worsening had significantly lower baseline soluble CD26 (sDPP4) levels compared to those completing 12 months of treatment.

Adverse events including grade 2-3 headache, injection-site reactions, and transient liver enzyme elevation led to treatment discontinuation in 4 of 17 patients; one further patient discontinued due to disease worsening, and side effects occurred more frequently than typically seen in primary immunodeficiency patients receiving s.c. IgG.
A cited study of adult housebound ME/CFS patients (Pendergrast et al.) found that 25% or more are confined to their homes or completely bedbound.

Severe ME/CFS symptoms (muscular, gastric, fatigue-based, neural, and cognitive) were described as potentially worse than those suffered by patients with multiple sclerosis or cancer, with abdominal pain sometimes severe enough to interfere with nutrition due to comorbid Mast Cell Activation Disorder.

Mental health consequences of severe pediatric ME/CFS include catastrophism, pessimism, depression, and isolation, contributing to a substantial loss of self as adolescents are deprived of school and social activities.

The most common classroom-observable feature of pediatric ME/CFS is a collection of attention, concentration, and memory deficits collectively known as 'Brain Fog', driven partly by post-exertional malaise from physical, cognitive, or orthostatic stress.

A case report/anecdote of two adult sons who have been homebound or bedbound for a decade describes severe light, sound, and touch sensitivities restricting computer use, and functional attention spans limited to irregular 20-minute intervals despite unimpaired intellect.

The authors reiterate that in their prior naturalistic evaluation, fatigue, physical functioning, and social adjustment all significantly improved following cognitive behaviour therapy in an NHS clinic for chronic fatigue syndrome.
Patient satisfaction with CBT for chronic fatigue syndrome was high at discharge, with over 90% at least slightly satisfied and 45% very satisfied, and satisfaction remained consistent at follow-up.
Patients who dropped out of the naturalistic CBT evaluation before completing outcome measures were more severely ill at treatment start than those who completed the course.
CFS patients with post-exertional malaise (PEM) had significantly higher overall fatigue as measured by the Fatigue Impact Scale compared to those without PEM.
CFS patients with PEM had significantly higher mental fatigue (CFQ mental sub-score) than those without PEM.
CFS patients with PEM had lower central (aortic) systolic blood pressure than those without PEM, with no difference observed in peripherally measured blood pressure.
No significant differences in peripherally measured blood pressure were observed between CFS patients with and without PEM.
CFS patients with PEM had higher normalized low-frequency component of R-R interval variability (LFnu-RRI), indicating greater sympathetic activity at rest, compared to those without PEM.
CFS patients with PEM had lower normalized high-frequency component of R-R interval variability (HFnu-RRI), indicating reduced parasympathetic activity at rest, compared to those without PEM.
CFS patients with PEM had higher LF/HF ratio of R-R interval variability, indicating sympathovagal imbalance favoring sympathetic dominance, compared to those without PEM.
A separate LF/HF sympathovagal balance measure was also higher in CFS patients with PEM compared to those without.
CFS patients with PEM had higher LFnu-dBP, an indicator of vasomotor sympathetic activity, than those without PEM.
CFS patients with PEM had higher LF/HF-dBP than those without PEM.
Logistic regression showed that a one-point increase in the mental fatigue component of the CFQ scale was associated with a 34% increased risk of PEM.
Logistic regression showed that a 1 mmHg increase in aortic (central) systolic blood pressure was associated with a 5% decreased risk of PEM.
Logistic regression showed that a one-unit increase in sympathovagal balance was associated with a 330% increased risk of PEM.

After correction for multiple comparisons via FDR, none of the observed between-group differences (fatigue, blood pressure, autonomic measures) between CFS patients with and without PEM remained statistically significant.

Transmission electron microscopy of myodural bridges harvested from Chiari malformation patients showed distinct ultrastructural collagen fibril damage in those with hypermobile EDS compared to those without EDS.
Real-time ultrasound at C1-2 showed increased cardiac pulsatory motion of the spinal cord in patients with EDS compared with healthy controls.

EDS patients without radiologically proven craniocervical instability showed irregular spinal cord displacement during head movements on ultrasound compared to healthy controls, suggesting a spinal cord motion disorder related to chronic neck pain and headache.
The title indicates a case report describing blepharochalasis syndrome occurring in association with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
Parent-reported fatigue was significantly higher in children with hEDS than normative data, corresponding to a large effect size.
Parent-reported fatigue T-scores were significantly lower (less fatigue) in children with MFS than normative data, a large effect.
The proportion of children scoring above the severe fatigue cutoff (parent-proxy) was significantly greater in EDS and hEDS subgroups than normative data.
Self-reported (pediatric) fatigue was significantly higher in the total HCTD group than normative data, a small-to-medium effect.
Self-reported pediatric fatigue was very largely elevated in the hEDS subgroup compared to normative data.
The proportion of children above the severe fatigue cutoff on self-report was significantly greater in the total HCTD group, EDS, and hEDS subgroups compared with normative data.
Disability (CHAQ-DI) scores were significantly higher than normative data across the total HCTD group and all subgroups (MFS, LDS, EDS, hEDS), with hEDS showing the largest effect.
The proportion of children with severe disability (CHAQ-DI Z-score <-2) was significantly greater than normative data across the total HCTD group and all subgroups, most markedly in hEDS.
Children with HCTD with severe disability did not differ significantly in age or sex from children without disability.
Assistance from another person for daily activities was required by 41% of the HCTD group overall, ranging up to 76% in hEDS.
Pain VAS scores over the last week were significantly higher than normative data in the total HCTD group and all subgroups, most extreme in hEDS.
General health VAS scores indicated significantly worse general health than normative data in the total HCTD group and all subgroups, with the largest effect in hEDS.
Children with hEDS reported significantly worse fatigue, disability, pain, and general health than those with MFS, LDS, and (for disability/pain) EDS subgroups.
Disability was significantly positively correlated with fatigue (both parent-proxy and self-report), pain, and general health in the total HCTD group.
General health was significantly positively correlated with fatigue and pain in the total HCTD group.
Pain was significantly positively correlated with fatigue (parent-proxy and self-report) in the total HCTD group.
In the hEDS subgroup specifically, disability was highly correlated with parent-reported fatigue, pain, and general health.
In the MFS subgroup, disability was moderately correlated with parent-reported fatigue and general health.

Pain VAS scores of the HCTD-group Parent-Proxy fatigue did not differ significantly overall between the total HCTD group vs normative data (Parent-Proxy analysis), while pain reporting missingness was not associated with age or sex.

A heterozygous COL1A2 c.2701G>A (p.Gly901Ser) variant, previously reported as pathogenic for moderate-severe and lethal osteogenesis imperfecta, was identified in a proband clinically diagnosed with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

A heterozygous COL1A1 c.133C>G (p.Leu45Val) variant was classified as Likely Benign, being observed in healthy adults, but the authors speculate it may act as a disease modifier reducing severity of the co-inherited COL1A2 mutation.

Biochemical analysis of cultured dermal fibroblasts from the proband showed overmodified, slower-migrating α1(I) and α2(I) collagen chains in both medium and cell layer fractions compared to three controls, plus an additional intracellularly retained overmodified band in the cell layer.

The proband presented generalized joint hypermobility with a Beighton score of 9/9, recurrent joint dislocations (shoulders, wrist, knees), bruising tendency, prolonged bleeding, postural hypotension, hypertrophic scarring, mild hearing loss, and early-onset osteopenia (DXA Z scores -2.1 lumbar and femur neck).
Postural hypotension was noted in the proband, but formal evaluation excluded autonomic dysfunction.
The proband had low 25-(OH)-vitamin D levels (15.2 ng/mL, below the deficiency threshold of 20 ng/mL) while other bone metabolism markers (calcium, phosphorus, PTH, alkaline phosphatase) were normal.

The proband's mother carried the identical COL1A1 and COL1A2 variants as the proband but exhibited only mild osteopenia and short stature, with no joint hypermobility, blue sclerae, dentinogenesis imperfecta, fractures, or cardiac/hearing abnormalities, illustrating marked clinical variability of the same genotype.

The proband showed minor vascular involvement, including right carotid artery kinking and mild valve insufficiency, consistent with reports of a higher rate of vascular events in OI/EDS overlap cases and arginine substitutions in collagen type I linked to arterial rupture in EDS.

Morlino et al. (2020) proposed the term 'COL1-related overlap disorder' after describing 21 individuals with clinical suspicion of EDS carrying pathogenic COL1A1 (n=5) or COL1A2 (n=8) variants typically causative of OI, supporting a wider phenotypic spectrum between EDS and OI.

The review found that pathophysiologic GI changes from malnutrition in the esophagus, stomach, and intestines do not consistently correlate with reported GI symptoms in patients with anorexia nervosa and ARFID.
Celiac disease and inflammatory bowel disease contribute to disordered eating through associated somatic GI complaints.
Pelvic floor dysfunction and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome contribute to disordered eating through both somatic and functional GI symptoms.
Functional GI symptoms remain problematic during treatment of restrictive eating disorders, and it is unclear whether they are functional in nature and whether they resolve or persist with treatment.
A 47-year-old woman with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome developed bilateral facial subcutaneous emphysema after blowing her nose, attributed to a defect in her left nasal cartilage.

The authors state this is the first reported case of sudden facial subcutaneous emphysema following nose blowing or sneezing occurring in a patient with a connective tissue disorder, out of only eight such cases previously found in the English literature.
In fibromyalgia, pain is driven by dysregulation of central pain processing, whereas in small fiber neuropathy pain results from loss or dysfunction of intraepidermal small nerve fibers.

Higher pain intensity, stabbing pain and paraesthesia, allodynia, dry eyes/mouth, altered sweating pattern, skin colour changes, reduced hair/nail growth on lower extremities, and warm/cold hypoesthesia are more commonly reported in small fiber neuropathy than fibromyalgia.
Headache or temporo-mandibular disorder point toward a diagnosis of fibromyalgia rather than small fiber neuropathy.
Pain distribution is typically length-dependent in small fiber neuropathy but can also involve the whole body.

Post-traumatic stress disorder and history of physical or sexual abuse in childhood or adulthood are more suggestive of fibromyalgia, while anxiety and depression are common to both fibromyalgia and small fiber neuropathy.
Inflammatory disease or musculoskeletal disease is frequently reported as comorbid with fibromyalgia.
Metabolic disorders (especially diabetes mellitus), neurotoxic exposure, Sjogren's syndrome, sarcoidosis, and HIV are the main diseases associated with small fiber neuropathy.
