Skin biopsy, quantitative sensory testing, laser evoked potentials, confocal corneal microscopy, and electrochemical skin conductance can help discriminate between fibromyalgia and small fiber neuropathy.
Warm or cold hypoesthesia is more commonly reported in small fibre neuropathy than in fibromyalgia.
Pain distribution in small fibre neuropathy is typically length-dependent, though it can also involve the whole body.
Headache or temporo-mandibular disorder are symptoms that point more toward fibromyalgia rather than small fibre neuropathy.
Anxiety and depression are common comorbidities in both fibromyalgia and small fibre neuropathy.
Post-traumatic stress disorder and history of physical or sexual abuse in childhood or adulthood are more suggestive of fibromyalgia than small fibre neuropathy.
Inflammatory disease or musculoskeletal disease is frequently reported as comorbid with fibromyalgia.
Metabolic disorders (especially diabetes mellitus), neurotoxic exposure, Sjogren's syndrome, sarcoidosis, and HIV are the main diseases associated with small fibre neuropathy.

Skin biopsy, quantitative sensory testing, laser evoked potentials, confocal corneal microscopy, and electrochemical skin conductance can help discriminate between fibromyalgia and small fibre neuropathy.
In 8 of 10 systemic mastocytosis patients whose elevated urinary (2,3-dinor)-11β-PGF2α normalized with aspirin therapy, urinary LTE4 excretion paradoxically increased by an average of nearly 13-fold.
Increased urinary excretion of the PGD2 metabolites 11β-PGF2α and (2,3-dinor)-11β-PGF2α has been documented in patients with systemic mastocytosis and mast cell activation syndrome.
Aspirin, a COX1/COX2 inhibitor, can prevent symptoms caused by increased baseline and/or episodic release of PGD2 in mast cell disease.
In a case series of 18 patients with mastocytosis or MMAS, none experienced an allergic reaction or anaphylaxis after receiving a COVID-19 vaccine (Pfizer, Moderna, or Janssen).
Even among the subset of patients (about 22%) with a prior history of anaphylaxis to other triggers (venom, food, idiopathic, exercise/heat), COVID-19 vaccination was well tolerated without reaction.

Antihistamine premedication practices before vaccination were inconsistent (some patients premedicated 30-60 minutes prior, some took only their home regimen at a different time, and two took no antihistamine at all), yet all patients still tolerated vaccination without reaction.
The average serum tryptase level among the 18 vaccinated mastocytosis/MMAS patients was 44.56 ng/mL, with a wide range reflecting disease heterogeneity.
A GWAS summarized in this issue found four SNPs in the ABCA2, OTX2-AS1, HLA-V, and PDE4DIP genes were more prevalent in mastocytosis patients than in a control cohort.
The same GWAS found five SNPs (in RPTN, CYP2B6, OR51Q1, FTCD genes, and rs9828758 near RP11) were less prevalent in mastocytosis patients than in a control cohort.
About 4-6% of the general population carry germline TPSAB1-alpha copy number gains, a condition termed hereditary alpha tryptasemia (HaT), resulting in elevated basal serum tryptase levels.
Hereditary alpha tryptasemia prevalence is significantly higher (15-20%) in patients with systemic mastocytosis than in the general population.
Hereditary alpha tryptasemia is associated with more severe Hymenoptera venom-induced anaphylaxis occurring concomitantly in systemic mastocytosis patients.
Hereditary alpha tryptasemia appears more common in patients with idiopathic anaphylaxis and mast cell activation syndrome than in controls.
Tyrosine kinase inhibitors midostaurin and avapritinib, which target KIT, are discussed as current treatments for advanced systemic mastocytosis, alongside other novel drugs.

Viral dsRNA binding to TLR3 on rat peritoneal mast cells triggers release of IFN-α/β, chemokines/cytokines (CCL3, CXCL8, TNF, IL-1β) and the lipid mediator cysLTs as part of an antiviral host defense response.
IgE-antigen stimulation of mast cells activates MAPK-dependent phosphorylation of LysRS at serine 207, allowing pLysRS to dissociate from the multi-synthetase complex (MSC).
The non-phosphorylatable LysRS S207A mutant, mimicking the dephosphorylated state, significantly reduced Ap4A production in mast cells.
Overexpression of the phosphomimetic LysRS S207D mutant increased Ap4A concentration and enhanced transcription of MITF target genes in mast cells.
Biacore binding analysis showed HINT1 binds specifically to Ap4A, but not to related dinucleotides Ap3A or Ap5A, and this binding affects the MITF-HINT1 protein complex.
USF2 transcription factor activity is similarly regulated by the interaction of HINT1 with Ap4A, analogous to the MITF-HINT1 mechanism.

Mast cell mediators such as tryptase are present in the cerebrospinal fluid of multiple sclerosis patients, supporting an inflammatory response that activates peripheral mononuclear cells and causes microvascular leakage.

LysRS interacts with RNA-DNA hybrids to delay cGAS recognition, and LysRS-dependent Ap4A production attenuates STING signaling, regulating autoimmune responses, suggesting LysRS-Ap4A as a pharmacological target for autoinflammatory diseases.
HINT1-deficient mice show increased susceptibility to both spontaneous tumors and tumor proliferation, consistent with its role as a tumor suppressor.

Ap4A regulates MITF activation through HINT1 polymerization, which blocks the MITF-HINT1 interaction and releases MITF to increase transcription of downstream genes c-Met and c-Kit involved in cell proliferation and migration.
Nuclear translocation of ERK-phosphorylated Ser207-LysRS is associated with improved mean disease-free survival in cancer patients with EGFR mutations compared to those with wild-type EGFR.
Membranous and nuclear LysRS participate in invasive cell dissemination, an important step in cancer progression identified in colon cancer spheroids.
Knocking out Ap4A hydrolase in dendritic cells increases intracellular Ap4A concentration, functionally enhancing antigen cross-presentation by DCs.
LysRS is highly expressed in various cancer tissues, including colon, lung, gastric, breast and thyroid cancer cells, reflecting a noncanonical role in immune response and tumor metastasis.
Clec12b mRNA is preferentially expressed in skin mast cells in mice, but not in mast cells from trachea, tongue, esophagus, or peritoneal cavity, nor in most lymphocytes and myeloid cells.

Using a newly generated monoclonal antibody (TX109) recognizing both mouse and human Clec12b, flow cytometry confirmed that Clec12b protein is expressed only on skin mast cells and not on other immune cell types in various mouse tissues.
In humans, Clec12b is expressed on skin mast cells but not on circulating lymphocytes and myeloid cells, indicating cross-species selective expression.
Serum CPA3 levels were increased in SARS-CoV-2-infected patients compared with symptomatic SARS-CoV-2-negative patients and identified severe COVID-19 cases.
Serum serotonin levels were decreased in SARS-CoV-2-infected patients compared with symptomatic SARS-CoV-2-negative patients and served as a good predictor of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Serum CPA3 levels correlated positively with C-reactive protein, circulating neutrophil counts, and quick SOFA score in COVID-19 patients.
In anesthetized male and female mice, pregnenolone constricted the middle cerebral artery in a concentration-dependent manner with a maximal diameter decrease of approximately 22-35%.
Pregnenolone evoked similar vasoconstriction in intact and de-endothelialized in vitro pressurized MCA segments, indicating the effect is endothelium-independent.
The BK channel blocker paxilline (1 μM) abolished pregnenolone-induced constriction of the MCA, implicating BK channels in the response.
Cell-attached patch-clamp recordings on freshly isolated MCA smooth muscle cells showed that 10 μM pregnenolone reduced BK channel open probability (NPo) by an average of 24.2%.

In cell-free inside-out membrane patches, pregnenolone inhibited BK channel activity in a concentration-dependent manner paralleling the whole-cell and in vivo effects, with maximal inhibition at 10 μM.
In MCA myocytes from KCNMB1 knockout mice, pregnenolone still decreased BK channel NPo, showing the regulatory β1 subunit is not required for the effect.

Reconstitution of slo1 channels into artificial binary phospholipid bilayers showed that 10 μM pregnenolone inhibited channel NPo similarly to native membranes, confirming direct channel sensing of the neurosteroid.

When slo1 channels were reconstituted into artificial binary phospholipid bilayers devoid of any other membrane proteins or cellular components, pregnenolone still inhibited channel activity to a degree similar to that seen in native smooth muscle membranes, indicating direct sensing of the neurosteroid by the slo1 protein itself.
Pregnenolone failed to constrict middle cerebral arteries isolated from KCNMA1-/- mice, demonstrating that the slo1 α-subunit is required for the vasoconstrictive action of pregnenolone.
Exosomes from red cell units (EXs-RBC) and from normal plasma (EXs-nor) showed similar levels of the exosome marker proteins CD81 and ALIX.
Tryptase-1 mRNA expression was significantly increased in HMC-1 mast cells exposed to EXs-RBC compared to EXs-nor.
PGD-2 mRNA expression was significantly increased in HMC-1 mast cells exposed to EXs-RBC compared to EXs-nor.
Immunofluorescence and western blot confirmed increased tryptase-1 protein expression in HMC-1 cells after EXs-RBC exposure, reaching statistical significance by 4 hours.
Multiple inflammatory mediator mRNAs (IL-6, TNF-α, IL-4, IFN-γ, CCL2, CXCL1, PAF, LTB4, VEGF) were upregulated in HMC-1 cells exposed to EXs-RBC compared to EXs-nor.
Secreted protein levels of IL-6, TNF-α, IL-4, CCL2, CXCL1, PAF, LTB4, and VEGF were increased in supernatant of HMC-1 cells exposed to EXs-RBC compared to EXs-nor, measured by ELISA at 8 hours.
Phosphorylation levels of JNK, P38, and ERK1/2 were upregulated at 2h and 4h in HMC-1 cells exposed to EXs-RBC, while total MAPK levels did not change significantly.
TLR-3 mRNA and protein expression increased in HMC-1 cells after EXs-RBC exposure, with protein expression significantly increased by 4 hours.

MAPK pathway inhibitors (SB203580/P38, SP600125/JNK, PD98059/ERK1/2) significantly reduced EXs-RBC-induced expression of tryptase-1, PGD-2, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-4, IFN-γ, CXCL1, CXCL5, and LTB4 in HMC-1 cells, but did not affect PAF or VEGF.

A TLR-3/dsRNA agonist complex increased, while a TLR-3 inhibitor (poly A:U context reversed) decreased, EXs-RBC-induced expression of tryptase-1, PGD-2, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-4, IFN-γ, CXCL1, CXCL5, and LTB4 in HMC-1 cells, with PAF and VEGF unaffected.
CCK-8 assay showed no significant change in HMC-1 cell viability after 24h treatment with PBS, EXs-nor, or EXs-RBC, indicating observed effects were not due to cytotoxicity.
Peanut-specific IgG and its subclasses IgG1-IgG4 were higher in peanut-allergic children than in non-peanut-allergic children.
Milk-specific IgG4 was lower in cow's milk-allergic children compared to non-cow's milk-allergic (tolerant) children, the opposite pattern from peanut allergy.
No difference in allergen-specific IgG isotypes was observed between allergic and non-allergic children for milk or egg, apart from milk-specific IgG4.
Basophils and LAD2 mast cells expressed IgG receptors on their surface, but surface-bound IgG and IgA were not detected on either cell type.
Blocking FcγRIIα or FcγRIIβ receptors did not modify allergen-induced activation of basophils or mast cells in either allergic or tolerant children.
Bone marrow-derived mast cells lacking Sirt6 showed augmented FcεRI-mediated signaling and degranulation compared to wild-type cells after IgE cross-linking.

Mast cell-deficient Kit(W-sh/W-sh) mice reconstituted with Sirt6-knockout bone marrow-derived mast cells developed more severe passive systemic anaphylaxis than mice engrafted with wild-type mast cells.
Mice engrafted with Sirt6-knockout mast cells also developed more severe passive cutaneous anaphylaxis compared to wild-type mast cell-engrafted mice.
Genetic overexpression or pharmacologic activation of Sirt6 suppressed mast cell degranulation and blunted passive cutaneous anaphylaxis responses.
Sirt6 deficiency increased PTPRC (CD45) transcription via increased histone H3 acetylation, leading to enhanced FcεRI aggregation in mast cells.
The Sirt6-PTPRC-FcεRI regulatory axis identified in murine mast cells was recapitulated in human cord blood-derived mast cells.
Exposure of human nasal epithelial cells (hNECs) to ozone-aged black carbon (O3BC) at concentrations above 50 μg/ml progressively reduced cell viability.
Cell survival rate in O3BC-treated hNECs was negatively correlated with O3BC concentration above 50 μg/ml.
Exposure to pollen allergen alone did not alter hNEC viability at any concentration tested.
Combining pollen with low-dose O3BC synergistically decreased hNEC viability compared to O3BC alone.
Pollen alone (200 μg/ml) significantly altered expression of 49 genes in hNECs (23 up-regulated, 26 down-regulated).
O3BC (25 and 200 μg/ml) altered expression of 29 genes in hNECs (11 up-regulated, 18 down-regulated).
O3BC at 200 μg/ml altered expression of 124 genes in hNECs (38 up-regulated, 86 down-regulated), more than at 25 μg/ml.
Combined exposure to O3BC (25 μg/ml) plus pollen (200 μg/ml) altered a far greater number of genes (544 total) than either agent alone.

Most of the differentially expressed genes (87.8%) induced by combined O3BC+pollen exposure did not overlap with genes altered by either agent alone, indicating a largely distinct synergistic transcriptional response.
GO enrichment showed that O3BC (200 μg/ml) alone predominantly up-regulated hypoxia/oxidative stress response genes in hNECs.

GO enrichment showed that combined O3BC and pollen exposure up-regulated genes related to innate immune/inflammatory processes, including neutrophil and macrophage chemotaxis, phagocytosis, and mast cell activation/degranulation.

Combined O3BC and pollen exposure differentially expressed a set of genes central to mast cell FceRI signalling, degranulation and mediator release, including FCER1G, FGR, LAT2, SYK, FES, RAC2 and VAV1.
IL1B, CSF1, CCL2, TLR2, LPL, IGF8, SPP1, CXCL8, FCER1G and IL1RN were identified as the top 10 upstream regulators of the inflammatory transcriptional response to combined O3BC and pollen exposure.
RT-qPCR confirmed that pro-inflammatory IL1B mRNA was up-regulated in hNECs exposed to O3BC (25 and 200 μg/ml) and to the combination of O3BC (25 μg/ml) plus pollen (200 μg/ml).
RT-qPCR confirmed CSF1 mRNA was over-expressed in hNECs exposed to O3BC (25 μg/ml) alone and in combination with pollen (200 μg/ml).
RT-qPCR confirmed FCER1G (mast cell FceRI gamma chain) mRNA was over-expressed in hNECs exposed to pollen alone (200 μg/ml) and to the combination of O3BC (25 μg/ml) plus pollen (200 μg/ml).
The minimum incidence of definite small fiber neuropathy (SFN) in central Switzerland was 4.4 cases per 100,000 inhabitants per year.
The calculated minimum prevalence of definite SFN in the reference population was 131.5 per 100,000 inhabitants.
More than one-third of the 84 patients with definite SFN were classified as idiopathic, with no identifiable underlying etiology.

Within the apparently autoimmune SFN (aaSFN) subgroup, patients had the highest proportion of women and the largest proportion of non-length-dependent SFN compared to metabolic and idiopathic subgroups.
Quantitative sudomotor axon reflex testing (QSART) was abnormal in 63.0% (46/73) of tested patients with definite SFN.
Stimulated skin wrinkling (SSW) was abnormal in 53.3% (40/75) of tested patients with definite SFN, and showed only a moderate correlation with abnormal epidermal nerve fiber density (ENFD).
The painDETECT questionnaire screening was positive for a neuropathic origin of pain in 48.2% of respondents, unclear in 19.6%, and negative in 32.1%.
Among the three etiologic subgroups (idiopathic, apparently autoimmune, metabolic), the apparently autoimmune group reported the highest average, maximum, and current pain intensity levels.
One patient with an apparently autoimmune SFN etiology had postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) as part of a systemic rheumatologic/autoimmune presentation.

The authors note that a prior randomized, double-blind, controlled trial found that intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) treatment had no significant effect on pain in patients with painful idiopathic small fiber neuropathy, in contrast to an earlier uncontrolled retrospective study reporting 74% symptom improvement with IVIG.
Sensory discomfort was reported as a presenting symptom in all 84 patients, while autonomic symptoms were reported in less than half.
Burning pain (91.1%) and tingling/prickling sensations (78.2%) were the most commonly reported sensory disturbances among patients who completed painDETECT.

Fabry disease (assessed via alpha-galactosidase A activity) was screened for as part of the etiologic work-up but is noted, based on cited literature, to be an unlikely cause of SFN in this population.
The large majority (79.2%, 19/24) of genetically confirmed SCA6 patients showed no neurophysiological evidence of a peripheral neuropathy on nerve conduction and related studies.
One SCA6 patient with impaired glucose tolerance had a mild sensorimotor polyneuropathy involving both large and small fibers, suggesting a comorbid rather than SCA6-intrinsic cause.
One elderly SCA6 patient had a length-dependent axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy, consistent with age-related large fiber involvement rather than an SCA6-specific process.
Two SCA6 patients had minor sensory abnormalities on nerve conduction testing, with one of these having comorbid type II diabetes and a history of chemotherapy.
One SCA6 patient had minor small fiber abnormalities detected on neurophysiological testing without an identified comorbid cause reported.
Median neuropathy at the wrist (carpal tunnel-type findings) was present in 41.7% (10/24) of SCA6 patients, a common comorbid entrapment neuropathy rather than SCA6-related neuronopathy.
All somatosensory evoked potentials tested (15/15) were normal in SCA6 patients, arguing against central sensory pathway/neuronopathy involvement.
Autonomic function testing (including tilt table and quantitative sudomotor axon reflex testing) was normal in the large majority of SCA6 patients tested.
In patients with small fiber neuropathy, wearing postural insoles for 6 weeks significantly reduced foot pain intensity during mobilization measured by VAS.
In patients with ankylosing spondylitis (nociceptive pain), wearing postural insoles for 6 weeks significantly reduced foot pain intensity during mobilization measured by VAS.
Global pain intensity and disease-specific activity/functioning scores (BPI, BASDAI, NPSI, DN4) all improved after 6 weeks of postural insole use in the respective patient groups.
Improvement in posturo-podiatric clinical outcomes did not correspond to a difference in clinical pain scores between patients with positive versus non-positive posturo-podiatric changes.
In the ankylosing spondylitis group only, mean velocity of center of pressure displacement (a stabilometric measure of postural control) significantly decreased after 6 weeks of postural insole use.
No significant change in stabilometric mean velocity of center of pressure was found after postural insole use in the small fiber neuropathy group.

The reduction in mean velocity of center of pressure correlated with the reduction in Brief Pain Inventory score in the ankylosing spondylitis group, suggesting improved postural control relates to reduced pain interference in daily activities.

The authors conclude that in neuropathic pain (SFN), mechanisms other than postural changes likely contribute to the analgesic effects of postural insoles, in contrast to nociceptive pain from spinal osteoarthritis (AS).

Unlike in the ankylosing spondylitis group, patients with small fiber neuropathy showed no significant change in stabilometric mean velocity of center of pressure displacement after 6 weeks of wearing postural insoles.

The authors conclude that in neuropathic foot pain (SFN), mechanisms other than postural/biomechanical changes likely underlie the analgesic effect of postural insoles, unlike in nociceptive pain from spinal osteoarthritis (AS) where postural control improvement appears more relevant.
IGFBP-1 levels in induced sputum supernatant were significantly higher in systemic sclerosis patients than in healthy volunteers.
TGF-β levels in induced sputum were significantly increased in SSc patients compared with healthy volunteers, without difference between SSc-ILD and SSc-nonILD subgroups.
IL-8 levels in induced sputum were significantly higher in SSc patients compared to healthy volunteers.
YKL-40 levels in induced sputum were significantly increased in SSc patients versus healthy volunteers, an original finding not previously described in this airway compartment for SSc.
MMP-7 levels in induced sputum were significantly higher in SSc patients compared to healthy volunteers.
IGFBP-2 sputum levels showed no significant difference between SSc patients and healthy volunteers.
MMP-9 sputum levels showed no significant difference between SSc patients and healthy volunteers.
IGFBP-3 and TNF-α were undetectable in induced sputum of both SSc patients and healthy volunteers.
Among all serum parameters tested, only serum IL-8 was significantly higher in SSc patients than in healthy volunteers, though at concentrations roughly 100-fold lower than in sputum.
In SSc patients, induced sputum IL-8 levels correlated negatively with FEV-1% and FVC%.
In a longitudinal subset of 14 SSc patients, induced sputum IL-8 levels correlated positively with the annualized change in KCO (∆KCO%).
In the longitudinal subset, induced sputum TGF-β levels correlated negatively with the annualized change in FEV-1 (∆FEV-1%).
In the longitudinal subset, induced sputum IGFBP-2 levels correlated positively with the annualized change in KCO (∆KCO%).
Induced sputum IGFBP-2 levels correlated positively with the modified Rodnan skin score in SSc patients.
The weight of induced sputum samples was significantly lower in SSc patients than in healthy volunteers, while cellularity was similar between groups.

Sputum and serum levels of MMP-7 and YKL-40 were positively correlated in healthy volunteers, but these correlations were lost in SSc patients, suggesting intense local bronchioloalveolar production of these proteins in disease.

Within the SSc-ILD subgroup, induced sputum IL-8 levels showed a trend to increase with greater severity of pulmonary involvement (mild < moderate < severe), though the small subgroup sizes limit interpretation.

In non-TB-infected control lung tissue, tryptase-positive mast cells (MCT) were the predominant mast cell phenotype, more abundant than double-positive (MCTC) cells, while chymase-only mast cells (MCC) were not detected.
Isolated chymase-only mast cells were rare in normal lung, as all chymase-positive cells observed were also tryptase-positive (i.e., MCTC rather than pure MCC).
Both mast cell phenotypes (MCT and MCC) were abundant at inflammatory (granulomas, pneumonia, vascular and airway walls) and fibrotic areas of TB-infected lungs but were absent near necrotic sites.

Tryptase-positive mast cells in inflammatory regions of TB-infected lung tissue contained intracellular vacuoles with Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens, indicating mast cells store or harbor the pathogen.

Mast cells were seen intermixed with lymphocytes/macrophages in incipient (early) granulomas but were largely excluded from the necrotic core of mature, well-organized granulomas, being confined to their periphery instead.
IL-17A-positive mast cells were observed in tissue neighboring typical granulomas and mixed within incipient granulomas, suggesting mast cell-derived IL-17A contributes to granuloma maturation.

In fibrotic areas of TB-infected lung, double-positive MCTC mast cells were the most abundant phenotype, exceeding MCT numbers, indicating a phenotypic switch from tryptase-only to tryptase+chymase mast cells at sites of TB-induced fibrosis.

Mast cells at fibrotic areas of TB-infected lung expressed TGF-β and displayed disorganized granular content suggestive of activation or partial degranulation, implicating mast cell TGF-β in fibrogenesis.

No colocalization/association between mast cells and TNF-α was observed in the TB-infected tissue examined, contrasting with mouse models where MC-derived TNF-α is implicated in granuloma maintenance.
The patient developed severe orthostatic hypotension with compensatory tachycardia, with blood pressure falling and heart rate rising markedly from supine to standing position.
Endoscopic evaluation confirmed gastroparesis with retained solid food in the stomach ~14 hours after last meal, consistent with autonomic GI dysmotility.
Initial IVIG therapy for five days produced no noticeable improvement in the patient's neurological symptoms.
An initial 6-session course of plasmapheresis produced only a slight, transient improvement in strength before relapse of weakness and worsening autonomic symptoms.
A second 6-session cycle of plasmapheresis resulted in moderate improvement of the patient's neurological symptoms.
Oral pyridostigmine led to significant improvement in gastrointestinal symptoms, tachycardia, orthostasis, and motor strength after other treatments had failed.
Midodrine and fludrocortisone were required at up-titrated doses to allow the patient to tolerate standing due to refractory orthostatic hypotension.
Myalgia was refractory to tramadol, acetaminophen, and pregabalin, but responded to morphine and gabapentin.
Persistent diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting were refractory to cholecystectomy and a broad range of standard antiemetic and GI medications.
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy for acalculous chronic cholecystitis with reduced ejection fraction on HIDA scan yielded no further improvement in the patient's symptoms.

Nerve conduction studies showed severe sensory neuropathy and diffuse demyelinating neuropathy in the bilateral lower extremities with normal upper extremity conduction, indicating predominance of sensory over motor deficits.
Anti-ganglioside (GQ1B) IgG antibody testing was negative, which does not rule out GBS/Miller-Fisher variant but limited definitive subtype diagnosis.
Lumbar puncture showed elevated CSF protein with normal white blood cell count (albuminocytologic dissociation), supporting the diagnosis of GBS.
EBV serology showed elevated VCA IgG and EBNA IgG consistent with past infection rather than acute EBV, so EBV was not considered an acute trigger.
Despite a targetoid skin lesion raising suspicion for Lyme disease after hiking, Lyme antibody screening was negative, though confirmatory western blot was not obtained.
Campylobacter enteritis was proposed as a likely antecedent trigger for the patient's GBS via molecular mimicry against axonal gangliosides, despite negative stool/antibody confirmation.
Dysautonomia occurring in GBS is associated, per prior literature, with increased mortality and worse functional outcomes.

Crtap-/- mice have thinner, hypercellular Achilles and patellar tendons with reduced tendon volume at 1 and 4 months of age compared to wildtype and heterozygous mice, a phenotype absent at postnatal day 10.
At 1 month of age, Crtap-/- Achilles tendons showed decreased ultimate load and linear stiffness on biomechanical testing compared to heterozygous and wildtype mice.

FACS analysis of 5-month-old patellar tendons showed a significant decrease in CD45-CD31-CD146+CD200+ progenitor-like cells (~2% vs ~4% in wildtype) with a concomitant increase in CD146-CD200+ cells in Crtap-/- mice.

TEM analysis of FDL, Achilles, and patellar tendons at 4 months revealed an increase in small (20-60nm) and large (>200-340nm) collagen fibrils with reduction in mid-range fibril diameters, and irregular fibril alignment, in Crtap-/- mice compared to wildtype, with the patellar tendon showing the most pronounced changes.

Stable HP collagen cross-links were increased in FDL, Achilles, and patellar tendons of Crtap-/- mice at 1 and 4 months compared to wildtype, with the patellar tendon showing a 5- to 10-fold elevation.

Heterozygous Crtap+/- mice showed intermediate, tissue-specific phenotypes (e.g., increased collagen cross-links in Achilles tendon at 1 month, altered fibril distribution in FDL and patellar tendons) that were milder than homozygous Crtap-/- mice, suggesting a semi-dominant effect of CRTAP dosage.

RNA-seq/IPA analysis of Achilles tendons identified 178 differentially expressed genes (99 up, 79 down) between wildtype and Crtap-/- mice, with predicted activation of TGF-β1 and inhibition of dystrophin (DMD) as upstream regulators, and enrichment of cell adhesion and ossification-related GO terms.

RNA-seq/IPA analysis of patellar tendons identified 519 differentially expressed genes (224 up, 295 down), with minor collagens (Col9a3, Col9a1, Col22a1) and ECM proteins (Lum, Fn1) among top changes, GO enrichment for metabolic/proliferative/angiogenic processes, and predicted highly significant activation of TNF, IL-6, FGF2, and TGF-β3.

qRT-PCR confirmed upregulation of tendon markers Scx, Tnc, Lum, Tnmd, Fn1, and Thbs3 in Crtap-/- Achilles tendons at 1 month, with modest downregulation of Col1a1 and no change in Col1a2, Col2a1, Col3a1, Col9a2, or CD31.

Immunohistochemistry at 4 months showed increased alpha smooth muscle actin (αSMA), MMP2, and phosphorylated NFκB, along with increased immature collagen (Herovici staining), in Crtap-/- patellar tendons compared to wildtype, consistent with excess matrix remodeling and tissue inflammation.
Crtap-/- mice displayed significant reductions in horizontal and vertical spontaneous motor activity in the open-field assay at 4 months of age compared to heterozygous and wildtype mice.

Crtap-/- mice showed reduced motor coordination and endurance on the rotarod assay (reduced latency to fall at later trials) and increased forelimb/hindlimb foot slips on the grid foot slip assay compared to heterozygous and wildtype mice, with no differences during the initial learning phase.
Crtap-/- mice exhibited markedly reduced grip strength (mean 0.62 N) compared to wildtype and heterozygous mice (approximately 1.3 N), along with reduced latency to fall on the inverted grid assay.

Ectopic chondrogenesis was observed at either end of the patellar tendon in some (but not all) 4-month-old Crtap-/- mice, a phenomenon associated with tendinopathy, while articular cartilage volume and surface were not significantly changed.
Patients infected with SARS-CoV-2 had an increased adjusted relative risk of loose stools compared with uninfected controls 5 months post-infection.
Patients infected with SARS-CoV-2 had a significantly increased adjusted relative risk of chronic fatigue compared with controls 5 months post-infection.
Patients infected with SARS-CoV-2 had a significantly increased adjusted relative risk of somatization compared with controls 5 months post-infection.
Gastrointestinal sequelae at 5 months were greater among patients who experienced diarrhea during the acute phase of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
During the acute phase of SARS-CoV-2 infection, more than 40% of patients reported fever, dyspnea, loss of smell/taste, weight loss, diarrhea, myalgia, arthralgia, and asthenia.

Continuous 12-week intake of the LG21 strain showed no statistically significant difference from placebo in ΔTmax-AUC, the primary endpoint measuring change in gastric emptying over the intake period, in the per-protocol population.
The odds ratio for a ≥30% improvement in delayed gastric emptying after 12 weeks was 4.1 favoring the LG21 group over placebo, though this did not reach statistical significance.
Change in salivary amylase concentration was significantly reduced in the LG21 group compared to placebo after 12 weeks of intake, suggesting an effect on autonomic (sympathetic) activity.

Among LG21 recipients, baseline salivary amylase concentration was strongly negatively correlated with the change in amylase after 12 weeks, indicating a greater reduction in participants with higher baseline (more stressed) autonomic state; no such relationship existed in the placebo group.
Gastric emptying rate after ingestion of a liquid meal following 12 weeks of intake was suppressed (trend) in the LG21 group compared to placebo across the full 90-minute measurement period.

In a strictly defined subgroup excluding high-appetite and suspected pan-enteric dysmotility participants, the odds ratio for improvement in delayed gastric emptying with LG21 versus placebo increased to 9.0-10.7, and a significant group difference in improvement rate (LG21 80% vs placebo 0%) was found.
In the strictly defined subgroup, global impression of overall gastric condition showed significant improvement after 6 weeks of LG21 intake compared to placebo.
In screening of individuals with stomach upset, mean gastric emptying Tmax was significantly longer in women than in men.
There was no statistically significant interaction between treatment group and gender on the odds of improvement in delayed gastric emptying.

Adverse events (colds, gastrointestinal symptoms, sleep disorders, headache, arthralgia) occurred in both groups (13 placebo, 19 LG21), all non-serious, transient, and judged not causally related to the test food.
In mice with myocardial infarction, treatment with the cAMP analog MAC improved ejection fraction, fractional shortening, and stroke volume compared with untreated MI mice.
CTGF mRNA and protein expression in both infarct and non-infarct areas of the heart was significantly higher in MI and MI+MAC groups than in sham-operated mice.
MAC treatment significantly lowered CTGF mRNA and protein expression in both infarct and non-infarct heart areas compared with untreated MI mice.
TGF-β1 mRNA and protein expression in infarct and non-infarct areas was significantly higher in MI and MI+MAC groups than in sham mice.
MAC treatment did not significantly change TGF-β1 mRNA or protein expression compared with untreated MI mice, unlike its effect on CTGF.
In primary mouse cardiac fibroblasts, TGF-β1 stimulation for 24 hours significantly increased CTGF mRNA and protein levels compared with untreated control cells.

Forskolin (an adenylate cyclase agonist) significantly increased intracellular cAMP levels in TGF-β1-stimulated cardiac fibroblasts compared with TGF-β1 alone, while TGF-β1 alone did not change cAMP versus control.
Forskolin-induced elevation of cAMP significantly reduced CTGF mRNA and protein expression in TGF-β1-stimulated cardiac fibroblasts compared with TGF-β1 alone.
Forskolin treatment significantly lowered p44/42MAPK mRNA and protein levels in TGF-β1-stimulated cardiac fibroblasts compared with TGF-β1 alone.
Forskolin treatment significantly increased PKA mRNA and protein levels in TGF-β1-stimulated cardiac fibroblasts compared with TGF-β1 alone.

Adding the MAPKK inhibitor PD98509 to forskolin/TGF-β1-treated fibroblasts further reduced CTGF mRNA and protein levels compared with forskolin/TGF-β1 alone, indicating cAMP suppresses CTGF via the p44/42MAPK pathway.
At 4 months after mild SARS-CoV-2 infection, shortness of breath, anosmia, ageusia and fatigue were present in 8.6%, 12.4%, 11.1% and 9.7% of followed patients respectively.
Post-COVID syndrome (defined as at least one of anosmia, ageusia, fatigue or dyspnea) was present in 27.8% of followed patients at 4 months and 34.8% at 7 months.
Relative to the entire initial cohort of 958 patients, 12.8% had long-lasting post-COVID symptoms at both 4 and 7 months.
At 7 months, anosmia (14.7%), shortness of breath (13.6%), fatigue (14.7%) and ageusia (11.0%) remained the most common persisting symptoms.
Male sex was associated with a lower risk of developing post-COVID syndrome compared with female sex.
A greater number of acute-phase symptoms was an independent predictor of developing post-COVID syndrome after 7 months.
Diarrhoea during acute COVID-19 was an independent predictor of post-COVID syndrome after 7 months.
Anosmia during acute COVID-19 was the strongest independent predictor of post-COVID syndrome after 7 months.
Ageusia during acute COVID-19 was associated with increased risk of developing post-COVID syndrome in univariate analysis.
Lower baseline SARS-CoV-2 IgG titre (measured 6 weeks after symptom onset) was associated with a higher risk of developing post-COVID syndrome at 7 months.
SARS-CoV-2 IgG titers progressively declined from the first to the third clinic visit over the follow-up period.
Even after mild acute COVID-19, 11% of patients could not fully return to everyday activities or work 7 months after infection onset.
Patients who dropped out of follow-up reported similar rates of post-COVID symptoms as those retained in the study, suggesting minimal attrition bias.
Pre-existing comorbid conditions (preconditions) prior to SARS-CoV-2 infection were not significantly associated with risk of post-COVID syndrome.

The authors hypothesize, citing another report, that endothelial dysfunction in brain capillaries could be a physical correlate of post-COVID fatigue, though this was not directly tested in this cohort.

The authors propose that SARS-CoV-2 entry via the ACE2 receptor in the nasal epithelium may cause olfactory neuroepithelial injury underlying anosmia, based on prior literature rather than this study's own data.

Citing external literature, the authors note that pulmonary vascular angiogenesis occurs more frequently in COVID-19 than influenza, proposed as a possible explanation for persistent dyspnoea and anosmia in PCS.

Citing Gaebler et al., the authors note SARS-CoV-2 persistence in intestinal biopsies of asymptomatic individuals 3 months post-infection, proposed as a possible link between viral persistence and post-COVID diarrhoea/PCS.

A 2008 patient organization questionnaire cited in the Health Council report found that the proportion of ME/CFS patients reporting improvement after CBT was roughly equal to the proportion reporting deterioration.

A patient organization questionnaire cited in the Health Council report found that a majority of ME/CFS patients experienced substantial diagnostic delay, with 80% diagnosed more than a year after symptom onset and 40% waiting four years or more.
The Health Council report characterizes ME/CFS as a multisystem illness that may involve the immune, metabolic, cardiovascular, central nervous, neuro-endocrine, microbiome and genomic systems.

Cooperating patient organizations asserted that there is sufficient evidence of immune dysfunction and frequent orthostatic intolerance in ME, along with objective brain abnormalities reported across a series of studies.

Patient organizations expressed ambivalence about the IOM diagnostic criteria adopted for the Health Council advisory, preferring the more extensive International Consensus Criteria (ICC), which they argued better captures the breadth and interrelation of ME/CFS symptoms.
Patient representatives stated that the effectiveness of CBT and graded exercise therapy (GET) for ME/CFS is unproven and that these therapies can cause harm to patients' wellbeing.

H2O2-induced oxidative stress altered the cytoplasm permittivity and conductivity of L6 skeletal muscle cells compared to normally cultured cells, as measured by single-cell broadband impedance spectroscopy.

Reflection and transmission coefficients (ΔS11 and ΔS21) of normally cultured cells were tightly clustered and closely resembled the cell-free solution across 9 kHz to 9 GHz, indicating minimal deviation in unstressed cells.
Oxidized L6 cells showed a wide distribution of dielectric properties in the GHz range, deviating in both positive and negative directions from normally cultured cells.

Calcium imaging directly supported that calcium flux contributes to the observed deviations in electrical impedance (S parameters) seen in oxidized cells, consistent with simulation-based hypotheses of ion alterations.
Autoantibodies against M1 acetylcholine receptors are demonstrated in ME/CFS patients and their occurrence is associated with reduced binding of M1 AChR ligand in the brain on PET imaging.
Autoantibodies against β1 and β2 adrenergic receptors were found in patients with ME/CFS.

β-adrenergic receptor autoantibodies occurring in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy, orthostatic hypotension, and POTS contribute to autonomic dysfunction and fatigue, features shared with ME/CFS patients.

Neurotransmitter receptor autoantibody levels correlate significantly with immunoglobulin levels, T-cell activation, and other autoantibodies such as ANA and TPO antibodies, suggesting broad immune activation.

In prior studies, depletion of CD20+ B cells with rituximab led to complete or at least partial remission in a majority of ME/CFS patients, an effect thought to reflect wash-out of autoantibodies after elimination of antibody-producing plasma cells.
In an observational study of ten patients with post-infectious ME/CFS, immunoadsorption using an IgG-binding column for 5 days induced rapid improvement in seven patients.
Extracorporeal apheresis (INUSpheresis) achieved a significant reduction of total IgG and all neurotransmitter receptor autoantibodies of up to 50%.
Extracorporeal apheresis (INUSpheresis) reduced inflammatory proteins such as CRP and RANTES in ME/CFS patients.

Extracorporeal apheresis conducted over 2 or 4 days induced significant clinical symptom improvement in ME/CFS patients based on disease-specific scores, with patients having a clear infection-triggered increase of autoantibodies showing the most sustained benefit.
Testing of HPA-axis function in post-COVID-19 patients who had received dexamethasone showed no blunting of adrenal cortisol levels, an unpublished observation.
Post-COVID-19 patients showed elevations of neurotransmitter receptor antibodies similar to those observed in other forms of infection-triggered ME/CFS.

In three post-COVID-19 patients, extracorporeal apheresis (INUSpherese) significantly reduced neurotransmitter autoantibody levels and alleviated CFS symptoms while maintaining sufficient levels of the patients' anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibodies.

According to the authors' clinical experience, replacement with antioxidants and vitamins is insufficient to produce major improvement in the clinical signs of post-COVID/ME-CFS fatigue syndrome, despite a possible contribution of oxidative stress.
The authors state that cognitive behavioral therapy is not likely to be sufficient to help patients with post-COVID/ME-CFS fatigue syndrome.
Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal hypofunction has been described in ME/CFS patients as a consequence of activated immune-inflammatory pathways.
An 11-year-old boy developed chronic fatigue syndrome following recovery from dengue haemorrhagic fever.
Investigations in the patient were largely normal except for a mild elevation of liver function tests.
Treatment with physiotherapy and nutrition counselling did not resolve symptoms, as the patient continued to have symptoms at 1-year follow-up.

Qualitative analysis of letters to the editor written by CFS/ME patients identified 13 mechanisms of symbolic violence (e.g., non-recognition, institutionalized un-care, delegitimization, invisibilization, silencing, isolation, self-blaming) reflecting societal dismissal of the illness.

Multiple Correspondence Analysis showed that structural mechanisms of symbolic violence (non-recognition, disintegration) combined with more symbolic mechanisms to produce the observed overall effects of symbolic violence against CFS/ME patients.
Baseline performance validity test (ASTM) scores were not significantly associated with cognitive behavioral therapy outcomes at follow-up in CFS patients.
CFS patients who had a missing follow-up assessment had lower baseline ASTM performance validity scores than those retained for follow-up.
Patients who did not complete follow-up assessment reported higher levels of physical limitations at baseline compared to those retained.
CFS patients with lower baseline ASTM performance validity scores completed fewer CBT therapy sessions, indicating reduced treatment adherence.
Among CFS patients retained in CBT treatment, response to therapy was comparable between those with low versus high baseline ASTM performance validity scores.

Self-rated clinical global impression scores of 'much worse' or 'very much worse' were reported by 4% of participants after graded exercise therapy versus 8% after control interventions, with no statistically significant difference.
Withdrawal from treatment occurred in 12% of participants after graded exercise therapy versus 10% after control interventions, with no statistically significant difference.
More participants dropped out of trial follow-up after graded exercise therapy (11%) than after control interventions (7%), a statistically significant difference.
After three months of neurocognitive rehabilitation exercises, hEDS patients with chronic low back pain showed significant improvement in pain intensity measured by the numerical rating scale.
The McGill pain questionnaire total score significantly improved after the neurocognitive rehabilitation intervention.
Fatigue severity, as measured by the fatigue severity scale, significantly decreased after the rehabilitation program.
Kinesiophobia (fear of movement), measured by the Tampa scale, was significantly reduced after treatment.
Pain-associated disability, measured by the Oswestry disability index, significantly improved after the rehabilitation program.
The majority of patients (88.9%) achieved a clinically meaningful reduction in pain (minimal clinically important difference) on the NRS after the intervention.
42% of patients achieved a clinically meaningful reduction in disability (minimal clinically important difference) on the ODI scale after the intervention.

Prior quantitative sensory testing in hEDS patients showed no somatosensory nervous system damage but an increased wind-up ratio, suggesting pain in hEDS may arise through central sensitization rather than peripheral neuropathy.

A modified Nominal Group Technique with 9 women with HSD/hEDS identified education about the condition, self-help strategies, and how to judge information about HSD/hEDS as priority behaviour change techniques.
Participants prioritised training in activity pacing, assertiveness and communication skills, and preparation for symptom changes expected during pregnancy.
Participants identified a need for environmental restructuring and enablement via occupational therapy support to maintain independence at work and home.
Participants wanted modelled behaviour narratives illustrating how other people with HSD/hEDS have coped with the psychosocial impact of their condition.
Participants reported poor access to psychological support and occupational therapy and a general lack of knowledge about HSD/hEDS as barriers to self-management.
Qualitative interviews with EDS/HSD patients showed that work participation is highly valued, providing income and social relationships.
Full-time work weeks were found to be too demanding a burden for many EDS/HSD patients, indicating difficulty matching work to personal capacity.
Flexibility to vary workload and schedule was reported by patients as contributing to sustainable employability in EDS/HSD.
Physically demanding tasks such as lifting heavy objects or repetitive movements were reported to sometimes exceed patients' personal capacity, contributing over time to leaving the labor market.

Belgian government support instruments (e.g., specialized job coaching and employer financial support) were reported to be actually used by EDS/HSD patients and helped several participants return to or remain in work.
Across the included RCTs, physiotherapy interventions produced significant improvements in pain regardless of the specific type of intervention used.
Physiotherapy interventions in hEDS patients led to significant improvements in proprioception across the included RCTs.
Inspiratory muscle training was found to benefit functional exercise capacity in hEDS patients.
Quality of life was systematically improved across the physiotherapy intervention studies in hEDS patients.

A 16-year-old girl with joint hypermobility and type III EDS and MRKH syndrome (46 XX, absent uterus/cervix/upper vagina) progressed from a 1-cm to a 7-8-cm vaginal dimple within 2 months of starting vaginal dilation, a rate faster than typically observed.

The authors conclude that recognizing EDS in patients with Müllerian anomalies undergoing vaginal dilation is important for safety, due to increased tissue elasticity raising risks of accidental urethral dilation, tissue prolapse, and theoretical vaginal perforation.

Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS type IV) is caused by autosomal dominant mutations in COL3A1 leading to a deficit of type III collagen, a key constituent of arterial walls and the digestive tract.
EDS type IV (vascular subtype) accounts for approximately 5% of all Ehlers-Danlos cases, within an overall EDS prevalence of about 1 in 5000 people.
EDS4 patients undergoing surgery, including cholecystectomy, are at increased risk of visceral perforation, aneurysm rupture, and other major complications due to tissue friability.

Elective cholecystectomy in a controlled setting was chosen over a watch-and-wait approach for gallstone disease, since EDS4 patients are at increased risk of requiring emergency surgery for complications like cholecystitis or gallstone pancreatitis.

A multidisciplinary perioperative plan involving upper GI and vascular surgeons, cardiology, and anesthetists, including vascular surgeon standby and HDU booking, was used to minimize complication risk for cholecystectomy in this EDS4 patient.

Hem-o-lok clips were used instead of mechanical clipping devices to secure the cystic duct and artery, as mechanical clips were felt to risk shear-force division of friable tissue in this EDS4 patient.
A standard laparoscopic approach was chosen over open surgery to reduce the risk of postoperative wound herniation given tissue fragility in EDS4.
Preoperative antiplatelet therapy (Ticagrelor), taken for a prior stented dissected coronary artery, was stopped in coordination with cardiology prior to surgery.
On postoperative surveillance over two years, the patient's renal artery and splenic artery aneurysms and carotid bulb dilatation remained largely stable, with only about 2 mm growth overall.
EDS patients pose additional anesthetic risk during endotracheal intubation due to cervical atlantoaxial subluxation from cervical ligament laxity and temporomandibular joint dislocation.

A patient with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome experienced multiple postoperative complications over a decade following total temporomandibular joint reconstruction, including two failed total joint replacements.

The case raises the question of whether Ehlers-Danlos syndrome should be considered an absolute contraindication for total temporomandibular joint reconstruction due to risk of postoperative complications.

The patient exhibited classic EDS-hypermobility type features including finger and cervical spine hypermobility, hyperextensible skin, a hypermobile temporomandibular joint with 7 cm mouth opening, and a positive Gorlin's sign.
The EDS-HT patient had significant co-occurring conditions of Takayasu arteritis with bilateral renal artery stenosis (4 years) and schizophrenia (3 years, untreated at time of surgery).

A tailored anesthetic protocol avoiding neck hyperextension, using minimal airway pressures during mask ventilation, gentle laryngoscopy with manual in-line stabilization, and careful joint positioning/padding resulted in successful nasal intubation and surgery without complications.

Invasive blood pressure was targeted within 10% of baseline with meticulous urine output monitoring to protect renal perfusion given the patient's bilateral renal artery stenosis from Takayasu arteritis.
Discussion notes that EDS-HT patients can have associated cardiac anomalies such as valvular prolapse and conduction disturbances, requiring vigilance during anesthesia.

The authors recommend avoiding NSAIDs in EDS due to increased risk of gastric bleeding and compromised renal perfusion, and using extra care to protect the eyes from pressure-related globe rupture or retinal detachment.
A novel PLOD1 variant c.2T>C (p.?) was identified in compound heterozygous state in a female newborn with kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
A novel PLOD1 frameshift variant c.1462del (p.Arg488Glyfs*9) was identified as the second compound heterozygous allele causing kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in the same newborn.
The authors propose that prenatal hydrocephalus should be considered as part of the differential diagnosis for kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, expanding the recognized perinatal phenotype.

A patient with a previously unreported homozygous pathogenic B3GALT6 variant presented with a complex phenotype more severe than spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia with joint laxity type 1 (SEMDJL1), including dural ectasia and aortic dilation as new associated features.

The authors note the diagnostic utility of repeating sequencing in patients with previously uninformative exomes, especially those originally analyzed with early-generation enrichment capture methods, which enabled identification of the causative B3GALT6 variant.

The patient exhibited generalized joint hypermobility of the fingers, wrists, elbows, and knees, scoring 8 out of 9 on the Beighton Criteria, supporting a diagnosis of hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (JHS/hEDS).
A cited study found that hypermobile joints were present in up to 60% of individuals with lipedema, supporting overlap between lipedema and joint hypermobility/connective tissue disorders.
A single-site study of 100 consecutive lipedema patients found 74% had a history of eating disorders, with 16% anorexia nervosa, 12% binge eating, and 8% bulimia.
In women with lipedema, the aorta was found to be dilated during both systole and diastole, supporting lipedema as a connective tissue disorder.
A loss of elasticity in calf tissue has been reported in women with lipedema, consistent with connective tissue pathology.
A UK study found that 93% of patients presenting with lipedema signs and symptoms were not recognized as having lipedema by their treating physicians.

Literature suggests extra-articular features of JHS/hEDS such as gastrointestinal problems, temporomandibular disorders, and food intolerances may contribute to development and maintenance of disturbed eating behaviors and significant weight loss.

In this case, the patient's anorexia nervosa was judged more likely related to feelings of being overweight due to unrecognized lipedema than to somatic extra-articular hEDS features, since she lacked those somatic problems.

This case demonstrates that lipedema, though often associated with higher body weight and BMI, can also present in underweight women, as this patient had lipedema fat accumulation despite a low BMI history from anorexia.
The patient's mother and sister also had disproportionately shaped and enlarged lower-body fat distribution, suggesting a familial pattern of lipedema.
Lipedema prevalence is estimated at approximately 11% of the female population based on the most cited estimate.
Anorexia nervosa has a lifetime prevalence of about 0.9% in women, an annual death rate of 0.56%, and is the psychiatric disorder with the highest mortality rate.
Cervical range of motion (CROM) correlated positively with generalised joint hypermobility (GJH), whether assessed as a continuous or dichotomous age- and gender-specific Beighton score.
Cervical range of motion decreased with increasing age across the lifespan.
Age, gender and extent of generalised joint hypermobility (as a continuous Beighton score) together explained 19-51% of the variability in cervical range of motion.
Cervical extension range of motion declined with age more than flexion, with the greatest loss occurring in the second and third decades of life.

A 56-year-old man with vascular EDS and a 50-mm type III postdissection thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm was successfully treated with a 2-stage endovascular procedure (left subclavian debranching followed by TEVAR and t-branch), with aortic remodeling and no endoleak at 3.5-year follow-up.

A 47-year-old man with vascular EDS and a 67-mm postdissection TAAA, following prior TEVAR and candy-plug for a ruptured false lumen aneurysm, developed aneurysmal false lumen dilatation distal to the candy-plug and was treated with fenestrated EVAR (F-EVAR) two years later.
Overall, endovascular repair of postdissection TAAA was found to be feasible and safe with good short-term outcomes in these two patients with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

A 75-year-old male with Marfan syndrome developed a splenic capsule rupture requiring emergency splenectomy the day after a routine outpatient colonoscopy with polypectomy, representing the first reported case of splenic rupture in a Marfan syndrome patient.
A systematic review conducted by the authors found Ehlers-Danlos syndrome to be the heritable connective tissue disorder most frequently implicated in cases of splenic injury following colonoscopy.

Vascular EDS carries an adverse instrumentation-related perforation rate of approximately 10%, though this may be under-reported and possibly less frequent than in Marfan syndrome or other EDS subtypes.

A prior multivariate analysis found connective tissue disease to be significantly associated with colonoscopy-related perforations, with a stronger association than non-metastatic cancer, renal disease, pulmonary disease, vascular disease, or ongoing anticoagulation use.
Splenic injury is a rare but highly morbid complication of colonoscopy, occurring at a rate of approximately 0.20 per 10,000 procedures and carrying a high mortality rate.

Ligament laxity, a core feature of heritable connective tissue disorders, is proposed to allow excessive downward stretching of the splenocolic ligament during colonoscopy, stretching and rupturing blood vessels without tearing the ligament itself.

Colonic histochemical samples from patients with heritable connective tissue disorders have shown weakened tissue layers from the submucosa through the muscularis propria, predisposing to inside-out colonic injuries during colonoscopy.
Marfan syndrome, an autosomal dominant heritable connective tissue disorder, affects approximately 2.5 per 10,000 individuals.

In Marfan syndrome, a rare additional splenic entity known as "wandering spleen" can occur, characterized by ligament weakness and propensity for splenic avulsion, more commonly seen in pediatric populations.

The patient's laboratory workup on presentation showed a marked hemoglobin drop from a baseline of 11 g/dl to 6.7 g/dl, with thrombocytopenia (62 k/ul), elevated lactic acid (8.92 mg/dl), hypoalbuminemia (2.7 g/dl), and elevated creatinine (2.12 mg/dl), consistent with hemorrhagic shock from splenic rupture.

Splenocolonic adhesions may be more likely in Marfan syndrome patients due to their propensity to develop accelerated vascular aneurysms requiring frequent surveillance and surgical repairs, potentially predisposing to splenic injury during colonoscopy.
Delta heart rate measured during the deep breathing test differed significantly between fibromyalgia patients with and without cardiac autonomic neuropathy.

Delta heart rate during the deep breathing test showed the best diagnostic performance for identifying cardiac autonomic neuropathy in fibromyalgia patients, with high sensitivity and negative predictive value.
The 30:15 ratio from the lying-to-standing test was a candidate index of cardiac autonomic neuropathy but did not differ significantly between CAN and non-CAN fibromyalgia patients.
Higher pain catastrophizing scores were associated with higher Glx levels in the insular cortex.
Higher pain catastrophizing scores were associated with higher tNAA levels in the insular cortex.
Higher pain catastrophizing scores were associated with lower myo-inositol levels in the posterior cingulate cortex.
Clinical pain severity was positively correlated with Glx levels in the insular cortex.
Clinical pain severity was positively correlated with Glx levels in the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC).
Clinical pain severity was positively correlated with tNAA levels in the anterior midcingulate cortex (aMCC).
Clinical pain severity was negatively correlated with mIno levels in the anterior midcingulate cortex (aMCC).
Clinical pain severity was negatively correlated with myo-inositol levels in the thalamus in women with fibromyalgia.
Evoked pain sensitivity was negatively correlated with tNAA levels in insular cortex in women with fibromyalgia.
Evoked pain sensitivity was negatively correlated with tNAA levels in midcingulate cortex (MCC) in women with fibromyalgia.
Evoked pain sensitivity was negatively correlated with tNAA levels in posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) in women with fibromyalgia.
Evoked pain sensitivity was negatively correlated with tNAA levels in thalamus in women with fibromyalgia.
Fibromyalgia patients showed reduced conditioned pain modulation (descending pain inhibition) compared to healthy controls.

Individuals with the genetically inferred TSPO high-affinity binder (HAB) variant showed reduced conditioned pain modulation compared to mixed/low-affinity binders (MLAB), in both FM and healthy control groups.
There was no significant interaction between TSPO polymorphism and group (FM vs HC) on the CPM score, indicating TSPO effects on pain modulation were not FM-specific.
Fibromyalgia patients required significantly lower pressure input to reach subjective pain ratings of 10 and 50 mm VAS, indicating increased pressure pain sensitivity compared to healthy controls.
TSPO polymorphism had no significant main effect or interaction on calibrated input pressures needed to reach P10/P50 pain ratings.
During the low-threat (green cue) condition, TSPO HAB carriers rated the mid-intensity pressure stimulus as more painful than MLAB carriers.
In contrast to the green-cue condition, TSPO polymorphism did not significantly affect pain ratings of the mid-intensity stimulus after the red (high-threat) cue.
Fibromyalgia patients rated the green-cue mid-intensity stimulus as more painful than healthy controls.
Fibromyalgia patients rated the red-cue mid-intensity stimulus as more painful than healthy controls, with the group difference changing over the course of the paradigm.
Absolute thalamic glutamate concentrations were significantly higher in TSPO HAB carriers compared to MLAB carriers, regardless of FM/HC status.

No significant main effects of TSPO polymorphism or group on rACC glutamate concentrations, though a near-significant TSPO×group interaction showed higher rACC glutamate in FM HABs vs MLABs and the opposite pattern in HC.
No significant effects of TSPO polymorphism or group, nor their interaction, were found for GABA concentrations in either rACC or thalamus.

Positive correlations between glutamate and GABA concentrations in the rACC were seen across all subjects, in FM, HAB, FM HAB, and HC HAB groups, but not in MLAB carriers; a significant negative correlation was found in HC MLAB for relative concentrations.

Positive correlations between glutamate and GABA concentrations in the thalamus were found across all subjects, in FM, HAB, and FM HAB groups (absolute and relative), and additionally in HC, MLAB, and HC MLAB groups for relative concentrations only.

Conditioned pain modulation (CPM) scores correlated positively with both glutamate and GABA concentrations in the rACC in fibromyalgia patients, TSPO HABs, and FM HABs, but not in healthy controls or MLAB carriers.
No significant correlations emerged between the CPM score and glutamate or GABA concentrations in the thalamus.
The distribution of TSPO genetic variants (HAB, MLAB) did not differ between FM and healthy control groups.
No differences in pain-evoked BOLD signal in the rACC or thalamus regions of interest were found between TSPO genotypes or between FM and HC, for either cue color condition.
No significant correlations were found between pain-evoked BOLD signal and glutamate or GABA concentrations in rACC or thalamus.

TSPO polymorphism showed no main effects or interactions with group on clinical measures including pain ratings (VAS), bodily pain (SF-36BP), anxiety/depression (HADS), catastrophizing (PCS), or pressure pain threshold (PPTmean); within FM alone, TSPO also did not affect FM duration, tender points, or FIQ.
Compared to healthy controls, fibromyalgia patients had higher pain, anxiety, depression, and catastrophizing scores, and lower pressure pain thresholds.

A large US inpatient database study found CRPS was diagnosed in 0.07% of discharges and was associated with female gender, Caucasian race, higher income, depression, drug abuse and headache, while obesity, diabetes, hypothyroidism and anemia were associated with lower CRPS rates.
A commercial/Medicare claims database study found CRPS prevalence of 1.2%, positively correlated with female gender, long-term disability, and multiple pain diagnoses.
CRPS is 2-4 times more prevalent in women than men across multiple studies.
Fibromyalgia is strongly and independently associated with a CRPS diagnosis, increasing risk up to 2.5-fold compared with controls.
Male CRPS patients were more likely than female patients to have depression, kinesiophobia, and use passive pain coping strategies.
Autonomic imbalance in CRPS patients manifests as skin color changes, tachycardia, decreased heart rate variability, low cardiac output, and excessive sweating.

In the acute (warm) phase of CRPS, decreased sympathetic outflow leads to compensatory upregulation and sensitization of peripheral α-1 adrenergic receptors, causing vasodilation, warmth and erythema.

Intradermal phenylephrine (an α-1 agonist) injection provoked hyperalgesia in CRPS patients, and those with hyperalgesia had greater cutaneous α-1 adrenergic receptor expression; CRPS-II and acute-phase patients showed higher receptor expression than chronic-phase patients.

A case study found significant degeneration of A-alpha nerve fibers with sparing of A-delta fibers in a CRPS patient, suggesting increased A-delta nociceptive activity may underlie allodynia and hyperalgesia.

Passive transfer of serum IgG from CRPS patients into mice with hind paw incisions caused increased hypersensitivity to painful mechanical, cold and heat stimuli, but not tactile stimulation, and patients with higher pain had higher IgG titers.

Using in vitro beating cardiomyocyte assays, patients with longstanding CRPS had elevated functionally active serum autoantibodies with alpha-1 adrenergic, beta-2 adrenergic, and M2 muscarinic agonist activity, which were generally absent in patients with other chronic pain conditions.
Among HLA genes studied in CRPS, HLA-DRB1 was the most significantly upregulated and HLA-DQB1 the most significantly downregulated, implicating the adaptive immune response in CRPS pathogenesis.

In post-amputation CRPS patients, a DNA methylation study found 48 statistically significant differentially methylated CpG sites, of which all but seven were hypomethylated compared to non-CRPS patients, with many related to immune function.

A case-control study found PTSD criteria were met by 38% of CRPS patients versus 10% of non-CRPS chronic pain controls and 4% of healthy controls; most CRPS patients with PTSD had symptoms predating their CRPS diagnosis.
A meta-analysis of three RCTs (875 patients) found daily 500 mg vitamin C supplementation for 50 days significantly reduced 1-year risk of CRPS following wrist fracture.
A meta-analysis of four RCTs (181 patients) showed a significant reduction in pain among CRPS-1 patients taking bisphosphonates compared to placebo.

Low-dose naltrexone, which inhibits microglial activation and reduces inflammatory response, has been used off-label for chronic pain syndromes including fibromyalgia and CRPS, though evidence is limited mainly to case studies.

A large randomized trial comparing dorsal root ganglion (DRG) stimulation to spinal cord stimulation (SCS) found higher treatment success rates, longer persistence of effects, and improved quality of life with DRG stimulation, with comparable safety.

A study identified IL-37 and GM-CSF as novel serum biomarkers in CRPS, with decreased IL-37 suggesting suppressed regulatory immune activation and increased GM-CSF reflecting a predominantly pro-inflammatory state.
Expanded populations of CD4+ and CD8+ lymphocytes have been documented in CRPS patients across multiple studies, suggesting an antigen-mediated T lymphocyte response.
Exposure to green light-emitting diodes (GLED) stimulated release of β-endorphin in the central nervous system of male rats.
GLED exposure stimulated release of proenkephalin in the central nervous system of male rats.
Gene editing of the µ-opioid receptor showed it is required for GLED's antinociceptive effect in naïve rats and in a model of HIV-induced peripheral neuropathy.
Gene editing of the δ-opioid receptor showed it is required for GLED's antinociceptive effect in naïve rats and in a model of HIV-induced peripheral neuropathy.

Green light-emitting diode exposure reversed thermal and mechanical hypersensitivity in a rat model of HIV-induced peripheral neuropathy, mediated via modulation of the spinal endogenous opioid system.
Prior clinical studies in migraine and fibromyalgia patients showed that green light-emitting diode exposure is a pragmatic and safe therapy to manage chronic pain.

The authors state that a validated MCAS diagnosis requires typical symptoms plus a substantial rise in serum tryptase during an acute attack above the patient's own baseline level, along with symptomatic response to mast cell-targeted therapy.
The paper reports that alternative, nonspecific diagnostic criteria for MCAS that have been proposed in the literature often lack specificity and validation compared to the consensus criteria.

The authors note that use of nonspecific criteria has led to an increasing number of patients being misdiagnosed with MCAS, causing confusion and frustration and sometimes delaying recognition and treatment of the actual underlying condition.
Safranal significantly reduced serum IgE levels in the OVA-induced asthma mouse model compared to OVA-treated mice.
Safranal reduced OVA-induced infiltration of inflammatory cells and mucus secretion in lung tissue on H&E and PAS staining.
OVA challenge significantly increased mast cell infiltration in lung tissue (toluidine blue and c-kit IHC), and safranal treatment reduced this mast cell infiltration.
OVA challenge increased Th2 cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) and decreased IFN-γ in lung tissue; safranal reversed this by decreasing IL-4/IL-5/IL-13 and increasing IFN-γ.
Safranal decreased OVA-induced CD4+ and Foxp3+ T cell infiltration in lung tissue.
High-dose safranal suppressed activation of the NF-κB and MAPK signaling pathways in splenocytes from OVA-treated mice.
RNA-seq of safranal- and DNP-HSA-treated BMMCs identified 13 immune-related differentially expressed genes, with Ccl7 and Cxcl10 showing the strongest protein-interaction relatedness.
Safranal decreased Cxcl10 levels in lung tissue of OVA-treated mice.
Safranal showed no significant cytotoxicity in bone marrow-derived mast cells (BMMCs) at concentrations up to 100 µM.
Safranal significantly reduced the percentage of β-hexosaminidase released from DNP-HSA-activated BMMCs, a marker of mast cell degranulation.
Safranal significantly inhibited production of TNF-α and IL-6 in DNP-HSA-activated BMMCs.
Safranal treatment dose-dependently decreased LTC4 production in DNP-HSA-activated BMMCs.
Safranal inhibited phosphorylation of cPLA2 and nuclear translocation of 5-LO in activated BMMCs.
Safranal inhibited phosphorylation of MAPK pathway proteins ERK, JNK, and p38 in DNP-HSA-activated BMMCs.
Safranal inhibited phosphorylation of IKK and IκBα in the NF-κB pathway in DNP-HSA-activated BMMCs.
Safranal inhibited nuclear translocation and DNA-binding activity of the transcription factors p65 (NF-κB) and AP-1 (c-Jun/c-Fos) in activated BMMCs.
In a passive systemic anaphylaxis (PSA) mouse model, serum LTC4 and histamine levels rose in the vehicle group and were reduced by safranal treatment.
Phosphorylated p38 and JNK protein levels in lung tissue showed a decreasing trend with high-dose safranal but did not reach statistical significance compared to the OVA model group.

The authors developed an isothermal proximity CRISPR Cas12a assay (iPCCA) that uses proximity hybridization rather than crRNA-target binding, allowing Cas12a to serve as a universal amplifier for DNA/RNA targets without a PAM domain, achieving a limit of detection of 1 fM for synthetic DNA after optimization.

Using iPCCA to directly measure IL-6 mRNA from total RNA of allergen-sensitized bone marrow-derived mast cells (BMMCs), IL-6 gene expression increased following IgE/allergen-mediated mast cell activation, peaking at 1-3 hours post-stimulation.

By conjugating iPCCA hybridization probes to polyclonal anti-IL-6 antibodies via streptavidin-biotin chemistry, the assay detected IL-6 protein directly and quantitatively in an isothermal, wash-free format down to 100 fM.

The temporal IL-6 expression pattern measured by iPCCA in activated mast cells closely matched the authors' earlier reverse-transcription PCR-based measurements, supporting iPCCA as a validated PCR-alternative method for quantifying this mast cell activation marker.
Hereditary alpha tryptasemia, caused by extra copies of TPSAB1, was found in 7.5% of a random biorepository population.
HαT was found more than twice as frequently in patients with mastocytosis (18%) compared to the general/biorepository population (7.5%).

Individuals with HαT did not differ from controls without HαT in clinical symptomology or medical history, including reflux, hypermobility, dysautonomia, flushing/pruritus, and hymenoptera allergy previously reported to be associated with the trait.
Average baseline serum tryptase levels were higher in individuals with HαT compared to controls without the trait.
Urinary mast cell activation products did not differ between individuals with HαT and controls.
Macrophages, marked by F4/80, infiltrated the injured tendon early after burn/tenotomy, appearing at 3 days, peaking at 7 days, and persisting up to 3 weeks.
Mast cells, marked by CPA3 and tryptase, infiltrated the tendon injury site early, peaking at 7 days and persisting up to 3 weeks after burn/tenotomy.
Macrophage depletion with clodronate liposomes markedly reduced heterotopic bone formation and blocked chondrogenesis and inflammatory cell infiltration at early stages.
Mast cell stabilization with cromolyn sodium reduced heterotopic ossification formation and blocked chondrogenesis and inflammatory cell infiltration at early stages.
SIRT1 expression was suppressed 7 days after burn/tenotomy compared to sham, coinciding with peak immune cell infiltration.
Direct SIRT1 activation with the agonist SRT1720 HCl significantly reduced heterotopic ossification formation as well as monocyte-derived macrophage and mast cell infiltration at early stages.
Acetylated NFκB p65 expression was dramatically increased after burn/tenotomy trauma but was inhibited by SIRT1 activation with SRT1720 HCl.

Molecular docking showed quercetin has high binding affinity to the SIRT1-activated pocket (ARG266, SER267, GLN337, SER433, SER434) comparable to the known SIRT1 agonist SRT1720, interacting via hydrogen bonds.
Quercetin restored SIRT1 protein expression, which was attenuated during monocyte-to-macrophage transition, M1 polarization, and mast cell activation in THP-1, BMDM, and P815 cells.

Quercetin significantly inhibited acetylated NFκB p65 expression during monocyte-to-macrophage transition, M1 polarization and mast cell activation; EX527 (SIRT1 antagonist) restored acetylated p65 despite quercetin, while SRT1720 abrogated it, confirming a causal SIRT1-NFκB relationship.

Quercetin dose-dependently decreased expression of the macrophage surface markers CD11b and CD14 and reduced cell adhesion/pseudopod formation in PMA-stimulated THP-1 cells, indicating decreased monocyte-to-macrophage transition.
Quercetin significantly downregulated production of TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6 and MCP-1 during PMA-induced monocyte-to-macrophage transition in THP-1 cells.
Quercetin dose-dependently reversed BMDM polarization to both M1 (INOS+) and M2 (CD206+) subtypes and reduced MCP-1-directed migration in a Transwell assay.
Quercetin restrained transcription and secretion of TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, MCP-1, IL-10 and TGF-β upregulated by LPS or IL-4 stimulation during BMDM polarization, in a dose-dependent manner.
Quercetin dose-dependently limited secretion of IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6 and MCP-1 induced by A23187 and PMA in P815 mast cells, with 20 μM reaching maximum inhibitory effect.
Quercetin at 20 μM significantly inhibited histamine and tryptase release from P815 mast cell granules, though the dose-dependent effect was not as prominent as for cytokines.
In the murine burn/tenotomy model, quercetin dose-dependently inhibited heterotopic ossification formation as confirmed by micro-CT quantification.
PDGFRα+ osteoprogenitor cell accumulation at the injury site was dramatically decreased after quercetin treatment, with higher doses exerting a better effect.
Toluidine blue staining showed that mast cell infiltration in tendon tissue after burn/tenotomy was significantly suppressed by quercetin.
Burn/tenotomy led to markedly increased presence of both M1 (F4/80+INOS+) and M2 (F4/80+CD206+) macrophages in tendon tissue, which was reduced by quercetin treatment.
Immunohistochemistry showed burn/tenotomy increased tissue TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, MCP-1, TGF-β and IL-10, and quercetin lowered accumulation of these cytokines in a dose-dependent manner.

EX527 blocked quercetin's inhibitory effects on monocyte-to-macrophage transition, macrophage polarization, cytokine production, and mast cell degranulation in vitro (THP-1, BMDM, P815), while SRT1720 partly or fully reproduced quercetin's effects, confirming SIRT1 dependence of quercetin's actions.

In the murine burn/tenotomy model, co-treatment with EX527 caused quercetin to partly lose its inhibitory effect on heterotopic ossification formation, along with restored monocyte-derived macrophage and mast cell infiltration and acetylated NFκB p65 expression.

Exogenous expression of EGFP-tagged βENaC in isolated mouse middle cerebral artery segments increased the pressure-induced constriction response, with approximately 2-fold greater peak myogenic tone compared to EGFP-alone controls.

Mechanical/morphological properties and vasoconstrictor responses to KCl and phenylephrine were identical between EGFP-βENaC and EGFP-only transfected middle cerebral artery segments, indicating the increased PIC effect was specific rather than a general change in contractility.

The authors propose that βENaC is critical to the pressure-induced constriction response and hypothesize that inflammation-mediated downregulation of βENaC may contribute to cerebrovascular dysfunction, though this was not directly tested.
