Mast cell degranulation and Th2 cytokine (IL-4, IL-13) production in response to activating agonists require NADPH oxidase activation as an obligate signaling step.
Low micromolar concentrations of bilirubin inhibit agonist-induced mast cell degranulation and adhesion molecule upregulation in vitro, mimicking the effect of heme oxygenase-1 induction.
Hydrogen sulfide acts in vitro to stabilize mast cells and slow proliferation of airway smooth muscle and airway fibroblasts.
DNP-HSA stimulation of IgE-sensitized RBL-2H3 mast cells triggered significant release of the degranulation marker β-hexosaminidase, confirming establishment of a valid mast cell activation model.
DNP-HSA stimulation increased transcription of the inflammatory cytokine/chemokine genes TNF, CCL2, and IL4 in activated RBLs.
RNA-seq of IgE/Ag-stimulated vs non-stimulated mast cells identified 191 differentially expressed genes (116 upregulated, 75 downregulated).
IgE/Ag stimulation increased c-Fos and FosB mRNA levels in mast cells, while Fosl1 and Fosl2 mRNA levels were unchanged.
Western blotting showed increased c-Fos and FosB protein along with increased c-Fos phosphorylation at Ser32 in activated mast cells.

IgE/Ag-stimulated mast cells showed increased Egr1 mRNA and EGR1 protein levels compared to non-stimulated cells, consistent with RNA-seq data, and c-Fos protein interacts with Egr1/Egr2/Egr3/IL-4/Ccl2 in network analysis.
shRNA-mediated knockdown of c-Fos (shFos) decreased EGR1 mRNA and protein levels compared to negative control shRNA-treated mast cells, indicating c-Fos drives EGR1 expression.
ChIP assay confirmed that c-Fos directly binds the Egr1 gene promoter, supporting transcriptional activation of EGR1 by c-Fos.
T-5224 exposure up to 50 µM for 24 h did not show cytotoxic effects on RBL-2H3 cells, supporting its safety for use in the concentration range tested.
T-5224 reduced AP1-luciferase reporter activity, confirming selective AP-1 inhibitory action in mast cells.

T-5224 reduced β-hexosaminidase release and suppressed IL4 release in DNP-HSA-activated RBLs, and decreased degranulation-associated morphological changes including cell elongation and F-actin decomposition.
T-5224 pretreatment dose-dependently decreased EGR1 transcription and translation in IgE-stimulated RBLs, with a stronger effect at 20 µM than 10 µM.
T-5224 dose-dependently inhibited phosphorylation of p38, JNK and ERK1/2 MAPK proteins in activated RBLs.
T-5224 did not affect BMMC viability but inhibited β-hexosaminidase and histamine release in IgE/Ag-stimulated BMMCs.
T-5224 pretreatment dose-dependently reduced IL4 mRNA, IL4 secretion, and Egr1 mRNA expression in BMMCs, and inhibited all three MAPK pathways (p38, JNK, ERK).
In the passive cutaneous anaphylaxis (PCA) mouse model, T-5224 attenuated IgE/Ag-induced dye diffusion, ear thickness, and dye extrusion, with effects comparable to the anti-allergy drug ketotifen.

In the OVA-induced active systemic anaphylaxis (ASA) model, T-5224 attenuated the OVA-challenge-induced drop in rectal temperature, with treated mice maintaining a temperature similar to non-sensitized controls.
T-5224 significantly diminished serum histamine elevation following OVA challenge in the ASA mouse model, with a similar reduction observed for serum IL-4.
In an oxazolone-induced atopic dermatitis mouse model, T-5224 attenuated ear skin thickening/swelling.
T-5224 significantly decreased mast cell infiltration in the dermis in the OXA-induced atopic dermatitis model.
T-5224 attenuated eosinophil infiltration into skin tissue in the OXA-induced atopic dermatitis model.
T-5224 (20 µM) did not affect the differentiation of precursor cells into mature bone marrow-derived mast cells.
Among 186 type 2 diabetes patients, 24.7% had pure small fiber neuropathy and 17.2% had mixed fiber neuropathy involving both small and large fibers.
Patients with pure small fiber neuropathy had significantly lower corneal nerve fiber density compared with those without diabetic peripheral neuropathy.
Corneal nerve branch density was significantly lower in pure small fiber neuropathy compared with non-DPN patients.
Corneal nerve fiber length was significantly lower in pure small fiber neuropathy compared with non-DPN patients, and progressively decreased further in mixed fiber neuropathy.
Neuropathy disability score and cardiovascular autonomic reflex test abnormalities were significantly greater in mixed fiber neuropathy than in both non-DPN and pure small fiber neuropathy groups.
Cold thresholds were significantly decreased in both pure small fiber neuropathy and mixed fiber neuropathy compared with non-DPN, with further decrease in mixed vs pure SFN.
Warm thresholds were significantly higher in both pure small fiber neuropathy and mixed fiber neuropathy compared with non-DPN.
Vibration perception threshold was significantly higher in both pure small fiber neuropathy and mixed fiber neuropathy compared with non-DPN.

Nerve conduction velocities of all tested nerves were significantly reduced in mixed fiber neuropathy compared with non-DPN and pure small fiber neuropathy; tibial motor NCV also declined in pure SFN vs non-DPN.
Corneal nerve fiber density and corneal nerve fiber length were significantly correlated with neuropathy symptom score, cold thresholds, warm thresholds, and all tested nerve conduction velocities.
Corneal nerve fiber length showed a significant negative correlation with vibration perception threshold.
Corneal nerve branch density was significantly correlated with warm thresholds and sural sensory nerve conduction velocity.

ROC analysis showed corneal nerve fiber density had the best diagnostic performance for pure small fiber neuropathy, with an AUC of 0.791, optimal cutoff 26.0/mm2, sensitivity 78.3%, specificity 70.4%.
ROC analysis showed corneal nerve fiber length had an AUC of 0.778 for diagnosing pure small fiber neuropathy, with cutoff 17.7 mm/mm2, sensitivity 91.3%, specificity 50.9%.
ROC analysis showed corneal nerve branch density had an AUC of 0.710 for diagnosing pure small fiber neuropathy, with cutoff 38.5/mm2, sensitivity 60.9%, specificity 73.2%.

Mixed fiber neuropathy patients had significantly longer diabetes duration, lower BMI, higher HbA1c, and higher frequency of diabetic retinopathy compared with both non-DPN and pure small fiber neuropathy groups.
There was no significant difference in demographics and clinical data between the non-DPN group and the pure small fiber neuropathy group.
An indirect ELISA for antiplexin D1-IgG showed 75% sensitivity and 100% specificity compared with the tissue-based immunofluorescence assay (TBA), with 96.6% overall coincidence.

Plexin D1-IgG was detected by ELISA in 12.7% (8/63) of all SFN patients, including 15.8% (6/38) of idiopathic SFN and 8.0% (2/25) of secondary SFN patients, compared with only 3.6% (2/55) of healthy controls.
Both secondary SFN patients who were plexin D1-IgG positive also had diabetes mellitus, suggesting antibody emergence may follow chronic small fiber nerve damage.
Plexin D1-IgG corrected OD values correlated positively with disease duration in SFN patients but not with age at sampling or age at onset.
IgG subclass analysis of plexin D1-IgG-positive patients revealed IgG2 predominance (87.5%), with 5 patients having only IgG2, 2 having predominant IgG2 with weak IgG1, and 1 having only IgG1.
SFN patients with plexin D1-IgG had significantly longer disease duration at serum sampling than plexin D1-IgG-negative SFN patients, and a higher frequency of pricking pain.
No sex preponderance was found in plexin D1-IgG-positive idiopathic SFN patients, contrasting with a previously reported female preponderance (75%) in idiopathic SFN generally.

Intrathecal injection of purified IgG from three plexin D1-IgG-positive neuropathic pain patients induced significantly higher mechanical pain reaction rates in mice compared with control IgG at multiple von Frey filament strengths 24 hours after injection.

Preabsorption of patient plexin D1-IgG with recombinant human plexin D1 extracellular domain abolished the mechanical pain hypersensitivity effect in mice, and IgG from plexin D1-IgG-negative inflammatory disease controls and healthy controls did not induce hypersensitivity.

IgG from one plexin D1-IgG-positive patient (patient 1) significantly shortened hot plate withdrawal latency in mice compared with control IgG, an effect abolished by rhPlexin D1 preincubation, though this thermal effect was not seen with IgG from the other two positive patients.

Intrathecal plexin D1-IgG from patients significantly increased the percentage of pERK-labeled (activated) DRG neurons, predominantly small neurons, compared with control IgG 24 hours after injection, an effect abolished by preabsorption with rhPlexin D1.
The pain-provoking and pERK-activating effects of plexin D1-IgG were transient, with no significant mechanical or thermal hypersensitivity or pERK increase observed 48 hours after injection.

Plexin D1-IgG selectively bound IB4-positive unmyelinated C-fiber type small DRG neurons on tissue sections, consistent with its role in mechanical pain sensation, and binding was abolished by preabsorption with rhPlexin D1.

Plexin D1-IgG was not detected in collagen-vascular/autoimmune disease patients without neuropathic pain, either in this study or a previous one, suggesting the antibody does not emerge in autoimmune disease unless neuropathic pain develops.
Global IBS prevalence estimates differ substantially depending on diagnostic criteria, being higher under Rome III than Rome IV.
Females are more frequently diagnosed with IBS and tend to experience more severe clinical symptoms than males.
IBS subtype distribution differs by sex, with constipation-predominant IBS more common in females and diarrhea-predominant IBS more common in males.
A study found significantly higher serum estradiol levels in females with IBS compared to healthy controls.
Males with IBS exhibited fewer male secondary characteristics on a male-trait score, suggesting reduced androgenic action may play a role.
A study reported higher testosterone levels in male IBS patients compared with healthy male controls, contrasting with the male-trait score finding.
Women with polycystic ovary syndrome, who have elevated androgen levels, show higher IBS risk than other females.
ERα and GPER receptor expression are upregulated and positively correlated with gut pain in IBS-D patients.
TRPV1-expressing sensory fibers are increased in colonic tissue from IBS patients and positively correlate with abdominal pain scores.
Estrogens sensitize and upregulate TRPV1 expression in sensory neurons in rodent and in vitro studies, a potential mechanism for sex differences in pain perception.
Treatment with DHT elevates TRPM8 expression in vitro, suggesting androgens modulate cold/pain receptor expression.
A study investigating a TRPM8 polymorphism found an association with increased IBS risk.
GPER mRNA levels are reported higher in IBS-D compared with IBS-C patients or healthy individuals, implicating GPER in bowel habit alteration.
The HPA axis stress response in IBS patients was found to be enhanced in males but blunted in females, highlighting sex-specific dysregulation.
A study found that autonomic nervous system imbalance in IBS preferentially occurs in males.
In a female-only IBS study, parasympathetic activity was lower in IBS-C patients than IBS-D patients, though autonomic function overall did not differ from healthy controls.
Female IBS patients show greater brain serotonin synthesis compared with healthy females, a difference not observed in males with IBS.
Alosetron, a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist, is more effective in treating IBS in females than males, possibly due to sex differences in drug metabolism and receptor signaling.
A 5HT2A receptor polymorphism is suggested as a risk factor for IBS, and the receptor is linked to smooth muscle contraction.
Mast cell abundance is correlated with clinical symptoms in IBS including abdominal pain, bloating, and depression.
IBS patients who experienced childhood trauma are more likely to suffer from somatization and psychological distress.
Genome-wide DNA methylation profiling of peripheral blood mononuclear cells from IBS patients identified genes with altered methylation status.
Stress during the COVID-19 pandemic exacerbated clinical symptoms in IBS patients.
Rectal sensitivity increased during menses in IBS patients but not in healthy volunteers, indicating hormonal modulation of visceral sensitivity specific to IBS.
Low FODMAP diet improves IBS symptoms while modulating gut microbiota composition and reducing SCFAs, which act as histone deacetylase inhibitors affecting epigenetic processes.
The number of mast cells per gram of omental adipose tissue was significantly lower in patients with T2D compared to both non-T2D and pre-T2D patients.
Mast cell numbers per gram of subcutaneous adipose tissue were significantly lower in T2D patients compared to non-T2D patients.
The normally higher mast cell density in omental versus subcutaneous adipose tissue was preserved in non-T2D and pre-T2D groups but was lost (no significant difference) in the T2D group.
A CD34+ integrin β7+ mast cell progenitor subpopulation was identified in both o-WAT and s-WAT but was absent in colonic mucosa negative-control samples, supporting a resident WAT progenitor pool.
Mast cell progenitors were more abundant in o-WAT than s-WAT and appeared to decrease with T2D status in both adipose depots.
In linear discriminant analysis separating T2D status groups, the number of mast cells in o-WAT was among the strongest correlates of the discriminant axis, alongside age and waist-hip index.

Random Forest analysis ranked the number of mast cells in o-WAT and s-WAT as the third and fifth most important variables (by mean decrease in Gini index) for discriminating T2D status, ranking above HDL, BMI, and waist-hip index.
A previously reported cohort from the same group found that after bariatric surgery, mast cell numbers increased 10-fold in o-WAT and 4-fold in s-WAT, alongside reduced tissue inflammation.

A cited study (Goldstein et al.) found that in patients with obesity, higher mast cell numbers in o-WAT were associated with lower cardiometabolic risk, greater weight loss after bariatric surgery, and higher hepatic insulin sensitivity.

A 15-year-old boy diagnosed with familial exudative vitreoretinopathy (FEVR) was found by whole exome sequencing to carry a heterozygous deletion mutation in a gene associated with Loeys-Dietz syndrome (LDS), yet showed no systemic features of LDS.
Despite carrying the LDS-associated gene mutation, the patient showed no systemic abnormalities typically associated with Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
At baseline, TGF-β1 protein was upregulated primarily in the glandular epithelium of idiopathic subglottic stenosis (iSGS) tissue.
CCN2 (connective tissue growth factor) was mainly upregulated in stromal fibroblasts surrounding TGF-β1-positive glandular structures in iSGS tissue at baseline.
Serial intralesional steroid injections (SILSI) with triamcinolone reduced fibroblast infiltration and increased matrix remodeling in iSGS subglottic tissue, correlating with clinical improvement.
SILSI treatment induced MMP9 expression, counteracting the profibrotic effects of TGF-β1 in iSGS tissue.
SILSI treatment repressed CCN2 expression in iSGS tissue while inducing MMP9, without altering TGF-β1 levels.
SILSI treatment did not significantly affect TGF-β1 levels despite altering CCN2 and MMP9 expression.
Treatment of primary iSGS-derived fibroblasts with TGF-β1 in vitro recapitulated aspects of the in vivo disease, inducing CCN2 and repressing MMP9 through changes in histone acetylation.
Triamcinolone counteracted the TGF-β1-driven coregulation of CCN2 and MMP9 by impairing SMAD2/3 binding to their promoter regions, rather than through changes in histone acetylation.
Nearly one in five shoulder arthroplasty patients had at least one functional somatic syndrome (fibromyalgia, IBS, chronic headaches, or chronic low-back pain) documented in their record.
Patients with functional somatic syndromes were more likely to be women, chronic opioid users, report more allergies, carry a diagnosis of anxiety, and have non-degenerative shoulder pathology.
Presence of at least one functional somatic syndrome independently predicted lower 2-year postoperative ASES scores after shoulder arthroplasty.
Presence of at least one functional somatic syndrome independently predicted lower 2-year postoperative SANE scores after shoulder arthroplasty.
Presence of at least one functional somatic syndrome independently predicted greater residual pain at 2 years after shoulder arthroplasty.
There was a dose-response relationship whereby each additional functional somatic syndrome was associated with progressively worse ASES/SANE scores and increasing residual pain.
Presence of at least one functional somatic syndrome independently predicted lower 2-year ASES scores after shoulder arthroplasty.
Presence of at least one functional somatic syndrome independently predicted lower 2-year SANE scores after shoulder arthroplasty.
Presence of at least one functional somatic syndrome independently predicted greater residual pain 2 years after shoulder arthroplasty.
A greater cumulative number of functional somatic syndromes was associated with a stepwise decline in ASES and SANE scores and a stepwise increase in residual pain.
Patients with functional somatic syndromes incurred higher hospitalization costs for shoulder arthroplasty.
Hospitalization costs rose in a stepwise manner as the number of functional somatic syndrome diagnoses increased.
ME/CFS patients perceived that others in their social environment viewed their illness as changeable (instability attributions) more than the scale midpoint.

Unexpectedly, ME/CFS patients perceived that others viewed their illness as less controllable (lower than the scale midpoint), contradicting the prediction that ME/CFS would be seen as a mental-behavioral stigma.
Perceived others' attributions of ME/CFS to physiological causes did not differ significantly from the scale midpoint.
Perceived others' attributions of ME/CFS to psychological causes were above the scale midpoint, indicating patients believe others psychologize their illness.

Participants' own controllability attributions for their illness were significantly lower than their perceived attributions of others (i.e., patients see themselves as less responsible than they think others perceive them to be).
Participants' own instability attributions for their illness were significantly lower than their perceived attributions of others.
Participants themselves attributed their illness more to physical than psychological causes, on average rating close to 'completely physical.'
Own controllability attributions were positively correlated with own instability attributions and with perceived others' controllability and instability attributions.

Own instability attributions were negatively related to perceived others' controllability attributions and unrelated to perceived others' instability attributions, suggesting patients may be more aware than others of symptom variability.
In a path model, perceived others' controllability and instability attributions for ME/CFS positively predicted perceived stigma.
Perceived stigma predicted lower functional status across nearly all SF-36 subscales (except vitality) and lower satisfaction with social roles and activities.

Indirect effects from perceived others' controllability and instability attributions to functional status (except vitality) and satisfaction with social roles and activities via perceived stigma were significant, supporting stigma as a mediator.

A reversed path model in which functional status/satisfaction with social roles predicted attributions, which in turn predicted stigma, showed indirect effects only for satisfaction with social roles and activities, not for functional status, providing weaker support than the hypothesized model.
ME/CFS patients show gut dysbiosis with increased proinflammatory Proteobacteria and decreased butyrate-producing Faecalibacterium and Bifidobacterium species.
ME/CFS patients show increased gut wall permeability allowing bacterial products to enter the circulation.
Abundance of various gut bacterial taxa correlates significantly with severity of pain and fatigue in ME/CFS.

ME/CFS patients (vs healthy controls) show increased proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1A, IL-17a, TNF-α) and anti-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1RA, IL-4, IL-13), particularly within the first 3 years of illness.
Levels of multiple cytokines correlate significantly with symptom severity in ME/CFS patients.
ME/CFS patients show decreased natural killer cell cytotoxicity with diminished cytolytic protein expression and cytokine production.
ME/CFS patients show increased numbers of activated CD8+ cytotoxic T cells bearing CD38 and HLA-DR activation markers.
T cell exhaustion is reported in ME/CFS, typically in longer-duration illness.
Some ME/CFS patients have autoantibodies against β-adrenergic and muscarinic cholinergic receptors, and more broadly against CNS and autonomic nervous system targets.
ME/CFS is characterized by reduced ATP generation from glucose via the TCA cycle, reduced fatty acids and acyl-carnitine, and reduced amino acids via the urea cycle.
Redox imbalance is a consistent metabolomic finding in ME/CFS, including increased pro-oxidants (peroxides, superoxides, isoprostanes) correlating with symptom severity.
ME/CFS patients show decreased antioxidant levels, including reduced α-tocopherol and TBARS levels that correlate with symptom severity.
ME/CFS shows increased nitrosative stress with elevated iNOS, nitric oxide, peroxynitrite, and nitrate, particularly following exercise.
Brain MRI in ME/CFS patients shows elevated ventricular lactic acid consistent with oxidative stress.
Neuroimaging studies report widespread activation of astrocytes and microglia (neuroinflammation) and glial cell hypoperfusion/metabolic dysfunction in ME/CFS.
ME/CFS is associated with downregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis.
ME/CFS patients show disordered sympathetic and parasympathetic activity with reduced cerebral perfusion, i.e., dysautonomia documented by autonomic nervous system testing.
Postexertion neuromuscular studies in ME/CFS show reduced anaerobic threshold and peak work, especially after a second exercise challenge 24 hours later, along with increased muscle lactic acid.

Concomitant psychiatric disorders occur in 50-80% of ME/CFS patients but typically develop after illness onset, and pre-existing psychiatric disorders are no more common than in the general population.
Controlled studies of the antidepressant fluoxetine in ME/CFS patients demonstrated no benefit.

In a cohort of over 70,000 COVID-19 survivors compared with nearly 5 million matched non-COVID controls, COVID-19 patients had significantly more persistent respiratory, cardiovascular, nervous system, metabolic, and gastrointestinal disorders at 4 months.
Hospitalized COVID-19 patients had significantly more persistent post-acute organ system disorders than hospitalized influenza patients.
Reported frequency of neurological signs/symptoms in acute COVID-19 inpatients varied widely by cohort: 36% in Wuhan, 57% in Spain, and 82% in Chicago.
SARS-CoV-2 RNA was not detected in the cerebrospinal fluid of 30 COVID-19 patients with a range of neurological complications.

In a study of 58 COVID-19 patients (81% with encephalopathy), viral RNA in CSF was infrequent (7%), but 40% had elevated CSF albumin suggesting blood-brain barrier breakdown, and 41% of a subset had elevated CSF IL-6.

A post-COVID-19 clinic reported high rates of persistent neurologic symptoms among patients never hospitalized for pneumonia/hypoxemia: brain fog (81%), headache (68%), paresthesias (60%), dysgeusia (59%), anosmia (55%), and myalgias (55%), lasting more than 6 weeks.

In 194 acute COVID-19 patients screened against 2770 extracellular/secreted proteins, autoantibodies were found against cytokines, chemokines, lymphocyte receptors, endothelial targets, and CNS targets including the orexin receptor, with autoantibody profiles correlating with illness severity.

Single-cell sequencing of olfactory epithelium showed ACE2 receptor expression in support cells, stem cells, and perivascular cells but not in olfactory sensory neurons, raising uncertainty about the mechanism of COVID-associated anosmia.
MRI of the brain in 37 individuals with severe COVID-19 disease revealed multifocal white matter hemorrhages.
Autonomic dysfunction is proposed to contribute to post-COVID illness, similar to its role in ME/CFS.
Up to 20% of people who recover from acute COVID-19 develop a lingering illness without evidence of obvious organ injury, termed post-COVID-19 syndrome or 'long COVID.'

In a large cohort study, COVID-19 patients surviving 30 days had significantly more persistent respiratory, cardiovascular, nervous system, metabolic, and gastrointestinal disorders at four months than matched non-COVID controls.
Hospitalized COVID-19 patients also showed significantly more persistent multi-organ disorders than hospitalized influenza patients.
The reported frequency of neurological signs and symptoms among hospitalized acute COVID-19 patients varied widely across cities: 36% in Wuhan, 57% in Spain, and 82% in Chicago.
Acute ischemic events and intracranial hemorrhage occurred in 1-4% of acute COVID-19 patients, including young adults without known vascular disease.
Autopsy studies of COVID-19 patients with neurologic disease have reported low levels of SARS-CoV-2 RNA and protein in the brain along with astrogliosis and microglial activation.

A study found viral RNA, protein, and particles in olfactory epithelial cells and dendritic projections of olfactory neurons extending into the mucosa and brainstem, along with microthrombi and infarcts, providing a mechanism for anosmia, dysgeusia, and CNS invasion.

Single-cell sequencing of the olfactory epithelium found that the ACE2 receptor is expressed in support cells, stem cells, and perivascular cells, but not in olfactory sensory neurons themselves, raising the question of the mechanism of COVID-associated anosmia.
SARS-CoV-2 RNA was not detected in the cerebrospinal fluid of 30 patients with a wide range of neurological complications, suggesting neuropathology is not due to direct CNS viral replication.

In a study of 58 patients (81% with encephalopathy), SARS-CoV-2 RNA in CSF was infrequent (7%), but 40% had elevated CSF albumin indicating blood-brain barrier breakdown, and 41% (7 of 17 tested) had elevated CSF IL-6.

Autopsy and CSF studies together suggest that COVID-19 neuropathology more likely reflects a host response to the virus and microvascular damage, with endothelial dysfunction proposed as central to pathology in both acute COVID-19 and its long-term consequences.
Brain MRI in 37 individuals with severe COVID-19 disease revealed multifocal white matter hemorrhages.

A post-COVID-19 clinic reported that even patients never hospitalized for pneumonia or hypoxemia had persistent neurologic complaints beyond 6 weeks, including brain fog (81%), headache (68%), paresthesias (60%), dysgeusia (59%), anosmia (55%), and myalgias (55%).

In 194 acute COVID-19 patients, screening for autoantibodies against 2770 extracellular and secreted proteins revealed autoantibodies against cytokines, chemokines, lymphocyte receptors, endothelial targets, and multiple CNS targets including the orexin receptor, with autoantibody profiles correlating with illness severity.
Autonomic dysfunction has been proposed to contribute to post-COVID illness, similar to its role in ME/CFS.
Before the COVID-19 pandemic, ME/CFS was estimated to impact 836,000 to 2.5 million Americans (an estimated 10 million worldwide) and to cost up to $24 billion annually in the USA.
Economists have estimated that cumulative future costs of post-COVID chronic illness in the USA may reach as high as $4.2 trillion.

The NIH announced in early 2021 that it would invest $1.15 billion in studies of ME/CFS and post-COVID illnesses, supported by an NIH-backed biorepository of plasma, serum, and cells from well-characterized patients.
Controlled studies of the antidepressant fluoxetine in people with ME/CFS demonstrated no benefit.

Psychiatric disorders that manifest before the onset of ME/CFS appear to be no more frequent than in the general community, although 50-80% of patients develop concomitant psychiatric disorders after illness onset.
ME/CFS patients showed significantly increased mental and physical fatigue on the FSMC questionnaire compared to controls.
ME/CFS patients scored lower than controls on physical-related SF-36 parameters, but not emotional-related parameters, indicating physical but not emotional functional limitation.

ME/CFS patients scored significantly higher (27 times higher) than healthy controls on the COMPASS-31 questionnaire, indicating severe autonomic nervous system dysfunction comparable to patients with ANS failure.
FSMC total fatigue score positively correlated with COMPASS-31 weighted autonomic dysfunction score across participants.
FSMC total score correlated negatively with SF-36 physical functioning score.
No significant differences in glycolysis (ECAR-based parameters) were found between ME/CFS patients and controls in PBMC bioenergetics profiling.
ME/CFS patients showed significantly lower mitochondrial coupling efficiency in PBMCs compared to controls.
Mitochondrial coupling efficiency correlated negatively with disease duration and positively with SF-36 general health score.
Protein carbonyl content, a marker of oxidative protein damage, showed a non-significant tendency to be higher in ME/CFS patient PBMCs than controls.
Cathepsin W (CTSW), involved in MHC class I pathway, was one of the two most significantly increased proteins in PBMCs of ME/CFS patients.
HLA-E, an MHC class Ib protein, was significantly increased in PBMCs of ME/CFS patients.
MLKL, involved in TNF-induced necroptosis, was significantly lower in PBMCs of ME/CFS patients than controls, indicating altered immune response.

LAMTOR1, part of the ragulator complex that recruits mTORC1 to lysosomes, was significantly increased in ME/CFS patients' PBMCs, together with mildly elevated LAMTOR5, suggesting increased mTORC1 activity.

Pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphatase regulatory subunit (PDPR) was significantly lower in ME/CFS PBMCs, potentially reflecting reduced pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDH) activity and impaired mitochondrial ATP production.
Pantothenate kinase 2 (PANK2), involved in CoA biosynthesis, was significantly lower in ME/CFS patients' PBMCs, potentially reflecting lower cellular CoA levels.
VNN1 (pantetheinase), responsible for recycling vitamin B5, was significantly lower in ME/CFS PBMCs, potentially indicating lower cellular CoA levels and impaired mitochondrial energy production.
ATP synthase F1 subunit epsilon (ATP5F1E) was significantly lower in ME/CFS PBMCs, potentially indicating insufficient ATP synthase activity.

SLC25A24 (calcium-binding mitochondrial carrier protein SCaMC-1) was significantly lower in ME/CFS PBMCs, potentially reflecting impaired ATP-magnesium/phosphate exchange between mitochondria and cytosol.
SLC16A3 (monocarboxylate transporter 4, MCT4), associated with lactate export in glycolytic cells, was significantly increased in ME/CFS PBMCs.
MCCC2, a subunit of 3-methylcrotonoyl-CoA carboxylase involved in leucine catabolism, was significantly lower in ME/CFS PBMCs.
SUCLG1, a citric acid cycle enzyme subunit (succinate-CoA ligase) catalysing succinyl-CoA to succinate conversion, was significantly lower in ME/CFS PBMCs.
Hexokinase 2 (HK2), catalysing the rate-limiting first step of glycolysis, was significantly increased in ME/CFS PBMCs.
PCK2, a mitochondrial enzyme involved in gluconeogenesis and lactate recycling to support cellular biosynthesis, was significantly increased in ME/CFS PBMCs.
The phosphatidylcholine PC(36:4) was nominally less abundant in plasma of ME/CFS patients than controls before multiple-comparison correction.
The ether phosphatidylcholine PC-O(34:4) was nominally less abundant in plasma of ME/CFS patients than controls before multiple-comparison correction.
Plasma steroid levels (17-hydroxyprogesterone, testosterone, androstenedione, cortisol) were not significantly different between ME/CFS patients and controls.

Prior open-label studies show 35-40% of ME/CFS patients experience significant health improvement when treated with dichloroacetate, a known PDH activator, supporting the relevance of PDH dysregulation in ME/CFS.

CVB1 strain 10796 infection of PANC-1 cells produced fragmented mitochondrial networks and downregulated mitochondrial fusion proteins mitofusin-1, mitofusin-2, and OPA1, unlike the ATCC strain or uninfected cells which retained filamentous mitochondrial networks.

Early ultrastructural study of 50 ME/CFS patient muscle biopsies found mitochondrial degeneration including branching/fusion of cristae, swelling, vacuolation, myelin figures and secondary lysosomes, leading authors to propose a viral-induced mitochondrial disorder.

In a study of quadriceps muscle biopsies from nine ME/CFS patients, researchers found inversion of the cytochrome oxidase/succinate dehydrogenase ratio and reduced activity of several mitochondrial matrix enzymes including NADHtr, COX, succinate dehydrogenase, cytochrome c oxidase, and citrate synthetase.

Two recent studies found normal mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and respiratory chain complex activity in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls, though this was inferred using plasma creatine kinase as a surrogate marker rather than direct muscle assay.

Extracellular flux analysis of skeletal muscle cells found ME/CFS patient cells had reduced oxidative phosphorylation compared to controls when supplied with glucose as substrate, but no abnormality when supplied with galactose or fatty acids.
Gastrointestinal tissue from two ME/CFS cohorts (n=165, n=416) showed 82% positive VP1 staining, compared to 20% in healthy controls (n=34) and 83% in functional dyspepsia patients (n=66).
Both ME/CFS and functional dyspepsia patient cohorts showed dsRNA staining, indicative of persistent enterovirus infection, in 64 and 63% of patients respectively.

Three ME/CFS post-mortem brain autopsy studies detected enteroviral genomic RNA and VP1 capsid protein in the hypothalamus, brainstem, cerebral cortex, medial temporal lobe, lateral frontal cortex, occipital lobe, and cerebellum.

Across 20 serological ME/CFS studies from the 1970s-1990s, 16 found an increased prevalence of CVB antibody signals in ME/CFS cohorts, ranging from 8-90% positive versus 0-65% in healthy control cohorts.
A 1997 neutralization test study for 11 enterovirus serotypes found that 100 of 200 tested ME/CFS patients had elevated enteroviral titers.
A tissue culture study using Hep-2, VERO, and monkey kidney cell lines found enterovirus positivity in 17 of 76 ME/CFS patients compared to 2 of 30 controls.
Four Northern blot studies of muscle tissue biopsies all detected viral RNA, indicating enterovirus prevalence of 21-50% in ME/CFS patients versus 0-1% in control cohorts.
Two RNAseq studies of blood samples (taken before or after exercise stress) were negative for enterovirus RNA in ME/CFS patients.

5 of 17 RT-PCR-based reports (on peripheral blood leukocytes, muscle tissue, and feces) found no significant difference in enterovirus prevalence between ME/CFS and control cohorts, but in-silico analysis showed these largely used primer sets with low comprehensiveness (as low as 0-56% coverage of known EV serotypes).
A quantitative summary/meta-analysis of rigorous data found no significant increase in brain white matter lesions in ME/CFS patients.

ME/CFS patients show altered brain characteristics including reduced cerebral/brainstem/cortex blood flow, impaired connectivity between vasomotor center, midbrain and hypothalamus, increased neuroinflammation in hippocampus/thalamus/midbrain/pons, reduced cerebral glucose metabolism, and lower brain glutathione.

ME/CFS patients show high prevalence and severity of postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), delayed gastric emptying, impaired thermoregulation in adolescents, and abnormal cardiac output, indicating autonomic nervous system dysfunction.

A muscle tissue study found no VP1 immunohistochemical staining in a cohort of 30 ME/CFS patients despite RT-PCR detecting enterovirus RNA in 13 of the same 30 patients, suggesting latent infection without detectable virion production.
A triple-cell-culture (green monkey kidney, RD, HeLa cells) fecal study found no enterovirus-positive samples in a cohort of 12 ME/CFS patients.

A proportion of individuals who contract EBV-induced mononucleosis remain ill 6 months or more with symptoms diagnostic of ME/CFS, and some ME/CFS patients show impaired immunological response to EBV.
A subset of ME/CFS patients with reactivated herpesvirus infections show symptom improvement upon anti-herpesvirus drug treatment.
Individual-level intra-class correlation coefficients showed variable agreement between parent and child reports of ME/CFS symptomatology and HRQOL in the ME/CFS patient dyads.
Control group parent-child pairs also showed varied agreement on HRQOL and symptom measures by ICC, indicating reporting discrepancies are not unique to ME/CFS families.
Group-level comparisons using paired-sample t-tests supported the existence of systematic discrepancies between parent and child reports of ME/CFS symptomatology and HRQOL.

Participants predominantly used their primary care physician, ME/CFS self-help services, and alternative medicine, while specialized physicians, mental health services, and hospital care were used less frequently.

The majority of participants reported barriers to accessing ME/CFS medical care, primarily geographical reasons (lack of specialists, travel distance), financial/insurance reasons, and lack of information about services.
Overall satisfaction with medical care from the most frequently visited physician (usually a GP) was significantly below the scale midpoint, indicating low patient satisfaction.

Among the subsample treated by an ME/CFS specialist, satisfaction with specialist care was significantly higher than the scale midpoint and higher than satisfaction with non-specialist care for the same patients.
The majority of participants were unable to work due to ME/CFS, with 59% on disability and only a minority working part-time or full-time.
Nearly all participants reported chronic, long-standing illness, with the majority having had fatigue/energy problems for over 2 years or since childhood/adolescence.
Three quarters of the sample reported that their ME/CFS began after an infectious illness, consistent with prior research on infectious triggers.
Confirmatory factor analysis supported a single-factor structure of the German DSQ-SF with acceptable model fit after allowing correlated errors between specific symptom-item pairs.
Higher ME/CFS symptom frequency/severity (DSQ-SF) was strongly correlated with lower physical functioning and greater bodily pain on the SF-36.
Moderate correlations were found between ME/CFS symptom severity (DSQ-SF) and SF-36 subscales of social functioning, general health, vitality, and mental health.
Only small correlations were found between ME/CFS symptom severity and the SF-36 role physical and role emotional subscales, suggesting discriminant validity of the DSQ-SF.
Ninety percent of participants reported having received a formal diagnosis of ME/CFS.

German official diagnostic guidelines on fatigue recommend cognitive-behavioral therapy and graded exercise therapy, which the authors note as a potential insurance-related barrier since other treatments may not be covered.

The authors cite a separate German study finding that half of chronic COVID-19 syndrome patients fulfilled the Canadian Consensus Criteria for ME/CFS six months post-infection, suggesting long COVID as a driver of increasing ME/CFS prevalence.
Among 130 COVID-19 survivors, 91.5% (119/130) reported at least one new persistent symptom at 3 months post-discharge, with a median of 9 symptoms.
At 6 months, 88% (115/130) of patients still reported at least one persistent symptom, with a median of 9 symptoms, indicating a slow decline from 3 months.
Fatigue was the most frequent persistent symptom, reported by 53% (69/130) of patients at 3 months post-discharge.
The rate of post-COVID fatigue decreased over time, from 53% at 3 months to 46.9% (61/130) at 6 months.
Patients with fatigue at 3 months were significantly older (53.9 ± 13.5 years) than those without fatigue (48.5 ± 13.3 years).
Patients with fatigue had a significantly longer hospital stay (17 ± 14 days) compared with those without fatigue (13 ± 10 days).
There was a non-significant trend toward more women among patients with fatigue (40.5%) compared with those without fatigue (27.8%).

At 3 months, additional common persistent symptoms included dyspnea on effort (50.8%), short-term memory loss (45.4%), sleep disturbances (45.4%), myalgias (40.8%), tachycardia (40.8%), postural dizziness (39.2%), anxiety (39.2%), depression (35.3%), and joint pain (38.5%).

Patients with fatigue at 3 months had significantly higher prevalence of dyspnea, tachycardia, sleep disturbances, postural dizziness, constipation, muscle pain and joint pain compared with those without fatigue.
Using the CDC Fukuda 1994 criteria, 17.6% (23/130) of post-COVID-19 patients met case definition criteria for ME/CFS.
Using the Canadian clinical case definition, 15.3% (20/130) of patients met ME/CFS criteria.
Using the International Consensus Criteria (2011), 19.2% (25/130) of patients met the diagnosis of ME.
Using the Institute of Medicine (SEID) case definition, 13% (17/130) of patients met the criteria for ME/CFS.
After multivariate adjustment, age 40-50 years was independently and positively associated with post-COVID fatigue.
Female sex showed a trend towards association with post-COVID fatigue but did not reach statistical significance in multivariate analysis.
At hospital admission, patients acutely infected with SARS-CoV-2 showed decreased lymphocyte counts and elevated neutrophil counts, CRP, ferritin, D-dimer, IL-6, and VEGF.
Orthostatic intolerance symptoms consistent with autonomic dysfunction were common, with 39.2% of patients reporting postural dizziness and 16.9% reporting lightheadedness after hospitalization.
Among 197 ME/CFS patients, 40 (20.3%) experienced new or non-typical symptoms after exposure to a PEM stressor.

27 of 197 patients (13.7%) experienced new or non-typical symptoms specifically during the prodromal phase between stressor exposure and onset of baseline symptom exacerbation, with this phase lasting more than 3 hours in 85.1% of them.

Patients who experienced prodromal new or non-typical symptoms before baseline symptom exacerbation had significantly lower PEM intensity than the rest of the study population, and this difference persisted after adjustment for sex and age at disease onset.
PEM frequency did not significantly differ between patients with prodromal new or non-typical symptoms and the rest of the study population.

Mood disorders (emotional lability, irritable mood, lack of motivation, depressed mood) were the most frequent prodromal new or non-typical symptom, occurring in 37% of patients with prodromal symptoms, and regressed spontaneously with PEM recovery despite absence of underlying psychiatric conditions.
Nausea was a frequent prodromal new or non-typical symptom, preceding baseline symptom exacerbation in 29.6% of the subgroup with prodromal symptoms.

Paresthesia, with patient-specific but variable topography (hemi-facial, perioral, one-sided, or diffuse), appeared suddenly as a prodromal symptom in 22.2% of patients with prodromal symptoms, lasting hours to days, and was never reported outside PEM episodes.
No association was found between the type of PEM stressor and the specific nature of prodromal new or non-typical symptoms experienced.

Among patients with comorbid reactional depression and/or fibromyalgia, medication intake did not differ significantly between those exhibiting prodromal new or non-typical symptoms and the rest of the study population, suggesting medication did not mask the emergence of warning signals.
Oral melatonin plus zinc supplementation for 16 weeks significantly reduced physical fatigue (FIS-40 physical domain) compared with placebo.
The FIS-40 cognitive domain showed a trend toward improvement in the melatonin plus zinc group over 16 weeks that did not reach statistical significance.
Overall FIS-40 total score improved markedly at 16 weeks in the melatonin plus zinc group but did not reach statistical significance, while the placebo group's early improvement was lost by 16 weeks.
Discontinuation of melatonin plus zinc after 16 weeks caused a significant worsening of the SF-36 physical functioning domain at 4 weeks post-treatment.
Discontinuation of melatonin plus zinc caused significant worsening in the SF-36 mental health domain at 4 weeks post-treatment.
The SF-36 physical component summary score improved significantly at both 8 and 16 weeks in the melatonin plus zinc group, with no significant between-group differences.
Global PSQI sleep quality index improved significantly in both melatonin plus zinc and placebo groups at 8 and 16 weeks, and worsened in both after 4 weeks of treatment withdrawal.
After treatment withdrawal, sleep latency, sleep duration, sleep disturbances and sleep medication use worsened significantly in the melatonin plus zinc group compared with the 16-week visit.

Skin fragility in hEDS is attributed to decreased expression of FLG, which encodes profilaggrin/filaggrin important for skin barrier formation, leading to disrupted keratinocyte differentiation and decreased skin integrity.
Bleeding symptoms in EDS/hEDS range from mild bruising to severe or fatal bleeding, with bruising, hematomas, and menorrhagia being the most common symptoms.

A review of 112 papers totaling 467 EDS patients found hematoma formation, especially after minor trauma, was the most frequently reported vascular-related complication, mostly subcutaneous, with management (transfusions, ICU admittance, surgical drainage) described specifically for musculocontractural EDS patients.

Ascorbic acid supplementation is recommended to decrease bruising tendency in EDS patients because it acts as a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases involved in collagen biogenesis, potentially increasing dermal stiffness and integrity.

A case report of a 23-year-old male EDS patient with a hematoma showed minimal improvement in bleeding time with daily DDAVP alone, but adding intramuscular conjugated estrogen normalized bleeding time and stopped ongoing hemorrhagic episodes; estrogen's effect lasts longer (10-15 days) than DDAVP's (6-8 hours).

A study of perimenopausal and postmenopausal women found increased risk of venous thrombosis in women taking conjugated estrogen compared with non-hormone users and esterified estrogen users, indicating caution is warranted when using conjugated estrogen for bleeding prevention in EDS.

In hEDS, atrophic cutaneous scars show abnormal, smaller flower-like collagen fibers with irregular interfibrillar spacing and elastic fibers with granulo-filamentous deposits and stellate hyaluronic acid-like globules, particularly in the reticular dermis, reflecting defective collagen fibrils that decrease dermal stiffness.

Patients with hEDS have increased surgical risks including bleeding, delayed wound closure and tissue repair, and higher rates of unsatisfactory scarring, requiring modified surgical technique (gentle dissection, deep sutures, extended suture retention, support taping) and preference for nonsurgical approaches when possible.

Piezogenic pedal papules are benign herniations of elastic tissue and subcutaneous fat through the reticular dermis, exacerbated by compressive forces such as prolonged standing, and have been demonstrated to be associated with EDS, likely due to inherent connective tissue weakness; painful papules are more common in EDS patients than in the general population.

Treatment options for painful piezogenic papules include reducing athletic activity, avoiding prolonged standing, weight loss, orthotics, compression stockings, and localized injections of betamethasone/bupivacaine or deoxycholic acid, though no standardized treatment exists.

Hyperextensible skin, a hallmark of hEDS due to collagen defects, is diagnosed with the rubber-glove skin test where a skin fold from the dorsum of the hand is classified as hyperextensible if it stretches more than 1.5 cm or beyond the wrist.

Livedo reticularis, a bluish-to-lavender net-like rash exacerbated by cold, commonly affects young women and is inferred to be associated with hEDS via defective collagen causing structural defects underlying the benign cutis marmorata form.

Elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS), typically seen in vascular EDS, has also been documented in hEDS; a case study of a 26-year-old woman with vEDS showed EPS lesions with coarse elastic fibers extruding into the epidermis, following a history of easy bruising, prolonged wound healing, and atrophic scarring.

hEDS lacks a known genetic mutation and specific genetic markers, making diagnosis reliant on clinical criteria and predisposing it to misdiagnosis as fibromyalgia, Marfan syndrome, or other connective tissue disorders due to overlapping features of skin hyperextensibility, joint hypermobility, and tissue fragility.
