The patient's common hepatic arterial aneurysm rapidly expanded from 7 mm to 14 mm in diameter within 7 days, with new proper and left hepatic arterial aneurysms also appearing.
Prophylactic endovascular coil embolization completely occluded the hepatic arterial aneurysms with no intraoperative or postoperative complications and no recurrence over 14 months of follow-up.
Prior literature reports high mortality rates for invasive procedures in vEDS: 30% for open surgery and 24% for endovascular therapy.

In a series of 30 interventional procedures in vEDS patients, 30% (9/30) were prophylactic and resulted in good survival with no hospital deaths, whereas 33% (10/30) and 7% (2/30) were performed for large aneurysms and rapid aneurysm expansion respectively.

A known vEDS diagnosis prior to invasive therapeutic procedures was associated with fewer intraoperative deaths (0% vs. 14%) and fewer postoperative complications (14% vs. 62%) compared with cases where the diagnosis was unknown beforehand.
Among elective (non-emergency) procedures in vEDS patients, those with a known diagnosis had fewer postoperative complications (5% vs. 55%) than those without, with no in-hospital deaths.
In one published article, use of NBCA along with coils for embolization was associated with intraprocedural rupture and iatrogenic intimal injury in 43% (3/7) of cases.
Patients with vEDS have a reported median life expectancy of 51 years, primarily due to vascular complications such as arterial rupture.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in this patient was caused by a mutation in the COL3A1 gene, which encodes type III collagen.
The patient presented with an aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, which was the initial manifestation prompting ICU admission.
Endovascular coil treatment attempted for the aneurysm was complicated by dissection of the left iliac artery and abdominal aorta, illustrating the vascular fragility characteristic of the disease.
Postmortem genetic testing identified a mutation in the COL3A1 gene, confirming the diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome that had been clinically suspected.

Clinical suspicion of vascular EDS was raised based on the pattern of vascular/haemorrhagic complications together with distinctive physical features and medical history, but diagnosis was often unrecognized until major complications occurred.
Women with hereditary disorders of connective tissue had a higher overall rate of perioperative complications following pelvic floor reconstructive surgery compared with matched controls.
The age-adjusted relative risk of perioperative complications in HDCT patients versus controls was 1.4 with a confidence interval crossing the null.
HDCT patients had significantly more Clavien-Dindo grade I and grade II complications than controls following pelvic floor reconstructive surgery.
HDCT patients had a higher hospital readmission rate than controls after pelvic floor reconstructive surgery.
There was no difference between HDCT patients and controls in the incidence of specific individual complication types.
There was no difference in recurrence of pelvic organ prolapse (10%) or stress urinary incontinence (11%) between HDCT patients and controls.
Autoantibodies purified from patients with fibromyalgia, but not from healthy controls, were able to produce fibromyalgia-like symptoms when transferred into mice.
FMS patient antibodies, unlike control antibodies, bound to and stimulated satellite glial cells into an activated state known to mediate chronic pain by augmenting neuronal activity.

Fibromyalgia presents with heterogeneous symptoms including widespread pain and tenderness, fatigue, sleep disturbance, and impaired cognition, with abnormalities noted in the neuroendocrine system, autonomic nervous system, and sleep implicating nervous system involvement.
Passive transfer of IgG from fibromyalgia patients into mice caused increased sensitivity to noxious mechanical and cold stimulation.
Nociceptive afferent fibers in skin-nerve preparations from FMS IgG-treated mice showed heightened responsiveness to cold and mechanical stimuli, indicating direct peripheral sensitization.
Mice treated with FMS IgG showed reduced locomotor activity and reduced paw grip strength compared to controls.
Mice treated with FMS IgG exhibited a loss of intraepidermal innervation, resembling small-fiber pathology.
Transfer of IgG-depleted serum from FMS patients had no effect on mouse sensory or motor phenotypes, indicating the pathogenic activity resides specifically in the IgG fraction.
IgG from healthy control subjects had no effect on mouse sensory or motor phenotypes, in contrast to FMS patient IgG.
Patient IgG did not directly activate naive sensory neurons, suggesting an indirect mechanism of sensitization via non-neuronal cells.
FMS patient IgG labeled satellite glial cells and neurons in the dorsal root ganglia both in vivo and in vitro.
FMS patient IgG bound to satellite glial cells and neurons in mouse dorsal root ganglia both in vivo and in vitro.
FMS patient IgG also labeled myelinated fiber tracts and a small subset of macrophages and endothelial cells within mouse DRG, but did not label any cells in the spinal cord.
FMS patient IgG did not bind to any cells in the mouse spinal cord, suggesting a peripheral rather than central site of action.
FMS patient IgG was shown to bind directly to human dorsal root ganglia, supporting relevance of the mouse findings to human disease.
The authors propose that therapies aimed at reducing IgG titers in fibromyalgia patients could be an effective treatment strategy.

Fibromyalgia patients show intramuscular pressure that is almost three times higher than that of comparison subjects, suggesting a possible mechanism for the muscle pain and tenderness characteristic of the condition.
Repeated administration of compound 48/80 significantly increased the gastric ulcerogenic index compared to control rats, indicating mast-cell-mediated gastric mucosal damage.
Pretreatment with dehydroleucodine (40 mg/kg) significantly reduced the ulcerogenic index compared to the compound 48/80 group.
Pretreatment with xanthatin (40 mg/kg) significantly reduced the ulcerogenic index compared to the compound 48/80 group.
Pretreatment with 3-benzyloxymethyl-5H-furan-2-one (40 mg/kg) significantly reduced the ulcerogenic index compared to the compound 48/80 group.
Pretreatment with the reference mast cell stabilizer sodium cromoglycate (40 mg/kg) significantly reduced the ulcerogenic index compared to the compound 48/80 group.

Lactone-treated groups (DhL, Xt, But, Crgl) showed ulcerogenic indexes not significantly different from the control group, and no differences were observed among the lactone-treated groups themselves.

Histological staining showed that compound 48/80 induced morphological signs of mast cell degranulation in the gastric submucosa, whereas mast cells in lactone-treated groups showed a stabilized morphology similar to controls.
Rats treated with compound 48/80 alone had higher serum serotonin concentrations than control rats, indicating serotonin release upon mast cell activation.
Rats pretreated with dehydroleucodine, xanthatin, 3-benzyloxymethyl-5H-furan-2-one, or sodium cromoglycate showed lower serum serotonin levels than rats treated with compound 48/80 alone.
Administration of the lactones after compound 48/80 treatment (rather than before) had no effect on the gastric lesions induced by the mast cell secretagogue.
The paper reports that a passively sensitized mast cell activation test can reliably diagnose chlorhexidine allergy.

Mast cell-deficient mice infected with Listeria monocytogenes had roughly 100-fold higher bacterial burden and impaired neutrophil mobilization compared to control mice, indicating mast cells are required for bacterial control.
In response to bacteria, mast cells generate proinflammatory responses from the cell surface but not type I interferon responses, which are instead induced from endolysosomal compartments.

The threonine-leucine amino acid pair in CDC domain 4 binds specifically to the hydroxyl group of cholesterol in cholesterol-rich membrane regions but not to free cholesterol, explaining cholesterol-dependent membrane recognition.
All eight CDCs studied were found to possess high-affinity lectin activity, identifying host cell surface glycans as additional candidate receptors independent of cholesterol binding.

Sublethal doses of SLO rapidly activated bone marrow-derived mast cells to degranulate and produce mRNAs for TNF-α, IL-13, IL-4, IL-6, and GM-CSF, with TNF-α production dependent on protein kinase C and p38 MAPK activity.
P2X7 receptor expression levels affect the degree of SLO-induced plasma membrane perforation in the human mast cell line HMC-1, providing a protective effect against toxin-induced damage.
Sublytic concentrations of SLO suppressed the oxidative burst in neutrophils, functioning as a virulence factor that helps bacteria escape ROS-dependent innate immune killing.
LLO and PFO suppressed the oxidative burst in murine macrophages by preventing localization of NADPH oxidase to the phagosome.
Low concentrations of SLO prevented release of IL-8 and elastase from neutrophils and blocked formation of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs).
Low levels of SLO reduced bacterial internalization by keratinocytes by disrupting clathrin-dependent uptake pathways and integrin-mediated signaling in cholesterol-rich membrane domains.

In vivo, SLO injected into ears of mast cell-deficient mice engrafted with BMMCs produced a stronger inflammatory response than in mast cell-deficient mice without engraftment, confirming mast cells drive the SLO-induced inflammatory response.

Exposure of rat RBL-2H3 mast cells to S. pneumoniae strains caused dose- and time-dependent degranulation that was only partially calcium-dependent and was not accompanied by TNF-α or IL-6 production.

PLY stimulation induced release of the antimicrobial peptide cathelicidin LL-37 from human lung mast cells, which showed antimicrobial activity against S. pneumoniae, suggesting mast cells limit pneumococcal dissemination.

Mouse BMMCs degranulated and released IL-6, CCL2, CCL3, and CCL4 (but not IL-1β, TNF-α, IFN-γ) upon S. pneumoniae exposure, in a PLY-dependent but TLR-independent manner, with responses varying by pneumococcal serotype.

Mast cell-deficient mouse strains showed no significant effect on disease phenotype in experimental pneumococcal meningitis, contradicting an earlier study reporting reduced inflammation, lower bacterial outgrowth, and longer survival in mast cell-deficient mice.

LLO triggers BMMC and RBL-2H3 mast cell degranulation and cytokine synthesis in a calcium-dependent manner, involving both extracellular Ca2+ influx and release from intracellular stores via IP3R and G-protein/tyrosine kinase-linked PLC activation.

Cholesterol-inactivated LLO (CL-LLO) still binds and aggregates plasma membrane rafts and induces tyrosine phosphorylation pore-independently, but unlike active LLO it fails to induce Ca2+ release in mast cells, indicating pore formation is required for calcium signaling.

Contrary to Gekara et al., Jobbings et al. found LLO-mediated mast cell degranulation was enhanced in the absence of extracellular Ca2+ (while antigen/PMA-ionophore-mediated degranulation was inhibited), and LLO induced transient downregulation of surface c-kit (CD117) without affecting FcεRI expression.
In response to L. monocytogenes, mast cells release TNF-α, IL-6, osteopontin, IL-2, IL-4, IL-13, GM-CSF, and chemokines CCL2, CCL3, CCL4, and CCL5 in a MyD88-dependent manner.

Live S. equi bacteria induced profound secretion of IL-4, IL-6, IL-12, IL-13, TNF-α, CCL2, CCL7, MCP3, CXCL2, and CCL5 from BMMCs, whereas heat-inactivated bacteria caused only a minimal cytokine/chemokine response, with weak degranulation observed overall.
The proinflammatory cytokine response of mast cells to S. equi was abrogated entirely when bacteria lacked the sagA gene encoding SLS, confirming SLS as the necessary bacterial trigger.

Escherichia coli α-hemolysin induced release of histamine, leukotrienes, and proinflammatory cytokines from human intestinal mast cells; this response was inhibited by blocking extracellular Ca2+/calmodulin-calcineurin signaling (cyclosporine A) and by MAPK p38/ERK inhibitors, indicating a distinct signaling pathway from FcεRI activation.

Sublytic concentrations of the plant/steroid glycoside pore-formers saponin and digitonin triggered IL-6 and TNF production in mast cells similarly to bacterial SLS, phenocopying CDC/SLS-mediated cytokine induction.
DHM at 100 μM inhibited IgE-induced proliferation of KU812 mast cells more effectively than 10 μM, without causing cytotoxicity.
DHM treatment reduced intracellular ROS levels that were elevated by DNP-IgE challenge in KU812 mast cells, as measured by flow cytometry.
DHM treatment significantly reduced IgE-induced upregulation of TNF-α in a dose-dependent manner in KU812 mast cells.
DHM treatment significantly inhibited IgE-induced IL-6 cytokine levels in KU812 mast cells.
DHM treatment reduced IgE-induced activation of NF-κB in KU812 mast cells.
DHM suppressed IgE-induced phosphorylation/activation of p38 MAPK but did not affect ERK or JNK phosphorylation.
DHM reduced IgE-induced tryptase release from mast cells from 1.75 ± 0.1 μg/mL to 1.13 ± 0.211 μg/mL, representing about 64.5% of the IgE-only group level, indicating attenuated degranulation.
DHM treatment suppressed the phosphorylation levels of STAT5 in IgE-activated KU812 mast cells.
Combining pimozide, an FDA-approved STAT5 inhibitor, with DHM further enhanced reduction of DNP-IgE-induced phospho-STAT5 compared to either agent alone, indicating synergy.
KU812 mast cells sensitized with DNP-IgE and stimulated with DNP-HSA showed significant hyperproliferation compared to non-sensitized mast cells.

The review discusses the mas-related G protein-coupled receptor X2 (MRGPRX2) as a proposed mechanism underlying immediate drug hypersensitivity reactions via direct mast cell activation independent of IgE sensitization.

The basophil activation test (BAT) is described as having diagnostic value for IgE-dependent allergies and certain forms of autoimmune urticaria but has practical weaknesses including a narrow post-collection processing window, non-responder cells, and difficulty standardizing large batch analyses.

The passive mast cell activation test (pMAT), using mast cell lines or cultured mast cells (including those derived from peripheral blood CD34+ progenitor cells) passively sensitized with patient sera or plasma, is reviewed as a flow cytometric diagnostic approach for IgE-dependent allergies.

Flow-induced constriction of isolated middle cerebral arteries (MCAs), a key mechanism contributing to cerebral blood flow autoregulation, was greatly and significantly reduced after traumatic brain injury (TBI) compared to intact rats.

Blocking TP receptors with SQ 29,548 significantly reduced flow-induced constriction in intact MCAs, but had no further effect on the already-reduced constriction seen after TBI, suggesting this signaling pathway is impaired by TBI.
HET0016, an inhibitor of CYP450 4A, substantially and significantly inhibited pressure+flow-induced constriction of MCAs, implicating this enzyme in the combined autoregulatory constrictor response.
TBI significantly reduced pressure-alone, flow-alone, and combined pressure+flow-induced constrictions of MCAs compared to intact vessels.
Arachidonic acid (AA)-induced dilation and constriction responses of MCAs were significantly reduced after TBI compared to intact vessels at both concentrations tested.
mRNA expression of the 20-HETE-producing cytochrome isoform CYP4a1 in MCAs was substantially reduced after TBI compared to intact rats, corresponding to reduced vasomotor responses.
mRNA expression of the 20-HETE-producing cytochrome isoform CYP4a3 in MCAs was substantially reduced after TBI compared to intact rats.
20-HETE-induced constriction of MCAs, mediated via TP receptors, was significantly reduced in vessels from TBI rats compared to intact rats.

U46619 (thromboxane-prostanoid receptor agonist)-induced constriction of MCAs was significantly reduced after TBI compared to intact rats at both concentrations tested, indicating reduced TP receptor sensitivity.

The authors hypothesize, without definitive proof, that altered 20-HETE production after TBI may reduce inhibition of BKCa channels (previously shown to be upregulated and H2O2-activated after TBI), potentially contributing to reduced MCA constriction, though this remains unresolved.
Leukotrienes and prostaglandins derived from ω6 arachidonic acid act on multiple cell types in the tissue microenvironment to either promote or suppress allergic responses.
Specialized pro-resolving lipid mediators derived from ω3 eicosapentaenoic acid and docosahexaenoic acid modulate the tissue microenvironment to positively or negatively regulate allergic responses.
CD300a is an inhibitory receptor on mast cells that recognizes externalized phosphatidylserine and, upon binding, inhibits FcεRI-mediated mast cell activation.
CD300f is an inhibitory receptor on mast cells that recognizes extracellular ceramides and, upon binding, inhibits FcεRI-mediated mast cell activation.
The inhibitory CD300-lipid axis downregulates IgE-driven, mast cell-dependent type I hypersensitivity through distinct mechanisms.
Increased mucosal mast cell density in the colon and ileum has been reported in the majority of published studies of IBS patients.
IBS is associated with increased density of degranulating mast cells and mast cells positioned near nerves, which correlates with abdominal pain frequency and severity.
Both mast cell and eosinophil densities are increased in pediatric IBS.
Increased densities and activation of mast cells and/or eosinophils have been demonstrated in functional dyspepsia in both adults and youth.
Mast cell degranulation in the proximal stomach may be linked to visceral hyperalgesia in adults with functional dyspepsia.
A history of allergy has been associated with increased duodenal eosinophils in adults with functional dyspepsia.
In children with cow's milk allergy, mucosal application of milk increases mast cell and eosinophil density/activation and mast cell-nerve proximity, mirroring changes seen in FAPDs generally.
Anxiety and depression have been associated with increased mast cell and/or eosinophil density in youth and adults with FAPDs.
Stress-induced CRH receptor activation results in mast cell degranulation, disrupting the epithelial barrier and increasing antigenic exposure.
In adults with documented food allergies, cold stress produced increased luminal jejunal tryptase and histamine release comparable in magnitude to that induced by direct food allergen exposure.
Preschoolers with allergic disease have an increased risk of developing IBS at school-age, with earlier IBS onset in those with food allergies and the highest risk associated with allergic rhinitis.
A history of atopic dermatitis significantly increases the risk of childhood IBS.
Allergic proctocolitis early in life is a risk factor for subsequent development of functional abdominal pain disorders.
Children with food sensitization have lower overall microbiota diversity, with reduced Bacteroides and increased Firmicutes colonization.
A placebo-controlled trial of a Bifidobacteria probiotic in children with allergic rhinitis and intermittent asthma showed significant improvement in allergic rhinitis symptoms.

In a study of 220 adults with IBS and/or FD, food-specific IgE tests were positive in 38%, but only 4% had a true IgE-mediated food allergy confirmed by elimination-rechallenge, similar to general population prevalence.
Another study found no difference in food-specific IgE levels between adults with FD/IBS and healthy controls.
The authors' prior study found no increase in immunoreactivity (IgE, skin prick test, IgG, IgG4, atopy patches) to common food allergens in children with FD and duodenal eosinophilia.
Colonoscopic allergen provocation testing (COLAP) was positive in 46% of food-antigen challenges in adults with suspected food-allergy-related GI symptoms, versus none in controls.
In a mouse model, bacterial infection causes loss of oral tolerance resulting in mucosal food-specific IgE and increased visceral pain via IgE- and mast cell-mediated mechanisms.
The superantigen-producing bacteria Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes are more commonly present in the microbiome of IBS patients.
In children with FAPDs, local pollen counts are associated with pain onset and are as strong a predictor as affect or sleep disturbances.
During birch pollen season, adults with birch pollen allergy show increased duodenal eosinophils and IgE-carrying mast cells, along with oral allergy syndrome.
In patients with birch pollinosis, mucosal COLAP testing with rBet v 1 was positive in 81% of those with GI symptom history, 22% of those without GI symptoms, and 0% of healthy controls.
Increased mucosal TH17 density has been demonstrated in pediatric IBS and in pediatric FD associated with chronic gastritis, comparable to levels seen in H. pylori- and Crohn's-associated gastritis.

In a confocal laser endomicroscopy food-challenge study of 155 adults (108 completers), 70% had a positive reaction, and positive patients were 4x more likely to have another atopic disorder, with increased permeability, lymphocyte density, and eosinophil (but not mast cell) activation.
Food-specific IgG titers are not related to symptom severity but correlate with mast cell density and degranulation in FAPD patients.
In a small case series, omalizumab (anti-IgE) improved symptoms in patients with FAPD symptoms and mucosal eosinophilia, though the reduction in eosinophil density was not statistically significant.

Two placebo-controlled trials of ketotifen (a mast cell stabilizer and H1 antagonist) in adults with IBS both showed improvement in abdominal pain and other IBS symptoms along with improved visceral hypersensitivity.
In a pediatric study of children with abdominal pain and diarrhea, oral cromolyn was shown to be as effective as diet restriction guided by skin prick testing.
A study of 10 children with egg allergy found no benefit from oral cromolyn in preventing egg reactions.
A study of 20 adults with IBS and documented food intolerances found that oral cromolyn allowed patients to tolerate their offending foods.
Another adult study found oral cromolyn to be comparable to an elimination diet, with both treatments performing better in patients with positive food skin prick tests.
Another adult study found oral cromolyn improved mast cell activation, abdominal pain, and stool consistency.

A biologic targeting Siglec-8 (expressed on mast cells and eosinophils) eliminated eosinophils and inactivated mast cells, and in phase II trials decreased antral and duodenal eosinophils while improving symptoms.

H1 antagonists, alone or combined with H2 antagonists, have been reported effective in children and adults with functional dyspepsia in uncontrolled studies, with response in adults predicted by elevated duodenal eosinophils.
Ebastine, an H1 antagonist, decreased visceral sensitivity in adults with IBS.

Montelukast, a cysteinyl-leukotriene receptor antagonist, effectively treats pain in children with functional dyspepsia and duodenal eosinophilia, but the effect is independent of changes in mast cell or eosinophil density or activation.

In a prospective study of adults with functional dyspepsia and duodenal eosinophilia, treatment with the proton pump inhibitor pantoprazole was associated with improved symptoms and reduced mucosal eosinophil density.
A placebo-controlled trial of a Bifidobacteria probiotic in children with allergic rhinitis and intermittent asthma demonstrated significant improvement in allergic rhinitis symptoms.
In adults with documented food allergies, cold stress induced increased luminal release of tryptase and histamine in the jejunum at a magnitude comparable to that induced by food allergen exposure.
Through activation of CRH receptors, stress results in mast cell degranulation, disrupting the epithelial barrier and increasing antigenic exposure.
During birch pollen season, adults with birch pollen allergy showed increased duodenal eosinophils and IgE-carrying mast cells along with oral allergy syndrome.
Birch exposure was associated with increased intestinal eosinophil and mast cell densities, and patients with gastrointestinal symptoms had increased IgE to birch (rBet v 1), hazelnuts, and apple.

In patients with birch pollinosis, colonoscopic allergen provocation testing with rBet v 1 was positive in 81% of those with a history of GI symptoms, 22% of those with pollinosis and no GI symptoms, and none of the healthy controls.

In a mouse model, bacterial superantigens Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes, which cause non-specific T lymphocyte activation, are more commonly present in the microbiome of IBS patients and are implicated in loss of oral tolerance and mucosal food-specific IgE-mediated visceral pain.
Skin colonization with Staphylococcus aureus in patients with atopic dermatitis has been associated with an increased risk of food allergy.

In a study using confocal laser endomicroscopy, 70% of 108 completers challenged with four common food antigens (all SPT/specific IgE negative) had a positive test, and those with positive tests were 4 times more likely to have another atopic disorder; positive responses were associated with increased permeability, lymphocyte density, and eosinophil (but not mast cell) activation.
Food-specific IgG titers are not related to symptom severity in FAPD patients, but they correlate with mast cell density and degranulation.

In functional dyspepsia associated with chronic gastritis (but not in its absence), gastric and duodenal TH17 density was greater than controls and comparable to that seen in Helicobacter-pylori-associated gastritis and Crohn's-associated gastritis.
Mast cell density in the upper esophagus of SSc patients significantly correlated with the percentage of acid exposure time on 24h pH testing.
Mast cell density across the entire esophagus (upper plus lower) also significantly correlated with acid exposure time percentage in SSc patients.
Overall esophageal mast cell numbers were similar between SSc patients and healthy participants.
Gene expression for mast cell-related pathways was significantly upregulated in the inflammatory intrinsic subset (IS) of SSc esophageal biopsies compared to proliferative or normal-like IS.
Intrinsic subsets (inflammatory, fibroproliferative, and normal-like), originally defined from skin biopsies, could also be identified in SSc esophageal biopsies via microarray gene expression.
SSc patients with inflammatory intrinsic subset profiles in the esophagus demonstrated more tryptase staining, suggesting mast cell-targeted therapy could be relevant for this subgroup.
SSc patients with an inflammatory intrinsic subset (IS) esophageal gene expression profile showed increased tryptase staining, a marker of mast cells.
The authors suggest that mast cell-targeted therapy may be a useful therapeutic approach for SSc patients belonging to the inflammatory intrinsic subset, though additional studies are warranted.
Bladder biopsies from some BPS/IC patients show suburothelial infiltration of mast cells, leukocytes and lymphocytes along with increased vasculature and bladder wall thickening.
Increased numbers of suburothelial mast cells are specifically found in patients with type 3 (Hunner lesion) BPS/IC.
Activated mast cells secrete vasoactive factors, neurotrophins and cytokines that lead to visceral and neurogenic inflammation in the bladder.
In non-lesion (type without Hunner's ulcer) BPS/IC, mast cell count and perineural inflammation are notably absent or reduced.
Bladder biopsies from BPS/IC patients show abnormal expression of uroplakins, chondroitin sulfate and tight junction proteins consistent with urothelial barrier defects.
Amitriptyline (or nortriptyline) improves BPS/IC symptoms in up to 50% of patients compared with placebo plus behavioral modification.
Oral pentosan polysulfate, the first FDA-approved treatment for BPS/IC, reduces pain, urgency and frequency with efficacy ranging widely between 21% and 56% versus placebo.
Intravesical lidocaine instillation improves symptoms in 30-50% of BPS/IC patients, increasing up to 70% when combined with bicarbonate and heparin.
Intravesical DMSO produces symptom improvement in 47-87% of BPS/IC patients with minor side effects.

Intravesical GAG replenishment therapy with hyaluronic acid and chondroitin sulfate has demonstrated efficacy in RCTs but the effect magnitude is generally limited, often requiring combination therapy.
TRPV4 knock-out mice do not develop cystitis-induced pain, implicating TRPV4 in bladder pain signaling and identifying it as a potential treatment target.

A clinical trial of the FAAH inhibitor ASP3652 in women with mild/moderate BPS/IC failed to show improvement in pain or LUTS compared with placebo, though it was safe with no psychotropic side effects.
In patients with multiple sclerosis, cannabinoid treatment has been reported to improve urgency and incontinence episodes by up to 50%.
In a phase IIa trial, the selective P2X3 receptor antagonist gefapixant reduced pain and improved urinary urgency and global impression of change compared with placebo after 4 weeks in BPS patients.
Water-filled (empty) intravesical liposomes showed equal efficacy to oral pentosan polysulfate in clinical trials of BPS/IC.
Onabotulinum toxin (BoNT-A) filled liposomes trialed in pilot studies showed no superiority over placebo in BPS/IC patients.
Intradetrusor injection of BoNT-A can palliate BPS/IC symptoms through chemical denervation, inhibition of sensory bladder function, and anti-inflammatory action.
Epidemiologic studies report an association between BPS/IC and other chronic pain/fatigue syndromes including fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome and chronic fatigue syndrome.
Some studies report increased sympathetic tone with decreased cortisol levels in BPS/IC patients, suggesting a possible autonomic etiology.

In an animal model, infection with an O-antigen-deficient E. coli mutant caused allodynia that persisted long after the infection was cleared, suggesting infection can trigger sustained sterile inflammation and pain in the bladder.
A phenotype-directed (UPOINT) multimodal treatment approach resulted in clinically significant improvement in BPS/IC symptoms at 1-year follow-up.
BPS/IC is reported to impact quality of life more severely than long-term hemodialysis, Crohn's disease, systemic lupus erythematosus or rheumatoid arthritis.
Intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD), assessed via PGP9.5 immunofluorescence, did not differ significantly between RLS patients and healthy controls.
Two RLS patients with comorbid impaired glucose metabolism met morphometric criteria for small fiber neuropathy based on published normative IENFD values.
Dermal nerve bundles in RLS patients showed increased density of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive adrenergic nerve fibers compared to controls.

An increased ratio of immature CD105-positive to mature CD31-positive endothelial cells within dermal capillaries was observed in RLS patients compared to controls, suggesting endothelial cell activation.
Asymptomatic TTR mutation carriers showed unexpectedly early small nerve fiber loss well before their estimated predicted age of symptom onset.
Asymptomatic carriers exhibited skin denervation at the proximal thigh site, suggesting a non-length-dependent pattern of small fiber neuropathy in ATTRv.
Ankle IENFD correlated with disease severity as well as with sural nerve SNAP amplitude and QST parameters, supporting its use as a marker of disease progression.
Patients at earlier disease stages did not show significantly different ankle IENFD compared with asymptomatic carriers.
Early-stage ATTRv-PN patients showed significantly worse QST parameters, more small fiber neuropathy symptoms, and greater neuropathic pain than asymptomatic carriers despite similar ankle IENFD.
One quarter of patients undergoing ligamentum teres reconstruction (LTR) in this systematic review had a diagnosis of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS).
Among EDS patients undergoing LTR in one series, outcomes were mixed: most improved, but a subset required conversion to total hip arthroplasty or failed to reach a clinically important improvement.
Reoperation rates after LTR were broadly overlapping between patients with and without EDS across the included studies.
Across the seven included studies, 9 of 28 hips (32.1%) required a subsequent reoperation after ligamentum teres reconstruction.
Complications after LTR were rare, occurring in 2 of 28 hips (7.1%), including traction-related labial blisters and a suture abscess.
Modified Harris Hip Score improved after LTR compared with preoperative scores across studies.
Non-arthritic Hip Score improved from preoperative to postoperative time points after LTR.
Visual analog scale pain scores decreased from preoperative to postoperative after LTR.
Studies using anchors for acetabular graft fixation during LTR reported higher reoperation rates than studies using button fixation.
No difference in reoperation rate after LTR was found between athletic and non-athletic patients.
Ligamentum teres pathology has been reported in a substantial minority to near-majority of consecutive patients undergoing hip arthroscopy.
Complete ligamentum teres tears occur in a wide reported range of hip arthroscopy patients and are more common with greater bony deformity severity.
Among professional athletes with femoroacetabular impingement undergoing hip arthroscopy, ligamentum teres pathology (partial and complete tears) was highly prevalent.
Professional hockey athletes undergoing hip arthroscopy for FAI showed a very high prevalence of ligamentum teres pathology.
Young female patients participating in activities requiring extreme hip range of motion, such as gymnastics and ballet, are noted to be at greatest risk of ligamentum teres tears.

Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is described as a genetic connective-tissue disorder causing increased ligament elasticity and joint hypermobility, predisposing to joint instability and injury including of the ligamentum teres.

EDS patients undergoing hip arthroscopy are considered a treatment challenge, with concerns that persistent or iatrogenic instability after standard hip arthroscopy correction may be due to unaddressed ligamentum teres pathology.
Prior investigations cited by the authors found higher rates of complete ligamentum teres tears in patients 30 years or older, in female patients, and in patients with low body mass index.
COVID-19 death rate was highest among UK Biobank participants living with obesity compared to overweight or normal/underweight participants.
A larger proportion of overweight or obese UK Biobank participants were tested for, tested positive for, and were hospitalised with COVID-19 than participants of healthy weight.
Older UK Biobank participants (70-82 years) had higher COVID-19 testing rates than younger participants, though younger participants had higher positive test rates.
Older UK Biobank participants had substantially higher rates of COVID-19 hospitalisation and death than younger participants.
Asian and Black ethnic groups in UK Biobank had higher COVID-19 testing rates and higher positive test rates than White, Mixed or Other ethnic groups.
The Black ethnic group had the highest percentage of COVID-19 hospitalisation and death among UK Biobank participants.
Testing, positive results, hospitalisation and death from COVID-19 were all higher for the most deprived quintile of UK Biobank participants than the least deprived quintile.
No supporting evidence was found for gender differences in COVID-19 testing rates or positive test outcomes in the UK Biobank cohort.

The data-driven Foresight obesity classification, though not built using obesity or COVID-19 outcome data, differentiates COVID-19 prevalence and severity across its seven classes in the UK Biobank cohort.
The Active workers class had an above-average positive COVID-19 test rate but low hospitalisation and death rates, likely reflecting their younger age.
The Retirees with healthy lifestyles class had higher-than-average testing but lower-than-average positive tests, hospitalisation and death rates.
The Stressed and not in work class had high COVID-19 testing rates along with above-average hospitalisation and death rates.
The Deprived with less-healthy lifestyles class had the highest COVID-19 testing rate and the highest hospitalisation and death rates of any class.
The Comfortable professionals class had below-average testing, positive test, hospitalisation and death rates.
The Comfortable families class had the lowest overall testing rate but a high proportion of positive results among those tested, alongside the lowest hospitalisation and death rates of all classes.
Roughly one quarter of SARS-CoV-2 infected individuals had not fully recovered to their pre-infection health status 6-8 months after diagnosis.
Female sex was independently associated with a higher likelihood of not having fully recovered compared to males.
Severe to very severe acute symptoms and presence of comorbidities were associated with non-recovery among initially symptomatic participants.
More than half of participants had a Fatigue Assessment Scale score indicating relevant fatigue at 6-8 months post-infection.
Participants aged 40 years or older were less likely to experience fatigue than those aged 18-39 years, with no evidence of association with sex, symptom severity, or hospitalization.
A quarter of participants reported dyspnea of mMRC grade 1 or higher, associated with female sex, initial hospitalization, higher BMI and presence of comorbidities.
About one quarter of participants reported symptoms of depression, one third anxiety, and 16% stress, at 6-8 months post-infection.
Lower education status and unemployment, but not age, sex, hospitalization, or symptom severity, were associated with depressive symptoms in multivariable analysis.
More than two thirds of participants were categorized as non-recovered or experiencing fatigue, dyspnea, or depression, with only partial overlap between these outcomes.
Over half of participants reported impairment in at least one EQ-5D-5L dimension, most commonly pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression.
Two fifths of participants had at least one healthcare contact related to COVID-19 since acute infection, including GP visits, hotline calls, and rehospitalization.

18% of participants reported a new physician-diagnosed medical condition since infection, of which 35% were considered COVID-19-related, most frequently respiratory, neuro-cognitive, cardiovascular, and skin disorders.

Initial hospitalization, severe acute symptoms, female sex and age ≥40 years, as well as non-recovery, dyspnea, fatigue and depression, were associated with increased likelihood of further healthcare contacts after acute COVID-19.
One quarter of participants reported new or ongoing symptoms since acute illness, with fatigue, cough, sore throat and headache most common, and higher rates among females.
Increased IgM and IgA responses to LPS, indicating bacterial translocation, form part of the 'causome' contributing to ME/CFS pathophysiology.
Lowered coenzyme Q10 constitutes the 'protectome' component of the ME/CFS model, reflecting reduced antioxidant protection.
Increased lysozyme is part of the adverse outcome pathway (AOP) feature set contributing to the ME/CFS model.
Increased CD38+ T cell activation is a key AOP feature contributing to the ME/CFS nomothetic model.
Increased cell-mediated immune activation (CMI) is one of the AOP features linked to ME/CFS.
Increased IgM responses to oxidative specific epitopes and NO-adducts (IgM OSENO), indicating autoimmune responses to oxidatively modified neoepitopes, are part of the AOP model of ME/CFS.

A combined PLS-derived latent vector of CMI + CD38 activation, IgM OSENO, IgA LPS, and lysozyme (all positive contributors) plus coenzyme Q10 (inverse contributor) explained 31.6% of the variance in the physiosomatic symptom dimension of ME/CFS.
Cluster analysis of PLS-derived latent scores identified a distinct ME/CFS subgroup characterized by increased lysozyme levels.
A second ME/CFS subgroup was defined by increased cell-mediated immune activation together with CD38+ T cell activation and depressive symptoms.
A third ME/CFS subgroup showed increased bacterial translocation markers together with autoimmune (OSENO) antibody responses.
ME/CFS patients had significantly reduced quality-of-life scores across all SF-36 domains except emotional role, compared with healthy controls.
ME/CFS patients had significantly higher disability scores across all WHO DAS domains compared with healthy controls, with the highest disability reported for life activities.
Eosinophil counts were significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than healthy controls, although within normal clinical reference range.
The majority (86.7%) of ME/CFS patients reported an infectious trigger prior to onset of symptoms.
On average, ME/CFS patients were diagnosed at age 29.6 years and had experienced symptoms for a mean of 14.93 years at study entry.

All ME/CFS patients reported cognitive difficulties, pain, sleep disturbances, sensory disturbances, and cardiovascular disturbances, while immune and gastrointestinal disturbances were each reported by 93.3% of patients.

In healthy controls, overnight treatment with the TRPM3 agonist pregnenolone sulfate (PregS) significantly reduced TRPM3 co-localisation with actin at the NK cell membrane compared with untreated cells.
Combined PregS and ononetin (TRPM3 antagonist) treatment further reduced TRPM3-actin co-localisation in HC NK cells compared with PregS alone.
In ME/CFS patients, overnight treatment with PregS or PregS+ononetin did not significantly alter TRPM3 co-localisation with actin compared with untreated cells.
In healthy controls, PregS and PregS+ononetin both significantly reduced TRPM3 co-localisation with PIP2 at the NK cell membrane compared with untreated cells.
In ME/CFS patients, combined PregS+ononetin treatment significantly increased TRPM3 co-localisation with PIP2 compared with untreated cells, an effect not seen in HC.
At baseline (control IL-2 condition), TRPM3 co-localisation with actin at the NK cell membrane was significantly reduced in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
At baseline (control IL-2 condition), TRPM3 co-localisation with PIP2 at the NK cell membrane was significantly reduced in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
Following combined PregS+ononetin treatment, TRPM3-PIP2 co-localisation was significantly higher in ME/CFS NK cells compared with HC, reversing the baseline deficit.
Baseline NK cell cytotoxicity was significantly reduced in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls at the 6.25:1 effector:target ratio.
Overnight stimulation with IL-2 significantly increased NK cell cytotoxicity in both healthy controls and ME/CFS patients across all effector:target ratios.
In healthy controls, PregS and PregS+ononetin treatment did not significantly alter NK cell cytotoxicity compared with IL-2 alone control condition.
In ME/CFS patients, PregS and PregS+ononetin treatment did not significantly alter NK cell cytotoxicity compared with IL-2 alone control condition.
A non-significant trend toward decreased NK cell cytotoxicity following PregS/ononetin treatment was noted in ME/CFS patients compared with HC.
A prior systematic review/meta-analysis estimated global ME/CFS prevalence at 0.89%, with women affected 1.5-2 fold more than men across categories.
Latvian administrative (ICD-10) data suggest ME/CFS-related diagnostic codes cover about 0.8% of the population, higher than in other comparable countries.
Both diagnosed ME/CFS patients and undiagnosed persons with CFS-like symptoms had an identical female proportion of 82.7%.
Diagnosed ME/CFS patients reported on average 7-8 distinct symptoms, with 9% reporting more than 10 symptoms.
Most undiagnosed respondents (85.3%) met the Fukuda symptom threshold of more than three long-term CFS-like symptoms, despite having no formal ME/CFS diagnosis.
ME/CFS patients underwent on average 6 investigations before diagnosis, and 43% waited more than 12 months from first symptoms to diagnosis.
A majority of both diagnosed ME/CFS patients (73.9%) and undiagnosed persons (66.2%) reported below-average household income, indicating financial strain associated with the illness.
Diagnosed ME/CFS patients spent on average EUR 1140 per year on symptom relief, versus EUR 979 per year for undiagnosed persons.

64% of ME/CFS patients reported medication (prescription/OTC) was effective, and 52% reported non-medication approaches (physiotherapy, psychotherapy, osteopathy, homeopathy, nutrition, supplements) or complex methods were effective.
Among former COVID-19 patients surveyed 6 months post-infection, 44.2% reported at least one CFS-characteristic symptom and 16.7% reported four or more Fukuda-criteria symptoms simultaneously.
95% of former COVID-19 patients with CFS-like symptoms reported that symptom onset occurred after their COVID-19 infection, suggesting COVID-19 as a possible causative trigger for CFS.

Symptom profiles differed across groups: 'difficulty concentrating' predominated in ME/CFS patients, 'depressed mood' predominated in undiagnosed persons, and 'psychological distress (anxiety)' was notably higher in undiagnosed and former COVID-19 patients than in ME/CFS patients.

On the EQ-5D-5L, former COVID-19 patients reported significantly lower severity (better health-related quality of life) across mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression domains compared to ME/CFS patients and undiagnosed persons.

Self-reported quality of life using a VAS scale did not differ significantly between diagnosed ME/CFS patients and undiagnosed persons, both before illness onset and in the past year, and both groups' pre-illness QoL was relatively low (<75/100) for their age.
The authors predict that the number of undiagnosed ME/CFS patients in Latvia may increase by at least 15% as a consequence of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Assuming ~15,770 undiagnosed ME/CFS patients in Latvia each spend EUR 979 p.a., the estimated total direct medical cost exceeds EUR 15 million annually, potentially increasing by at least 15% due to COVID-19.

A prior literature review of GPs' knowledge found that disbelief and lack of understanding of ME/CFS among general practitioners is widespread and contributes to diagnostic delays that constitute a risk factor for severe, prolonged disease.
A large literature review (1161 studies, 1979-2019) found the most commonly cited causal factors for ME/CFS were immunological, psychological, infectious, and neuroendocrine mechanisms.
A significantly higher proportion of ME/CFS patients regularly used supplements compared with the general Australian population.

Vitamin and mineral supplements (multi- and single-vitamin/mineral) were the most frequently taken supplement category, each used by 70.8% of ME/CFS patients, with zinc, vitamin D, and magnesium the most common single supplements.
Non-nutritive supplement use (e.g., probiotics, CoQ10, melatonin) was far more prevalent in ME/CFS patients than the general population, particularly probiotics.

ME/CFS patients had significantly higher daily intake of total, monounsaturated, and polyunsaturated fats, linolenic acid, and long-chain omega-3 fatty acids, but lower saturated fat intake, compared with the general Australian population.

ME/CFS patients had significantly lower daily intake of total carbohydrates, total sugars, and starch, but higher dietary fiber, compared with the general population, with no difference in total energy intake.

ME/CFS patients showed significantly higher daily intakes of natural folate, vitamin C, vitamin E, magnesium, potassium, and iron, but lower intakes of folic acid, vitamin B6, vitamin B12, iodine, sodium, and zinc, compared with the general population.
Daily caffeine intake was significantly higher and daily alcohol intake significantly lower among ME/CFS patients compared with the general population.

ME/CFS patients had significantly higher daily intake of water, herbal tea, gluten-free bread, pasta/noodles, cream, yoghurt, fruits, vegetables, eggs, and chicken, but significantly lower intake of total sugars, sausages, processed meats, and all alcohol types compared with the general population.

Three of seven SF-36 HRQoL domains yielded significant regression models when adjusted for sociodemographic factors and diet/supplement variables: role limitations due to physical health, bodily pain, and general health perceptions.
Use of herbal supplements was positively associated with scores for 'the role of limitations due to physical health problems' in ME/CFS patients.

Use of evening primrose oil supplements was negatively associated with scores for 'the role of limitations due to physical health problems', though this was based on only one participant taking the supplement.

Vitamin C supplement use was positively correlated with 'general health perceptions' scores but negatively correlated with 'general mental health' scores (the latter model was not statistically significant).
CoQ10 supplement use was negatively associated with 'the role of limitations due to emotional problems' scores, though the overall regression model was not statistically significant.
Higher daily long-chain omega-3 fatty acid intake was negatively associated with 'bodily pain' scores in ME/CFS patients.
Higher daily alpha-linolenic acid intake was negatively associated with 'general health perceptions' scores, while higher daily iodine intake was also negatively associated with the same domain.

Higher daily total folate intake was positively associated with 'the role of limitations due to physical health problems' scores, and daily saturated fat intake was positively associated with 'bodily pain' scores.
Higher daily calcium intake was positively correlated with 'general health perceptions' scores (significant model) and with 'social functioning' scores (model not significant).

Daily folic acid intake was positively associated with 'social functioning' scores but negatively associated with 'the role of limitations due to emotional problems' scores (the latter model not statistically significant).
Despite being the most commonly used supplement category, multi-vitamin/multi-mineral supplements showed no statistically significant association with any of the seven SF-36 HRQoL domains.
Sociodemographic factors were significant predictors in some HRQoL models: employment and education predicted bodily pain, and age and gender predicted general health perceptions.
Creatine kinase (CK) levels were significantly lower in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls.
Among patients, CK was lower in those with severe function impairment compared to those with moderate or mild impairment.
Creatinine levels were significantly lower in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls.
Creatinine was lower among patients with more severe function impairment than those with moderate or mild impairment.
Creatinine was higher in patients fulfilling only Fukuda and CCC ('non-ICC') than in those also fulfilling the ICC criteria.
Potassium levels were significantly lower in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls.
Potassium decreased with worsening functional impairment among patients.
Potassium decreased with longer illness duration among patients, the only blood test significantly associated with illness duration.
Sedimentation rate was significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than in healthy controls, consistent with possible low-grade inflammation.
Leukocyte counts were significantly higher in patients than in controls, though the difference was small (0.53-point difference).
Lymphocyte counts were significantly higher in patients than in controls.
Neutrophil counts were significantly higher in patients than in controls, consistent with prior reports.
Monocyte counts were significantly higher in patients than in controls.
Ferritin was significantly higher in patients than in controls, consistent with prior literature.
Vitamin B12 was significantly higher in patients than in controls, with no correlation to severity, illness duration, or diagnostic criteria, possibly reflecting supplement use.
P-calcium was significantly higher in patients than in controls, an effect the authors could not readily explain.
ALAT was significantly higher in patients than in controls.
Among patients, ASAT and ALAT levels were associated with function impairment severity, though the reported direction is inconsistent between the Results and Discussion sections of the paper.
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) was significantly higher in patients than in controls.
LDL-cholesterol was significantly higher in patients than in controls, though within normal range, consistent with a previously described unfavorable lipid profile.
Free T4 was significantly higher in patients than in controls; prior literature has reported both elevation and reduction of free T4 in ME/CFS.
CRP did not significantly differ between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls, despite other inflammatory markers being elevated.
There was no significant difference in BMI between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
The Norwegian version of the DSQ showed high sensitivity but low specificity for detecting symptoms consistent with a CCC diagnosis of ME/CFS.

ME/CFS patients in subgroup S3 (infection trigger confirmed by lab test) showed significantly reduced CMV seropositivity compared to healthy controls, consistent across a wide range of seropositivity cutoffs.

Before correction for multiple testing, ME/CFS subgroup S1 (non-infection trigger) showed significant negative associations (lower seropositivity) with EBV-VCA, EBV-EBNA1, and VZV antibodies compared to healthy controls, depending on the cutoff used, but these did not survive correction for multiple testing.

A putative association between ME/CFS subgroup S0 (unknown infection status) and EBV-VCA antibodies was observed only at a single cutoff (37 U/ml), while no other significant associations were found for this subgroup with any herpesvirus.

No significant association was found between ME/CFS subgroup S2 (infection trigger not lab-confirmed) and seropositivity to any of the herpesviruses tested (CMV, EBV-VCA, EBV-EBNA1, HSV1, HSV2, VZV, HHV6).

The proportion of severely affected ME/CFS patients differed significantly among trigger subgroups, with only ~9% severely affected in the non-infection/unknown subgroups (S0, S1) versus ~30% in the infection-triggered subgroups (S2, S3).
VZV serology showed the highest discriminatory power among all herpesviruses tested, with an AUC of approximately 0.75 distinguishing subgroup S2 from healthy controls at cutoffs below 15 U/ml.

Overall, most unadjusted AUCs comparing seropositivity between ME/CFS subgroups and healthy controls fell between 0.50 and 0.60, indicating limited predictive power of herpesvirus serology to discriminate ME/CFS subgroups from controls.

Stratifying ME/CFS patients by infection vs. non-infection disease trigger and performing a sensitivity analysis across a range of seropositivity cutoffs revealed significant herpesvirus serology associations (subgroups S1 and S3) that were not detected in the original unstratified analysis of the same UKMEB dataset.
One third of ME/CFS patients had detectable antihypothalamic antibodies (AHA) versus none in healthy controls.
More than half of ME/CFS patients had detectable antipituitary antibodies (APA) versus none in healthy controls.
ME/CFS patients had significantly lower ACTH/cortisol levels compared with healthy controls.
ME/CFS patients had significantly lower GH peak/IGF-1 levels compared with healthy controls.
Patients with high antibody titers (≥1:32) had significantly lower ACTH/cortisol and GH peak/IGF-1 levels and more severe ME/CFS than those with middle/low titers or antibody-negative patients.
Initiation of cannabinoid-based treatment drastically reduced chronic pain in an 18-year-old woman with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, improving her quality of life.
With continued self-administration of cannabis, the patient was able to completely eliminate her opioid requirement for pain management.
In a case series of 20 EDS patients (classical/classical-like and vEDS), most reported mild dyspnea (MRC grade 1), with a smaller proportion reporting more severe grades.
EDS and HSD patients reported markedly greater dyspnea burden on the SGRQ than healthy controls, especially with walking on flat ground.
In 162 EDS patients versus 221 matched healthy controls, cough, sputum production, and nocturnal cough/wheeze were significantly more common.
JHS patients had intermediate respiratory symptom burden—more than healthy controls but less than EDS patients.
Despite a three-fold higher symptom-based suggestion of chronic bronchitis in EDS patients, the strictly-defined actual prevalence of chronic bronchitis was very low.
GERD is a common, self-reported contributor to chronic cough in EDS patients.
Asthma prevalence is substantially increased in EDS and JHS patients compared to controls.
Serum IgE was above normal in a substantial minority of EDS and JHS patients, suggesting an atopic phenotype.
Asthma in a subset of EDS patients may be associated with mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS), though the prevalence of this overlap remains unclear.
In a case series of 21 hEDS patients, over a third had chronic or recurrent dysphonia with fibroscopic evidence of vocal cord discoordination or hypotonia.
A retrospective case series of 9 EDS patients found painless dysphonia, fluctuating hoarseness, weak voice, dysphagia, recurrent laryngospasm, and subglottic stenosis.
Speech therapy improved vocal cord performance in EDS patients with dysphonia, based on self- and observer-rated evaluations.
Using FEV1/PEFR ratio as a marker, a subset of EDS and JHS patients met criteria for upper airway collapse.
In a prospective parallel-cohort study, EDS patients had markedly higher rates of obstructive sleep apnea than matched controls, with a substantial proportion being symptomatic.
Among EDS patients, those with OSA had higher daytime sleepiness scores and worse quality of life across all SF-36 dimensions than EDS patients without OSA, with severity-dependent effects.
As in the general population, obesity, male sex, and older age were predictors of OSA among EDS patients.
In a case series of 20 vEDS patients, a quarter had at least one hemoptysis episode not attributable to anticoagulation or coagulopathy.

In a multicenter retrospective case series of 96 vEDS patients, pneumothorax or hemothorax occurred in about a fifth of patients, often preceding diagnosis and preceding intestinal complications by years.

Biochemical analysis of lung tissue from a vEDS patient post-bullectomy showed lower collagen III levels and reduced type III procollagen production relative to type I, compared to control fibroblasts.
Celiprolol reduced major vascular complications (systemic arterial ruptures or dissections) in vEDS patients in a randomized controlled trial.
Tranexamic acid has been used to manage recurrent hemoptysis in vEDS patients.
Among 20 EDS patients, chest wall abnormalities including pectus excavatum, thin ribs, scoliosis, and straight back syndrome were commonly observed.
Inspiratory muscle strength (SNIP) was reduced in hEDS patients relative to predicted values, with a tendency toward greater resting lung volumes.

In a small case series of nine vEDS patients, fibrous lung nodules arose from pleural and non-alveolar tissue pathology, and pulmonary hematomas showed no residual lung tissue, only surrounding compressed parenchyma with hypothesized fibrotic organization.

Among 20 EDS patients (16 classical, 4 vEDS), chest wall abnormalities were common: mild pectus excavatum in 6, very thin ribs with increased downward slope in 3, mild scoliosis in 4, and straight back syndrome in 3.
Inspiratory muscle strength was reduced in hEDS patients as measured by sniff nasal inspiratory pressure, with a tendency toward greater resting lung volumes.

In a randomized controlled trial of 20 hEDS patients, six weeks of inspiratory muscle training (IMT) improved inspiratory muscle strength, FEV1%, and six-minute walk distance compared to standard care without IMT.
